ANUVADA NUN MALAI iii

OM NAMO BHAGAVATHE SRI RAMANAYA

FOREWARD
(For the first Tamil edition)

Among the wealth of poetic works that Bhagavan so 
graciously bestowed upon the community of devotees, his 
works of translation, having a greatness of their own, carve a 
special niche for themselves. Each Sanskrit original that has 
been selected is in itself, a gem in the spiritual realm and his 
rendering it in Tamil, brings to the fore the beauty and clarity 
of it all in chaste Tamil, that they may aptly be deemed as not 
mere translations but original compositions.

Though all Tamil-knowing devotees can recite these 
verses with ease and pleasure, their content being deep and 
unfathomable, the dire and long-felt need for an annotated 
version of it, phrase by phrase, with a paraphrase and a 
commentary facilitating easy recitation and providing a fillip 
for a  fruitful and an in-depth study of these works, is now 
fulfilled.

The author of this text of commentary in Tamil, Smt. 
Kanakammal, is deeply devoted to Bhagavan. Even when 
young she sought and surrendered to Bhagavan. She listened 
to the works of Bhagavan explained by the scholar devotee 
of Bhagavan, Sri Muruganar, who himself was one who 
gained clarity by hearing and enjoying the content of all the 
works of Bhagavan explained to him by Bhagavan himself. 
He elucidated in all his writings and conversations (what 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   3 06-05-2011   10:53:37



iv ANUVADA NUN MALAI

he was taught by Bhagavan). The Path of jñāna, which he 
unflaggingly followed. Smt. Kanakammal shares with us what 
she learned from Muruganar through this text.

The service of Smt. Kanakammal is indeed commendable.
K. Swaminathan

Dharmalaya
Madras

2nd November1989

ANUVADA NUN MALAI v

PUBLISHER’S NOTE

This volume, a sequel to the earlier one, The Commentary 
on the original Compositions of Bhagavan, deals with the 
Works of Translation from the Sanskrit originals by Bhagavan.

Devotees desirous of knowing the true import of these 
verses sought Smt. T.R. Kanakammal and were amply 
rewarded by her expositions.

While narrating to the devotees small incidents and 
anecdotes associated with Bhagavan, she not merely virtually 
relived those days and successfully recaptured the spirit and 
mood that prevailed in the old Hall then but also transported 
them to that heavenly atmosphere of yesteryears. When 
explaining the profound contents of the works of Bhagavan, 
she, with consummate skill, would drive home even very 
subtle points, not easy of comprehension.

One wonders how one with no access to academic excellence 
through higher education could deal with ease on such abstruse 
subjects with such clarity. The clue perhaps is provided by what 
she confided, shortly before she got merged in Bhagavan.

She vividly described an incident which she could neither 
call a dream nor a vision in which Bhagavan asked her to open 
her mouth, put out her tongue and wrote something on. She, 
however was so thrilled by this gesture of great grace that she 
did not register then or recall now what he wrote and with 
what and in what script.

Earlier were the days, she, inspired by Swami Ramakrishna 
Paramahamsa and Swami Vivekananda was all afire with 
spiritual longing to find her master and used to spend her days 
together with reading and praying for it. Her father, worried 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   5 06-05-2011   10:53:37



vi ANUVADA NUN MALAI

that given her strong leanings to spirituality, more so her 
dislike to get entangled in married life and saṃsāra was afraid 
that she might quietly give them the slip. Hence his watch over 
her became closer and at night he used to sleep in the same 
room more or less blocking the way. One night, when she feel 
sleep after a day of tearful prayers, she suddenly woke up to 
find Swami Vivekananda standing before her blowing vibhuti 
(the sacred ash) all over her. The whole room was filled with 
the strong fragrance of the spreading vibhuti and woke his 
father up, who exclaimed in wonder: “Where and how this 
smell of vibhuti had emanated so suddenly?”

Very often she used to remark, “How does it matter 
whether we attain jñāna or not? The singular blessing of 
beholding him, moving in his presence and sitting at his feet, 
is mukti enough for us.” Lest this should dishearten and leave 
the devotees of later years languishing at having missed this 
blessing, she would quickly add, “The very fact of your having 
been drawn, in spite of his physical absence reveals that you 
are all a chosen few.” Gladdening their hearts this would lift 
them up. She would further add, “Those who came to him 
after seeing him once are great indeed; but greater still are 
those who have been drawn to him even without seeing him.”

That which capped them all causing a joyous thrill in 
the hearts of women devotees was the remark of Bhagavan 
recalled by her, "The penance that women observe in 
Arunachala bears fruits greater and quicker, quoting the 
example of Devi Herself who claimed the very half of Siva 
by observing severe penance here.

This is exemplified by the way she got absorbed in 
Bhagavan on the day of his Jayanthi, in his very presence and 
in the midst of all his devotees.

We do hope that this volume, like the earlier one would 
fulfil the keen desire of the devout to comprehend adequately 
and absorb in full the true import of the works by Bhagavan.

ANUVADA NUN MALAI vii

General Introduction To The Translated Works

Shaped by divine will and not by human design, all the 
works of translation from Sanskrit by Bhagavan dwell on the 
quintessence of Advaitic knowledge and ways and means of 
attaining the same.

Each translated verse is an upanishadic verity couched in 
dulcet verses of elegant poetry with alluring alliterations and 
scintillating rhymes. When recited to set tunes, the sonorous 
sound falls sweet on the ears and guides smoothly the inward 
journey. This is an instance where Absolute verity walks hand 
in hand with the Muse of Poetry decked at her best. Almost 
all the works remind repeatedly  that we are all (amritasya 
putra) children of Immortality. It is certain that if the contents 
of these verses are comprehended in full and the instructions 
adhered to, one will reach the cave of the Heart and drink the 
elixir of immortality.

The adoption of the literary format of the four lined veṇbā 
metre in place of the couplets in the Sanskrit Texts of Devi 
Kālōttaram, Sarva Jnanottaram, Bhagavad Gītā and Ātma 
Bodham is deftly used to render each verse more than a mere 
translation by compacting it with the intended import as well.

Texts like Devi Kālōttaram and Ānma Sakshatkara 
Prakaranam, advocate swarupa dhyana and instruct the 
seekers to follow the direct path of jñāna giving up the 
performance of all actions traditionally considered holy or 
obligatory and emulating the traits and conduct of realised 
souls. While the former has caused many to cock an eyebrow, 
the latter, namely emulating the behaviour of a jñāni some say 
is like pulling the cart before the horse.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   7 06-05-2011   10:53:37



viii ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Jñāna is both the goal and the way. The seekers is the one 
who is sought. The knowledge so sought is attainable only 
through the path of knowledge. Who are all competent enough 
to follow this path? To one who so wonders Bhagavan provides 
the answer, “He, whose mind has been purified by spiritual 
practices or by accumulated merit of past lives and who has 
distaste for the body and sense objects is fit for enquiry”. 
(Ramana Gītā, Chap. VII, Verse 9).

The fruit of all the practice, traditionally considered holy 
and virtuous, is to ensure  purity of mind with which one 
embarks upon the path of knowledge. Hence while engaged in 
the path of enquiry, to revert to such practices, is like sliding 
down to the lower rungs of spirituality ladder. Bhagavan 
assures, “Failure to perform prescribed actions is not sinful. 
For Self-enquiry itself is the most meritorious and the most 
purifying” (Ibid, Chap. V, Verse 19).

As for a sadhak, emulating the behaviour of a realised 
soul, Bhagavan says, “What is natural to the state of Self-
Realization forms the disciplinary course in the other state” 
(Talks, no. 491) and what was practised with effort once 
becomes spontaneous after attainment. Therefore one should 
take the Self-enquiry, giving up the Vedas and Agamas, for 
control of the mind is the sum and substance of all yogas, is 
what is taught by Devi Kālōttaram and Sarva Jnanottaram. 
They both may aptly be termed Moksha Gītā and Mukti Gītā 
respectively for they sing the nature of the divine glory of our 
own state and reveal the ways to achieve it, therefore leading 
us from darkness to light and from death to immortality. 

It is not a wonder that all the verses selected from 
Bhagavad Gītā by Bhagavan either advocate jñāna or 
surrender – the only two effective ways of attaining the Self.

Ātma Bodham also advocates the path of Knowledge 
delineating the nature of the Self. “Jñāna lakshanas are  stated 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   8 06-05-2011   10:53:37



ANUVADA NUN MALAI ix

in the śāstras to be an incentive to a seeker happiness. The 
methods are given. If they are followed the result will be jñāna 
having those lakshanas.” (Talks, no. 610).

Though Dakshinamurthy Stotram, Guru Stuti and 
Hastamalakam are all four lined verses in Sanskrit, Bhagavan 
has added new dimensions to them by dwelling on the glory of 
the Ātman and using various and significant epithets, though 
he followed the same format of veṇbā  metre.

In the Dakshinamurthy Stotra, while the refrain in the last 
line of each verse is the same, “May our obeisance be to that 
Guru Sri Dakshinamurthy” Bhagavan has provided various 
epithets to the lord in the refrain such as: 

Talaiyuru Guru (the primal Guru), 
Sattiyar Guru (The Guru with the power of perfection),
Tavaruru Guru (The Guru realized by ascetics),
Chalamaru Guru (The Moveless Guru),
Tadaiaru Guru (The Remover of obstacles to jñāna),
Charachara Guru (The Teacher of the world of moving 

and unmoving), 
Tazhal Vizhi Guru (The Teacher with the eye of jñāna),
Talamuru Guru (The Teacher of the world),
and Taṇarut Guru (The Teacher of the form of compassion 

and cool quietude).
Similarly in Hastamalakam in Sanskrit in verse 3 to 13, 

each verse ends with the same refrain, namely, saha nithya 
upalabdi Swarupaha aham ātma – He, the ever attained form 
of Reality, I am, while Bhagavan has described the Self in all 
Its nature in appropriate terms. The epithets are: oriyal nitta 
siddhai – the homogeneous, changeless and ever experienced 
content I am; arivuru – form of Awareness; advaya – non-dual; 
anittamil – Imperishable; adaitalnittu – never new but ever 
realized; alavīlā – boundless; aruvanāi – formless; alaidalil 
– moveless; ādalil – ever fixed and ahamila – egoless.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   9 06-05-2011   10:53:38



x ANUVADA NUN MALAI

The same applies to Guru Stuti also. As against the refrain 
in Sanskrit (That Thou Art), the adjective that Bhagavan had 
used are: That primal Sachchidananda; That which never sets; 
That which transcends all objects known; That uncreated and 
imperishable; That without an origin, middle and end; That 
True flawless Awareness; That which remains as the concealed 
content of the Vedas and That true Content known by deep 
enquiry.

Bhagavan’s mastery as a bard of Tamil Language and a 
Seer of Truth Absolute is most evident in the consummate skill 
with which the ‘link words’ are introduced though ostensibly 
to facilitate easy recitation by the two groups, they are loaded 
with significant import which preempt the content of the 
succeeding verse creating an eager anticipation of what is to 
follow.

These delightful translations provide the cream of the 
Upanishads – the crown of Vedas – and those who have no 
knowledge of Sanskrit need have no regrets for this single 
work, provides all there is to know by the study of them. 
Listening to or singing them, coupled with the endeavours to 
practise its teachings will definitely lead one to the Land of 
the Self. It is the experience of many that a mere listening of 
it hills one into the husked silence of the mind, a peep into 
which a provided for a very brief period at the conclusion of 
Parayana every evening in his holy shrine.

Śrī Devikālottara 
Jñānāchāra Vichāra Padalam

Avathārikai (Origin)
Bestowed by Sri Bhagavan

In the Text of Devi Kālottara, one of the upāgamas 
bestowed by Lord Paramasiva on Devi out of compassion, 
this canto, on vichāra of jñāna and achāra expounding the 
quintessence of all the āgamas, namely, the jñāna and achāra, 
fit to be attained by mature souls at the end of their ripened 
wisdom being verily the boat that, rescuing and bearing 
the souls fallen into and struggling in the grievous ocean 
of transmigration constantly sinking and surfacing, ferries 
them in this direct path to the shore of liberation. May all the 
mumukshus, perplexed not lose their way and wander, tread 
with this aid the direct path and obtain that supreme state of 
tranquil Bliss.

The Historical Background to this Translation
The Vedas are the Light of jñāna that reveal and illumine 

the path to attain the Content Beyond of the Upanishads, the 
crown of the Vedas, and dwell at length only on the Advaitic 
or the non-dual Content.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   1 06-05-2011   10:53:38



2 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

The purpose of the Āgama Śāstras is to explain in great 
detail, the forms of various deities – forms of Saguna Brahman 
– the process of making (sculpting), erecting and consecrating 
them, the ritualistic modes of worship specific to each of 
them, the structure and the architectural design of the temples 
that are to house those deities radiating grace, the erection of 
temple towers and the procedural details for the conduct of 
consecration ceremonies of these temples.

The erection of temple tanks and wells related to such 
temples is also expatiated upon by the āgamas in an admirable 
manner. All the temples of India have been constructed 
conforming strictly to the rules laid down by the āgamas. In 
the same way the form of the deity of worship in any temple 
and the procedure of worship followed will be found to adhere 
to rules of any one of the āgamas.

Even the temples with Vedic method of worship will 
strictly conform to rules of āgama śāstra as far as the structure 
and construction of temples are concerned.

The āgamas, twenty-eight in number, have expanded 
into many subsidiary Āgamas called upāgamas of which Devi 
Kālōttara – the Jñāna Kanda – is one.

During the Virupaksha days of Bhagavan’s stay 
in Tiruvannamalai, one devotee, Ramalingam, the son 
of Chinnaswamy, a priest of the main temple, brought 
some manuscripts in palm leaves collected from his 
relative’s house in Vriddhachalam wherein some āgama 
śāstras were found written. Among these this āgama, a 
Sanskrit text in Grantha script (a mixture of Sanskrit 
and Tamil) with complete orientation toward advaitic 
truth was also found.

Bhagavan while leafing through the scripts was amazed 
with wonder to see two upāgamas that instructed pure and 
perfect advaitic or non-dual jñāna, among āgamas that dwell 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   2 06-05-2011   10:53:38



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 3

elaborately on kiriyai and chariyai*. These two texts spoke 
very clearly of nirākāra Parabrahman – the formless Content 
Beyond. Both these were in the form of instructions by Lord 
Siva, one to Devi and the other to Lord Skandha.

One Kuppuswamy rājā, of Tanjore, with the intent of 
collecting advaitic oriented āgamas, had entrusted the work to 
his friend, Yajnarama Dikshitar, who went to various places to 
collect them. When he had come for the darshan of Bhagavan, 
he disclosed his mission.

Immediately Bhagavan, reminded of the earlier 
manuscripts, spoke about them to Dikshitar, who on hearing 
this, brought them from Ramalingam and sat copying some 
of them. Bhagavan, finding that both were in accordance 
with his own experience, thinking ‘why should we be quiet’, 
copied both in a small note book, in Devanagari script, in a 
beautiful hand that looked like print. But having misplaced it, 
when he started to write some verses in veṇbā metre in Tamil, 
these verses of Devi Kālottara came to his mind one by one, 
and the translation, a veṇbā for each verse – 85 verses, was 
accomplished, without the original, in chaste and clear Tamil.

*	 Charya, Kriya and Yoga are terms used in Saiva Siddhanta.
	 Charya (physical activity) is rendering service in shrines like 
cleaning the premises gathering flowers and worshipping the 
Lord. This leads to sālokya mukti wherein the devotee abides in 
the sphere of the Lord.
	 Kriya (physical and mental activity) consists in ritualistic 
worship of Siva inwardly and outwardly and leads to sāmīpya 
mukti where the devotee is close to the Lord.
	 Yoga calls for contemplation it and leads to sārūpya mukti 
wherein the devotee attains the form and various insignia of the 
Lord. All are considered as various rungs that lead to jñāna or 
spiritual realization.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   3 06-05-2011   10:53:38



4 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

While Bhagavan was in Virupaksha Cave itself, these 
85 verses were printed and published by ‘Ramaneeya Vani 
Printers’ of devotees of Bhagavan. It ran into a second edition 
in 1924.

After many years, when Bhagavan came to reside near 
the Samādhi Shrine of Alagamma, when Ramana Nūl Thirattu 
(The Collected Works of Bhagavan) was first published, this 
text was also added to it after being perused and pruned by 
Bhagavan.

A few years later, at the instance of a devotee, Bhagavan 
translated Ānma Sakshatkara Prakaranam – a veṇbā for 
each verse consisting of 62 verses. The subsequent edition of 
Collected Works included this as well.

The greatness of this text can be gleaned from the fact that 
Bhagavan, without anybody’s urging, on his own, translated 
this text. Bhagavan’s liking for this text is due to the fact that 
it dwells only on Brahman instructing repeatedly to give up 
everything, thereby confirming and emphasizing the Vastu 
Lakshana and releasing the minds of the seekers from the 
confusion caused by other distractions and pre-occupations. 
The write up ‘Origin’ provided by Bhagavan himself is proof 
enough of this.

6 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Paraphrase:
Of all the rare embodiments, life in a human body is 

indeed the rarest. Of the various austere vows, the vow 
of ahiṃsā or non-killing is indeed the greatest. Of all the 
Gods to be meditated upon the Lord with the (third) eye 
on the forehead is indeed Supreme. And the Truth that 
Devi Kālōttaram declares is indeed the highest.
Commentary: 

Of all the births the human birth is supposed to be the 
rarest of all.

Vivekachūḍāmaṇi declares that only through God’s grace 
can be had three things that are difficult to get indeed: a human 
birth, the desire for spiritual freedom and the company of a great 
soul. Human embodiment, obtained after countless inferior 
embodiments, is most suited for the attainment of Ātmajñāna, 
much easier than in other worlds so much so even the denizens 
of the celestial worlds yearn for birth in the world of humans.

Ahiṃsā or non-violence, often celebrated as the highest 
charity is the best of all (dharma) vows to be observed "For 
those who aspire for spiritual freedom, there is no rule more 
sanctifying than the avoidance of all injury to living beings 
by mind word, or action" (Bhāgavatam, 7.15.8)

A traditional hymn lists eight flowers worthy of being 
offered to the Lord:

Please the Lord with flowers eight
Flower of ahiṃsā ranking high
Second control of senses five
Compassion for all, flower nice
Forbearance a flower special
Flowers of peace and tapas
Likewise flower of dhyāna
With Truth are flowers holy

Paraphrase: 
Oh mind! Meditate in the heart on the elephant-faced 

God, verily the form of non-dual Silence, the Universal 
witness and Supreme ambrosial Bliss and grace that shines 
resplendently as the mighty blossom of spiritual wisdom 
(of aspirants who follow the path of jñāna) revealed in 
this text Devi Kālōttaram which Siva graciously fed into 
the ears of Devi through His holy mouth. 
Commentary: 

This text is addressed by Lord Siva (Deva) to Devi, 
Parvathy. The phrase ‘the Lord fed this into the ears of Devi’ is 
a highly delectable expression employed to convey an import 
of special significance. While the normal usage is ‘heard’ 
this phrase meaning ‘revealed into’ distinguishes that which 
falls accidentally and is heard, from the deeper and subtler 
connotation of the phrase, namely “making it register firmly 
in the heart”. What one reaps by observing the path of jñāna 
advocated by this text, is the ‘mighty fruit’ of Bliss Supreme. 
Like the farmer who gains the windfall of a bumper crop out 
of all proportion to the labour he has expended, the expert 
aspirants of Truth, treading diligently this path of jñāna reap the 
‘greatest yield’ (māvilaivam) of the celestial or ambrosial Bliss. 

What the meticulous adherence to the direct path of jñāna 
advocated by Devi Kālōttaram can bestow on one is much 
more than what an expertise can in any other path.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   8 06-05-2011   10:53:38



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 9

The Bliss of Absolute silence is gained by the ripeness 
of contemplative experience. 

The term mōnakkari stands for the ‘Silent Universal 
Witness’ or ‘Still-Immaculate Aloofness’. The content of the 
word kari is twofold, a witness and an elephant. According 
to the hoary tradition of paying obeisance to Vinayaka, the 
first and foremost, the elephant-faced god, the embodiment of 
Praṇava (OM) and the remover of obstacles before the start 
of any work, Lord Ganesa is invoked by praying “oh mind, 
think of that Lord”... At the same time in conformity with 
the advaitic experience, the state of Universal Witness, ever 
shining as one’s natural state of absolute silence, is invoked 
by “oh mind, dwell upon that Silent Witness”.

Thus the prayer is so worded that it is made applicable 
both to the elephant-faced God as also to the Universal 
Awareness.

Devi: Thus spoke the Divine Mother:

says: Oh Maheswara! the Lord of all celestial beings!

of Transcendental wisdom knowing which the means 
to mukti and the code of conduct to be practiced can be 
known in order that all humanity may attain Release, out 
of Thy Compassion. 
Commentary: 

In this verse Devi, espousing the cause of the jīvas and 
on their behalf, requests Lord Siva to reveal the way by which 
the means of Release can be perceived; that is, the most direct 
way to Supernal Wisdom that will at once grant mukti rather 
than going round about. The paths to Release are many and 
human life-span is so short. To avoid the jīva meandering 
in various less direct paths and wasting precious time, the 
way that would offer mukti as if on a platter is beseeched for. 
Further she emphasises that the bliss of liberation, being one’s 
own, is attainable by all.

The infinite compassion of Devi for the jīvas prompts 
Her to venture thus; but while so requesting she reveals her 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   10 06-05-2011   10:53:38



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 11

modesty by saying that the compassion of the Lord, Her 
Master, is more legendary and proverbial than her own.

The jīva steeped as he is in ignorance can never know the 
way to wisdom. The Universal Mother, out of over flowing 
compassion for the jīvas, that they may be lifted up on their 
behalf requests the Lord with eagerness and humility to 
graciously bestow that jñāna, for, but for His grace, not even 
an atom moves. Āchara (good and disciplined conduct and the 
body of practices to be followed) provides the ways and means 
to purge the mind of all its impurities thereby restoring pristine 
purity to an aspirant. Following the āchara by itself cannot 
result in mukti. It’s sole purpose is to discipline the mind of a 
seeker of Truth and make it competent enough to pursue Ātma 
vichāra. Āchara functions like a fence, in the initial stages, 
insulating the sādhak from the impact of the phenomenal world. 
Hence Devi requests for both jñāna and āchara.

Iswara: The Supreme Lord:

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 13

As it transcends thought and mind, all attempts to describe 
it become inadequate. So it is called odariya, difficult to be 
spelt out.

That the Supreme wisdom can be attained and revelled in 
by all is expressed by the phrase yavārumē jñānamura (that all 
may attain jñāna). The bliss of Release is ever present – never 
attained anew – and an attainment which is the birthright of 
every being. Beings cannot be without it for It dwells as the 
inmost being of man.

Manivachakar the great, praises the Lord (Siva) thus: 
“Hail the Feet of Him who not for an instant (not even for the 
batting of an eyelid) quits my heart.” The jīva imagining that 
he has been alienated from That wallows in the trammels of 
sorrow and misery. In order that such jīvas may be released 
from misery and attain jñāna, the Lord instructs the means 
to jñāna. Here Kalajñāna is the intellectual pathway to 
perfection. Jñāna is also spiritual wisdom. The word jñāna 
is applied to both the goal – of perfection – and the way to 
the same.

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 15

Siva proclaims to the whole world that this Kalajñāna 
stands supreme among all the treatises of jñāna. This is the 
royal road to knowledge and the gateway to Release and 
hence walking the other paths would be quite infructuous. 
He exhorts the jīvas to pivot all their concerted energies to 
tread this path declaring emphatically the futility of other 
paths in facilitating the dawn of awareness. If wisdom does 
not dawn by the teaching of Kalajñāna, nothing else can 
make it dawn. 

Jñāna here stands for that perfect, whole, objectless, 
Awareness.

Once a few learned Sanskrit scholars were seated in 
the hall discussing portions of the Upanishads and other 
scriptural texts with Bhagavan. Sub-registrar Narayana 
Iyer felt how great and fortunate were these people to be so 
learned and to have such deep understanding and ability to 
discuss with Bhagavan. He also felt miserable for he knew 
nothing. After the pandits took leave Bhagavan turned to 
him and said “What? Looking into my eyes and studying 
my thoughts, this is only the husk! All the book learning and 
capacity to repeat the scriptures by memory is absolutely 
of no use. To know the Truth, you need not undergo all this 
torture of learning. Not by reading do you get the Truth. Be 
Quiet, that is the Truth. Be still, that is God.” (R. Narayana 
Iyer, Fragrant Petals)

“A visitor: Can one realise the Truth by learning the 
scriptures and study of books?

B: No. So long as predispositions remain latent in the 
mind realization cannot be achieved. Śāstra learning itself 
is a vāsanā. Realization is only in samādhi.” (Talks no. 230)

All scriptures – right from rare Vedas to Purāṇas – are 
all apara knowledge. Knowledge that helps to secure release 
from bondage of the world is jñāna. Muruganar affirms:

intense faith and earnestness in the heart and free of any

Commentary: 

The adanāl (therefore) refers to the statement made in the

no other path can make him gain it. Therefore one is advised 
to follow this path with faith and without fear or doubt, with 
no thought of anything else. Fearlessness lies in giving up the 
other ways that have hitherto been followed.

Bhagavan affirms: “Because Reality is one, jñāna yoga is 
the direct path... In the shortcut of Svarūpa vichāra no fear or 
confusion arises because of the non-dual nature of the Self.” 
(Pādamālai, page 208)

If confusion assails the mind, consternation will follow 
blocking further progress of sādhanā. Hence devoid of any 
doubt in mind, with zest and fervour, one should practice the 
ways advocated here. Śraddhā, or faith, confidence and belief 
is the mainstay of the sādhanā like the root of a plant. It is 
indispensable to remain rooted to the ground of jñāna. This 
path of Kalajñāna will undoubtedly lead one to liberation.

In the wake of obstacles in the pursuit of this path, 
one must, without becoming weary, pursue the same path 
persistently without slack but with zeal and perseverance with 
no room for doubt.

Commentary: 

Claiming rights of possession on objects outside of us is

ahankara, the ego sense, the chief obstacle to gain Release is 
this sense of ‘mine’. Sense of ‘mine’ follows the ego-sense. 
While removal of ‘mine’ leads to chitta suddhi, purity of mind, 
removal of “I” is jñāna. Getting rid of ‘mine’ helps annihilation 
of the ego sense. Therefore mukti will remain out of reach as 
long as this lasts. However the removal of mamadai should not 
be replaced by hatred, towards objects and persons thinking

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 19

they are not ‘mine’. Compassion towards all is the hallmark of 
a true seeker. Such a one does not engender fear in any being.

The serene peace and universal benevolence springs from 
the truth that whole manifested existence is ensouled by the 
Supreme Essence. Therefore ahiṃsā means not merely non-
killing, and non-injury but non-resistance as well. Bhagavan 
confirms this truth: “If one abuses another or injures him, 
the remedy does not lie in retort or resistance. Simply keep 
quiet. This quiet will bring peace to the injured but make an 
offender restless until he is driven to admit his error to the 
injured party.” (Talks no. 517)

Yet one should not stop at being the seat of refuge for 
all beings mistaking it for the ultimate goal of human life but 
must possess intense desire for Release as well. Further the 
emphasis is on the steadfast adherence to this path instructed 
in Devi Kālōttaram, with a mind held firm and not allowed to 
wander in any other path for progress can be registered only 
by adhering to a single path (eka vazhi) with all the mental 
energies concentrated on it.

The antidote to the various mental modes like agitation, 
turbulence and restlessness is compassion alone which 
quietens the mind. That whatever is performed must be 
accompanied by total faith and whole-heartedness is indicated 
by isaindu nirka abide steadfastly and in conformity with what 
this text instructs.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   21 06-05-2011   10:53:39



22 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Wind, moveless or stilled, is not wind but ether. Mobility 
is the very nature of the wind. A cyclonic wind, besides serving 
no useful purpose, causes only havoc. But a gentle and smooth 
wind is hailed as the blessed zephyr or southern wind and its 
arrival is awaited with eager anticipation and when it does 
arrive we enjoy its comforting embrace.

The speed with which the mind flurries about is even 
faster than that of the fastest wind and hence the comparison. 
Instead of following a single current or line of thought it keeps 
alternating among various thoughts creating new ones, then 
flows in all directions in an uncontrolled manner, creating in 
the process grief and pain. The mind, faster than wind creates 
havoc like the cyclonic storm. One who makes his mind 
tranquil wields enormous powers and he equals the celebrated 
celestials, a list of whom these verses provide. The several 
titles and posts mentioned have the distinction of possessing 
unparallelled supremacy in specific fields. The mighty hero 
who has stilled the mind is competent enough to desire and 
acquire all these titles together at the same time.

The Lord explains by these two verses that the state of 
no-mind is the highest to be attained.

He who is ruled by the mind is a mere man. One who rules 
the mind is a mighty hero indeed. When the mind that tends to 
rule one is subjugated, the cause of potential grief and disgrace 
is transformed and one who accomplishes this performs 
actions fit to be hailed and hymned and he elevates himself to 
the status of Gods. Yoga Vasishtam extolls such brave men as 
follows: “In that state which the wise ones who are conversant 
with Self-knowledge and who are experienced in the path (to 
such knowledge) reach, the wealth of God Indra becomes 
equal to a decaying piece of grass. I do not see in the nether 
world, on the earth and in heaven, that pleasure or sovereignty 
which indeed surpasses wisdom (Self-Knowledge).” (Verses 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   22 06-05-2011   10:53:39



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 23

2264 and 2265). Restraint of the mind therefore is extolled by 
all spiritual classics as the highest reach of yoga. 

It would be in the fitness of things to call such a one as 
one with a non-existent mind. On enquiry it is found that 
mind is a non-existent entity and this being so why is it said 
that the mind on its own will not subside and that it has to 
be brought under control by force and stilled? Mind and 
mental perceptions are mere appearances otherwise known 
as nescience. That it is but an illusion, which, when rendered 
naught by the grace of the guru, it will be realized that there is 
neither a mind nor the need to bring it under control by force. 
But as long as nescience persists everything appears as true. 
Hence the exhortation to control and still it.

Bhagavan emphasizes: “There is no entity by name mind. 
Because of the emergence of thoughts we surmise something 
from which they start. That we term mind. When we probe 
to see what it is, there is nothing like it. After it has vanished, 
peace will be found to remain eternal.” (Talks no. 238).

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   24 06-05-2011   10:53:39



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 25

Reality. That itself is Pure awareness and the state of firm 
abidance. Moreover that alone is the svadharma (one’s 
natural duty) of the discriminating mumukshus. Further 
that alone is the holy pilgrimage to rare and sanctified 
tīrtās capable of annulling the sinful acts. That alone is 
the best of charity. That alone is excellent tapas. There is 
absolutely no doubt in this. Know this for certain.
Commentary: 

Any means adopted to control the mind is good 
enough. The means are not as important as the end – the 
accomplishment of a steady and still mind. The means, at 
times, may be laudable but becomes purposeless if the goal 
is not achieved. Extinction of the mind is the only way to 
Liberation. All seekers of sat, therefore, must take to this royal 
road as the one to be relied upon and practice accordingly. 
Remaining simply as the Awareness of Being as ‘I am’ comes 
with complete subsidence of the mind. Hence the Lord calls 
the extinction of mind itself as awareness. It is also called 
the nature and or state of firmness, for a totally subdued and 
quietened mind is a pre-requisite for abidance in the natural 
state without ever slipping from it. “Vichāra is the process and 
the goal also. ‘I AM’ is the goal and the final Reality. To hold 
to it with effort is vichāra; when spontaneous and natural, it 
is Realization.” (Talks no. 390). 

The code of righteous conduct that seekers after Truth 
are called upon to practise has control of mind as their first 
and foremost duty. As there is none better, it alone is called 
dharma. It is their svadharma (one’s dharma). Bhagavan 
explains svadharma as follows:

“sva – one’s own, i.e. of the Self of the Ātman
 para – the other’s, i.e. of the non Self, of the anātma
 Ātma dharma is inherence in the Self.” (Talks no. 58)

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   25 06-05-2011   10:53:39



26 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

There is no dharma greater than this. Chitta suddhi or 
purification of the mind is important and indispensable for 
seekers after mukti. The purpose of pilgrimage to holy rivers 
and tanks is to purify the mind by absolving it of the effects 
of sins in previous births. A mind well subsided is tantamount 
to obtaining the fruit of a dip in holy waters. Incidentally one 
of the minor Upanishads says: “the best sādhanā is Tattva-
chintanam” – meditation on the Supreme. Next to it comes 
śāstra chintanam – meditation on various scriptural teachings; 
still lower to it is mantra chintanam meditation on mantras 
into which one is formally initiated and the lowest is tirta 
yatra – pilgrimage to holy places and baths in sacred waters.”

Charity is a useful means or sādhanā to annihilate the sense 
of ‘mine’ and destroys the unholy thoughts of the mind. Mere 
control of mind achieves the purpose of charity as well. Hence 
that becomes dhana or ‘charity’. While Bhāgavatam (11-19-20) 
proclaims ahiṃsā as the best charity, Bhagavan states, “Dana, 
dharma, nishkama karma are all tyaga only. ...When the nature 
to give away is developed it results in jñāna.” (Talks no. 581). 
For tyaga of ‘mine’ and ‘I’ alone is jñāna.

The aim of all tapas that seekers with great difficulty 
perform is to achieve the annihilation of mind that enables one 
to abide firmly in the Self. This indeed, is the characteristic 
of tapas. The Self remains attained already, what is aimed to 
be attained by tapas then is not mukti but the extirpation of 
the mind only. Taittiriya Upanishad says: “Seek Brahman 
through penance.” and later on, “penance is Brahman.” Mukti, 
after all, is release from the bondage of worldly attachments.

The observance of all austerities is to remove the self 
– created bonds; when the mind subsides in its source all 
shackles loosen and fall off on their own.

Among the various virtuous acts enjoined upon a seeker 
after Truth, the means by which a subjugated mind is held 
firm that way, indeed, is the best of all. 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   26 06-05-2011   10:53:39

by Him need not be doubted but must be known as the Truth. 
It is imperative for a seeker to engage himself wholeheartedly 
in this noble enterprise.

28 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

by the Supreme awareness of the Transcendental content,

Commentary: 

Prajñā is Absolute Knowledge from which vijñāna or 
relative knowledge proceeds.

Paramam Prajñai (Supreme Awareness) is the objectless 
awareness of the Transcendent Content. The mind, moveless, 
merges in the Whole Content. Moving away from It, it 
becomes restless.

When the moveless wind abides in ether, it becomes the 
form of ether and does not appear as an entity other than ether. 
When it begins to move, losing its hold, it becomes an object 
other than ether and assumes the form of wind. Wind moveless 
and stilled, is space but when it starts to move it becomes wind. 
Likewise moveless and stilled mind is space of Awareness or 
motionless awareness, that is Brahman, but once it moves it 
becomes worldly bondage. This is an irrefutable Truth.

Saṁsāra is not a separate zone or circle existing 
somewhere for one to get caught up in. It is nothing but  of 
the mind which gets caught and struggles in the bondage 
created by itself. Mind, moveless, is absence of saṁsāra and 
verily mukti. A wise seeker of sharp intellect must inhere the 
mind constantly in the objectless Awareness, namely, the 
Transcendent Content and immerse and dissolve it in the form 
of That. This is the royal way.

While answering a question as to how to achieve this, 
Bhagavan answered “By practice. The mind is the intelligent 
phase leading to its own destruction, for Self to manifest.” 
(Talks no.240)

One who lives in solitude is still a saṁsārin (a bound 
person) if his mind is restless. One is freed of the bondage of 
mind if one abides in the sanctuary of Silence. “Apart from 
the Self there is no solitary place outside. Wherever you exist 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   28 06-05-2011   10:53:39



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 29

keeping company with the mind, that place is without doubt a 
crowded place.” and “Solitude amounts to making the mind 
still. This can be done in a crowd too, solitude cannot efface 
one’s thoughts. Practice does it. The same practice can be 
made here too."” (Talks no. 156)

Mukti is to remain with only the awareness, or the 
sphurana, of ‘Being’. This, again is an irrevocable law. There 
is no scripture, beyond this, to expound more or make it clearer.

The attainment of that state of Truth does not demand 
extraordinary physical strength but only a sharp intellect with 
fortitude and perseverence. Chittam idu means the stage has 
reached its finality, that is, with the mind moveless mukti is 
realized. Hence the Lord calls it chittam idu, this is most certain. 
On stressing the need for persistent pursuit of this Bhagavan 
says: “Mind control is not one’s birthright. The successful few 
owe their success to their perseverance.” (Talks no. 398)

Commentary: 

Ekāntam means the Silent haven of the space of Pure 
Awareness where one remains as That, the tad ekam where 
one sees nothing else, hears nothing else and understands 
nothing else. The bliss gained and revelled in as Self is infinite 
and beyond compare. It has nothing equal or higher to it, and 
being endless, it is indestructible. All other joys are external, 
limited and fleeting and differing in quality and quantity. 
Happiness is neither in the of enjoyment of perceived object 
nor in the mind, nor in the contact between the two. The 
transient happiness which we strive to obtain from objects 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   30 06-05-2011   10:53:39



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 31

is not real but an imagination of the mind as in the case of 
dream pleasures. But here the joy of the stilled mind is one’s 
own eternal Self. The source of all the pleasures of the world 
is that Bliss. All sense happiness is the minuscule part of that 
Bliss but in different garbs veiled by names and forms. The 
greatest sense of happiness is the distracted reflection of a 
mere ray of happiness of That. The dog while chewing a dry 
bone, unaware of the fact that the blood is from its own gums, 
imagines that it is from the scarce remnants of flesh sticking 
to the bone. A musk deer, unaware that the source of fragrance 
is itself, roams all over in search of the source of the fragrance 
that emanates from its own body. Likewise the source of all 
happiness is That, which one gains and experiences, when all 
that, that appears due to denotative knowledge have subsided 
along with the stilled mind into that one unsublatable Self. 

Can this be gained by accomplishment of any action? In 
that stillness of mind when the ‘I’ alone, the unsublatable is, 
after all the non I (the mind) has been sublated, the infinite Bliss 
gained is actionless. It is only the mind with the senses, moved 
by the three gunas, that engages in the activities of the world. 
Along with the stilled mind, doership and enjoyership of the 
jīva identifying himself with the body, cease. The mere form 
of awareness will not be associated with the quality of kriya 
or action. There is absolutely no action there. Any action by 
itself becomes an obstacle to the Bliss revelled in. Bhagavan in 
Who am I? says: “Activity is creation; activity is the destruction 
of one’s inherent happiness.”

When such highest and boundless happiness is available 
at hand when the appearance of many and objects have all 
subsided with the mind, absolutely with no action of any 
kind, which learned man of discrimination will leave it alone, 
unrevelled in? This does not require any deep contemplation 
to know and decide upon. Is it not? Hence the Lord says: “Let 
the answer be from Thyself.”

Commentary: 

Vishaya jñāna is ordinary thought processes (vrittis) 
dealing with objects and matters of the empirical world. When 
the mind is emptied of all these vrittis (that is mind minus the 
objective knowledge) it is called nirvishaya jñāna (objectless 
awareness). Nirvishaya jñāna is a form of chit sakti (power 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   32 06-05-2011   10:53:39



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 33

of awareness) and is called akandakara vritti (unbroken 
consciousness). Akandakara vritti is one in which all the senses 
and the antaḥkaraṇa become infinitised and then become the 
form of chit. As Bhagavan remarks: “ Subject and object – all 
merge in the Self. There is no seer nor objects seen. The seer 
and the seen are the Self.” (Talks no. 145). Until awareness 
of objective knowledge is obliterated, objectless awareness 
cannot dawn. When a seeker attains that objectless awareness, 
the earlier yearning and resolve to gain mukti also vanishes. 
When the thought of bondage no longer remains can thought 
of release linger? – a truth, the last verse of Uḷḷadu Nārpadu 
emphasizes. Attainment of moksha is also a resolution and 
a desire. Mahātmas say: “Sunder your desires, sunder your 
desires, even if they be for the Lord.” However elevated the 
thoughts or desires or resolves may be, with the extirpation of 
objective knowledge all thoughts are annihilated, lock stock 
and barrel. Never will they raise their heads again.

But such a dhira – the brave hero – even if he be desireless 
of mukti, mukti will claim him as It’s own without fail! When 
one attains perfect wisdom, all arts and scholarship, wealth 
and even the eight types of famed wealth, will seek him out 
on their own and abide with him desiring thereby to have their 
exalted status elevated further, for such a jñāna-siddha does 
them proud by granting them a chance to shine in all their 
glory and lustre.

On the other hand, when other than jñānis claim 
possession of them, they fade out losing their light and glory 
like the waning moon in the sky. 

Nothing can equal the lustre and glory of perfect jñāna. 
Seekers of Truth must have "objectless awareness" or 
nirvishaya jñāna as their goal and when that is accomplished 
Release follows automatically.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   34 06-05-2011   10:53:39



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 35

imaginary knowledge. When the ego part is broken down, 
difference is extinguished and there is absence of movement, 
the mind, having become still, calm and deep, except for the 
awareness of being. This aspect of awareness of existence is 
the form of chaitanya. The entire universe appears to exist 
by the strength of the saṁkalpa of sakti and as such mind is 
also an aspect of sakti. Sarvam Sakti dhyānam is explained by 
Bhagavan in Ramana Gītā, Chapter 12: “The one transcendent 
Power is known by two names, the Self, because it is ground 
and power because of the power of Creation.” (Verse 26). Siva 
is unmanifest whereas Sakti is manifest. Her manifestation 
is the display of Cosmos on pure Consciousness. “Diversity 
in Reality would not arise in the absence of movement. 
The movement cannot exist apart from Reality.” (Ibid, 
Verse 23). The support is inactive though Energy is active and 
changing, called Māyā. But the distinction between the two, 
the Substratum Self and Energy, the Substance and Attribute, 
and the supported or prakāśam (Effulgence) and vimarsam 
(manifestation) is only an illusion. “Self Awareness can be had 
in two ways, through its activity or experiencing it as such, 
by its attributes or by being one with it... By understanding 
the source of activity through activity, one gets established in 
the Self.” (Verses 30 and 31). When Kapali Sastri questioned 
Bhagavan whether the ‘activity’ is eternal, Bhagavan answered 
in the affirmative saying though there is no absolute creation 
or destruction, every moment there is creation and destruction 
and only sages can understand this ‘activity of Reality’ or 
Leela of Kaivalyam or Sakti of Svarūpa. What this verse 
of Devi Kālōttaram instructs is to go beyond the illusion of 
manifestation and by enquiring into the origin of ‘I thought’, 
to remain as simply “I am”. 

Manam (mind) is called so by its very nature of going 
over thoughts again and again (mananam). When all things 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   35 06-05-2011   10:53:39



36 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

that the mind is attached to are destroyed, what remains is 
the all pervading formless, Partless Awareness – “I am”- the 
wisdom to be attained by a seeker.

“The mind nature disappears somewhere. The Conscious 
nature (of pure awareness) remains quite clear, without 
disturbance and without division as the All, having a nature 
which is not mutilated (or stunted) and absolutely Real.” 
(Yoga Vasishtam, 2271).

Everything with form is contained in space. Space, itself 
formless, contains everything though it itself is not contained 
by anything. The true and Transcendental Content, being 
formless and partless, remains pervading everywhere. The 
characteristic of vastu or True Content is to contain everything 
within Itself. If it is contained in anything else It is then not 
vastu. Therefore It is called nirakaram – formless. Nishkala 
jñāna (Partless, Whole and Unfragmented Awareness) is the 
state when mind is devoid of all attachments or support to lean 
to. Awareness of existence is the knowledge of the Ātman. That 
which shines in its own Self-revealing effulgence without the 
intervention of any other medium – the awareness of the Self 
without the admixture of any other upadi or adjuncts – is the 
characteristic of the Ātman. That is nishkala jñānam (partless 
or indivisible consciousness).

Of all the sixteen kalas (parts), even if all the rest were to 
get destroyed, the awareness of existence, the one kala, alone 
will never perish. All the kalas are contained in the body and 
the world (the 16 kalas within the body are: pranan, śraddhā, 
space, air, fire, water, earth, organs, mind, food, vigour, self-
control, mantras, rites, world and name). All these mere names 
and forms, get merged in their source and lose their distinct 
and separate existence; they become the Self on which they all 
depend for their existence. The universe is not outside of that 
Self. It is like the creation of the dream world which has no 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   36 06-05-2011   10:53:39



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 37

existence before going to sleep and after waking. It was only 
an appearance projected by the ‘I’, the consciousness. Being 
just an appearance, it cannot exist without consciousness. 
On waking up, the whole of the dream world becomes non-
different from the ‘I’ that projected it. The dream world did not 
exist even during the time of witnessing the dream. The waking 
world similarly never exists different from the consciousness 
aspect. Remaining with the aspect of awareness of Being is 
nishkala jñāna. Referring to this once Bhagavan said: “the 
spark of jñāna will easily consume all creation as if it mere 
a heap of cotton. All crores of worlds...topple down when 
the atomic bomb of jñāna comes down upon them” and in 
the same context he said: “Aham (I am) is the first name of 
God. The first letter in Sanskrit is A .... and the last letter Ha 
... and ‘Aha’ thus includes everything from beginning to end. 
The word ‘Ayam’ means that which exists, self-shining and 
self-evident. Ayam, Aham, Ātma all refer to the same thing. 
In the Bible also “I am” is given as the name of God.” (Day 
by Day, 22.11.45)

forms and the Consciousness seeing them. That is to say, 
Siva is the background underlying both the subject and the 
object, and again Siva in Repose and Siva in Action, or Siva

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   38 06-05-2011   10:53:39



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 39

to me, I can then say that Siva is not pratyaksha.” (Talks no. 
450). Thus Bhagavan explains how Siva remains as ‘I am’ in 
all. Once Parvathy did tapas. “In her dhyāna she saw a bright 
light. She thought: “This cannot be Siva for it is within the 
compass of my vision. I am greater than this light.” So she 
resumed her tapas. Thoughts disappeared. Stillness prevailed. 
She then realised that BE-ing is Siva in His true nature.” (ibid) 
Here the triputi, seer, seen and the sight merge into One.

There is nothing apart from oneself to be perceived 
when one remains as the non-dual Perfect Content. As there 
is nothing to be perceived, perception disappears and only 
void remains. But the ‘void’ is not inert or insentient. It is just 
the awareness of ‘I’ with everything else as void. As nothing 
apart from chit is, it is void. When the void that remains as 
the perceived object also disappears, there is nothing other 
than ‘I’ and it is called mahaśūnya. Śūnyatta is Ātman in the 
doctrine of the Buddhists. “Śūnya (void or blank), ati śūnya 
(beyond śūnya) and maha śūnya (immense void), all mean the 
same, i.e., the Real Being only.” (Talks no. 333)

That state that establishes the identity of the perceiver 
as the paravastu, ‘the Content Beyond’, where the perceiver 
alone remains without perception is called parayogam (the 
Supreme Yoga) here. This is the royal route for the jīva to get 
liberated, and is called the seed of moksha. 

If the Bliss of mukti is to be harvested the seed to be sown 
is ‘void’. That is also the seed of everything. It is the nucleus 
for the appearance of the entire universe. We, ever the form 
of Awareness, are chinmatra only, Awareness alone.

Saint Thayumanavar describes this very beautifully in a 
verse in Ānandakkalippu:

	 The mind was born there
	 And died, was resolved there
	 Seat of all states there

Paraphrase: 
Discarding the direct way of seeking the light 

of Awareness and abiding as the Self taught by this 
Kalajñāna, contemplate never, and not even in the 
least, on the various chakras located in the celebrated 
Shadadhara (six centres), the subtle nāḍīs that create 
ten types of sounds, deities, like Ganesa residing in the 
lotuses of varying number of petals in the centres of 
these chakras, and their respective mantra aksharas and 
the different deities that have expanded into many, right 
from the three mandalas of sun, moon and fire.

1. Chakras or plexuses are spiritual centres located 
along the spine, six in number through which kundalini 
sakti rises.

2. Nāḍīs referred to above are subtle nerves called 
Ida, Pingala and Sushumna running along the spine, one 
to the right, one to the left and one in the centre of the 
spine.

3. Each chakra is conceived as consisting of lotuses 
of varying number of petals and each is presided over by 
a particular deity.

4. Aksharangal are the mantras or the sacred sound 
syllables respective to the various deities to be used in 
their worship.

5. Mandalas are circles or mystical diagrams used to 
invoke the deities in occult science and practices.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   41 06-05-2011   10:53:40



42 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Commentary: 
Swerving away from this direct path of Kalajñāna that 

helps one accomplish the goal of liberation with certainty, a 
seeker should not move over to other paths, is emphasized 
by the Lord in this verse. This indeed, is the most direct and 
best path to Release.

Giving up of the practice of kundalini yoga is well nigh 
an impossibility for those who practise it. The process of 
worship of the deities specific to these six plexuses involves 
the fixing (mentally) of the deity due to each chakra in that 
chakra, chanting the mantra of the deity the prescribed number 
of times, obtaining the siddhi or favour of that particular deity 
and then moving ahead to the next one, where similar ritualistic 
procedures will have to be followed.

What is gained is given up and the worship of what is to 
be gained is embarked upon and the seeker gradually becomes 
weary of ceaseless activity.

What is once worshipped as real has been discarded as 
unreal yielding place to another, which, though appearing 
real then, will subsequently be discarded as unreal. What is 
manifest and comprehended may be differentiated as real and 
unreal. But the unmanifest and uncomprehended deep rooted 
nescience will never be known by them, much less, overcome.

Some yogīs, as the fruit of ceaseless toil in the field, 
bind sound forms in their nāḍīs or subtle nerves with the 
capacity to create ten types of sounds. Success in this demands 
long-standing discipleship under a perfect guru with strict 
disciplines governing food and sleep. 

Yogīs, highly adept and skilled in this art, often produce 
sounds of praṇava (OM), Hrimkara (sound of Hrim), the seed 
letter or mantra of Devi, and other ten types of sounds by 
pressing certain nāḍīs. This is a strange form of worship that 
causes awe and wonder on the onlookers. Likewise deities in 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   42 06-05-2011   10:53:40



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 43

the three mandalas (circles) are also worshipped and favours 
are won (the three mandalas are those of sun, moon and fire).

But none of these can bestow that bliss of Release. “To 
imagine muladhara at the bottom, the Heart at the Centre, the 
head at the top of all these is all wrong. In one word, to think is 
not your real nature.” (Talks no 184), and again “Ātman alone 
is to be realized. Its realization holds all else in its compass... 
Those who speak of these have not realized the Ātman... The 
upanishads say para leena – meaning that sushumna or such 
nāḍīs are all comprised in para i.e. ātma nāḍī. For jñāna they 
must come to the Heart. Hridaya is the alpha and omega.” 
(Talks no 57). Hence a serious seeker should steer clear of such 
ways. These are just like the feats of magic performed by some 
in the empirical world and no more. Thus it can be seen that 
such feats are treated with contempt and indifference. They 
may surprise and spell bind the audience, but are obstacles in 
the path of sādhanā.

Further great saints like Kannudaiya Vallalar, the author 
of Ozhivil Odukkam consider acts of meditating on the 
(imagined) deities in the adharas and while proceeding from 
one to the other, undergoing grief and agony at the prospect of 
giving up the worship of that deity and creating and destroying 
subsequently other deities as one advances from one to the 
other, as grievous sins. To create and destroy the deities that 
create and destroy us is a mighty sin. These actions performed 
within, by the mind, are as much the cause of grief as the 
actions performed in the external world.

Most importantly in these paths lest dangers should arise 
and assail one, the guru must always be by the side of the 
seekers. But the path of Kalajñāna permits one to proceed 
fearlessly. The direct path, though may be prolonged due to 
the persistence of vāsanās on the part of the seeker, is a clear 
and straight path free of pitfalls and dangers. Once, while 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   43 06-05-2011   10:53:40



44 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

emphasising the need to abide in the Heart centre, Bhagavan 
said: “People who are midway may not know about the 
merits and demerits of other paths, but one who has climbed 
the summit and sits there observing others coming up is 
able to see all the paths. He will, therefore be able to tell 
people who are coming up to move a little to this side or that 
or to avoid a pitfall. The goal is the same for all, you see.” 
(Letters 18-1-1949).

Yoga Vasishtam also speaks of the same. “Let one meditate 
on this Supreme Siva who is ever abiding in the body. This 
one is the highest yoga. This one is the highest practice.” 
(Verse 1687).

Paraphrase: 
Seekers who aspire for everlasting release need 

not endeavour to practice the hosts of mantras meant 
for worship of diverse deities. Practices of yoga like 
pranayama and kumbhaka (retention of breath) that bind 
the movement of life-breath, dharana (concentration) and 
all-else, (all of which) are but one great fetter.
Commentary: 

If mukti alone is the cherished goal, none of the above 
need be observed, by the serious and intense seekers. Mind 
ensures a long life for itself by the chanting of the japas and 
will never die. But everlasting life demands the death of 
mind. Hence the host of clusters of mantras will never aid 
the attainment of everlasting bliss.

In days of yore these hosts of mantras numbered many 
crores, but with the passage of time, many have dropped off 
and have dwindled and only a few are available as worthy 
of being imparted as upadēsa. These are referred to here as 
mantrakkūttam – hosts of mantras.

In the yogic practice of pranayama when the life breath 
is controlled, breath will subside with mind. As long as breath 
is forcefully held or impounded within (sthambanam), so long 
will the mind subside. Once the breath is released, the mind 
will arise and assume its nature of indulgence in thoughts. 
This, often called manolaya, will not destroy the mind. Mukti 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   45 06-05-2011   10:53:40



46 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

is unattainable without manonasa, the annihilation of the 
mind. In sthambana and pranayama, the mind and breath, in 
subtle and gross form, remain, indicating the non-removal of 
the non-self and, therefore, the unattainability of the joy of 
Release. Stopping the vital breath without stilling the thoughts 
is like tying an elephant to a stone with the flimsy coir rope 
or trying to cover the sky with a piece of cloth instead of the 
simple process of closing the eyes.

Secondly dharana (concentration) or upasana or japa of 
a mantra, all involve the use of the mind. What is desired is 
mukti – a state of no-mind. But these practices strengthen the 
mind’s nature and make it more active in its functions. Any 
activity is an obstacle to stilling the mind. The means and 
goal in these paths, far from being in unison, are diametrically 
opposed to each other. Hence the Lord warns the seekers 
against resorting to such devious paths.

During the last illness of Bhagavan many homas were 
performed for the speedy recovery of his health. After the 
Mritunjaya japam was over, the people concerned asked him, 
if they could proceed with Mritunjaya homam. He nodded 
his assent and as soon as they left turned to Venkataratnam 
and said “Extinction of ego and abidance in Self is the 
Mritunjaya homam. In Devi Kālōttaram, verses 16 and 17 
it is stated that one should not get immersed in mantrams, 
homams and such things. Also in Sarvajñānottaram verse 
35 it is said that abidance in the Self itself is the mantra, the 
devata, the diksha, the tapas, the homam and the dhyāna.” 
(Letters – Brahmanirvana).

The difference between the path of jñāna and upasana 
is often explained thus. Realization of the non-dual Absolute, 
whose very nature transcends all action and inaction, does away 
with the difference among the falsely superimposed concepts of 
doership, of instruments of action and action and their results. 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   46 06-05-2011   10:53:40



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 47

In the case of the snake in rope the right knowledge dawns when 
the rope is illumined by the light which at once removes the 
false knowledge. No meditation in the false snake or real rope 
is involved as in nondualistic jñāna path. Upasana involves a 
continuous flow of similar modification of the mind in relation 
to some object with name and form.

The relative merits of karma, upasana and jñāna are 
given in a simple verse. “Karma (actions) are for purification 
of the mind, upasana for concentration and jñāna for moksha 
– thus proclaims Vedānta with a tom-tom: “Karmāni chitta 
suddhyartam aikagryentham upasanam mōkshārtam brahma 
vij nanam iti vedānta dindimah.”

Paraphrase: 
Listen to Me carefully. That Transcendent content, hailed

Commentary: 

That the Absolute Content can be known only through 
pure Awareness is being lucidly taught. None of the display 
of skilful actions, performed with the idea that that Supreme 
Content is outside of oneself and invoking it in an idol, 
worshipping it with puja, or activities like Suryanamaskar 
– propitiating the Sun-God – or the chanting of very holy 
panchakshara (the five letters on Namasivaya) or ashtakshara 
(the eight letters Om Namo Narayanaya or Om Namo 
Vasudevaya) or contemplating on deities, is there. 

That Content Beyond transcends all these and cannot be 
reached by any of these. Moreover all worships are performed 
with some desire in view which is conjured up and projected 
by the mind. All these are still in the realm of the mind with the 
triad of the worshipper, worship and the worshipped. Whereas 
in jñāna, Simple Awareness, all triads merge, the dualities 
disappear, the subject and object coalesce into the non-dual 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   48 06-05-2011   10:53:40



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 49

Infinite Being. These modes of actions, though attractive but 
expansive, after being gone through for a length of time, will 
land them ultimately in the path of jñāna for this ‘toll-gate’ is 
inescapable. Only a master of wisdom ever in the experience of 
the Self can forewarn the serious seekers at the very outset of the 
devious nature of such practices. Eternity can never be attained 
by transient or non-eternal sādhanās performed temporarily. 
Ātman, actionless, cannot be attained by the performance of 
action. As Ātman is ever attained and seeks nothing outside of 
Itself what one is to meditate upon is the Awareness of Being in 
the subject and object, without the subject and object, and then 
the meditator becomes one with the Absolute. This stage can be 
experienced simply as Awareness. Here the word ‘meditation’ 
loses its usual connotation of being simply a mental process and 
assumes a different significance. Trying to invoke the Ātman, 
that is All-pervading and never away from anything, in an idol 
to offer worship is akin to contain the floods of a swollen river 
by putting an obstacle in its way. “ Those who go to another 
God, having abandoned the Lord in the Cave of the Heart, long 
for a precious stone, giving up the celestial kaustukha gem 
in their hands.” (Yoga Vasishtam, Verse 1679). The highest 
fulfilment arises only from the knowledge of this Supreme 
God of Gods who is the Supreme Self; but not through the 
pain of religious practices. While the one who dwells within as 
the worsipper, worship and the source of worship, attempting 
to know Him through worship, japa and dhyāna is equal to 
trying to measure, with a ladder the sky that provides space for 
it and the one who attempts to climb on it. “Meditation is the 
respectful offering of water (in worship) in the form of pure 
Awareness. The Awareness that is meditation is the flower. This 
God who is of the nature of one’s own consciousness is not 
worshipped by oblations or gifts and the wiseman worships that 
mere consciousness beyond the deity-consciousness through 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   49 06-05-2011   10:53:40



50 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

every object obtained, with an even and whole intellect.” (Yoga 
Vasishtam, 1689, 92, 94).

There is a verse in Avadhuta Gītā that seeks pardon of 
the Lord for three sins: for going on pilgrimage ignoring the 
all pervasive and beyond the space nature of the Supreme, 
trying to meditate by setting at naught the Vedic declaration 
of Ātman, Brahman being beyond the reach of the mind and 
finally by praising, trying to confine the Lord who is beyond 
speech, within speech.

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 51

Paraphrase: 
For those, whose minds gaining restlessness, are 

forever expanding, clinging to external objects, that are 
the ‘other’ of oneself, factors causing fresh bondage keep 
increasing in countless numbers. If the externalised and 
ever roaming mind is turned inwards and made to abide 
in its natural state know that one will not be afflicted in 
the world by any misery or agitation.
Commentary: 

Mind, when abandoning its natural abode, emerges 
out, becomes externalised and holds on to gross objects 
outside and subtle objects within. The Kathopanishad says: 
“Lord has created the senses with an outgoing tendency. 
Only a rare discriminating spiritual hero, aspiring for 
liberation and immortality turns the senses and the mind 
inward by withdrawing them from their objects and realizes 
the Self”. (11-1-1).

The eyes can only perceive and not hear and the ears 
can only hear and not perceive. No one instrument can do 
the office of another. When all the instruments are present 
and functioning, mind-presence has to be there, for in the 
absence of the mind nothing can be cognized. One becomes 
aware of objects when one’s awareness envelops the objects, 
permeates them and identifies itself with them. The nature 
of the mind being ever restless and outgoing, and objects of 
the external world being impermanent, the mind changes the 
objects it holds on to frequently becoming even more restless 
and further ramified into thought-forms.

Only an expanded mind absorbs many things and 
gathering and assimilating the absorbed things becomes 
the very cause of bondage, and the quality of the object 
held on to determines the nature of that bondage. The 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   51 06-05-2011   10:53:40



52 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

inconstant mind purged of its defilement of desires and 
attachments to sense objects must be steadied, senses must 
be controlled coupled with faith that permits no intellectual 
doubt to assail it.

The only way to curtail the mind, will be to turn the mind 
inward, empty it of its contents and inhere it in its natural 
abode. An objectless mind shines as the Supreme Content. 
Restless and perpetually moving, the mind with attachments 
renounced, becomes stilled and abides in the Silence of the 
Supreme. The mind which perceives all objects cannot itself 
be perceived, for often it refuses to part with its subject-hood 
which is like committing suicide of itself. The mind can 
become an object only to the Ātman. This is what happens 
when the mind is inward-turned and made empty of its content. 
The awareness envelops the Ātman, the Subject, all the senses 
become (tanmayam) the form of the subject into which the 
mind and its pseudo subject-hood are dissolved – True Subject. 
This is the state of sarvaśūnya as there is nothing apart from 
it and it is not available for other modifications than the 
akhandākara vritti where all the antaḥkaraṇas, inner organs, 
have also become infinite. 

If only the mind could be elevated to this exalted state, 
none of the misery and fear in the world or the endless 
suffering can ever approach one. Attachment to objects 
(vishaya) is death. Release from this bondage is liberation. 
With this Release as sādhanā Release must be attained.

Paraphrase: 

Unite with that Truth, the all-pervading, immaculate 
Perfect Whole, the non-dual Ātman, without an inside or 
outside (within or without), bereft of all conceptions of 
directions such as up, below or centre, which assumes

and self-luminous, therefore self-revealing, requiring no

Commentary: 

The Reality, That which is, is all pervasive filling 
everything and everywhere. It is behind and beyond the 
world and in the world. It is within and without, up, down 
and centre, pervading each and every object through and 
through like the warp and woof of a cloth. Hence It is the 
form of all forms. Just as one fire takes different forms 
according to the thing it burns, so does the Eternal Ātman, 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   53 06-05-2011   10:53:40



54 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

though One, takes a form according to the form It indwells 
and is outside of all forms.

Chandhogya Upanishad states: “That alone is below and 
above, behind and in front, in north and south and is all this and 
It is the ‘I’ in all which alone is below, above...” This should 
not be mistaken for the individual ego. This is the Ātman in 
all, the only One non-dual Absolute. Purusha Suktam says 
only one fourth of the Brahman is manifest. He pervades all 
with non-being nowhere. As such there is no concealment and 
therefore no ‘within’ or ‘without’.

Hence imagined directions cannot be ascribed to It. 
Uncircumscribed by directions, It is the place of rising and 
subsidence of all the perceivable forms. But It Itself remains 
formless for if It has a form for that form to occupy space It has 
to resort to the formless space. Even that space not being other 
than Itself, it is formless. When ether or space, the subtlest of 
all elements, is all-pervasive, holding all the worlds, planets 
and the stellar systems in it, what to speak of the Self which 
is the cause of ether itself and therefore more pervasive than 
ether? Hence That, which is the cause of appearance of all 
the perceivable objects of the phenomenal world is said to be 
formless. That which has form is bound, by space and time 
and Reality, the Satvastu, being formless, transcends time, 
space and directions.

Likewise that which knows everything can be known 
only by Itself for there is no other consciousness competent 
to reveal It. The Self becomes aware of the Self when the 
senses, mind, intellect etc. are silenced in the stillness of 
Awareness; Awareness becomes Conscious of Itself. Being 
both knowledge and the object known It is the subject for it 
can be known only by Itself. It is the universal Subject, with 
never failing consciousness, who is described as the bird of 
beautiful plumage in the Vedas. It is well known as the ‘I’ in all.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   54 06-05-2011   10:53:40



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 55

That Content which illumines everything else shines in 
Its own Self-revealing effulgence, requiring no other luminous 
agent to reveal It.

Therefore It is Perfect – and verily all the objects – yet 
devoid of the impact of any on It. It is omniscient; yet It Itself 
cannot be known by any. It illumines all objects yet It cannot 
be illumined by them. The Lord exhorts the seeker to conjoin 
the Self with that Perfect, all Pervasive Whole.

Paraphrase:

Commentary: 

The present condition of saṁsāra experienced by all the 
jīvas in the world is what has been aspired for by them in 
previous lives and to gain which actions were duly performed 
by them. The consequences of these actions are being reaped 
now in the present life. Whatever action was performed by 
the jīva, be it good or bad, is now fructifying as effects. Yoga 
Vasishtam expresses the same in the following verse: “By 
what, where and in which manner any desire is entertained 
in the mind (and accordingly actions performed), that desire 
is obtained, as if bringing forth the fruit, by that, there, 
then and in that manner.” (Verse 698). This body has been 
fashioned by the mind, of its own accord for the sake of the 
desires cherished and actions performed to attain them, as if 
it were a vessel or a covering in the manner of the cocoon of 
a silkworm, or as an earthen pot created by a potter. Hence 
this body composed of five elements is a product erroneous 
by fashioned by the mind.

However all actions are flawed and will not grant that 
blemishless release. Actions – fruits – actions becomes the 
grievous cycle of saṁsāra plunging the jīva into the ocean 
of karma and grief ad infinitum Hence actions are described 
as ‘full of flaws’. What should be done then? is the question. 
Whatever is outside of oneself is flawed. Withdrawing the 
perception and goal away from them, one should turn the 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   56 06-05-2011   10:53:40



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 57

mind inward and concentrate it on the Transcendent Content, 
That cannot be seen  and establish the identity of oneself with 
Brahman, the All. Vichāra Bindu Upanishad says: “Just as 
you think so you become. Think ‘I am the body’, body you 
will become. Think ‘I am Sat-Chit-Ānanda‘, Brahman you 
will become.” (Verse 8).

As thoughts have tremendous force in impelling one to 
act, it is of utmost importance to eschew worldly and worthless 
thoughts and develop ātma chintanam.

The same instruction is offered in Ānma Sakshatkara 
Prakaranam “Meditate on that which is beyond the reach 
of thought”. Contemplation on the formless will render 
the contemplator himself formless. This is the best way 
to destroy one’s form. In verse 3 of Ashtakam Bhagavan 
speaks of the same idea “To dwell without thought upon 
Thy nature is to lose one’s identity like a doll of sugar in 
an ocean”.

What is called ajata Siddhanta is expounded in this verse. 
Only if there be such a thing as creation can there be cause-

nor any of the other things exists and what exists in the past, 
is present and future is the natural state of the Self. There is 
neither avidya nor illusion nor bondage, nor a concept called 
‘mind’. Nothing indeed is born and nothing perishes. All is 
one, without beginning or end, an undivided and unbroken 
mass of consciousness. Therefore acts of merit and demerit, 
experiences of pleasure and pain, ‘going’ and ‘coming’ to 
worlds, this and others, birth and death, being born in 84 lakh

     “What is the Self’s self-tranformation
	 As the world? A twist of straw

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 59

	 Appearing as snake? Look hard
	 You see no snake at all. There was
	 No transformation, no creation, none
	 No world at all.” 

(Guru Vāchaka Kovai, Verse 87)
But then, what can be the purpose of all the scriptures 

speaking of the process of creation in various ways? It is not 
the intent of the śāstras to preach exactly the way in which 
the world came into ‘being’ but to induce and enthuse the true 
seeker to enquire and know the primal cause of the appearance 
of the world.

“Q.: How has Srishti (creation) come about? Some say 
it is due to karma. Others say it is the Lord’s lila or sport. 
What is the truth?

Bhagavan: Various accounts are given in books. But is 
there creation? Only if there is creation (do) we have to explain 
how it came about. All that, we may not know. But that we 
exist now, is certain. Why not know the ‘I’ and the present 
and then see if there is creation.” (Day by Day, 17-2-1946).

If, in reality, the process of creation be true, there should 
be no contradiction in the accounts of creation detailed in 
the śāstras; but different ways of creation are spoken of in 
different śāstras. An intense seeker must glean and sift the 
truth from the very diversity of descriptions detailed in them 
that the process of creation is far from being real. This is the 
real intent and purpose of the śāstras. Hence the Lord says: 
“All these spoken of are not true”. 

“The scientic and theological explanations do not 
harmonise. The diversities in such theories clearly show 
the uselessness of seeking such explanations. Such 
explanations are purely mental or intellectual and nothing 
more. Still all of them are true according to the standpoint 
of the individual. There is no creation in the state of 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   59 06-05-2011   10:53:40



60 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

realization. When one sees the Self the world is not seen. 
So see the Self and realize that there has been no creation.” 
(Talks no. 455)

But the very same śāstras, when they speak of the Ātman, 
instruct its nature in one voice. There is no room for difference 
in this aspect. That alone is the Truth at all times (past, present 
and future) is evident enough.

When there is no such thing as world how can ‘worldly 
jīva’ exist? This is like the mouth chewing the face and 
smiling away. An aspirant, therefore, fortifying himself 
with the requisite strength of mind and impressed by the 
truth that the world appearing with the reality of existence 
is truly non-existant, must seek the source, the ‘I’, the 
pure Awareness, on which all these are imagined. Hence 
scriptures proclaim: “Brahman never grows by action nor 
is It reduced.”

Paraphrase:

is verily that Content Beyond which exists without any

derives its ‘Being’ from and is illumined by, that
