Commentary: 

The earlier verse negated creation of the world and the 
worldling jīva, bound by attachment. This verse instructs that 
the appearance of the entire Universe is but the very form of 
that Transcendent Content that has no support for Itself. That 
Content, clinging to which as support and stay, the entire 
Universe stands, remains Itself unsupported (niralambham) 
without any support. But It is the support of everything else. 
This is the characteristic of vastu or Vastu Lakshana. A yogī 
who has turned the mind inward merges all the objects seen 
in the world in that Form along with himself, and becomes 
one with It.

Reality of an effect rests on its cause as that of cotton 
fabrics in cotton. Cotton, the causal substance, is real and its 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   61 06-05-2011   10:53:40



62 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

fabrics are one with it. Water is the cause and waves, bubbles, 
drop and froth are all but water. In the same way fields, tanks, 
country and places are not other than earth.

Though the world manifestation is experienced it 
cannot be conceived as separate from the all-pervading Self. 
Cognition of unity of all existence in this way or unifying 
all the objects and the forms of worlds in that Supportless, 
all-pervasive Satcitānanda is called pravilapa dhristi, or 
bhāvaadvaita or Sarvātma bhāva. Other than that Self, the 
form of Bliss, there is not even an iota of a world. It is this 
Awareness (the Self) that reveals the world and without this 
awareness the world is inconceivable. Hence yogīs see the 
world as Brahman.

If things are seen as other than the support – the True 
Content – then the mind will not become single-pointed.

Verse five of Upadēsa Undiyar of Bhagavan is in perfect 
agreement with this. “Worshipping the eight forms (ether, air, 
fire, water, earth, sun, moon and the living beings) as the forms 
of God Himself is perfect worship of the Lord.”

The path of enquiry consists in enquiring who he is who 
sees the world as many, thus seeking his source. Unifying all 
that is perceived into that paravastu is called Pravilapa mārga 
(the path of pravilapa). The Vaishnava doctrine of Sarvam 
Vasudeva mayam jagath (Everyting in the world is the form 
of Vasudeva) belongs to this path. This is a very effective 
practice and guide to destroy the sense of ‘mine’.

A yogī discarding his separate identity and losing himself 
in that Niralambha Paravastu attaining ‘oneness’ with it, 
becomes niralambha. The state where one becomes the very 
thing he has clung to is the ultimate state, with nothing higher 
to it and is mukti.

If one proceeds to unify one by one the perceived objects 
in that Self, infinite other things will ever remain to be 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   62 06-05-2011   10:53:40



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 63

unified. If he himself becomes that form or at-one-ment with 
It, everything else becomes That. Bhagavan also says: “See 
just yourself as Brahman. Then see the world as Brahman.”

Gītā states:
brahmārpaṇaṁ brahma havirbrahmāgnau brahmaṇā 

hutam |

	 The offering is God
	 The oblation is God

The Mundaka Upanishad says: “Brahman before, 

Brahman behind, to right and left stretched forth below 
and above. Brahman indeed is the whole world, the widest 
extent.”

Various other upanishads proclaim the same truth. 
Tejobindu Upanishad (Verse 5): “This is Supreme, hidden 
in mystery, the resting-place (of all) and imperceptible; it is 
Brahman, without support, of the nature of unlimited space, 
atomic and subtle. That is the Supreme abode of Vishnu.”

Katopanishad: “Most glorious is this support. This is the 
supreme-most support. He who has realised this support comes 
to revel in the Brahma world.” (2-17) and Brihadaranyaka 
Upanishad (4-12-14): “The world manifestation is experienced, 
it cannot be conceived in separation from the all-pervading 
Self. It is consciousness that reveals it and without the 
revealing Consciousness, its existence is inconceivable. 
Therefore the wise see the world as Brahman.”

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   64 06-05-2011   10:53:41



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 65

of saṁsāra. Śūnya or the state of Śūnya or void is one where 
other than pure awareness there is naught else. In us, the form 
of Awareness, when the void that is known as an object is also 
removed, there is nothing other than ‘I’. This is mahaśūnya.

In all the books on Vedānta, the question of ‘void’ or of 
nothing being left behind is raised by the disciple and answered 
by the guru. Bhagavan explains this: “It is the mind that sees 
the objects and has experiences and that finds a void when 
it ceases to see and experience, but that is not ‘you’. You are 
the constant illumination that lights up both the experiences 
and the void. It is like the theatre light that enables you to see 
the theatre, the actors and the play while the play is going on 
but also remains alight and enables you to say that there is no 
play on when it is all finished. Or there is another illustration. 
We see objects all around us, but in complete darkness we do 
not see them and we say I see ‘nothing’; even then the eyes 
are there to say that they see nothing. In the same way you 
are there even in the void.” (Day by Day, 21.7.46)

The ‘I’, the awareness, is the witness of the three bodies: 
the gross, subtle and causal, and of the three states: waking, 
dream and deep sleep, and of the three times: past, present 
and future and also of this void. In Vivekachūḍāmaṇi (verses 
212 and 213) the disciple says, “After I eliminate the five 
sheaths as non-self, I find that nothing at all remains.”, and the 
Guru replies that the Self or That by which all modifications 
(including the ego and the creatures) and their absence (that 
is the void) are perceived is always there. “First one sees the 
Self as objects then one sees the Self as void, then one sees 
the Self as Self, only in this last there is no seeing because 
seeing is being.” (Ibid). This is that mahaśūnya referred to 
in this verse and that is our natural state. When that void is 
meditated upon, the form of ego melts away and one becomes 
that ‘void’. One who does not meditate on that ‘void’ is fated to 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   65 06-05-2011   10:53:41



66 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

become a saṃsārī, bound by various attachments – a bondage 
that is self-created – like the silkworm that binds itself in the 
cocoon it makes for itself.

Like the space that supports and yields room for all the 
perceived objects, Ātman is the support and substratum of 
the world, the jīva and Iswara. Though It is called a Śūnya 
it is not an inert void, for Perfect Truth is Its Existence. It is 
Sat, Chit and Ānanda. Verse 218 of Vivekachūḍāmaṇi affirms 
this: “This non-existence (śūnya) is Self-witnessed. For it is 
perceived by the Self. Hence the Self that witnesses is itself 
the Supreme Self, not anything else.”

Paraphrase: 

All beings in this world belonging to the four kind

Commentary: 

What is called Māśūnya (the Great void) is but the 
natural state. All that is perceptible going out of perception 
and becoming void and only the Self shining with the aspect 
of just the awareness of mere existence is that, aham amsattu 
ecchunyam of verse 14 (the void with just the aspect of ‘I’ as 
being). This void is not inert but shines with the sphurana of ‘I 
am’, for that void which is without a parallel is the effulgence 
of pure wisdom. Completely devoid of visible phenomena 
and which consists of the aspect of ‘I’ only is considered the 
seed of liberation.

Sleep is also a void. But there, just as the perceived world 
becomes void, the jīva, not conscious of himself, gets plunged 
into dark nescience, where nothing is known. He is aware of 
neither the world nor of himself. But the “great void” is the 
state of deep sleep brought on in jāgrat. Sleep was not a state 
of complete non-exiestence. True, there was no gross or subtle 
object to be grasped by the mind, as in waking and dream 
states. But none can deny existence of oneself then, which 
stands proved by the cognition, on waking, of the absence of 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   67 06-05-2011   10:53:41



68 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

break in one’s existence. And everyone says “I slept well”. 
Without the existence of the experiencer ‘I’, the experienced, 
(here the good sleep) and the process of experiencing, the 
above statement cannot be made. They must have been there 
but not as the ‘triad’ but as one homogenous consciousness. 
All the three have coalesced into pure Awareness, freed of all 
objectivity and therefore, the subjectivity also. But in sleep one 
is covered by the veil of darkness which can be cut asunder 
by contemplating that great void where, with the perceived 
world phenomena removed, he alone remains. Everything else 
remains void and that is the Reality.

It has been calculated and spoken of in the śāstras that 
there are about 84 lakhs of species born in the four ways 
(sweat-born, seed-born, egg-born and womb-born). Invariably 
all the beings, which ever species they belong to have sorrow 
and misery as their lot. Not a single being escapes this fate. 
The hope for happiness after a protracted period of grief 
also is shattered for the horizon of happiness keeps receding 
further and further for ever. The only way to put away this 
grief permanently is to seek and find one’s source of origin.

Pain or pleasure, happpiness or misery, all appear and 
disappear on that support, ‘The great void’. The entire 
cosmos, all the worlds of sentient and insentient beings, 
rise from and fall into, that void. Considering oneself as a 
separate entity other than the True Content is the cause of 
all this overwhelming malady of perpetual grief and misery. 
Non-attachment to externals is the pre-eminent condition to 
attain the competence to contemplate the void. With this and 
vairagya which is verily the entrance to the state of mukti, 
one should contemplate the void repeatedly with non-desire 
everywhere. Then alone one secures bahya anālambanatva 
(the state of no external support) which alone will facilitate 
this contemplation.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   69 06-05-2011   10:53:41



70 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

one must abide firmly in the natural state, devoid of the 
universe, called māśūnya.
Commentary: 

Narkriyai – Good kriya (activity), is to worship Siva 
within and without as per the agamic injunction: Sarchariyai 
– good chariya is to worship Siva in Saguna form in temples 
coupled with good conduct. These are prescribed with a view 
to attain knowledge or jñāna. After the dawn of wisdom the 
observance of these becomes redundant and is to be given up.

A ripe and competent seeker gains the siddhi of a mantra 
by constantly chanting it within. When the deity respective to 
the mantra by the strength of his upasana (worship) appears 
before him, the seeker holds on to the form as the support 
within, lest it (the form), should slip away. This is called 
salambha yoga (yoga with support). This must also be given 
up. Nothing need be held on to as He (the Self) remains the 
support of everything. Though a seeker is advised to give 
up all the aforesaid three namely, kriya, chariya and the 
salambha yoga, often the seeker is reluctant to abandon what 
was achieved with such a prolonged and, difficult endeavour. 
The toil and trouble apart, he delights in it still. Having been 
a ripe and disciplined seeker, all his actions by way of kriya 
and chariya have yielded their fruits to him. He hesitates to 
renounce the form that has all along served him as support and 
fears whether he would find himself at sea if he gives it up.

Only a guru, ever abiding in the experience of the Ātman, 
can remove the salambha yoga of a disciple and make him 
niralambha (supportless). After parting ways with this yoga 
where should be abide? The Lord answers: “in That that 
is worldless”. He cannot abide in the worldless void if he 
himself is of gross form. Unless he also becomes the space 
of awareness, he cannot abide in that ‘worldless void’ – that 
space of awareness.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   70 06-05-2011   10:53:41



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 71

It is axiomatic that the two substances uniting with each 
other must be of the same kind. If a jīva with upādhi desires 
to commingle with the upādhi-less Absolute Content, he must 
jettison his upādhis and become upādhi-less. As long as fuel 
burns, smoke and fire will manifest. As long as the jīvabodha 
is there, the actions of kriya and chariya will go on. Just as with 
the exhaustion of fuel, the smoke and fire disappear, with the 
annihilation of jīvabodha all actions (kriya, chariya, etc.) will 
die a natural death. If these actions are given up the jīvabodha 
will be stilled : what moves as jīva becomes Siva when stilled. 
What Yoga Vasishtam says must be borne in mind. “The worship 
of God consisting of worship of idols and the like is declared for 
those who have intellects which are not perfected. On account 
of His being of the nature of perception situated within the reach 
of everybody, nothing whatever such as invocation or mantras 
is employed for Him. (1682 and 1683). “Abidance in pure 
Consciousness alone is the highest meditation. That alone is 
considered as the highest worship and without that meditation on 
Pure Awareness, the Self is not known at all by other expedients. 
Therefore the wise man worships that mere Consciousness 
beyond the deity consciousness.” (1693 and 1694).

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 73

He is a Śūnya-jñāni or a hero of valour who annuls this

the weapon of Śūnya-bhava. No ‘others’ exist for a jñāni with 
Śūnya bhava. As per the dictum “yad bhāvam, tad bhavati 
(As is the attitude or bhāva so it becomes), the perception 
depends on the bhāva.

This great weapon of the bhāva (attitude) of Śūnya is 
like the Brahmastram (the mighty missile) of “Who am I?”of 
Bhagavan. Hence it is called the Śūnyamam attiram, the 
‘missile of Śūnya’.

A Śūnya jñāni is one who abides in the heart without 
perception with just the awareness of existence “I am”.

In this verse the word Satti (sakti) lends itself to a 
different interpretation too, namely, energy. The sakti that 
invests all activity with creativity cannot be seen. This sakti 
principle is the highest of all principles. All betwixt pātāla 
the nethermost, and sakti celebrated as the highest principle 
are all interdependent on one an other. A hero of valour is 
one who with his stance of Śūnya renders them all naught. 
Bhagavan provides the logical reasoning to give up the desire 
to attain the various lokas, enamoured by the promises of 
celestial pleasures. “‘Lokyate, iti lokah’, what is perceived 
is the world.” (Talks no. 518) Whatever perceived, is, but a 
superimposition on Pure Awareness. He further clarifies it in 
Ramana Gītā (in Chap. 14, Verses 16, 17). To the question 
whether Kailasa, Vaikunta, Surya Mandala are true he replies: 
“like other planets, these worlds are also projected on beings 
by marvellous power of Sakti.” and again to a similar question 
by Rangan, Bhagavan shot back “All are the concoctions of 
Māyā” (Power of the Presence, Part I, page 27). Therefore 
all these worlds have only as much relevance and reality as 
the world we live in.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   73 06-05-2011   10:53:41

Commentary: 

A mind that revels in sense-objects never says ‘enough’. 
On the other hand as it experiences them, the desire acquires

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   74 06-05-2011   10:53:41



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 75

and intense musing over it, it becomes restless and agitated. 
Hence is the comparison to the monkey, proverbially restless.

As fire when fed with ghee leaps up in raging flames, the 
fire of desire, fed with the gratification of desires, swells up 
demanding more and more of it. Hence the Lord says “desire 
in sense-objects never leaves”. One does not grow by acquiring 
something or wither away by losing it. One remains always 
what one is. Starving the mind of sense objects and empirical 
matters is the only way to make a restless mind quieten down. 
As long as it is outward-bent, it keeps gathering vishaya-
matter. Not only should it be turned inward but be established 
also in the ‘all-void’ state.

Establishing it in the Śūnya state is like keeping a dot 
in the sky. When so established, with nothing to hold on, it 
gives up its restless and oscillating nature. The thought that 
the enjoyment of sense-objects is the ultimate goal of life 
gets removed. One becomes aware of the peace of the state 
of śūnya bereft of vishaya or objects.

Organs of perception and the inner organs becoming 
subdued and still then, with desire for sense objects dying, 
the mind merges in Śūnya, loses its form and gets dissolved.

Once a visitor said “one must become satiate with the 
fulfilment of desires before they are renounced”. Sri Bhagavan 
smiled and cut in “fire might as well be put out by pouring 
spirit over the flames. (All laugh). The more the desires are 
fullfilled, the deeper grows the saṁsāra. They must become 
weaker before they cease to assert themselves. That weakness 
is brought about by restraining oneself and not by losing 
oneself in desires.” (Talks no. 495)

Another devotee expressed a different doubt “The state 
of Realization is one of desirelessness. If a human being is 
desireless, he ceases to be human.” Bhagavan replied, “state of 
desirelessness in sleep made you no less happy than now. You 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   75 06-05-2011   10:53:41



76 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

did not feel any want. You did not make yourself miserable 
by not entertaining desires. But now you entertain desires 
because you are limited in human frame. Why do you wish 
to retain these limitations and continue to entertain desires?” 
(Talks no. 520).

In the state of Śūnya all these limitations along with mind 
get dissolved. Hence the joy and peace of that state (if the state 
of sleep is an indication) must be infinite.

Commentary: 

Tattva or principle is the innate nature or characteristic

ninety-six principles in creation. Śāstras say that creation, in 
its entirety, is comprised of ninety-six principles. That Content 
which is mingled non-differently in and as not other than, all

from the true import of ‘I’ which is other than the ‘I am the 
body’ sense, the true Content – Awareness of Being – shines. 
Excepting the dehātma bhava it is mingled in all principles and 
shines as sarvatho mukham-with countenance everywhere – all 
pervading. It inheres in everything and illumines everything.

This non-different perfect substance is what remains 
everywhere with Its non-being nowhere. When the natural 
and full state of God is constricted and looked upon as “I am 
the body”, the Lord becomes alien to us. The phrase aham 
aham enbatarku aniyamahi (other than the sense of ‘I am the 
body’) explains this.

If this attitude of fragmenting is annihilated, what remains 
is the all-pervading Reality.

People with dehātmabhava are those who, instead of 
becoming food for the Lord, try to make the Lord subservient 
to them.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   79 06-05-2011   10:53:41



80 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

The Lord exclaims, “Look! What a wonderful thing is 
this! The action of that vastu strikes wonder indeed!”

Like a single lamp lighting up thousands of other lamps 
without its radiance getting dimmed in the least and like a 
guru, transforming meet and ripe disciples into illumined 
souls of his own stature of Selfhood, the Ātman transforms 
one who immerses himself in that form of Bliss, into its own 
form of all-pervading Bliss – Awareness.
This Supramundane experience is beautifully described by Sri 
Sankara in verses 481 and 482 of Vivekachūḍāmaṇi: “Having 
realized the oneness of Brahman and Ātman the modifications 
of the intellect have completely ceased and their interaction 
with the objects has melted away. I neither know ‘this’ nor the 
‘not-this’. What is this Bliss par-excellence? Where is the limit 
of this Bliss? I do not know” and further “like the hailstone 
dropping into the ocean and disappearing into the ocean by 
melting into it, even so the mind has merged in an infinitesimally 
small droplet of that infinite Bliss and I am now immersed 
in that Bliss without the least trace of the modification of the 
mind. The supreme glory and magnificence of Brahman filled 
with the torrents of the immortal nectar, cannot be described 
in words, nor even thought of by the mind.” As a tiny proof 
of this, Annamalai Swami’s reminiscences can be recollected 
here. When, one day, he was helping Bhagavan have his bath 
he questioned him about the Ānanda experienced by people 
who take herbs like ganja (hashish) to induce a state of Bliss. 
Bhagavan immediately enacted saying: “‘Oh ganja! The users 
feel immensely happy when they are under its influence. How 
shall I describe their happiness! They simply shout ānanda! 
ānanda. . .’ Saying so, He walked as if tipsy. The bhaktas 
laughed. He appeared as if He stumbled, placed His hands 
round Anamalai Swamy and cried ‘ānanda! ānanda!’” and 
he touched Annamalai Swamy. (Talks no. 560)

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   81 06-05-2011   10:53:41



82 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

fire starved of fuel, with flames abating, gradually gets 
extinguished.
Commentary:

When the flames of fire from a hearth blaze forth 
exuberantly, feeding it with more fuel will not make it subside 
or die down. When starved of fuel, the fire quietens of its own 
accord and comes to rest. If the mind is to gain peace and 
tranquillity, it should be deprived of objects of attachment it 
has clung to so far. The more the gratification of the senses, 
by way of enjoyment of sense objects, the more entrenched 
the vāsanās become and the mind, by repeatedly musing over 
them and caught in the fire of desire struggles and suffers.

“Knowledge is enveloped, O Arjuna, by this insatiable fire 
of desire which is the constant foe of the wise.” (Bhagavad 
Gītā, Chap. III, Verse 39)

“Only for those who have snapped asunder
 The bonds of desire does the fake
 Phenomenal world cease to appear.
 Snap, then, without a thought desire
 Even for a beatified bliss
 Of radiant Silence.”

 (Guru Vāchaka Kovai, Verse 378)
When all the three, namely, body, speech and mind are 

deprived of possible holds of attachment, the mind that has 
ramified into various modes of thoughts by running after 
objects, gradually contracts and shrinks getting erased by 
degrees and finally dissolves. There is no other path, higher 
or better than this to destroy the mind and achieve peace. 
Starving the mind out of thoughts makes the mind cease from 
being affected by worldly objects and forming attachments.

Bhagavan’s instruction to control desires is recorded by 
Mudaliar, as follows: “If a desire can be got rid of by satisfying 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   82 06-05-2011   10:53:41



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 83

it, there will be no harm in satisfying such a desire. But desires 
generally are not eradicated by satisfaction. Trying to root 
them out that way is like pouring spirits to quench fire. At the 
same time, the proper remedy is not forcible suppression, since 
such repression is bound to react sooner or later into forceful 
surging up with undesirable consequences. The proper way to 
get rid of a desire is to find out, ‘Who gets the desire? What 
is its source?’ When that is found, the desire is rooted out and 
will never again emerge.” (Day by Day, 12-4-46)

Mundaka Upanishad also corroborates this as the content 
of the following verse: “As fire deprived of fuel is extinguished 
in its own hearth so when the mental vrittis are decimated 
(vāsanā kshaya) chitta is extinguished in its own seat.” (VI. 
34). A piece of advice that Bhagavan proffers to Annamalai 
Swamy was: “Fire, debt, sense-objects and poison. Even a 
drop of any these is capable of destroying us.” (Power of the 
Presence, Part III, page 203)

The story of the king Yayāthi which occurs in Mahabharata 
is an illustration of this. He gave himself up so much to the 
enjoyment of sense-pleasures that finally he became a slave to 
his desires. When he lost his youth (by a curse) still impelled 
by the desires for the pleasures of the senses he (due to a divine 
boon) exchanged his old age with the youth of his youngest 
son, young in years but advanced in virtue, while the other 
sons refused to comply with his request. With the youth thus 
borrowed he spent a dissipated life. But what he witnessed in 
the forest once served as an eye-opener to him. He was already 
regretting his excessive indulgences in sensuous pleasures and 
his consequent steep fall spiritually.

In the forest he saw a homakunda where homa had just been 
completed by the sages or rishis dwelling in the forest. The fire 
was raging with flames leaping high earlier. Even as he was 
watching he realised that just as the leaping flames rose erect and 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   83 06-05-2011   10:53:41



84 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

unquenched, his desires when gratified, only waxed strong. As 
the homa had just been finished it was no longer fed with ghee, 
the flames ebbed down gradually, burning the remaining fuel 
and with nothing to feed on, got extinguished on their own. It 
then dawned on Yayāthi that even as his desires were gratified, 
fresh ones sprang up stronger clamouring for gratification and 
not feeding them with the objects of senses would eventually put 
them out even as the fire starved of fuel got put out and attained 
shanti. Finally he exchanged his youth for old age and spent the 
rest of his life as a vanaprasta in a forest.

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 85

Paraphrase: 
Therefore the various states (experiences) that 

overtake and engulf us like infatuation on perceiving an 
object of desire, and the consequent delusion, swooning 
caused by shock and dreaming, along with sleep 
enveloped in darkness and wakeful state and others that 
are spoken of, all must be relinquished. Know this.
Commentary: 

Infatuation, delusion and swoon are various states of the 
same avastha or experience. When an uncontrollable desire 
for an object is entertained, made intense by constant thinking 
of it, the mind totally enticed away by that object, loses its 
balance and struggles to gain poise. This is called infatuation.

The excessive longing for the object that is unattainable 
leads to the stunning of the mind. Consequent to non-
attainability of an object the pangs of separation lead to shock 
and loss of consciousness. Unexpected happenings heard or 
seen also lead to shock and swooning.

Along with these, the three states of dream, sleep and 
wakefulness which envelop the jīva and among which the jīva 
keeps alternating, should all be relinqiushed. None of these is 
desirable for they are all the retinue of the primary nescience 
and are candidates fit to be destroyed leaving no residue 
behind. “Accomplishment of this will yield you inestimable 
gain”, says the Lord.

Infatuation, delusion and swooning pertain to the state of 
wakefulness, which, along with dream and sleep, are states 
of and the characteristic of the mind. Though they and the 
pairs of opposites we suffer from in jāgrat and dream appear 
to be of the Self, in reality they are not. They are also a mere 
dream. If they were the qualities of the Self, they would 
appear in sushupti as well. In sushupti, the world and body 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   85 06-05-2011   10:53:41



86 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

are not, and hence, there is unawareness of anything. “The 
unawareness is owing to the absence of relative knowledge 
and the happiness to the absence of (seething) thoughts.” 
(Talks no. 617). But ‘Being" continues uninterrupted through 
all these three stages and beyond. The Self is the basis of 
all the experiences. It remains as the witness and support of 
them all. Reality is different from these states. The Self is the 
knower of the three avastas. Though the various states come 
and go the “Awareness” of the knower is ever constant and 
imperishable. The three states are mere phenomena appearing 
on the Self which is itself stationary and also a state of simple 
awareness. None can remain away from the Self at any 
moment. Therefore the one who knows the Sūtra – the silver 
thread of Consciousness that runs through everything – gains 
release.

“There is a fixed state. Sleep, dream and waking states 
are mere movements in It. They are like pictures moving 
on the screen in a cinema show with the difference that the 
realised being does not see the world as being apart from the 
Self.” (Talks no. 607). “The Self is the fourth state, the other 
three go on changing... All the three are ideas of the mind.” 
(Talks no. 487).

That one must wake up from the dream of all these three 
states to reality is the import of this verse.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   87 06-05-2011   10:53:41



88 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

as a resident in this gross body – a strange and wonderful 
manifestation among all those created.

It is extremely difficult to make this tenant vacate. Harder 
is the task of driving out his companions. This tenant still poses 
himself as the lord of the house he has subtly and stealthily 
occupied and reigns over with liberty to boot.

The seat of these four is the office of the chief-secretariat 
of their reign. Their decisions are the commands issued to 
the organs and senses. The only way to evict the dictatorial 
impostor who rules with such flamboyance is to totally ignore 
him when he will simply take to his heels and disappear as 
subtly as he came.

But the Lord, the Master of all is hidden behind all this 
cloak of māyā – a power of the Lord. This māyā is the lila 
of the Lord which in the words of Lord Krishna “is difficult 
to cross”.

He is hidden behind all the objects, concepts and precepts 
and also the subject.

He is veiled as it were by the objectivity of the objects 
and the subjectivity of the subject. One cannot but admire 
how unfathomable and indescribable is the nature of māyā 
that every man, though he is identical with the Supreme Entity 
in reality, and despite being repeatedly so instructed by the 
scriptures and the guru, not grasping the fact but accepts as his 
Self the non-selves like the aggregate of the body and senses 
with the idea of ‘I am so and so’.

One should meditate that one is residing in the body and 
is therefore different from the bodies three and should free 
oneself from the actions done by the body and mind which 
do not pertain to the real ‘I’, the Ātman, who always is apart 
from and is witness of all the three states. Therefore the Ātman 
is to be meditated on as different from the body, organs and 
vital force along with their activities.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   88 06-05-2011   10:53:42



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 89

He is also to be meditated on as internal to everything 
in the sense that He is subtler than the subtlest, pervading 
as a thread pervades the cloth, and therefore beyond senses 
and mind. In the final dissolution of the mind, with the three 
bodies and the world dead, the Ātman alone, Eternal, remains.

No mortal ever lives by prana or the organs, but all live by 
That on which all these depend for their existence – the Ātman; 
even as pranan, indriyas, mind and buddhi cannot awaken a 
sleeping man on their own except for the presence body-mind of 
the indweller, the real I, this kshetrajna who must be separated 
from the body-mind through enquiry by combine an inward-
turned mind must be known as the true Content of ‘I’.

No wonder Āchārya Sankara declares: “I shall declare in 
half a verse that which is stated in tens of millions of scriptures. 
And that is: Brahman alone is the Truth. All the Universe is 
mithya, an appearance superimposed on the Reality which is 
Brahman. And the individual jīva is verily Brahman alone and 
not anything other to Him.”

The silent sermon of the Lord within goes unheard and 
unfelt due to the furore caused by this crowd. So long as 
the mind under the cover of avidya works relentlessly in 
combination with the senses and prana, so long does the world 
and the individuality of jīva continue. The mind emptied of all 
its contents must be made to abide in Ātman that is worldless 
by contemplating that mahaśūnya, the form of pure awareness. 
Thus jīva becomes the form of that chit.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   90 06-05-2011   10:53:42



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 91

indulge in thoughts.
Half of the life span, which is but a fair for two days, is 

spent in sleep while the rest is spent in constantly thinking 
of something or other and running after them. The chase 
becomes endless and does not end with the attainment of the 
object of desire, but higher aspirations follow, that demand 
the expending of energy and effort only to end in heaving and 
hawing leaving with longing in case of non attainment.

Mind is verily like a bag of mustard seeds. As the seeds 
fall out of the bag and scatter all over making it impossible 
to gather them, thoughts from a distracted mind run in all 
directions led by the senses and gathering the mind becomes 
difficult. Due to this constant and shifting thought processes 
the mind loses its moorings becomes reckless and acts 
indiscriminately. Gradually educating the mind on the 
excellence of remaining in one’s natural state and instructing 
on the futility of running after worldly objects make efforts to 
anchor it in the Self, is the instruction provided here.

Endeavouring this just once will not do. Constant vigil 
and perseverance are required to accomplish it.

Sleep is a state granted by the Lord to the jīva. None can 
go beyond it. Even if sleep is not desired, it will not let one 
go out of its grip. It automatically envelops one in spite of 
the resistance.

The state of man is such that either he sleeps or thinks on 
scattered topics, or indulges in reveries. Hence the mind loses 
all its grandeur and comes to ruin. When the mind is not turned 
inward on its own accord, it should be made to turn within 
and abide in the Self by constant perseverance and matured 
practice. Till then endeavour has to be sustained. Here as Lord 
Krishna exhorts in Gītā in the pursuit of sādhanā “vairagya 
and abhyasa (dispassion and practice) are the sine-qua-non. 
”. “The three bhavanas (samsaya bhavana, asam bhavana 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   91 06-05-2011   10:53:42



92 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

and vipareētha bhavana) – sleep, tossing of the mind, mind 
turning towards objects, depression, building castles in the 
air, diseases, etc. are the chief obstacles in the attainment of 
Self-Realization.” (Sivajnamrita Upanishad, Verse 14). While 
samsaya bhavana relates to doubts in scriptural verities, 
asam bhavana is doubt in the non-duality of the Supreme, 
and vipareētha bhavana is the perverted conception of Self 
as the body. All these can be overcome only by the enquiry of 
the Self or ‘Who am I?’. Similarly eradication of vrittis that 
manifest during dreaming and deep-sleep states will help one 
in attaining the Bliss of the Self. 

The content of this verse echoes the content of some 
verses in the celebrated Mandukya Upanishad (3-42, 44, 46) 
“With the help of that proper process one should bring under 
discipline the mind that remains dispersed amidst objects of 
desire and enjoyment and one should control the mind even 
when it is in full sleep, for sleep is as bad as desire. One should 
wake up the mind, merged in deep sleep; one should bring 
the dispersed mind into tranquillity again; one should know 
when the mind is tinged with desire; one should not disturb 
the mind established in equipoise. When the mind does not 
become lost nor is scattered, when it is motionless and does 
not appear in the form of objects, then it becomes Brahman,”

On speaking of obstacles to Self-Realization Bhagavan 
said: “Some say there are nine, sleep is one of them.”

“As the mind tends to go out, turn it inwards then and 
there. It goes out owing to the habit of looking for happiness 
outside oneself; but the knowledge that the external objects 
are not the cause of happiness will keep it in check. This is 
vairagya or dispassion. Only after perfect vairagya the mind 
becomes steady.

“The mind is only a mixture of knowledge and ignorance 
or of sleep and waking. It functions in five ways:

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   92 06-05-2011   10:53:42



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 93

a) Kshipta (active)
b) Moodha (dull)
c) Viskshipta (distracted)
d) Kashaya (latent)
e) Ekagrya (one-pointed)
Kashaya is only the latency of tendencies and not the 

tendencies themselves such as attachment, repulsion, etc. ” 
(Talks no. 344)

“Destroy the power of mind by seeking it.” (Talks no. 345)
Bhagavan said to another devotee that there are five states:
“1. sleep
  2. before waking, a state free from thoughts
 3. sense of happiness of that freedom from thoughts 

(rasasvada)
4. the internal movement of the vāsanās (kashaya)
5. complete waking with (distraction) vikshepa. The 

second of those should be made permanent.” (Talks no. 623).

if it ever attains steadiness, should not be disturbed on any

as to how the mind, till now wandering in a scattered way, 
has come so swiftly and suddenly to be still, it should not be

of mind, the mind out of a sense of shame, may rise up to 
consider its assumed status all along or it may try to come 
out, out of gratitude for a sadguru who taught the method 
of enquiry. But not allowing it to get disturbed, it should be 
left to reside firmly in that state, is the instruction. The mind 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   94 06-05-2011   10:53:42



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 95

dislodged and isolated from its source becomes the seat of 
thoughts. If it is bound as to abide in the Self, its source, it 
becomes quiet and still.

A mind that has ceased to function becomes a temple of 
Awareness-Bliss. Unless it experiences the bliss it will not 
subside. But Bliss is unattainable unless the mind becomes 
still. But the ultimate goal of human birth is to keep it bound 
and still somehow. None can confront and overcome the innate 
nature of its movement.

The way to conquer and still the mind is to ignore it 
by rejecting it as unreal, false and as a mere appearance. If 
the Self, the real ground for the mind, is sought and abided 
in firmly, the mind, with none to pay attention to it, will be 
gradually ground out of existence.

The natural state is one where the stilled and steady mind 
is left undisturbed.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   96 06-05-2011   10:53:42



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 97

Like the movement of the reflected image of the moon 
seen in water in motion, thoughts flowing in all directions 
make the mind restless. Removing the perception of the image 
in moving water and directing it on the support of the reflected 
image of the moon – the moon in the sky- it will be found to 
remain still. In a similar way, if the mind, letting go of the 
attachments to objects, attaches itself to its Truth, it becomes 
still and steady. This is the sādhanā that a sincere seeker has 
to engage himself in. “When the mind, with its attachment 
to vishaya annihilated is fully controlled within the heart 
and thus realises its own essence, then that supreme state is 
gained. The mind should be controlled to that extent in which 
it gets merged in the heart. That is jñāna (realization) and 
this is dhyāna also, all else is argumentation and verbiage.” 
Amritabindu Upanishad, Verses 4 and 5). A spiritual classic 
called Vichāra Chandrodhyam enumerates several ways 
whereby the mind can be made to lean on that supportless 
Form and become that Form itself. When thoughts flit from 
one object to another, know the gap between the two to be 
chidākāśam. That is the state of Svarūpa Stiti of Real Form 
where the mind is thoughtless. The state completely devoid of 
all saṁkalpas is one which is Svarūpa Stiti. The state where 
the mind with all instruments have become completely stilled, 
rocklike, is another.

The state released from jāgrat, swapna and sushupti is 
the state of svarūpa stiti. The place where the ego-sense has 
become extinct, consequent on the mind being stilled and made 
extinct that which shines as sentient then that is the real state.

The aspect of ‘being’ of all objects is not other than jñāna 
(as mentioned in verse 13 of Devi Kālōttaram).

In the triputi of perceiver, perception and perceived, that 
body of awareness, which is between the subject and object 
but which is without subject and object, that is svarūpa stiti.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   97 06-05-2011   10:53:42



98 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

In the interrugnum of the mental journey from one place to 
another, the mind sentient but without thoughts is in Svarūpa 
stiti.

The nature of you when the mind is put away very far 
from you, be of that form.

Between one and the world, that is between what is 
perceived and the perceiver the perception (or darsana) that 
is the form of Ātman, the Self, abide in that.

Bhagavan himself used to give three instances where 
the Svarūpa Stiti prevails namely the interval between two 
thoughts, the interval between sleep and wakeful state and the 
state when one is looking at an object far away, exemplified 
by the familiar sight of Bhagavan looking steadfast, at the 
Hill, his own Self.

Paraphrase: 

At the time of dissolution, when all the other elements 
of creation get dissolved, the ether that had pervaded 
all these elements remains pure and unsullied by them. 
Likewise the Self, though pervading countless forms in

Commentary: 
At the time of deluge or dissolution when the four 

elements are dissolved, none of the qualities of the other four 
elements, sully ether though it is admixed with all four of them. 
Ether being extremely subtle remains free of any blemish. 
None of the flaws of the other four elements will taint ether.

Ether also pervades the inside and outside of all objects 
yet none of the qualities of the objects it pervades attaches 
itself to ether. Likewise the Content Beyond pervades all the 
forms of the universe, yet none of the upādhis can taint that 
Content which shines beyond compare. That Content, the 
silver thread of Awareness like the single string on which many 
pearls are threaded, runs through everything with name and 
form, yet remains Immaculate without being sullied by any.

The auspicious and unauspicious actions of the world 
will not touch the Sun. Just as the earth cannot muddy ether 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   99 06-05-2011   10:53:42



100 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

nor water can drench it nor fire can burn it nor air can dry 
ether, all the flaws of actions done by beings on earth cannot 
touch the Content Beyond that pervades all the forms. An 
illustration oft quoted by Sri Ramakrishna Paramahamsa is 
that of a man reading the holy Bhagavatha with the help of 
a lamp while another forges a signature under the self same 
light and the light is not affected by either of the two actions. 
In line is Sankara’s celebrated illustration, which refers to the 
Sun’s rays, falling either on the waters of holy Ganges or on 
that of the gutters do not sully the sun, the least . In the same 
way the shadow of a man may fall either on holy waters or 
on despicable stuff, but the man himself does not become by 
that very fact holy or defiled.

The Ātman is reflected in the medium of attributes, like 
the sun reflected in water and fire appearing in the fuel. 
But this reflection is seen only in identification with the 
medium, namely, the body in which it reflects. He is not 
apprehended in His distinctiveness by ordinary people. But 
wise men, by churning their whole being with the churning 
rod of discrimination discover the Ātman residing within 
themselves. “The ether in the jar is not in any way affected 
by the smell of garlic merely through its connection with the 
jar. Even so the pure Ātman is not, through its connection 
with the limiting adjuncts, affected by the properties thereof.” 
(Vedāntasāra Upanishad, Verse 10).

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   101 06-05-2011   10:53:42



102 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

a true scholar. On the other hand, he, who has learnt to keep

The way to this is to make it abide in its place of origin. 
The mind that constantly oscillates between thoughts is the 
seed of the misery of transmigration. Just as wind stilled 
becomes ether and ether moving becomes wind, mind in 
motion is saṁsāra and a moveless mind attains mukti.

True scholarship consists in realising, the futility of 
knowledge and in knowing the Truth that the knowledge of 
all arts is but ignorance, but enquiring and knowing who the 
knower of arts is, in truth, real knowledge.

Therefore by all means – even if it means adopting 
supreme endeavour – one should make the restless mind still. 
That indeed is the fulfilment of the purpose of human birth, 
so rare to obtain, for a moveless mind is verily Siva and a 
moving mind is a jīva. The raison d’etre of a human life is 
the attainment of this Ātman. “If here (in this life) one is able 
to comprehend Him (Brahman) before the death of the body, 
he will be liberated from the bondage of the world; if one 
is not able to comprehend Him, then he has to take a body 
again in the worlds of creations.” (Kathopanishad, 4-4). This 
wealth possessed by the possessionless is the greatest wealth 
that can never be plundered. One who does not enjoy the Self 
is called a krupana (miser). “Therefore which wise man will 
indulge in the unreal abandoning the experience of Supreme 
bliss? When the moon is shining giving infinite delight, who 
will desire to look at the painted moon?”(Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, 
Verse 523).

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   103 06-05-2011   10:53:42



104 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Commentary: 
One way to make the mind single-pointed is to fix it in 

any of the six chakras and meditate upon it. Bhagavan says, 
“A few advise seeking realization in the head (sahasrara); a 
few between the eyebrows; a few in the heart; others in the 
solar plexus. If realization amounts to gaining the paranāḍī, 
one might enter it from the Heart. But the yogī is engaged in 
cleansing the nāḍīs; then kundalini is awakened which is said 
to rise up from the coccyx to the head. The yogī is later advised 
to come down to the heart as the final step.” “The space, the 
magnitudes and the paradox are all in the mind only. How 
do they exist there? Inasmuch as you become aware of them, 
you must admit a light which illumines them.” (Talks no. 474)

The reason the seeker is advised to avoid it is that any 
support held onto by the mind, makes it move away from its 
real ground and does not further the cause of anchoring the 
mind in its Origin. Releasing it later from the grip of that 
support to make it niralambha (supportless) calls for more 
of an endeavour than was required to develop it. The real 
dharana (fixing or holding) is to annul the mind.

In truth dharana is also a bhavana – an attitude – and any 
bhavana is kanda or fragmenting the Absolute. If the mind 
has to transcend bhavanas to reach the state of bhavanatita, 
the only sādhanā is to remove all bhavanas. “It is all meant 
to help the bhavana (imagery). There are books dealing with 
six centres (shadchakra) and many other lakshyas (centres) 
internal and external. The description of the Heart is one 
among so many lakshyas. But it is not necessary. It is only 
the source of ‘I’ thought. That is the ultimate truth.” (Talks 
no. 392)

The various forms and mantras held on to within must be 
given up along with the possible potential supports that it can 
attach itself to. Endeavour of a high order is required for this. 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   104 06-05-2011   10:53:42



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 105

The mind devoid of support, either external or internal, 
will, of its own accord, giving up its restlessness, become 
tranquil and still.

If support ‘within’ is taken away, the mind will roam about 
trying for a support ‘without’. This is its very nature. When it 
is deprived of both the possible holds of support, seeking and 
securing rest from its restless roaming, it becomes quiescent.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   105 06-05-2011   10:53:42



106 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Paraphrase: 
While meditating, if sleep (the state of dullness 

devoid of awareness) overtakes you, awaken the mind 
and keep it that way. While awake, if the mind wanders 
moved by thought waves, curb and make it still. If the 
state devoid of both sleep and movement is attained (the 
state with only the awareness of being as “am”) abide 
still in it with no movement.
Commentary: 

The mind when deprived of the internal supports by 
way of bhavanas entertained within and also restrained from 
holding on to vishaya (objects) of external world as supports, 
thus starved of holds within and without, is stupefied and 
plunges into sleep.

The mind cannot remain without a support either 
from within or without. When thus isolated, cut off from 
all attachments, its only refuge is slumber. Sleep unsought 
envelops and engulfs one within it. Urakkatinindrum 
unarttiduha – one should awaken oneself from such sleep.

Awakened from sleep, the mind must be completely 
deterred from running after thoughts and thoughts must be 
wiped out in their entirety. The continual struggle of averting 
sleep on the one hand and preventing indulgence in thought 
while awake on the other, is the sādhanā needed here. The 
state devoid of both sleep and thoughts will be attained and 
that is the real state. “Even a single effort to still at least a 
single thought, even for a trice goes a long way to reach the 
state of quiescence. Effort is required and it is possible in the 
waking state only.” (Talks no. 609)

One should remain as peaceful and quiescent as in deep 
sleep with no contact (mental) of sense objects: yet at the same 
time one should be awake “alone”.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   106 06-05-2011   10:53:42



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 107

The thoughts in the waking state form the obstacle to 
gaining the stillness of sleep. In this practice there is effort 
here; there is awareness also; the thoughts are stilled; so there 
is peace of sleep gained. There is awareness of the waking 
state and the stillenss of sleep. It is called jāgrat-sushupti.

But why is the stillness of sleep preferred? The happiness 
of sleep is due the absence of the seething thoughts. In sleep 
the consciousness of the body-mind and all the elements of 
transient personality have dissolved into nothingness. There 
the Ātman (the single thread of awareness that continues) 
remains through all states sleepless but without the “I” sense 
and individuality. The peace and happiness enjoyed at the 
time of experience is only recollected. A diver can make his 
discovery public only after he comes out of water. In the same 
way a sleeper cannot express the joy because he cannot contact 
the organs of expressions until he is awakened by vāsanās. 
The experience of bliss of Brahman in sleep is said to be the 
negative aspect of such bliss as it is the result of absence of 
thoughts. It is transitory and the counterfeit of “Supreme Bliss”.

But the ‘I’ that is stripped of its personality, the ‘I’ of 
sushupti that is, the thoughtless state of the mind must be felt 
and experienced while awake. But some fear that the Self 
then is dissolved, thinking that a man robbed of his jewels is 
destroyed. The light of supreme consciousness in the ‘I-sense’ 
is to be traced which, being a ray of the Self-luminous Truth, 
leads to the source of union with the Truth. If one is free from 
thoughts and yet aware, one is that Perfect Being. 

Bhagavan often indicates the Self (or the pure ‘I’) of the 
transitional stage between sleep and waking must be held for 
realization. “If the transitional I be realised the substratum 
is found and that leads to the goal.” (Talks no. 314). Tripura 
Rahasya and other works point out that the internal between 
two consecutive saṁkalpas represents the pure aham (‘I’).

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   107 06-05-2011   10:53:42



108 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Therefore by giving room for sleep one looses oneself 
in the darkness of sleep, when enquiry is impossible. If the 
mind moves, convergence of the energies of mind is difficult 
to achieve. The mind, though void of vishaya, struggles to 
remain isolated from both these for want of ripeness.

Without resorting to either, we are exhorted to remain 
in samādhi. “Samādhi means sleep in waking state (Jāgrat 
sushupti). Bliss is overpowering and the experience is very 
clear, whereas it is different in sleep.” (Talks no. 372).

If one remains at peace oneself, there is only peace all 
about.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   108 06-05-2011   10:53:42



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 109

Paraphrase: 
That state of the mind (if it were to exhibit a tendency 

to fly outward) when, with nothing to cling to as supports 
that are binding, remaining faultless and pure with 
supports removed and devoid of desires and attachments 
called the nature of mind, is indeed the hallmark of 
Release gained through jñāna. Bear this firmly in mind.
Commentary: 

Mind, when forsaking its base, rushes outward, cannot 
stand on its own legs without an ashraya, a support to lean on 
and attach itself to It clings to one object till it becomes weary 
of it and then jumps to another and so on till it is caught up 
in endless whirlpools of thought waves with no respite. That 
the mind is nothing but a bundle of thoughts is proved here.

Purity of mind is achieved when the supports (as vishaya) 
it leans on are all severed. All the impurities and blemishes of 
the mind are the concomitant outcome of these attachments. 
Once it beccomes devoid of supports and therefore pure, none 
of the attachments and desires can touch it, much less, defile it.

Such a state of mind without anything to hold on to – pure 
and flawless- where no fresh attachments can bind – is the very 
nature and characteristic of jneya mukti, mukti born of wisdom.

Of all the states of mind the most terrible is the one 
afflicted with attachments and desires. Releasing it from the 
clutches of these is a very difficult sādhanā, but achievable 
none the less.

The profound wisdom born of experience as expressed 
in Bhāgavatam goes thus:

“āśā hi paramaṁ duḥkhaṁ 
nairāśyaṁ paramaṁ sukham”
Desire is the source of the most poignant of sorrows and 

desirelessness, of the most intense delight.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   109 06-05-2011   10:53:42



110 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

The hallmark of release or jneya mukti described in the 
śloka is the content of an Upanishadic verse as well. “The 
sages declare that Brahman is That, one with the Content 
of Supreme Bliss devoid of all vrittis, One with nirvana 
(Release); indescribable, devoid of origin, united to the 
originless Content of Awareness (the jneya vastu) and knowing 
All.” (Mandukya Karikai, III-47). The jīva minus jīvabhava 
is verily That.

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 111

Paraphrase: 
On renouncing completely all objects of attachment

Commentary: 

To remain firmly poised in the heart is feasible only for a 
mind bereft of all its attachments. Otherwise only a perpetual 
struggle between the mind merging in the heart and the 
vāsanās expelling it out recurs.

The strength to inhere firmly in the heart is aquired only 
when vāsanā kshaya or dissipation of vāsanās is achieved for 
it is the crowd of vāsanās that propel the mind out compelling 
it to function in various ways. Once the mind is stationed 
securely in the Heart, Perfect Awareness flashes in all its 
effulgence. One should learn to stay poised thus without letting 
the form of Pure Awareness slip away but make the abidance 
firm and strong.

The constant inhering in that state of perfect Knowledge 
will dissolve the mind in it to make it one of its own form. A 
mind dissolved will no longer be touched by any attachment, 
like a burnt rope. Like the light of the gem, cut, polished and 
freed of its flaws, the mind becomes blemishless and the light 
of grace of the Lord will shine in all its luminosity in it. A 
mind lit up by the light of the Supreme transcends all worldly 
bonds. A mind devoid of bondage gains the bliss of release.

The Lord exhorts here that until this True Awareness is 
strengthened constant practice is a must. Mind is the cause 
for both bondage and liberation.

“There is bondage when the mind is attached to any 
person, object, place or condition whatsoever. There is release

112 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

when the mind is unattached to any person, object, place or 
condition whatsoever. Attachment is death. Non-attachment 
is eternal life.” (Swaroopabodha Upanishad, Verse 9).

Commentary: 

What is called Śūnya or Void is the True Content of 
Transcendence. Why is that Supreme Content, that Existence-

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   112 06-05-2011   10:53:43



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 113

Knowledge-Bliss called Śūnya? There, nothing but the mere 
Awareness of ‘Being’ as ‘I am’ shining in self-revealing 
knowledge, utter remains to the exclusion of everything else. 
Hence It is called Śūnya; but It is not insentient. This is what 
is called Bhuma in the Upanishads. “Bhuma is that in which 
one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, understands nothing 
else. That which is Bhuma alone is immortal. But that in which 
one sees something else, hears something else, understands 
something else is the finite which is mortal.” Further it is said 
that the greatness of Bhuma is that, “That alone is below and 
above, behind and in front; in north and south and is all this. 
This Bhuma is the ‘I’ in all, the Ātman”, is the instruction of 
Sanatkumara to Narada in Chandogya Upanishad.

The entire cosmos including everything – stationary and 
moving – appears and disappears on this void by the saṁkalpa 
or resolution of māyā. Brahman, the cause of all forms that 
appear is called nirakara (formless). Brahman, the form of 
light that illumines the whole world, is called Śūnya.

Contemplation of this Śūnya dissolves gradually the 
vāsanās of the contemplator till they melt away to become void 
when the meditator also comes to abide as the form of Śūnya. 
Constant poise in that state of void ultimately destroys the 
seeds of vāsanās. Along with the seeds of actions – the cause 
and nucleus of the dyad – birth and death – are also dissolved 
forever. The meditator and the meditated upon become one, 
the form of Śūnya. It is the subject and object at once, even 
as the room space and atmospheric space are one when the 
walls of the room no longer exist. What remains is infinite 
Bliss, eternal Release. “That such a one will unfailingly attain 
that state” means he will remain thereafter as the very form 
of Bliss of Release.

“The state in which no ‘other’ is, no ‘other’ heard, 
no ‘other’ seen, know that this and this alone is cosmic 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   113 06-05-2011   10:53:43



114 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

consciousness.” ( This is a rendering by Muruganar of a verse 
in Chandogya Upanishad).

While referring to this state once Bhagavan after quoting 
this verse from Chandhogya Upanishad (7. 24. 1) said while 
“all upasanas are ways to winning it one must not get stuck in 
the upasanas, but must query ‘Who am I?’ and find the Self.” 
(Talks no. 634) and on another occasion “Bhuma alone is. It is 
Infinite. There arises from it, this finite consciousness taking 
on an upādhi (limiting adjunct). This is abhasa or reflection. 
Merge this individual Consciousness into the Supreme one. 
That is what should be done.” (Talks no. 68)

“What is not obtained from oneself endowed with 
repeated practice and absence of worldly desires, by whom 
the serpent in the form of organs of sense has been overcome, 
that is not obtained from the triple world.” (Yoga Vasishtam, 
Verse 1664). What such a one with repeated practice of 
contemplation of Śūnya attains “is the ultimate abode. That 
is the tranquil state. That is the Eternal and Blessed Felicity. 
Delusion does not again disturb one who has obtained repose 
there.” (1593).

Worship of Gods and Goddesses to gain mukti and

Commentary: 

Indulgence in actions, experiencing the fruits of actions 
and entertaining thoughts related to objects of experience – all 
of which being other than the Self, the non-Self – cause the 
mighty bondage of saṁsāra.

Merit is gained by the worship of deities and demerit 
accrues by harming lives. While merits are the cause of 
happiness, demerits bring in misery. In the process of 
experiencing the fruits of actions that are contrary to each 
other in nature, desired objects of the external world and the 
knowledge of them and of other vishaya (objects and matters) 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   115 06-05-2011   10:53:43



116 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

are acquired. All these, including thoughts on them, are the 
bondage of saṁsāra, that deludes every one.

When fruits of actions experienced are not in tune with 
the desires of the experiencer, dislike and disappointment are 
engendered which induce him to indulge in vicious actions. 
Consequently pain follows and assails him whether he likes 
it or not.

Actions thus bind the jīva in many ways and the Lord 
calls it the “mighty bondage of saṁsāra”.

The only way out of this interminable cycle is to catch 
hold of and annihilate the karmi, the doer of karma – that 
manifests as the actions-fruits-actions ad infinitum.

Saṁsāra is not something separate or apart from us. All 
the aforesaid shackles together form the bondage. When the 
bonds increase, the bondage becomes mighty. Saṁsāra is a 
delusion. Deva and Devi refer to idols of worship. 

“Liberation is obtained not by places of pilgrimage, nor 
by charity, nor by religious ablution, nor by learning, nor by 
meditation, nor by yoga, nor by religious austerities, nor by 
sacrifices.” (Yoga Vasishtam, Verse 1649). Further Bhagavan 
says wanting God as a bright being mounted on a bull is a 
vision with origin and must also end; hence transient. The 
Thevaram which sings “Our Light is ever shining forth from 
within! With mind clear, live in God!” speaks of the Eternal 
and Ever-experienced Being, taking us directly to the Reality. 
(Talks no. 512).

“In the matter of crossing over worldly existence (or 
attaining liberation) dwelling in forests is not the means; nor 
even residence in one’s own place; nor painful performance of 
religions austerities; nor the renunciation of religious rites; nor 
taking refuge in such rites; nor eulogies of the various fruits of 
actions in religious practices, oh Rama; therefore I say: there 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   116 06-05-2011   10:53:43



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 117

is no means other than knowledge for the mind having the 
bondage (of the world) like fetters, in crossing over worldly 
existence.” (Yoga Vasishtam, 1647, 48, 52)

Once when a pandit was referring to several bondages to 
realization, Bhagavan sat up and said: “Yes, that is so. They 
are bondages of the past, the future and the present.” Bhagavan 
continued, “the present bondages are of four types: vishaya 
asakti lakshanam – great desire for material things, buddhi 
mandyam-inability to grasp the teaching and exposition of the 
Guru, kutharkam – to understand perversely the teaching of 
the Guru and viparyaya duragraham – to feel egotistically ‘I 
am learned in Vedas’, etc. The first can be overcome by sama 
(tranquility), by curbing the evil propensities of the mind 
(dama), by detachment (uparati), by indifference to external 
things titiksha. The second by hearing the teaching of the Guru 
over and over again, the third by reflection and the fourth by 
profound meditation. If in this way the obstacles are removed 
and destroyed the seekers get confirmed in their belief that 
they are themselves embodiment of the Self (Ātma Svarūpam).

Future bondages arise from acts done without anyone 
knowing that they are sinful. How to recognise it? A future 
bondage is recognised when some action presents itself 
which makes him feel that he wishes to do it because the 
doing of it is an act of human kindness and sympathy. That 
future bondages result in rebirths is authoritatively stated in 
scriptures.” (Letters, 25 and 26 Sep. 1947).

Paraphrase: 

All external bondage or attachments that are leaned 
onto or depended on are called dwandwa (dyads). When 
dyads are transcended the One non-dual Supreme Content 
shines of Its own accord. A realised yogī, who has risen 
above the dyads is a bond-free jīvanmukta (liberated 
while embodied). When he gets released from the body 
he becomes a videha mukta.
Commentary: 

Dwandwa(the dyad) itself is a bandha (bondage). 
Whatever is a cause of attachment in this world, is verily a 
bondage. When pleasure is experienced, pain follows close at 
its heels like smoke accompanying fire. Sin and pain exist quite 
at the end of every expectation of pleasure as soot exists at the 
ending of a flame. When an object is desired with great longing 
whatever comes in the way of obtaining it is discarded with 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   118 06-05-2011   10:53:43



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 119

dislike and even hatred. While we intensely seek something at 
the same time we discard something as unwanted. We derive 
inordinate happiness in the company of the most loved ones 
and grieve at the time of parting from them. Thus pleasure 
is only for pain and life is only for death. Thus bound by the 
cords of desire and overcome by the fetters of dwandwas 
mortals are bound like birds bound by strings.

We do not have a choice, of retaining the beneficial one 
and rejecting the other of the dwandwas, for they are always 
inseparable. Dependence on these dwandwas can never 
yield permanent happiness. But permanent happiness can 
be gained and the True Content can also be realized if only 
the dependence on the pairs of opposites is given up. The 
Realization of Purnavastu will grant bondageless freedom – 
mukti, the state of eternal Bliss.

Therefore a serious seeker after Truth is instructed to give 
up these dyads and attachments. One, who having known the 
delusion of the world, gives up the dwandwas, remains without 
desires and abides in the Real state of bondageless freedom, 
is hailed as a jīvanmukta as long as he remains in a human 
frame. When he gets released from the body he is called a 
videha mukta. One, who, while in a body experiences himself 
as bodiless awareness is a jīvanmukta indeed.

Therefore all that a mumukshu has to do is to annihilate 
the jīva bodha, the form of ego, that clouds his real nature 
and know himself as the Self – that is bondageless – which is 
jīvanmukti – the Supreme state.

Bhagavan once said: “Name and form are the past 
bondages. The fact, is ‘that which is’, is only one. It is 
omnipresent and universal.” In order to explain the past 
bondages Bhagavan narrated a story from Vasudeva Mananam. 
A brahmin with a large family acquired a she-buffalo and 
by selling its products he maintained his family. He was 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   119 06-05-2011   10:53:43



120 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

fully engaged in tending the she-buffalo cow. All his family 
members passed away one after other. So he concentrated 
all his affection on the buffalo but which also unfortunately 
passed away. Disgusted with life he took to sannyāsa. He 
was unable to concentrate, for the buffalo he loved so much 
appeared in his thoughts. When he expressed this difficulty 
to his guru, the guru realising that it was his past bondage 
said:: ‘the Brahman is said to be asti, bhati and priyam. Asti 
means omnipresent; bhati means lustre; priyam means love. 
The buffalo being an object of your love is also Brahman. It 
has a name and form. What you should do is to give up your 
own name and form as well as those of the buffalo. If that 
is done what remains is the Brahman itself. Therefore give 
up names and forms and meditate.’ The brahmin did so and 
attained realization.” (Letters, 25 Sep. 1947).

“The Self light alone is immaculate. Having given 
up all conceptions of duality may you look equally 
upon all. That the quiescent jñāna is Brahman will now 
become an object of direct perception to you, o child.” 
(Swaroopabodha Upanishad, Verse 5).

The body is the outcome of prārabdha karma and till the 
prārabdha karma is not exhausted, it will not fall off. But once 
it is exhausted, neither all the piety not wit can make it last a

 “The Lord of life has placed the demon
	 Ego as a sentry strict
	 To make certain that the body lasts
	 Until one eats the last bite
	 The fruit that one has earned by deeds."” 
                                   (Guru Vāchaka Kovai, Verse 571)
While every jīva experiences his own prārabdha, the Lord 

remains shining as the Immaculate and uninvolved Witness 
in the heart. The discerning men of dispassion who are fully 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   121 06-05-2011   10:53:43



122 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

aware that the course of life is as per one’s prārabdha, do not 
get agitated by anything. Whether one likes or not, the fruits of 
one’s past deeds unfailingly come to be experienced by one.

A wise man therefore, should not attempt to give up the 
body out of desirelessness. Once the prārabdha is spent out, 
the burden of the body is cast off. It is this very prārabdha 
that guards and protects the body and destroys itself after its 
exhaustion for which it awaits the order of none. This is the 
secret of karma. The body is not an obstacle to the attainment 
of the bliss of jñāna. Nor can the bliss come on its own with 
the body’s extinction. Mere pronouncement will suffice to 
prove that a pot is nothing but mud. Should it be proved by 
breaking the pot? While that the body is insentient and impure 
is known, it need not be proved by destroying it. In the same 
way when a dreamer is surrounded by fire in a dream, the 
only way for the dreamer to get over it is to wake up from the 
dream. The only way to attain that joy of release is to remain as 
the uninvolved and moveless witness, untouched by the inner 
organs and the body realising that they are but impermanent 
off-shoots of māyā.

Bhagavan says while it is ‘ego’ that is to be killed, killing 
the body is like beating the chair to beat the one who is seated 
on the chair.

Once Chadwick, while cycling round the hill, on seeing 
a bus thought ‘why not by concentrating on the Self, throw 
himself in front of the bus’ so that he could gain mukti and 
later spoke about it to Bhagavan. Bhagavan replied that it 
would not work. Thoughts would spring involuntarily while 
he fell, fear and shock would cause them and thoughts coming, 
life would continue and that he would have to take another 
body. If he could still his mind sufficiently so that such a 
thing would not happen, then what was the need of suicide?” 
(A Sadhu’s Reminiscences, page 90).

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   122 06-05-2011   10:53:43



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 123

Bhagavan while explaining why should there be suicide 
at all said “Because he is unhappy and desires to put an end to 
his unhappiness. He actually does it by ending the association 
with the body which represents all unhappiness. For there must 
be a killer to kill the body. He is the survivor after suicide. That 
is the Self.” (Talks no. 340) and again “The eternal, blissful 
and natural state has been smothered by this life of ignorance. 
In this way the present life is due to the killing of the eternal 
pristine Being. Is it not a case of suicide? So then everyone 
is a suicide.” (Talks no. 53).

Renunciation of the non-self alone can bestow mukti and 
bliss and complete renunciation cannot happen by giving up 
the body, or by the austere living of an ascetic in hermitages. 
The mind, like the seed, is the origin of everything, and when 
the origin of everything is renounced, everything is surely 
given up.

As Pattinaththar sings “The fruit of actions found us a 
body and when that spent, the body, not even the size of a 
small grain of it, will remain. Remember the feet of Siva.” So 
if we have a body clinging to us, nature will go on acting till 
the body is shaken off as a discarded shell. The divine dwells 
as the inmost being of man and cannot be distinguished. This 
light, the concealed witness is imperishable and endures from 
birth to birth, untouched by birth or decay. It is the jīva who 
undergoes these changes, but if he is completely harmonized 
by the divine as the divine it will be realized that “I am” 
eternal. Therefore having obtained, as a result of good fortune 
a human body – rare to obtain – and captained by a competent 
guru and favoured by the Grace of God, if one fails to utilise 
them and cross the ocean of saṁsāra, he should be called one 
who has committed  suicide, a killer of his own spiritual self.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   124 06-05-2011   10:53:43



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 125

sarira (body). This is the temple of chit. That chit, bound by 
nothing, is indescribable as either big or light but remains as 
the Space of space and Light of light, bigger than the biggest 
and subtler than the subtlest. This is the ‘centre’ Hridayam. 
It stands for the Self and “It is to the body what the sun is to 
the world.” (Ramana Gītā). This must be enquired and known 
for it is Sat-Chit-Ānanda. This Ānanda, when realised, reveals 
its absence in the object as it lacks any affinity to the essential 
glories of the Lord, happiness and Peace. 

The Ātman shines with the sphurana of ‘I am’ forever in 
the firmament of Awareness of the Heart, without rising and 
subsidence. That Ātman, the Sat, or ‘That which is’ is also the 
chit, the Awareness that knows Itself. That Content, taintless 
and moveless is ever the form of Peace serene. This shanti is 
verily the form of Bliss. These three, Existence, Consciousness 
and Bliss are not mere properties of the Ātman. They are the 
very nature of Sat-Chit-Ānanda, the True Content.

In that Self, the Sat-Chit-Ānanda, the phantom ego 
appears with the dehātma buddhi the idea of “I am the 
body”and the attachment to it. When this is obliterated, what 
remains is the ‘Aham’, the reality. When ahamkara sheds its 
akara (form) what is, is Aham only. Anything other than ‘I am’ 
is from the mind, the great deluder, something that adds to the 
pure consciousness – an adjunct to pure consciousness – and 
limits it. Immediately it destroys the perfection, the wholeness 
and the pristine purity of Consciousness. 

“Ātma is always Sat-Chit-Ānanda. Of these, the first two 
are experienced in all the states, whereas the last one is said to 
be experienced in sleep only. The question arises how the true 
nature of the Self can be lost in the waking and dream states. 
It is, really speaking, not lost. In sleep there is no mind and 
the Self shines as Itself, whereas in the other two states what 
shines forth is the reflected light of the Self.” (Talks no. 566).

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   125 06-05-2011   10:53:43



126 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

When the mind is shorn of all its upādhis or adjuncts it 
becomes the very form of Reality. That is the Bliss of release. 
Mukti and Bliss are one and the same. Mukti itself is Bliss.

As long as one’s transitory personality – consciousness is 
active, the Fullness, silence and Peace cannot be experienced. 
The Ātman is vimala and nichchala, taintless and unmoving. 
The Self, the chit is unaffected by the contacts of the senses 
created by māyā whose sportive activities in the world leave 
no pollution in It even as the atmosphere is unsullied by its 
own movement everywhere. Māyā is nothing but the power 
of Brahman.

Bhagavan, in Ashtakam, speaks of māyā as a wonderful 
Power not apart from the Lord.

Paraphrase: 
Meditate unceasingly and with great devotion on 

that form of Awareness that shines untouched by any 
adjunct, (in the form of ego), that Supreme Content, “Siva

Commentary: 

Ātman, though permeating everything in creation – 
which is a play of māyā – is bereft of any upādhi or adjunct 
and is untouched by the insignia of the manifestations of the 
phenomenal world, like name, form, rise and subsidence. One 
should ever meditate with great devotion and zeal as “That 
form of awareness Siva, I am”. In the highest meditation 
which this text and the Upanishads prescribe, the Chit, that 
Siva, which is to be meditated upon is the Awareness in the 
subject and the object. It is called Samanya Chaitanyam, 
“Simple pure Awareness” that is like the sky everywhere, Full, 
as the substratum of all names and forms and as the form of 
Asti, Bhati, Priyam (Sat, Chit and Ānanda) and without any 
change. When one contemplates this Space of Pure awareness 
totally devoid of all attributes he becomes full with Ānanda 
pervading all directions – that is – he becomes the very form 
of the space – Awarneness.

Devotion and zeal are indispensable in the search for 
Truth. The Lord, if sought with love, is easily attained. “From 
head to foot as heart I melt not” so saying Manivāchakar 
melts in ‘pious rage’ and devotion. An yearning with devotion 
helps a heart as hard as stone to melt away in devotion. A 
heart hardened by an assertive ego becomes soft with melting 
devotion and finally dissolves away.

A constant meditation with this type of sincere love and 
devotion severs all the other attachments with no residue left.

Bonds become bonds only when the jīva volitionally 
embraces them, for, they being insentient, cannot bind him 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   127 06-05-2011   10:53:43



128 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

on their own. The jīva, though pseudo in nature, has an aspect 
of ‘awareness’ which enables him to attach himself to them. 

If only the jīva would centre all his attachments on binding 
himself to the Supreme Siva, all the other bonds are rendered 
naught. A ceaseless meditation on the one devoid of bonds is 
the way to cast off bonds.

Thirukkural voices the same idea:
“Paṭṭṛuha Paṭṛṭaṭṭrān Paṭṭṛinai appaṭṭṛinai 
  Paṭṭṛuha Paṭṭṛu Vidarku” (350)
The only attachment that will help sever all other bonds 

and attachments, is the attachment to the Lord, who is the 
boundless source of all things.

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 129
