Paraphrase: 
Give up totally by a discriminative intellect, all body-

based notions and attitudes spoken of about the country 
one lives in, the caste one is born into, the blemishless 
community, the varna and ashrama that one belongs to and 
hold on only to the natural state – the Self – the ‘origin’ 
of the ego ‘I’ and always practice meditation unceasingly.
Commentary: 

Nationality, caste, community and the code of conduct, 
pertaining to them, varnashrama, the commandments and 
injunction relating to the code of conduct belonging to them, 
observances of daily rituals and worship – are not merely 
mental attributes from the strangle-hold of which the seekers 
should free themselves, but are also definite obstacles in the 
way of Release. All of them are body based and as such they 
belong to the realm of non-self. Hence the Lord exhorts the 
sādhaks to renounce them totally. Bhagavan says: “There 
is varnashrama in some form or other in every land. The 
significance is that one should hold on to the single Ātman 
and not swerve there from. That is the whole gist of it. Ātma 
dharma is inherence in the Self.” (Talks no. 58).

Again in Who am I? Bhagavan says: “Living as the Self 
is the essence of all dharmas. All others merge there.”

Varnashrama dharma bears fruits only when observed 
successfully: that is, one must realize that he is not the doer but 
that he is only a tool of some Higher Power. “Let the Higher 
Power do what is inevitable and let me act only according to 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   129 06-05-2011   10:53:43



130 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

its dictates. The actions are not mine. Therefore, the results of 
the actions cannot be mine.” If one thinks and acts so, where 
is the trouble? Be it varnashrama or loukika dharma (worldly 
activities) it is immaterial. Finally it amounts to this

Sva – ātmanah (of the Self)
Para – anātmanah (of the non-Self)” (Talks no. 58)
A striver should always seek the origin of the ego, his 

Self, renouncing all bhavanas or attitudes. If he continues 
persistently in this practice of seeking the Self, by the sheer 
strength of this attitude, he will attain that state. “Rather 
be fixed in the Self. Inherence in the Self” is the sum and 
substance of the teaching.

But if a mind divorced from the practice of the above 
disciplines is not turned inward it comes to ruin losing its 
balance thereby losing both the here and the hereafter. Hence 
the exhortation to practice the method of seeking the Self 
thereby avoiding the failure to derive the best advantage of 
a human birth.

All the aforesaid disciplines will completely disappear 
with the disappearance of the jīvabodha with the dawn of 
enlightenment just as when the head is severed, the vital breath 
also leaves the body.

Paraphrase: 
(Fearless due to the absence of a second entity as there is 

no other), I alone am. No one belongs to me; nor do I belong 
to anyone. I see none who can claim me as his. There is also 
none, whom I can claim as mine. I (the Self) alone am.
Commentary: 

The characteristic of the “true content of I” the Content 
Beyond, (called vastu lakshana) is described in this verse. 
There is none and nothing other than “I" is established 
with certainty. When it is pronounced “I belong to none” 
‘I’ becomes the Master. But this master has no article of 
possession whatsoever.

If so do ‘I’ belong to anyone else? But I can see none who 
can lay such a claim on me. Though I may belong to none 
is there any whom I can claim as mine? However seen, it is 
certain that there is none except ‘I’ – I alone AM.

As nothing else has existence other than ‘I’, my true 
form is that non-dual, Full and Pure Awareness that shines 
without a second. That is Ātman. As the Ātman shines in its 
own effulgence with nothing and none other than Itself it has 
been affirmed “I see nothing else”. That the True Content of 
‘I’ is just ‘One’ is proved here.

132 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

“No one owns Me; I own nothing
I am neither slave nor master
No duty binds Me. I am
Neither doer nor enjoyer.”
                                 (Guru Vāchaka Kovai, Verse 1246)
Once Bhagavan explained this śloka thus: “Aham – ‘I’ is 

only one. Egos are different. They are in the One Self. The Self 
is not affected by the egos. ‘I’ is one only. ‘I’ is the Truth. All that 
follows is meant to refute the sense of duality.” (Talks no. 284).

This very idea occurs in different scriptures and holy 
books. B.V. Narasimhaswamy has chosen this very śloka for 
the motto of the eleventh chapter of his book, Self-Realization. 
Bhāgavatam also says: “In his real nature this Ātman has none 
specially dear or inimical to him. None is one’s own and none, 
another’s. Without the attachments as a friend or a foe, He is 
the One being that stands as the witness of all who do good 
and bad actions. He is the unconcerned witness of all that is 
high and low, ever free. He does not share any enjoyment or 
suffering nor does he accept anything, even the sovereignty 
of that state as the fruit of His actions.”

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   133 06-05-2011   10:53:43



134 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Commentary: 
At the very outset this verse expounds the mantra “I am 

Brahman” (Aham Brahmasmi) – the celebrated mahavakya. 
In Tejobindu Upanishad, this is described as Lord Siva’s reply 
to Lord Shanmukha who wants Him to describe the direct 
experience of the Ātman. There the Lord says “I am of the 
form of the transcendental Brahman, Pure Consciousness, the 
Alone. I am the direct experience, ‘I am the All’ and yet the 
all, if separated from the Ātman, is asat.” I am that avikara 
Brahman – changeless Brahman. This body is afflicted with the 
disease of death; but it is the dwelling place for the deathless, 
bodiless, Ātman. The one associated with the body is afflicted 
with desires, dislikes and diseases. But these do not touch the 
one who is bodiless (the one who is awake by the knowledge 
of the unembodied Self). “That Vidwan who sees that lustrous 
Supreme Self, who remains as Brahman, the source, the creator 
and the Lord, he sheds merit and demerit, free of taints, attains 
oneness with Him, the Supreme.” (Mundaka Upanishad, 
3-1-3). I am the Lord, the cause and creator of the universe, 
of the form of guru, Jñāna personified. One who abides in 
the experience of this certainty without slipping ever from 
that state annihilates the bondage of saṁsāra and becomes a 
mukta. He ensures the cessation of all sorrow and attains the 
Ātma loka, and firmly poised in mukti enjoys eternal Bliss.

The one who follows paths contrary to this is in bondage.
It is this all pervading infinite space of Pure awareness 

that has verily taken the form of Guru. Guru is not different 
from Ātman. At the time the mumukshu, purged of all his 
impurities, becomes ripe, matured and fit enough to absorb 
the descent of grace, the Lord appears assuming the form of 
guru and instructs the Truth and makes him turn inward and 
one-pointed. The Lord or Iswara, Guru and Ātma are one and 
the same. Guru is not only without but within too. Until the 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   134 06-05-2011   10:53:43



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 135

dehātma bhava is removed, the guru from without pushes the 
mumukshu in and He himself pulls him from within. When one 
subsides within, that sakti will be understood is the upadēsa 
of Bhagavan.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   135 06-05-2011   10:53:44



136 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

intense enquiry within, investigating one’s true nature. “The 
sādhak must remain as the Self. If he cannot do so he must 
ascertain the true meaning of the ‘I’ and constantly revert to 
it whenever the other thoughts arise. That is the practice.” 
(Talks no 647).

The jīva clings on to the body as ‘I’ and thereby 
experiences inseparable identity with it. When this ignorance 
and its product, the body, are sublated through enquiry into 
his real ‘Being’ he realises the Fullness of his Being. Seeing 
the Self as Self through the gnoetic Eye or Eye of wisdom 
is ‘realization’. The Self or Being has always been the same 
and only the ego that came in-between is eliminated. One’s 
true nature being ever the same, it has been lost in bondage. 
He is ever the Self luminous Consciousness. It is a state of 
perfect tranquillity with the mind stilled and this serenity 
of peace is joy Supreme. “If you identify with the Absolute 
Consciousness, having dissociated thyself from the body, you 
will enjoy this very moment Supreme Peace, eternal bliss and 
highest knowledge. You will be absolutely free from bondage.” 
(Vichārabindu Upanishad, Verse 7)

When the Ātman is realized as the sole existence nothing 
else is seen. An enlightened man who dwells in the Self 
always, does not even know or feel that he has a body, much 
less that he is doing anything. To him the experience of objects 
in the waking life is like the perception of the dream world 
in memory after one wakes up from sleep.			 
Bhagavan describes that state succinctly:

“The Sage self-realized, knows not 
Whether the transient body comes 
And stays, or dies and leaves, even as 
The senseless drunkard knows not what 
Happens to his clothes.” 
                  (Assorted verses by Bhagavan, Verse no. 24)

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   136 06-05-2011   10:53:44



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 137

To such a person, the body acquired by prārabdha is like 
a garland round the neck of a cow.

The body, never the form of joy of “I”, is mistaken for the 
true ‘I’ out of ignorance and delusion that is responsible for all 
the evils and misery of human life. This knot of Ahankara – I 
sense – when, through vichāra developed by discrimination, 
is rent asunder, the True ‘I’ is perceived by the gnoetic Eye, all 
desires vanish and one attains the joy of peace serene. Such 
a realized muni or sage resembles the deep ocean, still and 
calm, but deep and profound, unperturbed and unfathomable. 
Such a one whose mind is absorbed in the Ātman as pure Self 
Awareness without any experience inside or outside or of objects 
is totally unaware of his body and he is in Supreme Peace.

All Upanishads glorify such a one who has woken up to the 
knowledge of one’s real form that is bodiless. Kathopanishad 
proclaims: “The wise man, who knows the Ātman as bodiless, 
seated firmly in perishable bodies, Great and All-pervading 
does never grieve.” (I, 2-22). Vivekachūḍāmaṇi also states: 
“The absence of ‘I’ in the body, though it follows him like a 
shadow, is the mark of a jīvanmukta and with prajñā firmly 
established he enjoys that bliss that is continuous and the world 
to him is a forgotten thing.” (Verses 432, 429).

He who is described in all the scriptures as unborn,

Commentary: 

This verse declares vastu nirnayam (ascertainment of 
the True Content) that Vedantic texts speak of. The accepted 
modes of proof of this are Śāstrapramanam (declarations of 
Vedantic texts), anumana (inferential logic), spiritual wisdom 
handed down by elders and anubhuti (direct experience). 
The proof of vastu niraṇaya is offered in this verse with the 
authority of scriptural proclamations.

Ātman is ever present and is called ‘unborn’. Birth is 
the nature or dharma of the gross body. When birth is not 
even the nature of the subtle body, how then can it be the 
nature of Ātman? If we ascribe birth to the Ātman then death 
also will have to be ascribed and no more can It be termed 
eternal but will be perishable which goes against the Vedantic 
declarations. That Content, that is never born and shines as 
the Lord of all the worlds and beings, moving and unmoving 
in it, is hailed and hymned by all the scriptures.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   138 06-05-2011   10:53:44



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 139

It is spoken of as all-pervading, pervading everywhere 
in and out of all with forms, but Itself is without a form and 
remains as the Transcendental Space of Awareness. It is 
the formless form of Awareness that illumines everything 
else. When He is perceived as the intelligence of all beings 
in an undifferentiated manner, from Brahma, the Creator, 
down to an ant, then He is called Kutasta. The Noumenon 
is interwoven like the warp and woof of all that is perceived 
as the phenomenal world. “Residing in limiting adjuncts of 
differentiations He manifests Himself as interwoven in all 
bodies like the thread through the jewels, then He is called 
Antaryamin, Internal Ruler.” (Sarvopanishad, 3).

Moreover, though it is admixed with all qualities, It 
transcends all the qualities and is unaffected by these qualities.

In the presence of the Self māyā creates the three, God, 
jīva and jagat. The world has thus sprung from the power 
of māyā. But ignorance and bondage resulting from the 
phenomenal world are not apart from Ātman but Ātman or 
Brahman is apart from the phenomenal world, and beyond 
the māyā. This is what Lord Krishna says in Gītā in Chapter 
9, Verses 4 and 5: “By Me, all this Universe is pervaded 
through My unmanifested form. All beings abide in Me but 
I do not abide in them. Behold My divine mystery. My spirit 
which is the source of all beings sustains the beings but does 
not abide in them.”

Therefore, I, the birthless Self, the Sky of Awareness, am 
not affected by the dharma of the body (which is other than I) 
and therefore am devoid of all qualities and upādhis.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   140 06-05-2011   10:53:44



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 141

am free from sorrow. I am forever Brahmamayan – the

Commentary: 

Vijñāna matran (just Awareness) (Prajñāna ghana) 
(condensed mass of consciousness) refers to remaining 
with just the awareness of ‘I am’. It is a condensed mass of 
consciousness in which there is complete absence of the world 
as it stands. “It is that jewel of consciousness which shines 
forth in every body-casket. It is that moon in which sparkle 
these rays of light in the form of the collection of worlds.” 
(Yoga Vasishtam, 1214 and 16). Being concomitant with the 
world and also in its absence Pure Consciousness alone is the 
ultimate Truth.

Therefore ‘I’, the form of awareness, am the cause of all 
that is known as the tainted world, the product of māyā. There 
is nothing that is the cause of ‘Me’, the form of Awareness.

The Ātman is the purest of all purities. Though the Self 
remains in and out of all the worlds in all the avasthas that 
appear in beings, like the sky, it is not touched by any and 
unattached to any. 

‘I am free of all attributes’. ‘I’,the form of mere 
awareness, is untouched by the dharma of jīva, like the 
impurity of being caught up in the grievous cycle of repeated 
embodiments through birth and death due to endless karmas. 
‘I’ who am other than all these, though in them, is untouched 
by their impurities. Therefore, I, the form of taintless Self, 
am Pure. Mukta is the one who is freed of bondage, vimukta 
is one who is totally freed of everything. ‘I’ the form of 
mere awareness, am not the doer of actions, am devoid of 
sanchita and prabrabdha and hence am vimukta. As It is 
vijñāna (knowledge) and visuddha (most pure), It is vimukta 
(released), therefore no grief or sorrow can approach It.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   141 06-05-2011   10:53:44



142 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Further that Content being subtler than the subtlest, 
filling everything and every being is neither graspable nor 
releasable. “That is described as the Sky of Consciousness 
which, though everything always, is not anything, having 
ascertained everything in every way in this manner: ‘This is 
not That, this is not That’”. (Yoga Vasishtam, Verse 1241).

What is ungraspable cannot also be let off.
Abiding as the natural and mere sphurana (throb) of Sat, 

or shining with the mere awareness of merely “I am”, wholly 
immaculate beyond knowledge and ignorance, attributeless, 
Perfect Silence released from all bondage and imaginary 
illusions is Brahman and that Brahman I am. “That alone 
is Brahman, without component parts, without doubt and 
without taint. Realizing “I am” that Brahman one becomes 
the immutable Brahman.” (Amritabindu Upanishad, Verse 8).

and above his head. He never transgresses the limit of the body.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   143 06-05-2011   10:53:44



144 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

The jīva never regards anything except the body as ‘I’ 
and is incomparable in asserting when his claim of ownership 
over other things. He is exceedingly smart in deciding what 
are ‘mine’.

Quite contrary to this, Pure Consciousness that shines as 
the whole and unfragmented, in all the principles is alien only 
to the ego-sense -‘I am the body’. We are instructed that this 
chit, quite different from – and other than the insentient body 
– must be known as ‘I’. It is the mind that projects the idea 
that ‘I am this’ and ‘I am that’. Chit or awareness is simply 
knowing (Being), “I am” as “I am”. The whole universe has 
consciousness as its ‘Eye’, the instrument of cognition. On 
Consciousness all this is established and consciousness is the 
support of the whole cosmos. Though existing everywhere, 
it cannot be physically perceived or grasped by the senses or 
the mind. It is without organs such as eyes, ears and the rest. 
Though this Brahman is formless, nameless, It is well-seated 
and well known as the ‘I’ in all.

It is that which is not uttered by speech but by which speech 
itself is uttered. It is that which is not thought of by the mind but 
by which the mind itself thinks. It cannot be seen by the eyes but 
is the one by which the eyes are able to see. Likewise It cannot 
be known by any of the sense organs, be they the inner organs 
or the motor organs. That transcends all the organs. 

Both in the cases of knowledge of objects and the 
ignorance of them “I know” exists. All pervasive, Full 
everywhere of the form of immortality “I” in us never dies. 
But the Self, ‘I am’, is other than the perishable body.

Brahmanubhava Upanishad ecstatically excalims: “I 
am Akanda – Ekarasa Cinmatra Brahman. I am Prajñāna-
ghana Brahman. I am Vijnana-ghana Brahman. I am Chit-
ghana Brahman. I am Ānanda-ghana Brahman.” (Verse 
506). Bhagavan never missed an opportunity to instruct that 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   144 06-05-2011   10:53:44



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 145

the ‘I’ in us is the ‘other’ of the body and ‘we’, the blessed 
children of immortality, are simply the form of “I am”, the 
Awareness, of Being, eka chit. Child Indra, a daughter of G.V. 
Subbharamiah, was initiated into the mantra ‘Deham naham 
Koham Soham’ (Body I am not; Who am I? He, I am). After 
seeing a corpse, when seeing another young girl, described her 
fear to Bhagavan. Bhagavan remarked: “Why are you afraid 
of corpses? You should only be afraid of living corpses.” On 
another occasion he stated in so far as we carry the burden 
of the body referring it to ‘I’, we all are as much impure as 
the pall-bearers of a corpse to the cremation ground and this 
impurity cannot be removed, by holy dips in any sacred water 
except in that of Ātma tirta.

Paraphrase: 
I am the Lord of all perceivable creations, moving 

and motionless. I remain as the mother, father and father’s 
father of all these creations. The aspirants for mukti, the 
mumukshus, contemplate with concentration and fervour 
only upon Me, the exalted and good state of Turiya.
Commentary: 

Since the form of Chit, the primal cause, shines also as 
the effect, namely the world with all its moving and non-
moving objects, it is declared “I am the Lord of all”. Besides 
being the mother and father called Prakriti (māyā or nature) 
and Purusha He shines also as the Father – the substratum 
– for the appearance of these two. It means “I am the primal 
cause of them all, the substratum of all of them and remain 
as the transcendent principle.” This verse reemphasizes what 
the Lord declared in the Gītā: “I am the father of this world, 
the mother, the supporter and the grandsire I am the goal, the 
upholder, the Lord, the witness, the abode, the refuge and the 
friend. I am the origin and the dissolution, the ground, the 
resting place and the imperishable seed.” (Chapter 9, Verses 
17 and 18), and again “Know Me Partha, to be the eternal seed 
of all existences. I am the intelligence of the intelligent; I am 
the splendour of the splendid.”

The Ātman, thus though creating the world of names 
and forms, making it appear real with true existence, is Itself 
without a name and form. A mumukshu must ever contemplate 
that nameless, formless,  Ātman in the heart. His mind then 
gets purged of its impurities of vāsanās or latencies and 
merges in the Ātman. Then, That, which alone forever is, 
will remain, with all else extinct. A serious aspirant for mukti 
must strive hard to accomplish this. That is the turiya state. 
“Turiya is only another name for the Self. Aware of the waking, 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   146 06-05-2011   10:53:44



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 147

dream and sleep states we remain unaware of our own Self. 
Nevertheless the Self is here and now, it is the only Reality. 
There is nothing else.” (Talks no. 353). It is significant to note 
that Devaraja Mudaliar always addresses Bhagavan ever in 
the ‘good Turiya’ state as ‘Father and Mother’ rolled into one 
and refers to himself as ‘the child of Ramana’. (Ramana chei).

Turiya or pure Consciousness is Ātman, the true Self 
of man and living beings. It’s nature is Truth (Satyam), 
Knowledge (Jñānam) and Infinity (Ananthan), Good (Sivam, 
Nal in Tamil) and Beauty (Sundaram), Peace or (Santam) 
and Non-dual (Advitīyam). Turiya alone is the Reality behind 
all experiences, the reality behind the universe; so much so 
Āchārya Sankara, at the commencement of his commentary 
on the Mandukya Upanishad, pays his obeisance to Turiya 
(the Awareness-Pure) and invokes it to protect us.

Commentary:

charity done with a view to attain the Lord is termed the rarest.

Besides these, construction of temples, providing tanks

and progeny. Purta comprises works of civic utility such as 
planting trees, building water tanks, etc. ordained in scriptures.

all these ways” (All these works are called "purtham while 
the earlier verse spoke of ishta – desire based and the other 
purushartam – to wards the attainment of the highest goal of 
humans).

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 151

“In Me alone is everything born, in Me does everything 
rest and in Me everything is dissolved; I am that Brahman 
secondless”, says the Lord.

All things moving (jangamam) and unmoving (sthavaram) 
are all but Me. Other than ‘Me’ there is no other ‘Being’. ‘I’, 
the One, remain as the entire world. Know this, declares the 
Lord. The scriptures say Sarvadeva namaskara: Kesavam 
Pratigacchati- All prostrations to all devatas reach only 
Kesava – the Supreme Brahman. 

When one perceives the Content Whole with a perception 
transformed into one of jñāna (wisdom) the universe made up 
of five elements shines as the substance of jñāna, Ātman. This 
is the import of the Lord’s declaration. “Everything is Me, the 
One, Know thus.” This is precisely the upadēsa of Bhagavan 
in Upadēsa Undyar “Worshipping everything preceived as 
the form of Lord is the best worship.”

	 Himself as space and celestials stands
	 Himself as body life and matter stands
	 Himself as sea, hill and dale stands
	 Himself – all world’s Lord Supreme.

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 153

“I am not the gross body perceptible to the physical eye. 
Nor am I the subtle body or the causel body. The five kosas 
of which the body is made up I (the Self) am not.” 

The gross body, the food sheath, is subject to birth and 
death, is impure, undergoes changes at various stages and 
is finally destroyed and is therefore asat. The subtle body 
comprises of pranamaya kosa, subject to hunger and thirst, is 
strong or weak and when joined with karmendriyas earns the 
name articulator, giver and mover and in the absence of indriyas 
earns epithets as deaf and the mute. The second component of 
the subtle body, manomaya kosa has desire, greed, fear, hatred, 
jealousy and ahankara. The third component, vijñāna maya 
kosa is associated with pleasure and pain, the sense of doership 
and enjoyership. The jnanendriyas (organs of perception) 
connected with manomaya and vijñānamaya kosas have the 
qualities of seeing, hearing and tasting. 

The causal body of the Ānandamaya has the qualities of 
knowledge, ignorance and the sukha (bliss or joy) of sleep. 
But none of the changes the five kosas are subject to, is for 
‘Me’ the Self, since the appearance and subsidence of the kosas 
with their changes are clearly known by ‘Me’, the Self. I am 
changeless, the form of Knowledge.

All the three bodies made up of five kosas are but the form 
of pain. As ‘I’, remain apart from them and know them all, ‘I 
am’ changeless, the form of jñāna and as such ‘I am’ the most 
loved by all beings as objects witnessed by me. And ‘I’ remain 
the support of all. It is because of the Self that husband and 
wife become dear to each other. Son, wealth all these become 
dear due to the love of the Self.

Ātmanastu kamaya sarvam priyam bhavathi – “Everything 
becomes dear due to love of the Self. Ātman alone must be 
perceived, must be heard, must be thought of, must be known 
definitely.” (Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, 2.4.5)

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   153 06-05-2011   10:53:44



154 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Therefore, the immortal, non-dual, indivisible, formless 
Ātman, which is distinct from the three bodies and five sheaths 
and which is the Witness of the three states is to be realized 
as one’s own by constant, protracted and deep meditation. 	

In truth, in the real form there is no universe at all. Both 
in days of ignorance and knowledge, in all the three states 
when the world, the form of misery appears and disappears, 
I do not appear and disappear with them. The three states 
and the worlds that rise and disappear in them are naturally 
known by Me. ‘I am’ forever. If not, there is none else who 
can know the three bodies, the three states and the virtueless 
worlds seen in them, so says the Lord.

“This ‘I’ is the one who experiences the waking, dream 
and sleep states. The three states are changes which do not 
affect the individual. The experiences are like pictures passing 
on a screen in the cinema. The appearance and disappearance 
of the pictures do not affect the screen. So also the three states 
alternate with one another leaving the Self unaffected. The 
waking and dream states are creations of the mind. So the 
Self covers all. To know that the Self remains happy in its 
perfection is Self-Realization.” (Talks no. 487)

As ‘I’, the Self, the form of awareness, is the support of all 
these, the world, fragmented into all its multiplicity of names 
and forms, when shorn of the illusion of names and forms, only 
the essence of awareness, a condensed mass of consciousness, 
the perfect, whole jñāna, the Self eternal, remains.

The world, the cause of delusion, with its diversity of 
names and forms, was in its unmanifest state, the form of One 
and Bliss to start with.

This can be explained with an analogy. The peacock with 
its fan-like turquoise plumage of magnificent colours and 
patterns, while in the nucleus of the egg, remains uniformly 
the same colourless embryo without its splash of colours.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   154 06-05-2011   10:53:44



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 155

If the truth of the world needs to be known, it can only be 
known from the absolute state of Ātman, is the Lord’s instruction.

The body appearing as "I am this or that" with all its 
inauspicious vāsanās and couched in triputis is not true, either 
in the past, present or future.

The pragmatic waking world, the illusory dreaming 
world, and the complete void of the deep sleep – all these 
and the body in all its states – are illumined by the light of 
consciousness, the Ātman-Brahman. Though in deep sleep 
(sushupti) we daily go to the city of Brahman in the heart 
cave, we, veiled by nescience are unable to realise it just as 
people who walk over the buried treasure are unable to know 
and much less unearth it. The ego or the subtle body constitues 
the heart’s knot and does not die out without the knowledge 
of the ever attained Self and due to its proximity to the Self 
appears imperishable. The consciousness which manifests 
Itself there is called the kshetrajna, the knower of kshetra. 
Jothirbindu Upanishad says “Just as you take out the butter 
from the buttermilk by the process of churning, even so you 
will have to take out the Ātman from the panchakosas by the 
churning of constant meditation.”

Commentary: 

The Content Beyond, unbound by Time; transcends 
Time, hence It is called the unborn. It lends the knowledge of 
awareness to all knowledge that can possibly be known but 
Itself remains beyond the comprehension of all knowledge so 
gained. Therefore It is called vijñānam.

None can say that It originated at such and such a time, 
being more ancient than the most ancient. Just as space in a pot 
and all the pervading space are one and the same, irrespective 
of the pot’s existence or destruction, so too the True Content 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   156 06-05-2011   10:53:44



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 157

or the Light of Consciousness as such has never been ever 
born, nor will It ever perish. Hence It can only be indicated 
by the word Purānam (ancient). 

Being subtler than subtletely Itself It has no form. Being 
unborn It has neither death. It is devoid of the effect of māyā 
world and the body and therefore of all the taints of the world 
and forms, gross or subtle. It is free from the faults of the stains 
like hunger, thirst, grief, delusion, old age and death, and of 
changes like birth, growth, etc.

There is no blemish or nescience or avidya in That. 
There is nothing else other than That, making comparison or 
claim of equality impossible. Truth cannot be communicated 
without reference to objects which are but mere illustrations 
only, yet the objects of illustrations can never be the Truth by 
themselves.

Being the support of everything else, That Itself is without 
a support. That Content, formless, dwells ever in the heart-cave.

Kanappohadu.... (cannot be seen). Here by negating the 
capacity for the eyes to see the Truth, the intention is to negate 
the capacity for all the other sense organs to feel or know the 
subtle Truth as an object. The eye being an instrument to see 
can only see objects other than itself, it can never hope to 
see itself, as a telescope cannot be used for viewing the very 
eye of the observer himself. This Ātman, the subtlest of the 
subtle, resides in the inmost recesses of the heart, the holy of 
holies, in us.

A verse in Kathopanishad (Mantra 12) expresses the same 
content: “The wise sage who by means of meditation on the 
Self, recognises the Ancient, who is difficult to be seen, who is 
hidden in the cave of the heart, who dwells in the abyss, who 
is lodged in the intelligence, he renounces joy and sorrow”.

Kaivalyopanishad also declares, “I am minuter than the 
minute, I am likewise the greatest of all, I am the manifold 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   157 06-05-2011   10:53:44



158 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Universe. I am the Ancient one, the Purusha and the Ruler, I 
am the Effulgent One and the All-good.” (Verse 20)

It is beyond being conceptualized or visualized or 
comprehended by mind or intellect and cannot be known as 
an object through the senses. The Ātman is asparsa and the 
method for attaining It is called asparsa yoga, the yoga of 
non-contact; for there is neither the subject to contact nor the 
object to make contact with. It can at best be described as “It 
is” or merely ‘is’. 

“That vastu, Akshara, is imperceivable, untouchable 
(beyond physical contact), without a source and devoid of 
colour, ears, eyes, hands and legs, eternal, everywhere, all-
pervading, highly subtle and cannot be diminished. Wise men 
enquire and know that Source of all.” (Mundaka Upanishad, 
1.6) and verse 21 of Kaivalyopanishad declares, “Without 
arms, legs, am I, of unthinkable power; I see without eyes, I 
hear without ears. I know all and am different from all. None 
can know me, I am always in intelligence.”

Paraphrase:

Commentary: 

That Brahman which is Sanātana, unlike the asat which 
abides at one time and disappears at another, the most ancient, 
is also antharamil – is everywhere within and without, with 
no interspace in It.

Therefore that Sat, that Brahman alone ‘Am I’. When one 
meditates for a prolonged period of time with Soham attitude 
he becomes perfectly still, quiescent and gains immortality. 

The one and only aim of all meditations is to directly know 
and realize that the meditator is always non-different from 
Brahman, the ‘object’ of meditation and the act of meditating. 
Even at the time of thinking of an object, the mind is really one 
with the object. In the meditation of Soham also the result is 
the attainment of oneness with the object of meditation which 
is Brahman. In this meditation, the mind, without any support, 
holds on to the sat vritti, the most auspicious modification 
of the mind “I am Brahman verily”, which is the bestower 
of Supreme Bliss for this leads to complete stillness devoid 
of modifications of the mind with complete forgetfulness of 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   159 06-05-2011   10:53:45



160 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

all thought, and culminates in identification with Brahman, 
which is termed Samādhi and Jñāna.

“Does not one find some kind of peace while in 
meditation? That is the sign of progress. That peace will be 
deeper and more prolonged with continued practice. It will 
also lead to the goal.” (Talks no. 73)

In Nirvana Shatkam, Sankara details the meditation on 
Sivoham (Soham), I am Siva (Brahman). In the first instance 
‘I’ is not the mind, the intellect, ego or subconscious, nor is ‘I’ 
the senses of hearing, seeing, smelling, tasting and touching; 
nor is ‘I’, the five elements; but ‘I’ is the all-auspicious Siva, 
of the form of consciousness, Bliss. Next, are negated the five 
pranas, the five upapranas, the seven datus (blood, flesh, 
fat, bone, marrow and semen), the five kosas, the five motor 
organs, and ‘I’ is affirmed as the nature of consciousness, 
Bliss; then likes-dislikes, greed, delusion, passion and jealousy 
(shatūrmi – the six defects) and the four purushartas (dharma-
cosmic law, artha-wealth, kama -desire and moksha -release), 
including liberation – for liberation is the counterpart of 
bondage; both of which need be transcended – are negated 
and ‘I’ is affirmed as the nature of Pure Consciousness,Bliss.

Then comes the negation of merit and demerit, happiness 
and misery, sacred sound sylables and holy waters, the deities 
and sacrifices, enjoyer, enjoyed and what is enjoyed, fear of 
death, distinctions in social status, parents, one’s own birth, 
relations and friends, preceptors and disciple. Finally the 
negation of all these must be followed by the afrmation of 
the truth “I without form and thoughts, am, the all-pervasive 
Lord, with organs everywhere, always in a state of equipoise 
where there is neither bondage nor liberation but the pure 
Consciousness-Bliss-Absolute – the Great Siva-Brahman.” 
In short, that hymn is the condensation of this treatise.

Brihadaranyaka Upanishad.

Paraphrase: 
Oh, Noble Lady, the form of Awareness! I have 

expounded until now, the nature of Knowledge, the 
Svarūpa lakshana of jñāna (the characteristics of It), in 
order that everyone may attain the state of mukti (abiding 
as Ātman) which, however, is ever attained. Now, with 
perfect repose and attention hear me pronounce on the 
conduct, way of life, and practices to be observed by the 
seekers.
Commentary: 

The Lord says that “mukti, the unalterable state of Eternal 
Bliss is attainable by all and, the nature and characteristic of 
jñāna, the ways and means of achieving it, were all spelt out 
by Me”. Now He proceeds to instruct about the ācharas – 
practices – to be observed, as requested by the Devi earlier.

Āchara is the traditional way of life and other observances 
prevalent from ancient times. This is called purvāchara – 
āchara practiced and handed down from the time of the 
forefathers of our great culture. The observance of āchara 
or practices pertaining to a particular community or kula is 
called kulāchara and those pertaining to a particular religion 
(madham) are called madhāchara. Likewise there are 
kalāchara (kala-art, pertaining to arts), desāchara (desam-

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   162 06-05-2011   10:53:45



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 163

country, pertaining to regions) and the āchara followed in 
Mutts – the treasure houses of jñāna – called jñānāchara 
and the observances of disciples (sīdar) called sidāchara or 
sishtāchara.

What is dealt in further detail here is the body of disciplines 
and practices to be observed by the seekers of knowledge. 
The essential basis of any āchara is to safeguard and protect 
the execution of endeavours to accomplish the ideal or the 
goal chosen, even as a fence protects young plants. By strict 
adherence to the prescribed āchara (discipline and conduct) 
the mind is restrained within bounds without dissipating 
its energies in distractions due to its essentially fissiparous 
tendencies. Practice of āchara helps the mind remain still 
and moveless by purging it of its impurities and by providing 
clarity and momentum to the pursuit of Ātma vichāra. 

The Lord says “I shall deliberate in detail, the disciplines 
of āchara so that all can gain release and also those by 
observance of which they may not slip from the state so gained. 
And listen with a single pointed attention.”

While some of the ācharas that He spells out relate to the 
purity of the body, others pertain to the purity of speech and 
mind to facilitating the plunge inward. Āchara is nothing but a 
command or an injunction to perform or observe some things 
and desist from others. The type of Āchara, and the practical 
observance or execution of it, verily reveal the character and 
conduct of a person.

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 165

Commentary: 
The Lord who bade Devi listen to him describe the 

āchara for seekers in the earlier verse now enumerates all 
the observances normally practiced earnestly by seekers 
of Truth and exhorts that giving them up in toto is the only 
āchara demanded of them. “It is enough that a person becomes 
antarmukti (inward-turned). The śāstras are not needed for an 
inward-turned mind. They are meant for the rest.”         
(Talks no. 513).

All the prescribed ācharas are only for the attainment 
of purity of mind and single-pointedness. For a jñānābhyasi 
(a practiser of jñānamārga), with his mind clear and pure, 
none of these need be observed. “He whose body, words and 
mind have grown pure, to him every foot step is a place of 
pilgrimage; he whose heart is impure and defiled, to him then 
even, the holy Ganges is a thing more hated and worse than 
the Kikata country.” (Devi Bhāgavatam, 4-8-28)

Scriptures very emphatically declare non-performance of 
actions by a mature person pursuing Self-enquiry is no sin, 
for Self enquiry is itself the meritorious and most purifying 
of actions. 

“One who has firmly set his foot on this path of enquiry 
for Realization, need not care for Vedic commandments on 
works.” (Bhāgavatam, 11-20-4).

But Brahman or Ātman is Sarva Rasah – all essence – and 
bathing in it is the holiest of dips.

These ācharas are not only redundant, but may prove 
even a hindrance in the path, because observance of āchara 
is external while the path of jñāna is inward-turned.

Places where the rivers like the Ganges and the Yamuna 
flow are holy dips in them, daily homas like Ganapathy Homa 
and Samithadhana, chanting of sacred mantras (japas) like 
panchakshara, ashtakshara, daily worship of deities, etc. are 
all not for them.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   165 06-05-2011   10:53:45



166 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Besides these, Brahma yagna performed by nithyagnihotris 
(those who perform ritualistic offering in fire daily), 
vaisvadevam, sthali pākam (various kinds of homas) or the 
much celebrated yagas (elaborate ritualistic offerings in fire 
on a big scale) like vajapeya or those that occupy the pride 
of place as of exceptional greatness and other exalted deeds 
performed in agni are not for them.

The ritualistic portion (karma kanda) of Vedas that 
deals with these yagas and yajñas is sweet with promises 
of enjoyments as fruits of ritualistic works but they do 
not enlighten man on his ultimate good. Worship is only 
meditation within. There is no other worship of the Supreme 
Self equal to this. This God, who is of the nature of one’s own 
Consciousness, is not worshipped by oblations.

They are means to stimulate men of inertia to higher goals.
The heavenly joys of celestial worlds promised as rewards 

of such ritualistic karma are as transient and dreamlike as 
those of this world and end only in misery and they cannot 
life-long be mistaken for Satchitānanda.

In fact the performance of karma is enjoined only for 
release from karma which ironically entails more fetters, 
though golden.

The Vedic rituals, even if performed without any 
interruption and hindrance or breach of procedure yield only 
perishable results and requires repeated embodiments. Since 
all joys from Brahma loka to Vaikunta are imagined in the 
Ātman – Jñāna, paroksha and aparoksha (indirect and direct) 
– is the best yagna. 

Even Ganga, the greatest of sanctifying agencies, can 
purify men only through long and continuous contact. But men 
who are in contact with ‘That’ can purify even that Ganges. 
Ātma tirtha is the one everybody should have a dip in and 
there is nothing greater or holier than that. Bhagavan very 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   166 06-05-2011   10:53:45



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 167

emphatically declares: “The body is a corpse. So long as one 
is in contact with it, one must bathe in the water of the Self.” 
(Talks no. 252).

As for puja and devotion, Bhagavan says “Meditation on 
the Self is devotion to the Lord Supreme, since He abides as 
this Our very Self.” (Stray Verses, no. 13).

Therefore a seeker after truth must prevent his mind 
from being enticed away by any of these practices; but 
gathering his mental energies and intent on Ātma vichāra must 
pursue it rigorously. Gītā declares “na hi Jñāna sadrusam, 
pavithramiha vidyate”- nothing purer than Jñāna is known. 
(Chap. 4, verse 38).

Natesa Iyer was an exemplary devotee of Bhagavan. 
He was a very self-effacing man, always ready to serve the 
devotees of Bhagavan at all times of day and night. 

He did his panchāyatana puja (daily worship of five 
deities) in the area adjacent to the cowshed for a long time 
and it had become a life-long habit with him. When Bhagavan 
would walk by the cowshed every morning Natesa Iyer would 
invite Bhagavan to inspect his idols to which worship would 
have just been completed. Bhagavan also would look at them 
and nod his approval. 

One day when as usual Natesa Iyer invited Bhagavan to 
view the Gods Bhagavan looked up and asked him, “Are you 
still doing this?”

Iyer felt a strong quivering sensation fill his body as 
Bhagavan spoke these words. Realising that Bhagavan wanted 
him to abandon this practice, he threw the box containing the 
idols reverentially into the Pāli Tīrtham and felt no remorse 
or regrets afterwards. Mahānirvana Tantra (a hymn) states:

“I bow to Thee, the pure Consciousness
  .............................................................
 The Purity of all purifiers

Who stands complete within and without.”

Commentary: 

Vedantic texts prescribe various types of yamās and 
niyamās (canons of internal and external disciplines) for 
seekers right from āsana (posture) to ahara (food) in great 
detail. The greatness and glory of hallowed kshetras (places) 
and the deities that remain spreading grace in such places, 
procedures of ritualistic worship, the profferring of puja and

the most holy Ganges and other holy waters on earth and 
pilgrimage to holy cities like Ayodhya, Mathura, Maya, Avanti, 
Kasi, Kanchi and Badri called mōkshapuris (cities that grant

170 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Release) are explained elaborately in their respective Sthala 
Purāṇas – Purāṇas pertaining to those holy places.

Similarly offering of thila tharpana (sesame seeds and 
water) for the manes and forefathers, thirta pindas (offering 
of food for the manes at holy waters) and observance of 
srārdha ceremonies (performance of homa, offering oblation 
in agni for the welfare of the departed souls on their death 
anniversaries) are also dwelt in at great length in the Vedas.

Observance of celebrated vows on Mahasivaratri, 
Vaikunta Ekādasi, Pradōsham, Janmāshtami and Sri Rāma 
navami and the fruits of such observances are spoken of in 
Vratha kalpas (compendium on such observances).

Thēsār Vrathangal refer to potent and instantly fructifying 
vrathās of great fame, vrathās that are full of tejas or light 
that assure enlightenment. Performance of Puthra kamēshti 
yaga desiring progeny, Sudarsana homa to vanquish enemies, 
Varuna sukla japa praying for rains are all capable of yielding 
the desired results immediately.

The performance of all these karmas demands mental 
activity but what is required of a jñānābhyasi (a practiser of 
the path of jñāna) is to restrain the mind within, in an effort 
to know the Self. Therefore not even a single one of them is 
necessary or recommended.

Karma, be it good or bad, is not an antidote for karma. 
Karma begets results which again give place to karma. No 
karma can permanently efface the joys and sorrows resulting 
from karma. All karmas good, bad or expiatory ones, are the 
products of avidya. It is with the same linga (subtle) sarira 
with which a man performs actions here without stop till 
liberation, that he enjoys the fruits of action in the hereafter. 
This ‘I’ sense rooted in the subtle-body uses the gross body as 
an instrument. Therefore effects of action accrue to the subtle 
body which transmigrates with tendencies acquired from 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   170 06-05-2011   10:53:45



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 171

works and enjoys them in other worlds. Karma is prescribed 
for the release from karma. The Lord says “Oh, Uddhava 
abandon reliance on the scriptural injunctions and prohibitions, 
the ways of work and of renunciation, what you have learnt 
and what you hope to learn – surrender your entire being, 
body, mind and soul to Me – the all comprehending One, the 
Essence within all embodied beings.” (11-12-14, 15). In the 
words of Bhagavan, “but for those who follow the jñāna or 
vichāra mārga (the path of Self-enquiry) their sādhanā is itself 
quite enough for acquiring all daivic qualities; they need not 
do anything else.” (Day by Day, 18th July 1946).

“Through nāma-japa, the person who owns the name 
is reached....For the thinking mind, that is intent upon 
enquiring into the Self, ‘I’ is like a name. At this stage of 
practice, Self-enquiry is thinking of a name or a japa.” 
(Advent Souvenir, page 89).

Bridharanyaka Upanishad says “aham nāma abhavat” 
(He became ‘I’ named). 

That is the first name of Reality.
Bhagavan very emphatically remarks that the eradication 

of the identification with the body is charity, spiritual 
austerity and ritual sacrifice, it is virtue, divine union and 
devotion. It is heaven, wealth, Peace and Truth, it is grace, 
it is the state of divine silence, it is the deathless death, 
it is jñāna, renunciation, final liberation and bliss. And 
again “Only the Pure Being-Consciousness is the true God 
who is worthy of being worshipped by the assembly of 
the jīvas. As consciousness is the real nature of Siva only 
enquiry into consciousness is the true worship of Siva”. 
(Pādamālai, page 57, Verses 97 and 98).

Tapas, as Bhagavan indicated to Ganapathi Muni, is to 
let the mind subside where ‘I’ rises and japa is to let the mind 
subside where the sound of mantra rises from.

172 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Is it not a wonder then that Ganapathy Muni, extremely 
gifted from childhood, having mastered all the Sanskrit 
scriptures and performed crores of japas yet wanted to know 
from Bhagavan, who was not formally trained in any of these 
but ever steeped in the Self, what true tapas is?

This is but a proof of what the scriptures declare: That rare 
soul whose mind gets firmly fixed in that Pure Awareness even 
for a kshana (equal to 4/5 of a second) through deep reflection 
and meditation on Brahman attains the result which is greater 
than what one gets through holy baths in all the sacred waters, 
through offering in charity the wealth of the whole world to 
pious and worthy souls, through propitiation of all the manes, 
gods and the hosts of celestials by offering libation of water 
and other rituals, through the chanting of holy mantras billions 
of times and through hard penance practised for long periods, 
all put together. Bhagavan reaffirms it in Ramana Gītā (Chap. 
11, Verse 19): 

“Natural abidance in the Self alone is difficult penance.
 By such penance one is ripe from moment to moment.”
During his early days of life at the ashramam, Muruganar 

used to perform the ritualistic ceremonies prescribed on 
the death anniversaries of his parents. Muruganar knew 
that Bhagavan did not consider rituals important. Not 
withstanding it, once for his mother’s ceremony, he brought a 
large jack fruit with the intention of serving it to everyone in 
the ashram during lunch in memory of his mother. On seeing 
him with the fruit Bhagavan exclaimed: “I see the vāsanās 
have not yet released thir hold.” Immediately Muruganar 
exclaimed that he would henceforth never repeat such an 
act. It is true Bhagavan’s answers to questions varied from 
individual to individual and they were in tune with the 
level of competence of the devotee. But to devotees of the 
“inner circle” – those who followed Self-enquiry or who had 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   172 06-05-2011   10:53:45



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 173

surrendered totally to him – he always suggested refraining 
from actions.

Ramanatha Brahmachari, gave up his family and a 
potential career to be with Bhagavan. Once when Bhagavan 
found him fasting as he had to perform ceremonies for his 
ancestors he told him, “Now that you have come to me, you 
need not perform these any longer...You are not bound by 
these rituals anymore.”

Lord Krishna also says: “Abandoning all duties come to 
Me alone for shelter. Be not grieved for I shall release thee 
from all evils.” (Gītā, Chap. XVIII, Verse 66).

“Not letting the proud and frenzied mind roam about 
suffering in the company of senses but resting it in the heart 
with Siva, Pure Awareness, is tapas according to ascetics.” 
(Guru Vāchaka Kovai, Verse 409).

The karmas enjoined by the śāstras, called vihita 
karma (positive commandments) and the canons of conduct 
prescribed for the respective ashramas, even observances of 
ordinary dharmic (virtuous) acts, meritorious acts of offering

be given up in entirety is the advice. The only fruit of karma 
is chitta suddhi (purity of mind) which paves the way for 
jñāna. “Chittasya Suddhaye karma na tu vastūpalabdhayē 
vastu siddhir vicharena na kinjith karma kotibihi” (vastu is 
attainable only by vichāra and never by crores of karmas) – 
(Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, Verse 11) One should start with karma 
(desireless) and then continue karma with meditation and 
therefore practise pure meditation leaving off karma and 
finally attain jñāna. 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   174 06-05-2011   10:53:45



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 175

Action, of whatever nature performed, is the charasteristic 
of desire. Jīva is verily the form of desire. Therefore worship 
of a deity or performance of karma, for fulfilment of desire, 
is worship of desire.

All karmas performed with a desire to enjoy happiness 
in any form in this world or in higher worlds come under 
apara vidya or those in the realm of ignorance. The result 
of karma itself is called loka – world – that which is seen or 
experienced. But yat drishyam tat nasyam – whatever is seen 
is perishable. Therefore all the worlds attained by karmas are 
thus perishable.

One who indulges in thoughts other than those of the Self, 
gets deluded by the diversity of objects seen which manifest 
themselves with distinctions such as merit and demerit in 
them. This necessitates the distinction between those actions 
to be followed (vihita karma) and those to be eschewed 
(nishita karma). As there is nothing other than the Self, a 
discriminating seeker has to transcend both.

As for the observance of auspicious times and days, they 
can adversely affect only worldly actions by the mind. For 
those in the pursuit of Enquiry,

	 “Auspicious is each day; benevolent
	 In aspect every planet; lucky
	 Is each conjunction. Every hour
 	 Is fit, fine and fresh for the bright
	 Unfading worship of the Lord.”
					     (Guru Vāchaka Kovai)
It may be remembered here that a hymn of Thevaram 

called Kolaru Pathikam, by Saint Jñānasambhandhar, asserts 
that all planets are auspicious for devotees of Siva and ends 
by saying anai namadhe (this is my command) thus stamping 
it with Supreme authority. Once, while reading this hymn, 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   175 06-05-2011   10:53:45



176 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Bhagavan tapped his chest thrice when he pronounced these 
words. What more proof need there be to impress on seekers 
that observances of all karmas are superfluous, nor is there 
any auspiciousness or inauspiciousness, in time or space, for 
seekers who have embarked on the path of enquiry. Just like 
the alluring speech of parents to persuade their children to 
take medicine, the Vedic statements imply an indirect purpose. 
As a medicine is given to cure a disease, so the karmas are 
ordained in the Vedas in order to free man from karma and 
not for continual indulgence in them, which makes one sink 
deeper in it. Karma is not an end itself. Just as the action 
in dream comes to naught on waking up, by the dawn of 
enlightenment, of the jñāna of ‘I am Brahman’, all the sanchita 
karma, done by body, speech and mind, gets destroyed, says 
Adhyatmopanishad: “Aham Brahmeti vijñānath kalpakoti 
shathargitam sanchitam vilayam yanti prarabadhath swapna 
karma vat”

Vichāra Bindu Upanishad exhorts “Virtue and vice, 
pleasure and pain are of the mind, not thine, Hey Saumya! 
Neither doer nor enjoyer art thou, Indeed thou art ever free. 
Renounce the ideas: I am the doer, I am the enjoyer. Be happy.” 
(Mantra 10).

The advice contained in the Upanishads (of Narada 
to Sukha) is this: “Do thou relinquish dharma (virtue) and 
adharma (vice) as well as truth and untruth. Having renounced 
both truth and untruth, do thou renounce that by which thou 
hast renounced these. Renounce dharma by suppression 
of the action of the mind, adharma by having no vicious 
thoughts, truth and untruth by knowledge and knowledge by 
ascertainment of the Supreme." In the Absolute, virtue, vice, 
duty or the absence thereof find no place.

Therefore the Self abidance that flourishes when one 
realizes one’s own true nature is the supreme dharma of sat-

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   176 06-05-2011   10:53:45



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 177

āchara. Living as the Self is the essence of all dharmas. “All 
other dharmas merge there.” (Pādamālai, page 134).

Cast away in toto all the highly praised practices 

and disciplines of the religion you are born into, without

of dharma end up as bondage. All the mental conflicts

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   177 06-05-2011   10:53:45



178 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

into, the caste-based dharma (code of conduct) and the 
attachments for them – put them all away from you.
Commentary: 

One is necessarily born in a particular caste, belonging 
to a particular religion. It is but natural for such a one to 
live observing the code or canons of conduct relating to that 
particular caste and religion. This habit is inherited from days 
of yore. All these ācharas of caste and religion, we are told 
with sternness, to renounce in their entirety, for they all end 
up as bondages. 

Whatever act is performed one is bound by the fruit of 
that action. Unless the fruit is exhausted as experience it does 
not get spent; nor does it end with it; but goading one into 
further action through latencies, plunges one into the ocean 
of karma and drowns one in it. 

Saṁkalpas (resolutions of willing and wishing) are subtle 
in nature but actions are gross in nature. Saṁkalpas are the 
subtle seeds for the flowering of them into actions. Whatever 
saṁkalpas were willed earlier appear as real life experiences 
later on. External karmas are the gross manifestation of 
subtlest saṁkalpas. Movement of the subtle mind is karma. 
That which is ‘moveless’ is Brahman. Akarma is Brahman. 
Vāsanās of the caste one is born into, the caste-behaviour and 
the attachments to them, all cause further embodiments and 
will not ferry one across to the shore of mukti.

The nature of embodiment is determined by the quality of 
acts performed. Avidya or nescience gives rise to desire which 
in turn gives rise to karma. Karma is the cause of embodiments 
which reinforce nescience. Jīva bhava is not just the result of 
nescience, but jīva bhava itself is the nescience!

Bhagavan, in an answer to the question whether if the 
seeker after Truth refrains from following the dharmas of 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   178 06-05-2011   10:53:45



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 179

varna and ashrama his sādhanā would become impaired, 
states “the Supreme purpose of all other observances is 
abidance in jñāna. Therefore there is no strict injunction 
that one who ever practises the path of jñāna is bound to 
adhere to the disciplines of the respective ashrama he is in. 
If he follows the dictates of varna and ashrama it is to be of 
help to the world. He does not gain anything by observing 
them nor does he lose any by non observance of them.” 
(Spiritual Instructions, II, no. 30).

Therefore, without pondering over the nature of actions, 
and without the least hesitation, all karmas must be abandoned, 
and they must be put away in such a way as not to give them a 
chance to delude the mind again in the form of fresh or  even 
renewal of old attachments. 

The truth is that all karma, of whatever kind, will lead to 
fresh bondage. That is why it is said in Ozhivil Odukkam that 
a Guru who prescribes fresh karma or action of any sort i.e. 
rituals or other sacrifices to anyone who, after trying various 
karmas comes to him for peace, is both Brahma and yama to 
the disciple, he only creates fresh births and deaths.	  

Once Narada approached Sanatkumara beseeching him 
for instructions for attaining peace and tranquility which has 
been eluding him all along. Sanatkumara, after initiating 
him into a very potent mantra, gave elaborate instructions 
as to the conduct of the worship of the deity whose mantra 
he was initiated into. It required collection of 1008 flowers 
of a particular colour for each day. This act and the process 
of worship proved to be onerous, and to his dismay, Narada 
found that, the cumbersome process robbed him of even the 
little peace of mind that he had had before he approached 
Sanatkumara. He went back to his preceptor and requested 
him to be released of the new karma he had taken on. 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   179 06-05-2011   10:53:45



180 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Then, Sanatkumara taught him the secret of and the path 
of knowledge. Karma can not liberate a seeker but only 
strengthens his fetters.

All the entities other than the Ātman are false. So the body 
and all the institutions, ends and practices based upon this 
false multiplicity like varanashrama, social order, the duties 
and religious practises based on it, all resolves , positive and 
negative, and doubts are all equally false like the objects seen 
by a dreamer. Of all ācharas (external religious observances) 
Sat-āchara – abidance in the Self – is the best. Living as the 
Self is the essence of all dharmas and one’s own dharma 
(swadharma) is to abide in one’s Svarūpa.

Therefore “There is no need for a mantra or japa or 
dhyāna or anything of the sort, because these are our real 
nature. All that is needed is to give up thinking of objects 
other than the Self. Meditation is not so much thinking of 
the Self as giving up thinking of the non-self. When you 
give up thinking of outward objects and prevent your mind 
from going outwards and turn it inward and fix it in the Self, 
the Self alone will remain.” and “Regulation of life, such as 
getting up at a fixed hour, bathing, doing mantra japa, etc., 
observing rituals, all this is for people who do not feel drawn 
to Self enquiry or are not capable of it. But for those who can 
practise this method all rules and discipline are unnecessary.” 
(Day by Day, 18-7-46).

182 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Commentary: 
Of all the obstacles that block the spiritual progress of an 

aspirant in the spiritual path, siddhis are the most dangerous. 
Only he who escapes the lure of siddhis can make it to the 
state of mukti from where one never returns to the earthly life.

Rasayana siddhis, siddhis akin to alchemy are equally 
powerful as the ashtamasiddhis (eight fold) like anima and 
mahima. They are broadly classified into pāthālanjanam 
bhūtanjanam and chōranjanam.

The alchemy like pāthālanjanam reveals treasures lying 
buried under the earth. Bhūtanjanam commands mastery over 
the five elements by which their qualities are controlled and 
conditioned to one’s will.

Moving to and fro invisible to others and to make what is 
invisible to others visible is called chōrajanam. The movement 
of siddha purushas imperceptible to others is like this. A 
withered and dead tree can be turned green and live or a green 
and flourishing tree with fresh verdure may be made to wither 
away and die, by these siddhas.

Even if these siddhis come to the seeker directly, on their 
own, the seeker should abjure them without getting caught 
up in them by developing mental attachments to them. The 
word oruvuha (thou shalt remain anchored away from these) 
is verily a command for the seekers.

The powers of siddhis are legion and countless are the 
miracles that can be performed with them. An elephant in 
rut, capable of breaking a stone pillar it is tied to, can be 
made to obey commands. Cruel predators like tigers and 
bears can be bound, unable to open their mouths. One 
can ride on the back of the lion, the king of animals. The 
venomous cobra can be taken out from the ant hill and 
made to dance. Iron can be transformed into gold. One 
can become invisible to the whole world. Devas can be 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   182 06-05-2011   10:53:46



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 183

ordered to stand in attendance on and a youthfulness, that 
withers not, can be enjoyed, one can walk on water and 
lie on fire. Such incomparable siddhis can be gained but 
restraint of chitta (mind) and remaining still is rarer and 
more difficult than all these, says Thayumanavar.

“The highest siddhi is realization of the Self.” declares 
Bhagavan. (Sat Darsana Bhashya, XXII)

“The eight great siddhis will reach the presence of and will 
sport before those whose hearts are naturally established in 
Seld-abidance. Those who rejoice, having subsided in Sivam 
will not pay even the slightest attention to these (siddhis) that 
only cause sorrow.” (Pādamālai, page 131, v. 32 63).

Showing that which is not, as if it is, is siddhi. Enjoying 
‘what is’ is jīvanmukti.

The best example of someone who already had 
thaumaturgic powers and learnt to move away from them 
by the advice of Bhagavan is that of Humphreys. He asked 
Bhagavan “Can I perform miracles?” “The master noticed 
his bent, and fearing his yielding to meretricious charms of 
siddhi showed him that the chief thing was to push on in one’s 
effort to reach the Highest, the Self.” He said, “Clairavoyance, 
clairaudience and such things are not worth having, when 
much far greater illumination and peace are possible without 
them than with them”. Further “when the whole thought 
in meditation is fixed unmovably on ‘That which sees’ the 
result will show in four or five months time – in all sorts of 
UNCONSCIOUS clairvoyance, in peace of mind, in power 
to deal with troubles, in power all round, always unconscious 
power.” (Self Realization, Chap. 18).

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 185

Furthermore, they drag the jīva to vile ways and lowly 
behaviour causing the ruin of him. How can people, who long 
only for stale gruel, know or enjoy the plentiful nectar that 
flows in the high Heaven of Infinite Awareness? For a mind 
enveloped in such wicked ways, the horizon of Release recedes 
forever. Bliss of Release lies in the Supreme Awareness, where 
the mind, stilled from its activity, is hushed into silence but 
never in a mind that revels and dances among the siddhis.

Bhagavan, in verse 16 of Supplementary Verses to Reality, 
speaks of this:

   “Peace of mind is moksha, ever present.
	 Siddhis arise from movement of the mind.
	 How can those who hanker after siddhis
	 Know moksha’s bliss, the stillness of the mind?”
If an aspirant were to indulge in siddhis that come and 

sport, on their own, half way through the pursuit of the path 
of jñāna, the net gain is the pompous growth and swelling of 
the roots of the ego and not the release from bondage. With 
the waxing of the ego, the strangle hold of bondage grows in 
size and strength. This is the import of what is meant by “this 
is but bondage for the jīva”. Bhagavan clarified a doubt of a 
devotee in this respect by answering thus: “People anxious 
for siddhis are not content with their idea of jñāna and so 
want siddhis associated with it. They are likely to neglect the 
Supreme happiness of jñāna and aspire for siddhis. For this 
they are going through the bye-lanes instead of the royal path 
and so will likely lose their way... In fact jñāna comprises all 
and a jñāni will not waste even a thought on them. Let people 
get jñāna and then seek siddhis if they so desire” and again

“In Halāsya Mahima (the glory of Madurai) there is a 
chapter on eight-fold siddhis. There Siva says that His bhakta 
never wastes a thought on them. Again Siva says that he 
never grants boons. The desires of the devotees are fulfilled

according to their prārabdha only. When Iswara himself says

who displays them. Therefore siddhis are not worthy of any 
thought. Jñāna is to be aimed at and gained.” (Talks no. 57).

Paraphrase: 
In all states of being, driving away the weariness of

Commentary: 

No cause should be entertained, resulting in an adverse 
effect on the progress of the yoga that is practised, even if it be 
due to extraordinary or special reasons. The mind should ever 
be anchored on the thoughts of Ātman. If, due to any doubt 
in the efficacy of this royal path of Kala jñāna, chosen and 
practised, if a seeker is lured by the thrill or joy of proffering 
worship in a kshetra or to the deity of a kshetra, that delusion 
should be rejected forthwith. The natural Awareness shining 
in perfect stillness in the Heart within the temple of this 
body, is the real God Supreme and not any name and form. 
Constant remembering of and abiding as That constitutes true 
worship. (Kshetra is the holy place where a deity dwells and 
kshetrapida is the temple where the presiding deity resides 
spreading grace.). 

A number of pilgrimages to holy places and worship of 
deities there coupled with holy dips in sanctified waters has 
fruited in seeking Ātmajñāna and choosing this direct path by 
ripened competence. But the residual vāsanās like the thrill 
of the joy of worship and the zeal left behind by the seeker’s 
performance of such actions in the past may try to propel him 
again into the same fields of actions.

It is but natural to experience delight even at the mere 
thought of it for he had performed it all earlier whole-heartedly. 
But all these are positive hindrances to the experience of the

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   188 06-05-2011   10:53:46



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 189

Paraphrase: 
Oh my dear wife, listen. Only that discerning man 

who never harms any form of life like insignificant 
insects, worms, crawling, birds, trees, shrubs and creepers 
and never does any act that brings about the destruction 
of these, is a true practicer of jñāna, ever seeking true 
Awareness, the form of wisdom. Know this.
Commentary: 

Ahiṃsā or non-injury is the noblest and foremost of all 
the vows, to be observed by a seeker of liberation. Bhagavan 
once remarked: “Ahiṃsā stands foremost in the code of 
discipline for the yogīs”. A devotee then said, “Plants have 
life” and Bhagavan completed, “So too the slabs you sit on.” 
(Talks no. 23).

Even if one does not directly destroy them, actions 
causing their ruin should be refrained from.

A wise man of discrimination must remain ever seeking 
the Self, causing no injury to any life. This is the true hallmark 
of one who practises the direct path of jñāna. All forms are but 
forms of the Lord. A rigorous adherence to this principle of 
non-injury by itself will enable one reach the shore of mukti. 

Bhagavan was very emphatic about this rule. When 
someone asked whether one should endure the mosquito bite 
and not kill him, his answer was, “You do not like to suffer 
yourself. How can you inflict suffering on others? Just keep 
off mosquitoes since you suffer by their stings.” (Talks no. 53).

Bhagavan found all nature pulsating with life and light. 
While the ordinary perception is vitiated by attitudes of 
distinction towards fellow human-beings, animals, insects 
and trees, for jñānis like Bhagavan, there is but one yardstick: 
that no harm should befall even a blade of grass. Once when 
Bhagavan saw an ashram worker cutting down ripe coconuts 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   189 06-05-2011   10:53:46



190 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

he enquired whether the rod used had a bamboo or iron bit 
attached to the end of it. When he was told that it was an iron 
piece, he silently walked away. But paying no heed to what 
transpired the use of iron sickle was continued. Sometime 
later during this operation, a coconut fell on the forehead of 
that man and struck his nose very painfully. When Bhagavan 
came to know of it, he remarked, “Now he will know what 
is to be hurt and how much his iron sickle must have hurt the 
uncomplaining trees.” (At the Feet of Bhagavan, page 36).

Once Bhagavan caught someone plucking fruits from a 
tree during night and chided, “Won’t you let the tree sleep in 
peace? Can you not pluck the fruits during the day time? Have 
a heart. Merely because the tree cannot express its woe should 
you be so cruel?” (Krishna Bhikshu in Unforgettable Years).

Ramakrishna Paramahamsa also once complained of 
unbearable pain in his body when one of the visitors was seen 
walking on the lawn grass.

Once a sadhu was seen helping a scorpion that had 
accidentally fallen into the water of a river and struggling. 
The sadhu who had gone to the river, saved the scorpion with 
a help of a leaf and left it on the bank of the river, but was 
stung by the scorpion. But by mistake it again fell into the 
river. The sadhu, not withstanding the sting of the scorpion 
saved it again in the same way but unfortunately, this time 
also was stung by it. A third time, a fourth, fifth time also 
the same thing happened. Everytime the sadhu helped it but 
he got stung in the process. One who was observing all this 
asked the sadhu why did he have to save it in spite of being 
stung by it so many times. The sadhu replied, “To sting is its 
dharma; to save it is my dharma.” He is true one of wisdom, 
and a true practiser of jñāna.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   191 06-05-2011   10:53:46



192 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

of non-injury to all beings right from insects, birds, plants, 
the plucking of leaves and flowers, even for the worship of 
the Lord is, condemned here.

The pleasantly odoriferous cuscus root held most 
auspicious in worship and the fragrant holy basil leaves, the 
venerated vilva leaves held indispensable while proffering 
worship to Siva, the aromatic leaves of masipatram (Indian 
wormwood, Artimesia India), maruvu (another aromatic plant 
with fine smelling leaves), davanam (wormwood, artimesia) 
and kadirpachchai (austriasa) should not be removed from 
the mother plants heartlessly.

The mere, but kind, thought on the helplessness of the 
leaves and flowers that wither away, supportless when severed 
from their mother plants is indeed a sublime one containing 
the essence of the truth of ahiṃsā. 

The worship of the Lord is at its best when everything 
in creation is regarded as one’s ownself and no harm of any 
kind is meted out to them. As for naivedya or offering to God, 
Bhagavan said, “A little of what belongs to God is returned and 
nothing more. It is like pinching a small quantity of jaggery 
from a jaggery image of Lord Ganesa and offering it to him 
as Naivedya. To remain free from thoughts is the best offering 
one can make to God.” (Unforgettable Years, page 89).

He further commands that however vile, wicked and harmful 
beings may be, no harm need be done to them even if angered 
by them. Even animals, naturally wild and harmful, forget their 
natural instincts and become sadhus (tame and calm) on seeing 
such men, the very personification of mercy and compassion.

History speaks of two big cheetas lying down like meek 
lambs in the benign presence of Ēsanya Jñāna Desikar of 
Arunachala on either side of him which is proof indeed of wild 
animals becoming satvic in the presence of men practicing 
ahiṃsā.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   192 06-05-2011   10:53:46



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 193

The true hallmark and the distinctive characteristic of 
a man of knowledge is a life that means no harm or injury 
to any, not being harmed by any, with malice and anger 
towards none and in turn none with reason to harbour hatred 
or anger against him. Such a life is an authentic one worthy 
of emulation. 

That flowers should not be plucked callously was 
once taught by Bhagavan very effectively and forcefully to 
Lakshmiammal, his childhood playmate at Thiruchuzhi, when 
they were going round the Hill. At Sonatirtam captivated by 
the beauty of a laburnum tree (cassia fistula) in full bloom, 
luxuriantly laden with golden yellow flowers in profusion, it 
Lakshmiammal started to pluck them all. 

Bhagavan, on seeing Lakshmi plucking flowers asked: 
“What are you doing?” A shocked Lakshmi replied that she 
was plucking flowers for puja. Bhagavan noticed a heap of 
flowers already plucked on a cloth spread over the ground, 
and asked “There is plentiful already, why do you still pluck?” 
Lakshmi replied, “This tree so richly laden with blossoms, 
stands with such a profusion of flowers all of which are simply 
wasted. That is why, Bhagavan.” Bhagavan immediately 
spoke, “Yes, yes! Only you planted it, watered it. Don’t you 
have even this liberty? In your opinion if it is in such full 
bloom, it will not be beautiful. You have seen the beauty of 
it all. Nobody else should see it. Hence denude it completely. 
That is the fruit of worship.”

Lakshmi was taken aback. She, on realizing her mistake 
was startled and agitated. Subsequently whenever she saw a 
tree with flowers in profusion, folding her hands in reverential 
worship, she would mentally offer them all to Bhagavan saying 
“Iswara, oh Lord, all this is an offering unto you.”

When Bhagavan was in Virupaksha Cave, Echamma 
decided to do puja with a lakh of tender tulsi (basil) leaves 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   193 06-05-2011   10:53:46



194 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

to the picture of Bhagavan and Seshadri Swami in her house. 
When she was half way to her target summer had set in, and 
the leaves became scarce though she wandered all over the 
mountain to collect them. Tired, she ventilated her grievances 
to Bhagavan, who said “If you cannot get the leaves, why not 
pinch yourself and do puja?” When she said “That will be 
painful”, Bhagavan retorted “Won’t it be painful for the tree 
or bush when you pluck the leaves?”

These incidents prove beyond doubt the truth of the 
dictum that no flowers should be plucked heartlessly.

Mudaliar records another incident of harm done to a life 
incurring the displeasure of Bhagavan. Once a snake was 
seen by Chinnaswami and others in the ashram premises 
somewhere near Bhagavan’s hall. Suddenly cries as to “what 
kind of snake is it?” was heard and “Beat it, beat it”, followed 
by the noise of actual heating. Bhagavan immediately cried 
out “Who is beating it?” But the remonstrance went unheard 
and the snake was killed. Bhagavan said, “If these persons 
are beaten like that they will know what it means.” (Day by 
Day, 10-12-1945)

Everyone knows the episode of Bhagavan being stung 
by a host of hornets when their nest was accidentally brushed 
by his thigh while he was walking up the hill to reach the big 
banyan tree mentioned in Arunachala Mahatmyam, intrigued 
by the huge leaf of that tree he saw on the bank of a stream. 
Bhagavan patiently stood there allowing the mountain hornets 
to sting him thinking “for the misdeed I have committed, I 
must receive appropriate punishment.” Muruganar frames a 
question on this in a verse:

	 Putting your foot in what you thought
	 Was a green herb bush, you had it stung
	 By hornets till it swelled up big.
	 Why should you regret and pay for

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   194 06-05-2011   10:53:46



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 195

	 This accident at fault as if
	 It were intentional?
Bhagavan too replied in a verse:
	 If hornets sting and cause to swell
	 A foot that crushed their hidden nest
	 Should not the man regret the event
	 Accidental though it was?
Such is the compassion of a jñāni, who sees everything 

as the Self. The seeker should try and consciously cultivate 
the perception of viewing everything as the Self is the advice.

plucking of flowers and severing of leaves is prohibited for a
