Steering clear of from the performance of such worship, 
never should one resort to a whole host of heinous and cruel 
acts labelled as Kshudra karma, actions like chanting and 
performance of homas by which mastery over the exercise of 
cruel and destructive powers is gained with a view to harm 
enemies or persons disliked and to wreak vengeance on others.

Mārana is the way of causing ruination of persons or 
things that one does not like by the potent power gained by 
the repeated chanting of certain mantras intended for that 
purpose. Mārana homa is aimed to cause such death.

The homa that the rishis of Daruka forest performed to 
destroy Siva belonged to this category. Whatever emanated 
from the homa kunda, the fire pit, into which oblations were 
offered, was meant to kill Siva.

Undesirable paucity of strength and want of power of 
influence in chasing away one’s enemies or undesirable 
elements needles one to have recourse to Uchchādana 
(chanting of) the most potent mantra with infallible potency 
in achieving the intended purpose of driving people away.

Incited by jealousy at the close and cordial intimacy 
between two inseparable friends, some resort to the use of 
the power of mantras called vidveshana, thereby sowing 
seeds of discord between them that culminate in enmity and, 
inveterate hatred.

Sthambana is the use of the power of those mantras 
whereby the faculties, specially the faculty of speech, are 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   198 06-05-2011   10:53:46



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 199

immobilised or made to freeze, of one with name and fame, 
extensive erudition, excellent capabilities, sharp intellect and 
a life of honour and wealth. 

The one against whom this power is invoked becomes 
virtually dumb with qualities of head lost, sharpness of intellect 
blunted, courage replaced by cowardice and excellence of the 
power of speech frozen.

The highly extolled lives of others arouse the basest 
instincts of jealousy in some to assume such monstrous 
proportions as to force them to resort to such vile practices 
called abhichara or black magic. Such, indeed, are the lowest 
of the lowly.

The product of abhichara, if baulked of its prey, returns 
in fury to devour the sender. 

Bhagavan once stated that abhichara prayoga (resorting 
to black magic) is condemned in Devi Kālōttaram and by such 
practices one compasses one’s own ruin. “Avidya (ignorance) 
is itself bad and makes one commit suicide. Why should black 
magic be also added to it?” and he later said “bhakti is the 
remedy open to the victim of black magic.... This black magic 
is said to have been used even against the greatest saints in 
India since time immemorial. The tapasvis of Daruka forest 
used it against Siva Himself.” (Talks no. 517).

Arthur Osborne has recorded an instance of the practice 
of black magic of this type that he was subjected to. A friend 
of him who was a devotee of Bhagavan went to Kerala and got 
attached to a guru there and was frequently writing letters to 
Osborne to join him under that guru. When no response was 
evinced, the letters assumed a serious and threatening note. 
Osborne was in the habit of placing every letter he received 
for the perusal of Bhagavan. But one day while he was 
working in the garden, a half animal of huge size and of black 
hue suddenly jumped on him from behind and menacingly 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   199 06-05-2011   10:53:46



200 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

caught at his throat. Osborne was unperturbed and suddenly 
the sphurana of Arunachala Siva started spontaneously in his 
heart and kept up steadily till the beast loosened its hold and 
disappeared. When he reported this to Bhagavan, he remarked, 
“That is all they can do.”

It is but natural for beings to be afflicted with fever and 
be cured. Unlike this the fever invoked in one by virtue of the 
power of mantras chanted by another with evil intentions will 
not be contained by drugs or medicine, but will subside only 
when the chanting of mantras is discontinued. Activating evil 
spirits and powers of planets through the power of mantras 
causing irremediable ills and thereby unsettling others or 
subjecting persons of well-being to sudden and fast possession 
of uncontainable fury or causing people to be possessed by 
evil spirits and other such lowly acts are called abhichara.

“Good men worship the Gods, the passionate worship the 
demigods and the demons and others worship the spirits and 
ghosts.” (Gītā, Chapter XVIII, Verse 4) 

The other kshudra karmas are subordinating others to one 
through unethical and wrong means causing attraction and 
infatuation in others towards oneself even if those persons 
have no love or inclination towards one. Those on whom the 
power is exercised, losing their self-will, become bound like 
tame-lambs.

Such a kshudra upasaka worsipping such kshudra 
devathas (lowly deities) gains siddhi in the mantras respective 
to such deities. None of these is worth the slightest attention by 
a striver after Truth. They (such karmas) should be abandoned 
in their entirety. 

For the performance of such kshudra yoga, a figurine is 
made out of wood or stone or in a skull or of dried leaves, in 
which mantra is invoked and chanted continuously. A seeker 
who is wise and knowledgeable should keep himself as far 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   200 06-05-2011   10:53:46



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 201

away from any of these as possible. “Abandon puja in stone 
or wood” means this. This can also be interpreted in a general 
way as an instruction to avoid worship only in images of stone 
and wood, as the Lord is everywhere.

The uselessness of worship of such kshudra devatas is 
revealed by an incident that Yogi Ramiah once related to 
Bhagavan. A professional conjuror was displaying tricks in 
a street. A large crowd had collected and being curious, the 
yogī also joined the throng. By materialising real articles the 
conjuror had deluded the audience in an illusion, magical 
and spell binding. After exhibiting many such feats, he asked 
everyone what he wanted and materialised it immediately. 
When yogī’s turn came, he asked for hot and crispy pakoras 
(a tasty snack made out of gram flour). Immediately he waved 
his hand towards the sky and the next instant a packet of hot 
pakoras was in his hands which he handed over to the yogī. 
Wondering how the magical product would taste, he tried one 
and found it to be hot and tasty and was greatly astonished. 
After finishing the show the magician went round with an old 
tin box seeking and collecting money. When he came to yogī 
Ramaiah, the yogī questioned him “just as you materialized 
everything for others you can also materialize your needs and 
be happy without having to beg”.

But the story he heard made him feel sad. In order to 
make a kshudra devata carry out his commands he performed 
protracted worship of that deity in a cremation ground and 
finally he succeeded, but the condition was that he should 
never ask anything either for him or for his family. On finding 
out the futility of this upasana for himself, when he tried to 
wriggle out of the whole thing, the fruit of the act of worship of 
that kshudra devata had to be gone through otherwise, the deity 
threatened to devour him. Caught in such an entanglement 
he had to live the life of a beggar for the rest of his life. This 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   201 06-05-2011   10:53:46



202 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

is very much similar to the fate of. Dr. Faustus who sold his 
soul to Mephistophles.

Therefore, a seeker, by a careful enquiry into the worlds 
achievable by karma, must realize that the Supreme Content 
devoid of any action cannot be achieved by any karma.

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 203

Paraphrase: 
Renouncing the various mudhras practiced in the 

worship of deities dwelling in holy kshetras and the great 
yagas (sacrifices) that are performed with great fervour 
to please these deities and the vāsanās that the mind has 
become impregnated with on account of such practices in 
the past, contemplate only on the Self, the All-pervading 
Awareness, to gain eternal release.
Commentary: 

The kshetra pidas refer to the six plexuses or chakras 
imagined in the body and the devatas, to the deities presiding 
over the respective chakras. Kshetras may also stand for 
holy kshetras (centres of pilgrimage) and devatas, the deities 
presiding over these kshetras (holy places).

When the mind is fixed in any of these chakras or deities 
presiding over the chakras or kshetras, the mudhras (various 
mystic postures made by joining the fingers of the hands) 
appropriate to these deities are adopted and there are also 
various yogas associated with them. The Lord instructs that 
all these must be given up.

Even after such external practices are given up, the 
vāsanās that the mind has become impregnated with by virtue 
of having practised them along, will linger on. These manifest 
as thoughts about them. Extinguishing all thoughts of them 
must be the endeavour of a striver after Truth. Similarly yagas 
and yajñas also are to be eschewed.

Contemplation of the chit, the form of Awareness, is all 
that a seeker must practise. When the mind becomes single-
pointedly concentrated on that, all else drop off by themselves 
thus proving Bhagavan’s utterance in verse 5 of Ashtakam 
“When once a photographic plate is exposed to sunlight, can 
it receive impressions subsequently?”

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   203 06-05-2011   10:53:46



204 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

The mind that contemplates the content of Truth will be 
untouched by worldly attachment. Adhyatmic vāsanās are 
very much like the vāsanās of worldly attachment and hence 
excepting thoughts of Ātman all else must be banished from 
the mind is the exhortation of the Lord in this verse.

While worshipping the deities of the various chakras one 
moves from the lower plexus to the higher which involves the 
contemplation of one deity and then abandoning it and moving on 
to to the other. What appeared once as the True Content becomes 
false when one moves to another chakra. This being the case 
how can that nescience or jīvabodha which is unmanifest and 
strongly entrenched become fit enough to be abandoned as false? 
All these mental activities are carried on on the basis of the firm 
conviction of the Truth of jīvabhava – the nescience. Hence all 
mental activities must be given up is the exhortation. 

Bhagavan explains this: “Such concentration (on chakras) 
may lead to a sort of laya in which you will feel a certain bliss, 
but care must be taken not to lose the thought ‘I Am’ in all 
this.... Whatever the centre or object on which you concentrate, 
he who concentrates is always the same.”(Day by Day, 18 
and 22-7-46) and “nature of the one who concentrates must 
be known which is the goal of all sādhanās.”

(Verse 74 and 75 are kuḷakam - to be taken together)

Paraphrase: 
He is a mahayogī without a taint who is even sighted 

in the heart, equipoised towards all objects, without 
longing and affection for any object, with equanimity in 
the midst of happiness and misery, between friends dear 
as life and foes, non-different, evenly disposed towards 
a shred of pot and a costly piece of gold and with a mind 
turned inward, never swayed by desires nor yielding to 
gratification of the senses with objects of senses, who has 
destroyed the mamakara, the idea of mine within, has 
fortified the mind with discrimination and with fear and 
desire towards nothing, but ever revels in the Self alone.
Commentary: 

The natural attitude of an average man is one of 
indifference towards common place and ordinary objects, but 
towards valuable or uncommon objects the approach is one of 
desire with a view to gain possession of it. A mental attitude 
equal towards all perceived objects and persons, whatever be 
the difference in their nature, is a sine-qua-non for a seeker.

Dame Fortune being fickle and never the same life 
alternates between joy and sorrow. Elation of spirits in times 
of prosperity and dejection of spirits at times of adversity 
must be replaced by an attitude of equanimity towards both. 
An attitude of non-difference and equality between friends 
and foes must be developed consciously, instead of one of 
heart-felt pleasure and warmth at the sight of a bosom friend 
and of anger enmity and agitation roused by the sight of a 
foe, hated whole heartedly. The Antarātman in another body 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   206 06-05-2011   10:53:47



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 207

is hated by one with the sense of “I am the body”. He is a 
bheda darsi, one with diversity of perception, and such a one 
does not enjoy peace at heart.

“He who (behaves) alike to foe and friend, also to good 
and evil repute and who is alike in cold and heat, pleasure and 
pain and who is free from attachment is dear to Me.” (Gītā, 
Chapter XII, Verse 18)

A broken piece of pot of clay and priceless precious gem 
must be viewed equally with feelings and intention totally 
unchanged and uninfluenced by the difference in their nature 
and value. The best example of this can be seen from the life 
of Saint Appar.

Appar stayed in Thiruppakalur for sometime worshipping 
the Lord of that place, by singing many a decade on Him 
serving Him with reverence and love in his inimitable role of 
a servitor of the Lord. He rid the holy precincts of the temple 
of weeds thorns, bushes, shrubs, stones and pebbles on the 
pathways and grounds surrounding the main temple used by 
the devout. The Lord, with a view to reveal to the world his 
desirelessness for land and gold and his equanimous attitude, 
enacted a lila (divine play). While Appar was clearing the 
ground, with the hoe, wherever the hoe entered into the earth, 
He made that place fully strewn with priceless gems and 
precious stones. But Appar regarding them as nothing more 
than pebbles removed them with the hoe and threw them 
away, along with the stones and weeds. This proves that for 
the servitors of the Lord a priceless gem is no more than a 
clod of earth.

Gītā extolls such persons thus: “ He who regards pain 
and pleasure alike, who dwells in his own Self, who looks 
upon a clod, a stone, a piece of gold as of equal worth, who 
remains the same amidst pleasant and the unpleasant, who is 
firm of mind, who regards both blame and praise as one, who 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   207 06-05-2011   10:53:47



208 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

is the same in honour and dishonour, same to friends and foes, 
who has given up all initiative of action, he is said to have 
transcended the gunas. (Gītā, Chap. XIV, Verse 24 and 25).

Seekers may also remember how Saint Ramakrishna 
during his days of sādhanā, once held a piece of gold on one 
hand and a clod of earth on the other saying repeatedly “this 
is gold, this is sand”, for sometime, then threw both on them 
into the Ganges as valueless.

A couple, vanaprasthas, leading an ascetic life preparatory 
to embracing sannyāsa order, were walking in the forest. The 
husband was walking ahead and the wife following him at a 
little distance. The husband saw a shining bar of gold on the 
path. He, thinking that if his wife were to see it, she might 
feel attracted by it, covered it with earth. The wife who came 
after a few minutes, had noticed her husband’s action and also 
divined the sound motive behind his action. She asked him, 
“Why do you cover earth by earth?” It then dawned on the 
husband that while he still entertained the feeling of difference 
between gold and sand, his wife, free from such an attitude 
of distinctions, had more dispassion and equal vision which 
he himself was yet to attain and possess.

Unless an aspirant is equipped with an attitude of 
equanimity, he cannot realize the Content Beyond that is 
equally pervasive everywhere. Birds of the same feather alone 
can flock together.

A seeker should never allow the mind to entertain desires 
within for the enjoyment of sense-pleasures. “A sense object is 
more virulent than the poison of a king cobra. The latter kills 
only him who swallows it; the former brings about the death 
of him who merely looks at it.” (Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, Verse 78).

Hence vishaya (objects of sense pleasures) are worse than 
visham (poison). While the deer, elephant, moth, fish and the 
black bee meet with death, each guiled just by one of these 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   208 06-05-2011   10:53:47



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 209

senses, a man in whom all the five are active, falls certainly 
into the trap of transmigration unless he frees himself from 
the cord of sense attachment. Though the objects of senses 
are outside of us, the desire for them is strongly implanted 
within, on account of which, we claim ownership of and 
bind ourselves to, such objects as ‘mine’. ‘I’ and ‘mine’ are 
the strong and forceful factors, that cause the ruination of the 
life of jīva. When the sense of ‘mine’ that regards as one’s 
own what are outside, is relinquished with nothing to hold 
on to, ‘ego’ or ‘I’ will subside of its own accord. Hence the 
Lord instructs the seekers to give up the sense of ‘mine’ that 
consumes sense objects out of desire, by saying un mamadhai 
otti.

The accomplishment of this task requires an intellect 
that is robust and steadfast and a dispassion that is total and 
everlasting.

Just as even at the time of thinking of an object, the mind 
is already one with the object, while meditating on Brahman, 
that mahaśūnya, the mind and the senses attain oneness with 
the object of meditation, namely, Brahman. A dhira who 
has such extraordinary strength of mind, to abandon the 
‘mine’ and ‘I’, will have neither fear nor desire. He is called 
a māyogī, who ever revels in Ātman, free of fear or desire. 
Ānanda Bindu Upanishad states the same idea “Where there is 
no ‘I’ there is Release; where there is ‘I’, there is bondage. Man 
is bound by ‘mine’ but is released by ‘not mine’.” (Verse 6).

“Every gift implies unselfishness. That is the whole 
content of nishkama karma (unselfish action). It means true 
renunciation. If the giving nature is developed it becomes 
tyaga. .... Dana, dharma, nishkama karma are all tyaga only. 
When ‘mine’ is given up it is chitta suddhi (purified mind). 
When ‘I’ is given up it is jñāna. When the nature to give away 
is developed, it results in jñāna.” (Talks no. 581).

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   209 06-05-2011   10:53:47

Paraphrase: 
Flawless, ever equipoised, neither elated when highly

Commentary: 

The same-sightedness which a mighty yogī espouses is 
further explained in this verse.

One will not feel dejected or hurt when others revile at 
him, if he remains with the attitude of “Who is there that is 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   210 06-05-2011   10:53:47



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 211

alien to me? What does it matter what people say of me? What 
matters if I praise myself or blame myself?”

Likewise even when others praise one, if one remains in 
a state of equipoise unswervingly with the attitude of “what 
does it matter if one praises or blames oneself?”, sorrow born 
of censure or elation born of flattery or praise cannot touch one.

There is bondage when the mind wishes for anything, 
grieves at anything, feels unhappy at anything. There is 
Release when the mind wishes not, grieves not, feels not happy 
or unhappy at anything. (Vedāntasāra Upanishad, Verse 8).

In short Brahma Jñāna is the release from the 
trammels of one’s own mind. Such a release alone 
leads to the attainment of Moksha or real Swarajya. 
(Brahma Rahasya Upanishad, M. 20).

A yogī must be permanently equipoised with an even 
perception towards all lives, be it a cow or a venomous snake. 
Gītā says: “The wise see the same in a brahmin endowed 
with wisdom (the knowledge of the Self) and humility, 
a cow, an elephant, a dog and a (low-born) dog-eater.” 
(Chapter 5, Verse 18).

	 In my sight ‘I’ only am
	 And ‘you’ are not. In your sight
	 ‘You’ only are and ‘I am not’
	 In the sight of the Self, the Self alone
	 Exists and nothing else
	 In truth I, you, and all are nothing
	 But the Self.

(Guru Vāchaka Kovai, Verse 1245)
Such equanimity, even-sightedness and equipoise betwixt 

contrary circumstances can simultaneously dwell forever only 
in a yogī with jīvabodha dead. Gītā also affirms it: “He who 
sees the Supreme Lord abiding equally in all beings, never 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   211 06-05-2011   10:53:47



212 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

perishing when they perish, he verily sees. For, as he sees 
the Lord present, equally everywhere, he does not injure his 
true Self by the Self and then he attains to the Supreme goal.” 
(Chap. 13, Verse 28).

Such an yogī of even-sightedness indeed attains 
Brahmanhood. In short he is undistracted among distractions. 
Is not instructing the mumukshus to cultivate the nature of 
jīvanmuktas like putting the cart before the horse? A pen 
picture of the truly natural and exalted state is given in advance 
to act as a guide to destroy jīvabhoda. This can be understood 
in two ways. Cultivating these qualities will help one attain 
that state; or only when one abides in that state such qualities 
will manifest themselves. The goal is the same viewed either 
way. Bhagavan remarks “What is natural to the state of Self-
Realization forms the disciplinary course in the other state.” 
(Talks no. 491).

Paraphrase: 

One must eschew indulgence in fruitless disputations 
with others and also association with groups of worldly 
men speaking and seeking worldly matters. Vain quarrels 
among groups differing in faiths should be avoided. 
Keep away from and do not mingle with religious bodies 
learned in śāstras. Vile abusive language as well as

Commentary: 

A serious discriminating seeker who seeks to abide in 
the silence of mind and speech must eschew indulgence in 
vain debates and disputations, which, besides causing mental 
distress and agitations fattens the ego and makes it wax in 
size and strength. The very indulgence in arguments is due 
to the assertion of the ego. A love for the display of one’s gift 
of excellence in grandiloquent speech makes one seek out an 
audience. Hence verbal wrangles and the groups of worldly 
men associated with it must be steered clear of. 

“Skill in fluent speech, the proficiency in explaining 
the śāstras, the scholarship of the learned, all make 
only for personal enjoyment but not for liberation.” 
(Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, Verse 60).

Bhagavan very often used to say all books on the spiritual 
paths say “look at thyself” but when seekers unheeding, ponder 
over śāstras and discussions on them, they laugh at men.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   213 06-05-2011   10:53:47



214 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

As mentioned by Bhagavan in Ātma Vidya Keerthanam 
“Of what avail is knowing things other than the Self? And 
the Self being known, what other thing is there to know?” 
and again in Who am I? “to quieten the mind, one has only 
to enquire within oneself what one’s Self is; how could this 
search be done in books?”

Kalaham (putting one against the other or generating 
quarrel) has for its very nature the expertise in the 
reprehensible art of sowing discord where there is 
harmony. A mere clamour or noise is transformed into 
a formidable storm by creating misunderstanding and 
amity is converted into discord. Equally dangerous is the 
host of scholars of scriptures and śāstras. They lacking 
direct experience use their vast learning and scholarship 
to wax eloquent in vain dialectics and engage themselves 
in arguments. Brihadaranyaka Upanishad (4.4.21) also 
emphasizes, “Let that dheera (wise man) intent on realizing 
Brahman, attain prajñā. He need not acquire knowledge of 
the śāstras which is nothing but a burdensome exercise of 
speech.” Besides all texts teach the way to attain the Self 
after knowing which what is required is endeavour in the 
path informed. Of what avail can be the repeated reading 
and discussions of the śāstras?

If the Supreme Truth is not known (realized) learning 
of śāstras is of no use. If it is known (realized) then too 
knowledge of and the display of it is of no use.

A person cannot become a king by merely saying ‘I am a 
king’ if he has not killed the enemies and if he has not acquired 
the wealth of the whole earth. Those who have ‘attained’ do 
not dispute and those who dispute have not ‘attained’. They 
simply jump into the fray to prove their skill in śāstraic lore. 
Kannudaiya Vallalar compares them to the ‘pestle’ of the 
grinding stone, that mechanically goes over and over what is 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   214 06-05-2011   10:53:47



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 215

fed into the stone, totally unaware of the taste or the fragrance 
of what it helps to grind.

Those who possess a mere knowledge of śāstras and the 
observance of the practices bereft of the actual experience 
are no better than these grinding stones and are to be avoided 
diligently. They, who trying to attain the Ātman through such 
arguments, are like those who instead of walking with an 
umbrella or with shod feet to protect themselves from the 
heat of the sun and thorns instead trying to, accomplish the 
impossible task of covering the entire earth with leather or 
spreading a cloth over the entire sky. 

In the words of  Bhagavan “The Self is the real book, 
you can glance anywhere in that book; nobody can take 
it away from you. Whenever you are free turn toward 
the Self. Thereafter you may read whatever you like.” 
(Madhavatirta, Power of the Presence).

In short there is no māyā in whom there is no vidvadva 
– the prop of māyā.

Finally just as one discards with contempt vile and 
abusive language one should abandon also extolling verses 
of praise and flattery. These cannot be a greater foe in the 
guise of a friend than flattery for the ego to emanate and 
assert itself with a pompous flamboyance and vigour. One 
would do well to remember here the upadēsa of Bhagavan 
in verse 37 of Supplementary verses to Reality “If a man 
yields to the vile harlot of flattery, escape from thraldom is 
hard indeed.” Bhagavan never said anything good or bad of 
anyone. But if he were to hear about the demise of anyone he 
knew, he would immediately speak of the good qualities of the 
departed person. When somebody questioned Bhagavan about 
his not correcting people who behave strangely, Bhagavan 
replied “correcting oneself is correcting the whole world”. 
He said, “Who is to correct whom? Is it not the Lord alone 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   215 06-05-2011   10:53:47



216 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

who has the authority to correct everyone? All that we can 
do is to correct ourselves. That itself is correcting others.” 
(Ramana Darsanam, page 24).

Bhagavan never liked people to talk ill of others and 
would take the side of the accused party. Once when a 
rich lady complained that the out-caste boy whom she 
had adopted scooted away with some of her jewellery. 
Bhagavan said “Your jewels made you lose your boy.” 
(Moments Remembered by V. Ganesan).

Paraphrase: 
All distractions like jealousy that surges tumultuously 

from the heart, malicious tale-bearing (calumny) against 
others, pompous display, desire, consequent hatred 
when desire is thwarted, the desires that keep constantly 
springing up in the heart, anger, fear and grief must be 
removed gradually and completely.
Commentary: 

To turn green at the prospect of the well-being and 
prosperity of others is a demoniac trait and a sure gate-way 
to ruin and hell. An individual who allows jealousy to invade 
and aggrandise his heart gains neither happiness here nor 
the hereafter. History is replete with countless instances of 
deterioration and destruction as proof of this. In fact most of 
the maladies that the world suffers from today stem from envy.

“Those who forbear, get to rule the world while the 
jealous, like demons, are ruined” is an old saying. 

One who is a slave to pomp and show is the one who 
drowns indeed in the deep ocean of delusion and saṁsāra. He 
is one who forever desires to be viewed as incomparable by the 
world which in turn, necessitates the recourse to endless wants 
and desires. The sense of contentment eludes them forever. 
This is called raga – desire. When the aforesaid factors go 
against the wishes of a person and become adverse, hatred sets 
in. Desire thwarted, naturally inturn, yields to hatred. Desire 
becomes a driving passion for an object and hatred against 
what stands in the way of gratification of that passion, results 
in anger. When anger and passion transgress all proportions, 
detestable actions are resorted to. Fear of retribution for sinful 
deeds turns such a one into a grief-stricken coward. This 
‘chain-reaction’ results in a grievous life of misery. Gītā refers 
to this specifically when Arjuna asks why is sin committed 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   217 06-05-2011   10:53:47



218 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

at all? “This is craving, this is wrath, born of the mode of 
passion, all devouring and most sinful. Know this to be the 
enemy here.” (Chapter IV, Verse 10)

“As fire is covered by smoke, as a mirror by dust, as an 
embryo is enveloped by the womb, so is this (knowledge) 
covered by passion. Enveloped is Knowledge, O son of Kunti 
by this insatiable fire of desire which is the constant foe of 
the wise.” (Chapter III, Verses 37 to 39)

Hence He exhorts: “Delivered from passion, fear and 
anger absorbed in Me (the Self), many purified by the austerity 
of Knowledge, have attained to My State of being (Ātman).” 
(Gītā, Chapter IV, Verse 10)

Therefore attempts must be made consciously to put all 
these away from one gradually, is what the Lord prescribes 
for the attainment of Knowledge. Gradually – and to the 
extent possible – one must retire from the pursuit of ‘desires 
and ritualistic’ karmas. One becomes free to the extent one 
renounces, which is the way to eliminate sorrow, delusion and 
fear and establish one in Bliss.

Paraphrase:

Commentary: 

All the dyads like birth and death, good and bad, likes 
and dislikes must be despised and driven away as if dreams 
so that they do not follow one like shadows, to cause misery. 
Dwandwas (dyads) give rise to bandha or bondage.

“Identification with body is dvaita or duality and non-
identification is advaita.” (Talks no. 35).

The mind is the creator of the subject and object and is the 
cause of dualistic idea. When thoughts arise duality is present. 
The phenomenal world created by the mind teems with 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   219 06-05-2011   10:53:47



220 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

multiplicity. Duality or dwandwa, the belief in the existence 
of a second entity including that of the body, is the cause both 
of bondage and fear. Therefore the mind must be merged in 
the ego and the source of the ego must be sought. In the Self 
there is no duality for It is one only without a second and when 
one seeks the seer and finds the Self, the Heart springs open 
and all dyads and triads fly away.

The Lord exhorts one thus rid of ego to live in solitude, 
for living in a crowd may exteriorise the mind.

	 Of all the many qualities
	 Desirable in an earnest seeker
	 Of imperishable moksha, none
	  Is more essential than love
	  For the bliss of solitude.
		                     (Guru Vāchaka Kovai, Verse 908) 
Besides living in ekantha, solitude, far from the 

maddening crowd, one should aim at the solitude of the Self 
that is free from all attachments.

This solitude which is freedom from vāsanās, thoughts, 
memories and expectations, which are the bondage in reality, 
must be preferred.

In Upadēsa Manjari Bhagavan clearly states, as an answer 
to a question as to what is the meaning of dwelling in solitude 
(ekānta vasa): “As the Self is all-pervasive, it has no particular 
place for solitude. The state of being free from mental concepts 
is called "dwelling in Solitude.”

Once a priest wanted to know the meaning of the phrase 
Vivikta deśa sevitvam aratir jana saṁsadi (resort to solitary 
place and dislike a crowd of people), (Verse 10 in Gītā, 
Chap. VIII), Bhagavan replied “Vivikta deśa is that where 
there is nothing but the Supreme Self, the Paramātma. Aratir 
janasaṁsadi means to remain without getting mixed up with or 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   220 06-05-2011   10:53:47



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 221

absorbed by the five senses (vishayas). It is these five senses 
that rule the majority of people. Vivikta deśa is that state in 
which they are in abeyance.” (Letters, 28th Sep. 1947).

One who, rid of all attachments, stays ever established 
in the Solitude of the Self, becomes omniscient even while in 
the body and shines radiant like a thousand suns with a face 
cool, joyous and like a full blown lotus. In short he is verily 
the effulgence of Brahman.

He remains as the All and his Awareness is total. He 
remains as the ‘Eye’ of Consciousness, which alone is and sees 
everywhere. This pure awareness is Supreme omniscience. 
Though he may appear to be with a body in the perception 
of worldly men, in his perception, he is simply Awareness 
unembodied. In truth, in his perception there is nothing else 
but the Self, the unbroken Wholeness. He shines as All, and 
personifies total Awareness. Therefore true omniscience is 
direct experience of this non-dual Self and nothing else.

	 Contented with whatever comes
	 Free from duality and envy
	 The even minded Seer may act
	 And is not bound.
			    (Assorted Verse by Bhagavan, 26)
The contents of this verse and the previous one are also 

contained in Tejobindu Upanishad which declares, “Brahman 
is not known to those who are possessed of avarice, delusion, 
fear, egotism, lust, anger and sin, heat and cold, hunger and 
thirst, or mental resolve and indecision, or pride of birth 
or vanity in having read a mass of books on mukti. Nor is 
Brahman known to those who are sensitive to fear, pleasure 
and pain, honour and disgrace. To one free from these ideas, 
the Supreme Brahman becomes manifest – to one whose 
highest refuge is Brahman; yea, that Supreme Brahman 
becomes manifest to one whose highest refuge is Brahman.”

The state of liberation hailed high is attainable only 

by the siddhi of jñāna that destroys ignorance and is

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   222 06-05-2011   10:53:47



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 223

Commentary: 
Excepting Jñāna nothing can help one attain mukti. 

Siddhis acquired and practised, even if they be countless, 
cannot ensure the Supreme Release. The hankering after 
siddhis by one enticed by the lure of them, clouds one’s vision 
of the Truth of their fruitlessness in securing the attainment of 
jñāna. Siddhis are also time-bound and after a lapse of time, 
these powers hoodwinking him, desert him, leaving him a 
piththa (a madman) and not a siddha.

Instead of remaining as All, the Whole, the Infinite 
Awareness, desiring worthless siddhis is like begging for 
stale gruel from the Lord of unbounded munificence, who is 
prepared to offer anything that is asked for including Himself. 
“In high Heaven where nectar flows in plenty, who would 
ask for old sour gruel? It is like the bee seeking the flower 
of nettle when the lotus, full of honey, is nearly.” (Alavandar 
Stotra Ratnam). If a seeker after mukti mārga (path of release) 
were to distract himself with miscellaneous siddhis, half way 
through his inward journey, his ego and bondage, the very 
things he set out to annihilate, gaining growth and strength, 
bar the door to eternity.

Siddhis convert the mind into an agitated slurry and the 
bliss of Release or shanti attained on the stillness of mind 
recedes as one beyond reach. While the zeal and rigour of 
the endeavours demanded for the acquisition of siddhis is 
manifold more than what worldly actions require, how can 
there be scope for peace in the pursuit of them?

Although the powers appear to be wonderful to those 
who do not posses them, in truth they are only transient. It 
is foolhardy to aspire for that which is transient. There is no 
joy in the trivial. All these wonders are contained in the one 
changeless Self. Ramana Gītā, verses eleven and twelve 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   223 06-05-2011   10:53:47



224 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

of chapter 5 says, “the entire Universe is condensed in the 
body, and the entire body in the Heart. Thus the Heart is the 
nucleus of the whole Universe”. But acquisition of siddhis 
demand concentration on different parts of the body for the 
different siddhis. “But the Heart comprises all. That is what 
is tought to Svetaketu by the illustration of the seed of a fig 
tree. The source is a point without any dimensions. It expands 
as the cosmos on the one hand and as the Infinite Bliss on the 
other. That point is the pivot. From it a single vāsanā starts, 
multiplies as the experiencer ‘I’, experience, and the world. 
The experiencer and the source are referred to in the mantra. 
Two birds, exactly alike, arise simultaneously.” (Talks no. 616)

Siddhis and jñāna lie in opposite directions and directing 
the mind towards siddhis is an impediment to progress in the 
royal road to mukti. An assorted verse by Bhagavan reiterates 
this:

“Oh my son, A conjuror, himself without getting deluded, 
deludes the men of the world by the illusion he creates.

But the siddha first deludes himself and then foists his 
delusion upon the world. What a wonder is this!”

Lord Krishna declares in Bhāgavatam, “All the siddhis 
that are found to accrue by birth, drugs, austerity, mantras, 
etc. can be had by the practice of the highest yoga (of union 
with the Self). But these others enumerated cannot yield what 
is attained through the practice of yoga alone.” (11-16-34).

Commentary: 
The eight-fold siddhis may flock together and sport, of 

their own accord, before some yogīs in the course of their 
spiritual journey towards the goal of Knowledge, or they may 
not even approach some others. Whether siddhis will dance 
attendance or not on a yogī on the path of jñāna will be decided 
by the inborn latencies, or pūrva vāsanās of the yogīs . But 
a yogī of blemishless and immaculate heart will not bestow 
even a passing thought on them. He does not exult when 
siddhis attend on him nor is he driven to despair when they 
don’t. He remains totally oblivious of them for he remains as 
the blemishless form of Ātman, Awareness Pure and Whole. 
Tranquility of mind vouchsafes for him the joy of Release.

The jñānis who have gained the jñānasiddhi, the perfect 
siddhi of the grandeur of liberation alone are those who 
have gained the summum bonum of all siddhis and the entire 
gamut of all other siddhis abides in them in toto, manifest or 
unmanifest, like many a cosmos lie concealed and unmanifest 
in space.

Bhagavan, in Ramana Gītā declares: “By effortless 
abidance in the Self, the siddhis may in course of time come 
to the seer and if prārabdha lies that way, even a jñāni may 
sport such powers. Just as to the sage the world appears as 
nothing but the Self, even so the play of siddhis is regarded by 
him as nothing other than the Self”. (Chap 11, Verse 20 and 
21) and “They know nothing who think that jñāna is devoid of 
power. For a jñāni abides in his real state (of Being) which is 
the plenitude of power and all – round perfection.” (Verse 26)

   “There the one who does not delude himself
	 As the beholder of outer objects
	 But knows his real status as
	 The mighty Self Supreme, rejects

The body (dwelt in by the Self) is the form constitued

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   227 06-05-2011   10:53:47

seated in that body itself. Right from the one unfragmented

Commentary: 

In this very body, this city of nine gates, made up of the 
five elements, the Lord, well seated in harmonious unity, holds 
His court (durbar). The principle of Siva with no division or 
fragmentation pervades everywhere indivisibly within and 
without of everything with no place where it is not, like the 
ether that fills all objects within and without, and as such 
pervades the human body made up of the five elements. This 
body is verily then Brahmapuri, the city of Brahman. 

In the space of the heart-cave, that is verily the temple of 
Awareness, He, subtle, incorporeal and all-pervasive, resides 
truly and well. That which is not contained by any cannot be 
called by any name. It is Space of space, Light of light, greater 
than the greatest and smaller than the smallest, beyond mind 
and speech and is All.

The cause – the principle of Siva – appears as the effect – 
the manifest world. Right from the sand-dunes of the earth up 
to Mahesa, everything is the form of Siva. The sarira (body) 
and the sariri (indweller of the body) are both aspects of Siva. 
The ‘Being’ or ‘Sat’ of Siva – the cause – lends substantiality 
or reality to the world – the effect. All the multifarious names 
and forms of the plurality of the world are the manifestation 
of the expansive grace of Siva, the one who shines without 
a second.

All the worlds are manifestations and expressions of His 
glory and splendour even as the effulgence of the sun is the 
sun’s splendour.

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 229

There is no world but for the body. The body is not apart 
from the mind. The mind does not function but for the light 
of Awareness. That awareness or chit is not other than Sat, 
the True Content.

This Awareness is so to say, the ‘Eye’ of cognition 
of the whole Universe. On It is established all this. This 
Prajñānam, Pure Awareness, is Siva the Omniscient Lord. 
Therefore Prajñānam is Brahman in His manifestated forms 
and unmanifested forms both and is also the Indweller in 
all and the Controller of all. Right from Iswara down to the 
clump of grass, a particle of sand, the invisible atom and its 
subdivisions are naught else but He. That Awareness you are 
and therefore you are verily that Siva who is within you well 
seated. Therefore Tat Tvam Asi – That Thou Art. 

“He, when known, destroys the ocean of saṁsāra. 
Therefore knowing thus one attains the fruit of Kaivalya. 
Verily one attains Liberation.” (Kaivalya Upanishad)

is a Pūrna Kāma (one who has accomplished all there is to 
accomplish) and nitya trupta (who is ever satisfied). The bliss

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 231

of his greatness.
Who ever worships such a sage revelling in Siva’s radiant 

Bliss with offer of water for bath, clothes to wear, tasty food to 
eat and with sandal paste and flowers, besides having darsan 
of him, is extremely fortunate and blessed.

Such a jñāni must be worshipped with the triple identity 
of body, speech and mind and to the traditional shadrasa, 
the six types of tastes like sweet, sour, bitter, salty, spicy 
and astringent, for the palate, must be added the seventh, of 
‘melting devotion’.

Mundaka Upanishad declares (2.1), “They who worship 
the sage who knows Brahman, the support of all, the pure 
effulgent being in whom is contained the Universe, cross the 
boundary of birth and death.” 

Though it is customary to go with offerings while visiting 
such a sage, a heart filled with love and devotion is the best 
offering to a jñāni which makes material offerings a mere 
trifle and redundant.

A Siva yogī who desires nothing is the only one fit 
for bhoga or enjoyment. Silken clothes, sandal paste and 
beautifying ornaments may be apt for a queen but not for 
a penniless widow. So is bhoga apt only for a jīvanmukta 
and not for others who resemble simply stone rollers. 
(Ozhivil Odukkam, Poduvilupadēsam 59).

“Whatever lokas or bhogas are resolved by the 
mind by one with a pure and clear mind, those lokas and 
bhogas are attained by him. Therefore one who desires 
the Supreme attainment must worship an Ātmajñāni.” 
(Mundaka Upanishad, 3-1-10).

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 233

Commentary: 
If one with no other desire in his heart except of mukti, 

worships such a sage beyond compare, he gains that Supreme 
Awareness. A jñāni who ever abides in the natural state that 
transcends the desires and dislikes,on account of the mind 
having been annihilated, is totally bereft of the idea or desire to 
grant Release to the one who worships him. The very merit of 
the virtuous deed of worship of such an enlightened soul will 
fructify as fulfilment of the desire with which one worshipped 
him. This is the Content of the sentence “One who worships, 
his merit earns”.

The presence of a jñāni is like the pure transparent crystal 
or a clean mirror facing another mirror. The state a jñāni abides 
in is devoid of a sense of doership. Whatever be the desire 
with which one worships him gets automatically fulfilled and 
the agency of granting the desire cannot be attributed to him.

Nor is he the one, who, disliking his slanderers metes out 
punishment to them. He being an akarta, a non-doer, does 
nothing. The fruit of the vile deed of calumny fructifies as 
punishment for them. If anyone wrongs a jīvanmukta, the sin 
and blame will be a burden too heavy for him to bear – birth 
after birth.

Neither bestowal of blessing nor pronouncement of curses 
is in him.

It is the fruit of the austerities of Mother Earth that a sage 
aware of his form as the Lord’s, treads on the earth.

His glory is extolled as one who, having gained the 
transcendent state, has seen the Self within as God Supreme, 
now walks abroad, free from attachments, with the Lord 
Himself walking beside him as his guard to protect him from 
all harm. 

Those who reach his presence and bask in it also are made 
immortal, they themselves gaining that Supreme awareness.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   233 06-05-2011   10:53:48



234 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Those who obey the gracious wishes of a great saint 
and render physical service, gain freedom from bondage and 
wealth of grace and live a rich life with all its aims fulfilled.

Mudaliar records Bhagavan’s quoting from Brahma 
Gītā, “To stay where a jñāni, who is none else but the 
Supreme Self, stays is mukti. He who serves a jñāni is so 
great that I permanently bear on my head his feet. None can 
equal the spotless and supreme jñāni, neither Siva, Vishnu 
nor I, Brahma. Who else then can equal him?” and from 
Kurunthirattu, “ Vishnu will carry on his head all that a jñāni 
wants. Siva will follow him everywhere. While virtuous kings 
and all the devas do obeisance to the dust of such a jñāni’s 
feet, Brahma will beg that those feet may be placed on his 
head!” (My Recollections of Bhagavan Sri Ramana, page 32)

Adi Sankara in his Manīsha Panchakam says, “the holy 
feet of that rare soul is worthy of worship by even the king 
of celestials, the ruler of the three worlds.” Such sages are a 
collyrium to clear the eyes of those who approach them of 
egotism and their spirit diffuses itself. An incident recorded 
by Ramanānandha Swarnagiri in his Crumbs from His Table 
speaks of the great reverence in which Ganapathi Muni held 
Sri Bhagavan. “When we came to a place, where Bhagavan 
was said to have sat in the evenings he (Ganapathi Muni) took 
a small quantity of the earth and smeared it on his forehead. 
He also dropped a small bit of the earth into his mouth and 
said – The very ground on which such a holy person sat was 
sacred. His footprints were worth all the spheres that rolled 
in the heaven.”

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   235 06-05-2011   10:53:48



236 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Commentary: 
The Kala jñāna that was requested for by Parasivai, Devi 

Parvathy, from Siva, is to liberate the crores of jīvas on earth. 
The Lord, on the pretext of instructing the Devi, bestowed 
this Ātmavidya or Paravidya so that all ripe souls can gain 
release from saṁsāra.

Devi, at the very beginning of the text itself, requested the 
Lord to bestow that “by which people may get liberated and 
the way to gain it”. From this, it is clear that the attainment of 
mukti is the basic right of all. The Lord also commences the 
instruction by saying “If wisdom does not dawn on one by 
this, even if he were to learn crores of treatises true Awareness 
will not dawn”, meaning that this text stands foremost and 
Supreme, and beyond compare, in instructing on and imparting 
true jñāna.

“Such a highly lauded text on jñāna and the exalted 
āchara, I have disclosed, just as you had requested. If there 
is more that is desired to be known do tell me”, says the Lord.

Thus ends the 65th canto called “Jñāna āchara – canons 
and desciplines” for seekers in the Jñāna Kānda called Sri 
Devi Kālōttaram, a text of 24000 verses.

The Tamil rendition of these Sanskrit verses – the best 
among all great treatises is a great blessing for the community 
of believers in general and seekers of Pure Knowledge in 
particular. This text, the extensive and intensely subtle content 
of which has been condensed in Kali veṇbās in chaste Tamil 
that is sweeter than honey, by Bhagavan will for ever shine and 
abide with unfading fame in the world of scholars and seekers.

Commentary: 

Ātman is the ever existing Reality. Lord Siva, who 
instructed Lord Subrahmanya then, remains the form of the 
Self, ever and even now. He who graciously expounded the 
upadeśa to Guha then in Sanskrit, now, seated as the Ātman 
in my heart, imparts it in Tamil. There is but just one change 
in what continues to exist from then on to now. Then the Lord 
spoke Sanskrit, the language of the Gods and now Ramana 
Aryan (the noble Ramana), reveals it in chaste Tamil. It is 
but meet and proper and ideal too that Lord Guha who is also 
hailed as the Lord of Tamil is instructed in Tamil, a language 
as ancient as Sanskrit having withstood the test of time.

It is the unshakeable and deeply entrenched faith of many 
devotees that Guru Ramana, the teacher, is but an incarnation 
of Lord Guha, the Lord of hilly terrains and the language of 
Tamil. Many a devotee hailing Bhagavan Ramana as Lord 
Skanda has hymned his glory in dulcet verses. Some even 
had had darshan of him as Lord Skanda. 

When viewed in this light it will be seen that Guha, now 
incarnated as Guru Ramana, the guru, speaks in Tamil the 
instructions that he received from Lord Siva then, to enlighten the 
mumukshus, the serious seekers, thus keeping up the Guru-Sishya 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   239 06-05-2011   10:53:48



240 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Parampara (lineage). It is worth recalling here the fervent prayer 
of Arunagirinatha, the renowned bard-saint of Arunachala in the 
last verse of “Kandar Anubhuti” wherein he pleads to Guha to 
come as Guru and bestow grace. This Tamil rendition of the text 
is the response of Bhagavan, Guha incarnate.

Moreover when the upadeśa is reiterated in Tamil by 
Bhagavan who as Skanda had also received it directly, the 
contents get conveyed exactly and excellently, become error-
free and are registered easily and firmly in the hearts of the 
listeners leaving no room for any doubt. Repeated parayana of 
this rare and majestic text is capable of lifting up the sadhak to 
the exalted level of Atmānubhava (experience of the Ātman).

It is a divine dispensation that the Absolute Itself, 
remaining as all and everything, instructs the chosen ones at 
appropriate times so ordained by the omnipresent Lord.

Once Siva, on receiving upadeśa of Praṇava (the content 
of OM) from Guha, conferred on Him the title “Preceptor of 
even the Father-Swaminathan” (the Lord of even the Lord). 
Now the same preceptor to Father receives instructions from 
the Lord. This text contains the body of Instructions that Guha 
received from Iswara. 

Ganapathy Muni hails him as “Karthikeya in human form” 
(Maharishi Ramanam Karthikeyam narākritim) in Ramana Gītā 
and in Ramana Chatvarimsat as follows: “Only the names differ 
for Sanatkumara and Skanda are synonyms for you, who now 
are in Arunachala and not residing in Tiruttani or Swamimalai 
and once before, you taught the secret of the science of the Self 
to Sage Narada, who served you as a disciple.” (Ramana Gītā, 
Chapter II, Verses 8, 9, 11). He also extols him as “a renowned poet 
in Tamil, a language worshipped by Agasthya and other sages” 
(Kumbha yōni mukha mouni pujithē, dravidē vachasi vishrutam 
kavim). Bhagavan himself composed a verse, on the request of 
T.K. Sundaresa Iyer, with himself as Subrahmanya: “Destroyer 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   240 06-05-2011   10:53:48



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 241

of darkness (of nescience) in the virtuous, cave-dweller, 
imperishable one compact of light, Sun eternal, wielder of the 
javelin of Awareness, Ramana, in the Heart-Cave, Him let us 
adore.”

Ganapathy Muni’s conviction that Bhagavan is Lord 
Skanda incarnate was firmly believed in by many and 
was often confirmed by Bhagavan himself. Once when 
Arunachaleswar’s vibhuti was brought to him, he applied it 
to his forehead saying in an undertone “The son is contained 
in the Father” with a voice choked with emotion.

While in Virupaksha Cave many scholars visited Bhagavan 
and composed verses in Tamil in his praise. Perumalswamy 
lamented his inability to compose such verses. Bhagavan who 
came to know of this immediately composed a verse and wrote 
beneath the verse Perumalswamy’s name. The song in lilting 
and rhyme very much like Arunagirinathar’s Thiruppagazh 
celebrated Bhagavan as Skanda. Later on, a commission of 
enquiry that questioned Bhagavan showed him this verse 
in his own handwriting in praise of himself as Skanda. 
Bhagavan said, the handwriting was his own but the ideas were 
Perumalswamy’s. “Do you not agree with the statement made 
in it?” he was asked. “In the same way as an idol is praised as 
Subrahmanya” was his reply. Once an upāsaka of lord Skanda 
came to Bhagavan and spoke with longing of his unfulfilled 
desire. Though he had been worshipping the Lord for so long 
he has not been bestowed till  then even once with a vision of 
the Lord. Muruganar who happened to be there promptly said 
“All your tapas has borne fruit today. Look in front of you the 
Lord.” Puzzled, the gentleman looked up. Immediately with 
tears streaming down his eyes, wonder and joy writ large in his 
face he exclaimed: “Yes. Yes, true.”; for Bhagavan appeared 
as Lord Skanda to him then.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   242 06-05-2011   10:53:48



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 243

Commentary: 
Reality, being formless and extremely subtle, is 

incomprehensible by the mind and remains, therefore, beyond 
the domain of the mind. As it stands permeating everything, the 
jīva remains verily as That. How then can the mind objectify 
and know the truth of the Self?

Manadināl ut koḷḷap pohādu means this Reality cannot 
be pointed out and made known the way earth is pointed out 
and made cognizable with a stick. It is beyond the purview of 
denotative knowledge so much so Kathopanishad declares: 
“The Ātman, subtler than the subtle, greater than the greatest 
is seated within the heart of each living being. He who is free 
from willing and wishing, with his mind and senses composed 
beholds the majesty of the Self and becomes free from sorrow.” 
(II-20). The eye that perceives everything cannot see itself, 
the all-perceiving one. The mighty Awareness that lends 
awareness and thus illumines all sentient things cannot itself 
be seen by that awareness which is illumined by It. The eye 
can know the seen but what is seen does not know the eye.

“I am minuter than the minute, I am likewise the greatest 
of all, I am the manifold Universe. I am the Ancient One, 
the Purusha and the Ruler, I am the Effulgent One and the 
All-good” (Kaivalyopanishad, Verse 20). Therefore the 
exceedingly subtle Supreme Self cannot be either seen by the 
gross eye or known by the subtle mind.

Siva says He would teach a way to attain such a formless 
Self, the unsurpassed form of Bliss. 

An extensive and deep study of all the texts of Vedānta, 
and an enquiry into them, will reveal that they all stop with 
the teaching, “Know Thyself”, “Enquire and know the Self 
within you.” No amount of śāstraic scholarship can enlighten 
one on knowing ‘That’. Beyond that one has to engage oneself 
in Ātma vichāra within. Since only a suitable approach can 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   243 06-05-2011   10:53:48



244 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

reveal the knowledge of a subtle object, Siva declares, after 
delineating the nature of Reality, “I will teach you a subtler 
way”, implying, no fear or hesitation or doubt as to its 
attainability need be entertained.

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 245

and which Supreme Vijñāna (Knowledge of Reality) has

Commentary: 

Parōksha refers to knowledge grasped by the intellect. 
Aparōksha means the knowledge that is known and felt as the 
most intimate and direct experience. Siva says that He will 
impart that parōksha jñānam (intellectual knowledge) which 
will lead one to aparōksha, a direct experience of the Self.

Preparation for a headlong plunge into the practice after 
observing śravaṇa and manana with great faith is called 
parōksha jñāna.

The mind, due to nescience, has become impregnated 
with vāsanās. When all these vāsanās are burnt up by intense 
sādhanā what remains is the condensed essence of jñāna in the 
form of awareness of simply “Being”. But for the realization 
that it is this awareness of the Self that remains within the 
Intellect, illumines and activates it, the aparōksha jñāna 
cannot come about. Real knowledge dawns only when, with 
the knowledge that can be comprehended by the intellect, the 
awareness that activates the intellect, is known.

This knowledge of the Self is beyond the scope of 
denotative knowledge or objective knowledge which can be 
objectified and pointed out specifically as ‘that’ or ‘this’. This 
is the experience of the Self by the Self and is called aparōksha 
jñāna. The first line of the verse means this.

Sivahood is attained when one, controlling the cunning 
and thieving senses, totally eschewing exteriorisation and 
banishing oscillation and imagination of the mind, remains 
anchored in the awareness of simply “Being”, one’s real form. 
One becomes Siva Himself by knowing and being in that 
state. All that is perceived is the very form of Siva to jñānis 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   245 06-05-2011   10:53:48



246 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

who abide as the form of Self, the state of Grace. The second 
line of the verse ‘edanai arindon Sivaneyam’ speaks of this.

Siva further says “the knowledge which hitherto has not 
been imparted by Me to anyone, that, I shall tell you now” 
referring to that Sivajñāna by which one realizes the state of 
Siva and remains as Siva.

The world, the form of five elements will appear the form 
of Siva, the form of jñāna, if perception of the jīva is changed 
into perception of jñāna. The jīva also becomes Siva Himself. 
Unless one becomes oneself Siva first, the perceived world 
will not appear as Siva. Siva proceeds to impart the way to 
gain the experience of becoming Siva Himself. Bhagavan 
once explained Parōksha and aparōksha jñāna in this way. 
“In Vasudeva mananam, it is related that one has to gain 
conceptual realization (parōksha jñāna) with the help of a 
Guru by the act of hearing (śravaṇa) and manana and then 
gain intuitive experience (aparōksha) by spiritual practice and 
by consequent complete maturity of the mind.” But Vichāra 
Sāgara says “intuitive experience is always present, the 
only obstacle is conceptual knowledge (parōksha). Spiritual 
practice is required to remove that obstacle. It is all the same. 
Those who are able to overcome the three-faced obstacles (the 
triputi of jīva, jagat and Iswara) are likened to the naked light 
in an windless place or to the ocean in a waveless state; both 
are true. When one feels the Self within one’s body, it is the 
naked light in a windless place, when one feels that the self 
is all pervading, it is like the waveless ocean.” 

(Letters, 28-9-1947).
In jñāna or in contemplative experience one sees the 

presence of one substance persisting through numerous modes. 
When the permeating substance alone is seen to the exclusion 
of all changing modes apprehended as different from It, then 
that understanding is called Vijñāna. (Bhāgavatam, 11-19-15).

248 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Commentary: 
Śāstrās on paravidya bear ample evidence to reveal 

that Ātma Vidya is instructed only by a guru to a disciple. 
And this lineage of guru – sishya continues. All Vedāntic 
texts will be in the format of gracious upadeśa given by a 
fully realized saint to a meet or ripe disciple who had taken 
to him as the saviour. Never will it be the one given by a 
guru suo motto. Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, most of the Upanishads 
and Kaivalya Navaneetham are all classic examples of this 
wherein the guru says: “since you have asked me, I have 
given this upadeśa”.

The tradition is always in the form of instructions on 
Ātma Vidya by a guru to a disciple, who, seeking a Sadguru 
and a way to redeem himself from the unbearable miseries of 
birth and consequent saṁsāra, had surrendered to the guru. 
This tradition of jñānopadesa from guru to disciple has come 
down to us through the ages from time immemorial. The 
core of ahankara cannot be cut asunder but by the guru’s 
grace and upadeśa. Hence the line “idu guru parampariattup 
pondadam”: it is passed down through a long line of gurus. 
The intricate maze of philosophy of different schools is meant 
to clarify matters and reveal the Truth. But in fact they create 
confusion where no confusion need exist. “To understand 
anything there must be the Self. The Self is obvious. Why not 
remain as the Self? What need to explain the non-self?” asks 
Bhagavan.” (Talks no. 392). 

Discussions conducted in search of the Self is vada. 
Dissensions and disputations are to be eschewed if Ātma jñāna 
is to be gained. Various contentious arguments like māyāvada 
or prakriti vada fatten the ego and help them grow in lieu of 
annihilating them. Thoughts and words must simultaneously 
subside if Satyam, the Truth, buried deep in wasteful but 
sophisticated systems of philosophy, were to shine as the form 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   248 06-05-2011   10:53:48



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 249

of the Self. The birth of Ānma Sākṣātkāra takes place on the 
death of the ego. Simultaneous engagement in disputations and 
sādhanā with Ānma Sākṣātkāra as the goal is like travelling 
westward when eastward lies the destination. Suri Nagamma 
records the following: Bhagavan once remarked, “Ancients 
have said that the superabundance of book knowledge is the 
cause of the rambling of the mind and that will not carry you 
to the goal. A mumukshu should understand the essence of 
the śāstrās but should give up reading of śāstrās as that is 
inimical to dhyāna. What books had I seen and what Vedānta 
discourses had I heard except to close my eyes and remain 
peaceful and quiet?” (Letters, 2-7-1949).

The truth is beyond the pale of words and mind; while 
disputations and discussions are not even ordinary modes but 
thoughts rendered mighty and forceful by a fattened ego. The 
truth that can be known solely by a pure satvic mind, turned 
inward, steering clear of imagined illusions can never be 
known by indulgence in metaphysical disputes.

The purpose of teaching this upadeśa of Ātma Vidya is 
to release mumukshus from being tossed about by waves of 
transmigration in saṃsāric ocean and help them reach the 
shore of mukti. 

Thayumanavar describes the grievous nature of the 
transmigratory cycle thus:

	 “The seas are many and the mountains are many;
	 So many are deeds done and deeds to be,
	 For deeds so many, many are the bodies
	 As multitudinous as sands of sea
	 Wouldst Thou not drive afar, O God, All-Filling
	 The gathering clouds of ignorance from me,
	 That I, before I leave this present body
	 May draw near Thee and Lord abide in Thee.”

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   249 06-05-2011   10:53:48

The Content Beyond, with Sarvathō mukham (countenance 
everywhere) pervades all the places and remains the form of 
witness perceiving everything.

In devotional hymns it is usual to praise the Lord as 
nirguna. For instance the Venkatesa Suprabhatham hymns 
chakshushē sarva lōkanām – Eye of all the worlds.

The Purusha Suktham hails the Lord as one with Visvatho 
mukam – with the face everywhere.

Kaivalya Upanishad says “Without arms and legs am I 
of unthinkable power. I see without eyes and I hear without 
ears. I know all and am different from all. None can know 
Me. I am, always Intelligence.” (Verse 21).

Commentary: 

He who abides by nature in all perceivable objects is the 
Perfect, whole One. This does not mean that He abides in 
objects that are different from or other than Him. He remains as 
all the perceived objects, He ensouls them as the Sat or “being” 
in all of them, pervading all of them within and without, He 
Himself remains filling everything being Himself Full, is the 
true import of the line ellamahi iruppan – who is as everything. 

That He remains as the face everywhere (omnipresent) 
eyeing everything as simply the uninvolved Witness is 
declared by the phrase engum mukhamulān. Escape from acts 
performed ignoring or concealing the Holy witness within is 
impossible, is the content of this line. 

He is the one who cannot be thought of by the mind 
though he has countenance everywhere.

How can the one who remains within the thinking mind 
be thought of by the mind? As emphasized by Bhagavan in 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   251 06-05-2011   10:53:48



252 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Verse 22 of Forty Verses on Reality, “How can the mind know 
the Lord, who illumining the mind, resides in the mind?” He 
is beyond the realm of mind.

The content of ‘I’ or Ātman is one, who, becoming all the 
principles, fills them as their content, yet transcends them all. 
He is the one who remains as the unsublatable content that 
can neither be rejected nor accepted, of a homogenous nature 
within and without and is the form of all.

Vedāntic texts explain this as follows: objects, place, 
time, the quarters, varna and ashrama exist at one place 
and time, but do not at another; one object does not become 
another. But Brahman or Ātman, devoid of origin and end 
is not restricted or divided by time. As It is everywhere It 
is not restricted by place. As It remains as all the objects It 
is not restricted by objects. Filling all quarters, pervading 
everywhere, and without an origin and end, Ātman is 
Whole, Full and therefore Sarvatho mukham – with face 
everywhere.

Yoga Vasishtam declares (Verse 1197): “It has the 
boundary of its hands and feet on all sides, It has Its eyes, 
heads and mouths everywhere. It has Its ears all round. It is 
established in the world pervading everything.”

Purusha Sooktham proclaims “All this is Purusha. What 
is manifest now and will manifest in future are all He.”

Lord Krishna in Gītā declares :With hands and feet 
everywhere, with eyes and heads and mouths everywhere, 
with ears everywhere – He exists enveloping all!” (Chap. 
XIII, Verse 13)

Brahmanubhava Upanishad emphasizes that Brahman is 
the only reality thus: “I am the All. I am the All-in-All. I am 
the one in All. I am the All in one. I am the Many.”(Verse 22).

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   253 06-05-2011   10:53:49



254 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

mind. The upadeśa begins with the instruction of the subtle 
way which is to meditate on Siva as “He – I am” (soham) 
unceasingly.

Guha is urged to contemplate that Siva – the whole 
and prime Content – who, pervading within and without all 
principles, yet transcending them all, remains beyond the reach 
of speech and mind devoid of a name and form as “I am”. He 
is asked to contemplate on His own Real form as against the 
differentiated stance, “He is different from me.”

Bhagavan also has emphasized this point in verse 8 of 
Upadeśa Undiyār as follows “Better than viewing Him as 
other (than oneself) is to hold him as the ‘I’ within.”

“That Ātmatattva cannot be known either by eyes, 
speech or other senses, or by tapas or karma. A man of 
pure heart perceives that Impartite Whole by dhyāna.” 
(Mundaka Upanishad, 3-1-9).

Once when a gentleman asked Bhagavan “What is my 
tattva (truth)?” Bhagavan answered: “You are yourself the 
tattva. Is there a different one to know the tattva of another? 
How can you exist apart from the tattva? The very fact of your 
existence makes you to ask the question. Your very existence 
is the tattva. Give up the habiliments of the tattva and remain 
in your essential nature. Tattva always remains shining and 
single.” (Talks no. 565).

As He is the One non-dual form of Self who has nothing 
else to be spoken of as “This or That”, He is the one whom 
speech and mind cannot approach or associate with and much 
less describe. All descriptions of Him become halting and all 
known standards are rendered inadequate and imperfect. He 
is beyond the range of activities of the mind in the form of 
resolutions, positive and negative, which are pure imaginations 
of the mind so much so the Upanishads emphatically declare: 
“Unable to reach, speech and mind return.”

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 255

“That Siva, who is beyond the grasp of speech and mind – 
‘I am’ is how one should contemplate upon, is the injunction, 
which is precisely what is laid down by the mahavakya ‘Aham 
Brahmasmi’.

“A person is enabled to realize only after hearing the 
mahavakya. Hence the Upanishadic text is the eternal Truth to 
which everyone who has realized owes his experience. After 
hearing the Self to be the Brahman the person finds the true 
import of the Self and reverts to it whenever he is diverted from 
it. Here is the whole process of Realization.” (Talks no. 647).

Tam yatha yatha upasathe tathaiva bhavati - in whatever 
stance or bhava one meditates, in a similar way one has 
darshan of the Ātman. The best of all stances is to think of 
oneself as the “Absolute Content”. The contemplation of ‘I 
am that Siva’ destroys the delusion of considering the body as 
the Self and a separate individual and eventually uproots the 
ego. Viewing oneself as simply Awareness is Siva Chintanai. 

“Think on what is beyond thought” is the same as saying 
“engage in the thought of Siva with a mind that is non-
differentiated and focused on with a single stance. With the 
elimination of distinctions, the thinker ‘dies’ and then none is 
left behind to think. What remains, after ‘thinking’ is given up, 
is only Sivam – Sivahood rendering dhyāna redundant for one 
who meditates becomes the object of meditation. Hence the 
instruction is “Contemplate Siva with an unfragmented mind”.

yad bhavam, tad bhavati – As one conceives so one 
becomes.

There is a humorous incident recorded by Suri Nagamma 
regarding this. Annamalai Swami was looking after the 
constructions in the Ashram. Whenever he came into the hall, 
Bhagavan used to enquire about the construction of something 
or other. A devotee, puzzled, asked Bhagavan why whenever 
Annamalai Swami came he spoke only of the construction

is concerned only about construction work and he is amply

bhavam tad bhavati.

Commentary: 

endrum uladai (ever present) means the Ātman undergoes no 
change due to time, and remains ever the same. It is imperishable 
because It is eternally present. Only objects that exist at one 
point of time and cease to exist at another, suffer changes. 
Ātman, the ever present content, is changeless. It transcends the 
grasp of the inner organs like mind and intellect and therefore is 
unfathomable and indescribable as ‘this’ or ‘that’.

The Ātman is firmly established. While mind and other 
instruments and senses wander in sense objects the gross body 
will not move. Even if crores of bodies move, the elements of 
which they are made are moveless. Similarly though residing 
in all that is moving, the Self remaining as the Self, is simply 
the Witness of all that moves and does not move Itself. 

Present everywhere, permeating everything and 
everywhere, It dwells in everything and infills everything. 
It has no source or pre-existing cause for Itself. As there is 
absolutely nothing, not even an iota of anything as other 
than ‘That’, It is incomparable. “Know that the Ātman 
is the repository of all these exaltedness, is unexcelled, 
incomparable, all-pervading and formless.”

Where the error of seeing, hearing and knowing along 
with the ego that cognizes them gets annihilated totally, that 
is the non-dual jñāna or Ātma jñāna. Perishability is to that 
with a form. The formless cannot be made to perish. Hence 
It is called Eternal.

“The Supreme Consciousness is known as Bhuma” 
(Chandogya Upanishad). “Bhuma is the Supreme” – where 
one sees none other, hears none other, knows none other “that 
is Perfection”- Yatra nanyat pasyati, nanyat srunoti, nanyat 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   257 06-05-2011   10:53:49



258 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

vijnāti, sa bhuma. “It is indefinable and indescribable. It is as 
It is. It alone is. Nothing else.” (Talks no. 68).

Bhagavan further explains how to attain that perfection: 
“In the sunshine cotton does not burn; but if the cotton be 
placed under a lens it catches fire and is consumed by the 
rays of the sun passing through the lens. So too, though the 
awareness of the Self is present at all times, it is not inimical 
to ignorance. If by meditation the subtle state of thought is 
won (to fix attention on the pure ‘I’ after the subsidence of 
all thoughts) then ignorance is destroyed…..Mental states 
are of two kinds. One is the natural state and the other is a 
transformation into forms of the objects. The first is the truth 
and the other is according to the doer (kartru tantra). When 
the latter perishes, the former will remain over.”

The means for this end is meditation. Though this is 
with the triad of distinction (triputi) it will finally end in pure 
awareness (jñānam). “Meditation needs effort; jñānam is 
effortless. Meditation can be done, not done or wrongly done, 
jñānam is not so. Meditation is described as kartru tantra (as 
doer’s own), jñānam as vastu tantra (the Supreme’s own).” 
(Talks no. 624).

within the realm of mind, It eludes all stances as well. Hence

That moveless Supreme Self cannot be known by the

of perception.

Vidayam kadandolir Vedyam: It transcends the realm of 
all objective knowledge. When the Sun and moon set, fire 
subsides and speech becomes silent, what shines as light for 
man is the light or effulgence of the Ātman. This light does 
not belong to the body. Even a blind man while dreaming 
perceives various sights. This does not belong to the mind 
either. Mind is the form of food and has no light of its own. 
This light makes everything else shine. But nothing can make 
it shine. The light of Ātman through the intellect in the mind 
and through the mind in the instruments in other organs shines. 
That is why even this insentient body appears to be with 
sentience. Ātman appears to take the form of whatever object 
is lit up by its light, just as sunlight when reflected through a 
coloured glass acquires colour of that glass. When the light 
of Ātman comes through the intellect It appears to think. In 
truth Ātman thinks nothing. This Ātman remains the form of 
knowledge for the mind outward bent and within the Cave 
of the Heart remains the light of the Self. “Brahman or the 
Eternal is the Mind of the mind, the Life of the life, the Ear 
of the ear, the Eye of the eye and the Tongue of the tongue. 
He shines by his own brightness. By His light all these are 
illumined”. (Vichāra Bindu Upanishad, Verse 3).

absolute silence in the void of objective knowledge and when the 
din and roar of the senses is silenced through meditation tranquil

Paraphrase: 
I indeed am the Supreme, Pre-eminent Lord, the form 

of Siva, not renounceable by any. I am the form, essence 
and basis of all mantras; yet I remain transcending them 
all as the One Beyond, devoid of origin and dissolution 
and without activity of any kind, like creation and 
dissolution, of the Universe.
Commentary: 

The entire Universe consisting of moving and unmoving 
objects and the ashta moortha or eightfold form, all of which 
are the expanded manifestation of the five elements and 
the outcome of their compounding with each other (Panchi 
karanam), are all the form of Siva. Hence the jīva who falls 
within this manifestation has necessarily to be Siva. This is 
the content of the assertion ‘Siva am I’.

mantirangal yavin māyānum:- The content Absolute, 
that shines as all is also the form of mantra and the deity the 
mantra stands for. Various hymns describe this principle. 
Viswam Vishnu: Vishnu is verily the universe while another 
proclaims “I am verily the form of all mantras.”; so much so 
a saint-composer sings: “Siva verily sound personified.”

I am worldless, transcending all the mantras devoid of the 
fivefold krithya (actions) of creation, sustenance, dissolution, 
veiling and anugraha (benediction). This state is called 
“abidance, yet non-abidance”.

The Absolute is the limit of all negations as well as 
affirmations. It is not all this and yet It is all this and transcends 
all this. Ātman-Brahman is beyond saguna and nirguna. He is 
neither and at the same time both these also but transcends all.

He who remains as chit and achit (sentient and insentient) 
world and jīva, also shines as the Formless, Attributeless and 
untouched by any of their qualities.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   262 06-05-2011   10:53:49



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 263

A seeker must realize that Brahman shines in all 
things known. What exists (asti), what shines (bhati) that 
is Ātman. That which is not has neither existence nor light. 
The Consciousness of Ātman alone shines. That Content of 
Akshara, like a lamp makes everything appear, revealing 
itself by its own light. It has also attained this jīva-bhava. This 
bhavana or stance is an aid to Self-Knowledge.

Once a group of Andhra devotees, after going on a 
pilgrimage to various places came to Bhagavan and one of 
them asked Bhagavan to explain the meaning of Paratpara 
Rupam, (the form of Supreme Being) and Bhagavan replied, 
“you have come after worshipping various Gods. Though He 
is one in all, that which is above all is paratpara rupam. After 
visiting various temples it has occurred to you to wonder what 
that Supreme Being is which is the source of all these Gods”. 
Suri Nagamma records while Bhagavan was saying this “the 
Supreme Being was dancing on his face”. After they went 
away Bhagavan explained again “Paratpara rupam means 
the form or figure of the Supreme Being which is the highest 
of the high”. (Letters, 2-5-1946).
