Paraphrase: 
All the visible (known) and invisible (unknown) 

objects, the ‘unmoving’ objects like plants and moving 
ones, like creatures and humans, all devoid of a ‘being’ 
without ‘Me’, are all pervaded by Me. I am the Lord of 
the Universe. All things shine forth because of (illumined 
by) Me.
Commentary: 

The Lord declares His form as the limitless sky of 
Awareness in this verse. Just as ether pervades everything, 
the Lord abides, bodiless, in all things. The various forms 
of moving and unmoving objects cognizable by the five 
instruments of perception are mere appearances of the formless 
content of Truth. Whatever is perceived is not apart from the 
True content yet remaining in the True content and as the True 
content, the perceived appear with various names and forms 
– all differences imagined on It.

All that is subject to appearance and disappearance 
including worlds and bodies are all imagined in the 
Self who is the stay and support of all of them. In short 
the Noumenon permeating everything interpenetrates 
everything like the warp and woof of the matrix of all 
that is perceived as the phenomenal world. The line 
icharuvamum ennal paravidap pattanavam (all this is 
pervaded by me) explains this.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   264 06-05-2011   10:53:49



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 265

As the myth of this world and the objects in it are imagined 
appearances on the True content and as there is no being apart 
from the Truth, the Lord declares “They are all Me”.

The space of pure Awareness, the True content, is the 
substratum for the expanded appearance of the worlds. The Sat 
Vastu, permeating all the unreal phenomenal objects, makes 
them all appear as if real. But though admixed with them yet 
like the sky untouched by their nature and attributes, It shines 
in blemishless splendour. The content of the line elam ennal 
tane vilangm (all shines by Me) is this. 

The phenomenal world is a superimposition on the 
Noumenon. ‘What is’ is only the Reality that pervades the 
unreal, phenomenal world. Therefore, the spiritual aspirants 
through discriminative intelligence and introspection must 
seek and find the Ātman permeating everything in the body-
mind complex just as milk is sought and found in cows, fire 
in fire sticks, cereals in the soil and water under the ground. 
He is the indweller in all bodies and is the infiller of all.

A celebrated Azhvar sings in ecstasy as Nindrathellam 
Nedumal – “All that stands is the great One.”

The content of this verse has been the import of many an 
Upanishadic verse. Verse 21 of Brahmanubhava Upanishad 
says:

 	 “I am the manifested Brahman
	   I am the unmanifested Brahman
	   I am the Immanent Brahman
	   I am the Transcendental trigunatita Ananta Brahman
	   I am Karana Brahman
	   I am Kārya Brahman”.
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad says: “He who dwells in all 

beings but is within them, whom none of the beings knows, 
whose body is all beings and who controls all beings from 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   265 06-05-2011   10:53:49



266 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

within, is the Inner Controller – your own Self and Immortal”. 
(3-7-15). A seeker often wonders how to perceive everything 
as Brahman. Bhagavan has the answer: “Ancients say drishtim 
jñānamayim krtwa Pasyeth brahmamayam jagat”. (change 
your perception into one of jñāna and perceive the world as 
Brahman). The world is as we see it. If we see it as material 
it is material. If we see it as Brahman, it is Brahman. That is 
why we must change our outlook. Can you see the picture in 
a film without the screen? If we remain as we are, everything 
adjusts itself to that attitude”. (Letters, 20.08.49) “With that 
(perception of jñāna) absolute awareness realized, look 
without and you will realize the Universe to be not apart from 
the realized Absolute”. (Talks no. 311).

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 267

Paraphrase: 
I shine ‘as all’, right from the lofty principle of Siva 

down to this Universe and the various tiers of worlds 
teeming with a variety of forms, diverse and unlike each 
other. The objects of creation in their entirety abide and 
stay established in Me. 
Commentary: 

No two leaves are alike in creation, either in form or 
content. No two forms are similar. Even in the same object, 
the form seen that day not be the same the next day. Constant 
change is the order of creation.

Objects differ from each other in form and nature. The 
nature of one object will not be exhibited by another. Even the 
species of homosapiens do not manifest the same character at 
all times. The world, with change as its intrinsic nature, never 
staying at the same place, rolls on forever. 

The world is nothing but the conglomeration of an 
aggregate of varied forms and qualities. Many such worlds, it is 
said, exist in successive tiers in creation. Of all the principles in 
these myriad worlds of creation, the most exalted is the principle 
of Siva, encompassing within itself all the others. Siva mudal 
ivvulaham ira (right from Siva down to the earth) refers to this. 
“It is that from which emanate the Gods, Vishnu and others, like 
rays of light from the sun and from which infinite worlds arise 
like bubbles from the ocean. It is that towards which multitudes 
of visible objects proceed like waters towards the great ocean 
and which illuminates the object as well as the Self like a lamp”. 
(Yoga Vasishtam, Verses 1207 and 1208).

Right from the principle of Siva down to this earth, I am, 
who shine as all, their support and stay.

The unperceivable Supreme content is the basis for the 
perceivable world, just like the unperceivable roots provide the 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   267 06-05-2011   10:53:49



268 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

anchor for a tree seen laden with flowers in a riot of colours. 
The unfragmented and undifferentiated content is the basis 
and support for the world of infinite differences. The world 
of jīvas ridden with and subject to the play of three gunas, 
has the attributeless Nirguna, that transcends the three gunas, 
as its aim to be achieved. In that Content, that pervades and 
infills everything, and remains as all, devoid of anything as 
void or śūnya, right from Siva everything stays firmly fixed.

Our physical perception is confined to this terra firma. 
But there are worlds and worlds and they are called anda koti 
(crores of worlds), just as the firmament houses countless 
constellations of stars.

The Brahman or Ātman as ‘Being’ provides substantiality 
for all the worlds seen and heard in all the three states and 
they all have our Being as the form, just as all the dream 
worlds seen are ultimately of the form of the dreamer. Other 
than the form of ‘Self that ever shines as Being, the world is 
not the ‘other’. The Brahman-Ātman that shines as ‘being’ in 
everything is of all forms.*

* The Sata Rudriya occurring in Yajur Veda visualizes Him as the 
all-pervading Supreme Reality immanent in every atom of this so 
called creation. Herein Rudra is depicted as the Creator, Protector 
and destroyer, the mortal and immortal, the real and the unreal, the 
good and the bad, the sinful and the meritorious being and doing, 
in short, everything in creation. The whole hymn praises Him 
as manifesting all and everything by naming them all including 
things that are opposed to each other. “Prostration to the Creator 
of the whole universe, the ruler over vegetable kingdom, to the 
all-pervading one, to the valiant confronter of the enemies, to the 
protector of Dharma, to the chief of thieves, to the elusive lord of 
rogues and plunderers; to Him who is in the atoms, in the dust, 
in the dry and in the green, to Him who is in difficult terrains, in 
the green grass, to Him who is in the earth and in the rivers with 
mighty waves”.

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 269

A lady, Rama Bai, greatly devoted to Bhagavan, once 
queried “Bhagavan, śāstrās speaks of the existence of many 
worlds yet not all of them are perceptible to our eyes, we 
know only this world”, Bhagavan answered “Yes, we have 
been given an embodiment suited to this world. Hence what 
is in this world alone is perceived. A form, proper and suited 
to the respective world, will make that world known.” As is 
the eye so is the perception.

Worlds symbolically stand for parts while the universe or 
creation stands for the whole and creation is a phenomenon 
on a single Reality.

“That one Supreme Ruler, the soul of all beings who 
makes his one form manifold…those wise men who perceive 
Him as existing in their own Self to them belongs Eternal 
Happiness and to none else”. (Kathopanishad, 5-12)

“That which is above the sky, below the earth and in 
between the two, that which is in the past, present and future 
and that in which the space is woven as the warp and woof is 
the Akshara Brahman”. (Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, 3-8-7).

Paraphrase: 
Know that in this world whatever is directly and well

Commentary: 

This verse declares the Supreme Content straightaway 
without recourse to metaphors or comparisons. All that is 
perceived with the eyes is within the seer. All that is heard 
through the ears is contained in the listener. All that arises 
within and without, with body as the centre, are contained in 
the dehātman (one who looks upon the body as I). Whether a 
perceiver or a listener or a jīvātman, all the three are not other 
than the true Content.

“Pervading them all and indwelling all of them is Me.” 
says Siva.

Since the origin of the perceiver, listener and the ego 
attached to the body is not other than the True Content, all 
that is perceived, heard and all that pertains to the ego, the 
dehātman, are all ‘He’ without whom no mind can think, 
without whom no sruti can be heard, without whom none of 
the worlds will be seen, without whom the sun and moon will 
not shine, without whom the body will not move, that Absolute 
Content pervading and permeating everything remains as all, 
is the truth expounded by Lord Siva.

On this One silver string of Consciousness all names, 
forms, all that is heard and thought are strung. Though this 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   270 06-05-2011   10:53:49



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 271

verse speaks of what is seen and heard, the functions of other 
instruments are also to be inferred. 

The above three verses explain together the form of the 
Self, Siva – Paripoornam (The Fullness of Siva). That one 
should identify oneself with That, the Absolute Consciousness 
that repletes all creations, was taught by Bhagavan to a 
Zamindarini, a lady devotee – in following way. She was a 
frequent visitor and once before leaving begged for Bhagavan’s 
blessings and regretted her inability as a married woman of 
responsibilities to stay on in Bhagavan’s presence for long, 
to which Bhagavan replied “Guru is where one is.”. “Should 
one look upon the whole world as Brahman or should one 
look upon one’s own Self as the most important?” she asked. 
Bhagavan answered “We exist. And the world is Brahman 
itself. What then is there to look upon as Brahman?” She was 
taken aback. Bhagavan continued “We undoubtedly exist. The 
world also exists, as Brahman. We should make our vision 
as the all-pervading Brahman. Ancients say: Drishtim jñāna 
mayim kritwa”. (Letters, 20-9-49).

Therefore a mumukshu should think that in all the objects 
of the world known, Brahman is shining. What is not, has 
no being, no revealing light. Ātma Chaitanya indeed shines. 
When the Lord is Infinite and all perfection, the world also is 
infinite and perfect. There cannot be two infinities. “Just as 
sugar pervades the juice of sugar cane and sweetness pervades 
sugar so also this subtle Ātman pervades the whole world and 
this whole body.” (Vichārabindu Upanishsad, Verse 3).

ĪsavÅsya Upanishad says: Īsā vāsyam idam Sarvam – All 
this (this world) is enveloped by the Lord.

Lord Krishna also speaks of the same principle in 
Gītā: “There is nothing whatever that is higher than ‘I’, O 
Dhananjaya. All that is here is srung on Me as rows of gems 
on a string.” (Chap. VII, Verse 7).

272 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Ul veli pattri olir – Everything is strung in the single 
string of Consciousness Existence. 

Brihadaranyaka Upanishad says, One who knows that 
“string and the indweller of all, is the knower of Brahman, 
knower of worlds, knower of devas, knower of elements, 
knower of Self and knower of all”. (3-7-1).

Sankara in Manīsha Panchakam speaks of the same 
“Brahmaivāham idam jagat-cha sakalam chin mātra 
vistāritam”- “I am Brahman alone, also all this universe which 
is the expansion or expression of the pure Consciousness. I 
am the essence and also the expansion, the world before me.”

Sage Yajñavalkya in Brihadaranyaka Upanishad teaches 
this to his wife. The magical display of sound and sight that 
the world is, cannot be grasped as apart from Ātman just as 
the various musical notes that emanate while playing on the 
instrument Veena cannot be taken apart from the particular 
sound of the instrument itself without which the notes cannot 
have their existence. Likewise when salt dissolves in water 
the water wherever taken from will remain salty. In the same 
way this limitless Brahman is the condensed essence of 
Consciousness permeating everything.

Paraphrase: 
Though one remains ever the Self to be known and 

though one thinks “the Self I am; I am not the body”, 
still one, who out of delusion, imagines the Paramātman 
Siva he wants to become, is different from and other than 
oneself (Self) and worships Him thus (in dual attitude) 
will not attain Sivahood by the strength of that upāsana. 
Know this.
Commentary: 

The jīva renouncing the thought of clinging to the body 
as the Self starts contemplating “I am the Self”. But however 
great be the strength of this dhyāna, that which he thought 
as the Supreme Self and which form he wanted to attain, 
he will not attain. The very desire to attain Siva implies the 
dual attitude that Siva and he are different. Siva becomes the 
‘other’. Sivahood does not belong to the realm of objective 
knowledge; it can never be objectified and known. This form 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   273 06-05-2011   10:53:49



274 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

of dual worship is the outcome of a deluded mind. Hence He 
declares “avvattralal Sivattuvam eidan” (By that way he will 
not attain Sivahood).

Further, both the thoughts ‘the body-I am not’, ‘the 
Self I am’, centre on objects that are other than the Self. As 
long as Siva is contemplated on as the ‘other’, Sivahood is 
unattainable.

Sivahood shines where he who thinks so, subsides or the I 
(the jīva) becomes silent. The very endeavour of worship thus 
carried on with so much longing and enthusiasm, becomes the 
obstacle to attain Him. Instead of knowing Him as the ‘other’ 
by objectifying Him, ‘becoming food for Him’ will help one 
attain Sivahood.

While the Lord Supreme, whole and sole, stands as 
flawless true awareness, for one to claim a separate being apart 
from Him, even for worship is utter folly. “To spring and leap 
from the unbroken sky of Pure Awareness is the heinous sin 
of violating the true dharma of the unity of Being by dividing 
it into two”. (Guru Vāchaka Kovai, 776 and 777).

Only in the state where an attitude of duality prevails, 
one perceives and knows ‘the other’. When everything shines 
as the Ātman what will he perceive, what will he know and 
by what? By what can ‘That’ by which all this is known be 
known? Attempting to know it will become then like the lamp 
that went to see the sunlight or the salt doll that entered the 
sea to measure its depth. Just as fire cannot burn itself so also 
the Self cannot perceive the Self as an object. Knowledge 
itself is the Supreme Content. When the knower and the 
known become one what is ‘knowing’ then? Unless the one 
who worships becomes food for Siva, Sivahood cannot be 
known. That is why Bhagavan sings in verse 101 of Akshara 
Mana Malai: 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   274 06-05-2011   10:53:49



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 275

“As hailstone in water let me melt as love in
Thee who art Love itself, Arunachala!”
Kannudaia Vallalar, the author of Ozhivil Odukkam, 

illustrates this truth with a beautiful example.
The flame from the wick in a lamp shines slowly eating 

away the wick and finally swallows it completely. Instead 
of offering one’s jīvahood as food (like the wick) in small 
measures to that Great Awareness, that out of infinite grace 
revealed the Self, till one (the jīvabodha) is fully consumed 
and becomes extinct without even a trace of individuality 
(Vyakti) contemplating Siva as an object apart is to reject 
Siva, who ever remains nondually the Self, as Awareness, as 
the one other than the Self.

276 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Paraphrase:
Uproot from the mind and totally discard by all 

means the attitude of ‘otherness’ (or the perception of 
distinction) that thinks that Supreme Siva is someone else 
other than me and I am someone other than Siva. Practice 
unceasingly the non-dual attitude of oneness devoid of 
distinction and otherness that asserts “I am indeed none 
other than Siva.”
Commentary: 

The Sivasvarūpa that permeates and shines everywhere – 
and never away from anything even for a moment – pulsates 
within the jīva as his own Self with the Sphurana ‘I-I’, that is 
most directly experienced ever. To look upon the Sivasvarūpa 
that shines as his very Self as something other than himself 
and to think that he, as distinct from Him, exists as a separate 
entity is an attitude, divisive and fragmented. It should be 
uprooted and discarded, is the exhortation.

In truth Siva and jīva are one in substance. Is there a gap 
or interspace as other than that Content, to part or fragment 
and move that Content, the unfragmented, unbroken whole, 
which permeates and fills everywhere as the limitless space 
and shines with ‘non-being’ nowhere?

Everything is the imagination of the mind. Mind, itself 
an imagined entity, caught up in its own web of imagination, 
can be retrieved from it only by switching over to the stance 
of ananyabhava that of regarding, and contemplating ‘Siva’ as 
his very Self from the earlier stance of anyabhava where Siva 
was regarded as the ‘other’ of him. This stance of ananyabhava 
(the attitude of non-distinction) is to be practiced unceasingly.

View forever that sādhanā, the way to attain mukti and 
sadhya or attainment are states not distinct from the Ātman. 
It is worth recollecting here the content of verse 37 of Uḷḷadu 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   276 06-05-2011   10:53:50



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 277

Nārpadu which says that the doctrine of duality during search 
and of unity on attainment is false.

The practicer of upāsana, whether he worships or 
meditates, does it in an attitude of duality regarding Siva 
as different from the Self. When plants are pruned, only the 
excess growth is removed. If it is to be removed we uproot 
it. Likewise, deeply entrenched attitude of ‘otherness’ in the 
mind is the one that has to be uprooted. Hence the Lord says: 
“bhinna bhavattai peyarttiduha”. Srutis declare “yata yata 
upasate tadeva bhavati” – as he worships so he becomes. 

Anna Sivan (that Siva) who, to be attained is worshipped: 
Entering within simply with the attitude of “He I am”, ever 
practice the non-dual attitude. Unceasing meditation with 
this bhava erases the bhavana and what remains shines as 
the Truth. But what should be borne in mind is that the non-
dual attitude should not be simply mental but must be in 
terms of awareness of feeling. The Self is experienced when 
all bhavanas are transcended. Therefore a serious sadhak 
identifying himself with Brahman should realize that the 
Self, like the sky, is uncircumscribed and unaffected by any 
adjuncts.

Bhagavan has explained this ananya bhava in various 
places. Upadeśa Undiyār, Verse 8 says: “Better than viewing 
Him as other (than oneself) is to hold Him as ‘I’ within”. As 
proof he often cited what was revealed in an answer to Moses 
questioning who the Lord was, namely “I am that I am”. 
“Bhuma (Perfection) alone is. It is Infinite. There arises, from 
it this finite consciousness taking on an upādhi (a limiting 
adjunct). This is ābhāsa or reflection. Merge this individual 
consciousness into the Supreme One. That is what should be 
done”. (Talks no. 68).

Besides one who perceives distinction is subject to 
fear. He seeks protection. One who perceives unity is free 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   277 06-05-2011   10:53:50



278 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

of fear. In Upadeśa Manjari Bhagavan says: “The end of 
the path of knowledge (jñāna) or Vedānta is to know the 
truth that ‘I’ is not different from the Lord (Iswara) and 
to be free from the feeling of being the doer”. (Chapter 1, 
Answer to question 10)

And in “Who am I?”: “What really exists is Self (Ātma 
Svarūpa) alone. The world, soul and God are superimpositions 
in it like the silver in the mother of pearl; these three appear 
and disappear simultaneously. Self itself is the world; Self 
itself is the ‘I’; Self itself is God; all is the Supreme Self 
(Siva Svarūpa).”

Paraphrase: 
That yogī of ceaseless practice of this non-dual

Commentary: 

One who abides in the Ātman through the constant 
practice of the perception of non-difference, becomes that 
essence of oneness that pervades everything and for such a 
one, there is none other than him, the Self. He, by the strength 
of his bhavana, bears testimony to the scriptural statement 
yad bhavam tad bhavathi (as is the attitude so is the man) and 
beholds everything as the One Self. 

Muruganar describes the state of such a one with the 
perception (awareness) of non-difference as follows:

	 “In my sight ‘I’ only am
	  And you are not. In your sight
     ‘You’ only are and ‘I’ am not.
	  In the sight of the Self the Self alone
	  Exists and nothing else.
	  In truth I, you and all are nothing
	  But the Self”.
                                                     (Guru Vāchaka Kovai)
While I remain (as) the Vastu, in my awareness of 

non-distinction, other than ‘Me’ there is no entity as ‘you’. 
Likewise while you abide in the Vastu, in your awareness, 
other than ‘you’ as ‘Me’ there is none. I, you, He all are 
Ātman, when the nature of Truth is known. Thus the Ātman 
must be perceived only by the infinitised Consciousness of 
the antahkarana.

280 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

evvidattum eppodum imply that the Self is not parted 
or limited by Space and Time as Ātman is non-spatial and 
eternal. This verse reveals the way to behold the One all-
permeating Self in all physical forms, worlds and of the 
enjoyments of varied nature. When the Ātman abides in 
Himself no difference is experienced but when He abides 
in adjuncts, gross minded people think of Him as many, just 
like the sun reflected in different adjuncts like pans of water 
being looked upon as many and diverse. Therefore Sankara 
in Vivekachūḍāmaṇi exhorts: “O, noble soul! Spend your day 
seeing yourself everywhere thinking yourself as non-dual 
enjoying Atmānanda.” (Verse 525). 

According to Muruganar this verse also provides an 
answer to the question why should the Lord, the ocean of 
compassion, create the attachment-ridden world. 

The answer is that the world is not binding as such but 
the perverted perception of distinctions is the bondage. When 
enquired within ‘Who am I?‘ with an interiorised mind the 
perception (drishti) changes into one of jñāna and the world 
appears as it is – the form of Reality. The cognition of unity 
of all existence like the realization that the cotton that runs 
through the cotton fabrics is the reality, is bhavÅtita. A story 
is often told to explain the state of one with the perception of 
non-difference.

Once a monk was walking along a city, when a ruffian 
assaulted him for no reason and he fell unconscious on the 
ground. A little later, his disciple came in search of him and 
finding him in that condition did the needful to bring him back 
to his consciousness.

The disciple, just to confirm that the monk had regained 
his consciousness asked him whether he recognized him. The 
monk replied “Oh yes! Why not? It is He who assaulted me.” 
The disciple, worried that the recovery was not complete, 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   280 06-05-2011   10:53:50



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 281

told him that he was his disciple and the one who assaulted 
him had made good his escape. The monk smiled and said 
“Yes. He assaulted me. He escaped, He came back, revived 
me and is now talking to me.” The disciple then understood 
the significance of his master’s words. He was referring to the 
One whom he saw in all and in all actions.

Such a blessed one does not perceive anything separate 
from the Absolute – “na-anyat-pasyati, na-anyat-srunoti, 
na-anyat-vijnati “(Chandogya Upanishad, 7-24-1). He does 
not perceive anything else, he does not hear anything else, He 
does not know anything else. 

When he perceives he perceives nothing other than 
the Absolute. He perceives and he perceives not. This is 
divine perception. “Just as curd is a variant of milk even so 
the elemental space full of objects is a manifestation of the 
Supreme Space Transcendence. Thus Siva and the Saivite are 
non-different.” (Ribhu Gītā, Chap. I, Verse 35)

The Lord in Bhāgavatam speaks of the same:
“Whatever is grasped by the mind, words, eyes and other 

sense organs all that is I am. Know by enquiry. There is nothing 
different from Me.” (11-13-24).

When inhering in the thoughts of Ātman as Ātman – as

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   282 06-05-2011   10:53:50

and among what?
This delusion and perception of difference that hitherto 

were in him loosen their hold now and fall off by themselves.
The delusion of moha and perception of diversity, that 

were shunned and eschewed and demanding enormous energy 
to extinguish them at the time of sādhanā proved to be an 
insurmountable task. Now with inherence in the Ātman as the 
One Self they slip away by themselves and disappear leaving 
no trace behind.

All the organs of a yogī become immaculately pure by 
this – the best of all contemplations – contemplation with 
ātmabhavana. Highly famed Vedic texts declare that such 
yogīs will acquire the siddhi of sarvajnatva – of knowing

detectable verse in Supplementary Verses in a beautiful and 
poetic way: “Do know that for those who have known the 
Truth, the effulgent glow of wisdom, the sparkle of expansive 
intelligence and abiding prowess and all other excellences 
shine in unison of their own accord just as spring heralds 
luxuriant growth of trees in full bloom, adorned with fresh 
beauty and velvet verdure.” An indepth perusal of Bhagavan’s 
teachings will be of great help here. We are ‘That’, the Self, 
when the ‘I’ has not risen. Seeing the Self is seeing the Lord. 
As we are not two but the one non-dual Self to remain as 
Self is Ātma nishtai. This is the non-dual attitude or ekātma 
bhavana. Ātmabhavana is not remaining as other than Ātman 
but remaining the Self or being aware of the Self as Self. 
Bhavana in the language of siddhanta is the awareness as 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   283 06-05-2011   10:53:50



284 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Self. Bhavana is simply Awareness. It is like the saying “a 
river of the form of ocean.”

Since everything is the form of Ātman, and as there is 
nothing other than Ātman, if one, who is perpetually with 
Ātmabhavana, were to direct his mind toward something 
desired to be known, that knowledge will come to him on 
its own. But the word ellam – a perception born of Māyā - is 
true only from the relative or empirical plane, but from the 
Absolute plane it is non-existent. Hence an Ānmayogī devoid 
of delusion and vikarpa (perversion) or difference even if he 
were to see such things, will disregard them and give them 
no thought.

Prasnōpanishad (4. 10) says: tad aksharam vedhyate 
yas tu somya eva avivesa iti. Who ever comes to know 
that undecaying vastu he becomes a sarvajna and one who 
pervades and fills everywhere.

Chandogya Upanishad: The question what is that through 
the knowledge of which everything becomes known, is 
answered with TAT TVAM ASI” (That Thou Art).

This answer Uddhalaka Aruni made Svetaketu repeatsnine 
times. The same Upanishad also says (8-7-1): “He who has 
found out and understands that Ātman attains all the worlds 
and all the desires”.

Taittriya Upanishad (3.5) says: “a Brahmajñāni is 
one who can experience whatever he wills and can take on 
whatever form he wills and yet will remain full. As he has 
transcended likes and dislikes, like the Lord, what he resolves 
will come to pass”. But no jñāni ever cares for such powers. 
As Bhagavan said to Humphreys: “No master ever cared 
a rap for occult powers for he has no need of them for his 
daily life….The Master takes on these powers as a form of 
Self-Sacrifice”. (Self-Realization by B.V.Narasimhaswami, 
page 112).

286 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Commentary: 
He is unoriginated and without an end, and He is the 

Lord of all created beings. So the Vedic texts hail Him as the 
birthless one and as Iswara. Yet the One who is so hailed has 
neither a sarira (body) nor a quality. He is simply the formless, 
attributeless Self. That Self am I.

This very idea Bhagavan expounds in Upadeśa Undiyār, 
Verse 24:

	 “In the nature of their being
	  Isa and jīva are in substance one,
	  They differ only in adjuncts and awareness.”
When the upādhis (adjuncts) like jīva and Iswara are 

jettisoned both are of one substance. Vessels made of glass 
and clay with a burning lamp within are opposed to each 
other due to their upādhis (vessels). But by the nature of light 
within each they are one. Ātman being all-pervasive pervades 
everywhere and fills everything within and without. Therefore 
It is formless. Qualities and attributes that are abstract can 
arise and manifest only by holding on to something gross or 
with form. Ātman, formless, is beyond the state of qualities or 
gunas and cannot be held on to. The description gattiramillan 
gunamillan (devoid of form and attributes) explains this. 

As He remains as everything filling everything who 
else can ‘I’ be but ‘He’? If, not even an atom is other than 
Him, who else can this ‘I’ be? When the Self has expanded 
as the all – gross (physical) manifestation – the one calling 
himself as ‘I’ must also be ‘He’. There can be no doubt in this. 
Thayumanavar in Ennāt Kanni expounds:

“Thou weavest Thy Nature 
 Thou within me, when 
 Oh! When will I realize
 Within Thee Am I.” 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   286 06-05-2011   10:53:50



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 287

This verse is akin to the declaration of Mahavakya ‘Thou 
Art That’ or ‘Tat tvam asi” and voices the highest aspiration 
of the human soul.

The Infinite, seemingly limited and encaged in a body (a 
mere superimposition on the Ātman) struggles to regain its 
original nature of Infinity and complete freedom by trying to 
discard the upādhis like the body. All activities of man are 
always the effect of this eternal and undying urge of the soul 
within for the expansion of the individual into the Infinite.

Pūrnamadah Pūrnamidam Pūrnāt Pūrnamudachyate 
Pūrnasya Pūrnamadāya Purnamevāvasishyate. 

“The Invisible (Brahman) is the Full; 
 The visible (the world) too is the Full. 
 From the Full (the Brahman), the Full (the visible 

universe) has come. 
 The Full (Brahman) remains the same, even after the Full 

(the visible universe) has come out of the Full (Brahman).”. 
(Īsāvāsya Upanishad).

Paraphrase: 

He who does not know the truth of his eternal nature, 
The Ātman, is the jīva bound by the dharma of birth that 
is appearance, stay and disappearance. One who knows 
his own true reality is eternal and perfectly pure without 
the least defilement. He is verily Siva Himself. Know that 
there can be no doubt in this. Where is birth for him then?
Commentary: 

The word Sivam Itself means auspiciousness. So long 
as one fails to realize one’s true reality one can never get 
out of the Persian wheel of saṁsāra and its concomitant 
bondage of karma and attachment. The fruits of actions, 
which follow the actions of jīva or pasu, bind the jīva. In 
the course of experiencing the fruits, new tendencies are 
generated responsible for a subsequent birth. Once prārabdha 
gets exhausted the frame falls and another embodiment takes 
place, experiencing the fruits of actions of the previous birth. 
This transmigratory cycle goes on and on with embodiments 
high and low and experiences of pleasure and pain and the 
jīva comes to rack and ruin. With the world as the basis for 
‘mine’ and the body with the panchakosas as the basis for ‘I’, 
the jīva bears and carries both, as the donkey bears the burden.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   288 06-05-2011   10:53:50



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 289

Getting thus submerged in the ocean of saṁsāra caught 
in irremediable pain is what is meant by the line srishti mudal 
tanmam uru pasu tanavan.

A release from the dharma of srishti (birth) can be gained 
only by realizing Ātma dharma, the truth of one’s reality. The 
one who knows the truth of the Self, seated in the Self, shines 
as the basis of true awareness, his very nature. He is eternal and 
perfectly pure and is the Lord of all. This is the most certain 
eternal Truth and there need be no doubt in this.

Ajñāna is bandha and jñāna is moksha. In truth Lord’s 
creation never binds the jīva. The Ātman, the Self is 
untouched by any of the attachments – the Pasa (bondage) 
– of the Pasu (the jīva). Impelled by the flawed perception 
of assuming the insentient body with the five kosas as ‘I’ 
forces the jīva to superimpose the dharma of the perishable 
body on to the Self – like an elephant that throws sand and 
rubbish heap on its own head. This coupled with the act of 
māyā – namely the ignorance of his true Self untouched by 
anything – makes him wallow in the quagmire of saṁsāra 
in endless sorrow. 

Creation is nothing but the sheer imagination of jīva. The 
srishti (birth) of jīva is simply a self-fastened fetter.

The Rtm or order in the process of creation also manifests 
infinite compassion for the jīvas. In order that they be liberated, 
a jñāna guru who has become Siva Immaculate, by realizing 
his Fullness in human frame, is revealed to them. This divine 
solicitude with mercy destroys the bondage and takes them 
to the further shore of liberation. Such is the succour that the 
merciful Providence provides us with.

This divine state of union with Brahman is the ‘Brahmi 
stiti’ that Gītā speaks of: “esha Brahmi stitihi Partha nainam 
Prapya Vimuhyati stitvasyamanthakalepi brahmanirvāṇamry-
chchati”, (Chap. II, Verse 72).

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   289 06-05-2011   10:53:50



290 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

“This is the divine state, O Partha! Having attained 
thereto, one is (not again) bewildered; fixed in that state at 
the end one can attain to the bliss of God (brahma nirvāṇa).”

The Lord also states: “Among thousands of men 
scarcely one strives for perfection and of those who 
strive and succeed, scarcely one becomes Me in truth” 
(Gītā, Chap. VII, Verse 3), emphasizing also the truth, higher 
the goal, greater the difficulty of attaining it.

In Brihadaranyaka Upanishad Sage Yajñavalkya tells 
his wife, “Oh, Gargi, he who departs from this world without 
knowing this Immutable, is miserable”. (3.8.10).

In Kathopanishad, Yama, the Lord of Death, tells 
Nachiketas, “the way to Hereafter is not apparent to the 
ignorant man, who is childish, befooled by the glamour of 
wealth. ‘This is the world’ he thinks, there is no other; thus 
he falls again and again under my sway” and “The wise 
sage, who by means of meditation on the Self, recognizes 
the Ancient, who is difficult to be seen, who is hidden in the 
Cave of the heart, who dwells in the abyss, who is lodged in 
the intelligence, he renounces joy and sorrow”. (2-6 and 12).

292 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

gnoetic Eye or Eye of wisdom. The Self, ‘I’, remains within 
the five sheaths while texts and treatises are outside of them. 
The ‘I’ that permeates and interpenetrates the five sheaths but 
transcends them has to be sifted and known from among the 
panchakosas by sublating them into the unsublatable residue 
’I’ and cannot be attempted to be known from books that are 
outside of the Panchakosas.

“Para means ‘not relative’ or ‘beyond the relative’ that is 
to say the Absolute” says Bhagavan (Talks no. 273). It is clear 
that Brahman is spoken of in two aspects – form, formless – 
perishable and imperishable – as in one place; all pervading 
– capable of being perceived directly and imperceptible. Gītā 
also says: “There are two persons in this world, the perishable 
and the imperishable, the perishable is all these existences and 
the unchanging is the imperishable.” (Chap. XV, Verse 16).

The Supreme is that form from which all these beings are 
born, that by which they live and into which, when departing, 
they enter. “This form is not capable of being seen; with the 
eye no one sees Him. They who know Him thus with the 
heart, with the mind as abiding in the heart, become immortal” 
says Taittriya Upanishad (4.20). Though He is the Source 
of all that is, He is Himself unmoved forever. The Supreme 
in Its transcendental aspect is the Pure Self – unaffected by 
any action or experience, detached and unconcerned. In its 
dynamic cosmic aspect, It not only supports but governs the 
whole cosmic action and this very Self which is One in All 
and all in all, is present in the individual. The Real is the 
eternal, spaceless, timeless Brahman who supports this cosmic 
manifestation in space and time. He is the Paramātman who 
ensouls the cosmic forms and movements. The Supreme in 
Its absolute Self Existence is Brahman the Absolute, and as 
Lord and Creator is Iswara, the God. Bhagavan explains: 
“the Source is a point without any dimensions. It expands 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   292 06-05-2011   10:53:50



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 293

as the cosmos on the one hand and as Infinite Bliss on the 
other. That point is the pivot. From it a single vāsanā starts, 
multiplies as the experience ‘I’, experience and the world. The 
experience and the Source are referred to in the mantra, “Two 
birds exactly alike arise simultaneously”. “The world is not 
other than the mind, the mind is not other than the Heart, that 
is the whole truth”. “This is what is taught to Svetakethu by 
the illustration of the seed of a fig tree”. “Ahankara shoots up 
like a rocket and instantaneously spreads out as the Universe”. 
(Talks no. 616). Though the Self is nirguna (attributeless) and 
nishkala (partless) It shines as both Para, the Transcendental, 
and apara, the phenomenal, like Creation. That formless 
Content also shines as the gross form and the formless subtle. 
All objects can be known through sense-perception. But the 
Ātman, the Self, can be known only by remaining as the 
Self. Though He is nameless and formless, He can be known 
through meditation in the Heart having ‘Him’ as the ‘I’ in all. 
In the order of subtlety It is the highest.

This is indicated in the phrase Ner ariyattakkadu (to 
be known directly as aparōksha). Hearsay knowledge is 
Parōksha jñāna and is not firm. But knowledge born of one’s 
own realization – aparōkasha – is firm. There is no ‘knowing’ 
in this; only experiencing, the experience of the joy of jñāna 
alone is there.

The real form is devoid of the minutest distinction in Its 
inherent nature. When due to inadvertence, the Ātman slips 
away from this real form as jīva, It perceives manifoldness 
with a mental perception of distinction. In order to instruct 
such deluded minds the nature of non-difference of the 
Absolute, since those perceptions of manifold difference, apart 
from the mind, are not, these differences were explained with 
reference to the perception of the Ātman by the mind. This is 
only by way of courtesy and formal practice.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   293 06-05-2011   10:53:50

The Param or Transcendental is called Nirguna 

Brahmam (Jñāna that is nameless, formless, spaceless

perceptionless. The apara or phenomenal is Brahman that 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   294 06-05-2011   10:53:50



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 295

is manifest and shines as Saguna Brahman with the five-
fold functions like creation. Mantras (the form of sacred 
words and syllables) are the gross form of that Brahman. 
The subtle form of that Brahman abides established in a

Commentary: 

Parama nirvānam is the state of being the Ātman, shining 
with the sphurana of Ātman ‘I am’ simply as ‘Being’ and 
‘Awareness’, void of Perception. It is Śūnya, for there is 
nothing apart from the knowing Awareness. It is also called 
maha Śūnya when even śūnya as an object known is removed 
from ‘I’, the form of Awareness. This is also called nirguna 
Brahman. Bhagavan often used to say that when the ‘I’ of 
sushupti (deep sleep) is experienced in Jāgrat (wakeful state) 
it is Ātman or nirguna Brahman or Śūnya. 

This can be explained as follows: Waking is also a 
dream but a little less transitory than dream. The dreamer 
and the ‘I’ of the waking state have passing experiences in 
nature but without any substantiality. The experiencer of 
both the dreams were the dreamer (or dream-ego) and the 
jāgrat-ego. Who is the ‘I’ then? The witness of these two 
states. In deep sleep, the ‘I’ is the witness of that experience 
as well but there is no experience to be witnessed by ‘I’. 
Therefore the ‘I’ is not even a witness for there is nothing 
to be witnessed. But this sakshi bhava also has to be 
transcended. Dream incidents are unreal and equally unreal 
are the incidents of jāgrat. In both states nothing happens 
and therefore there is nothing to be witnessed. Hence It 
is not even the witness of the three states. The ‘I’ alone 
is, – the Sat-Chit-Ānanda – in all the three. Remaining as 
this is nirvāṇam. 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   295 06-05-2011   10:53:50



296 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

That form of jñāna that shines with the five-fold functions 
of creating the perceivable universe, protecting it, destroying 
it, veiling and bestowing grace is called apara or Iswara 
or Saguna Brahman. The form of mantra of Ātman, like 
the mahavakya is Its gross form, it being within the reach 
and grasp of the mind. The subtle form of the Self abides 
established in a mind of Ātmakara Vritti alone with love 
(Ātmakara Vritti is the thought-ramification of the form of 
Ātman). As God is love, in a mind with unwavering love, the 
subtle Self remains as condensed essence of consciousness 
devoid of the phenomenal or objective content.

Sarva Śūnya is that content that pervades everywhere 
and infills everything, with Its non-being nowhere and in 
nothing. Brahman, the Absolute, includes all and excludes all, 
is immanent in all and transcends all. This is akin to calling 
a top that spins too fast a ‘sleeping’ top on account of its 
seeming stillness. As long as there is the perverse perception 
of ‘otherness’ and many, the perception expands into manifold 
as ‘this’ or ‘that’. When the perception of distinction vanishes, 
it (perception) becomes void and One. This sight, devoid of 
drisya (seen), is nirvāṇa.

The state of mukti is to attain the pristine-pure life of bliss 
that shines simply as ‘Being’. This is the final verdict of true 
jñānis who have experienced the state of ‘Truth’ declared by 
the Vedas. Nothing remains to be attained beyond this.

The use of the word Parama (supreme) is very significant 
and revealing. Even the ordinary word sukha (pleasure) itself 
refers to bliss. The word parama sukha implies that no sukha 
(bliss) is greater than that. So is the use of the word parama 
shanti, supreme peace. Hence Parama Nirvāṇam refers to the 
exalted state of mukti.

Nirvāṇam literally means without form or to be blown 
out. Here it refers to the individual ego getting put out.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   296 06-05-2011   10:53:50



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 297

Transcendent and Immanent are otherwise known as 
Nirguna and Saguna, nirakara (formless) and Sakara (with 
form). Sakara Saguna refers to Gods like Rama and Krishna 
and nirakara saguna refers to mantras [(formulae) but with 
qualities like Shanti and Sathya]. 

The Form is present in the Formless even as a statue 
is present in the uncarved stone. The manifest is in the 
Unmanifest. Hence the manifest must be resolved into the 
unmanifest. Nirguna Nirvāṇa is known as Sat-Chit-Ānanda. 
When the unreal formful world is eliminated, ‘I’ the form 
of awareness, remains as the True Content, that cannot be 
sublated anymore. This is formless Brahman.

“Nirvāṇa is perfection. In the perfect state, there is 
neither subject nor object; there is nothing to see, nothing to 
feel, nothing to know. Seeing and knowing are the functions 
of the mind. In nirvāṇa there is nothing but the blissful Pure 
Consciousness ‘I am’.” (Talks no. 406).

Knowing anything other than realizing the whole prime

Endless listening to discourses on scriptures and śāstrās 
that dwell at great length on Ātman and the practice of śravaṇa 
and manana as an end in themselves do not serve the purpose. 
Such magical and clever display of words, sweet to hear, may 
amuse and astound the listeners but will not be a wholesome 
fare for the spiritually starved. One in pangs of hunger 
must himself eat to appease his hunger; instead listening to 
captivating critiques on the health and taste components of 
food items cannot become food; or may be food for thought 
but not for the stomach. Similar is this sabdajala (magical 
display) of words or excellence of discourses. So much so 
Acharya Sankara states vehemently in Vivekachūḍāmaṇi (The 
crown jewel of discrimination) that “Sabdajala maharanyam 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   298 06-05-2011   10:53:50



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 299

chitta bhramana karanam” (The wild forest of magical display 
of sounds is enough cause to stupefy the mind).

“The Scriptures are useful to indicate the existence of the 
Higher power (the Self) and the way to gain it. Their essence 
is that much only. When that is assimilated, the rest is useless. 
As one rising up in the scale finds the regions one has passed to 
be only steps to the higher stage and so on, the steps ascended 
become purvapaksha successively until the goal is gained. 
When the goal is reached it remains alone and all the rest 
becomes useless. That is how the śāstrās become useless… 
The essential soaks in the mind and the rest is forgotten. So 
it is with śāstrās”. (Talks no. 63).

Such continuous listening prevents a mind from following 
a particular path suitable to one’s temperament making it waver 
or jump from one to other causing indecision and consequent 
delusion. However said, ultimately one has to realize or know 
himself. The Self is not away from oneself or outside of him 
as the ‘other’. The essence of various expositions listened to 
is to “Know Thyself”. Bhagavan draws our attention to this 
very truth in Ānma Vidya Keerthanam wherein he says: “On 
knowing the Self within, the light of Ātman flashes within”. 
The power of clever display of words weans one away from 
the path of Truth and causes one to lose direction and struggle 
and wander in lanes and bylanes rather than march on the 
straight royal road to Release. Eternal happiness has to be 
sought only in the Eternal Vastu.

At their best, śravaṇa, manana and enquiry into śāstrās 
can be a guide and help to turn the mind inward. Their utility 
stops there. The goal and gain of a seeker should be realization 
of this Truth at all costs and never to allow the mind wander 
in fruitless occupations. There is no attainment greater than 
that of the Self. Even if Vedas and Vedāntas are churned well 
by one’s intellect, the nectar of aparōkshajñānam will not be 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   299 06-05-2011   10:53:51



300 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

attained without Vichāra or Aanvīshiki (Ātmayoga). Srimad 
Bhāgavatam proclaims that a person may be an adept in 
Sabda-Brahman (learned in the scriptures) but if his mind is 
not absorbed in Parabrahman, through spiritual disciplines, 
his efforts are futile like those of a person who maintains a 
sterile cow (hoping to milk it). (11-11-18).

Mundaka Upanishad says: “This Ātman is not obtained 
through the mere study of scriptures; nor through intellectual 
understanding; nor through much hearing of instructions from 
others. When the seeker prays by the Self for the Self alone, 
then the Ātman reveals Its real form”. (3-2-3).

Bhagavan very often used to say that all books tell you 
“look at yourself” but we continuously keep looking at the 
books instead. Once, a widely read scholar from the North 
came to have darsan of Bhagavan. Daily he would sit by the 
side of Bhagavan’s sofa and read aloud verses in Sanskrit 
from Upanishads and other scriptures continually. Others 
could neither meditate nor speak to Bhagavan. This went on 
for ten days. One day the scholar was found quietly seated 
in a corner like every other person and all were surprised. 
Bhagavan remarked humorously then: “Even the scholar has 
become silent like us”.

The look of grace from the sun of jñāna bestowed indeed 
the peace and quiescence on that man that could not have 
been procured by any other means, not even his extensive 
scholarship.

Ramakrishna Paramahamsa used to remark that if 
Almanac says there will be so much rain in a year squeezing 
the almanac will not cause the rain. Likewise, one has to 
realize oneself. 

Muruganar says:
Books of guidance all prescribe
Freedom from thought as the best way

Commentary:

The quality and grade of lives of beings in the world is 
varied and does not conform to any uniformity. Great are 
the variations and differences perceived among them. This 
is purely the outcome of jīvasrishti (creation by jīva). The 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   302 06-05-2011   10:53:51



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 303

quality and style of life experienced today by a jīva is the 
result of what he strongly resolved, aspired and endeavoured 
for, earlier.

Brihadaranyaka Upanishad also says “What it (the jīva) 
desires, it resolves, what it resolves, it works out; and what it 
works out it attains”. (4.4.5).

Ramakrishna Paramahamsa when he undertook various 
practices as part of his sādhanā, he assumed the bhava of an 
ideal servitor, namely Hanuman so intensely that he developed 
even a tail in the posterior of the body.

The jīva has gained the enjoyment of present life by his 
own volition and resolve. The most quoted example in spiritual 
lore for this is called the Bhramara-kīta nyaya- how a worm 
becomes a wasp. The worm confined to the mould on the 
wall by the wasp and constantly made to think of it in anger 
and fear of being stung, becomes converted into the shape of 
the wasp itself. Whether moved by fear or desire what one 
repeatedly thinks one becomes or gains that. Bhagavan has 
spoken of this. 

On whatever objects a person concentrates his mind, 
whether it be from love, animosity or fear that person attains 
the state of that object “like kita that turns into a brahmara 
or wasp”. Familiar examples are of Sisupala, Jayadharatha 
and Hiranya Kasipu, who by constant thoughts on the Lord, 
though born of hatred, attained the Lord ultimately .

But all that the jīva resolves and thinks out of delusion 
cannot be expected to turn good. Often, the contrary outcome 
is due to the absence of identity between thoughts and deeds. 

It is absolutely certain that every act comes back to him 
along with the attitude or bhava in which it was done. 

The experience of pain is but a grim reminder of his past 
sinful deeds. Understanding of this order in nature will prevent 
a jīva from further indulgence in sinful acts. But sometimes 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   303 06-05-2011   10:53:51



304 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

impelled by the strength of forceful vāsanās he is goaded 
to perform evil karmas. When he experiences the fruits of 
such karma, he bemoans that it was self-inflicted punishment 
caused by the reckless performance of abominable deeds done 
knowingly but uncontrollably. The jīva has neither the powers 
nor the wit to face and oppose the outcome of his own past 
deeds which is called ‘Fate’.

Tejobindu Upanishad (Verse 13) says: “Brahman is not 
known to those who are sensitive to fear, or pleasure and pain 
or honour and disgrace. To one free from these ideas, that 
Supreme Brahman becomes manifest – to one whose highest 
refuge is Brahman; yea, that Supreme Brahman becomes 
manifest to one whose highest refuge is Brahman”.

Mundaka Upanishad (1.10) proclaims: 
“Whatever world a jīva of a pure mind thinks (sankalpa) 

and whatever enjoyments he desires, gains that world and 
those enjoyments. One who desires great attainment must 
worship an Ātmajñāni.”

Siva exhorts Guha therefore to gain somehow the True 
Knowledge and realize that everything is but the form of 
Ātman with absolute certainty and blesses Him with eternal

Standing apart from and as other than the Ātman and 
realizing that everything is the Self cannot be whole or Perfect 
knowledge. Unless the one who so knows remains the Content 
of Ātman, the contemplation of everything as Brahman will 
not be real or possible. Bhagavan emphasized this point to a

as your form” ? Bhagavan replied: “One must first realize 
there is nothing but the Self and that he is that Self and then 
only he can see everything as the form of the Self. That is the 
meaning of saying – See the Self in everything and everything 
in the Self – as is stated in the Gītā and other books.” 
(Day by Day, 18-4-46).

Again to another question as to how the world, only a 
dream, should be harmonized with Eternal Reality Bhagavan 
answered that “it consists in the realization of its inseparateness 
from the Self… The Realized being sees the world not as 
separate from the Self”…for such a one this (the world) is the 
kingdom of Heaven. The Kingdom of Heaven is within you. 
That Kingdom is here and now.” (Talks no. 487).

As Bhagavan himself sings in Pancharatnam: “May 
Arunachala make my heart blossom so that His unbroken 
brilliance may shine forever and remain as all.”

Most importantly “Unnaik kandu ellamum unnuruvai” – 
(beholding Thee and everything – the cosmos – as Thy very 
FORM) The term ellam (everything) or all itself becomes 
contentless for one who remains (as) the content of Ātman. 
‘What is’ is Ātman alone. When one remains as That what else 
can be there? Who is there to see? When everything is Ātman 
what is there to be meditated upon as Ātman?

“The seeker ultimately reaches the Self and there finds

Being absorbed in the Reality the world is also Real. There

from the Self”. (Talks no. 316).

“Subject, object all merge in the Self. The seer and the

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 307

A  void devoid of everything is the content of Ātman which 
alone is. The inner awareness coupled with a void of mind 
(emptied of sankalpas and vikalpas) and remaining anchored 
in the Source, the Heart, is conveyed by the expression “Ātma 
chintai vallanai endrume vazh.” (Live forever as an adept in 
contemplation of the Ātman – as one with Ātman).

The spiritual heroes-those stita prajñās – abiding ever in 
the state of illumination are the adepts in this science of Ātman.

The ghost of the ego is the seed for the sprouting of 
various religious differences. The knowledge of the non-dual 
Ātman – jñānam and vijñānam, paroksha and aparoksha – is 
the seed of integration of all religions. The Lord instructs the 
way to live simply as the bliss of Being, a life of light of the 
effulgence of Brahmajñāna, never slipping from It.

Further He says the reason for His synthesizing and 
amalgamating, the essence of Truth is to somehow make one 
succeed in gaining the Ātma Vidya. Ways indicated by the 
Vedas and śāstrās are many; but the Content they indicate 
and earnestly attempt to reveal, is just One. Hence know the 
Truth that Sarvam (all) is Brahmamayam (the very form of 
Brahman) and live permanently in the Oneness of the Self. 
Here one is irresistibly reminded of the personal experience of 
the condensed essence which was couched in a beautiful song 
by the saint Sadasiva Brahmendra as Sarvam Brahmamayam. 
Everything that is perceived for such a one becomes Satyasya 
Satyam the truth of all truth for the Spiritual Essence sees 
only That everywhere. The world is a manifestation of the 
Glory of God and everything is His altar and Tabernacle and 
all creatures are His Expressions.

“What is even here (visible as the world) the same is there 
(invisible as Brahman); and what is there, the same is here. 
He proceeds from death to death who beholds here difference 
(between Brahman and the world).” (Kathopanishad, II-X).

Vedas, their holy recitation, courses of Vedic learning

Commentary: 

Śāstrās speak of ways and means of worshipping the 
deities and prescribe appropriate ways of elaborate procedural 
worship for specific deities. Thus there are various forms 
of worship laid down and observance of certain rules and 
disciplines is compulsory for undergoing apprenticeship in 
courses of Vedic learning.

The yajñas enjoined by the Vedas are also varied and 
the purpose and the rules of procedure to be followed are all 
prescribed in great detail in the Vedas.

While performing such yajñas, the fruit of the performance 
of the yagna will not accrue in its entirety, if dakshinas or 
offering of gifts to priests who help conduct the yajñas are 
not given away as per the dictates of the Vedas, all of which 
are set down in the Vedas.

Vedic commandments in this field are numerous. 
Sometimes it enjoins on the part of one who has the yajña 
performed, the gift of fixed heads of so many cows to the 
officiating priests. Brahmacharins who recite the Vedas during 
yajñas would be commanded to hand over the dakshinas 
received to their respective gurus. It also lays down the gift 
of land and villages duly accompanied by legal documents, 
declarations making them valid and encumbrance – free to 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   309 06-05-2011   10:53:51



310 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Vedic pundits who recite the Vedas. The authority and dignity 
accorded to Vedas in the domain of yajñas is truly vast and 
unquestioned. No yagna can ever be declared complete unless 
performed with strict adherence to such Vedic injunctions.

But in the state of the experience of the Ātman none of 
these aforesaid actions exists. The Self is immaculate, present 
everywhere; eternally existent and shines as the form of 
Supreme Peace. “Resort to that jñāna” says the Lord.

All the actions – by their very nature and by the nature of 
instruments involved – are limited and that which is unlimited 
cannot be the result of limited and finite actions. Hence 
Supreme knowledge is prescribed by scriptures as the only 
way to eradicate nescience. All karmas and the various lokas 
– with a view to attain which these karmas are performed – are 
all perishable. “The divine forms are only like bubbles in the 
ocean of Reality or like pictures moving on a screen”, (Talks 
no. 163) and “all lokas even the Brahma loka do not release 
one from rebirth”, (Talks no. 181) and “devotion is nothing 
more than knowing oneself”. (Talks no. 205).

Vivekachūḍāmaṇi defines Bhakti as “contemplation of 
one’s real form”. All Vedas are pointers to this one Truth and 
all endeavours are efforts to realize this Truth. Parōksha and 
aparōksha jñāna are the best yajñas.

This is reaffirmed by the Lord to Uddhava. “Therefore 
abandoning reliance on the scriptural injunctions and 
prohibitions, the ways of work and of renunciation, what 
you have learnt and what you yet hope to learn – surrender 
your being, body, mind and soul, to Me (the Ātman), the all-
Comprehending One, the Essence within all embodied beings. 
By that shall you be free from all fear through My grace.” 
(Bhāgavatam, 11-12-14 and 15).

“The non-performance of actions is no great sin for one 
engaged in enquiry, for that itself is the most meritorious and 
purifying of actions.” (Ramana Gīta, 7.19)

Paraphrase: 
Know that there is nothing other than the knowledge 

of the Self that provides a safe haven of refuge to the 
jīva who wanders seeking an asylum from drowning in 
the vast ocean of saṁsāra of repeated births and deaths.
Commentary: 

Saṁsāra is a never ending chain of events like birth 
and death. It is a grievous cycle of unceasing embodiment. 
A jīva born into the world experiences his prārabdha – the 
fruits of his actions of former births – and at the expiry of the 
prārabdha, dies immediately not even living for a second 
more. But he is born again, performs actions, good and bad, 
and takes more births appropriate to experience the fruits of 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   311 06-05-2011   10:53:51



312 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

them. In this vast and deep ocean of saṁsāra, the jīva gasping 
for relief and seeking a way of escape from drowning tossed 
about wanders hither and thither. What the jīva desires is not 
only relief from suffering that the saṃsāric life is full of but 
also happiness unpunctuated by suffering. In short, what he 
yearns for, is eternal happiness. But what he fails to realize is 
that Eternal happiness can be sought only in the Eternal and 
not in the transient. 

Hence a man caught in this quagmire can be made to 
reach safety only by one who is free and not himself stuck in 
the slush of saṁsāra. Relief from the bog of continual births 
and deaths can be had only by seeking refuge at the feet of 
Mahesa, the birthless and deathless. Some means may provide 
temporary relief but the only haven of permanent relief is the 
knowledge of the Self.

Bhāgavatam very emphatically and repeatedly states that 
this bhavasāgara (ocean of saṁsāra) can be crossed over as 
easily as puddles formed of calf’s hoofs with Ātmajñāna. 

A discriminating seeker must seek and obtain it 
disregarding all other means of refuge. The saṁsāra of birth 
and death, the outcome of anānma jñāna or ajñāna causing 
ignorance of one’s own spiritual stature can be overcome only 
by its opposite namely ātmajñāna which alone is the shore of 
mukti for one struggling in the sea of saṁsāra.

Therefore Nanyat dwaram ātmano vijñānaya! – There 
is no other way except Knowledge of the Self declares the 
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad.

The means to attain moksha is Self knowledge and not 
action. This is the purport of the Gītā Śāstra as declared by 
Sankara and not karma or bhakti as is commonly believed.

“Jnanenaivathu Kaivalyam” (Kaivalyopanishad) “By 
knowledge alone is Liberation” – “tam evam vidwan Amrita 
iha bhavati nanyap pantha ayanaya vidyathe” – One who 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   312 06-05-2011   10:53:51



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 313

knows That becomes immortal even here. There is no other 
way to him.

Therefore the balm for the clinging affliction of birth is 
Knowledge of the Self alone, the attainment of which leads to 
final disentanglement from all embodiments. Everyone at some 
point of time develops a mental state full of determination to 
follow only the light of the ‘Content’ that dwells in the heart. 
Then he frees himself from the bondage and becomes a hero 
spiritually.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   313 06-05-2011   10:53:51



314 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Paraphrase: 
Know that the one who, by becoming that very 

Parasvarūpa (the Content Beyond) realizes firmly 
the truth of that Paramātman, as ‘It is’, ‘firmly and 
forever’, though he (seemingly) attains and abides in 
all the different states of consciousness, even without a 
single effort he will attain Release – the Home of Mukti, 
without fail.
Commentary: 

The one who seeks to know the Self must first become 
the Self. One can never objectify and know the Ātman by 
remaining as an independent entity apart from the Self. “To 
know the Ātman” is a formal way of saying, – by way of 
courtesy; for becoming the Self is knowing the Self – the 
non-dual Infinite Being in whom all the triads have merged, 
the dualities have disappeared and the subject and object 
have coalesced. The first sentence of this verse “Paramahi 
apparamanmavai uramaha ullapadi unarvai” (Becoming the 
Self, know firmly the Self as It is) emphasizes this.

Unless the individuality of the jīva, the very form of the 
ego-ridden mind, is totally uprooted, the ego-mind by simply 
contemplating “I am that Supreme Self” cannot attain its 
Source the Self; hence the emphasis on “Paramahi” (becoming 
That).

Here a word of caution is administered by saying “Know 
the Self as It is firmly”.

A deluded mind lacking in firmness, strength and grit 
will attempt to know the Self as a form imagined by it by 
the sheer strength of its stance. Hence the caution to know 
the Self as ‘It is’ through a firm mind. One who realizes 
the truth by practicing in this way will remain unaffected 
by any state.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   314 06-05-2011   10:53:51



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 315

The Immutable Ātman, though remains ever realized, 
remains veiled by its own power of māyā. 

Māyā projects the three states of consciousness in the 
manokasa (ether of mind) and mounts the jīva, so attached 
to the body, on them and whirls him round in this merry-go- 
round. Yet none of these states can ever affect one who has 
known the Truth as It is by becoming It.

The jīva with the distorted perception of the world 
considers “Parama nirvāṇam” (Supreme release) as Turiya, 
the fourth state. But for that Mahayogī in whom the Supreme 
knowledge of the Self is firm, the Supreme awareness is 
mingled with all states, yet it remains beyond them as non-dual.

Though such a one appears to perceive like others all the 
different states, he, in truth perceives his own transcendent 
form in all these. This is conveyed by the last line which says 
“Though he abides in all states of consciousness, without an 
effort, he reaches HOME.”

Bhagavan explains the state of a jñāni who seems to 
go through the avasthas thus. “There is a fixed state; sleep, 
dream and waking states are mere movements in it. They 
are like pictures moving on the screen in a cinema show.” 
(Talks no. 607).

“The Self is the fourth state – the other three go on 
changing like the scenes in cinema. All the three are ideas of 
the mind. That which is beyond the three is the Self. A jñāni 
ever in Samadhi is like a light in windless place or the ocean 
without waves.

“Is the cinema screen affected by a scene of fire burning 
or sea rising? So it is with the Self.” (Talks no. 486).

“Real waking lies beyond the three states of waking, 
dream and sleep.” (Talks no. 476).

And in Day by Day, Mudaliar records: “The jñāni does 
not think he is the body. He does not even see the body. He 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   315 06-05-2011   10:53:51



316 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

sees only the Self in the body. If the body is not there, but 
only the Self, no question about the body or the states it goes 
through can arise.” (18th Jan. 1946).

Bhagavan once translated a verse from Bhāgavatam 
which explained this state of such a jñāni. The translation in 
English of that verse it is as follows:

“Just as the man blinded with drunkenness sees not 
whether the cloth he has is on, or not, so the Self-realized 
siddha knows not whether the perishable body is existent or 
non-existent whether by force of karma it has gone from him 
or come to him.”

“For the jñāni, all the three states are equally unreal. But 
the ajñāni is unable to comprehend this because for him the 
standard of Reality is the waking state, whereas for the jñāni, 
the standard of Reality is Reality itself. This Reality of Pure 
Consciousness is eternal by its nature and therefore subsists 
equally during what you call waking, dreaming and sleep. 
To him who is one with that reality there is neither the mind 
nor the three states, and therefore neither introversion nor 
extroversion.” (Maharshi’s Gospel, page 83).

Bhagavan who was always in the Sahaja Samadhi was 
ever awake and the body did not exist for him. The following 
two incidents explain this. When Swami Pravanananda 
recommended Dr. Kaviraj for treating Bhagavan, Bhagavan 
replied “Will anyone preserve after the dinner, the leaf on 
which he has eaten?” 

Dr. M. Anantanarayana Rao records (Surpassing Love and 
Grace): “Bhagavan was always awake, though in a state of 
Samadhi”. Once he went to him with a small pot containing 
an ointment which he had wanted. Anantanarayana Rao heard 
him snore lightly and thought he was sleep. “I stood thinking 
whether to keep the pot on the shelf quietly or wait till he was 
awake. Within a moment he opened his eyes, smiled and asked 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   316 06-05-2011   10:53:51



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 317

me why I was waiting without handing over the ointment to 
him. I replied that he was asleep…..Sri Bhagavan at once 
asked me how I concluded that he was asleep…. Bhagavan 
again closed his eyes and snored lightly.”

“At that time a bhakta – a new comer – came near the 
couch and prostrated, he at once opened his eyes and smiled 
at him. Again he reverted to the sleepy condition when an 
ashramite came and prostrated, he did not open his eyes, 
but practically on the ashramite’s heels came a new comer 
who prostrated and Bhagavan immediately opened his eyes, 
saw him and smiled.” Devaraja Mudaliar has recorded two 
instances which proved beyond doubt that Bhagavan ever 
remained as the Self. One was when Swami Rajeshwarananda 
had arranged for Bhagavan a tour various places in India. 
Bhagavan declined to go. “When telling us about it, he 
remarked ‘What is the use of my going anywhere? I cannot see 
anything.’ He clearly meant that wherever he goes, whatever 
he is shown he sees only the Self”.

The other was when A. Bose’s mother prepared 
various items, brought them and served them at lunch to 
Bhagavan and devotees. Telling her not to trouble herself 
making so many dishes he said, “All of you have many 
tastes but I have only one taste; your taste is in the many, 
mine is in the One. From these it was clear that Bhagavan 
was always in that transcendental state called Turiya”. 
(Devaraja Mudaliar, My Recollections, page 96-97).

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   318 06-05-2011   10:53:51



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 319

“That natural Bliss of Brahman, where the mind is not 
risen, does occur in heaven and the like, as a habitation 
of ice (or a lake of ice) does not occur in a sandy desert.” 
(Yoga Vasishtam, Verse1586). 

Gain of the Self is nothing but ātmasākṣātkāram or the 
direct experience of the Self. It is not far away. This Ātman 
who appears to be within the body is the Supreme Self and That 
is not confined to here or there. But that, filling everywhere 
and remaining as all, pervades everything. Contemplate and 
realize this truth, is the advice.

Man, discarding this most precious of all gains, and 
considering other cheap gains as worthy of attainment, 
ceaselessly toils and runs after them only to come to ruin. 
Finally weary and disgusted and overcome by frustration he 
gives them up. Ceaseless struggle and endless pain are all 
that he gets.

That attainment, after gaining which the desire for another 
gain does not arise is the greatest gain.

“That is the (ultimate) Abode. That is the Tranquil state. 
That is the Eternal and Blessed Felicity. Delusion does not 
again disturb one who has obtained repose there. Embodied 
beings, having reached through their heart that position of 
Supreme Bliss, do not value the visible world as kings do not 
(value) poverty.” (Yoga Vasishtam, Verse 1594).

That, is the only gain that is never away from him even 
for a moment, but ever remains with him.

Brihadaranyaka Upanishad (1-5-16) says: “This world 
of man is to be won through the son alone, by no other rite; 
the world of the manes through rites and the world of Gods 
through meditation”. But these lead to the attainment of the 
three worlds that are other than the Self (non-Self).

“What shall we achieve through children, we to whom, 
the Self we have attained, is the goal?” (4-6-22).
