Paraphrase: 

Ātman is neither the prana, the vital air; nor is it the 
apana. Nor is it the instruments, senses or the inner organs 
like the mind that are superior to them. It is Awareness 
– the all knowing Witness eternally Present, Partless, 
Content of Fullness. Attain the thought of that Content 
ever in thy heart and abide as That.
Commentary: 

This verse proves the Self by way of ‘Neti-Neti’ (not this-
not this). Of the five pranas in the body namely prana, apana, 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   320 06-05-2011   10:53:52



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 321

vyana, samana and udana though only two are mentioned the 
others can be inferred as included.

(That which keeps the body alive bringing in oxygen 
taking out carbon dioxide and converts food to energy is called 
prana. That which takes out waste from the body is called 
apana. That which digests the food is called samana. That 
which spreads the digested food as energy through the body, 
regulates circulation of blood and regulates movements of 
body and senses is called vyana. Finally that which takes out 
the soul from the body at the time of death is called udana.)

The instruments of action, organs of perception or the 
inner organs like the mind, intellect etc. that are superior to 
each other in that order are not Ātman either. If that be so then 
the question, what then is the Ātman is answered by proving 
the Ātman by proclaiming its characteristics. It is simply 
the Awareness that knows the five pranas, the instruments 
of action and perception, the inner organs like the mind and 
intellect. It is an ever present Fullness.

None of the above five pranas is the Ātman. It is wrong 
to identify the principle of prana, functioning in the body 
as the one who hears and replies, for prana and the indryas 
moved to action by prana, are as much unconscious entities as 
the body itself. The qualities of prana like thirst and hunger, 
strength and weakness as revealed in expression “I live well”; 
“I will die” exist only in jāgrat. In dream and sleep, strength or 
lack of it, hunger, thirst, living and dying are not known. But 
remaining as other than prana but aware of its functions and 
devoid of their virtueless nature is the Ātman, the Unmoving.

All indryas perform different functions and one organ 
of action will not perform that of another. Similarly one 
instrument of cognition cannot do the office of another. Each 
performs its own action only in jāgrat (wakeful state); none 
of them functions in dream and sleep. Remaining apart from 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   321 06-05-2011   10:53:52



322 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

these, aware of their rise, subsidence and functioning, is the 
unmoving Awareness-the Ātman.

Like one actor performing different roles, the one mind 
donning the costume of likes and dislikes appears in the outer 
world. In dream, it becomes the dream world of imagination. 
In sushupti (sleep), with no special knowledge it subsides 
unseen. Remaining as the ‘other’ and aware of the mind’s vile 
functions, as the witness of the mind that comes and joins in 
jāgrat and dream is the Self, the Awareness that is devoid of 
pleasure and pain (the sukha and dukha) of the mind. 

No mortal lives by prana or apana or the organs but all 
live by That on which all these depend for their very existence. 
The Ātman associating with the mind, prana, indriyas and 
the body makes them conscious entities. None of these can 
comprehend the Ātman as the indweller in all the creatures as 
the Witness-Awareness. Ātman is distinct from these faculties 
and their objects just as forms and colours cannot see the eye 
that reveals them. Just as a sense object does not grasp the 
sense that perceives the object, the senses cannot know the 
Ātman – the Witness – Awareness.

Prana, indriyas or mind and intellect cannot awaken 
a sleeping man on their own except for the presence of the 
indweller – The Witness – Awareness.

This Ātman or Self is that which a man cannot comprehend 
with the mind, that by which the mind is encompassed, that 
which man cannot see with the eye, that by which man 
perceives the activities of the eye. That Ātman, though be 
without limbs and sense organs, by being the witness of all 
cognitions, by nature nothing but the power of consciousness, 
is indicated by the cognitions themselves in the midst of 
cognitions as pervading all of them. 

Just as sparks coming from a fire do not illumine or burn 
that fire, the entities born of Ātman like the mind, prana, 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   322 06-05-2011   10:53:52



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 323

senses, buddhi and words cannot reveal That. Even Vedas 
attempt to explain That by their negative stance. Ātman is 
seen as many and momentary only when It is reflected in all 
these adjuncts.

Therefore that Awareness, which lends sentience and 
power to everything, making them all function as if endowed 
with natural sentience, is the mighty Awareness, Ātman.

The most exhaustive repositories of encyclopedic 
knowledge of the entire Universe cannot equal even a ‘whit’ of 
that Awareness. Though revealing everything It can be known 
by nothing and to know It one has to abide as That and know 
It. It is called ‘Fullness’ for It remains as the Awareness of 
awareness, vivifying everything.

Hence the Lord exhorts to hold that contemplation in the 
heart at all times, to approach It and abide as That, without 
the mind frittering away its energies on other thoughts. The 
contemplation of Ātman gradually grinds the thoughts till 
the mind becomes naught. What remains, with the mind 
obliterated, is one’s own Form of Awareness and That shines 
in all Its splendour.

Mundakopanishad says “That Supreme Purusha is full 
of Effulgence, formless, homogeneously present in and out, 
birthless, without prana, without mind and Immaculate. 
Pranan, Mind, all organs, ether, air, fire, water and earth that 
holds everything all rise only from Him.” (2-1-3 and 4).

Prana for the empirical jīva is the Truth (Sathyam) but 
Ātman from which everything including prana originates is 
sathyasya sathyam – the Truth of truth.

The five elements are the cause of the world and therefore 
Sathyam. But Brahman, the cause of them is sathyasya 
sathyam.

Saint Manivāchakar sings of the same with a melting 
heart as follows:

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   323 06-05-2011   10:53:52



324 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

	 Moving ever – as atoms ever wasting-Thou art One
	 Civan, who dwell’st in Perunthurai
	 Thou art not anything; without Thee nothing is
	 Who are they that can know Thee as Thou Art? 
Contemplation is never to ensure the life or longevity of 

the mind but to render it void of thoughts. Ātma chintanam 
is not to think of It by remaining apart from It. It, as Ātman, 
is unreachable by mind. Continual contemplation of It will 
annihilate the thoughts till the mind, void of its content-
thoughts- comes to a grinding halt, loses it form and becomes 
One with the Ātman.

Bhāgavatam hails the Supreme Brahman as follows in 
verses 6 to 8 in Skandam 10, Chapter 85:

“That prana and other energies which cause the world 
to evolve are not self energetic but they depend on Him to be 
effective. As a sharp sword depends on its wielder to strike 
an enemy, non-intelligent beings require a Prime Mover to 
initiate the movement and direct it purposefully……

O, Lord, Thou art the shine of the moon, the heat of the 
fire, the brilliance of the sun, the twinkling gleam of the stars 
and the flash of lightning. Thou art the motionless stance of the 
mountains and the earth’s power of bearing and its fragrance 
too. Thou art the power of water to quench thirst and enable 
life to survive”.

is All-pervading, Unbroken, Immutable and Blemishless. That 
Content Beyond is not confined to any specific place either 
within or without or far or near. Whoever posed questions 
to Bhagavan will receive the answer that the one who posed 
the question was the answer. In the same way if the question 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   325 06-05-2011   10:53:52



326 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

what is this ‘Being’ of the Ātman is asked, the one who seeks 
is the ‘Being’ of the Ātman is the answer. This is the Truth as 
well as the illustration. 

Ātman, being the highest in the order of subtlety, though It 
pervades everywhere, remains ‘untouched’ by or ‘unattached’ 
to any. Hence It cannot be said to reside in any object yet at 
the same time as It pervades the ‘inside’ and ‘outside’ of all 
objects it is said that there is no place where “It is not”. Infilling 
everything and pervading everywhere It remains as ‘All’. Apart 
from the ‘Being’ of the Ātman, there is no ‘being’ for any ‘to 
be’. In truth the unreal world appears so real and deludes due 
to the ‘being’ of the True Content on which it is superimposed. 

The entire Universe is mithya, an appearance superimposed 
on the Reality which is Brahman. And the individual jīva is 
verily Brahman alone and not anything other than Him.”

Once a devotee wanted to know the sign-boards in the 
journey towards the Self. Bhagavan replied “You know how 
far you are from Madras. Can you tell me how far away you 
are from the Self in order that you should seek it?” The devotee 
replied in the negative. Then Bhagavan questioned “Are you 
ever divorced from the Self? Is it possible to be divorced? Are 
not all these alien to you and the Self most intimate? Where 
should you go to gain the Self?” (Talks no. 427).

“Direct your look within and make it absolute. With 
that absolute awareness realized, look without and you will 
realize the universe to be not apart from the realized Absolute. 
Because your outlook is externally directed you speak of a 
‘without’. In that state you are advised to look within. This 
‘within’ is relative to the ‘without’ you are seeking. In fact, the 
Self is neither without nor within. Speaking of Heaven, one 
thinks of it as above or below, within or without since one is 
accustomed to relative knowledge. One seeks only objective 
knowledge and hence these ideas. Really speaking there is 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   326 06-05-2011   10:53:52



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 327

neither up nor down, neither in nor out. If they were real they 
must be present in dreamless sleep also. For what is real must 
be continuous and permanent”. (Talks no. 311).

While announcing the Ātman the One ‘Being’, the 
declaration that is “It is not in anything” is immediately 
followed up by the statement that “There is no place where It 
is not”. Is not this tantamount to a contradiction? Why is it so?

It is so instructed to suit the level and state of the seeker. 
Ātman is ever the same. Never is there a change in It. All these 
statements are intended to cater to seekers of varying degrees 
of competence or ripeness. When the seeker is sufficiently ripe 
he is told “anything that appears is not”.

Inside and outside, far and near, are all differences in 
space and time – the products of mental imagination –which 
are not in the Parandamam that is beyond the reach of mind. 
“Ātman is subtler than the subtlest, smaller that the smallest 
and at same time bigger than the biggest and greater that the 
greatest.”

Behind the greatest and smallest, He is hidden as the 
impelling energy, the Light of Consciousness. Therefore 
Parandamam is said to be neither ‘within’ nor ‘without’ neither 
far nor near. Unlike the various supports put forth by the mind 
(like objects and persons) when one has moved away from the 
Self, that Formless Ātman shines as the basis and support of 
all these imagined supports. Ātman is experienced directly by 
an inward turned mind and through the enquiry ‘Who am I?‘.

The word angē (there) stands here for the ‘Heart’. The 
best dhyāna is to gather and inhere the chindai (mind) in its 
Source, the Heart. The Lord exhorts “direct your mind” there. 
As inadvertence is death, He instructs not to give way to 
forgetfulness by saying endrum cheluttu ever direct your mind. 
In short the meditator should perceive the essence, presence 
and power of the Supreme Consciousness behind every object 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   327 06-05-2011   10:53:52



328 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

and every experience. In the ultimate sense nothing appears 
or disappears. There are none bound. There are no seekers 
performing sādhanā so as to get released from bondage. 
There are no mumukshus (seeker ‘of Release’), consequently 
there is no one released. The most certain conclusion of the 
philosophy on the Supreme is this. Thus proclaim the śāstrās, 
loud and clear, with conviction.

Devaraja Mudaliar has recorded an incident where what 
Bhagavan explains is the content of this verse.

One Mr. Tayal of Calcutta asked Bhagavan that he 
kept changing the centres on which he concentrated but 
while he concentrated on one, his mind got fixed on another 
on its own. Bhagavan replied “It is immaterial on which 
centre you concentrate since the real heart is in every centre 
and even outside the body. On whatever part of the body 
you may concentrate or on whatever external object, the 
heart is there….He who concentrates is always the same.” 
(Day by Day, 22-7-46).

“Brahmajñānis call it (Ātman) Akshara. It is neither gross 
nor subtle, neither short, nor long; neither red like fire; nor 
wet like water; devoid of shadow, measure, without an inside 
and outside.” (Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, 8-8).

and below, ever and everywhere, firmly fixed and beyond

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   329 06-05-2011   10:53:52



330 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

This Ātman without resorting to the aid of any other 
light, shines in Its own Self-revealing Effulgence. As there 
is nothing other than the Ātman as apart from It, It shines as 
Being, Bliss and Awareness. Though It pervades everywhere 
infilling everything It shines as Śūnya, with the non-being of 
anything else, and without the impact of anything and beyond 
the reach of speech and mind.

It may be of interest to know here that Sage Yajñavalkya 
with the reputation of being unbeatable in describing Brahman, 
answers in reply to the question by Garki “By what is 
unmanifested ether pervaded by?” He answered “Oh Garki! The 
knowers of Brahman say this Immutable Brahman is That. It 
is neither gross, nor minute, neither short nor long, neither red 
in color nor oily, neither shadow nor darkness, neither air nor 
ether, unattached, neither savour nor odour, without eyes or ears, 
without the vocal organ or mind, without vital force or mouth, 
not a measure and without exterior or interior. It does not eat 
anything, nor is It eaten by anybody.” In short It is devoid of 
all attributes, for It is one without a second. All these attributes 
are with reference to the mind but the relationship with mind 
ends with dream. The mind and its vishaya have no place there. 
Hence it is called Śūnya for there nothing can be specified and 
there is nothing through which anything can be specified.

That Brahman that is directly perceptible to Itself, That 
which remains desiring nothing else, That which remains as 
the indweller of all, transcending all afflictions like hunger, in 
which the ether is woven as warp and woof, that is the frontier, 
that is Supreme Refuge (Para gathi) that is ParaBrahman. 
Right from earth to sky in all things that are empirically true, 
that alone remains as the Transcendental Truth, says Sankara. 

The second mantra of the Advaitamrita Upanishad, a 
minor Upanishad states the same: “Brahman is within and 
without. He is above and below, He is in front and behind. 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   330 06-05-2011   10:53:52



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 331

He is in your right side and left side. He is everywhere, like 
the all-pervading ether. He is Chidakasa.”

One is instructed to contemplate more and more on 
this Ātman shining in Its own splendour. How to hold and 
contemplate in the mind that which is beyond the reach of 
mind? Even if It be so, It has to be contemplated on is the 
way prescribed. Even a stone when subject to constant and 
forceful rubbing gets worn out and loses its identity of shape 
and form; so mind constantly contemplating on one Vastu 
will wear out and waste away. This is the aim and intention of 
contemplation, not to attain Ātman but to annihilate the mind.

Ātman is an ever attained reality and cannot be gained 
anew. All sādhanā is to defeat, conquer and annihilate the 
mind. Hence the exhortation to contemplate more and even 
more. This is a subtle way of gaining the form that is beyond 
bhavanas by the sheer strength of bhavana.

The nature of Self is like the same sugar out of which two 
dolls – one master and the other a slave – are made. The forms 
differ but the substance is the same. The Self that pervades 
everywhere can have no distinctions; hence contemplate It 
more and more.

Paraphrase: 
That Ātman is not Śūnya, a void. Nor is It aśūnya 

(non-void). It is also a void and a non-void. This Ātman 
– the Whole – pervades everywhere, shines everywhere

Commentary: 

Śūnya is objectless Awareness. There is the non-being of 
everything else except Itself as Awareness. It is a void with 
none of the objects external or internal in the body, like the 
world, objects, senses, inner organs and their functions, names 
and forms, speech, mind, the three gunas, five elements, the 
three states, Pranan, sun and moon. Such a state, though 
baffling comprehension, is called Śūnya.	

Bhagavan explains the whole phenomenon of void: “In 
all books on Vedānta you will find this question of a void or of 
nothing being left, raised by the disciple and answered by the 
guru. It is the mind that sees the objects and has experiences 
and that finds a void when it ceases to see and experience but 
that is not ‘you’. ‘You’ are the constant illumination that lights 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   332 06-05-2011   10:53:52



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 333

up both the experiences and the void. It is like the theatre 
light that enables you to see the theatre, the actors and the 
play while the play is going on but also remains alight and 
enables you to say there is no play when it is all finished. Or 
there is another illustration. We see objects all around us but 
in complete darkness we say ‘I see nothing’; but the eyes are 
there to say so. In the same way you are there even in the void” 
and further, “the nature of Self, ‘I’, is illumination and all 
experiences and the absence of them contain the illumination 
which is the nature of the Self.” (Day by Day, 21-7-46).

The intellect on the one hand, and the objects grasped by 
them on the other, are nothing but consciousness which forms 
their substratum. The world of objects is transitory and has 
no ultimacy. Objects cannot be separated from Consciousness 
and shown to exist (like ornaments from gold) separately 
by themselves as they have no independent existence apart 
from Consciousness. Ātman shines unbroken as the basis 
and support of everything and illumining all. Ātman here is 
explained by way of both affirmation and negation.

Phenomenal knowledge becomes void in the Noumenon 
– the form of Ātman. Hence It is Śūnya. But if Ātman is void 
how can It shine remaining simply as Awareness of objectless 
Void?

Further it is everybody’s experience that one coming out 
of sushupti (where mind stands suspended) has a memory of 
blissful subject-objectless relationship. One knows nothing but 
the sense of bliss is recalled. The person who enjoys the bliss 
of sleep, the I of sushupti is the Self, can it be called Śūnya? 

“The object to be witnessed and the witness finally merge 
together and Absolute Consciousness alone reigns supreme. It 
is not a state of śūnya (blank) or ignorance. It is the Svarūpa 
(Real Self). Some say the mind arises from Consciousness 
followed by reflection (ābhāsa); others say that the ābhāsa 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   333 06-05-2011   10:53:52



334 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

(reflection) arises first followed by the mind. In fact both are 
simultaneous”. (Talks no. 68).

Only vishaya or objective content becomes void and not 
the Ātman. As the state of Ātman shines without a second, 
perception becomes void, but the residue, the perceiving eye 
(the perceiver) the unsublatable dhrik, remains as simple 
Awareness This is what is called “abiding, yet non-abiding”. 
Contradictory predicates are attributed to the Supreme to 
indicate the inapplicability of empirically known determinants. 
Perceived from one angle Ātman is Śūnya; viewed from 
another angle, It is non-void.

Yet ‘void’ and ‘non-void’ cannot shine but for ‘It’. Hence 
It is both Śūnya and aśūnya.

This Ātman though pervading everywhere is without 
the least partiality and equally and homogeneously fills 
everywhere It is totally unattached due to Its extreme subtlety. 
Ātman Unbroken, Undifferentiated, Egoless, Perfect Fullness 
shines everywhere as the detached or uninvolved Witness and 
as such there can be room for partiality. Contemplate that 
Ātman at all times is the directive.

The Supreme consciousness is called Śūnya lest It should 
be finitised by being given a name. Yet the Immaculate Eye of 
wisdom, the Ātman which completely negates the phenomenal 
perceivable world, cannot be called simply ‘void’. When 
attempts are made to perceive It, It becomes the perceiving 
Awareness and becomes imperceptible and void. Hence It is 
called “Neither Śūnya nor aśūnya”.

The infinite and mighty Awareness that is the source of 
all dualities experienced, like Gross and Subtle, Void and 
Fullness, is the Ātman. Contemplate That. Sage Vasishta 
instructs Rama on this thus: “That is the nature of the Supreme 
Self which is empty when there is a multitude of worlds, which 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   334 06-05-2011   10:53:52

void is, as it were, non-void and in which the non-existent 
world exists.” (Yoga Vasishtam, Verse 1218).

Tejobindu Upanishad says: “Though It is that which is 
not void, yet thought of as void, (but in reality) It transcends 
voidness and is firm-fixed. There is neither thinker nor thought 
nor the thinkable Still it is to be meditated upon.”. (Verse 10)

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   335 06-05-2011   10:53:52



336 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

of birth (dehātma bhava) untouched by caste, name and

Commentary: 

Afflictions are of many kinds. Hunger and thirst are of 
the prana, pain of old age and death of the body and avidya 
(nescience), asmita (egoism), raga (desires), dvesha (hatred) 
and abhinivesa (clinging to life) are of the mind. In addition 
there are the physical and mental ailments and diseases. 
While the latter is not so serious and are curable the mental 
afflictions cause Bhavaroga, the disease of birth. Hence Sage 
Vasishta instructs Rama: “The usual ailments perish just by 
obtaining what is wanted (or approved). Rama! Without 
Self-Knowledge the essential or ultimate mental affliction 
does not perish. The destruction of the essential of mental 
affliction is the one that removes the roots of all the plays of 
mental afflictions and physical ailments, as a river in the rainy 
season (removes) the roots of creepers on the banks.”  (Yoga 
Vasishtam, Verses 727 and 728). Ultimately “the ego is the root 
of all diseases. Give it up. There will be no disease”. (Talks no. 
164). B.V. Narasimhaswamy records in his Ramana Gīta the 
answer provided by Bhagavan to the question “Of what use 
is Ātma-vichara?” as Sarvaklesa nivrutti – destruction of all 
sorrow. Somebody, then, questioned whether this Sarvaklesa 
nivritti aspect of Ātma-vichara can be applied in the field of 
suggestive therapeutics or in the practical affairs of daily life 
to overcome painful experiences. Bhagavan affirmed it saying, 
“Yes. The Truth of the Self is one. It’s application are many. 
... People who come here make use of the Truth their own 
affairs.” Then Bhagavan went on to say how a lady applying 
the above Truth (that she is not the body of the five kosas but 
the affliction-free Self) to herself got over her ailments like 
dyspepsia and insomnia. So did Vasudeva Sastri get relieved 
of his sorrow at he lost his dear child in his presence. One 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   336 06-05-2011   10:53:52



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 337

who is not yoked to the thought of a body, is not troubled by 
the characteristic properties of the body. Bhagavan went on to 
add that there are no other means to achieve the destruction of 
all sorrow. In the mighty presence of an Ātmajñāni – a mere 
form of condensed awareness, such incidents were many. 
Bhagavan  affirms, “Such instances here are not infrequent.” 
(Ramana Gīta, page 31 and 32).

Therefore the only one unafflicted by any disease is a 
jñāni who has known the Self; all the rest suffer afflicted by 
the greatest of all diseases namely birth – the anavamala – 
which eats into the very vitals despite the care and pain taken 
to lead a life freed of afflictions. “That (akshara) cannot be 
seen; cannot be grasped; originless, casteless, without limbs, 
eyes and ears, eternal, present everywhere, all-pervading, 
highly subtle, inexhaustible, the source of all – that, dhiras the 
wise men, enquire and know”. (Mundaka Upanishad, 1-1-6).

The blessed one freed of all afflictions is the one without 
the anavamala.

Ātman is unidentifiable by any caste and does not belong 
to any of the classes of Yakshas, Rakshasas, Kinnaras, 
Gandarvas, Kimpurushas, humans, animals, cows or birds. 
The Ātman is the one enduring spirit in the many and 
momentary bodies. Like the prana or vital air, that, though in 
different bodies like cows, birds and human beings, does not 
imbibe the nature of those bodies, Ātman undergoes no change 
and is untouched by the nature and qualities of the mind and 
body. Though men are tall or short and are associated with 
exalted and lowly nature and birds and animals have special 
characters, the Ātman, devoid of differences of high, low and 
unattached, and non-distinctive in nature cannot be identified 
by any of these body-based distinctions.

Though the sunlight shines in all places the sun is always 
of the same form, pervasive, incomparable and shines without 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   337 06-05-2011   10:53:52



338 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

any distinction. The All-pervasive Brahman though in all 
human beings, animals and birds, is not touched or associated 
with them. That content eludes name, form and caste. Yet we 
chant thousand names to perform archana to a nameless one. 
Names such as ‘Self’ are invented for the Absolute, from which 
words turn away (without defining it) and which is known as 
liberated. Such names are not born from its inherent nature. 

He is formless and has no form. To those who know 
Him He has the form of wisdom. That the Lord in fact has 
no name or form is the experience of realized sages. Hence 
the Lord says: varnamodu nama rupangalum naṇṇidātam 
(It is untouched by caste, name and form). Therefore the 
Ātman is Immaculate without the blemishes of these qualities. 
Blemishes are associated with grossness. The more gross the 
nature, the more are the blemishes. Conversely, the more and 
more subtle an object is, the less and less are the flaws and 
faults. Fire is free from the impurities that the earth and water 
contain. The air is even less tainted. No impurity can ever 
touch ether on account of its very subtle nature. When ether, 
the subtlest of all elements, is itself unattached with anything 
even though it holds all the Universe and stellar systems in 
it, then that nothing can touch the Ātman, more pervasive 
than ether and subtler than subtlety itself, becomes easy of 
comprehension. 

Yoga Vasishtam (Verse 1202) states: “that Supreme 
Reality is so subtle that, in front of it, the ether is seen as having 
a gross nature like Meru mountain by the side of an atom.”

It is within and without, pervading each and every object 
through and through like the thread in a cloth. It is unfettered, 
feels no pain, and suffers no injury, being free of physical and 
subtle bodies, the causes for diseases and pain.

It is Immaculate, untouched by any taint of the body It 
dwells in, even as the sun is not at all affected in anyway, 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   338 06-05-2011   10:53:52



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 339

favourably or otherwise, by the healthy or defective condition 
of the eyes which are helped by the sun to see the objects or 
by the impurity or purity of the objects illuminated by It. 

‘The “I” in one. Contemplate ever on That’ is the upadeśa 
of the Lord. “The Ātman which is free from evil, old age, 
death, sorrow, hunger and thirst, whose desire is of the Truth, 
whose resolve is of the Truth, He should be sought, Him one 
should desire to understand”. (Chandogya Upanishad, 8.7.1).

340 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Paraphrase: 
Contemplate with a joyous heart the Ātman that is 

Self-supporting, bereft of an ‘other’ base or substratum 
for Itself, but firmly established, beyond a parallel to be 
compared with, intrinsically Immaculate, eternally existent 
and unknowable by any known standards of evidence.
Commentary: 

The above six verses delineate the characteristic of 
the Ātman and exhort that the Ātman must be meditated on 
ceaselessly like the flow of oil. 

There is nothing ‘other’ than the Ātman to bear or support 
It. Though It remains the substratum, base and the support of 
everything else, It needs no basis or support for It to hold on to. 
It rests on It’s own Glory (sve mahimnē). It is Self-supporting.

The common way method in empirical world to make 
things unknown known is by way of analogy or comparisons. 
But Ātman is beyond compare. Traditional attempts to explain 
that which is beyond comparison by way of pramanās 
(evidence) such as pratyaksha (direct perception), inference, 
scriptural knowledge and wisdom revealed by ancients and 
elders, all fail to prove It. 

Inferential logic that establishes the existence of fire on 
seeing smoke on the basis of the reasoning that “There is no 
smoke without fire” cannot explain away the Ātman. 

Therefore that being beyond mind, and speech, all the 
known means to right knowledge become inadequate and 
unequal to the task of revealing Brahman. 

“People want to see it (Ātman) as a blazing light, etc. How 
can it be so? It is not light, not darkness (na tejas, na tamah). 
It is only as it is. It cannot be defined. The best definition is “I 
am that I am”. The srutis speak of the Self as being the size of 
one’s thumb, the tip of the hair, an electric spark, vast, subtler 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   340 06-05-2011   10:53:53



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 341

than the subtlest, etc. They have no foundation in fact. It is 
only Being, but different from the real and the unreal; It is 
knowledge but different from knowledge and ignorance. How 
can it be defined at all? That state, beyond light and darkness, 
is called light since no other proper word could be found for 
it.” (Talks no. 122).

Though unknown by any known means of knowledge, 
It is not non-existent. That is an ever established Content of 
Pure Awareness, the uninvolved witness of the rise and fall 
of all the worlds, bodies and various states imagined on It. 

As the sky is homogeneously same in all the countries and 
in all the three tenses, the Ātman, aware of the rise and fall of 
everything that appears and disappears, is eternally existent.

The form, simply of ‘Awareness’, cannot mix with action 
and qualities. Devoid of ego, intellect, body, kosas and senses 
and therefore undefiled by the demons of attachment to sense 
objects and thoughts which alone carry the taints of dualities, 
the triads, distinctions and pleasure and pain, the dharma of 
antahkarana, It remains Immaculate and free of taint of any 
kind such as matter and its attributes. It is pure, stripped of the 
unreal veils superimposed on It. It remains unsullied by the 
activities of māyā even as the atmosphere is unsullied by its 
own movement everywhere. It is then that the beginningless 
Reality (Vāstava anādi) shines stripped of beginningless 
imagination (karpita anādi).

“As the sun, the Eye of the whole world, is not 
contaminated by the defects of the external eye, so being the 
innermost Essence in all beings Ātman is not contaminated 
by the external sorrows of the world.” (Kathopanishad, 5.11)

The Lord exhorts Guha to contemplate that Ātman with 
love and joy for it is the best way to attain It. The proper guide 
to attain the Vastu that remains already attained is an overflow 
of joy that melts the heart with love. When the desire and 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   341 06-05-2011   10:53:53



342 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

longing to attain and be the Self softens and melts the heart, 
turning inward and converging at the source becomes easy; the 
swell of the ego dissolves and in the place of extinction of the 
ego shines the ocean of love. As Bhagavan says in the verse 
“ariyadi idara jīvaradu”; “When the mind melts with love for 
Him and reaches the inmost recess of the Heart wherein He 
dwells as the beloved, the subtle eye of pure intellect opens 
and He reveals Himself as Pure Consciousness.”

from throngs of people of contentious beliefs, one should

Commentary: 

The Content of this verse is very much similar to the 
invocatory verse of Forty Verses On Reality by Bhagavan. 
The latter parts of both the verses are identical in their import. 
An approach to Ātma Sākṣhātkāra that is advaitic in essence 
and highly exalted, but least objectionable, is advocated in an 
admirable manner here.

The verse in Uḷḷadu  Nārpadu says: “Who could meditate 
upon the Reality called Heart (that exists free of thought)? To 
remain within the Heart, as It is, is truly to meditate (upon 
It)”. This must be compared with the latter lines of this verse 
which says “Know then that one should forever meditate the 
Self, seated in the Self, by the Self.”

Here even the “words” employed are in complete 
consonance with the content they imply.

An enquiry into the various ways suggested for the 
attainment of Ātman reveals an incongruity between what is 
said and the real state of the Self. But despite the contradiction 
it has to be so. Even the command or message of silence has 
to be conveyed by the use of speech like “Do not speak”. 
Likewise while saying “Meditate that which is beyond mind”, 
the words and the Content run counter to each other.

Yet in this verse, the use of the phrase “tannile tannale 
tannilamar tannaiye unnida vendum” (one must meditate on 
the Self, seated within oneself, by the Self, within the Self) 
with no words contradicting each other has the content that 
is in line with sādhanā (pracitce) and sadhya (attainment). 
Perfect agreement of the word and it’s content in intuiting the 
content it stands for, is very rare indeed.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   343 06-05-2011   10:53:53



344 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Release from the bondage of karma caused by the vāsanās 
of actions performed requires renunciation of attachment to 
actions. Desire is the effect of avidya or nescience and the 
effect of desire is action. Action isolated from the desire for 
action and the fruits thereof does not create attachment. Sakama 
karma – karma coupled the desire for fruits – incarnates as 
bondage of karma. Saṁsāra itself is the characteristic karma 
born of avidya. Hence performance of hundreds of crores of 
karma will not help one gain jñāna.

Shankara in Vivekachūḍāmaṇi says: “Not by yoga, not by 
Samkya, not by karma, nor by upāsana is liberation achieved. 
It is only understanding of the oneness of Brahman and Ātman. 
Not otherwise.”

Ribhu Gītā extolls this Truth in hyperbolic language,
“The Self is verily the Self itself by itself”
“The Self dissolves in itself”
“The Self is indeed the target of meditation for itself”
“The Self is indeed its own goal”
“The Self is indeed the oblation to itself”
“The Self is indeed the japa of itself.”
                                          (Chapter 36, Verses 9 and 10)
Further Ātman, the eternal, cannot be won by non-eternal 

or transient means like karma and the Self, action-less, cannot 
be obtained by action, for Ātman is ever attained. One who 
gives up everything including himself (ego self) attains to his 
real form and one who does not experience the ever-attained 
Ātman and leaves the world is declared by scriptures as 
“krupanah or miser”.

When desires born of nescience are given up and 
dispassion is developed ignorance gets exterminated by 
enquiry into the Self. “Then the Self perceives Itself by its 
own Self. This is the certainty of its inherent nature.” “The 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   344 06-05-2011   10:53:53



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 345

Self alone perceives itself. It investigates itself by its own 
Self. The Self alone exists here; not ignorance. Destruction 
of ignorance is considered Realization.” (Yoga Vasishtam, 
Verses 1752 and 53).

In Bhagavan’s words: “all karma of whatever kind will 
lead to fresh bondage.” (Day by Day, 27.3.46).

If one has to live within the four walls of society the 
necessity of conforming to its dictates induces such a 
renunciate to engage in actions perforce as before. Like the 
brahmara kita nyaya (the logic of worm and wasp) whereby 
a wasp turns the worm in the mud hole into one of its own 
kind by being constantly after it, the renunciate ends up like 
any other member of the society. All his conscious efforts to 
give up the desire for actions and their fruits become fruitless. 
Hence, such a one is advised to shun society, seek the sanctuary 
of solitude and live a sequestered life, far from the madding 
crowd.

Gītā also speaks of this in verse 10 of chapter XIII as 
“”Vivikta desasevitam Arati jana samsadi” (resort to solitude 
and abhor the society of men).

When somebody questioned Bhagavan about the place 
of solitude Bhagavan replied: “Vivikta desa is that where 
there is nothing but the Supreme Self, the Paramātma. Aratir 
jñānasamsadi means to remain without getting mixed up 
with or absorbed by the five senses (vishayas). It is these 
five senses that rule the majority of people. Vivikta desa is 
that state in which they are in abeyance”. (Letters, 28-9-47), 
and in Ramana Gītā he declares: “Even One who is always 
established in the Self is performing inviolable penance. There 
is no need for solitude for him.” (Chap. II, Verse 25).

Bhagavan while explaining yet another verse from Gītā 
(Chap.VI,Verse 10) explained: “living in seclusion – by a 
yogī, as a yogī (who has subdued his mind and senses, free

from desire and bereft of possessions, living in seclusion all

must remain steadily in the secret place called Ātman; realize

(Letters, 2-3-49).

The excellent means, then, is by the mind turned Self 
ward, one must meditate the Self seated within the Self as “I”. 
Yoga Vasishtam also speaks precisely of the same way: “Please 
the Self by the self. Worship the Self by the self. Having 
perceived the Self by the self, live in the Self by yourself.” 
(Verse 1665). Again an echo of this is found in Gītā also (Verse 
17 of Chap. XIII): “That the light of all lights is said to be 
beyond darkness. Knowledge, the object of knowledge and the 
goal of knowledge to be reached is seated in the hearts of all.” 

“If you abide as Consciousness by knowing Consciousness

objects will come to an end. Out of all the sādhanās that 
are worth performing knowing consciousness is the only 
excellent and definitive one. Knowing consciousness through 
consciousness means to abide as the Self, Pure Consciousness, 
bereft of the suttarivu (denotative knowledge). Know this to 
be the glorious meaning of the unique phrase ‘Summa iru’ (Be 
Still).” (Pādamālai page 56).

Commentary: 
The various thoughts that the mind is impregnated with 

can be classified under four categories like land of birth, 
caste, lineage and stage of life. These are bases for the myriad 
number of thoughts to spring from. All these must be wiped 
out without any residue, is the exhortation.

All entities other than the Ātman are false. The Ātman 
is bodiless and worldless. Therefore all the institutions, 
ends and practices based upon this false multiplicity, like 
Varnashramam, social order, the duties and religious practices 
based on it – and even the heavenly regions attainable through 
them – are equally false like the objects “seen” by the dreamer. 
Self-awareness is without any experience of inside and 
outside, and of objects pertaining to them and the nature of 
activities or karma based on them.

Only an Ātmajñāni, a stita prajñā, totally indifferent to 
and regardless of caste, country, family or ashrama, shines in 
his natural state forever. 

A verse in Ozhivil Odukkam [Avattait-tanmai (nature of 
the state of the sage), Verse 25] portrays the state of a jñāni who 
has renounced the practices pertaining to caste and family:

	 Enemies six abandoned
	 Hands as begging bowl
	 Earth as bed of eider down
	 With limbs to cover limbs
	 Freed from impact of pain
	 Of name, form, caste and acts
	 What religion can we name It?
What is the religion of one turned away from the six 

enemies namely, desire, hatred, delusion, greed, miserliness 
and malice and eating from the begging bowl of one’s hands, 
with mere limbs as cover in rain and cold, sleeping blissfully 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   348 06-05-2011   10:53:53



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 349

without the least impact of the pain of vāsanās arising out of 
one’s name, form, caste, action and profession?

Once Suri Nagamma read before Bhagavan a Verse from 
Telugu Bhāgavatam which expressed the same content when 
Bhagavan cited Kaupina Panchakam of Sankara and gave 
its meaning. “O Lord, Thou hast given me a hand to use as 
a pillow under my head, a cloth to cover my loins, hands 
where with to eat food, what more do I want? This is my 
great good fortune!”... “Is it really possible to say how great 
a good fortune it is? Even the greatest of kings wish for such 
happiness. There is nothing to equal it. Having experienced 
both these conditions, I know the difference between this and 
that. These beds, sofa, articles around one-all this is bondage.” 
(Letters, 5-12-1947).

One is asked, day in and day out, to contemplate on the 
Self. The Yoga Vasishtam says: “Rama! That continuance in 
the course of worldly life, accustomed to during hundreds 
of different births is not destroyed anywhere without the 
employment of repeated practice for a long time and wise 
men consider thinking of That, describing That, instructing 
one another about That and sole devotion to This alone is 
Practice “ (Verses 1779, 1781).

In short this is called akandakara vritti, while ordinary 
vritti consists of objective knowledge, akandakara vritti is 
vritti minus vishaya jñāna (knowledge of the objects). When 
the mind thinks of or sees an object, the senses and mind 
envelop the object and become the very form of that object. 
When the Self is thought of (wholly) the mind (and senses) 
all become the very form of the Self and when it continues to 
remain so, it becomes akandakara or Brahmakara.

being repeated. This is the excellent worship and exalted

Commentary: 

The novices among the seekers of the Self are initially 
taught upāsana of a mantra, murthy and dhyāna. Initiation 
into a mantra followed by constant repetition of it leads to the 
upāsana of the deity of the mantra and then meditation upon it.

None of these is required for one who is engaged in 
dhyāna of his own real nature which comprises all the three. 
In dhyāna of the Self, the triad becomes the one.

“Japa means changing to one thought to the exclusion 
of all other thoughts.” (Upadeśa Sāram). “That is the 
purpose; it leads to dhyāna which ends in Self-Realization.” 
(Talks no. 413).

“Enquiry consists in retaining the mind in the Self. 
Meditation consists in thinking that one’s self Is Brahman. 
Existence-Consciousness-Bliss”. (Who am I?).

‘Who am I?’ is the best japa. What could be more concrete 
than the Self? It is within each one’s experience every moment. 
Why should one try to catch anything outside, leaving out the 
Self? Let each one try to find out the known Self instead of 
searching for the unknown something beyond.” (Talks no. 81).

The aim of getting initiated into a mantra is to attain the 
Ātman, the content of that mystic sound, namely, the mantra. 
Therefore contemplation on one’s real form, the content of 
that mantra, is the best of all upāsanas. Hitherto the repetition 
of the mantra was carried on in the stance of mantra being 
different from the content of mantra whereas Svarūpa dhyāna 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   351 06-05-2011   10:53:53



352 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

-contemplation on the Self – being non-dual – eliminates the 
dual bhava.

“You are always repeating the mantra (of I) automatically. 
If you are not aware of the ajapa (unspoken chant) which is 
eternally going on, you should take to japa. Japa is made with 
an effort…to ward off other thoughts. Then japa becomes 
internal and also eternal. Finally its ajapa and eternal nature 
will be realized.” (Talks no. 312).

Worship of various deities is undertaken with a view to 
attain the Self. The Self being the most exalted of all deities, 
the worship of all deities is encompassed by It. One’s own 
form is not other than Ātman. Hence dhyāna of one’s own 
svarūpa (real form) is the worship of all deities and herein 
lies the true principle of dhyāna. “Know that as the worship 
of the Deity in which the Self God is worshipped by flowers 
in the form of tranquillity and awareness. The worship of a 
form is not worship”. (Yoga Vasishtam, Verse 1688).

Of the various ways advocated for the attainment of the 
Self, tapas or penance is indispensable and the foremost. The 
unrelenting faith and belief of all mumukshus is that the Self 
cannot be known in the absence of tapas. The goal of tapas 
being the knowledge of the Self, contemplation of the Self 
alone is truly tapas.

The quiescence of body, senses and mind gained by the 
unbroken awareness that this bewildering array of world – 
appearance, all self-made, veiling and revealing the Reality 
is tapas. There can be no greater and nobler tapas than to 
“Be still”.

The promiscuity of thoughts poses the greatest obstacle 
to the successful pursuit of japa, upāsana, dhyāna and tapas, 
capable of shattering or unsettling any effort. Their removal 
makes the aspiration a fait accompli. Hence He exhorts to 
extinguish them.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   352 06-05-2011   10:53:53



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 353

“Knowledge of the Self is the Supreme mantra.
 Knowledge of the Self is the Supreme Penance.
 Knowledge of the Self is the verily Vishnu
 Knowledge of the Self is Siva Supreme.”
			           (Ribhu Gītā, Chap. 36, Verse 22)
Finally Siva endorses svarūpa dhyāna with an emphasis 

so, as to instil and inspire undaunted courage. “That which 
is, is the one Reality. It may be represented by a form, japa, 
mantra, vichāra or any kind of attempt. All of them finally 
resolve themselves into that One single Reality. Bhakti, 
Vichāra, japa are only different forms of our effort to keep 
out the unreality…..Meditation or vichāra is thus a reversion 
to our true nature.” (Talks no. 402).

Hence inherence in svarūpa dhyāna is the performance 
of everything. 

“On account of his being of the nature of perception 
situated within the reach of everybody nothing whatever such 
as invocation or mantras (or sacred formulae) is employed 
for him.” (Yoga Vasishtam, Verse 1683).

Therefore abidance in Pure Consciousness is the highest 
meditation; the highest worship.

Paraphrase: 
The Self is ever without thoughts. Empty the mind 

– ever given to various kinds of thoughts – of thoughts. 
Compel the mind, that forever keeps thinking of 
something or other without a respite, to inhere firmly in 
the Ātman and let it not think of anything else. 
Commentary: 

The upsurge of mind is called thoughts. The rise of 
thoughts is a continuum, for before one thought disappears, 
another appears. The mind has no form except that of thoughts. 
What Bhagavan says in verse 18 of Upadeśa Undyiar may be 
recalled here “Thoughts alone make up the mind and of all 
thoughts, the “I” thought is the root.”

What is called mind is but the notion of “I”. In fact 
“there is no entity by name mind. Because of the emergence 
of thoughts we surmise something from which they start. 
That we term mind. When we probe to see what it is, there 
is nothing of it. After it has vanished, Peace will be found to 
remain eternal.” (Talks no. 238).

As the state of ‘no mind’ is the Ātman, the Self has no 
thoughts. If the mind united with thoughts is to be isolated 
from thoughts, the mind must be rendered thought-free. 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   354 06-05-2011   10:53:53



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 355

Mutually dependent on each other, mind lives as long as 
thoughts flourish and thoughts survive as long as the mind is. 
With the annihilation of one, the other perishes. Hence it was 
said “make it impossible for the mind to think”. But how to 
make the mind free of thoughts? The answer is to establish 
the mind united with thoughts firmly in the Ātman, one’s real 
form. Then thoughts will not arise. Mind when it emerges out 
from its source holds on to thoughts whereas while inhering 
in its source, it remains as ‘That’. In Who am I? Bhagavan 
speaks of the state of Self-attention as being Ātma-chintanai, 
the thought of the Self.

Once a devotee asked Bhagavan “How to train the 
mind to look within?” Bhagavan replied “By practice. The 
mind is the intelligent phase leading to its own destruction, 
for Self to manifest.” Then the devotee queried “How to 
destroy the mind?” Bhagavan said “Water cannot be made 
dry water. Seek the Self; the mind will be destroyed.” 
(Talks no. 240).

In fact, mind induced by Ātman, thinks of the Ātman. 
“The gain of thought of Ātman” (called smarana siddhi) itself 
is because of the Ātman. The real sādhanā of a seeker is to 
wage war with thoughts to gain the thought-free state. Though 
everyone wants to attain that, not everyone endeavours to 
practice the required exercise of preventing the fissiparous 
tendencies of the mind and inhering it in its Source. Bhagavan 
explains this practice as follows “Abhyasa consists in 
withdrawal within the Self every time you are disturbed by 
thoughts. It is not concentration or destruction of the mind but 
withdrawal into the Self.” (Talks no. 485).

In Gītā when Arjuna complains of the restlessness of the 
mind Lord Krishna replies: “the mind is difficult to curb and 
restless but it can be controlled, Arjuna, by constant practice 
and non-attachment “. (Chap.VI, Verse 35).

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   355 06-05-2011   10:53:53



356 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Earlier Krishna says “it should be achieved “little by 
little”, gradually (sanai sanai)...

Contemplation is possible only with the control of mind 
and control can be accomplished only by contemplation. It is a 
vicious cycle. Bhagavan says “Yes! They are interdependent. 
They must go on side by side. Practice and dispassion bring 
about the result gradually. Dispassion is practised to check 
the mind from being projected outward; practice is to keep 
it turned inward. There is a struggle between control and 
contemplation. It is going on within. Contemplation in due 
course will be successful.” (Talks no. 220).

The degree of freedom from unwanted thoughts and the 
degree of concentration on a single thought are the measure 
to gauge the progress.

There are various obstacles in the way of arresting 
the thought process. The three bhavanas like doubt, non-
understanding and perverse understanding of Truth called 
samsaya, asambhavana and vipareetha bhavana, sleep, 
restlessness of the mind, depression and building castles in the 
air. All these belong to the mind not to Self. Vichāra will help 
remove all these impediments. Adavaitamruta Upanishad in 
Mantra 6 says: “Withdraw the mind again and again from all 
sense objects. Make it one pointed. Fix the mind again and again 
on the Self. Become fearless. Be firm in the vow of Divine Life.” 
The Ātman is not gained by one who is destitute of strength. 
Further with the growth of sankalpa, this world will arise. If 
it is destroyed, the universe will disappear. Extinction of the 
sankalpas alone is moksha. The same Upanishad enumerates 
six minor obstacles, which are: forgetting of the nature of 
Self, postponement of meditation, and enquiry, appearance of 
darkness or light during meditation, perspiration and dejection.

Brahma Rahasya Upanishad mentions seven states of 
ignorance or ajñāna bhumikas called Bindu jāgrat, the rise of 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   356 06-05-2011   10:53:53



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 357

jīva, jāgrat (feeble conception of ‘I’ and mine), Maha jāgrat 
(I and mine becoming entrenched due to repeated births), 
jāgrat swapna (day dreaming), swapna (dreaming), swapna 
jāgrat (one in waking state remembering things of the past) 
and deep sleep. Bhagavan mentions five states:

“Sleep
 Before waking, a state free from thoughts
 Sense of happiness of that freedom from thoughts 

(rasasvada)
 The internal movement of vāsanās (kashaya)
 Complete waking with vikshepa (distraction)
 The second of those should be made permanent.” 

 (Talks no. 622).
A thought-free state is so hailed for it is full of Supreme 

Peace and bliss. Who will not desire it? Is it not thought, that 
seeking joy in ephemeral things, wanders in the outside world? 
How can it know that the very place of its own extinction is 
the place of perfect bliss. This ignorance caused by delusion 
causes the mind to struggle and suffer. The mind, restrained 
from flowing outward must be anchored in the Ātman.

or thought of by the mind. Yet It is not inconceivable.

Commentary: 

Ātman, ‘That which is’ is but One. Hence however 
described, it will only be indicative of It. Viewed from a 
different angle whatever said may not reflect It truly. But the 
vastu is one and the same about which descriptions are only 
indicative of and also not indicative of. 

This verse explains the All pervasiveness of the Ātman 
by methods of both affirmation and negation.

If anyone of the above statements is accepted as true 
or rejected as untrue, it becomes ‘alien’ or ‘other than’ the 
Ātman, but Ātman is non-dual or without a second. No state 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   358 06-05-2011   10:53:54



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 359

of existence or stage of being can exist without ‘That’. Hence 
Ātman remains as All is proved here. 

Ātman is not an object to be known. Therefore It is beyond 
the grasp of the mind. Hence chindikkat takkadalla – cannot 
be thought of. But mind seeking its source, with the thought 
of svarūpa grasps and merges in It. It is chindikka onnadadum 
alla: It is not inconceivable either.

Therefore It is avang mana gōcharam– It defies being 
defined and described.

The same can be stated differently. As long as there is 
jīvabodha, the mind thinks of the Ātman as other than itself. 
Hence the stand “Ātman is not inconceivable” becomes 
admissible. But the question how to meditate on it, when with 
the annihilation of the jīvabodha or the ego-sense, the mind 
becomes extinct, negates the earlier affirmation.

The principle of Truth, the basis of both, shines 
transcending both.

It is not the thinking mind (thought) chindai ala adu. 
Chittam or mind is insentient (jada) and cannot function but 
for the Light of Chit (Awareness). Mind functions as a separate 
entity in the Light of Ātman, borrowing the ‘existence’ aspect 
of the Ātman. But the Self exists without the mind but mind 
cannot exist without the Self. Therefore It is chindaiyumām 
– It is also the mind indeed. Yet the nature of rise and 
disappearance, the characteristic of the mind, is not in the 
Ātman. Therefore it is not chitta.

Though this principle appears to be a bundle of 
contradictions, viewed from each angle, the Truth from 
that point is admissible. ‘That’ remains as All, pervading 
everything. Everything is Its form as there is nothing apart 
from It. 

The nature of Reality transcends thought and expression. 
Even the Vedas attempt to explain It with the stance of 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   359 06-05-2011   10:53:54



360 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

“Neti- Neti” and cannot describe It directly but advocate the 
withdrawal of the effects of māyā like the superimposition 
of everything within the reach of senses. What is left after 
the negation of all, that is conceived of by the mind is simply 
‘mona’ the Great Silence. The Reality is the limit of all 
negations and affirmations. It is not all this, and yet It is all 
this and transcends all this. 

In its real nature, the Ātman, has none specially dear or 
inimical to It. None is Its own and none another’s. Without any 
attachment It is the One being that stands as the unconcerned 
witness of all that is high or low and good or bad. Right from 
celestial worlds and Brahma up to plant kingdoms, there are 
grades like best, moderate and low. Even among human beings 
there are variations in the grades of beings like blissful jñānis, 
yogīs, devotees and miserly jīvas. Yet in all these that exhibit 
such a wide variety of gradations, without any change, with 
‘Being’ as the form, the Self shines. Hence the Self is equal 
and uniform everywhere.

Once a devotee expressed his doubt about the impartial 
nature of the Ātman on the basis of Vedic declaration (from 
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad) which says “the Ātman reveals 
Itself to whomsoever It chooses”. Bhagavan replied that this 
should be understood in the proper way. Ātman chooses the 
one who chooses the Ātman to reveal Itself to him. Mundaka 
Upanishad also says (2.3): “When the seeker prays to the Self 
by the Self for the Self alone, then Ātman reveals Itself to him.” 
Ātman is a homogenous mass of consciousness like space all 
around, all-pervading without a break. Hence strutis declare: 
Brahman has neither inside nor outside. He is all-Full. He is 
one homogenous essence. He is a mass of knowledge. It is, 
as Bhagavan says, “ekarasa or Brahman is the only rasa.”

Gītā also speaks of the same in Verse 29 of Chapter XIX: 
“I (the Self) am (the same in) alike to all beings. None is hateful 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   360 06-05-2011   10:53:54



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 361

nor dear to Me. But those who worship Me with devotion, 
they are in Me and I also in them.” The Self has no friends or 
foes. He is impartial. He does not damn any nor effect any by 
capricious will. The only way to win His love is by faith and 
devotion and each must tread the path by himself.

Paraphrase: 
Meditate at all times the Self beyond the grasp of 

mind in terms of thought. Release the mind from the 
grip of attachments to objects and matters, fix it firmly 
in a state of desirelessness (making the mind devoid of 
content fit for dhyāna) and experience within that Bliss 
which is Full, attainable in abundance in that Ātman that is 
Partless, Formless, and Whole that transcends all canons 
(of philosophy and religion).
Commentary: 

The Supreme Content, the Pure or unmoded Consciousness 
is beyond the reach of mind. It is neither any of the objects 
known, nor is It the unknown. None of the senses can reach It. 
Since the Self is attributeless it is impossible to meditate upon It. 
Yet the scriptures declare that It can be known, meditated upon 
and realized with a purified mind, that is, a mind not tainted with 
desires. This verse also exhorts us to contemplate what transcends 
contemplation, a tall order, like the demand to mark a visible dot 
in space. The import of the first line of this verse means that the 
mind emptied of all its content must be made to die.

Any thought that springs from the mind other than “I 
am” becomes an upādhi by adding something to the Pure 
Consciousness, thus limiting It and defiling the immaculate 
purity and the wholeness of the Ātman. The propensity of 
the mind to attach itself to objects and persons is the rope 
of bondage of saṁsāra. When this is snapped, liberation 
is gained. The Self is there but the Consciousness of the 
transitory personality has come in-between concealing It and 
obstructing the Fullness and Peace. When “I” is eliminated, 
the Fullness shines.

The mind gains strength by thinking repeatedly of the 
same thing. Here the content that is asked to be dwelt upon by 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   362 06-05-2011   10:53:54



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 363

the mind is the limitless Pure ether, as space, that is beyond 
the grasp of the mind. The content of contemplation here, 
namely, the space or void of Consciousness gains strength by 
repeatedly being focussed on and the mind, on getting inhered 
in It, becomes unsupported and loses all holds and grounds 
that hitherto it was hanging on to. This is expressed by the 
line chindai nirasiriyam cheide (making the mind support 
less or hold less).

When the mind cognizes objects through the senses, the 
senses envelop the objects and the mind cognises it and gains 
identity with it (tatatmyam). When the inward-turned mind 
that is desireless contemplates the void of space, the inner 
organs in the same way envelop it and gain identity with 
the content of contemplation and become the very form of 
that which is contemplated on. That is why Yoga Vasishtam 
says: “the power (of repeated contemplation on something) 
manifested leads oneself to the state of the Self in a moment 
as the abundant mist of the rainy season (makes) the entire 
atmosphere (misty)” (Verse 1801).

Muruganar says:
	 He who sees this phenomenal world
	 As all Awareness, Self-Awareness
	 This Sage indeed enjoys with all
	 Five senses fully his own Self.

(Guru Vāchaka Kovai, Verse 62) 
Various tips are provided to make the mind hold less or

you are not the mind. And the Self will remain.” (Talks no. 264)

“The mind must be cut off, roots and branch. See who 
the thinker is, who the seeker is. Abide as the thinker, seeker. 
All thoughts will disappear”. (Talks no. 245).

“D. How is the mind to be stilled?

Meditation on “I am beyond speech and mind” will also

A devotee once queried Bhagavan: “It is possible to gain 
that Consciousness which is beyond thoughts?” Bhagavan 
replied “Yes. There is only one Consciousness which subsists 
in the waking, dream and sleep states... The present is only the 
“I” thought, whereas the sleeping “I” is the real “I”. It subsists 
all through. It is Consciousness. If It is known, you will see 
that it is beyond thoughts.” (Talks no. 43).

He should be meditated on as the all-pervading void 
of space, yet not external but as the innermost Self, yet not 
internal, untainted by anything that happens or does not 
happen, as simply the uninvolved Witness.

One, desireless and trained in concentration, will realise 
that his mind is non-different from Brahman, his own Self, 
the Self in all. Brahman is the all, in the all.

Once Swami Madhava Theertha questioned Bhagavan as 
to “How can daily life go on if the sight is fixed in the state 
where there is no existence of seer, seeing, seen?” Bhagavan 
replied “Jñānis fix their sight in the substratum even during 
vyavahara (worldly activities), nothing else becomes the Truth 
except adhishtana.” (Mountain Path, July 1981).

The Ātman, formless, pervades everywhere transcending 
all principles. Though formless, It is not Śūnya. It is full of 
Perfect and Absolute sukha. That alone is infinitely Blissful.

This formless Ātman is well nigh unattainable if the mind 
is not emptied of its contents, severed of its attachments to 
objects and rendered groundless and holdless. Such a mind 
experiences Perfect Bliss. “That which is Infinite is alone 
Bliss. There is no Bliss in anything finite. Raso vai Saha: He

alone is the Essence. (Incidentally Sanatkumara is identified

The Taittriya Upanishad says if the maximum human

incomparable. That which we call pleasure derived from sense

The mind while alive does no good but renders greatest

366 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

An incident narrated by Subbhalakshmi Ammal has great 
relevance to the content of this verse. She became a widow 
at the young age of 16 and during a pilgrimage she, along 
with her mother, visited Bhagavan at Virupaksha Cave. She 
somehow felt the feeling that Lord Arunachala Himself has 
come in human form. She returned after 15 years and while 
sitting before Bhagavan had an unforgettable experience of 
mental stillness. Next time, she picked up courage and went 
near him and asked “What is Ātma?” Bhagavan replied “To 
remain without thinking is Ātma”. She recalls “Then he looked 
at me and I felt my mind melt away into nothing. No thought 
came, only the feeling of immense unutterable Peace was 
there.” (Unforgettable years).

When Maurice Frydman pressed Bhagavan to say 
something for practical guidance for Self-Realization 
Bhagavan said: “Be still and know that I am God” and added 
a rider that the Lord said “Know and not think I am God.”

A devotee once said “however much we try, this mind 
does not get under control and envelops the svarūpa so that it 
is not perceptible to us. What is to be done?” Bhagavan, with 
a smile placed his little finger over his eye and said “Look, 
this little finger covers the eye and prevents the whole world 
from being seen. In the same way, this small mind covers the 
whole Universe and prevents the Brahman from being seen. 
See how powerful it is.” (Letters, 22-1-1949).

Paraphrase: 
That Content, pure, eternal, undifferentiated, 

ungraspable by mind, transcending thought, without a 
pre-existing cause for Itself, beyond illustrations and 
the pale of compare shines exalted. It is spoken of as the 
Supreme Bliss. Immerse and soak yourself fully in that 
form of Bliss through and through.
Commentary: 

Being Infinite, the Supreme Content with no difference 
or change, equally and eternally, shines everywhere infilling 
everything. Being highly subtle, with nothing more subtle than 
‘That’, nothing can wreak any modification in It. 

“Even the structure of the atom has been found by the 
mind. Therefore the mind is subtler than the atom. That which 
is behind the mind, namely, the individual soul is subtler than 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   367 06-05-2011   10:53:54



368 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

the mind. Further the Tamil Saint Manivāchakar has said of the 
specks dancing in a beam of sunlight that if each represents 
a Universe, the whole sunlight will represent the Supreme 
Being.” (Talks no. 15).

There is nothing beyond It. Nothing can make or mar it 
either. There is absolutely nothing that can cause a change or 
difference to It. So It is called nirvikarpam. 

Beyond the reach of mind, That remains ungraspable by 
thoughts just as a fruit, though seen by the eyes, its essence 
or rasa is not grasped. That Being, the source of everything, 
is Its own cause and shines without a cause to Itself. As there 
is nothing other than the Self, It is beyond being explained 
either by way of illustration or by comparing It to the likes 
of It. The Self shines as It’s own illustration and comparison. 
This is the meaning of the second line which states: “the 
Self is without anything as the cause or source of Itself and 
transcending illustrations and beyond the range of comparisons 
for recognition of likeness.”

If so, what exactly is the state of that Content? Without 
a beginning or an end or without rising and setting It shines 
and That is the farthest boundary of Bliss. The use of the word 
Parama (Supreme) indicates that it is the farthest point. Words 
like Parama sukham, Parama Shanti, Parama Priti (Supreme 
Satisfaction), Parama trupti (Supreme Contentment), Parama 
jñāni (Seer beyond compare) and Parama Vairaghyam 
(Supreme dispassion) all mean they are the ultimate in them.

One is told to immerse oneself fully in that Supreme 
Bliss and become one with That instead of remaining dually 
as the enjoyer of the bliss and the Bliss. The Upanishads say 
that the highest possible happiness which a human being can 
attain, or which the ten grades of beings higher than man, the 
celestials and gods like Brahma can attain, is like foam in the 
deluging flood of the bliss of the Self.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   368 06-05-2011   10:53:54



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 369

Bhagavan referring to this, once narrated a story. A king 
was passing through a forest in all his pomp and pageantry 
with his army and retinue behind him. He came across a man 
with not even a cod-piece on him, lying on the ground with 
one leg cocked over the other and laughing away apparently 
supremely happy and contented with himself and the entire 
world. The king struck with the man’s happy state sent for him 
but the ascetic took no notice of the message delivered to him 
and continued in his ecstatic bliss. The king when reported of 
this surmised that this was no ordinary man, himself went and 
said, ”Swami, you are evidently supremely happy and may 
we know the secret of this happiness and from which Guru 
you learnt it?” Thereupon the ascetic said, “I have twenty-
four Gurus. Everything, this body, the earth, the birds, some 
instruments, some persons, have all taught me” All the things 
of the world are classed as either good or bad. The good taught 
him what he must seek. Similarly the bad taught him what 
he must avoid. The ascetic was Dattatreya – the avdhuta, the 
example of renunciates.

Bhagavan “Samadhi is our natural state, if we give up 
the  states: vikalpās” and when someone asked the difference 
between sushupti ānanda and turiya ānanda Bhagavan replied 
“There are not different ānandas. There is only one ānanda 
enjoyed during the waking state, the ānanda of all kinds of 
beings from the lowest animal to the highest Brahma, the 
ānanda of the Self. The bliss which is enjoyed unconsciously 
in sleep is enjoyed consciously in Turiya... The ānanda enjoyed 
during jāgrat is upādhi ānanda.” (Day by Day, 2-2-46).

“You can have or rather you will yourself be the highest 
imaginable kind of happiness. All other kinds of happiness 
which you have spoken of as ‘pleasure’, ‘joy’ happiness, and 
bliss are only reflections of the ānanda which in your true 
nature you are.” (Day by Day, 15-5-46).

Those persons with tranquil minds, who have gone to the

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 371

Paraphrase: 
Abandoning all attachments to sense objects and 

matters and their vāsanās that follow us with each birth, 
quell the upsurge of the profuse ramification of thoughts. 
That day when the quiescent state of the stilled mind 
is realized, then there shines the one non-dual Ātman, 
spoken of as the Content of Supreme Bliss, ending all 
misery.
Commentary: 

The highest desirelessness for objects of enjoyment 
is declared as samadhi. Steadfast or firm tastelessness 
in objects of sense is alone declared as dhyāna . 
(Yoga Vasishtam, Verse 2089). Such a one lives abandoning 
thoughts. Vikshepa and sankalpa are to the mind. The Self is 
beyond tossing and wavering. It is the same unchanging pure 
chaitanya at all times.

The first and final step for the attainment of Supreme 
Bliss is to give up all attachment to the sense objects and to 
eradicate all thought-waves that like turbulent billows of the 
sea repeatedly keep buffeting the mind. When both these are 
successfully eliminated mona or the state of the thoughtless 
quiescence results. Then the form of non-dual Self pervading 
everywhere, shines as Itself. 

To a question how awareness can be obtained and 
cultivated, Bhagavan replied, “All that you have to do is to 
give up being aware of other things, that is of the non-Self. If 
one gives up being aware of them, then pure awareness alone 
remains, and that is the Self.” (Day by Day, 24-7-46).

The state of mona is the state of non-dual Self. This, 
variously called as swarupānandam, paramānandam, 
tanmayānandam, atmānandam is the highest of all Bliss.

One who practices the quelling of the mind, eschewing 
vishayas, destroys their effect, namely, the ramification of 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   371 06-05-2011   10:53:54



372 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

thoughts. But the mind starved of vishaya may lapse into 
slumber when, the thought-free mind, assuming a thought 
must be aroused from sleep and again must be merged into 
the thought free Self. Such a constant practice of switching 
the mind between merging and rousing will ultimately free 
the mind from both oscillation and sleep which then remains 
merely as the form of Awareness. 

Giving up vishaya or thoughts of sense objects may be 
easy but to eradicate their vāsanās is not that easy. The pure 
state of being without the least attachment to any object (non-
self) other than the Self but with great attachment to one’s 
own form, the Self, is the non-dual state of Silence or Shanti. 
Experiencing this directly is called ‘Supreme Bliss’. That is 
the state where the ego has been uprooted, root and branch, 
and where the Ātman shines eternally as Pure Awareness. Its 
intrinsic nature is immaculate Joy. This is called the unmani 
bhava. Though the Self is gained as if anew It has been – and 
is – eternal and beginningless. 

This Ātman cannot be won by a weak minded one. 
Ātman cannot be gained by one with the delusion (of having 
renounced the desires) or with tapas that is not freed of desires. 
The Ātman shines in the Heart the city of Brahman, in one 
who sincerely endeavours in proper way. 

Brahmarahasya Upanishad states: “The annihilation 
of vāsanās, destruction of mind and Tattva jñāna should be 
practiced together for a long time. Then only one can attain 
Self-Realization. It is attained through mind alone after 
abandoning its sankalpas and vikalpas, and when the five 
organs of knowledge are subdued.” (Verses 6 and 7).

Bhagavan explains this: “The mind is like akasa’(ether). 
Just as there are objects in akasa, there are thoughts in the 
mind. The akasa is the counterpart of the mind and objects 
are of thought.” “How will objects cease to be is the next 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   372 06-05-2011   10:53:54



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 373

question. Investigate the matter and ascertain the truth that 
the objective world is in the subjective consciousness.”... 
“the mind starved of ideas amounts to realization and the 
experience is like a mirror facing another clear mirror, i.e. no 
reflection.” (Talks no. 485).

After the attainment of unmani bhava (the mind – free 
state) Ātman is felt as if gained afresh. Though It is ever 
present, ramification of thought waves in jāgrat and getting 
drowned in sleep, forgetting oneself, It is not perceived, 
however striven for. This unmani bhava is the turiya state.

ashrama (acquired by choice) of the jīvas cannot cause

Commentary: 

The earth is contained within the ten quarters. There is no 
śāstraic injunction that one who practices Ātmayoga should 
face any direction. Full freedom is given in this regard.

Though the earth encompasses all the places within 
they are classified variously as Punya bhumi (holy land) 
karma bhumi (land of action), yoga bhumi (land of yoga), 
jñāna bhumi (land of knowledge) and bhoga bhumi (land of 
enjoyment). The denizens of these places may not be engaged 
in the activities germane to that land. Yet all these specified and 
non-specified places, without any distinction, are conductive 
to the yoga of the Self.

Likewise none of the auspicious periods of time like 
the early morning hours extolled as brahmi muhurtam (time 
propitious for spiritual pursuit), dawn, dusk and pradosha 
kala, held holy, have been specifically mentioned as specially 
suited to this yoga of the Self. Nor are there restrictions 
imposed prohibiting certain periods like Rahukalam or 
directions like facing south or other prohibitions on grounds 
of being inauspicious for certain practices. Whatever be the 
divisions of time, all of them, without exception, are suitable 
for Ātmayoga. 

When someone questioned Bhagavan as to “what 
time is most suitable for meditation?, Bhagavan replied, 
“What is time? It is only an idea. Whatever you think of 
it, it looks like that. Time is immaterial for jñāna path.” 
(Conscious Immortality, page 32).

All distinctions of caste, lineage and varna acquired by 
the accident of birth and the distinction based on ashrama 
prevail among the jīvas normally. Yet time, space, directions, 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   374 06-05-2011   10:53:54



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 375

countries, elements, jīvas, body, indriyas and Gods are all the 
effect of māyā – illusions – issuing from a mind that has been 
dislodged from the Heart called Brahmapuri (city of Brahman). 
Though this observance of the perception of the ‘nature of 
many’ or diversity may be conductive to the performance of 
actions in the empirical world, the Self, the One without a 
second, the form of Awareness, the substratum of all these, is 
beyond distinctions. The Self is abedha with no distinctions. 
There is no manifoldness in the Self. Manifoldness is in the 
adjuncts in which the Reality is apprehended, like the space 
or ether in different pots, or the sun in different reflectors. “ 
The Self is not related to the body and there is no body in 
the Self. They are mutually different as light and darkness.” 
(Yoga Vasishtam, Verse 906).

Svarūpa, the form of jñāna, is the same for all and 
transcends all these distinctions. When someone asked

other than the Self is devoid of distinctions. “ This Ātman 
is eternal and shines when apprehended by proper canons 
of knowledge. It does not need a place or time of purity.” 
(Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, Verse 532).
