Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   376 06-05-2011   10:53:55



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 377

Commentary: 
Nature does not allow herself to be duplicated in creation. 

The various lives created are classified into genus and species. 
Even the beings of the same species differ from each other in 
colour and form. Though cows are many in colour the milk 
they all yield is of the same colour. The differences of colour 
of the coats of the cows are not present in the milk. Jīvas are 
similar to like the cows with countless distinctions in qualities, 
forms and nature.

The non-dual jñāna that shines in the hearts of all of them 
is the same like milk. Jñāna, the essence of one Selfhood, 
shines distinctionless among distinctions. Jñāna is beyond the 
reach of distinctions. It persists through all the transformations 
and its effects or forms but suffers no distinction or diminution 
in the process as also when all these effects are eliminated. 
Anything with distinctions cannot be called jñāna.

The wise who know the Truth as ‘It is’ disregard the 
differences and know and perceive jñāna devoid of differences.

While the previous verse stated that jñāna within all 
beings is the same unaffected by caste, ashrama, etc., this 
one provides an example to illustrate it. 

Differences of colour and gender pertain to the gross 
body. The subtle body does not have these differences. How 
can differences exist in the Ātman, the most subtle among the 
subtle? That which shines within all that exhibit distinctive 
differences is Ātman, the non-distinct, the Self. Pal polum 
jñānamenap parttiduvar (will perceive jñāna as milk) thus 
He describes the perception of nondifference of the wise. 

There is a famous episode in Srimad Bhāgavatam. Once 
when Brahma could not answer highly subtle questions on 
aspect of yoga in their highest reaches by Sage Sanaka and 
others, the Lord appeared in the form of a Swan. The Sages 
questioned him as to who he was. He answered “How is this 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   377 06-05-2011   10:53:55



378 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

question relevant when ekātma (singleness) is the nature of 
Ātman? What speciality of Ātman that is devoid of caste and 
quality can I espouse and answer? Even if the question is 
with reference to the body it is meaningless for the bodies of 
all beings are made up of the five elements.” Thus the Lord 
taught them the Truth.

Therefore Yoga Vasishtam declares: “Human beings! 
There is not even a little relationship of this stainless Self with 
the body, as there is no relationship of gold with a particle of 
mud, though situated in it.” (Verse 907).

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 379

attachment and shines with countenance everywhere and

Commentary: 

There is no place where Brahman is not. It is the in-
dweller and the in-filler of everything abiding in the innermost 
recess of the heart. It resides even in the world of an atheist 
who attempts to disprove Its existence. 

“With countenance everywhere” means with perception 
everywhere. Face derives importance only from the perceiving 
power of the eyes it houses. Eyes are the proof of perception. 
The All knowing Witness, with Its omnipresence is described 
as “with face everywhere”. Brahman dwells everywhere 
through all, pervasive like the heat of fire in heated water 
or an iron ball – remains as All, yet identified with none, is 
omniscient and ever the same; hence the use of the phrase 
engum mukham meviadaha (with face everywhere). 

“I alone am the sky with unlimited boundary, endowed 
with a space, time and activities. Whoever perceived thus 
everywhere (at all times) he sees truly.

I am the Consciousness in the sky and the sun. I am the 
Consciousness in the cage of the five elements (the body).

I am the Consciousness in the Gods and demons 
and also in the movable and immovable things.” 
(Yoga Vasishtam, Verses 917 and 915).

While an earlier verse spoke of the conduciveness of all 
places, directions and time to the yoga of knowledge on the 
Self, this verse provides the reason for it namely the “all- 
pervasive nature of Brahman with face everywhere”. For those 
souls of true perception desirous of Liberation, Brahman alone 
is and therefore it was said “firmly establish your mind in that 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   379 06-05-2011   10:53:55



380 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Brahman”. Here place and direction also include Time. They 
are all simply superimpositions on that Brahman like snake 
seen on a rope or thief perceived on a post. Hence none of 
these, being mere illusions, will ever pose obstacles in the 
yoga of the Self as some tend to think.

When the perpetually oscillating mind is fixed in Ātman 
unceasingly and unswervingly the distinctions of the time, 
place and directions – the illusory limitations circumscribing 
the Ātman-fall away on their own even as a doll held in the 
hand of a sleeping child slips away.

The content that fills all things – sentient and insentient 
alike – and pervades everywhere remains concealed as content 
unknown to any due to the deluded knowledge of the mind. 
When the delusion departs, the Supreme content shines by 
Itself. A firm abidance in Brahman will drive the delusion away.

The buffeting of the waves is a phenomenon confined to 
the surface and not to the depth of the ocean. When the mind 
abides still in its source and form it shines serene and majestic 
like the deep unfathomed ocean. But when it slips from its 
source buffeted by the thought waves and troubled like the 
turbulent sea it becomes battered like the waves relentlessly 
dashing against each other.

Mind must be inhered in Brahman, by unceasing efforts, 
till it abides there firmly. The injunction that it should not 
think of anything else is to prevent the exteriorization. The 
adroit magician of the ego keeps creating the world; yet does 
not reveal its identity as the creator of the world but keeps its 
role under the wrap and remains in hiding. But when it abides 
in its source, Brahman, it divests itself of its magical form 
of māyā. The formless ghost of the ego, by creating forms, 
distorts the true Form. The ego, in hiding, must be exposed 
and made over to Brahman and thereafter no thoughts of place 
or direction should be entertained.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   381 06-05-2011   10:53:55



382 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

He has neither an ashrama (the stage of life) nor the 
observance of the prescribed code for that ashrama*. 
Such a dhira, a spiritual hero, or Hercules, has nothing 
to gain by performing any act and the fruits of action are 
not for him. Nor is there anything that needs be done by 
him. There is no Vedic injunction either enjoining him to 
do anything. Know this firmly.
Commentary: 

A jīva who turns a spiritual hero by burning his jīvabodha 
in the fire of jñāna and gains Liberation while even in a 
body needs no insignia to announce his status. One who has 
attained the Knowledge Supreme subsides in silence. He is 
without identifiable marks and no marks, social or religious 
or individual can identify him.

The practices followed in the family he is born into, 
the traditional cultural habits due to his lineage, practices 
followed in the name of country, the ritualistic observances 
of the religion or the obligatory acts of dharma of a particular 
ashrama and codes of conduct, are all needless for him.

All karmas performed in the practical world are sakama 
(with desire for fruits) always tainted with the desire for 
the fruits of them. The performance of a specific act is a 
sine-qua-non to enjoy a specific fruit while non-performance 
of it will not secure the fruit.

Observance of certain daily rituals are called Nithya 
karmas which are obligatory and while the non-performance 
of them may entail demerit no special gain accrues by 
performance of them, such as bathing, worship of the sun 

* They are four:	 The Brahmacharya ashrama
		T  he Grihastashrama
		T  he Vanaprasthashrama
		T  he Sannyāsashrama

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   382 06-05-2011   10:53:55



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 383

God three times a day and worship of and offering to deities. 
Performance of these becomes compulsory to safeguard one 
from a sin.

Naimiththika karmas prescribed for special occasions 
bestow extra-merit while performing them, but non-
performance entails no sin. Such special occasions are the 
beginning of summer and winter solstices, days of full moon, 
new moon, solar and lunar eclipses, etc.

The karmas performed for the manes (departed souls) 
are enjoined as obligatory called Pithru karmas. In addition 
Vedas and scriptures lay down certain special dharmas, the 
performance of which is a ‘commandment’.

The sage who knows Brahman has become Brahman 
Himself. His separate individuality having been consumed in 
the fire of jñāna, he has expanded as the Infinite and the drop 
has become the ocean.

When wisdom is attained karma drops off on its own, for 
karma and jñāna are mutually opposed as light and darkness. 
The law of karma holds sway only in the realm of non-self, 
where body-based distinctions of heredity, biological and 
social holds are prevalent. Therefore submission to any of 
these is not required. 

Every action is an expression of subtle sankalpa and 
desire. A jñāni who has transcended both fear and desire has 
no action to perform. A well has to be dug only till water is 
sighted, after which the spring will continue to yield. In the 
same way all karmas are only till Ātman is gained, then the 
inexhaustible Bliss is to be revelled in.

All actions by their very nature (by the involvement of 
impure instruments, motives and desires) are defective. The 
act of simply ‘being’ is greater than every other act. He may 
perform some actions but like the Lord he is the doer yet not 
the doer, kartaram akartaram, the best example being that of 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   383 06-05-2011   10:53:55



384 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

king Janaka and Jada Bharatha. Uttara Gītā declares: “For the 
yogī who has become accomplished as the result of having 
drunk the nectar of wisdom, no further duty remains; if any 
remains he is not a real knower of Truth.”

The best example of this can be provided from 
Bhagavan’s life. While Bhagavan’s mother was nearing her 
end, when he was invited by others for a meal Bhagavan 
declined but asked others to take their meal. When at night 
the mother ‘got absorbed” then “he rose up and in a voice 
free from pain said, ‘Hereafter we can eat. Come on. There 
is no pollution.’ And along with others took his meal.” 
(B.V.Narasimhaswamy in Self-Realization).

Bhagavad Gītā also speaks of the same “He has nothing 
to gain by actions done or to lose by anything undone. He is 
not dependent on anyone for the achievement of any goal.”

A jñāni has transcended all dharmas and karmas by virtue 
of his having been established in the Self and is therefore 
beyond the ‘dos’ and ‘don‘ts of the Vedic commandments. 
Scriptures and Vedas have granted him full freedom. 

A verse in Ozhivil Oddukam pen-pictures the state of 
such a jīvanmukta and says even Vedas and Agamas will 
wonder if it is said that the normal injunctions apply to him

	 Will stand in wonder
	 Who can say so?
It further goes on to say can there be action for a jñāni,

need a mount to fly on the sky? Can sky become the deep sea 
requiring a ship helmsman and a compass? What work will 
space and time perform except to remain as they are? 

Likewise for a jñāni will actions be required?
All works without exception have culminated in wisdom.
“Knowledge as a sacrifice is greater than any material 

sacrifice, oh Arjuna, for all works without any exception 
culminate in wisdom.” (Gītā, Chap. IV, Verse 33).

Therefore after gaining wisdom can work reappear? Can 
fuel burnt in the fire reappear or ghee churned from milk 
reappear in milk? Bhagavan himself has said that a jñāni is 
like a burnt rope. “The burnt rope still looks like a rope but 
it can’t serve as rope if you try to bind anything with it.” 
(Day by Day, 19-11-46).

What T.K. Sundaresa Iyer says is a fitting finale, 
“Bhagavan was above formal orthodoxy or unorthodoxy 
whatever he did was orthodox because he did it, since he was 
higher than Manu (the original law giver) and was himself the 
source of orthodoxy”. (Mountain Path, 1965).

The considered conclusion of the Vedas is that no 
injunction or karma can apply to the jñānis who have emerged 
victorious in the greatest austerity of annihilating the-self- the 
jīva-bodha.

“The inactivity is the basis of its corollary, activity. The 
useful wheel could not exist or move without a motionless 
centre. The sage relies on action less activity and carries on 
wordless teaching.” (Ella Maillart – Golden Jubilee Souvenir).

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   385 06-05-2011   10:53:55

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   386 06-05-2011   10:53:55



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 387

stay in any one place, or he may reside in a place and mingle 
intimately with the devout. Like everyone else he may sleep 
and wake up from sleep. But none of these poses a hindrance 
to his perpetual Self-abidance. Like the people of the world 
he eats when hungry and drinks when thirsty. This in no way 
deters his inherence in Ātman nor does it dislodge him from 
That.

When natural calamities like hurricane, unbearable cold 
and sweltering heat beset him he will give them no thoughts. 
Whatever state be happens to be in, not becoming one with 
it, he will be aloof and unaffected.

He who, as a seeker, thought every act as a bondage, now, 
in the realized state, remains as uninvolved witness without an 
impact of anything on him. Never dislodged from his natural 
state, supremely serene, he, the Self, remains as the Self.

Ātman is untouched by anything. So is an ātma-nishta, 
never one with anything except the Self. No avastha (state) 
– however intense and terrible – can approach the Supreme 
Content. Nothing can part or rend it asunder, burn It, drench 
or dry It.

The five elements with the functions of burning, parting, 
drenching and drying derive their power to do so from the 
Supreme Content, the Brahman. In the mere presence of the 
Self, all these happen. One who transcends the five elements 
and becomes Brahman will be unperturbed and unassailed 
by the elements. 

Ātman, the whole and Prime Content, is devoid of ‘going’ 
and ‘coming’, the three states of jāgrat, swapna and sushupti, 
afflictions like the enjoyable pleasures and grievous pain, 
hunger and thirst and the thoughts of doership with a view to 
rectify the afflictions – and most of all – the dehātma bhava 
that suffers most by the natural calamities.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   388 06-05-2011   10:53:55



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 389

Natural calamities like fire, or untoward happenings or 
sightings of apparitions like ghosts and ghouls do not cause 
fear in him.

Auvvaiyar, when questioned by Lord Subrahmanya 
“What is the most terrible of all things?” answered “Poverty”. 
In truth ‘poverty’ includes but mental penury, a shortcoming 
of the mind. Want of contentment in spite of the possession 
of inestimable wealth lands one in a state of abject penury. 
But one with contentment and no mental shortcoming is the 
possessor of all even if he is assailed relentlessly by poverty 
of everything else. When this is so, how can prosperity or 
poverty approach an ātma-nishta who has no-mind?

All diseases, whether raging fever or afflictions caused 
by the imbalance of the three humours like bile, phlegm and 
wind or ailments of the abdomen like acute indigestion and 
other countless diseases all assail the physical body made 
up of the five elements. But one abiding in the Self is bereft 
of “dehātma bhava”. How then can the ailments that assail 
the physical body affect him? He is one without a disease. 
Unperturbed by any such he is in the natural state forever.

But, for the onlookers, he seems to be in a body subject 
to the onslaught of the aforesaid diseases and at such times, 
he is described to be unperturbed and perfectly tranquil and 
at peace with himself. In truth he has no body and much less 
the diseases that affect it. All these changes pertain to the 
perception of distinctions of the onlookers and it is a mockery 
to say that he is afflicted by the diseases.

A verse in Ozhivil Odukkam portrays the preposterous 
nature of such a conception in a humorous way: “With 
whom can one compare people, who suspecting Lord Agni 
(Jadaragni, an aspect of fire that is believed to digest food 
eaten and facilitate absorption and assimilation) to suffer from 
indigestion, try to cure him by administering a concoction 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   389 06-05-2011   10:53:55



390 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

of dry ginger-paste in water (the traditional remedy for 
indigestion), then assuming him to be affected by cold cover 
him with stacks of hay to cure him of the cold and then grieve 
for not having resorted to them earlier or those who wash 
water, the purifier of all, with water or bury their shadows 
that follow them under sand or try to measure the shadow to 
know their height?”

While treating the one who digests for the sickness 
indigestion is the height of stupidity; equally stupid is it to the 
think that an ātmajñāni suffers from diseases like a common 
man.

“Neither pleasure nor pain nor good
  Nor evil ever touches this Knower
  Of Brahman, who has no identification 
  With the body, but who rests in Brahman.
  The Ātman is his wealth, power and everything.
  He always lives without the body-idea.
  He is always satisfied in his own Self.”
                             (Brahmarahasya Upanishad, Verse 9)
This and the preceding verse are a perfect pen-portrait of 

Bhagavan. Bhagavan always clad in a loin cloth was totally 
indifferent to extremes of weather. In midday in the height of 
summer, while the devotees walking with him, unable to bear 
the heat would be asked by Bhagavan to run or walk fast to 
reach a shade, he himself would walk in the same measured 
slow pace of his, unperturbed and unaffected by the heat of 
the sun or of the scorching earth on the unshod soles.

In an unusually cold winter when Manavasi Ramaswami 
Iyer had two shirts stitched and offered to Bhagavan he 
refused saying “did I ask for it?” During the days when a 
series of operations were performed one after the other, Dr. 
K. Subramanyam records “As far as Bhagavan was concerned 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   390 06-05-2011   10:53:55



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 391

he was ever the same serene blissful Self. He behaves as if 
the disease belonged to somebody else.” (A Tribute – Ramana 
Kendran Hyderabad)

While climbing a steep part of the mountain and a 
precariously perched rock, disturbed out of equilibrium 
accidentally came down heavily on him and his left thumb got 
dislocated,he simply pushed back the thumb into his socket 
with no sign of concern while his mother was shocked to 
behold his blood-splattered form. When numerous hornets 
attacked his thigh with needle like stings, Bhagavan simply 
stood still, allowing them to vent their anger for having 
disturbed their nest.

When Rangan was astonished to find in both his feet many 
thorns sticking out which he wanted to remove while some 
were old some were knew “Which thorn will you remove?” 
asked Bhagavan with a laugh and crushing the thorn with the 
same foot he happily continued to walk.

Once hearing the growl of tiger very near, the panic 
stricken devotees (though in the presence of the greatest 
asylum) sought asylum within the premises and bolted the 
door. Bhagavan remained where he was, unruffled. Yet if he 
found tigers near the tank in day time, he would advise them 
to go away as others would he afraid of their presence. Such 
incidents are numberless in the life of Bhagavan who was 
always in his natural state, called Brāhmi stiti. One who has 
attained this supreme state is never again deluded.
Once Bhagavan narrated the stories of Thondaradipodi Alwar 
and Kaduveli Siddhar. Even though they led a life of seclusion, 
circumstances forced them to live in the company of women 
for some time, yet they never swerved from their abidance in 
the Self. When Kaduveli Siddhar was jeered by the public for 
his apparent association with a woman he exclaimed, “If it 
is true that I slept day and night quite aware of my Self may 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   391 06-05-2011   10:53:55



392 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

this stone burst into twain and become the wide expanse.” 
And it did. Bhagavan continued, “Such a one is pure like the 
ether which is always itself clear, whether covered by dense 
clouds or cleared of clouds by currents of air.”. “Although he 
may appear grief-stricken…yet he evinces just the right love 
of and pity for the senses which he earlier controlled before 
he realized that they were mere manifestation of the Supreme 
Being. All his actions should be taken to be only divine 
manifestation on the plane of humanity.” (Talks no. 449).

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 393

Paraphrase: 
Bearing a body in the world, if I go from one place to 

another I am not the one who traversed up and down. It is 
the movement of only the sarira (body) and not the “I”, 
the Self. On close enquiry both ‘going’ and ‘coming’ are 
not for “Me”. Further I am not of the work of māyā the 
creator of the illusory appearance of the entire Universe. 
Remaining always the same, I was never immersed in the 
dharmas of creation that keep perpetually changing nor 
will I ever be so.
Commentary: 

Ātman pervades everywhere like the limitless sky and as 
such there is no “other” place than Itself for the Ātman to ‘go’ 
to and ‘come’ from. It is not possible to move this way or that 
way even for the space of a dot That content, that pervades 
everywhere without leaving the space of even a fraction of 
an atom unpervaded. How then can ‘going’ and ‘coming’ be 
effected? Therefore it is said ponavan vandavanu nanahen. 
“The one who had moved forward and came back is not Me.”

Bhagavan explains it: “ You do not leave one place for 
another. You are always stationary. The scenes go past you... 
We see a picture of a man running several miles and rushing 
towards us but the screen does not move. It is the picture that 
moves on and away.” We are forever like the screen. The true 
state of Being remains fixed and stationary. “The state of Being 
is permanent and the body and world are not.” (Talks no. 609).

The dharma or nature of prakriti or māyā is to create 
this illusory and perceivable world and subject everything to 
perpetual change. Sometimes torrential rains pour, at other 
times acute drought agonizes; sometimes blazing heat sends 
out heat waves and a tornado moves mountains. Prakriti 
creates jīvas, gives them youth and old age and subjects them 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   393 06-05-2011   10:53:55



394 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

to death. All changes like birth and death, health and ill-health, 
are all the handwork of prakriti or māyā. 

Endowing māyā with all these dharmas and inducing it 
to manifest them, yet remaining beyond the impact of them 
by transcending māyā, is the Self that ever shines as “I-I”. 
This is called Brahman. Its dharma is ever changeless but the 
ever-changing nature of prakriti is a strange wonder indeed!

On close enquiry it will be evident that the changes 
pertaining to the dharma of prakriti are not in the least to 
“Me”, the substratum of prakriti. I was never steeped in them 
(dharmas of prakriti) either before or now, nor will I ever be.

These dharmas of prakriti are indeed not for me in any 
span of time “I am beyond them and exist as I unchanged 
forever”. Actions of ‘going’ and ‘coming’ pertain to the 
upādhis or adjuncts while the Ātman is nirupadikan, devoid 
of upādhis. The Self unborn, ever remains as the witness of 
the upādhi deha (body) and the changes it is subject to. The 
condensed essence of jñāna as Awareness is the substance 
that persists always even when the upādhis It is associated 
with undergoes changes. It remains changeless and suffers 
no diminution. 

“It is upādhi (superimposed quality) only that comes, it 
alone goes; it alone does actions and enjoys; it is that which 
lives and dies. Like the Kuladri (mountain called Kula) 
(a mythological mountain personifying stability) I stand 
unmoving.” (Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, Verse 502). ‘Going’ and 
‘coming’ cannot be to the one without parts. How will, that 
which is One through and through, closely compacted and 
without intervening space, like the sky, ever ‘go’, ‘come’ or 
‘move’?

Bhagavan who ever remained as the Self All-pervading, 
on many occasions when requested by devotees to visit their 
places answered uniformly on all occasions “Where can I 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   394 06-05-2011   10:53:55



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 395

go?” or “Where to stay and where to go, there is no place to 
which I could go.”

In Mahavakya Ratnamala it is stated: “What is there for 
me to do, where am I to go, what am I to accept and what am 
I to discard, since I pervade the entire Universe like the waters 
of the final deluge.”

Bhagavan explains how “I am the body” sense is 
responsible to view the motionless Ātman as subject to ‘going’ 
and ‘coming’.

“People come by train and say ‘we have come’. It is the 
same thing with the body. For the Self, the body is a cart. 
The legs do the work of walking and people say “I walked, 
I came”. Where does the Self go? The Self does not do 
anything but appropriates to itself all these acts.” (Letters, 
28 May 1946). and again “When we ride in a carriage do we 
feel that we are in the carriage? Take the example of the sun; 
It shines in water in a small pot, in big rivers and in mirror. 
Its image is there. But just because of that does it think that 
it is all that? The same thing with us. All the trouble arises, 
if one thinks one is the body. If one rejects that thought, then 
like the sun, one will shine everywhere and be all-pervading.” 
(Letters, 21-11-47)

Once when T.K.Sundaresa Iyer expressed his distress at 
the prospect of having to go away from Bhagavan for taking 
up a new job Bhagavan asked him “How long have you 
been with Bhagavan?” “Forty years”, was the reply. “Here is 
someone who has been listening to my teaching for 40 years 
and now says he is going somewhere away from Bhagavan”, 
remarked Bhagavan. However, that the job fell through is a 
different matter.

Bhagavan who ever remained as the Self – all-pervading 
whenever requested to visit holy centres by devotees like 
Swami Rajeshwarānanda, uniformly answered: “Where can I 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   395 06-05-2011   10:53:55



396 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

go? Where can I come?” As a proof of the exalted state that he 
was in, Bhagavan’s assurance to the sorrow-stricken devotees 
during his final illness was simply a reassertion of this ever 
true state as the Self, namely, “Where can I go?”

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 397

Commentary: 
All actions have their source in prakriti or māyā. All 

actions are the effect of prakriti. Everything in the universe 
rises from prakriti (mula prakriti) and functions. Therefore 
it is spoken of as the origin of karmas. The power of māyā is 
such that, not being apart from the True content it possesses 
infinite powers that are wonderful. Bhagavan sings of this in 
Ashtakam “In Thee there is a wonderful Power.”

The poison in the fangs of the snake never harms itself 
but causes disastrous consequences when it strikes others. 
Likewise, māyākāryam – the action of māyā – is born of 
Reality, Brahman, and does not affect It in anyway. Only those 
who objectify and know it are assailed by it.

Karma means action. Actions, whether of the gross body 
or of speech or of mind and however exalted like learning 
and reciting of the holy Vedas, japa, tapas and dhyāna, are 
all forms of action – offsprings born of maya. Prakriti is the 
mother of all karmas.

Furthermore the effects of prakriti are cosmic in nature. 
The rising of the sun, the showering down of rain, the wafting 
of the wind, and blowing of icy air are the unfailing functions 
of the five elements – an aspect of prakriti. Bumper crops or 
failure of crops are the outcome of prakriti. All that is seen 
in nature is the act of prakriti and not of the Ātman. Just as 
clouds are the cause of rain, Prakriti is the cause of actions. 

A perfect tattva jñāni, (who knows the import of the 
tattvas) reflects naturally “I am the Immaculate, freed of all 
actions”. The Teacher of Gītā, expounds thus: “Nature is said 
to be the cause of effect, instrument and agent.” (kārya kāraṇa 
kartrtvē hetuḥ Prakritir uchyatē) (Chap. XIII, Verse 20).

“He who sees that all actions are done only by nature 
(Prakriti) and likewise that the Self is not the doer, he verily 
sees.”

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   397 06-05-2011   10:53:56



398 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Prakrtyai va cha karmāṇi kriyamāṇāni Sarvasah
Yah pachyati tatha’t mānam akartāram sa pachyati 
                                                      ( Chap. XIII, Verse 29)
The Self is Immaculate for It is devoid of the impurities 

and flaws of all the five elements, of the gross, subtle and 
causal bodies and the five functions of God. We the Self are 
not the world, jīva and God.

The flaws of the earth are slush, dirt, burning ghats, 
slums and of water turbidity, bubbles, foam, sedge, and of 
fire smoke, and spark and dust; fragrance, and stench are of 
air. Phlegm, bile, sweat, etc. are impurities of the gross body. 
Desire, greed, ego, miserliness, hatred and jealousy are of 
the subtle body. The jīva has the impurities of knowledge 
and ignorance. But we, the Ātman, is simply the Awareness-
witness of all these. As the sky is not connected with the 
clouds, so too I am not connected with the body. The sky, that 
is untouched by the cloud that is the result of combination of 
smoke, light, water and wind, is not made wet either by the 
downpour of rain by reason of its formlessness, subtlety and 
uncontaminability, so too there is no connection of the Ātman 
with the body made of the five elements. If so how will the 
actions contaminate the ‘indweller’ in the body? Therefore 
we are flawless and Immaculate. We, the Self, are without 
actions. For one travelling in a train, the land and trees appear 
to speed past, though one oneself appears not to move. On 
reflection, it will be known that trees and land do not move. 
Likewise though the ego functions, the self has no activity and 
while the ego subsides, the Self does not. The two functions 
of ramification and withdrawal that arise from the ego, due to 
superimposition, appears as if the functions are of the Self just 
as the trees appear to move fast for one in a running train. The 
Self without action and endeavour is simply the uninvolved 
witness of the ego that acts.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   398 06-05-2011   10:53:56

Commentary: 

Prakriti is a mixture or conglomeration composed 
of a host of tainted qualities, a variety of changes, flaws, 
shortcomings, dwandwas (dualities) like good and bad, likes 
and dislikes, pleasure and pain and the triads like world, 
God and jīva. An action is neither a painless pleasure, nor a 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   399 06-05-2011   10:53:56



400 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

flawless virtue. Prakriti is incapable of providing whole Bliss 
unalloyed with pain.

One who abides in the Self will not be bound by māyā 
replete with blemishes. The play of māyā with its phantasies 
of changes is for the one who has slipped from abidance in 
the Ātman. A jñāni, precisely because of his release from such 
māyā, has earned for him the name mukta, the one liberated 
while embodied.

The mukta, is the only spiritual hero (dhira) who shines 
untouched by the blemishes of māyā and all the rest are in 
some way enslaved by māyā. “Māyā māyāmitam akilam” (the 
whole world is enveloped in māyā). Māyā is anirvachaneeya 
(indescribable). Hiding its form it manifests its effects. Only 
when one staggers under the burden of delusion of māyā kārya 
(action of māyā) one can realize its form in its effects.

That is why Devi Mahatmya says “She, the Divine 
Mahamāyā, draws by force the minds of even the knowing 
ones and yea makes them over to delusion.” (Chap. I, Verse 55) 

The Lord proclaims in Gītā: “mama māyā duratyaya” 
(Indeed my māyā is difficult to cross over). 

Māyā wears many an attire to ensnare and enslave men.
Pride among the affluent, haughtiness among the learned 

scholars and erudite pandits, egoity among the royalty, 
indifference among the powered, nonchalance among the 
soldiers and the pride of lineage among men of good families 
are, to mention a few, garbs that māyā adorns herself with 
dexterity.

A jñāni is unaware of the body made up of the five kosas. 
He is bodiless in his perception and being unembodied, is 
without the five kosas which perform the actions. Hence he 
is an akarta and is not bound by māyā. 

Therefore even as actions done in a dream disappear 
on waking all karmas get extinguished upon the dawn of 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   400 06-05-2011   10:53:56



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 401

Knowledge. He is untouched by any action. “Just as a river 
does not continue its flow after its discharge into the ocean 
so also a person loses all movements after he merges in the 
Self.” (Talks no. 554).

Māyā that conquers all pays homage at the feet of 
ātmanishta and becomes his slave. Once Bhagavan himself 
described a state of jīvanmukta thus to one Mr. Knowles, well 
-versed in Eastern and Western philosophy “A jīvanmukta is 
the ever-aware Self, the Witness-Consciousness transcending 
space and time and causation, the fullness of being; how he 
is the non-actor, non-enjoyer and yet at the same time the 
greatest of actors, the greatest of enjoyers and so forth.” 
Mr. Knowles to whom this was too much to digest put a 
strange question “Are you or are you not speaking to us?” 
Bhagavan gave him a meaningful look and said in a most 
emphatic tone: “No, ‘I’ am not talking to you.” In an ecstatic 
mood, Knowless echoed, “No, Bhagavan is not talking to 
us. He simply is. That is all.” (At the Feet of Bhagavan, by 
T.K.Sundaresa Iyer, page 54). 

Between the two, mind and activity which are ever united 
like fire and heat, on the annihilation (or absence) of either, 
both just vanish.

That is called renunciation of action which is remaining 
desireless without feeling, without objects to be known, calm 
even, and without utterance. “Māyā does not bind such a 
one for.” declares Yoga Vasishtam. “The entire collection of 
worlds past, present and future is taken within, like a thread 
by a pearl, by that person by whom everything is abandoned.” 
(Yoga Vasishtam, Verses 2062, 2064, 2074).

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   402 06-05-2011   10:53:56



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 403

Darkness can be destroyed only by light which is opposed 
to it and not by any other means. Anything can be rendered 
naught only by what is opposed to it; for instance fire cannot 
be extinguished by fire but only by water, its opposite, which 
alone can put it out. The place enveloped by darkness is itself 
called the form of darkness. Darkness can be destroyed by 
the light of a lamp which, besides removing the surrounding 
darkness, also reveals itself. The Light of Ātman in the same 
way makes the veiling darkness born of the void of dark 
nescience extinct by It’s light of knowledge and reveals Itself 
without any veiling by shining in It’s own effulgence.

“For those in whom ignorance is destroyed by wisdom, 
for them wisdom lights up the Supreme Self like the Sun.” 
(Gītā, Chap.V, Verse 16).

The Ātman is the Supreme Consciousness by virtue of 
whom there is Consciousness in the world but whom the 
world does not and cannot make Conscious for Ātman is Self-
effulgent -a mass of radiance-, Self-revealing Awareness who 
is awake even when the entire world is asleep.

“The world, that is by the reflected light of the Self, is 
seen with the mind. When it is not itself so illumined, it is not 
aware of the world. If the mind is turned in towards the source 
of light objective knowledge ceases and the Self alone shines 
forth as the Heart.” (Talks no. 98).

Bhagavan further explains it with an analogy. “We see 
the pictures on the screen with the help of a small light in an 
atmosphere of darkness; if that darkness is dispelled by a big 
light can the pictures be visible? The whole place becomes 
luminous and lustrous. In the same way if you see the world 
with the small light called mind you find it full of different 
colours. But if you see it with the big light known as Self-
Realization (Ātma jñāna) you will find it is one continuous 
Universal light and nothing else.” (Letters, 25-9-47).

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   403 06-05-2011   10:53:56



404 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

The real or natural form can be attained only by 
destroying the veiling darkness. Unless the knowledge of the 
Self is attained, concealment will not be obliterated. How to 
dispense with this mutual dependence? This glorious act of 
grace can happen only by the grace of the guru. Seeking and 
grace go hand in hand. “Out of compassion for those (who 
are constantly devoted to Me-the Self) I reveal Myself.” says 
the Lord.

Whether Ātmasākṣātkāra dawned first leading to 
the destruction of ajñāna or removal of ajñāna led to the 
knowledge of the Self is unanswerable due to the difficulty 
of separating the two.

When sleep overtakes one, when was one awake or when 
did one start to slip into slumber is not easy to state. Did sleep 
come after wakefulness was lost or with the onset of sleep did 
wakefulness subside is unanswerable. Even as the age-long 
darkness in a cave is destroyed completely and immediately by 
striking a match-stick, the beginningless darkness of nescience 
is destroyed simultaneously with the dawn of knowledge.

The light of Ātman shines as the light of divine knowledge.
“One winter evening as Bhagavan was stretching 

himself on the sofa, without any occasion whatsoever for 
the utterance he said suddenly and spontaneously: ‘It is 
said that I took twenty minutes to realize – It is wrong (adu 
tappu)!’ After a few seconds he added: ‘it may be a moment 
(oru kshanam irukkalām)’. But again he corrected himself: 
‘even that is not correct (aduvum sariyillai). Where is time 
element in it? (time engē adīlē?)’” (Moments Remembered, 
V Ganesan, page 85).

Paraphrase: 
Like the light of the lamp that, with its ghee exhausted 

and its light and heat subsided, attains permanent rest and 
peace in the void, the yogī who ceaselessly contemplates 
the Ātman and the vijñāni who remains the Self and shines 
as such will attain eternal repose and quiescence in the 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   405 06-05-2011   10:53:56



406 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Self – the space of Awareness. There is nothing greater 
than the Ātman to be attained. This is the Truth.
Commentary: 

This verse explains the exalted state of a mahayogī, who 
has attained to the state of remaining as the form of ‘That’ in 
perfect repose by ceaseless contemplation. As long as there 
is ghee in the lamp, fed by the ghee, the flame of the lamp 
shines spreading its lustre. Once the ghee gets exhausted, the 
light gradually gets dimmer and dimmer and finally losing its 
heat and brightness, attains rest and peace.

A yogī ceaselessly contemplates on the Self as long as the 
mind is active. Like the ghee getting exhausted by the wick in 
the lamp, the mind gets gradually ground atom by atom and 
finally completely ground into extinction attains quiescence 
like the flame of the lamp that is blown out or like a candle 
that is snuffed out.

Dhyāna is an activity of the mind. Contemplation can go 
on only so long as there is a mind. The purpose of meditation is 
to swallow the meditator which is nothing but the annihilation 
of the mind.

Contemplation of the Ātman alone is capable of snuffing 
out the mind. Then the jīva-bodha dies and ātma-bodha shines 
in its place. This is parama nirvāṇam – the final Beatitude and 
there is no greater state than this. The ego and the sense of 
doership causing karma-fruit-karma continuum that forces a 
jīva into varied embodiments birth after birth, get extinguished 
by the dhyāna of the True Content like the ceaseless flow of 
oil. For one who has attained the Self, other siddhis become 
needless.

This state of Nirvāṇa is described by Yoga Vasishtam as 
follows: “That is declared as abidance in one’s real nature 
which is indeed the state, void of thinking, like what exists 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   406 06-05-2011   10:53:56



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 407

in the interregnum when the mind is going from one object 
to another object. That is considered one’s abidance in one’s 
real nature which is like the state within a stone, with all 
thoughts or imagination extinguished (but) freed from sleep 
or dullness” (Verses 2254 and 2255) and “Here that seeking-
nature vanishes somewhere like a lamp with its oil fully spent; 
only the state of the Highest Truth remains there shining 
without end.” (Verse 2270).

Yet this analogy causes is some the doubt whether one’s 
Self also would also cease to exist.

One Dr. Hand questions Bhagavan: “What is the nirvāṇa 
of Buddha?

B: Loss of individuality.
D: I dread that loss. Can there not be a human consciousness 

in nirvāṇa?” (Talks no. 176).
“Why fear to lose individuality? What is your state in 

dreamless sleep? Are you conscious of your individuality 
then?” and further “Are there two selves in that case?” (Ibid)

Even Upanishadic seers have raised and cleared this 
doubt. Nachiketas of Kathopanishad fame and Maitreyi in 
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad raised the same doubt.

Bhagavan has himself cleared this doubt: “Nirvāṇa is 
perfection. In the perfect state, there is neither subject nor 
object, there is nothing to see, nothing to feel, nothing to know. 
Seeing and knowing are functions of the mind. In nirvāṇa 
there is nothing but the blissful pure consciousness, ‘ I am’”. 
(Talks no. 406).

When the subject and object coalesce, who is there to 
understand That by which everything else is understood and 
through what can That be understood? 

Bhagavan explains “The spark of jñāna will easily 
consume all creation as if it were a mountain – heap of 
cotton. All the crores of worlds being built upon the weak 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   407 06-05-2011   10:53:56



408 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

(or no) foundation of the ego, they all topple down when 
the atomic bomb of jñāna comes down upon them.” 
(Day by Day, 22-11-45).

Then the ‘mind-nature’ disappears somewhere. The 
‘conscious nature’ remains quite clear, without disturbance 
and division but as the All.

As Yoga Vasishtam says: “The entity that is the mind, 
risen with a nature that is completely separated (from the body 
and the like) on account of its enlightened nature (that is pure 
consciousness) is without beginning or end and produces the 
fruit of oneness with the Highest Truth. I do not know where 
the mind is gone or where desire actions and the perceptions 
of joy and anger.” (Verses 2272 and 2274).

On attaining this highest Truth even knowledge that 
helped arrive at fulfilment becomes unreal immediately and 
even that along with ignorance perish in the fire of jñāna as 
the stick used for turning the funeral pyre.

uØan chelva-daha uœarn- though conceived by us as

Paraphrase: 

When an empty pot is carried from one place to 
another, though we feel that the space within the pot has 
also moved along with the pot, is it not the pot alone that 
has moved? The space does not move. Is it not? Likewise 
the Self that appears to be in the body (Itself, not moving 
by the movement of the body) remains motionless and 
fixed like space.
Commentary: 

This verse provides an example for the motionless nature 
of the Ātman explained in verse 47. The most celebrated and 
oft-quoted example of Vedāntic literature of space in a pot 
and space outside the pot is utilised here. Ghatakasa (space 
in a pot) and mahakasa (space unconfined) are the classic 
examples commonly used.

Though we normally distinguish between the two and 
say ‘the small pot space’ and ‘the large atmospheric space’ 
due to the apparent separation by the walls of the pot, they 
are not really different. They remain as one homogenous 
space undivided by the walls of the pot even when the pot 
remains as the pot because the walls of the pot are also of the 
same space which is both inside and outside. The walls are 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   409 06-05-2011   10:53:56



410 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

the effect of space and therefore non-different from space. In 
short ghatakasha was always mahakasa with the upādhi of 
the ghata (pot) removed. It is as ever. Space constricted by 
joining the index and the forefinger may be called triangular 
or circular depending on the shape produced by joining so 
the fingers. But the removal of the fingers renders the space 
as limitless as it ever is.

How can that which pervades everywhere providing 
room for everything else to stay, be carried? Like a pot that 
is immersed in water, water fills the inside and outside of 
the pot, in a pot with space, space fills the inside and outside 
of the pot and space cannot be carried. What changes place 
is only the pot but space remains motionless and fixed. 
Likewise when the body moves from one place to another, 
the Ātman that seems to reside within the body, is thought 
erroneously to move. What moves in fact is the body and 
not the Ātman.

The space though it provides room for the activities of 
the other four elements like air, fire, water and earth, remains 
untouched by the dharma or nature of any of them. The Ātman, 
like the space, is ‘moveless’.

When the jīvas being whirled around perpetually in cycles 
of birth and death, the belief that Ātman also moves along 
with, is a mental deception. Even if it is so perceived, it must 
be known that in the same way the sky remains as it is, Ātman 
also remains as It always is.

The Self in the individual experiences no change at all, 
though the subtle body of man may take various embodiments 
according to past karma. Akasa resembles the Self in its 
aspects of immutability and pervasiveness. Just as the all 
pervading akasa does not perish when the pots which held it 
are broken, so it is with the all pervading Self, at the repeated 
destruction of the body, It’s upādhi.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   410 06-05-2011   10:53:56

Commentary: 

The earlier verse spoke of the ‘moveless nature’ of space 
that has no ‘coming and going’ and that when a pot is carried 
it is the pot that moves and not the space in it. Once the pot 
is broken, it is said, the space within the pot will merge with 
the limitless, unparticularized space. In truth this is another 
phantasy or illusion of the mind. The space can unite only 
if it was divided ever. It is the jīvabhava that differentiates 
the space that remains pervading fully within and without, 
as ghatakasa (the space within the pot) and mahakasa (the 
space outside the pot).

The illusion born of imagination can be undone only by 
another illusion in tune with the adage, set a thief to catch a 
thief or use a thorn to remove a thorn and then throw both 
away. The True Content has no illusion whatsoever and 
however requires no antidote either.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   412 06-05-2011   10:53:56



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 413

Further it is said that the Ātman within the body, after the 
latter passes away becomes one with the Paramātman. But in 
truth there is no place that Ātman is not. Then with what can 
it merge? All these are illusions fabricated by the ego. The 
jīvātman and the Paramātman were never separated by the 
insentient body to start with. To say that on passing away of the 
body, the jīvātma will merge with the Paramātma is to satisfy 
the minds flawed with fragmented perceptions. Ātman, like the 
limitless sky, is indivisible. It is the support of everything like the 
akasa. It is One, and the whole Content and cannot be parted. 
Therefore on enquiry it will be found that in Ātman there is 
no room for union or division or individual and the aggregate.

The pangs of hunger experienced in a dream can be 
appeased only by food in dream. Food of jāgrat cannot satisfy 
the dream-hunger. Likewise for dispelling a delusion born of 
imagination, an antidote born of imagination is suggested. 	
     Amritabindu Upanishad also has two verses containing 
the same Truth. “When various forms like the jar are broken 
again and again, the akasa does not know them to be broken 
but He knows perfectly.” (Verse 14) (‘He’ stands for the ever 
manifest all-knowing blissful Self who knows that He is ever 
unborn and deathless).

“Being covered by ‘māyā’ which is a mere sound It does 
not, through darkness, know the akasa (the Blissful One). 
When ignorance is rent asunder, It being then Itself only sees 
the unity.” (Verse 15).

This verse explains why is it that Ātman which is 
omniscient is not always aware of its true nature which is Bliss. 
Māyā having no real existence is the cause of phenomenal 
world composed of form, sound, etc. Just as a man, though 
possessed of his faculties and senses, cannot find a particular 
thing, however near it may be, if he is blinded by darkness, 
so the Ātman does not know Its own nature as Existence-

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   413 06-05-2011   10:53:56



414 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Knowledge-Bliss through the covering of māyā or just as the 
akasa in a jar knows not that it is the same as the infinite akasa, 
so the individual soul being covered by the darkness of māyā 
does not know its real nature. When the pot is broken, there 
remains the one Infinite akasa. Similarly when the covering 
of māyā is rent asunder by jñāna, the Ātman shines it its 
essence of One only there being utter absence of differentiation 
between the subject and object. The one who knows this nectar 
of Supreme Content residing in the hearts of all beings as ‘I 
am this’ gets released from the grip of ignorance while in the 
body and destroys the vāsanās of avidya. 

Merging with the Ātman as One with the elimination of 
jīvabodha is the essence taught here. Even this is true only to 
a certain extent. There is no separate entity as jīva. Even that 
is the form of Ātman. This truth is easy of comprehension for 
those capable of perceiving akarma in karma and formless in 
form. However said ‘what is’ is just One. 

Bhagavan was a past master in converting every incident 
into a pointer to the ultimate Truth. Once, for example, 
Ramaswamy Pillai who carried his key-bunch with him (with 
which, he also used to keep the beat of time by jingling them 
during parayana), once had lost it. When he told Bhagavan 
about the missing key, Bhagavan said to him: “The key 
is where it always was. It is not lost. Only your memory 
is lost. Ātman (the Self) is always everywhere, but due to 
ajñāna (ignorance) we spend our time searching for it.” 
(Power of the Presence, Part I, page 28).

one, unperturbed by anything and in any state, will be content 
in the Self, supremely serene and peaceful. Bound by none of 
the attachments of prakriti, he is forever one with the Ātman 
and will remain like the sky untouched by the dharmas of the 
deha. This, in nutshell, is what has been revealed so far and 
is the import of the word endru.

The Lord is called adhikari for with the five-fold functions 
of creation, preservation, destruction, veiling and bestowing 
of grace, He is the mahā kartha. He is called ellam unar isan 
for infilling everything and pervading everywhere as the holy 
Witness He is ‘omniscient’ (All-knowing).

That, the Supreme Lord, Parameshwara with due 
authority of a guru instructed Kumara in ancient times is 
revealed in andru adhikarattodu ivvaru araindan. (Spake with 
authority, then). This was taught by the Lord the day it was 
listened to by Kumara. Andru may also be taken as nandru 
(well revealed).

Bearing this upadeśa in mind one who conquers all 
binding attachments and vanquishes the mind will gain 
liberation and in Absolute Awareness (like the Lord Himself) 
will eternally remain everywhere and as All, is the instruction.

Those conversant with the life of Bhagavan could recall 
countless instances as proof of the dictum stated in this verse, 
namely, that such a one remaining anchored in the plane of 
chit pervades everywhere as Absolute Awareness, though 
localised, yet transcending space and time.

A poor couple from Peru longing to see Bhagavan, whom 
they regarded as the second coming of Christ, willingly and 
happily bore hardships and privations to save money to be 
able to come to Bhagavan, came and stayed on for some 
days. One day, in the course of conversation, when the 
couple were describing the beach and seacoast of their town, 
Bhagavan astonished them and the listeners by describing 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   416 06-05-2011   10:53:57



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 417

minutely the beach paved with marble slabs, coconut palms 
planted between the marble benches, and the fifth bench 
where the couple used to sit and immediately noticing their 
astonishment he smiled and remarked “It does not matter 
how I can tell. Enough if you know that the Self is not limited 
by space and time, thus providing a tangible demonstration 
of God’s omnipotence, omnipresence and omniscience.” 
(T.K.Sunsaresa Iyer – At the Feet of Bhagavan).

How he went all the way to Punjab and claimed Poonjaji, 
though he remained rooted in Tiruvannamalai all the time is 
well-known. Equally well-known is the episode of granting 
the most needed succour to Ganapathy Muni at Tiruvottriyur 
by his physical presence and blessing though he never left 
Tiruvannamalai.

During the height of the First World War, the whole world 
felt that Great Britain and its allies would lose the war. One 
early morning when this was being discussed with anxiety by 
G.V.Subharamaiah and Subregistrar Narayana Iyer, Bhagavan, 
suddenly observed: “Um, but Russia?” Abruptly he cut short 
his speech and resumed silence. That Russia joined the Allies 
years later and that Germany was routed is history.

There are many such incidents of Bhagavan guiding 
people in distant places to Arunachala appearing either in 
dreams or in visions physically; the most outstanding of 
which is the story of Jadini Sundarambal recorded by Swami 
Abishktananda. This type of Leela of Kaivalya is not limited 
to this phenomenal world.

Once, to Venkateshwar, the brother of Krishna 
Bikshu, Bhagavan said “I have at this moment twenty 
different bodies working in twenty different lokas.” 
(Fragrant Petals, page 224).

Yet the Glorious example of Bhagavan remaining as 
Eternal Witness-Awareness is revealed when he described 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   417 06-05-2011   10:53:57



418 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

how Lord Dakshinamuthy tried to dispel the doubts of 
Sanaka and others initially by explaining verbally. As 
doubts still persisted, he assuming his ‘Grand Silence’, 
taught them and they understood. When Muruganar 
immediately responded saying such a story has never been 
recorded anywhere, Bhagavan shot back “It is indeed so.” 
(adu appadittan oi).

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 419

Paraphrase: 
Therefore men of discriminative perception totally 

relinquishing all attachments to the observances of Kriyai 
and Chariyai spoken of in the agamas, anchored in the 
blemishless and immaculate Ātman – the samadhi of 
Ātmayoga – and realizing by due enquiry that there is 
nothing greater that is worthy of attainment than this 
state, must destroy all vikalpas (thoughts of differences, 
doubt and uncertainty) and without the least recourse to 
them remain centred in the Self.
Commentary: 

Agamic scriptures – a component of Vedas - deal 
elaborately with kriya, chariya and parayoga with special 
emphasis on kriya and chariya. The methods of worship of 
the Lord, the procedural rules, rituals of worship, guidelines 
to be followed in the construction of holy temples that house 
the Lord, sculpting of the idols to be the worshipped as Gods, 
the structure and positioning of the yaga-kundas and all 
things related to temples are found in the agamas. All temples 
devoted to the worship of the Lord in immanent forms would 
have to adhere to some agamic rules.

The Lord instructs here that all that the agamas advocate 
is the form of action and are to be relinquished for they remain 
as obstacles to the practicer of the Ātmayoga. No action can 
be performed without the involvement of the mind. Since 
mind is the paramount block for yoga samadhi, mind and its 
action in the form of observance of agamic practices have 
together to be given up. It is totally paradoxical that a treatise 
on Agama contains such a directive, purely Advaitic in content. 
This is what prompted Bhagavan to select and include this 
work in his translation. “The non-performance of prescribed 
actions by a mature person pursuing Self-enquiry is no sin. 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   419 06-05-2011   10:53:57



420 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

For Self-enquiry is itself, the most meritorious of all actions.” 
(Ramana Gītā, Chap. 7, verse 19).

After studying the Vedas, the intelligent one who is 
solely intent on acquiring knowledge and Realisation, should 
discard the Vedas altogether, as the man who seeks to obtain 
rice discards the husk. A study of Vedas and the performance 
of the karma-kanda inculcated therein cannot bring on the 
utter annihilation of saṁsāra and the aim of the Vedas is the 
realization of the Self. A man of discrimination gives up the 
former as no more needful and exclusively devotes himself 
to the latter. “Of cows which are of diverse colours, the milk 
is of the same colour. The intelligent one regards jñāna as the 
milk and the many branched Vedas as cows”, Amritabindu 
Upanishad. This verity is also emphasized by the teacher of 
Gītā as follows: “As is the use of a pond in a place flooded 
with water everywhere, so is that of all the Vedas for the 
Brahmin who understands.” (Chapter II, Vese 46).  That is, 
all the benefit that accrues in the practice of the Karmakanda 
portion of the Vedas is included in the benefit accruing from 
Brahmajñāna.

When the impurity of anava (egoity) of the mind is 
rendered naught, one becoming the form of Immaculate 
Ātman, is ripe and competent enough to be established in 
yoga samadhi. A more exalted state than this is none. That, 
that condition is attained after due and deep enquiry is stated 
in the words idan melaha ayal ondrume indrena ornde. 

“That, after knowing which everything becomes known, 
That alone is Brahma Vidya which is worthy of being known 
by all the Vedas. That is the source of all Vidyas.”

In such a mind, no thought – by way of doubt, uncertainty 
indecision or difference (vikalpa) – must be permitted to 
arise lest thoughts should dislodge one from that exalted 
state where one is well anchored in. Instead of staying in and 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   420 06-05-2011   10:53:57



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 421

savouring the Bliss of the exalted state that one has attained, if 
thoughts as to the possibility of a higher state are entertained, 
the quiescence of samadhi will be disturbed. It is precisely 
to avoid the wavering of the mind that the Vedāntic śāstrās 
conclusively declare that there is nothing greater than this. 
Exterminate thoughts of distinction even before they approach 
the mind, is the upadeśa.

422 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Paraphrase: 
An Ānmayogī, constantly contemplating the Self 

and thus ever in Ātmaprajñā (Self-awareness) realizes 
his unembodied nature and ever remains merged in his 
natural state. Such a liberated sage of purity has the 
dharmas of that Form Beyond, as his own dharma. 
He shines, filling everywhere, within and without, and 
always moves as he pleases to all places (worlds) with 
no obstacle whatsoever.
Commentary: 

Vijñāna normally stands for Aparōksha jñāna – the 
non-mediated experience while jñāna for parōksha, the 
intellectual comprehension of the Ātman. While jñāna means 
knowledge, vijñāna is visishta jñāna or the great knowledge 
that is beyond both knowledge and ignorance. An ātmayogī 
who ceaselessly contemplates the form of jñāna, the Self, 
merges in the contemplated substance and becomes ‘That’ 
which is the natural state as well. By virtue of this abidance 
in the Self, the unembodied nature of the Ātman becomes his 
and his dehātma bhava, the feeling of Ātman in the body lost 
forever, he realizes himself as the dehi, the Self.

“When the purusha, effulgent like gold, shining as 
Brahman, the Source, creator and the Lord is seen by a vidwan 
capable of so seeing, he, shaking himself loose of all merits 
and demerits becomes blemishless and one with Supreme 
Brahman.” (Mundaka Upanishad, 3.1.3).

The Consciousness of the body lost forever, he immerses 
fully in his real form the Formless Self – which becomes his 
form. That true jñāni, gaining the unembodied nature becomes 
the ‘dharmi of all dharmas’ that is he becomes the dharmi 
with the dharmas of Sivasvarupa (the very form of Siva) as 
his dharma and shines everywhere, within and without.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   422 06-05-2011   10:53:57



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 423

He, at will, moves wherever he wants to and can also 
travel to any world as well.

Taittriya Upanishad says: “such a one taking the form he 
wills, he traverses the worlds.” (3.10.5).

One who is bound by attachment is not free. A mukta is a 
Realized one freed from all bondage of action. The exclusive 
privilege of experiencing freedom to the fullest extent of the 
word belongs to a mukta alone.

In Ramana Gītā Bhgavan says: “The Mahātma who 
abides in the Self and gets Release while yet alive, his life 
forces too get absorbed in the Self even here. The jīvanmukta 
may in time attain intangibility while the form remains. 
Disappearance of form (invisibility) ensues. Remaining as 
Pure Awareness alone, such a siddha disports himself as he 
likes. He can roam at will in all the worlds, assume as many 
bodies as he likes and even confer grace on others. (Chap. 
14, verses 8, 9, 10 and 15) and finally “the glory of siddhas 
is beyond imagination. They are equal to Siva. Indeed they 
are the very form of Siva. They have the power to grant every 
prayer.” (Chap. 18, Verse 26).

As Yoga Vasishtam says: “everything is indeed given to 
him who does not take anything whatever. Quite everything 
waits upon him who gives up everything. The absolutely full 
(or self-satisfied) state of the mind, free from thinking, which 
has obtained the desired object and is destitute of what is fit to 
be abandoned or acquired, is described by the word Samadhi.” 
(Verses 2081 and 2087).

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   424 06-05-2011   10:53:57



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 425

Chandogya Upanishad says: “That which is infinite 
alone is Bliss. There is no bliss in anything finite. The Infinite 
alone is Bliss”- “yo vai bhumo tat sukham nalpe sukham asti, 
bhumaiva sukham” The Bliss of the Self that is ānandaghana 
is the Bliss Absolute the rasa and It never diminishes. The 
bliss of a jñāni who abides as the Self, the Supreme glory 
and magnificence of Brahman transcending mind and senses 
and thereby the dualities including that of pain and pleasure, 
is indescribable, filled with torrents of the immortal nectar. 
Such a one manifests Supreme peace and joy in the absence 
of any object whatsoever which alone is the cause of pleasure 
and peace in ordinary mortals. 

The Self alone is the source of joy for such sages. Yoga 
Vasishtam speaks of them as follows: “Those persons with 
tranquil minds...have arrived at the utmost limit of enjoyment 
of pleasures.” (Verse 2094).

The Self is absolutely free, under the influence of none, 
with sovereignty vested in Itself. The mahayogī, who has 
flown out of delusion like a bird out of cage, is totally free 
remaining as the Self.

Further he dwells on the strength of the Ātman which 
is birthless and deathless. The order of creation is such that 
anything created is subject to growth, ageing and finally decay. 
None of the created can escape this law of nature. But the 
dharma of Sivahood that transcends creation will not be bound 
by this law. It’s dharma is described in detail in the Scriptures.

The Ātman, ever the same without the least difference, 
shines limitlessly with undiminishing lustre, and beyond 
circumscription, It possesses boundless and endless power. 
The Sivayogī who has gained Sivahood also becomes the 
possessor of all these qualities. Power becomes perfect 
and complete when knowledge becomes perfect. Hence 
omniscience – Sarvajnatva – is omnipotence both of which 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   425 06-05-2011   10:53:57



426 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

presuppose omnipresence. This is explained by the second 
line of the verse.

While the earlier verse declared that that sage as Sujñāni, 
addharuma dharumi who has attained Sivahood, will have the 
dharmas of Siva as his own dharma, this verse propounds the 
dharma of Siva and proves how they are also the dharma of 
the jñāni merged in Siva. 

He becomes the afflictionsless Self, attaining an 
immaculate body – attaining the form of space of Awareness 
– and remains merged with That. Such a jīvanmukta is one in 
whom act of Grace has been consummated and his body is 
simply the radiance of Eternity that he is. Such a one is wisdom 
personified as ‘Being’ whose body is knowledge.

As Yoga Vasishtam declares: “The lotus plant of wisdom 
that has seen the sun of Consciousness and is bearing the 
blossoms of virtue, blooms with a pure and superior lustre, 
beautiful like the sky at dawn.” (Verse 2250) and “Graces 
such as joy do not leave the face of such a one at any time. 
They neither blame nor rejoice at life as well as death”. 
(Yoga Vasishtam, Verse 2309). 

That Bhagavan lived as the repository of all qualities 
mentioned here is abundantly revealed from the reminiscences 
of devotees who were fortunate to behold him, to be in his 
presence and to be able to drink in the limitless nectar of his 
divine presence and power.

His presence was a ‘river of peace’, and spirituality 
‘radiated from every pore of his body’. Even to see him 
walking down the hill in the evening in the light of glinting 
sun rays on his body simply plunged or transported people to 
seventh heaven. He was a being so surcharged with Reality 
that coming into his presence was an entrance to altogether 
a different plane of existence and it effected a dynamic 
change. Some even experienced tangibly the radiance he was 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   426 06-05-2011   10:53:57



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 427

enveloped in. While some were receptive to his transmission 
of the experience of eternity by mere look, others, not ripe 
enough, shuddered. His body gave off a faint perfume and 
radiated tremendous peace.

“Mahātmas express in their faces whatever rasa (feeling) 
is appropriate to the occasion. But what can one say in the 
presence of the all-pervading vijñāna rasa which integrates 
all other rasas?” (Letters, 23-11-1945).

“To behold him appear on the hill and climb down is 
watching a glorious sunrise unfold, and as it approached 
became more and more radiant until the blazing sun itself 
was standing there” and this display of utter magnificence 
humbled everyone. (Roda MacIver – Moments Remembered).

Instances of his omnipresence, omniscience and 
omnipotence are legion yet he would divest them of the 
supernatural element and make them pass as natural 
coincidences. But these occurred too often to be dismissed 
so casually. 

Harindanath Chattopadhyaya wrote: 
“Eternity has worn a human face

in daylight; he shines in the Heart like the sun in the sky. He 
is a sage drunk with the joy of Consciousness.”

Paraphrase: 
Chanting the japa of holy names, worship of personal 

God in idols by offering of flowers to the chant of divine 
names, bathing in holy waters like Ganga that absolve 
one from sins and bestow merits, ritualistic observances 
like homa performed in fire – none of these or any other 
sādhanā – is necessary for an Ātmayogī.

Dharma or righteous conduct and adharma – non-
righteous conduct – and their fruits like merits and 
demerits are not for him. Offerings of libations of rice 
balls and ritualistic offering of water to manes and the 
performance of tarpana (with water and sesame seeds) 
for forefathers are not for him. Hear further from Me.
Commentary: 

Dharma Śāstrās give importance to namajapa, worship 
of Gods and performance of homas to lead a peaceful life. 
The same śāstrās that lay down the injunctions must also 
sanction their discontinuance as unnecessary, if the occasions 
demanded it.

The same Siva who commanded earlier the performance 
of the above actions declares them now as unnecessary just 
as a doctor, who prescribes diet restriction for a patient, lifts 
them after the cure is complete. Commandments of actions 
to be performed by various seekers have to be in accordance 
with their level of competence and degree of ripeness based 
on which injunctions given vary.

The novice or a starter in the spiritual path gains purity 
of mind by the performance of japa, worship, bathing in holy 
waters and ritualistic homas. As a result he attempts dhyāna 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   429 06-05-2011   10:53:57



430 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

with an inward-turned mind. Therefore these kriyas cannot 
be dismissed as fruitless as they prepare him for the inward 
journey. But their aim and purpose stop there and they cannot 
be considered as the be-all and end-all of human existence.

Kriyas which facilitate the attainment of the ‘Self’ by 
producing purity of mind, detachment and dispassion become 
redundant after the summum bonum of the spiritual experience 
of the Self. As Lord Krishna says fire which is kindled burns 
its fuel to ashes, even so does the fire of wisdom turn to ashes 
all work. All works have attained their consummation in the 
gain of wisdom. What more is there (for a realized soul) to 
be gained? (Guru Vāchaka Kovai, Verse 715).

“He is called a great renouncer by whom all righteous 
and unrighteous deeds (of the body), the thinking of 
the mind and desire,  are renounced internally.” 
(Yoga Vasishtam,  Verse 2079).

The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad says “Aham nama 
abhavat” (He became the ‘I’ named). That is the original 
name of Reality. Therefore “when all things perceived by the 
Self-oriented, thunder with the powerful voice of silence, in 
the egoless heart’s firmament the Lord’s own name of ‘I-I’” 
(Guru Vāchaka Kovai), where is the need of japa for them? 
They have become the form of jñāna which is but parabhakti 
that has consumed the ego. It is the feet of these holy sages 
that lend holiness and the cause for tirtas being tirtas by their 
contact. (Tīrtānām tīrtakāranam munihi Padotakena).

Regarding bathing in holy waters, Bhagavan says: “The 
Ganges is within you. This Ganges does not make you fell 
cold and shiver. Bathe in it.” (Talks no. 163) 

Regarding worship of forms, Bhagavan says: “Everyone 
sees only the Self. The divine forms are only like bubbles in 
the ocean of Reality or like pictures moving on a screen.” 
(Talks no. 163).

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   430 06-05-2011   10:53:57



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 431

Dana, dharma and nishkama karma are all tyaga only. 
When ‘mine’ is given up it is called chitta suddhi (purified mind). 
When ‘I’ is given up it is jñāna. When the nature to give away is 
developed it results in jñāna. (Talks no. 581). “Tyaga is giving up 
the possessions and the possessor too.” (Talks no. 163).

Then the question arises as to the observance of dharmas 
and rituals for manes. Dharma śāstrās very emphatically 
declare that they must be performed till one’s death. How 
then can they be given up?

The answer, by way of negative injunction, is very 
emphatic. None of these is prescribed and renunciation in 
toto is extolled as the greatest sādhanā here as uniformly 
emphasised by many Upanishads.

The mind’s hold and attachment to the earlier sādhanās 
like japa, worship and other rituals is so strong and deep that 
if such attachments are severed, the mind, starved of support, 
becomes worn out and finally extinct. Thus conquering all 
that, the mahayogī who shines as the austere king of Sivayoga, 
needs nothing and “the One established firmly in the natural 
state is incessantly performing the most difficult penance 
spontaneously.” (Ramana Gīta, Chap. II, Verse 18). Lord Siva 
proceeds (further) asking Kumara to listen to him.

Paraphrase: 
Know that none of the disciplines for Self-control 

like yama and niyama need be practiced by a mahayogī.

Commentary: 

This verse enumerates various sādhanās that are generally 
ranked high but which ātmayogīs are called upon to renounce. 
Niyamas or disciplines are absolutely essential for a mumukshu 
desirous of attaining his real form, the Self. They, functioning 
as fence, protect them from the onslaught of vishayas in their 
formative years and facilitate the growth of mental purity, 
essential to turn the mind inward.

Upavasam or fasts, vows like chandrayana purify the 
mind and heart. Upavasam means ‘living near’. Abiding (near 
or) in Brahman is true upavasa. The rest are all formal, none 
of which is necessary for him. Once a devotee asked Bhagavan 
about the significance of fasting. With a benevolent look 
towards him, Bhagavan said, “If all the activities of indriyas 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   432 06-05-2011   10:53:57



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 433

are given up, the mind becomes single pointed. When such 
a mind gets concentrated on God it is real upavasam. Upa 
means being near, vasam means living. Where is he going 
to live? He will live in his Self. Desires are the food for the 
mind. Giving them up is upavasam. If there are no desires 
whatsoever there is no such thing as mind. What remains 
then is the Self. One who can ‘fast’ the mind need not fast the 
body.” (Letters, page 677).

Hence Muruganar says:
“Absence of mental craving
For sense-enjoyments is true fasting
Abidance in the Self is worship true
Hence, those with pure, clear wisdom
Cherish as most precious
This fasting and this worship.”

(Guru Vāchaka Kovai, Verse 678)
There is no endeavour to engage in activities for he is 

a krita krityan one who has accomplished all that has to be 
done. Bhagavan affirms it. “Since such a one has no sense 
of doership, his karma, it is said, is completely destroyed. 
As nothing but the Self exists, no doubts arise for him. 
Once the knot is cut, one is never bound again. This is 
considered the state of Power Supreme and Peace Supreme.” 
(Ramana Gīta, Chap. IX, Verse 21 and 22).

Sankara emphatically declares in his Commentary on 
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad: “Even as there is no endeavour 
to indulge in activity, there is no need either to withdraw from 
any. Nivritti (withdrawal) is required for one who has pravritti. 
Hence there is nothing for him to abstain from.”

Along with niyama, upavasa, pravritti or nivritti, even the 
vow of holy celibacy, celebrated as the life-line of a seeker of 
the Self is discarded. Bhagavan explains it: “Realization itself

is naishtika brahmacharya (unflagging celibacy). The vow is

it is not a forcible attempt at it”. (Talks no. 491) and again: 
“Self Realization is designated by so many different names, 
Satya, brahmacharya, etc.” (Talks no. 491).

That yogī constantly moves in Brahman (Bramachari) 
and hence a mundane vow of celibacy is redundant to him.

Adornment with sandal paste and holy ash 
Their pujas with such components are sheer futility 

(General Verse 44)

Paraphrase: 
Discard leaping into fire or waters of a Holy River 

like Ganges or jumping from atop a hill to end life, all 
of which serve no fruitful purpose. Instead drink deep 
and experience the nectar of Siva jñāna and remain as 
the very form of Siva, Eternal and Immaculate, freed of
