Commentary: 

The only known way of escape from unbearable mental 
anguish for man is to discard the body. Man, unaware of 
a way to discard the mind attempts to give up the body 
instead. “Leaping into fire” has reference to the way some 
austere tapasvins end their life frustrated and distraught with 
unfulfilled desires for which such intense tapas was carried 
on by them. Performance of penance, standing in the midst 
of five fires (four around and the sun or another fire above) 
is a way of tapas, practiced to attain a desired end. One who 
performs such an arduous penance, in the event of failure 
to obtain the desired end, and unable to pursue the penance 
further leaps into the very same fire tended so far by him and 
drops the body. Ending one’s life in such a terrible way is 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   435 06-05-2011   10:53:58



436 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

often termed as ‘fierce’ or as asuric or demoniacal austerity. 
The Lord commands here to give up such practices.

Gītā also states “That penance which is performed with 
a foolish obstinacy by means of self-torture or for causing 
injury to others is said to be tamasic.” (Chap. XVII,Verse 18).

The performance of certain karmas to obtain desired 
results is specially advocated in some Sthala Purāṇas (history 
of holy places) in those auspicious kshetras (places).

“Jumping into water to end life” has reference to the belief 
and practice associated with Prayag (near Allahabad) called 
“The King among Tirthas”. Though river Ganga is held holy 
throughout its course its greatness is extolled specially in three 
places namely Gangotri in the Himalayas, where it originates, 
Prayag in the middle of its course and Ganga Sagar where 
it merges with the sea. Even among all these three Prayag is 
given the pride of pre-eminence.

Prayag is called Triveni where the three rivers, Ganga, 
Yamuna and mythical Saraswathy unite. The common belief 
is that who ever drops his body here with a sankalpa (desire 
or determination) to attain something, will have the desire 
fulfilled without fail. Even this, the Lord commands, is to be 
eschewed.

Hermits performing penance in the caves of mountains 
sometimes jump from those very hill tops and end their lives up 
unable to bear the frustration of failure and pangs of thwarted 
desire to achieve the desired object or end.

These are the ways of the ends of the desire-oriented 
seekers. Desireless austerity and gain of the Self have nothing 
to do with these. Bhagavan clarifies the phenomenon of suicide 
thus: “Suicide must be committed on the mind, where the 
suffering is deposited, and not on the body, which is insentient 
and feels nothing. The mind is the real culprit being, the 
creator of the anguish which tempts to suicide but by an error 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   436 06-05-2011   10:53:58



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 437

of judgement, the innocent insentient body is punished for it.” 
(Guru Ramana, page 43) and  suicide is committed to end 
“association with the body which represents all unhappiness. 
For there must be a killer to kill the body. He is the survivor 
after suicide. That is the Self. (Talks, no. 340). The story of 
Chudala and Sikhidhvaya in Yoga Vasishtam is a proof  of the 
content of this verse. The royal couple, becoming dispassionate 
decided to seek the Truth and performed sādhana. The queen, 
being more dispassionate, gained jñāna (earlier) the glow of 
which was seen all over her. The king, surprised, questioned 
her on the cause of glow in her face and was told that it was 
the glow of the Self that she had realized. But he disbelieved 
it. Then, much against her advice, he proceeded to the forest 
to perform tapas. After sometime, Chudala, taking the form of 
a Brahmin sage, Kumbha, appeared before him, was accepted 
as the guru and as per instructions received, he carried on 
his tapas, but not being able to renounce the ego he could 
not attain jñāna. Frustrated, when he was about to end his 
life by jumping from atop a mountain, Chudala, in the form 
of guru, appeared and instructed him that, “though he had 
renounced everything, his renunciation was not complete for 
he had not renounced his ego.” Then, by doing so, he attained 
realization. Bhagavan, while referring tot he story said, “The 
king had vairagya even while ruling his kingdom and could 
have realized the Self, if only he had pushed his vairagya to 
the point of killing the ego. He did not do it but came to the 
forest, had a time-table of tapas and yet did not improve even 
after 18 years of tapas... On Chudala’s advice to give up the 
ego he did and realized the Self.” (Talks, no. 404). Vairagya 
accompanied by ego is of no value whereas all possessions 
(including the body) in the absence of ego do not matter.

A true yogī seeking union with Self is undaunted by 
anything and by sheer perseverance attains It and enjoys the 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   437 06-05-2011   10:53:58



438 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

elixir of union with Siva. Such a one, who is Self-possessed, 
goes beyond everything and is free from seeking and satisfied 
only in the Self, neither acts nor desires.

“Complete renunciation, O virtuous King cannot 
happen by giving up the body, by renouncing the 
kingdom and by emaciation in hermitages and the like.” 
(Yoga Vasishtam, Verse 2070) and “The mind is the origin of 
quite everything. When the origin of everything is renounced, 
everything is surely given up.” (Ibid, Verse 2071).

instructed you here that is worthy of being known there

Commentary: 

The very word of God is indeed the Truth since God is 
Truth personified and needs no other truth to commend it as 
Satya-Truth. None can estimate the glory and greatness of 
this treatise on upadeśa, when the Lord Himself declares that 
there is nothing more exalted than this Truth and He affirms 
this fact not once but thrice over. This is proof enough of the 
sublimity and the most exalted nature of this discourse.

The countless texts that purport to teach Ātmabodha have 
branched off into various varieties functioning in different 
ways. Amongst all those ways of teaching that, this text 
instructing Ātma Sākṣātkāra (Being the Self), has Truth as 
its content is vouchsafed by the Lord Himself. Can there be a 
greater authority than this? Hence no doubt need be entertained 
in this. The affirmation rendered thrice is to strengthen the 
awakening in the jīva who is enveloped by the three-fold 
impurities of anava mala, māyāmala and karmamala.

Varahopanishad has a similar proclamation: “Realizing 
that Truth, namely, that condensed essence of consciousness 
that is Ānanda, non-dual and attributeless is one’s own form 
of Self and afraid of nothing, the state of Brahmavids is that 
everything is nothing but pure Awareness, Eternal Whole, 
Imperishable and Ānanda, namely Brahman and this is The 
Truth, The Truth, The Truth. ‘I am’ is the Truth, the Para-
Brahman. Nothing apart from ‘Me’ is.”

Chatusloki Bhāgavatham  in Bhāgavatham affirms this 
truth: “The Supreme Spirit is that ultimate substance. This 
universe which seems to have a separate existence is also 
Myself (the Brahman) deriving its substantiality from Me 
alone.” (2-9-32 and 35).

indiscrimination and himself being the immaculate Self

Commentary: 

One who is pure with discrimination is intelligent and

“He has come out of the association with the world. 
He is the one with the mental fever of pride cured. He 
has his delight in the Supreme Spirit. He is remaining 
quietly and is fulfilled. He is one possessed of pure mind.” 
(Yoga Vasishtam, Verse 2343).

That Sivayogī of clear intellect, rid of indiscrimination 
and of a pure heart, rid of taints, comes to possess a clear 
perception by which he perceives everything as the form 
of Siva. The effulgence of the sun is not other than the Sun. 
Likewise the seemingly real world that appears is nothing but 
the form of Paramātma. Just as mind, vital air and senses abide 
action-less in sushupti, after the gain of this perception the 
delusion of division like objects, action and awareness abides 
in the pure Awarenes. Contemplating Siva with this perception 
of purity he realizes Siva. The very usage of words amalam 
bhavittu (contemplating the blemishless purity) implies 
that the content is void of bhava. No stance or attitude can 
contemplate amala or purity. When bhavanas that are within 
the realm of mind become extinct, experience shines at once.

Remaining blemishless is to contemplate with the 
stance of purity. Similarly in the usage nirmala ānma (The 
immaculate Ātman), nirmala (pure) and Ānma are not two. 
Blemishless purity itself is Ātman. Yoga Vasishtam speaks 
of the same: “Rama! That body (or nature) of the Almighty 
God Pārameswari tanuhu (the body of the Absolute) which is

442 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

supreme Bliss, situated within all living beings, which arises 
at the end of all bhavas and on the dissolution of the mind and 
the ego, which is spontaneously accomplished through yoga 
and which is existing not far from (the state of) one asleep, 
is not accessible to words. It is experienced here only in the 
heart (or inmost being).” (Yoga Vasishtam, Verses 2261-2262).

When Bhagavan once explained to a lady “Drishtim 
jñānamayim kritwa” as changing the “vision as the all-
pervading Brahman” fully satisfied, the lady came out and 
sat on the veranda opposite to Bhagavan’s couch. Bhagavan 
was as usual silent and with a smile on his face. Looking 
at the radiant face of Bhagavan, she said involuntarily “ah! 
How beautiful Bhagavan is”. A devotee who heard the 
exclamation reported it to Bhagavan. With a slight nod of his 
head Bhagavan said: “Sivam Sundaram”.

Suri Nagamma records “How pregnant with meaning that 
expression is”. (Letters, 20th Sep. 1946).

To such a jñāni, the world and everything he perceives 
becomes the Satyasya Satyam for the ‘Special Essence’ (that 
he is) sees only that everywhere. It is that “Special Essence” 
that gives substantiality to the universe. What Lord Krishna 
says in Uddhava Gītā is worth recalling here. “Whatever is 
grasped by the mind words eyes and other sense organs all 
that is Myself (Self). Know that there is nothing different from 
Me.” (Srimad Bhāgavatam, 11-13-24).

In the ultimate sense “all this is Brahman.” Let us 
conclude with this verse from Amritabindhu Upanishad, “In 
whom resides all beings and who resides in all beings by virtue 
of His being the giver of grace to all-I am that Soul of the 
Universe, the Supreme Being, I am that Soul of the Universe, 
the Supreme Being.” (Verse 22).

Śrī Bhagavad Gītā Sāram

(THE QUINTESSENCE OF 
BHAGAVAD GĪTĀ)

Origin
Bhagavad Gītā – a book of life – is for the blossoming 

of the spiritual stature of man to its fullness. It is the most 
widely translated religious and philosophical text, next to 
the Bible. All savants and scholars, both in the orient and in 
the Occident have recognized its repute and universal appeal 
and have accorded it a pre-eminent position in the spiritual 
literature of the world. There is no scholar who has not 
showered encomiums on the Gītā, and no teacher of religion 
who has not proffered commentaries on it. All propagandists 
of religions consider it their prime duty to spread the message 
of Gītā offering their interpretations on it. It’s message 
is of imperishable significance and called “The Perennial 
Philosophy”.

Bhagavad Gītā consists of 700 verses divided into 
eighteen chapters. The Gītā, one of the corner stones of 
Hindu religion and philosophy, and the other two, namely, 
Upanishads and Brahma Sūtras are called the “prastana 
traya”, the three, providing efficacious ways to attain Brahma 
Sakshatkara – the realization of Brahman. It is both a Brahma 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   444 06-05-2011   10:53:58



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 445

Vidya and a Yoga Śāstra – the science of Reality and the art 
of union with that Reality.

Sankara, in his introduction to the commentary on Gītā, 
says: “The Gītā is an epitome of the whole Vedic teaching. 
It’s  aim chiefly is Supreme Bliss. A knowledge of its teaching 
leads to the realization of all human aspirations.”

Gītā contains the essence of Vedas and of Truth and is the 
cream of all scriptures. It is butter churned from these – the 
Butter of Bliss.

The popular hymn on the glory of Gītā says: “the 
Upanishads are the cows and the cowherd’s son Krishna 
is the one who milks. Arjuna is the calf and the wise man 
is the drinker of the nectarine milk.” It further hails it as 
Advaitāmruta varshinīm, that which showers the nectar of 
Advaita. It shows the way to salvation for those who wander 
in the region of variety and transience.

Some ardent devotees feeling the paucity of time found 
this text of 700 verses too long to be recited daily. Hence 
Gurram Subhramaiah beseeched Bhagavan to bestow on 
the devotees a short and summarized version containing the 
important verses, suitable for daily pārāyaṇa. Bhagavan, 
compassion incarnate, acquiesced in and gathered 42 verses 
of pearls, and strung them together; “Bhagavad Gītā Sāram” 
– a rare creation.

He further translated them into 42 Tamil verses in veṇbā 
metre and thus blessed the land of Tamil. The core teaching 
of Gītā shines forth clear and lucid in Bhagavan’s translation 
leaving no room for doubt. Anyone can comprehend it 
without a recourse to reference in extenso. The style adopted 
by Bhagavan is highly chaste and majestic as usual but the 
content is crystal clear as the water of the pellucid stream. The 
richness and cogency of ideas, and the order in which they are 
set, enrich this wealth and strike awe and wonder in the devout.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   445 06-05-2011   10:53:58



446 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

The compact size of the text is in contrast to the content 
that is at once profound and deep. This text by Bhagavan is 
both a blessing and a gift conferred on the world of seekers.

Like that of Lord Krishna, Bhagavan’ life is the best 
commentary on the Gītā. Concepts like stita prajñā, 
uninvolved Witness, vairagya, sannyāsa, detachment and true 
karma, stand authenticated as Reality in Bhagavan.

Bhagavan who quoted with ease extensively from various 
spiritual texts, quoted the most from Gītā and often explained 
and revealed the concealed content of the verses of Gītā that 
were rich with hidden layers of import.

Interestingly Bhagavan has never formally read the Gītā. 
“I have not read Gītā nor waded through commentaries for its 
meaning. When I hear a śloka I think that its meaning is clear 
and I say it. That is all.... They come out naturally. I realise 
that the Truth is beyond speech and intellect.... Their (reading, 
understanding and repeating) purpose is to know the Truth. 
The purpose having been gained, there is no use engaging 
in studies.” (Talks no. 418). One is apt to conclude that the 
Lord, who seated in the chariot of Arjuna and sang the “Song 
Celestial” in the days of Mahābhārata is none other than Sri 
Bhagavan. What Lord Krishna says in a later chapter “ Indeed 
I myself am the jñāni” is proved  now for the subtle facts of 
knowledge  that no commentator except Lord Krishna knew, 
poured out of Bhagavan inspiring forth and bearing testimony 
to the authority of the One Self. “Is the one who seated within 
as Ātman and speaks the same today any other than Lord 
Krishna?” asks Bhagavan.

Incidentally B.V. Narasimhaswamy, in his Self-Realization, 
declares that all the sixteen qualities of Rama (an avatar of 
Vishnu), fit Bhagavan pre-eminently.

Hence Viswanatha Swami says: 
“Glory be! Of that ancient Gītā

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 447

  Sung by the Lord Himself as Sri Krishna
  Is now given the quintessence
  Drawn by Him as Sri Ramana.”

sanskrit text...................

Just as our prostrations are due not only to the Lord who 
spoke the Eternal Truth but also to Arjuna who inspired him 
to dwell on this, our prostrations are due to Bhagavan and the 
devotees who were instrumental in bringing forth this rare 
text, Gītā Sāram, for the devotees.

By the addition of a single world, or by simply altering 
another, Bhagavan has enriched and (or) elaborated the 
content. While the Gītā is in the form of couplet, Bhagavan 
chose the veṇbā metre of four lines, so that what was said in 
brief is expanded and explained with no room for doubt or 
distortion.

Paraphrase: 
May Lord Krishna, the personification of grace, the 

teacher of Gītā, who, seated in Arjuna’s chariot as the

Commentary: 

Arjuna, the Pandava warrior, who in eager anticipation 
of the war was raring to fight till he came to the field, shrank 
from it on seeing the armies converged in the battle arena to 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   448 06-05-2011   10:53:58



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 449

fight in this fratricidal war. He, with mind clouded, became 
confused and his spirits drooped.

Lord Krishna, the teacher of Gītā, who by his upadēsa 
and words of grace dispelled the distress and despondency 
of Arjuna, encouraging him to stand by his swadharma (the 
dharma or duty of a varṇa and ashrama that one belongs 
to) and showed him the way to salvation, is invoked for the 
protection of all.

When, to whom, how and in which guise, the Lord will 
choose to bestow grace and instruct is something none can 
know or predict. Besides guiding Arjuna in the battlefield as 
his charioteer in the right path, the Lord, by instructing him on 
the righteous path in life prevented him from swerving from 
the path of dharma, even at the hour of worst mental crisis in 
his life, thereby enabling him to gain fame in the worlds here 
and hereafter. Nalvārttai (auspicious words of grace) refers 
to the profound and the uncommon words of wisdom and the 
instruction on the eternal dharma.

The removal of Arjuna’s afflictions by Krishna was not 
temporary but everlasting. The bane of saṁsāra, the very form 
of mamakara (mine), is the cause of all misery. The teaching of 
the Gītā by Lord Krishna, the embodiment of Compassion is 
precisely for the removal of the pain and struggle of saṁsāra.

The very thought of mahātmās ever with the purpose 
of uplifting the souls immersed in the grievous ocean of 
saṁsāra and leading them ashore is called krupa or unsolicited 
Compassion.

May Lord Krishna, full of such compassion, graciously 
protect us is the content of this invocation.

One becomes a fit receptacle of Lord’s Grace when one 
approaches the Lord in a spirit of total submission. The Guru 
with Compassion and full of concern takes him under his 
wings and protects. It is assured that if we too approach the 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   449 06-05-2011   10:53:58



450 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Lord the way Arjuna did, we will also drink the nectar that 
is Gītā.

In the entire Hindu and Buddhist spiritual literatures, 
the chariot stands for psycho-physical vehicle, the steeds are 
the senses, the reins are their controls but the charioteer or 
the guide is the Self or Ātman. Krishna, the charioteer is the 
spirit within us.

This invocatory verse originally written in Tamil by 
Bhagavan was later rendered into Sanskrit by Bhagavan 
Himself which runs as follows:

Pārthasārathi rūpeṇa śrāvayitvā śubhāṁ giram
Pārthasyārtiharo devaḥ kṛpāmūrtiḥ sapātunaḥ
Bhagavan once explained how this invocatory verse 

came to be written by him. One Mr. Krishnaswamy Iyer, 
wrote a commentary on Bhagavad Gītā, attached a picture of 
Lord Krishna on the first page of the manuscript and pressed 
Bhagavan to write something underneath. Then Bhagavan 
wrote this verse in Tamil and subsequently changed it into a 
śloka in Sanskrit.  It is found in Bhagavad Gītā Ratnamalika. 
Once Muruganar wrote two verses in praise of Vishnu, one 
pertaining to the body (kāyikaṁ), another pertaining to the 
word of mouth (vāchikaṁ) and insisted on Bhagavan writing 
the third one (mānasikaṁ) pertaining to the mind. The verse 
runs thus: “O! Swami, to relieve the burden of the earth, you 
took the avatar of Krishna and by your teaching through the 
Gītā, like ‘Whenever there is a decline of righteousness’, for 
the protection of the virtuous, you assured us that you would 
have several incarnations. To praise such a Lord and his 
various forms, Who am I?” This verse, incorporating verses 
from Gītā itself (Chap. IV, 7 and 8), ends very significantly 
with the poser “Who am I?”

Bhagavan later said, “These words of praise or ‘Who am 
I?’ have several meanings and could be interpreted in different 
ways by different people.” (Letters, 27-7-1948).

Paraphrase: 
With a heart overflowing with compassion (towards 

kinsmen, friends, preceptors and revered elders – turned 
foes and arrayed in the battlefield against him) and 
uncontainable grief, as Arjuna sat despondent with sorrow 
and with eyes welling up with tears, Krishna, the slayer 
of Madhu, sizing up the situation and bestowing a look

Arjuna’s grief may be dispelled!

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   451 06-05-2011   10:53:58



452 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Commentary: 
The great warrior Arjuna, who was raring to rush into 

battle without delay no sooner he reached the battlefield than 
he requested Lord Krishna to draw his chariot between the 
two armies arrayed and ready to fight. As Krishna did so, 
Arjuna beheld kinsmen, revered grandsires, and worshipful 
preceptors, dear uncles, loving sons, fathers-in law, cousins, 
companions and comrades in both the armies, ready to give 
up their lives and became aggrieved. Perplexed with a reeling 
mind and overcome with compassion he became dejected 
and was in total despair unable to move. Considering the 
implications of the forthcoming fratricidal war, its outcome, 
good and bad and overcome with inconsolable grief he stood 
transfixed with mind unsettled and immobilised and tears 
welled up in his eyes.

Waging war was not new to him. Countless were the 
battles he had fought and laurels won. His mighty arms had 
helped even the devas to win. Nay, he had fought against the 
very Parameshwara, though as a hunter in disguise. But then 
his heart had not been moved to pity or compassion when he 
slaughtered soldiers and kings in the arenas of battle. Why? 
Those slaughtered were enemies totally unrelated to him. But 
now, what he is about to engage himself in, is the decimation 
of his own kinsmen who stand arrayed and eager to fight as 
enemies ready to forsake their lives and riches. They are all 
bound to him by the bond of (blood) relationship.

Our of fear of slaying them in the battle, he refused to 
fight even it be for the gain of the three worlds, or at the cost 
of adherence to one’s own dharma and preferred the life of a 
beggar begging for food , than to have the blood of preceptors 
and cousins on his hand.

This compassion of Arjuna is not something that is natural 
to him. The true cause of refusal to fight in the war lies in the 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   452 06-05-2011   10:53:59



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 453

idea of ‘mine’. While true compassion has no room for selfish 
interests, his compassion was born of recoiling of his mind 
from an act aimed to hurt and an apprehension of death of 
his own people – objects of love and veneration. A true man 
grieves neither for the living nor for the dead.

The characteristic of true compassion is to relieve the grief 
of others. It has no mamakara in it. What Arjuna experiences 
is a seeming compassion, that springs from the bewilderment 
of the idea of mine concealed in it, in the absence of which 
there would have been no grief. What Krishna has for Arjuna 
is indeed true Compassion.

The first act of Lord Krishna to wipe out the grief of 
Arjuna who stood with tears of sorrow and mind rent with 
grief and dejection, is to bestow his look of grace on them. 
This  alleviation of grief by a mere look of grace is released 
by the sentence “looking at aggrieved Partha, that his grief 
be dispelled.”

This bestowal of look of grace always precedes bestowal 
of upadēsa. “Pārttu Madhusūdanan ivvārthai uraittān” 
(looking...... the slayer of Madhu spoke these words) reveals 
this truth.

Absorption of the upadēsa that is to follow is possible 
only if mental grief and intellectual cogitation are controlled 
to a certain extent. His look of grace is potent enough to effect 
such a feat which is explained by the phrase tuyar ahalap 
pārttu (looking so that his grief may be dispelled)

The Lord summarising the essence of all Upanishads and 
instructing it variously under different topics to suit the needs 
of the seekers of varying degrees of competence and bestowing 
it as upadēsa is meant by ivvārthai uraittān vahuttu uṇara.

Lord Krishna is celebrated as the slayer of Madhu and 
Kaitabha, the two demons. While Madhu is the personification 
of intoxication, Kaitabha is the demon of delusion. The hint is 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   453 06-05-2011   10:53:59



454 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

that the Lord who slew Madhu is disposed to remove Arjuna’s 
intoxication of egoistic attachment to his kinsmen and teachers 
born of a sense of ‘mine’.

Grief overpowers the discriminative faculty and sorrow 
and delusion constitute the cause of the transmigratory cycle. 
Self-Knowledge alone can destroy them.

Arjuna is a true representative of an average good man. 
Though he has known all along that the kauravas were his 
cousins, and was keen on facing them in a war, yet he abstains 
from the war in the last minute for he is yet to realize that 
wives preceptors and kinsmen are all dear not for their sake 
but for the sake of the Self.  All spiritual enquiry starts with 
such a churning of the heart.

The usage of the word pārthu (looking) in the Tamil 
rendering by Bhagavan is very beautiful and pregnant with 
significance (this word is not in the original)

Look of grace followed by upadēsa is to be known as 
sublime teaching. Bhagavan’s upadēsa goes even a step 
higher. He by a mere look of his, made the devotees, who came 
seeking him, ripe. None could escape that look of grace. Then, 
if need be, his words of grace would follow as instructions. 
This is the direct experience of all in his powerful presence.

Swami Madhavatirtha records “I found in the look of the 
sage the dazzling brilliance of the Sun. It seemed to pierce me 
to the core of my being, even as the light of the Lord passed 
into Devaki through the look of Vasudeva.... my mind was 
elevated into some spiritual realm of unutterable peace and 
happiness... It was natural for the individual self to subside 
in his presence.” (Power of the presence, Part I)

Chagganlal Yogi recounts: “It seemed the light of his 
eyes was suffusing my consciousness. Even without my 
being aware of it, his silent gaze brought about a subtle but 
definite transformation in me.” – Ibid. Lakshmana Swamy 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   454 06-05-2011   10:53:59



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 455

recounts “when I looked, the Maharshi looked intently at me 
for sometime; something like a lightning flash resulted in a 
flood of divine light shining both within and without.... The 
Self absorbed my whole being.”  Walter A. Keers says “He was 
a bomb that exploded the myth of my life. His look blasted 
away years of accumulated wrong ideas.”

Once Viswanatha Swamy, sitting in front of Bhagavan, 
in an attempt to write a verse on Muruganar, could not 
proceed beyond the first word ahatthāmarai.  Bhagavan 
finding him struggling, wrote the verse himself but signed it 
as ‘Viswanathan’. This verse, written by Bhagavan himself is 
the greatest testimony for the miracle his gaze did.

The meaning of this verse is as follows:
“Arunachala Ramana, dwelling in the heart-lotus smiled 

and steadily looked at me and slew my little separate self. 
So Singing so of this flow of grace, Muhavapuri Murugan 
composed his Sannidhi Murai equalling Thiruvachakam itself 
so that people of the world may be saved.”

Kitty Osborne narrates an incident that goes to prove 
beyond doubt that how a mere look of Bhagavan dispelled 
completely the utter grief of a lady. When Kitty was 10 
years old she was assigned the job of taking a lady guest 
to the presence of Bhagavan. That lady was tense, nervous 
and unhappy. The man whom she loved most dearly and 
married against the wishes of her parents was soon killed by 
a shark right in front of her eyes. The distraught widow was 
travelling to various ashrams asking why God had been so 
unjust to her. She was unhappy and aggressively angry. But 
after an hour in the presence of Bhagavan Kitty records “I 
will never never forget the change that had come over her 
in just an hour. She was calm, relaxed, peaceful and happy. I 
was so awed and intrigued.” When her mother asked her (the 
lady) about the change and she answered that when she sat 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   455 06-05-2011   10:53:59



456 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

down “Bhagavan had looked at her – just looked with such 
infinite Compassion that she felt that her questions were just 
not important any more. She sat there, felt at peace and not 
a word had been spoken. Bhagavan is Supreme indeed!” 
(Moments remembered, V. Ganesan – pages 11 and 12).

Once when Nayana, intrigued at Bhagavan’s speaking of 
Self-enquiry to one who apparently could not comprehend the 
meaning, asked Bhagavan how it could help him, Bhagavan 
replied in all innocence that he could teach only what he knew. 
Muruganar who was present there quickly interjected, “It 
depends on whom the upadēsa comes from and added further 
“does not the look of grace accompany the upadēsa. Today 
we are a witness to the upadēsa and the accompanying grace 
but we may not live to see its effect on him.”

Oh! Partha! Know that the body, the place for the 

experience of enjoyment is called kshetram or the field. 
One, who dwelling in the body, is aware of the body as

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   457 06-05-2011   10:53:59



458 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Commentary: 
Kshetram literally means ‘arable field’. Yajña kshetra 

is the place where yajñas are performed. Just as seeds are 
sown and crops of paddy are obtained again and again in 
the fields, this body is the field of actions where good and 
bad acts are performed which are the seeds for the crops 
of further embodiments. It is also an abode of enjoyment 
where the fruits of actions performed in countless births are 
(reaped) experienced as pleasure and pain. Finally this kshetra 
disintegrates and perishes (and goes back to earth).

The constituents of the field of kshetra are the five 
elements, the ego-sense, the intellect, the organs of action and 
the instruments of perception and the mind (the distinction 
between gross or subtle or physical and mental is within 
the kshetra itself). One who knows the body – from foot to 
crown-the kshetra or field as an object of knowledge is called 
kshetrajña by sages who abide as the Self. One identifying 
oneself with this insentient body or matter says ‘I’, giving 
high value to the embodiment of Consciousness and not 
to the Consciousness per se, the kshetrajña. This want of 
discrimination between the two leads to transmigration. 
Mistaking the kshetra for kshetrajña is called nescience or 
primal ignorance. The evils of delusion arise from ‘mine’, an 
effect of this  nescience.

Grief can be overcome only by the removal of this 
ignorance. Dawn of jñāna or Self-knowledge alone can 
dispel the darkness of ignorance. Thus all these factors are 
inter-linked.

Hence the Lord starts by teaching the eternal wisdom 
or knowledge of the Self to annihilate the primal cause of 
delusion and grief.

As everything outside of the Self – one’s Being – 
including the object that the body is – is transient and subject 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   458 06-05-2011   10:53:59



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 459

to change, the search for the Truth that abides within the body 
as kshetrajña – the Self – involves the renunciation of all that 
is non-self and is outside including the body.

But the jīva intertwining the body (matter) and the Ātman 
(the spirit within) together and binding them both deludes 
himself. While the body is the field of unconscious activity, the 
knower of the field (kshetrajña) is Consciousness, uninvolved. 
He is the silent and eternal witness that does not need the use of 
either the senses or the mind for its witnessing. The kshetrajña 
cannot be recognized as an object among other objects as a 
substance but can only be recognized as a subject. Hence the 
Lord, separating the insentient body and the inadvertence of 
the ego that regards the body as ‘I’ instructs that this body is 
not I and the Ātman is the real ‘I’ and in order that the jīvas 
may overcome their primal ignorance by becoming aware of 
this truth, even while in the body, proves it as the experienced 
awareness of the sages.

Jñānis who are experts in the science of Self-Knowledge 
distinguish between kshetra and kshetrajña and become 
aware of it as their direct experience and speak on the basis 
of that experience as proof. Bhagavan while describing 
his death experience says, “But with this death of the 
body am ‘I’ dead? Is the body ‘I’? This body is silent and 
inert. But I feel the full force of my personality and even 
the sound ‘I’ within myself – apart from the body. The 
material body dies, but the spirit transcending it cannot be 
touched by Death. I am, therefore, the deathless spirit.” 
(B.V.Narasimha Swamy, Self Realization, page 17). And again 
“In the vision of death, though all the senses were benumbed, 
the aham sphurana (Self-Awareness) was clearly evident and 
so I realised that it is that awareness that we call ‘I’ and not 
the body. The Self awareness never decays. It is unrelated to 
anything. It is Self-luminous. Even if this body is burnt it will 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   459 06-05-2011   10:53:59



460 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

not be affected. Hence I realised on that very day that ‘That’ 
was ‘I’.” (Letters, 22.11.45).

Traditionally the eighteen chapters of the Gītā are divided 
into three parts, the first six dealing with TVAM (Thou) 
and the next six with TAT (That) and the final six with TAT 
TVAM ASI   ( That Thou Art). That Bhagavan has chosen as 
the first verse of Gītā Sara, a verse from the last section of 
union of Ātman and Brahman is highly significant. This verse 
contains the eternal message of wisdom “Know Thyself”. The 
discrimination between the body and the knower of the body 
leading to the query of who am I is central to the core teaching 
of Bhagavan and essential for the knowledge of the Self.

Lord Krishna imparts the same instruction to Uddhava 
at the very outset in Bhāgavatam also. “Just as fire, because 
it has burning and lighting property, is different from the fuel 
it burns and illumines, so also the Ātman, the Self-luminous 
seer, is different from all objects seen including the gross and 
subtle bodies forming its instruments of perception. (11.10.8)

The jīva’s involvement in saṁsāra consisting of recurrent 
births and deaths arises from his identifications with the subtle 
and gross bodies. Knowledge of the Self will put an end to 
his entanglement in saṁsāra.

An interesting incident reveals how Bhagavan always 
lived as the kshetrajña. Once an American photographer who 
had come to the ashram took a photo of Bhagavan feeding 
the elephant from the temple. He sent the photo later with 
something written at the back. Bhagavan read it aloud: “A 
big Self which does not know the body and a big body which 
does not know the Self at one place.”. Someone remarked 
“Bhagavan always appears unconcerned about the body”. 
Bhagavan said, “That is it” and added Chintadhikshitulu said, 
“He is like a statue in a museum”. When somebody asked if 
Jada Bharata also got the name because he was the big Self 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   460 06-05-2011   10:53:59



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 461

who did not know the body Bhagavan replied “It means he 
was the personification of the Self who did not care for his 
body.” (Letters, 16th Jan. 1949).

Bhagavan once referred to the body as the “rented house.” 
(Letters,  18.2.49).

Paraphrase: 

Arjuna! Know Me as the kshetrajña or Ātman abiding 
within and together with all gross bodies called kshetras. 
That knowledge which can be known by enquiring into

Commentary: 

Right from Brahma down to the tiniest worm or insect, I 
am the indweller of all the bodies. Know ‘Me’ as the kshetrajña 
abiding, associated with these bodies. That knowledge that 
knows the truth of kshetra and kshetrajña as it is, by deeply 
enquiring into their truth is Ātmajñāna and that indeed is 
acceptable to Me.

Kshetra is the dwelling place of the Ātman. In the same 
manner, places dwelt in by Gods, the saguna form of Brahman 
are called kshetras and God is spoken of as the Lord of the 
kshetra. The body – the kshetra, is often called the city of 
nine gates and because it is dwelt in by Brahman, it is called 
Brahmapuri. The body is the temple and the indweller is God.

Kshetrajña, the one who dwells in the house is the 
possessor of the house or kshetra. Possession can never 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   462 06-05-2011   10:53:59



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 463

become the possessor. House cannot be the owner of the house. 
None thinks of the house one dwells in as oneself. Kshetrajña 
is different from kshetra in the same way fire in fuel, air in the 
body and all pervading sky in objects remain distinct from all 
the vestments of nature like the body with which He is found 
associated. Pursuing the enquiry into the nature of kshetra and 
kshetrajña, by the same logic, the knowledge that is gained 
is Ātmajñāna.

Just as gold smelters extract gold from the ore through 
the appropriate processes, so also an expert in the science of 
Ātma yoga extracts through enquiry the gold of the Supreme 
Ātman, from the mine of the body. Ātman is the one distinct 
from the body, a field of expression. Understanding these one 
should give up the false feeling ‘I am the body’ or ‘the body 
is mine’ – a feeling born of ignorance.

The one in every kshetra, whether be it of Brahma, Indra 
or a king is called kshetrajña. None of the kshetras will be the 
form of kshetrajña in them. Actions, good or bad, performed 
by body or mind, the resultant experiences of pain and pleasure 
– none of these will be either the form of kshetrajña or his 
dharma.

In all kshetras (fields) the knower of the field is One. He 
is one though in countless and variegated fields. He is devoid 
of the differences derived from the fields. Hence the Lord 
says “I am the all-knowing knower in all fields of actions.”

A deep enquiry into the nature and form of kshetrajña 
in everybody will reveal that ‘I’ is its form. This ‘I’, though 
due to differences of upādhis it is associated with, appears as 
many, the vastu in the form of sphurana of ‘I’ is but one only. 

On Him is superimposed the doership, the enjoyership, 
by removing which, the knower, who is transcendental by 
nature can be known. The field is an unreal projection of the 
mind, the product of nescience and the knower of the field is 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   463 06-05-2011   10:53:59



464 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

the substratum. The Lord identifies Himself with kshetrajña 
and Arjuna is asked to give up his identification with the ‘field’ 
-body- and instead to identify himself with Him. The man 
is different from the world and has identity with the Lord. 
Once this is realised, the reality of the world will be known. 
The Lord says: “enakku oppu” (this knowledge alone is true 
knowledge and acceptable to Me).

The knowledge or scholarship in other fields of 
knowledge, arts and science or of the whole world is not 
true knowledge. Those who know the Truth about what is 
permanent and impermanent never grieve for the eternal Self 
or for the impermanence of the body.

Bhagavan was living this Truth as ever the kshetrajña. 
Once when a lady devotee expressed sadness at having to 
go away from Bhagavan, he said “I am saying I am not this 
(tapping his thigh repeatedly) I am not this, you say ‘this is 
Bhagavan, this is Bhagavan’. What to do?”

Many devotees have recorded how he was awake even 
when the body snored or when the body groaned with pain 
and fever. He always was apart from the body but it was his 
last illness that proved that the body was just something he 
was wearing on. “When the flesh was being cut blood was 
flowing and I could see the radium needles that had been 
inserted into the flesh around the cancerous growth. Bhagavan 
was fully conscious but utterly indifferent to the procedures.... 
We were all consumed by the power of Bhagavan’s silence.” 
(Natesa Iyer, Face to Face, page 185).

A verse from Swarūpabōdha Upanishad aptly describes 
his state.

“The jīvanmukta though in sound sleep does not sleep; 
though dreaming, he does not dream; though awake, he is 
really not awake. He is always resting on his own swarūpa. 
His state is indescribable.” (Verse 14).

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   464 06-05-2011   10:53:59



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 465

The teacher of Gītā dwells on the same idea in Verse 7 
of Chapter 7 also where in he says “Beyond Me, the Supreme 
Lord, there is naught else, there O, Dhananjaya, All that is here 
is strung on me as rows of gems on a string.”

People around felt that Bhagavan is none but the one 
kshetrajña housed in all sariras. When someone served him 
more of an item than was served to others he looked up and 
said “Do you think I eat with this one mouth alone?”

Paraphrase: 
Arjuna! I am the Self, the form of Awareness, seated 

within the hearts of all beings. Know that ‘I am’ the 
beginning (creation or origin), middle (existence) and the 
end (absorption) of all beings, and I, the Primal content 
am the cause of these three.
Commentary: 

Once an young American wanted to know which verse 
of Gītā Bhagavan liked most. Bhagavan replied that he liked 
them all. But when he persisted in knowing the most important 
verse, Bhagavan mentioned this verse. (Letters, 11 Sep 1947).

The one who dwells in the sarira also remains as the form 
of the Universe of sentient and insentient beings. That which 
unceasingly pulsates within every body as ‘I-I’ is the form of 
Ātman. That indeed is the form of jīva. The Lord explains “‘I 
am’ the form of all beings. ‘I am’ the primal cause of their 
origin and absorption.”  He is the only reality in all that is 
manifested and He alone exists when after the cosmic deluge 
everything is absorbed into the unmanifest. He explains His 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   466 06-05-2011   10:53:59



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 467

all pervasiveness by saying that without a pre-existing cause 
for Himself, He remains the cause of the existence of all. The 
Lord here speaks of His divine glory.

The truth to be gleaned from this is that all beings are 
but the form of the Lord; for the Lord says though every 
perceivable being may think variously as ‘I am a scholar’, “I 
am an illiterate”, “I am a rich man” or “I am a poor man” “I 
am a fool” and so on, He dwells in the hearts of all of them. 
“I am”, is common to all. ‘He’ as ‘I’ is to be meditated upon 
as the origin, middle and end. A seeker should think that He 
is the prime whole content and there is naught else that is not 
‘He’. Thus absence of difference between jīva and Iswara and 
their union is spoken of here.”. “O! Arjuna, I am in the expanse 
of the Heart” says Krishna. “He who is in the sun is also in 
this man”, says a mantra in the Upanishads. “The Kingdom 
of God is within” says the Bible. All are thus agreed that God 
is within.” (Talks no. 200).

The form of Self though being the cause and end of beings, 
ever shines as ‘existence’ alone, untouched by the beings It 
houses in. The whole cosmos does not shine even a little in 
Him. The same thought is expressed in verse 5 of Guru Sthuthi: 
“Like all ornaments of gold are but gold, all the perceived 
world is but the form of Chit or Chinmaya”. Bhagavan while 
explaining this verse states “Chinmaya means Chit-Prakāśa, 
i.e. lustre of the Spirit. That light is always existent. “Arjuna I 
am the Self seated in the hearts of all beings.” Does that mean 
He is in the hearts of all beings with this material body? It 
means He is in the hearts of all beings in the shape of Aham 
Sphurana (effulgence of ‘I-I’) That effulgence of the Self is 
known as Chit-prakāśa or Chinmaya.” (Letters, 18-1-49).

The water in a mirage, both when it appears as water 
and when it is known to be a mirage and not water, appears, 
remains and disappears in the desert. This world and the beings 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   467 06-05-2011   10:53:59



468 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

in the world are all equally imagined appearances. In truth, 
there is nothing other than the Ātman. All beings appear from, 
remain in, and disappear into the Ātman. The world, apart 
from the Ātman, has no existence. “Know that all is the form 
of Ātman and that Ātman I am” says the Lord.

Knowledge of the Self is, therefore, knowledge of the 
Supreme Being, the Eternal Reality, that is the beginning, 
middle and end of all beings.

While clearing a gentleman’s doubt, Bhagavan once 
explained, “you think you are the individual, there is the 
universe and that God is beyond the Cosmos. So there is 
the idea of separateness. This idea must go. For God is not 
separate from you or the Cosmos.” Then quoting this verse 
Bhagavan said: “Thus God is not only in the Heart of all, He 
is the prop of all. He is the source of all, their abiding place 
and their end. All proceed from Him, have their stay in Him 
and finally resolve into Him. Therefore He is not separate.” 
(Talk no. 649).

The jñāni, who gives up the ego to become one with the 
Self thereby gives up the feeling that he is doing everything 
while he works. Then a devotee asked, “Lord Krishna himself 
has said that He is the kartha (doer) and He is the bhokta 
(enjoyer)”.  Bhagavan replied that when Mahātmās talk of 
this it is different. “For them Aham means Self (Swarūpa). 
It is not the ‘I’ which says ‘I am the body’.” Quoting again 
this śloka Bhagavan  continued, “The thing called ‘I’ is the 
all-pervading Self (Ātma). That which the sages speak about 
as ‘I’ is functioning of the Self only and not of the body..... 
when the ancients claim to be Iswara they do not talk of this 
body. Self itself is Iswara. That is Brahman, Ātman and all the 
rest. That which is always present is Aham. To be is Brahman 
according to Brahma Gītā. That which is Not is māyā. If you 
look at that which is Not, that which ‘Is’ remains as it is.” 
(Letters, 19-1-1949).

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 469

When Uddhava wanted to be instructed by Lord Krishna 
(in Bhāgavatam) He replied that when Arjuna, dominated by 
the ignorant man’s idea ‘I am the killer, he is killed’ wanted 
to withdraw from the battle, “I restored that hero’s balance 
of mind by rational instructions.” So saying He proceeds to 
instruct him and the very first verse is identical to this one: 
“Uddhava, I am the Ātman, the well-wisher and the master of 
all beings. I am the All-formed and I am simultaneously the 
one form from whom all creations spring, by whom all are 
sustained and in whom they all dissolve.”

11-16-9
This is very significant for this drives home the core 

teaching of Lord Krishna and Bhagavan namely “Knowledge 
of the Self is the Knowledge of the Supreme”.

The original Sanskrit verse of this Tamil translation is 
as follows:

It is I, O Gudakesa am the Self seated within the Heart of

The term Gudakesa, eminently fits Bhagavan, who was

Reality.

The term adiyām nānē can be interpreted in two ways.

origin, middle and the end.”. The introduction of this word

That the central teaching of this śloka is Self-enquiry, 
to know and be the Self, was emphasized by Bhagavan to 
a devotee who wanted to be touched by him. Bhagavan 
remarked “ātmaivaham Gudakesa” i.e. I am Ātman; Ātman 
is the Guru and Ātman is Grace also. No one remains without 
the Ātman. He is always in contact. No external touch is 
necessary.” (Talks no. 105).

One evening Bhagavan, accompanied by Ganapathy Muni 
was climbing down the Hill from Virupaksha cave to go round 
Arunachala. When they had both walked a few steps, all of 
a sudden, Bhagavan stopped and Ganapathi Muni as well. 
The full moon was shining bright in the starry sky. Pointing 
to it Bhagavan said, “Nayana, If the moon and all the stars 
have their being in Me, and the Sun himself goes round My 
hip with his satellites, who am I? who am I?” Ganapathy 
Muni immediately recognized him as the Great person of the 
Vedas, as described in Śrī Rudra, the Purusha Sukta and the 
Skamba Sukta of the Atharva Veda: “He is verily all these and 
That beyond; there is nothing that is not He.” Sri Kavyakanta 
Muni later made this revelation known to the devotees. 
(T.K.Sundaresa Iyer, At the Feet of Bhagavan, page 57).

Paraphrase: 
That whoever is born into the world is bound to die 

is an absolute certainty. Equally certain is that those dead 
will be reborn. This is an inexorable law ordained by 
the Lord. Why do you grieve needlessly in this which is 
inevitable? Tell me.
Commentary: 

It is a matter of common experience of all that for people 
born into the world, whether high or low, man or worm or 
insect, death is an inevitable concomitant. So is a birth too for 
one who dies. The sequence of birth and death is unavoidable 
and a matter of course. Even hatha yogīs who proclaimed to 
have lived for many centuries, having preserved their bodies, 
someday or other have fallen into the jaws of death. None 
can deny the proof of this direct perception. Birth and death 
following each other is an inexorable law. The Lord explains 
here the eternity of the Self and that it is needless and unwise 
to grieve over and get agitated over bodies which are but 
aggregates of elements. 

These words emanating from Lord Krishna establish the 
certainty of the rebirth of jīva. As the Sun rises, it will certainly 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   471 06-05-2011   10:54:00



472 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

set and if it sets, it will certainly rise and none grieves for it 
when it sets. Our ignorance of rebirths cannot negate them. 
Faith in the friendly advice of the elders of experience will 
help us a long away. Lord Krishna later says “Arjuna, many 
are my lives past and thine also; all of them I know, but thou 
knowest not.” (Chap. IV,Verse 5).

Such is life of man, that unasked he comes and unbidden 
he goes. Life is but a small interlude marked by birth and death 
in the eternity and the inevitability of both makes grieving 
either for the dead or rejoicing for the living  needless is the 
rational teaching of the Lord, the realisation of which is bound 
to bring poise and proportion to one and usher in the enquiry 
of Self to get out of this endless cycle. 

What Bhagavan once remarked is in tune with this: “Why 
mourn the dead. Mourning the dead is the chain forged by the 
mind to bind itself to the dead..... What if anyone is dead? What 
if anyone is ruined? Be dead to yourself, Be ruined yourself. 
There will be no pain if the physical outlook is given up and if 
the person exists as the Self..... Mourning is not the true index of 
love. It betrays the love of the object, its shape only. True love 
is shown by the certainty that the object of love is in the Self 
and that it can never become non-existent.” (Talks no.  203).

“Therefore the state of Being is permanent and the body 
and the world are not. They are fleeting phenomena passing 
on the screen of Being-Consciousness which is eternal and 
stationary.” (Talks no. 608).

Bhishma, Drona and others whose impending death 
Arjuna grieved and wept about would at some point of time, 
in future, even if not then, have to face death, for none can 
escape it. “Whatever is destined not to happen will not happen, 
try as hard as you may. Whatever is destined to happen will 
happen, do what you may to prevent it. This is certain”  This 
advice Bhagavan gave to his mother is eternally true.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   472 06-05-2011   10:54:00



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 473

Grieving only weakens and wearies the mind but can 
never bring back the dead. Lord Krishna further instructs 
Arjuna that if they are destined to meet a hero’s death in 
the battle field no amount of his grieving could prevent it. 
Hence he asks “Why do you needlessly despair about what is 
inevitable and unavoidable?”. This reminds one of the story 
in Buddhist literature where Buddha asked a lady grieving 
for her dead son to get sesame from a house where death 
had not visited at all. When she tried to get it, she realised 
the inevitability of  death and reconciled herself to this truth.

Further by saying “you tell me” He induces him to enquire 
and find out the truth for himself, even if he were to disagree 
with what Krishna says. The same advice Lord Krishna 
extends to Uddhava in Bhāgavatam as well. The association 
with sons, wives, dear friends and relatives is no better than 
chance gathering of a group of travellers in a caravanserai. 
Just as dream relatives change in the recurring dream states 
that follow sleep, so do those of the waking life change in 
repeated embodiments. A person will not get attached to home 
if he reflects on this truth and lives like a guest without any 
feeling of ‘I’ and ‘mine’ with regard to anything or anybody 
in life. (11.17.53 & 54).

Once when Bhagavan was living in the Pacchai amman 
temple, a muslim gentleman, who had taken lease of the 
tamarind trees there, was annoyed at the monkeys eating away 
the ripe tamarinds. In a fit of anger he threw stones at a monkey 
which died on account of it. Immediately all the other monkeys 
collected around the dead monkey and started to weep and wail 
over it. Bhagavan who was a silent witness to all these gently 
addressed the monkeys saying, “Those embodied will have to 
die one day. Why do you weep then? Even the one who threw 
the stone and killed the monkey will also have to die some day.” 
On hearing this, the monkeys, pacified went away finally. The 
stark truth, emanating from a jñāni, finds immediate acceptance 
and brings solace even to animals. Bhagavan remarks, “Birth 
and death are only ideas. They pertain to the body or the mind. 
The Self exists before the birth of this body and will remain 
after the death of this body. So it is with the series of bodies 
taken up in succession. The Self is immortal..... Mortality is 
only an idea and cause of misery; you get rid of it by realising 
the Immortal nature of the Self.” (Talks no. 486).

“Let the man find out his underlying Self and die and be 
immortal and happy.” is the teaching. (Talks no. 64). 

“True love is shown by the certainty that the object of 
love is in the Self and that it can never become non-existent.” 
(Talks no. 202).

A staunch devotee called Mahalakshmi amma and her 
husband, who lost all the male issues born to them , and 
another mother who brought the dead body of her son in the 
hope that Bhagavan would certainly bring the child back to 
life were spoken to at length by Bhagavan about life, death 
and the need to be conscious of the state transcending both. 
Since all experiences were centred around the individual, the

search for the source of ‘I’ alone would end all sufferings. 
These soothing words and advice, no doubt, loaded with power 
and grace, consoled their grief stricken hearts and filled them 
with serenity and peace.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   475 06-05-2011   10:54:00



476 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

ceasing to be, is not for the Ātman. He is never born and ever 
existent, imperishable and eternal. Even if the body is slain, 
he is not slain. He being ancient is the Primeval Being. Bear 
this in mind.
Commentary: 

Though Arjuna knows that the venerable preceptors 
and others cannot avert death and that it is a certainty, he 
is distraught with grief that he should be the cause of their 
death. The prime reason for his grief is his sense of doership, 
the feeling that “I will kill them” and “they will be killed by 
me.” Slaying and being slain are associated with the body and 
mind. The real nature of the jīva, namely the Ātman, neither 
slays nor is it slain. This verse dwells on this Truth.

Birth means having been non-existent and becoming 
existent and death means having been existent becoming 
non-existent. The body subject to birth exists for sometime 
and then dies. Even during the short span of life often called 
a fair for two days, it is seen with changes like childhood, 
youth, growth, old age and decay and finally it dies. This is 
but the nature of the body.

But the Self having been, never ceases to be. It is not 
born. It will not die. By negating the birth and death the Self 
becomes eternal and by negating the first and last change 
the intermediate changes also stand negated. Further growth 
is accession of new parts and decay is attrition of parts, but 
Ātman is Impartite and without a form and attributes and 
therefore is not subject to changes. But the Ātman being and 
knowing the body as an object apart from it and being the 
witness of birth, death and changes of the body is free of 
them and untouched by the dharma of the body. He is also 
tollōn, ancient, for being Impartite, He was new even in times 
of yore. Bhagavan pointed out that it was from this level 
that Jesus spoke when he said “Before Abraham was I am”. 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   476 06-05-2011   10:54:00



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 477

(Talks no.189). Therefore the eternal and ancient Ātman exists 
without being slain even if the body is slain. Hence the Lord 
says, “Therefore Arjuna, you the form of Ātman do not kill. 
Nor are Bhishma and others – the form of Ātman – killed. This 
is the Truth. Understand it well and bear it well in your heart.”

Lord Krishna reiterates this truth to Uddhava in 
Bhāgavatam. “The seer can never be the seen. Just as a man 
who observes the growth of a plant from its seed to decay is 
different from the plant, so also is the Ātman, the knower of 
the body and its transformations. The ignorant man incapable 
of distinguishing the Ātman from the body gets entangled in 
the objects of senses and consequently in the cycle of births 
and deaths.” (11.22.49).

Once a devotee conversant with Gītā plied Bhagavan with 
many questions. In the course of the conversation Bhagavan 
said, “The Truth was revealed to Arjuna even at the start. For 
the very first śloka of Sri Krishna’s upadēsa starts, no birth, 
no death, no change etc... Only Arjuna did not understand.” 
and finally Bhagavan concluded by saying “you are taught the 
Truth. Instructions have been given. See who you are. That is 
the whole instruction.”

	 Abiding, everlasting ancient too.

Bhagavan points out that in another verse in even the 

present birth is denied (natvevaham, Gītā, Chapter II, Verse 
12) wherein the Lord says, “Never was there a time when I 
was not, nor thou, nor these kings were not; nor will they not 
be in future. That which is unreal never exists. But that ever 
was even now is and will ever be.”

A verse with the same content occurs in Kathopanishad 
II-18: “The intelligent Ātman is not born nor does He die; He 
did not spring from anything and nothing sprang from Him; 
Unborn, Eternal, Everlasting, Ancient, He is not slain though 
the body is slain.”. Bhagavan proved the content of this verse 
in every way, while living and finally before he dropped 
the body by saying: “Where can I go?” Bhagavan's death 
experience is but an experiment of the truth of this verse and 
he came out of it as the undying Self, thus proving this eternal 
verity. “Henceforth death became a trifle, a mere name”, 
records B.V. Narasimhaswamy while describing his first death 
experience. Therefore death and life are two different aspect 
of one and the same event.

Paraphrase: 
This Ātman is uncleavable ever. He is incombustible. He 

cannot be made wet by water nor dried by the heat of the Sun. 
He is eternal and all-pervading. By this changeless nature 
like a pillar of rock, he is the same forever. He is immovable, 
remaining everywhere as the Self.
Commentary: 

This verse reiterates the Truth that Ātman is not associated 
with any of the dharma of the body. What holds good to 
sarira (body) with organs, cannot apply to the sariri (The 
Self) without organs.

Since the doctrine of the Self enunciated here is difficult 
for Arjuna to understand, the Lord repeats the truth in various 
ways so that somehow Arjuna may grasp and comprehend the 
Truth. The infinite compassion that beings must somehow 
know the Ātmatattva is the reason for such repeated 
instructions.

Just as a body of parts can be severed by a sword, Ātman 
being Impartite and without limbs, cannot be severed by a 
sword or any weapon. Hence it is said Ātman without limbs 
is uncleavable. Fire that burns everything to ashes cannot 
burn the formless Ātman. Ātman lends space for water. Even 
a deluge that may submerge the world in its entirety cannot 
drench it for It has no form or dryness. Neither the heat of the 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   479 06-05-2011   10:54:00



480 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

sun that dries up all objects in the world nor any other heat 
can dry the Ātman devoid of liquid content. Thus the elements 
that ruin one another cannot destroy this Ātman.

The Ātman who is indestructible is eternal -nithyan- 
or ever present. That which is not in one place cannot be 
called eternal, therefore He is omnipresent. Change means 
assumption of a new state after abandoning the previous one. 
He is changeless, therefore omnipresent. He is immovable as 
sthāṇu – unmoving like a pillar and the same forever. He is 
ancient by nature (Sanathanan) and not the product of any 
cause which also means It is ever new.

When mind and instruments wander in sense objects, the 
gross body will not move. Even if crores of bodies move, the 
elements are moveless. Though residing in all that is moving, 
the Self, remaining as the Self, is simply the witness of all that 
moves; hence he is sthāṇu.

The gross body moves among different houses, cities and 
countries. The subtle, joined with the causal, moves among 
varied worlds. Water moves around earth, fire moves water 
and fire is moved by the wind. Space that provides place for 
all these is the totality of Cosmic gross bodies. God who has 
all these as the body moves within. All these though like a 
swift bird try to run in all the ten different directions, the Self 
in all places and for endless time remains as the unmoving 
witness beyond measure. Hence It is achalam.

Action means mere movement even while in the same 
state. Even in the same state, It is not an object of action. 
Subjection to action means association with results of 
actions. But the eternal is unmoving, is not the result of any, 
therefore changeless and static. The omnipresent one being the 
controller of all, is not subject to their actions; for weapons cut 
one who is not within them. Self, the giver of existence and 
manifestation to weapons (and to the wielder of weapons) is 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   480 06-05-2011   10:54:00



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 481

their mover and the indwelling Self. So how can weapons or 
a wielder of weapons make it an object of their own actions?

Thus this Ātmavidya is repeatedly and clearly taught to 
make it easy of comprehension so that the jīvas caught in the 
bondage of saṁsāra may gain release. The Kathopanishad 
also proclaims the truth of this verse: “The Self is not born 
nor does it die. It has not come into being from anything nor 
does anything come into being from it. The unborn, eternal, 
everlasting and ancient one suffers no destruction with the 
destruction of the body.” and “If the slayer thinks, ‘I slay’ and 
if the slain thinks ‘I am slain’, then both of them do not know 
well.” “This slays not nor is ‘this’ slain” (Verses 18 and 19).

Commentary:

Ātman is destructible by none. Removal of any object 
demands some gap or interspace. How to make naught That 
which is never away from anything or anywhere? Hence the 
instruction to know It as Avinasi or Akshara or indestructible. 

Only gross objects, but not subtle can be destroyed. Can 
any get hold of the firmament in hand and make it naught? 
Who can annihilate the Ātman that is subtler than the subtle 
atom? That is in a changless state that is devoid of growth or 
decay, depletion or repletion. There is no change in It whether 
It is said to be existent or non-existent. Space – all pervasive 
– is not divided by the appearance of clouds in it. It is not 
possible for the clouds to change the magnitude of space. But 
space ever remains Itself. So is the Ātman, the substance of 
the universe, that appears and disappears.

Destruction is non-perception and non-being. Immutable 
is that Ātman which neither increases nor decreases. No 
addition or subtraction can be effected on Awareness that is 
eternal. Brahman known as Sat does not forfeit its own nature; 
for It is partless unlike the body, world etc. Neither in respect 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   482 06-05-2011   10:54:00

of its properties does it change for it has no property. Therefore 
none can bring about its destruction.

can . Here edanālum (by any) refers to the five elements in 
creation or parameshwara the creator of those elements.

“Not even Iswara, the Supreme Lord, can bring about the 
destruction of the Self.”

and that it is not unknown to anybody. The aim is to remove the 
superimposition of the attributes of the non-Self on to the Self.

Paraphrase: 
Listen Arjuna to this Truth. The unreal, asat (the 

non-existent, like world and jīvas) has no ‘being’. The 
Real content Sat, never indeed, has non-being: Therefore 
those seers who, knowing the real as Sat and the unreal

Commentary: 

The truth that Kshetras or bodies are impermanent. 
Ātman alone abides forever is the import of this verse. An 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   484 06-05-2011   10:54:00



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 485

externalised mind deluded by the might of māyā perceives 
a body but in the perception of the Self there is no ‘body’. 
Therefore it is said that even when the body appears ‘to be’ 
it is non-existent. Sat or real or ‘that which is’ is defined by 
seers as that in regard to which our consciousness never fails 
and unreal (asat) as that in regard to which our consciousness 
fails. Our consciousness of objects (world, body, etc.) varies 
but not that of existence. The asat or unreal or ‘that which 
is not’, is the phenomenon of passing show of the world that 
veils the unchanging reality that is manifest forever. This in 
a nut shell is the teaching of the entire Gītā by Lord Krishna 
which he pronounced in different ways in the beginning 
itself like “There was never a time when I was not nor thou 
nor these kings and this. ... But Arjuna could not grasp it. 
Later Krishna plainly says that people confound Him with 
the body, whereas in reality He was not born nor will He die. 
Still Arjuna requires the whole Gītā for the truth to be made 
clear to him”.  (Talks no. 46). And this summum bonum is 
the sum and substance of Bhagavan’s teaching as well, often 
described by devotees as the Brahmastra.

While reality is devoid of spatial, temporal and objective 
limitations, the unreal is limited by space and matter. 
Occasional occurrence is said to suffer from temporal 
limitations. All that is perceived falls within this limitation 
and therefore asat or ‘that which is not’. The perceiver alone 
is ‘what is’ and the Ātman.

Seers of Truth never deny the ‘existence’ or ‘being of Sat’ 
or ascribe ‘being’ or existence to ‘that which is not’ namely 
asat and insentient. The insentient and asat bodies become 
non-existent after remaining for some time. This body was not 
before it was born; nor will it be after its death. That which is 
not before and after appears to be in the middle for sometime. 
This interim appearance is also an imagined illusion; hence 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   485 06-05-2011   10:54:00



486 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

even during the time it appears to ‘exist’ or ‘be’, it is only 
non-existent, is the conclusion of the seers of Reality.

The world and body keep perishing every moment but not 
so perceived, for the senses, mind and intellect also belong 
to the same class to which the world belongs. How can the 
perishable perceive the perishable? Only the imperishable can 
perceive another perishable. The Ātman, the real perceiver who 
is bodiless (all the three bodies) and worldless is the witness 
of all these perishable phenomena. Therefore He is the Sat, 
the Real, or “That which exists”.

Such sages who remain as this witness, the real seers, do 
not see themselves as bodies but as the Infinite Self that is 
uncircumscribed by any upādhi.

Hence Ātman, ‘that which is’, the cause and substratum of 
all, ceases at no time to ‘be’. Time itself is an entity imagined 
by the mind. The world and jīvas – imaginary appearances 
projected by the illusory māyā - are non-existent ever.

The nature of gold remains the same before the ornaments 
are made out of it, after the ornaments are made out of it 
and later on when the ornaments are melted. The forms of 
ornaments made out of gold are destroyed but gold itself 
remains indestructible. Likewise the Ātman ever remains the 
same with no change in Its nature both when It is realized 
and when It is not known. Like the tenth man in the parable, 
the Ātman – both when eagerly sought by the jīva and when 
attained and experienced by the jīva – remains the same Self 
ever.

The jīva cannot perform any activity without the 
assistance of the world, body, senses, mind and intellect. It 
proves that all the activities take place in the world – rather 
than in the Self. The world, body, mind, senses and intellect 
are non-existent. Hence there is no karma in the Self. But all 
these appear to exist because of the light of the Real.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   486 06-05-2011   10:54:00



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 487

The Seers who have known both the non-being of the asat 
and the ‘being’ of the Truth are great tapasvins. Therefore, 
relying on the perception of Reality, Arjuna is advised to 
endure grief and banish delusion and remain with a serene 
heart firmly believing that dualities like birth and death, names 
and forms are unreal transformations that appear illusorily 
like a mirage. 

Just as Lord Krishna repeated the same Truth in different 
ways Bhagavan taught that very same truth to different 
devotees according to their Pakwa. He emphasizes “The Self 
alone is Real. All others are unreal. The mind and intellect 
do not remain apart from you” and “The whole Vedānta is 
contained in the two biblical statements, ‘I am that I AM’ and 
‘Be still and know that I am God’.” (Talks no. 338). Stillness 
is the sole requisite for the realisation of the Self as God, and 
again “‘I am that I am’. ‘I am’ is God – not thinking, ‘I am 
God’.” (Talks no. 354), and “Ātma vichara = disappearance 
of dehātma buddhi.” (Talks no. 337).

The original sanskrit verse is as under:

Paraphrase:

by reason of its subtlety, it is untouched by the qualities 
and changes of the objects it pervades or the objects that

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   488 06-05-2011   10:54:00



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 489

Commentary: 
If Kshetrajña or Ātman alone is ‘what is’, and the bodies, 

though appear to exist are not, who is this jīva who performs 
actions, good and bad, and who experiences pleasure and 
pain? If the jīva remains as the Ātman, will not the deeds, 
virtuous and vicious, and happiness and pain, be related to 
the Ātman too? If so how can the Self be said to be changeless 
and imperishable?

The transmigratory existence of saṁsāra, the performance 
of actions by the body, the experience of fruits of actions are all 
only to the jīva who identifies himself with the ahankara which 
is the cause of all the delusive experiences of divisiveness and 
the mind – an illusion of māyā.

When an object is broken and powdered as to lose its 
form, the most subtle atom of it does not undergo any change; 
likewise none of the changes of the gross body like birth, 
childhood, youth, growth, decay, changes of weather, hunger 
and thirst of the prana, strength or weakness of the subtle 
body like the actions of the indriyas or the deformation of 
the indriyas, desire, greed, hatred, miserliness, jealousy and 
ahamkara of the mind, pleasure, pain, sense of doership and 
enjoyership of the ego and of the causal body etc, knowledge 
and ignorance and the sukha (happiness) of sleep, are related 
to the Ātman, the subtlest of the subtle; just as the subtle ether, 
though all pervading and present in all places, is not stained 
or does not get related to anything on account of its subtlety.

The Ātman has never been subject to birth, He never 
grows, He never weakens or dies. He is the continuing 
witness of all the changing conditions of the three bodies. He 
is unchanging, present always and everywhere.

The same perception of nescience that imagines bodies in 
Ātman perceives the actions of merit and demerit and pleasure 
and pain in the Ātman. The one who so perceives is the jīva.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   489 06-05-2011   10:54:00



490 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

When the truth is known, one who saw a snake in a rope, 
or a person in a post overcomes the delusion. Likewise one 
who knows Brahman, the cause of the world, overcoming 
his delusion, gets established in the Self. This one, while he 
perceives the world and functions in the empirical world, is 
called the jīva. Changes in the bodies of the jīva and the world 
are the illusory projections of māyā, just like the illusory 
projections of the jīva in the dream state. They are not true in 
respect of Ātman. The one who dreams either before dreaming 
or after dreaming or during the dream undergoes no change. 
In the same way, perception of the empirical world or actions 
performed in it do not affect the Ātman.

Just as clouds wafted by the wind do not affect the sky, 
so the Ātman is not tainted by tenancy in the body. Ether 
pervading in all elements like air, fire, water and earth, by its 
innate property of subtlety, penetration and the nature of being 
unattached, is not tainted by their qualities like mud, ash etc. 
The Sun reflected in water is not affected by the attributes of 
water. The wind, though it moves everywhere, is unaffected 
by any. In the same way the Ātman, subtler than subtlety 
itself does not become tainted by the attributes of anything 
illumined by it because it is the illuminator. Ahankar or ego, 
the ‘I’ sense is māyā and therefore cannot be real. The effect of 
nescience has no effect on the Ātman. Ātman never subject to 
birth growth, changes or death, is the continuing witness of all 
the changing conditions. One who witnesses changes cannot 
be subject to changes. He is unchanging and all-pervading. 
The water of mirage cannot make the land slushy. Ātman, 
the most subtle, remains as the immaculate space, supreme 
everywhere. Bhagavan once remarked, “The Non-self is 
untouchable. The social untouchability is man-made whereas 
the other untouchability is natural and divine.” (Talks no. 308). 
and again “The soul remains always uncontaminated. It is the 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   490 06-05-2011   10:54:01



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 491

substratum running through all the three states.”, which is 
simply ‘I am’. The three states among which people alternate 
continually are like the pictures moving on a cinema screen 
which do not affect the screen. So “I am” unaffected remains 
throughout.

During his last illness Bhagavan appeared to be suffering 

from the point of view of the onlookers, while he himself was 
not touched by it. 

The moving story of Natesa Iyer, a kitchen worker, 
an ardent devotee of Bhagavan as recorded by V.Ganesan 
proves how Bhagavan still remaining as the indestructible 
Self, hears petitions and provides succour in times of need. 
When Natesa Iyer was asked to leave from the Ashram, a few 
years after Bhagavan’s nirvāna by the management and for 
days together he sat on the steps of the nearby temple as he 
had no place to go and he did not want to leave the precincts 
of his Sadguru’s ashram. On hearing this when Mr. Ganesan 
reported the unfairness of it all with tears to Muruganar he, 
in turn with a mischievous smile said, “you could have gone 
directly to Bhagavan and told him.... Did you feel you had to 
tell your story to a living human being? Is not Bhagavan still 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   491 06-05-2011   10:54:01

alive? And will he not listen to you if you go to his shrine and 
unburden yourself there? Go to the shrine.. and shout it as 
loudly as you are shouting here. He will not only listen to you, 
he will also take appropriate action. Have faith in Bhagavan.” 
He did as he was told and the next morning Natesa Iyer was 
found working in the kitchen in his usual place. The ashram 
management had asked him to come back. Countless devotees 
will bear testimony to the fact of Bhagavan extending such 
succour to this day.

Sadhu Natanananda bears testimony to this fact in a 
Verse (63.5) in his Ātma Gītā. “O mind!” He said, “when I 
am present everywhere where can I go?” where then can he 
go and how? Though he has given up the perishable body, he 
will always be present in our hearts as “that which is” beyond 
the knowledge of the senses. He who bestowed his grace more 
sweetly than one’s own mother will from now on also shine 
as our unseen guide and support.”
