Paraphrase: 
The Sun and Moon that shine in the firmament and 

fire cannot illumine this Ātman at any time. Know that 
state to be My Supreme Abode, attaining which they do 
not return to saṁsāra again.
Commentary: 

Lord Krishna explains his all-pervading real form of 
effulgence in this and the following verse lest Arjuna who 
was told that Kshetrajña is Iswara and Iswara is Ātman, and 
who perceives him only as Krishna should circumscribe the 
Supreme Brahman to a form and know it as such.

The light perceived in the world is normally classified 
as sunlight, moonlight and the light of fire – all of which 
can illumine only the physical world and none can illumine 
the Ātman. The light of their effulgence is not their own but 
is received from the Ātman; hence they are incapable of 
illumining the Ātman. That which is illumined by something 
is not able to illumine its own illuminator.

That state, attaining which one does not come back (edanai 
adainde madangaro) to the bondage of the world or saṁsāra, 
is ‘My Supreme abode’ (Paramam vidu) says Krishna.

Going always has return as an end and union will have 
separation as an end, but the ‘going’ that is mentioned here is 
going to the Supreme Abode which does not entail a return. 
One who attains Brahmanhood with the annihilation of the 
upādhi of jīvahood, does not come back to saṁsāra. Once 
a devotee quoting this śloka raised a doubt that since this 
Absolute state is beyond Cosmic Consciousness, those who 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   493 06-05-2011   10:54:01



494 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

reach Cosmic Consciousness have not escaped the clutches of 
ignorance, Bhagavan replied, “That is what is meant by saying 
that all lokhas, even the Brahma loka do not release one from 
rebirth vide Gītā: Reaching Me there is no rebirth. All others 
are in bondage. “Moreover as long as you think that there is 
gati (movement) as implied in the word gatva (having gone 
to) there is punaravritti (return) also. Again gati implies your 
purvagamanam (birth). What is birth? It is birth of ego. Once 
born you reach something..... Be as you are. See who you are 
and remain as the Self, free from birth, going, coming and 
returning.” (Talks no. 182). Therefore Paramam is nothing 
but remaining still and know that I am God.

Lord Krishna here clears another doubt of Arjuna. Arjuna 
perceives Krishna as his friend but Krishna speaks like the 
Supreme Lord. Lest he should think that the form of Ātman, 
the Supreme Lord, is something infinitely bigger like that 
of the form of Universe, He utters this verse. Further in the 
universal form, (Viswa Rupa Darsanam) he witnessed, in the 
form of Krishna, ‘Krishna’ seated as ‘Mahavishnu’ in His 
Abode Vaikunta. Therefore He simply reveals the Truth that 
all those are simply His abodes but not ‘Being’ or Supreme 
Abode, the Param damam or Paramam vidu. 

When Prof. Subbaramaiah asked about Viswarūpa 
darsana Bhagavan answered, “Visvātma darsana is Visvarūpa 
darsana, i.e. the Universal Self or the Cosmic Self is the 
Cosmos.” Sri Krishna started the discourse in Chapter II, 
saying “I have no form”. In chapter XI He says: “See my form 
as the Universe.” Is it consistent? Again He says “I transcend 
the three worlds,” but Arjuna sees the three worlds in Him. 
Sri Krishna says, “ I cannot be seen by men, Gods etc”. Yet 
Arjuna sees himself and the Gods in Him. No one could see 
and yet Arjuna was endowed with divine sight to see Him. 
Does it not look a maze of contradictions?”

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   494 06-05-2011   10:54:01



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 495

“The answer is that the understanding is wrong. Sthula 
dhristi on the physical plane is absurd; jñāna-dhristi (subtle 
understanding) is necessary. That is why Arjuna was given 
divya chakshuh (divine sight). Can such sight be gross? Will 
such interpretation lead you to a right understanding?

Sri Krishna says “Kalosmi” ‘I am Time’. Does Time have 
a shape?

Again if the universe be His form, should it not be one and 
unchanging? Why does He say to Arjuna “See in me whatever 
you desire to see?” That means that His form is according to 
the desires of the Seer. They speak of ‘divine sight’ and yet 
paint the scene, each according to his own view. There is the 
seer also in the seen. What is all this? Even a mesmerist can 
make you see strange scenes. You call this a trick, whereas 
the other, you call divine. Why this difference? Anything seen 
cannot be real. That is the truth.”

Even the form of Krishna that is being perceived by 
him, Vaikuntam, Mahavishnu, etc. have effulgence that 
is circumscribed. Even these like others are subject to 
disappearance.

The true form of Ātman pervades everywhere with 
limitless effulgence. “That is my Supreme Abode” – That 
abode is a mass of splendour that is illumined by nothing. 
So the Lord can neither be perceived by the sun (who is the 
presiding deity of the eye) nor thought of by the mind (whose 
presiding deity is the moon) nor be described in words (whose 
presiding deity is fire) .

Vīdu stands for both Abode of God and God. The Abode 
of God is an embodiment of light, just like the Sun and its 
light are one and the same.

“One who reaches that Abode returns not to saṁsāra” 
says the Lord. Thus the Supreme Abode is the Ātman Eternal – 
the realm of the Self which is the land of Knowledge Absolute. 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   495 06-05-2011   10:54:01



496 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Other forms however great or effulgent are circumscribed and 
finally go out of existence. Vaikuntam, Kailasam and Brahma 
lokam are not permanent. One who gains the Ātman, eternal 
and whole does not come back to the transmigratory saṁsāra 
is the instruction Lord Krishna delivers to Arjuna.

A verse with similar content is contained in Kathopanishad: 
(2.2.15)

“The Sun does not shine, neither do the moon and stars nor 
do these flashes of lightning shine. How can this fire? When 
he shines all these shine after Him; by His light all these are 
variously illumined.” 

The original Sanskrit śloka is as follows:

Paraphrase: 

That status hailed by the Vedas as birthless, 
imperishable and imperceptible (unmanifest) is spoken 
of as the highly exalted state, Akshara or the Supreme 
state. Further that status attaining to and having merged 
with which, they do not return to saṁsāra again, that is 
My highest Abode, hard to reach. Know this.
Commentary: 

Ātman, eternally manifest, is indefinable. Only forms can 
be perceived by the senses. Ātman is unmanifest and without 
a form and therefore imperceivable. Hence It is birthless or 
originless and as a consequence deathless or imperishable. 
Vedas, therefore, hail it as Unmanifest and imperishable.

Further those who go to celestial or higher worlds as fruits 
of meritorious deeds performed return to the earth after the 
exhaustion of their merit and have to follow the wheel of birth 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   497 06-05-2011   10:54:01



498 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

and death. None of the other lokas like Vaikuntam, Kailasam, 
Brahma lokam or the world of celestials is permanent. At the 
end of the yugas, they also perish when all the manifested is 
withdrawn. Except the imperishable Supreme Abode or Mukti, 
whichever higher worlds one goes to, one has necessarily to 
return to saṁsāra. Hence Lord Krishna states with emphasis 
and clarity here that state, attaining which one does not return 
to the saṁsāra of triple suffering as His Supreme Abode, called 
here as ariya vidahum -(the rarest of rare abodes) which is 
of the nature of Being, Self-effulgent bliss that is without an 
origin and end – the culmination of all human aspirations. 
There is nothing greater than this state. This is the ultimate. 
“This is the Truth and know it as such” instructs the Lord. 
“There is nothing higher than purusha. He is the culmination. 
He is the highest goal”. (Kathopanishad, 1.3.11).

In the Tamil translation of this verse Bhagavan’s usage 
of the phrase maruvit tirumbaro (reaching and merging with 
which they do not return) is delectable, at once majestic and 
suggestive of immense serenity. Inspiring seekers with courage 
and confidence, it sets afire the spiritual longing of the seekers 
by rekindling it with zeal and fillip, enabling them to march 
on relentlessly without yielding to weariness.

500 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Paraphrase: 
Without the pride of ahankara (‘Í’ sense in the body) 

and delusion, freed of all desires and attachments that 
cling to the mind, ever poised in the Self as the form 
of Self, liberated from the body – related and defective 
pairs of opposites like pleasure and pain, those undeluded 
jñānis attain and rule that everlasting state.
Commentary: 

The earlier verses spoke of the Supreme Abode. This one 
describes those who reach that state. The word mānam which 
means egoism also stands for measure. The jīva, limiting 
himself to the size of a body and considering the body as a 
measure of ‘I’, is attached to the body. Mōha is delusion born 
of nescience which is the cause of failure to realize the Ātman 
that remains within one as the very Self. This mōha or delusion 
leading to the non-perception of the Self and attachment to 
the body – the cause of misperception of the Self – must both 
be overcome and all desires and attachments the mind clings 
on to, due to vāsanās or latent tendencies must be annihilated 
by a spiritual seeker. The Ātman is the sole existence and the 
One appears as many. The deluded perceive only the many 
and get entangled in its aftermath namely desires, attachments 
and pairs of opposites. But the undeluded perceive the one 
existence and that light of discriminative intelligence helps 
them free themselves from ahankara or egoism, pride, 
attachment, desires and dualities. The duality of attachment 
and aversion is the cause of all sins.

But how to conquer desires? Bhagavan answers, “Desire, 
or lust, anger, etc. give you pain. Why? Because of the ‘I’ 
conceit; this I – conceit is from ignorance; ignorance from 
differentiation; differentiation from the notion of the reality 
of the world and this again from ‘I-am-the-body’ idea. The 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   500 06-05-2011   10:54:01



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 501

last can be only after the rise of the ego. The ego not arising, 
the whole chain of mishaps disappears. Therefore prevent 
the rise of the ego. This can be done by remaining in your 
own real nature; then lust, anger, etc. are conquered.” (Talks 
no. 575).

The consequences of all dualities end in sukha (pleasure) 
or dukkha (pain). A gain or sukha will certainly be lost 
ultimately. Hence all pairs of opposites may be clubbed as 
the duality of pain and pleasure.

“One should not give place to feelings of pleasure or pain, 
come what may. How do the events affect a person? You do 
not grow by acquiring something nor wither away by losing 
it. You remain what you always are.” (Talks no. 614), and “a 
man’s true name is Mukti.” (Talks no. 55).

charbu asai mattrinar means attachments (to body and 
world) removed and replaced by attachment to the Self.

How to become free from the stain of association of 
attachments? Bhagavan says “by Sat-sangha, which means 
(association) with Sat. Sat is only the Self.”

One whose mind is absorbed in the Ātman as pure Self-
Awareness is released from body – related dualities. He, with 
desires stilled, is constantly engaged in the contemplation of 
the Essence – the Supreme Self and becomes undeluded. He, 
having discarded the identification with the body, will not be 
of the body, though in the body. Only such people repair to that 
Paramapadam and such ascetics who have that imperishable 
status as their experience are called jñānis.

Desires, the defects of the mind, drag the individual down 
– and deeper – into the mire of saṁsāra. While association 
with friends and relatives delude the mind with desires and 
attachments, association with holy men (Sat sangha) removes 
the darkness of ignorance and the fear of saṁsāra just as fire 
removes cold, darkness and fear. Getting rid of the body-

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   501 06-05-2011   10:54:01



502 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

based ‘I’ and the world – based ‘mine’ is possible only with 
abidance in the Self.

Only those who inhere in the Ātman forever (ekkalum 
tannile tan nilaittar) alone can overcome ‘mine’. When the 
mind is made to inhere in the Ātman, all these defects get 
annihilated. When one with the pursuit of enquiry “Who am 
I?” plunges within, he perceives nothing other than jñāna. And 
inhering in the Self as Brahman, he becomes totally freed of 
all attachments and gains the ever-lasting state.

This and other verses describing a stita-prajña or jñāni 
in Gītā are a true pen-picture of Bhagavan. He is the epitome 
of all the qualities described in this verse. He had nothing to 
call his own and many have recorded how he moved about 
as if even the body did not belong to him. He enjoyed the 
Supreme blessedness of the state, free of wants of any kind. 
As Gītā says in the 52nd verse of Chapter II “He is the one 
who is satisfied in the Self by the Self”.

Swami Siddheswarananda says that Maharshi can best 
be described in the words of Gītā and enumerates numerous 
verses to show how they perfectly fit Bhagavan and explain his 
state (Golden Jubilee Souvenir), while Dr. T.M.P. Mahadevan 
states, “Bhagavan is a vivid and living commentary on that 
great scripture Gītā” so much so that he would advise “If 
anyone wants to understand the inner meaning of the Gītā, 
he must meet the Maharshi”.... The storms of the world 
never reached him. Sitting in the Ashram hall, he appeared 
to be the still point of the turning world... There was not the 
least adhyasa present in him. His last illness quite clearly 
demonstrated this. What a complete and utter detachment 
from the body he manifested in order to teach the world that 
the body is not the Self (Surpassing Love and Grace, page 
192). Bhagavan taught that we are not the body (the content 
of this verse) both by words and example.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   502 06-05-2011   10:54:01



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 503

Though an ashram grew up around Bhagavan in course 
of time he never regarded it as his. He never ordered anyone 
to do anything nor did he take anything for granted. His 
actions were like “actorless actions” or a chariot without a 
driver. Once a sadhu turned up in the morning half an hour 
before lunch (which was at 11 o’clock in those days). Seeing 
Bhagavan seated on the sofa and assuming him to be the head 
of the ashram, as in the case of other mutts he had visited, he 
went straight to Bhagavan and said “I am very hungry. Can 
you arrange for food to be given to me?” Bhagavan kept silent 
for a few minutes and then slowly said, “Wait for some time. 
Then a bell will go. Then along with everybody else, you can 
go to the dining hall where you will find a leaf spread in the 
centre of the hall overlooking rows of plantain leaves spread. 
Sit there, eat your fill and go.” He did not ask anybody to serve 
him food. He simply wanted to give him what was given to 
him by the ashram authorities which meal also he had earned 
by working in the kitchen in the wee hours of the morning. The 
administration getting wind of this and afraid that Bhagavan 
would precisely do that – give away his food to the sadhu – 
and might even go without food, hurriedly took the sadhu in, 
fed him well and quickly sent him away.

Neither elation nor distress was ever noticed in him, 
whether it was days of plenty or of dire straits as to the 
wherewithal of the next meal was unknown. Even when news 
of the Sarvadhikari Chinnaswamy being reportedly kidnapped 
was received or when he presented himself in the evening, 
there was no trace of any emotion on his face. He was one 
ever established in the Self, having transcended all pairs of 
opposites and the three gunas.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   504 06-05-2011   10:54:01



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 505

Paraphrase: 
He who discards living by the scriptural injunctions 

and lives instead prompted by the desires and the dictates 
of the mind following unworthy ways will never gain the 
ultimate goal of human life, the peace and happiness of 
this world or the exalted state of emancipation.
Commentary: 

This verse provides the rules for the journey within. 
Śāstras based on the Vedas form a body of knowledge which, 
instructing people on matters not known before, lead them 
into righteous paths paving the way for a dharmic way of life.

Śāstraic injunctions are of two kinds – inducive and 
restrictive. The positive injunctions command the performance 
of certain acts while others prohibit the performance of others. 
Those parts of Vedas that consist of these injunctions and 
prohibitions are called Smritis. Vedas distinguish between 
dharma – the means to achieve the ultimate goal of human 
aspirations namely mukti and adharma  – to be eschewed at 
all costs. “The Vedas are the exhalation of the Omniscient 
one ... and unflinching conviction in the authority of the 
Vedas is mandatory. Therefore strict adherence, with true 
faith and utmost loyalty, to these commandments is required.” 
(Ribhu Gītā, Verses 5 and 48).

Strict adherence to a life of dharma commanded by Vedas 
leads to the dissipation of vāsanās resulting in purity of the 
mind and thereby creates the competency for enquiry of the 
Self. Abandoning a life of adherence to the ways enjoined by 
the scriptures and leading an unrighteous life, dictated by the 
vagaries of desires, – like acting wilfully without performing 
what is enjoined and performing what is prohibited – cannot 
lead one to Liberation or peace. 

One who leads a life prompted by desires becomes a slave 
to the desire-ridden mind and achieves neither the perfection 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   505 06-05-2011   10:54:01



506 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

of Release nor secures the competence to achieve any end of 
man. Parting ways from the dharmic way of life, such a one 
suffers from the loss of peace of mind and the comfort of peace 
in the here, and forgoes the hereafter too. Siddhiyodu charane 
(attainment of perfection) here means success or fitness for 
reaching the highest human goal for purity of mind which 
is necessary, for the attainment of Release is gained by the 
observances of śāstraic injunctions –  positive and negative.

The intellect is not a competent authority to decide what 
is fit to be done and what is fit to be eschewed. In the very 
next verse the Lord declares tasmāt śāstram pramanam te 
(therefore let the śāstras be your authority and guide on this); 
hence śāstras alone are proof and guide to decide that.	

When the unrestrained and self willed action is regulated 
by the observance of canons of conduct, prescribed by the 
śāstras, purity of heart is gained which secures for one 
a deeper understanding of the meaning and goal of life. 
With the gain of mukti the ‘spontaneity of spirit’ takes 
over. Therefore a life of abidance by śāstraic injunctions 
is a stepping stone to a life of Release. Sadhu Natanananda 
remarks “Many religious traditions and scriptures have come 
into existence for the sole purpose of redeeming through 
grace-consciousness the intellectual world, which has been 
struggling hard to find the route to limitless contentment.” 
(Ramana Darsanam, page 6). The realized Mahātmās do 
not transgress the śāstraic injunctions for their experience 
is in conformity with śāstraic proofs. Here the Lord while 
instructing Arjuna reiterates and gives credence to śāstraic 
authority rather than authenticating it as hailing from Him.

Though Bhagavan’s core teaching is Self-enquiry and 
Surrender, he always encouraged people who were following 
a life of strict adherence to such śāstraic codes before they 
could come to Ātma-vichara so much so Sivaprakasam Pillai 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   506 06-05-2011   10:54:01



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 507

hymns him as “Long live the lotus feet of him who says giving 
up achara (adherence to such conduct) is disastrous”.

Once a relative of Viswanatha Swamy, an educated youth 
fired by the freedom struggle, while on a visit to the ashram, 
wanted to sit during lunch not with the Brahmins but with 
others who were seated on the other side of the screen. When 
Niranjananda Swamy asked him to move to the other side he 
questioned whether such distinctions were being followed in 
Bhagavan’s presence also. Bhagavan then said “I am the only 
one who does not follow all that. Come and sit next to me. 
Besides you do follow these rules in your house, don’t you? 
What rules you dare not break in your own house should not 
be broken here.” The young man quietly switched over to the 
other side. Bhagavan, a mukta purusha had transcended all 
that. But till one reaches that state or acquires the competence 
to carry on Ātma vichara, one has to follow the śāstraic 
injunctions which provide the purity of mind and heart to 
march further on the inward journey.

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 509

Commentary: 
Right from Brahma down to a blade of grass or a clod 

of earth everything is bound to perish. That which is born 
is subject to growth, decay and destruction. Deathlessness 
demands birthlessness. The Self alone is without a birth or 
death.

The Lord abides equally in all things – moving and 
unmoving – of various sizes, colours and forms. All beings 
endowed with the three gunas undergo birth, life and 
dissolution, are born in the beginning of the yuga or cosmic 
dawn and dissolve at the end of Cosmic night. They are born 
in various species that are forever revolving and never remain 
constant for a moment. But the Lord remains constant, uniform 
and the same in all forms from the highest to the lowest, all 
of which are characterised as dying. The Supreme Lord or 
Ātman, though abiding equally in all beings is imperishable 
when the beings It is housed in keep perishing. It is clear 
from this that though the Ātman resides in them It is not born 
with them. The world, jīvas and all that is seen are all the 
perishable manifestations of the one imperishable. All the 
worlds perceived in all the three states, jīva, God all have the 
Self – Being – alone as their basis excepting which everything 
else is perishable. The plants and trees grow and perish on 
the earth and become the earth itself. Jagrat, swapna and 
sushupti states rise, stay and perish in the witness (Self) that 
is aware of them. Likewise the worlds appear from, stay on 
and dissolve in the Self – the blemishless Awareness – and 
there is no second entity.

The Self that abides in all perishable beings must be 
perceived in the same way gold is perceived in all the 
ornaments of gold, mud is seen in pots of various shapes and 
sizes and yarn is seen in different types of cloth. The perception 
of many, though perishable, is due to the distorted perception 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   509 06-05-2011   10:54:02



510 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

caused by nescience. If the misperception is to be overcome, 
nescience has to be annihilated.

The moon, though the only one in the star-studded sky, 
appears as many for the one with scales in the eye. The reason 
for the perception of many is the disease of the eye and not 
the moon. When we hear a person saying he perceives many 
moons we say true perception is the perception of one moon 
only. Hence amongst people who perceive the form of the one 
Ātman as the world of many, as many disparate selves, only 
the one who perceives the imperishable Ātman, the single 
undivided Self equally in all, is the one who really sees. The 
ignorant one like a dreamer mistakes the unreal for real. He 
who sees his Self identified with the body does not perceive 
truly and he who sees himself identified with the Lord and 
sees similarly the Lord in everyone sees truly.

The one who realises the Truth and abiding peace is one 
who sees all animate and inanimate beings not as objects for 
fulfilment of desires but as the perishable manifestation of the 
Imperishable Lord. 

This verse speaks of the union of the Kshetra and 
the Kshetrajña. The Kshetra undergoes modification but 
Kshetrajña is ever the same. He is changeless devoid 
of transformation. Secondly He is imperishable among 
perishables. Kathopanishad says “From death to death he 
goes who sees here a manifold as it were”, “The realized being 
does not see the world as being apart from the Self and he 
possesses true knowledge and the internal happiness of being 
perfect whereas the other person sees the world apart, feels 
imperfection and is miserable.” (Talks no. 486). Bhagavan ever 
remained the fountain of the one Self and divine love welled 
up for the Self he saw all around, whether human beings or 
animals or plants making no difference. Everyone was the 
same to him be he a pontiff of a mutt or a Maharaja or an 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   510 06-05-2011   10:54:02



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 511

illiterate rustic. He lived the truth enshrined in this verse of 
Gītā. “The wise look with equal eye on a learned but humble 
Brahmin, a cow, an elephant, a dog and a chandala living on 
dog’s flesh.”. He never called any of the animals ‘it’ or treated 
it as being less than a human being records B.V. Narasimha 
Swamy. Squirrels or sparrows, monkeys and dogs, crows and 
deer, snakes, all received equal treatment and Bhagavan never 
brooked any violent treatment of plants and trees by way of 
plucking leaves or fruits.

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 513

Commentary: 
The unswerving stance that there is nothing other than 

Iswara is ananya bhakti. One possessed of this bhakti due 
to perfection of sravana, manana and nidhidhyasana of 
scriptural knowledge and Upanishadic utterances, becomes 
worthy of knowing the Lord as He truly is, namely, seeing 
everything as that form Supreme and finally knowing himself 
as the form of Supreme Self. With this knowledge nescience 
and its products become eliminated. The experience of the 
awareness of the Self, that is aware of everything as the form 
of the Lord, as the very Lord is the greatest bhakti called 
Parabhakti. The Lord can be known, seen and attained only 
through this Parabhakti. Parōksha jñāna, knowledge of the 
Supreme gained from scriptures or hearsay knowledge is not 
firm but aparōksha jñāna, that is born of one’s own realisation 
aided by Parōksha jñāna is firm.

Perceiving everything, being and non-being, as the form 
of Lord and meditating on Him with devotion without a sense 
of ‘otherness’ and never seeking any object except the Lord 
and when no object other than the Lord is cognised by the 
senses, it is called ananya bhakti. To such a one, the Lord says, 
He will vouchsafe the competence and worth of perceiving 
the Lord as He really is, in Essence.

Anniyam ennāda anbinal (not thinking of any other) also 
means not thinking of any other God or not harbouring any 
other thought. That is, devotion directed to naught else than 
the Lord at all times. One who worships with such an ananya 
bhakti or parabhakti will, by the Grace of the Lord, be blessed 
with the knowledge of Truth, the Lord’s form as It is, same – 
sightedness and aparōksha jñāna, the greatest bliss.

An ideal devotee is one who realizes by all the senses only 
one object, God. He adores God with all his spirit and heart.

Bhakti (ananya or prapatti) is not different from jñāna. 
“Merging into the Source, there is unity only. So it is with 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   513 06-05-2011   10:54:02



514 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

bhakti too. Realising the God of devotion, there will be unity 
only. God too is thought of in and by the Self. So God is 
identical with the Self. ... There is in fact no difference between 
bhakti and vichara.” (Talks no. 154). 

Surrender is bhakti yoga. To reach the source of the I 
thought is the destruction of the ego, is the attainment of 
the goal, is prapatti (surrender), jñāna, etc.” Talks no. 129 
Therefore either the thoughts are eliminated by holding on to 
the root thought ‘I’ or one surrenders unconditionally to the 
higher power. These are the only two ways for realization. 
Bhakti is not different from mukti. “The Gītā says: Brahmano 
hi pratishtaham. If that ‘aham’ is known, the whole is known.” 
(Talks no. 649). Absence of thoughts is bhakti. It is also mukti. 
Bhakti is being the Self (Swarūpa). Only one thought prevails 
to the exclusion of all other thoughts. That thought is of God, 
which is the Self or it is the Self surrendered unto God. What 
Verse 6 of Swaroopabōdha Upanishad states is of significance: 

“Give up the thoughts of not-self. Fix the purified mind 
in the Ātman, the indivisible and Infinite. Think always of 
the Self, the bliss Absolute which conduces to liberation and 
realise the Self”.

Commentary: 

There are a few words in Sanskrit the full import of 
which is difficult to be conveyed when translated into other 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   515 06-05-2011   10:54:02



516 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

languages. Words like dharma, satyam, śraddhā and many 
more belong to this category. The word śraddhā means faith, 
trust, confidence and much more and it relates to the Self. 
Bhagavan declares “Śraddhā, grace, light and spirit are all 
synonymous with the Self. Grace is the Self. It is not manifest 
because of ignorance prevailing. With śraddhā it will become 
manifest.” (Talks no. 381).

Gītā also proclaims Sraddhāvān labhatē jnanam 
(He who has śraddhā, gains jñāna. Chapter 4, Verse 39). 
Vivekachūḍāmaṇi defines śraddhā as “faith in śāstra vakyas 
and teachings of the Guru”.

In each one, faith conforms to his inherent nature or inner 
sense. Man is verily the form of his faith; as a man’s faith is, 
so is his character. As a man’s faith is, so is his conviction or 
nishta (state of being) and according to his conviction is his 
destination. His feelings and actions are shaped by his faith. 
Faith determines the sankalpa (willing or resolve) and propels 
one to act towards the attainment of the sankalpa and the 
confidence of attainment is certainly inspired by faith indeed. 
Nothing can be accomplished in the absence of faith.

Śraddhā is according to the nature of one’s antaḥkaraṇa 
which in turn is determined by vāsanās.

The births of jīvas are according to the actions performed 
and the qualities in association with which those actions were 
performed. The gradation of birth is determined by the nature 
of vāsanās or proclivities left behind by previous births and 
the strength of such vāsanās left behind dominates the inherent 
nature of the jīvas. This is nature’s general law. We are what 
we are on account of our past and we ourselves can fashion 
our future.

All the qualities an individual possesses have been 
imbibed from previous births. Even if the body were to fall 
the next minute, belief in the body’s continued existence is 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   516 06-05-2011   10:54:02



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 517

entirely due to the firm hold on faith, inspired by the eternal 
nature of the Self within.

Śraddhā depends on one’s swabhāva or inherent nature. 
Swabhāva follows the preponderance of gunas, (one over the 
others) which decides the nature of jīvas as satvic, rajasic 
or tamasic. That in which śraddhā is reposed will reveal the 
nature of the man and one’s way of life depends on one’s 
qualities or gunas.

Later the Lord goes on to say how good men worship the 
Gods, the passionate worship the demigods and demons and 
others – (who are) the dull – worship the spirits and ghosts.

Śraddhā, in its fullest sense means striving after the 
ultimate goal of all human aspirations and such śraddhā, 
earnestness, will make life eternal. When one with great 
śraddhā strives after Self-realization by focusing the gathered 
mental energies on that ideal, then He from within rakes 
up the heap and dust of vāsanās and gunas facilitating the 
vāsanākshya (annihilation of vāsanās) acquired from previous 
births. In short, faith, confidence and diligent endeavour itself 
is mukti for such a one.

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 519

Commentary: 
The greatness of śraddhā is explained in this verse. 

Faith or śraddhā in terms of aspiration to gain knowledge is 
necessary for attaining Ātmajñāna. This involves the practice 
of sādhanās observed with due śraddhā, complete subjugation 
of the senses, preventing the ramification of various thoughts 
propelled forcefully by strong predilections and constant 
and deep meditation on the Self. Such a one alone can gain 
knowledge. “The degree of absence of thoughts is the measure 
of your progress towards Self-realisation... The Self remains 
always in realisation... The obstacles are thoughts. Progress 
is measured by the degree of removal of the obstacles to 
understanding that the Self is always realised.” Therefore all 
one has to do is “Ātma samstham manah kritva na kinchidapi 
chintayet.” (Anchoring the mind in the Self, do not think of 
anything). (Talks no. 618).

Grace of the Guru and control of senses are indispensable 
for the attainment of Ātmavidya. “But Grace is not exterior. 
In fact very desire for grace is due to grace that is already 
within one.” (Talks no. 618). Śraddhai ullone (only the one 
with śraddhā) refers to one who has great faith and belief in 
the teachings of śāstras and guru. Conviction follows śraddhā 
leading to effective control of senses. Lest such a one should 
yield himself to indolence the Lord further advices “karuthil 
vidate karudhi” not to allow the mind to engage itself in the 
whirlpools of thoughts of objects of senses, but to live inward 
constantly in the parōksha – knowledge gained, from the 
scriptures and guru till it blossoms into reality as aparōksha 
jñāna where the Self touches Brahman and becomes It. Such a 
one attains to Supreme peace with ignorance and all its effects 
destroyed once and for all.

Human effort can achieve by itself nothing. One must pray 
constantly for the ahankara to melt away and then from within 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   519 06-05-2011   10:54:02



520 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

He rakes up the heaps of vāsanās and annihilates them. There 
is nothing that He does not know. A conception can never be 
hidden from the mother and a word can never be hidden from 
the heart. “All that you need to do is to find out its (I) origin 
and abide there. Your efforts can extend only thus far. Then 
the beyond will take care of itself. You are helpless there. No 
effort can reach it”. (Talks no. 197). “(This (jñānam) is called 
vastu tantra (The Supreme’s own) while human endeavour 
kartru tantra (doer’s own).” (Talks no. 624).

Commentary: 

Yoga means union. Mere desire for mukti cannot bestow 
knowledge of the Self. Not all with a desire for mukti can 
comprehend the Ātma tattva easily. One who meditates on 
the Lord, the principle of Para, with heart and soul and with 
a melting devotion, without hankering for gain, honour, fame, 
or for any purpose of his own, but out of love for the Lord (the 
Self) becomes a fit recipient of His grace and is granted the 
Supreme buddhi or jñāna yoga by which he reaches Him – the 
Supreme Lord – who is the very Self. “Love is not different 
from the Self. Love of an object is of an inferior order and 
cannot endure whereas Self is love. In other words God is 
Love.” (Talks no. 433).

Here Satbuddhi yoga means yoga of Enquiry or Ātma 
vichara that leads to the right perception of Reality.

eppodum – always. The meditation has to be constant for 
“no one succeeds without effort. Mind control is not one’s

perseverance.” (Talks no. 398).

Renouncing one’s own endeavour, taking Him as the 
sole refuge and continually thinking of Him, one is granted 
that Ātma-yoga which cannot be accomplished by human 
effort alone. He, the Mahātmā of all mahātmās, grants this 
by guiding one from within the Heart, His Abode.

This verse speaks of the boundless compassion of the Lord, 
the ripeness or Pakwa of the seeker and its outcome; namely 
the fulfilment of human birth. When, by His compassion, the 
seeker’s love and devotion become strong and steadfast, the 
way to Supreme Bliss is revealed. The Lord, considering the 
helplessness of the jīva, out of compassion rescues him and 
lifts him up to His own level. The seeker on his part must 
follow the path with intense śraddhā, due reverence and love 
and become the fit recipient of His grace.

Once a devotee asked Bhagavan “will bhakti lead to 
mukti?” Bhagavan replied: Bhakti is not different from mukti. 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   522 06-05-2011   10:54:02



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 523

Bhakti is being as the Self (Swarūpa). One is always that. 
He realises it by the means he adopts. Bhakti is to think of 
God; only one thought prevails to the exclusion of all other 
thoughts. The thought is of God which is the Self or it is the 
Self surrendered unto God. When he has taken you up, nothing 
will assail you. The absence of thought is bhakti. That is also 
mukti. The jnana method is said to be vichara (enquiry) That 
is nothing but Supreme devotion, Parabhakti – The difference 
is in words.” (Talks no. 650).

That Ātma yoga defined as Knowledge of right perception 
is nothing but Ātma vichara is abundantly clear by the 
translation of the Bhuddi yoga from Sanskrit into English as 
“the yoga of Enquiry” by Bhagavan. Whatever be the path 
followed, in the final instance, path of enquiry or jñāna mārga 
is, according to Bhagavan, the inescapable tollgate. Bhagavan 
in Ramana Gītā, Chapter 7, Verse 7 very emphatically 
declares: “Marvellous occult powers may be had through 
other means. But in the end freedom can come only through 
Self-enquiry.”

Paraphrase: 
I, dwelling in the Self (heart/intellect), of those

Commentary: 

The question why should not the Lord bestow wisdom

compassion incarnate – grants wisdom only to those who seek 
Him with perseverance.
	 Annavar ullattu amarnde (seated in the hearts of 
those) who seek him whole-heartedly. God dwelling within 
as the “Essence” grants them this wisdom – a truth very 
often emphasised by Bhagavan that the real guru, Self, is 
within. “There is a stanza in Kaivalya which says, ‘O’ Guru! 
You have been always with me watching me through several 
reincarnations, and ordaining my course until I was liberated.” 
The Self manifests externally as Guru when occasion 
arises; otherwise He is always within, doing the needful.” 
(Talks no. 425). So the lamp is lighted from within. 
	 Annavar (‘those’) refers to those who have devotion, 
faith and śraddhā towards the Lord, who seated within, dispels 
entirely the ignorance born of beginningless nescience by the 
blazing light of jñāna. 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   524 06-05-2011   10:54:02



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 525

	 Thus bhakti or devotion leads to the complete 
destruction of ignorance by the effulgence of jñāna of 
sparkling Awareness. Thus when love or devotion and 
knowledge arise the eternal is fulfilled in an individual. Bhakti 
is a means to jñāna. What one has to do is to seek Him who 
is seated within. “Seek within you and find Him there, Then 
you will have constant communion with Him. The message is 
always there. It is never silent. It can never forsake you; nor 
can you ever move away from (this) Master.”

	 Tollirul (timeless darkness or darkness of ages) means 
ancient or long-standing dense darkness, that is ajñāna or 
nescience. A Saiva saint sings: 			 

                  “Since when art Thou
	                Since then am I”.
Since the day the Lord began creation calling himself 

the “Lord of Creation” from then on I am. I am as ancient 
as you are. The jīva is as beginningless as Iswara himself. 
Hence the jīva’s ignorance with its product of the darkness of 
delusion is spoken of as beginningless. Darkness here includes 
both the beginningless nescience and the illusory perception 
resulting from nescience. It cannot be removed by any material 
phenomena, belonging as it does to the same class of darkness. 
In all the types of knowledge spoken of variously as academic, 
scientific, practical and medical and so on, nescience is mixed 
up and deludes the scholars.

The darkness of a room kept locked for years can be 
dispelled only by lighting a lamp and not by any action or its 
repetition or of announcing the darkness by many. 

Immediately on the lamp being lit, there occurs the 
manifestation of an already existing thing consequently it 
is not that something  uncreated is created. In the same way 
when ignorance is to be dispelled there is no need for any 
action or its repetition other than the rise of knowledge. The 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   525 06-05-2011   10:54:02



526 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

darkness of nescience is removed by the Self manifesting 
Itself. The one has become many. Unless the many become 
one, nescience will not be destroyed. When the compassionate 
Lord, seated within, dispels the nescience of the jīva by the 
light of knowledge, there occurs the manifestation of already 
existing liberation which is identity with Brahman.

Very often the idea of the “flame of knowledge” is 
expanded as follows. “This flame is fed on the oil of clear 
devotion and enlivened by the breeze of internal love of 
contemplation on Me (Self). It’s wick is intellect strengthened 
by impressions of striving to cultivate celibacy, etc. It is 
ensconced  in the sense of detachment where the gusts 
of attachment and aversions do not blow as the mind has 
withdrawn from the sphere of objects and has the lustre of 
right perception born of ceaseless one-pointed meditation.” 

The holy Ganges quells the thirst of everyone who comes 
to her and drinks the water. To say that the Lord bestows grace 
only on His devotees and not on all is like complaining that 
Ganges is partial in quenching the thirst, by one who, though 
aware of his proximity to the river shows no inclination to 
drink its water.

When this śloka was being read out in Bhagavan’s 
presence, a devotee asked Bhagavan, “ Is complete devotion 
a precondition for the Lord showing grace and would not the 
Lord naturally in His Grace be kind to all His children whether 
they are devoted or not?” Bhagavan replied, “How can one 
help being devoted? Everyone loves himself. If the Self were 
not his dearest object would one love it?” As the devotee could 
not understand Mudaliar intervened “Bhagavan has told us 
more than once the Lord’s grace is always ‘flowing’. There 
is no time at which it is not flowing and no person towards 
whom it is not.... Devotion is a condition precedent, not for 
the flowing of grace but for your being able to receive and 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   526 06-05-2011   10:54:02



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 527

assimilate the grace which is there always flowing.” Then Dr. 
Sayeed quoted a verse from Gītā which says that “the Lord is 
the friend of all, the sinner and the saint alike, but that He is 
specially in the hearts of those who cherish him and that such 
people are dear to Him.” (Day by Day, 7.1.46). Paul Brunton 
records after his experience in the presence of Bhagavan 
“Divine grace descends and acts only when it is invoked by 
total Self-Surrender.... It’s whisper can be heard in a mind 
purified by Self-Surrender and devotion”. (Ibid, 4.1.46).

But the same Devaraja Mudaliar once said to Bhagavan 
that Subbaramiah was shown more favour than others to 
which Bhagavan replied, “To me there is no distinction. Grace 
is flowing like the ocean ever full. Everyone draws from it 
according to capacity. How can one who brings only a tumbler 
complain that he is not able to take as much as another who 
brought a jar.” (G.V.Subbaramiah, Reminiscences). 

Divine grace is the most powerful force in the universe.
In fact Bhagavan says, “The Guru (the Self, the Lord) is 

always within you. Thayumanavar sings, “Oh! Lord, coming 
with me all along the births never abandoning me and finally 
rescuing me”. Such is the experience of realisation. Śrīmad 
Bhagavad Gītā also says the same in a different way, “We 
too are not only now but have ever been so.” (Talks no. 398).

Commentary: 

When, by the Grace of the all-compassionate Lord, the 
darkness is once and for all destroyed, Knowledge that is 
Full, lights up the Supreme like the Sun. Jñāna is the Sun of 
wisdom. As the sun, by its mere rising, dispels the darkness 
entirely but does not depend on any auxiliary agent, similarly 
knowledge of Brahman, the form of pervasive light, eradicates 
ignorance together with its effects, by its mere emergence itself 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   528 06-05-2011   10:54:03



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 529

without depending on any auxiliary and reveals the Supreme. 
“Can there be darkness before the Sun? Similarly can there 
be ignorance before the Self-evident and Self-luminous Self? 
If you know the Self there will be no darkness, no ignorance 
and no misery.” (Talks no. 364). The man of divine knowledge 
not only realizes that God is jñāna or knowledge (Prajñanam 
Brahma), and that he himself is Brahman (aham Brahma 
asmi) but also is able to instruct others as That Thou Art 
(TAT TVAM ASI) and that this soul is Brahman. (Ayamātma 
Brahma).

The smoke and darkness of ignorance roll off. Just as 
the beloved one cannot be seen in a room plunged in utter 
darkness, the Lord, the beloved of All, one’s own Self, cannot 
be seen in ignorance. “The Sun is brightness only. He does not 
see darkness whereas others speak of darkness fleeing away 
on the sun approaching. Similarly ignorance also is a phantom 
and not real. Because of its unreality, its unreal nature being 
found, it is said to be removed. Again, the sun is there and also 
bright. You are surrounded by sunlight. Still if you want to 
know the Sun you must turn your eye in his direction and look 
at him. So also Grace is found by practice alone although it is 
here and now.” (Talks no. 354). The way of gaining this jñāna, 
indispensable for the removal of ignorance as mentioned in 
the earlier verse is to fix the mind in Him with a heart melting 
with devotion. Jñāna, bestowed on those who become the fit 
recipients of it drives away the dense darkness of ajñāna just 
like the physical sun drives away the darkness of the earth.

More than the world perceived this gross body is

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   530 06-05-2011   10:54:03



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 531

gross body. Considered greater than the senses is the 
mind. Greater than the mind is the subtle intellect or 
understanding. Far greater than the intelligence is He 
who shines in Self-revealing effulgence – the Supreme 
Self. Know this.
Commentary: 

Ātman is greater than all knowable principles and having 
none beyond shines in its own Self-revealing effulgence. This 
verse gives the hierarchy of levels of consciousness.

Greater than the external gross body, circumscribed and 
perceptible to the eyes, are the senses by virtue of their subtle 
nature, internal position, pervasiveness, nature of penetration 
into things thereby gaining knowledge of the objects.

The senses know the objects but the objects cannot – and 
do not – know the senses. Senses live without objects but 
without the senses, the existence of objects is not proved. 
Senses illumine the objects but the objects cannot illumine the 
senses. While the senses remain the same, the objects go on 
changing. So senses are greater and more powerful and have 
a wider range of activity than the objects or the physical body. 
Every sense knows only its own object and not the objects of 
other senses; for instance the eye can only see and not hear 
and so on.

The senses do not know the mind while the mind knows 
all the senses and their objects.

Therefore mind, characterised by volition and indecision 
is superior to the senses, for but for the association of the mind 
none of the indriyas (senses) can function – a fact revealed by 
the state of deep sleep devoid of mind when all the indriyas 
retire and rest. The mind, being more subtle and having a wider 
range of activity than the senses, is superior to the senses and is 
their illuminator. The mind which is nothing but the aggregate 
of sankalpas and vikalpas is imaginative and analytic.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   531 06-05-2011   10:54:03



532 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Arjuna came to the battlefield with the resolve to fight 
but the vikalpa causing sorrow, delusion – and subsequent 
agitation – made him tuck tail not out of cowardice but out 
of misplaced sympathy and ignorance.

When one is agitated by the various sankalpas and 
vikalpas and the mind buffeted and oscillating from one to 
the other is caught in the horns of a dilemma of whether to do 
or not to do, then the function of the intellect is to counsel the 
mind and make one approach men of knowledge requesting 
help and guidance to be out of the horns of the dilemma.

The intellect, whose essence is discrimination, weighs the 
pros and cons of the situation and reasons out the best course 
of action to be taken. The mind does not know the intellect 
but the intellect knows the mind, its thoughts, senses and their 
objects. Therefore intellect is rated superior to the mind. In this 
hierarchy each can know objects of grosser forms than itself.

But He who shines as Himself distinct from all these is 
the Self – interior to all the perceivable objects inclusive of 
the intellect – the embodied jīva the witness of all. Therefore 
Bhagavan says: “Intellect is a tool of the Self. Intellect is not 
the Self, nor apart from the Self.” (Talks no. 115).

First of all, the eye is the onlooker while the form is the 
object to be seen. Then the mind is the onlooker while the 
senses such as eyes are the objects to be seen. Then the intellect 
is the onlooker and the mind is the object to be seen. At last 
the Self is the onlooker or witness of the dispositions of the 
intellect but the Self can’t be seen by anyone. But all the others 
(the senses, mind and intellect) can know knowledge only 
when accompanied by the Self. The Upanishads declare that 
“the Self is the Eye of the eye and Mind of the mind.”. “Self 
is That which man does not comprehend with the mind, that 
by which the mind is encompassed, that which man does not 
see with the eye, that by which men perceive the activities of 
the eye.”   (Brihadaranyaka Upanishad).

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   532 06-05-2011   10:54:03



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 533

The import of this verse is that consciousness must be 
raised gradually to a level higher and higher so that the jīvas 
become freer and freer. When living in the consciousness of 
the world that is reported upon by the senses we are under the 
sway of the senses and exercise and enjoy the least freedom. 
If we live by the dictates of the mind, we enjoy more freedom. 
When the intellect is allowed to rein in the mind, the level 
of freedom also goes up. But when consciousness, divorced 
from and the tampering by all these instruments, is raised to 
the level of Pure Awareness of the Self, where the Self alone 
shines in It’s revealing light, that is release or freedom from 
all shackles.  Hence the effulgent Being, who is the director 
of the mind and other organs, is He who is the Eye of the 
eye, Ear of the ear, Mind of the mind, Speech of speech, the 
Life of life. Giving up all Self-identification with these, and 
renouncing the world, one should become immortal.

The desires that reside in the mighty senses, mightier 
mind and still mightier reason and understanding can be killed 
only by sole reliance on the saving grace of the Lord. Hence 
an Upanishad says “Let the wise man sink his senses in his 
mind; his mind in his understanding, his understanding in his 
Self and his Self in God.”

Kathopanishad has a verse very similar to this verse from 
Gītā which runs as “Beyond the sense objects are the senses, 
beyond the senses is the mind, beyond the mind is the intellect, 
beyond the intellect is the Great Ātman.” (3.10)

	 The senses are called great, greater the mind

The substitution of the word ‘understanding’ for ‘reason’ 

by Bhagavan depicts the enlarged scope of intellect as it is. 
While the original declares “He is far greater” as a matter 

of fact, Bhagavan has used an additional world milirvān 'one 
who shines', emphasises His effulgence that is Self-revealing. 

Kathopanishad (1.3.34) describes Ātman as the master, 
body as the chariot, intellect the charioteer, mind the reins, 
indriyas the horses and the paths the objects of senses. 

While the Sanskrit verse, as it stands in the original (Sa: 
he is greater than intellect) lends itself for misinterpretation 
and some have taken this Sa: – He in the original – as referring 
either to jīva, the ego or desire. Bhagavan, to avoid such 
misconstruing has stated clearly with no room for ambiguity in 
his Tamil rendition of the verse as “Know the one who shines 
greater than the intellect as the Ātman (ānmāvām ennaṛi). 

As Kathopanishad says “There is nothing higher than the 
Purusha. (1.3.11) “He is the highest goal.” (Ibid).

Paraphrase: 

The ever victorious Arjuna! Thus knowing Him, the 
effulgent Ātman, the form of jñāna, as far greater than 
understanding (intellect) and steadying the wavering mind 
in the intellect and inhering that (ego Self) in the Ātman, 
conquer desire, the true enemy so hard to overpower.
Commentary: 

Arjuna is an ever-victorious warrior. Vanquishing and 
slaying enemies on the battlefield is child’s play for him; yet 
the enemies within, namely desire and attachment, make him 
tuck tail and appear a chicken-hearted coward. What he did 
not realise is that his real foe is the form of desire, reaching 
or staying of which foe is not accomplished that easily. Here 
the Lord exhorts Arjuna to kill desire, the foe within, which 
assuming numerous forms that are scarcely intelligible, is 
difficult to apprehend, much less to overpower or conquer. 
“Desire, the fickle monkey sets foot on places which are not 
fit to be mounted upon, endeavours to obtain the fruit and 
satiated, does not remain in one place for a long time. Of all 
the ills of worldly life it is desire alone that gives long-lasting 
grief” (Yoga Vasishtam, Verses 65 and 66).

The conquest of this foe – desire – by Arjuna will place 
him in the enviable position of a foeless hero.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   535 06-05-2011   10:54:03



536 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

The enemy ‘desire’ aggrandises the mind gaining entry 
through the gateways of the indriyas or senses and destroys all 
human goals. Desires are in the mind caused by the objects of 
the senses in the outside world. If desire is to be vanquished 
senses which function through the mind must be sublated. 
Therefore the mind must be turned away from the sense 
objects. The jīva knows the world only by dissociating himself 
from That and the Lord only by identifying himself with 
Him. The scriptures also very emphatically say “When all the 
desires of the seeker are rooted out, the mortal man becomes 
immortal and realizes the eternal.”     (Kathopanishad,  2.3.14). 

The conquest of desire is to be accomplished by 
establishing the mind with the help of intellect in That which 
is realized to be superior to the intellect. Bhagavan explains 
fulfilment of desires accomplish nothing to us: “You do not 
grow by acquiring something nor wither away by losing it. 
You remain what you always are.” (Talks no. 614). Further 
he explains that desire springs from ‘I’ conceit which is from 
ignorance and ignorance springs from differentiation which 
in turn arises from the notion of reality of the world and this 
from ‘I am the body’ idea -; an outcome of the rise of ego. 
Therefore the rise of ego has to be prevented. “This can be 
done by remaining in your own real nature. Then lust, anger 
etc. are conquered.” (Talks no. 575).

Thus desire, the matchless foe, outcome of I and mine, 
masquerades as the friend of the Self by making the mind 
regard as enemies what is outside and deceives the Self by 
donning the robe of a friend. “The sole enemy in this battle 
(within) appears in just one form – desire – and slay him” says 
the Lord. Therefore when the mind, steadied by the intellect 
to abide in the Self by Self, then the ego, petrified, loses its 
hold and dissolves itself in the Self.

None can foretell when this foe-in-friendly-guise will 
aggrandise the mind making the conquest of him very difficult. 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   536 06-05-2011   10:54:03



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 537

Ahankara is the root of all these and is hard to be vanquished 
on account of its complex nature and hidden recesses it 
occupies. While anger can be seen, desire lurks unseen.

This verse speaks of steadying the restless ego by the 
light of the eternal Self. He who knows this becomes truly 
independent and seeks guidance from no power that is outside 
except his inner light. Therefore the advice is to kill desire 
the strongest foe by steadily composing the Self by the Self 
and relying on Him.

Paraphrase: 
Know that even as the fire burning with leaping 

tongues of flame consumes all fuel fed into it and turns it 
into ashes, just so the fire of knowledge burns all actions 
and reduces them to ashes leaving no remnant behind.
Commentary: 

That the fire of knowledge of the Self consumes all karmas 
is explained in this verse with an illustration. The vāsanās of 
actions performed in countless prior births remain in the jīva 
in the form of seeds. But these seeds of vāsanās responsible 
for future births by generating their fruits (effects) are burnt 
away by the knowledge of the Self. The mind is the origin of 
quite everything as the seed is the origin of a tree. When the 
origin (cause) of everything is renounced, everything is surely 
given up. Hence Yoga Vasishtam declares, “Between the two, 
mind and activity, which are ever united like fire and heat, on 
the annihilation of either, both just vanish.”, (Verse 2062). 

	 Karmas are of three kinds namely prārabdha that has 
started to fructify, sanchita, accumulated karma waiting to 
fructify and agami, actions performed during the period of 
experiencing the prārabdha which will start to yield in future 
births. It is said that Self-Knowledge burns up sanchitam and 
agami i.e., works done in previous births before the dawn of 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   538 06-05-2011   10:54:03



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 539

Knowledge and which have not begun to bear fruits as well 
as those which co-exist with Knowledge but prārabdha will 
be exhausted only by experiencing the rest of the prārabdha. 
Bhagavan clarifies this: “The scriptures say that jñāna is the 
fire which burns away all karma (Sarvakarmani) (in Tamil 
karumam anaittum). Sarva (all, anaittum) is interpreted in 
two ways: 1. To include prārabdha and 2. To exclude it ‘As 
per the first’ if a man with three wives dies can two of them be 
called widows and the third not? All are widows. So it is with 
prārabdha, agami and sanchita. When there is no karta, none 
of them can hold out any longer. The second explanation is 
however given only to satisfy the enquirer.... From the jñāni’s 
point of view there is only the Self... There is no body or 
karma apart from the Self, so that actions do not affect him.” 
(Talks no. 383).

	 Those who have experienced the sublime thought-
free state are non-doers. Bhagavan explains “The activities 
of the wise men exist only in the eyes of others and not his 
own although he may be accomplishing immense tasks, he 
really does nothing. Therefore his activities do not stand 
in the way of inaction and peace of mind. For the knowers 
of Truth all activities take place in the mere presence and 
that he does nothing.” (Upadēsa Manjari, 2-25). He is 
simply the silent witness. The actions pertain to the body. 
The jñāni is like the sleeping passenger – or like a child 
interrupted from sleep and fed, being unaware of it. The 
child says the next day that he did not take the milk at all, 
and that he went to sleep without it. Even when reminded 
he cannot be convinced.” (Talks no. 82). A jñāni may 
appear to act but does not. His eyes are likened to the eyes 
of a dead goat. “They are always open, never closed. They 
glitter but they see nothing, though it seems to others that 
they see everything.” (Letters, 26-10-47). 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   539 06-05-2011   10:54:03



540 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

A jñāni’s perception is blind to the denotative knowledge 
of the world. For a man of Knowledge to perform actions, it 
is not essential that the world has to be real as such.

An Ātmajñāni without any attachment to the body, simply 
being a witness of all that is happening before, regarding both 
pain and pleasure as mere dreams, never getting dislodged 
from the state of remaining the Self, is established as the form 
of serene peace. Nothing exists here as purifying as the blazing 
fire of Knowledge in which all actions perish.

	 “When the knot (of ignorance) in one’s heart is broken, 
there is no fettering (or bondage) again by the qualities of 
Nature. By whom is a fruit that has fallen down fastened again 
to the stalk even with effort.” (Yoga Vasishtam, Verse 2275).

One whose undertakings are free from desire and

Commentary: 

This verse delineates the characteristics of a Stita Prajña 
or a Brahma nishta – one who is anchored in Brahman for 
purposes of easy identification so that mumukshus desirous 
of the Knowledge of the Self can seek them out.

Evan - ‘Who’, here stands for one who has realized the 
Truth. As there is no purifier like the fire of Knowledge and all 
works attain their consummation in Knowledge, he is one who 
is immaculate with all karmas burnt. He desires nothing and 
this wantlessness enhances the aura of his spiritual radiance. 

Ellamum stands for all his undertakings either mundane 
or otherwise that he may appear to engage himself in which 
are devoid of desires, resolution and the idea of agency or 
kartrutva bhāva. Therefore all his actions lose their binding 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   541 06-05-2011   10:54:03



542 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

potentiality; for “work performed with attachment is a shackle 
whereas work performed with detachment does not-affect the 
doer. He is, even while working, in solitude.” (Talks no. 20).

Whatever work an Ātmajñāni does will be perfect. He 
is already a pandita with the effulgence of Knowledge, pure 
with all karmas burnt and before undertaking an action, there 
will be neither the Sankalpa to do it in a particular way nor 
the sense of doership. But it will be a spontaneous action. He 
is one in whom the activities of the mind have ceased and 
therefore there is no room either for desire to act or resolve 
or desire for the fruits of actions. Hence he is one whose 
actions have been consumed. “Having attained to oneness 
with the Highest Truth, I do not know where the mind is 
gone and where desire, actions and the perceptions of joy and 
anger”.   (Yoga Vasishtam , 2274). All the actions of such a 
one will be executed more beautifully and skilfully than one 
who does with attachment. Such a one is a yati (monk) and 
yogī Supreme. “He does not arrogate to himself the function 
of being the actor. The actions go on automatically. Even the 
question of non-attachment for fruits of actions arises only if 
there is the actor.” (Talks no. 643). Bhagavan often used to say 
Gītā teaches “actorless action” and he perfectly exemplified 
the famous dictum of Gītā “Yogah karmasu kausalam” – Yoga 
or union with Brahman is skill in action.”. Bhagavan further 
explains how actions performed by such a one are not action. 
“Sri Krishna says in the Bhagavad Gītā ‘I am not the doer and 
yet the actions go on.’ It is clear from the Mahabharata that 
very wonderful actions were effected by Him. Yet He says that 
He is not the doer. It is like the sun and the world of actions.” 
(Talks no. 467). So was it with Bhagavan.

Even an ordinary chore undertaken by Bhagavan, be it 
either binding of a book, stitching of leaf-plates, cutting of 
vegetables (they will be uniform and equal in size) or carving 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   542 06-05-2011   10:54:03



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 543

of cups and spoons out of coconut shells (which he called 
as “our golden cups and silver spoons”) or even preparing 
dishes, all shone with consummate artistry and perfection. 
Anything he touched became pleasant, orderly. But he was 
totally detached from the outcome of them all. After working 
on them painstakingly and meticulously he would hand them 
over to anyone in need. After giving detailed instructions in 
the preparation of various items or sometimes preparing them 
himself, when served with during lunch, he would mix them 
all up and gulp them down.

The stita prajña of Gītā was Bhagavan in flesh and blood. 
Ashtavakra Gītā states “Even renunciation of actions by a 
deluded person is conducive to action while even performance 
of actions of a wise man leads to actionlessness.” Bhagavan 
provides examples for  both. “1. A child is fed while asleep. 
On waking up the next morning he denies having been fed. 
It is a case of inaction in seeming action. 2. The cartman 
sleeps in the cart when it jogs along the way in the night and 
yet he reaches the destination and claims to have driven the 
cart. This is a case of action in seeming inaction. 3. A man 
appearing to listen to a story nods his head to the speaker but 
his mind is otherwise active and does not really follow the 
story. 4. Two sleep side by side. One of them dreams that both 
of them travel round the globe and have varied experiences. 
On waking the dreamer tells the other that both of them have 
been round the earth. The other treats the story with contempt.” 
(Talks no. 607). While the first corresponds to the actions of 
a jñāni, the rest to ordinary mortals.

But the jñāni is fully aware that the true state of ‘Being’ 
remains fixed and stationary and that all actions go around 
him. His nature does not change and his state is not affected in 
the least. He looks on everything with unconcern and remains 
blissful himself.

Paraphrase: 
Total and everlasting beatitude of Brahman will be 

the direct, immediate (aparōksha) experience of those 
yatis or sannyāsins delivered from the cravings of desire 
and anger, devoid of thoughts and with a subdued mind, 
bereft of the bondage of attachments and who have 
realized the Ātman, the effulgence of jñāna.
Commentary: 

Raga or desire is defined as the attraction to pleasure. 
A mind, desire-driven, is the cause of bondage and a mind 
freed of desire is the cause of freedom in man. Desire is the 
root-cause of all disasters. Real saṁsāra and its aftermath 
start with desire which is the cause of all karmas, animating 
indriyas and organs to function. Desire wreaks havoc in men 
with its inseparable companions of fear and anger.

Non-attainment of the desired object creates anger 
towards impediments that thwart the desire. “From anger 
arises delusion; from delusion  confusion of memory and loss 
of reason and when reason is lost, man is lost” says the Lord 
in an earlier verse. With subsidence of desire and anger, mind 
becomes subdued. These are but the manifestations of the ego. 
When the ego is annihilated without a whit left behind, Ātman 
shines with no let or hindrance.

Further desire for perishable objects is kama. A man has a 
desire only when he lacks something. There is privation only in 
the unreal while the real Self is not wanting in anything. When 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   545 06-05-2011   10:54:03



546 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

one identifies oneself with the unreal one feels something 
lacking in him. This feeling of shortage gives birth to desire 
but those who have no identity with the unreal and who have 
realized the Self experience no privation. The mind and body 
of such yatis become the instruments of the Lord, a chariot for 
the Divine charioteer. They experience the bliss of Brahman 
as direct or aparōksha anubhūti and the Bliss of the knower 
is said to be the Supreme Bliss on a particle of which beings 
from Hiranyagarba (Brahma) down to the lowest being thrive. 
The bliss derived from the satisfaction of all other desires by 
those who consider themselves as separated from Brahman 
is but the distorted reflection of an infinitesimal fraction of 
the Bliss of Brahman.

True sannyās or renunciation is sacrifice of the mind. One 
might not have donned ochre robes yet whosoever has subdued 
the mind is a great yati or sannyāsi. Total bliss is natural to 
him and not what comes and goes like desire.

Kāma and krōdha (desire and anger) are simply thought 
movements. These inner enemies, like an intoxicating drink, 
drive one down the dark pit of despair. Therefore giving up 
thoughts in their entirety is a way to annihilate desire and 
anger and enter the gates of Heavenly Bliss. “Non-attachment, 
Illumination and desirelessness (vairagya, bhoda, uparati) 
these three will not remain separate from one another.” 
(Letters, 28-10-47). 

This verse contains the exposition of the entire fifth 
chapter, says Sankara and it is highly significant that Bhagavan 
has selected this verse.

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 547

The Bliss of the Eternal enfolds those
Who know themselves, weaned from desire and wrath
Subdued in nature and subdued in thought.
The only change introduced by Bhagavan is ‘Bliss’ for 

‘peace’ which is profound and striking. 
Bhagavan was the perfect proof of the content of this 

verse. Even conditions that appear most trying for ordinary 
mortals never moved him even a little from the state he was 
established in. The mind having disappeared along with 
its desire and anger once and for all during the first death 
experience, the rest of his life was a perfect demonstration of 
“His will being his will and His joy being his joy.”. He was 
the happiest and most powerful emperor, with earth as his seat, 
hands as plates for taking food, loin cloth for an apparel, the 
sky as the canopy and renunciation as his spouse so much so 
Ganapathy Muni sang of him: kara thamara sena supatravata 
- as the ideal renunciate.  “No want is the greatest bliss. It can 
be realised only by experience. Even an emperor is no match 
for a man with no want. The emperor has got vassals under 
him. But the other man is not aware of any one, besides the 
Self. Which is better?” (Talks no. 648). 

When the Maharani of Baroda sent a velvet shawl, 
Bhagavan refused to use it, however much persuaded overtly 
and covertly by others. Similarly silver tumblers and plates, 
costly walking sticks or wooden sandals with silver fittings and 
costly pens, all went untouched but were sternly commanded 
to be sent back, with “Of what use are these to me?” His 
quiescence of the Self was so powerful as to creep in and 
possess those in his presence and the lives of many devotees 
transformed hold testimony to this. 

Adangu manam uttrar: (those with mind quiescent) are 
jñānis in whose presence the quiescence of the Ātman in which 
they forever abide can almost tangibly be felt by those around

being plunged into it.

What they are abusing is your body... what greater enemy is 
there than the body, the abode of anger and similar feelings... 
If anybody abuses us, we should know that they are ‘waking 
us up’.” (Letters, 26-1-1946).

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 549

Paraphrase: 
Oh Mighty charioteer! Endeavouring for that Brahma 

nirvāna by a valourous and discriminative understanding, 
little by little (not obstinately and at one go) free the mind 
from thoughts and its nature of perpetual movement. 
Make it steady and still, fix it steadfastly in the Ātman 
and do not at all think of anything else.
Commentary: 

The mind always runs after objects of the external world 
due to vāsanās acquired from beginningless time. Turning it 
inward in an instant is not possible. With stoic discrimination, 
coupled with valour of a high order, it can be accomplished 
only little by little. The mind with restlessness as its nature 
bounces back like a rubber ball with renewed gusto if it is tried 
to be pushed in impetuously. “Practice is necessary. It is like 
training a roguish bull confined to his stall by tempting him with 
luscious grass and preventing him from straying.”     (Talks no. 
220). The mind must repeatedly be told that the Self alone is 
all this. This is the Supreme injunction. As Manivachakar says 
in Thiruvachakam “O, Humming bee! (namely mind) Why 
do you take the pains of collecting tiny specks of honey from 
innumerable flowers? There is one from whom you can have 
the whole store-house of honey by simply thinking or seeing 
or speaking of Him. Get within and hum to Him.”

The mind divested of all thoughts must be brought to a 
standstill and then fixed firmly in the Ātman. Mind emptied of 
thoughts acquires the fitness to inhere in the Ātman. “If thought 
seeks to comprehend Brahman, which is one’s own Self, it 
loses its separate identity and becomes ‘That’.” (Ramana Gītā, 
Chap. 4, Verse 8).

Once a gentleman complained that his mind was not 
steady. Bhagavan quoted this verse and also drew attention to 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   549 06-05-2011   10:54:04



550 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

another verse in the same chapter. When Arjuna complains that 
the mind is fickle, violent, powerful, obstinate and is as difficult 
to be controlled as the wind, the Lord replies “Doubtless, O 
mighty armed! The mind is fickle and hard to curb. But by 
constant practice and detachment (abhyasa and vairagya) 
it can be controlled.” It was then that Bhagavan quoted the 
24th verse from 6th chapter to explain vairagya. It runs thus: 
“Abandoning without exception all desires born of selfish 
will, restrain with the mind all the senses from every side.” 
As for practice Bhagavan quoted the present verse and for 
jñāna the following verse. It requires great valour to turn the 
adamantine mind inward but once it becomes a fait accompli 
no thought whatsoever should be entertained. “Looking at the 
mind with the mind, or fixing the mind in the Self, brings the 
mind under the control of the Self.”   (Talks no. 378). “The 
sādhaka must remain as the Self. If he cannot do so, he must 
ascertain the true meaning of the ‘I’ and constantly revert to it 
whenever thoughts arise. That is the practice.” (Talks no. 647). 
The mind must be cut off root and branch. One must see who 
the thinker is, who the seeker is and abide as the thinker, the 
seeker. Then all thoughts disappear. This is what is described 
as Ātmavile mannach cheidu” (made to inhere in the Ātman).

Mella Mella – gradually or little by little. The ways of 
sādhanā are said to be three in kind; those of a bird, a monkey 
and an ant. A bird while it flies with a fruit after pecking at it 
may let it slip. When a monkey with food jumps from branch 
to branch may let it fall. But an ant slowly and steadily, with 
heroic perseverance gathers food little by little and enjoys it 
in peace at leisure. This is the best way.
