Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   551 06-05-2011   10:54:04



552 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Commentary: 
Mind is extremely fickle and wavering by nature. Ever 

unsteady and never still, it keeps oscillating forever like the 
shuttle of the power loom. Getting hold of an object of any 
one of the five senses of perception it wanders forever and 
suddenly and swiftly passes from that one to the other. As it 
runs faster than the wind, steadying it and bringing it to a stand 
still is indeed a battle – royal. The Lord in this verse teaches a 
way to accomplish this hard task. Let the mind be instructed 
on the true nature (unreality) of the matter or object it has 
held on to so far, reduce them to empty appearances, let it be 
withdrawn and make it loosen its hold; resort to detachment, 
turn it inward and bring it under the sway of the Self. 

edu edanaip pattriye ehum (holding on to whichever 
object) refers to whatever causes the mind to go astray, 
become restless, unsteady and to wander away. The causes 
are: attachment and aversion, sound, sight, vishaya (matters) 
sleep vikshepa, kashaya, rasaswadha. Bhagavan explains 
these obstacles: vikshepa refers to the sense objects, kashaya 
are thoughts in the mind about previous experiences with the 
sense objects; rasaswadha otherwise called ananda where a 
feeling of separation from the source of ananda. But a yogī, 
each time it strays out, must withdraw it from whatever it has 
held on to, so that it becomes neither restless nor inactive. All 
vrittis must be annihilated. Just as swarms of flies come out in 
a continuous stream so also vrittis or thought waves gush out 
from the mind in a continuous current. Just as a soldier kills 
his enemy one by one when he emerges from the fortress, so 
also each thought even as it rises has to be killed at the source.

In this battle royal, the fight will truly be hard and often 
victory may temporarily rest with the mind. But the fight will 
have to be carried on without giving room for despair, bringing 
the mind every time it goes astray to the control of the Self. 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   552 06-05-2011   10:54:04



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 553

“When the five senses of knowledge come to rest together 
with the mind and the intellect too does not function, that state 
they call the highest.” (Kathopanishad ,2-3-10). Realization, 
is after all freedom from the tyranny of thoughts.

“Practice is power. If thoughts are reduced to a single 
thought, the mind is said to have grown strong. When practice 
remains unshaken it becomes sahaja (natural)... Ātman is the 
aim... one pointedness is the fruit of all practice... One may 
get it quickly; another after a long time. Everything depends 
on the practice.” (Talks no. 290). 

This verse again emphasizes the importance of vairaghya 
and abhyasa. Vairaghya is the absence of diffused thought; 
abhyasa is concentration on one thought only. The one is the 
positive and the other negative aspects of meditation.

Once a devotee from Andhra expressed the impossibility 
of stilling the mind specially in the midst of everyday life. 
Bhagavan answered, “Everyday life is not divorced from 
Eternal state. If spirituality is rightly understood, the active 
life will be found to be not different from it. Can the mind be 
got at by the mind on looking for it as an object? The source 
of mental functions must be sought and gained. That is the 
Reality. One does not know the Self owing to the interference 
of thoughts. The Self is realised when thoughts subside.” 
Whenever the turbulent mind wavers then and there pull it and 
bring it under control ‘Seeing the mind with the mind’ (manasā 
mana ālokya) so proclaim the Upanishads.” (Talks no. 376).

While Bhagavan quoted the earlier verse for abhyasa 
(practice), for jñāna he quoted this verse. Sacrificing the mind 
is real sannyāsa when it becomes like a lamp in a windless 
place.

Thus the Lord exhorts Arjuna to withdraw the fickle mind 
from wherever it goes wandering, still it and poise it back in 
the Self. Lord Krishna conveys the same idea in Bhāgavatam 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   553 06-05-2011   10:54:04



554 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

“Whenever the mind runs away under the stress of desires a 
discriminating person should draw it towards the heart again 
and again and concentrate there. Such a practice without break 
will soon subside in calmness as the fire that has consumed 
the fuel.” (7.15.83).

When the mind does not become lost, nor again it is 
scattered, when it is motionless and does not appear in the 
form of objects then it becomes Brahman. For obliteration of 
thoughts, Bhagavan emphasises:  “The Gītā’s method is the 
only one for it.” (Talks no. 287). Mind (Chittam) bereft of the 
letter ‘ta‘ (Chittam – ta = Chit) becomes consciousness. ‘Ta’, 
indicates association with worldliness just as a colourless gem 
manifests colour in the proximity of a china rose. (Sankara, 
quoted in Letters, 28-1-1947 as foot note).

Further Bhagavan assures us that “Even a single effort to 
still at least a single thought even for a trice goes a long way 
to reach the state of quiescence.” (Talks no. 609).

Paraphrase: 

That sage, who reining in all senses, mind and 
understanding from having their whimsical ways, has 
controlled and subdued them, has cast away completely 
desire, fear and hatred, solely intent on Liberation desiring 
nothing else and devoutly endeavouring for it, is the best

Commentary: 

This verse teaches the Supreme way of reaching the goal 
mukti. Tapas or austerity is focusing of senses and mind on a 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   555 06-05-2011   10:54:04



556 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

single thing to the exclusion of everything else so much so all 
senses and mind become the very form of what is focused on. 
Control or subjugation of mind, senses and understanding is 
the essential characteristic of tapas. However that alone will 
not suffice. One solely intent on Liberation desiring nothing 
else must continually be striving for it. One who observes such 
a continuous vigil alone is a muni, nay, the best among munis.

The word muni  means one who is adept in the discipline 
of manana. After listening to the Ātmatattva explained by a 
competent teacher, one who ceaselessly reflects upon what 
was heard with no other thought except that of mukti is muni 
sreshtan, the best among such munis.

Not all those who perform tapas can become sages. The 
rakshasas or demons like Ravana and Surapadma were great 
tapasvins yet they undertook penance and observed austerities 
for fulfilment of specific desires.

One who has controlled, in addition to the senses, mind 
and understanding, desire, hatred, fear and anger alone is 
called a mukta or a liberated one. Yet control of desires is not 
easy. Many devotees have repeatedly requested Bhagavan for 
effective ways of curbing desire and other passions. These 
vices of the mind are closely interrelated. There is no fear 
without desire and no anger and hatred without fear. These 
dualities are dependent on the mind and with the control of 
mind, they are easily controlled. But Bhagavan asks: “for those 
who have abandoned their ego mind, what other things besides 
that (mind) are left that are worthy of being renounced?” 
(Pādamālai,Verse 103).

After we have renounced whatever 
Can be renounced, That which abides
And cannot be renounced, is True
Being shining in the Heart
The fount, the flood of Bliss.
			            (Guru Vāchaka Kovai, Verse 836)

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 557

Bhagavan instructs that once whence all happiness 
including the one that appears to come from objects is seen, 
it will be realized that all happiness comes from the Self, and 
then one will always abide in the Self. “All experiences and the 
absence of them contain the illumination which is the nature of 
the Self. Without the Self, they cannot be experienced, just as 
without sugar not one of the articles you make out it can taste 
sweet”. (Day by Day, 21.7.46). Bhagavan further instructs 
“oudasinyam abhipsitam – Indifference is advised. But what 
is it? All these experiences are phenomena that pass on the 
Self. Once you know this “Will you love or hate them? That 
is the meaning of indifference”. Further “you know that you 
are not the mind. The desires are in the mind. Such knowledge 
helps one to control them.” (Talks no. 495).

The world’s ways bewilder and cause reaction only from 
minds attached to them, not those detached. Such a serene 
and Self-contained mind is like a vast ocean deep and calm 
untroubled by any ripple of desire, fear and aversion.  With 
the abiding of the mind in the Ātman, all else drop off by 
themselves and become non-existent. In fact ego’s destruction 
is the most flawless worship of the Lord.

Awareness is detachment, purity;
Awareness is propinquity to God;
Constant awareness is freedom from fear;
It is immortality; it is
Everything and all there is.
			          (Guru Vāchaka Kovai, Verse 438)

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 559

Paraphrase: 
One with a blemishless mind ever poised firmly in 

the Self and steadfast in this yoga, sees with the same 
sightedness the Self abiding everywhere and in all beings 
from Brahma down to a worm and sees all beings in him, 
the Self. Such a yogī of samadhrishti is most fortunate 
and highly blessed for he has attained all there is to be 
attained.
Commentary: 

When the sense of a separate and finite self with hopes, 
fears, likes and dislikes is destroyed, it abides in the Self and 
everywhere beholds the Self alone in all beings from Brahma 
down to a blade of grass. During the period and process of 
sādhanā one had to retreat from the world and external things 
to attain the vision of the Self but once the Self is realized, the 
world and everything else is withdrawn into and absorbed by 
the Self or the Self expands as All. Such a one is unified in 
consciousness with the eternal Self. The perception of such a 
one has for its object the identity of Brahman and Ātman. He 
sees the Self – which is indeed One, eternal, omnipresent, the 
inmost consciousness, the Witness present in all things, i.e., 
in all bodies moving or unmoving – to be different from the 
things Witnessed which are unreal, finite and sorrowful by 
nature and in that Self, the witness, he sees all things witnessed 
which are imagined as distinct from the witness. This insight 
filled with truth makes him see everything as indeed the same, 
be it concealed or subtle or remote.

Possessed of this cognition of the identity of Brahman and 
the Self and perceiving this identity without any distinction, 
such a one beholds one’s own Self abiding in all beings and 
all beings as one. One is the Self within, without, everywhere 
and in everyone. As the Self is bliss through and through, one’s 
heaven lies about everywhere.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   559 06-05-2011   10:54:04



560 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

With the attainment of the yoga of oneness in the Self, a 
steadfast oneness with all in the universe becomes the very 
nature of one’s being. Bhagavan declares: “The Self in all 
and all in the Self.” – That contains the whole truth. Even 
this is oupacharika (a courtesy). There is in fact nothing but 
the Ātman. The world is only a projection of the mind. The 
mind originates from the Ātman . So Ātman alone is the one 
Being.” (Talks no. 100).

While Lord Krishna utters the verse as a statement, 
Bhagavan by using the two words danniyan andattavan (That 
yogī is most fortunate and blessed) has extolled such a sage.

That Bhagavan remained as the Self in all and saw all 
in the Self was experienced by many a devotee on several 
occasions. His samadhristi (equal sightedness of seeing the 
Self everywhere) was obvious in all aspects of daily life and 
towards all without exception be it birds or beasts, pandits 
or illiterates, people good or bad or belonging to various 
echelons of society. He never referred to an animal as ‘it’ but 
always as ‘he’ or ‘she’ or ‘lads’ or Lakshmi. The animals were 
always fed first. Then the beggars and finally the devotees: 
The animals were equally the recipients of his grace as the 
devotees. When Krishnaswamy, the attendant beat monkeys 
who played mischief in the old hall, Bhagavan told him, “It 
is not the monkeys that are receiving your beatings. It is I, the 
suffering is mine”. Once when workers, with long bamboo 
sticks were thrashing violently a mango tree to bring down 
the fruits, a large number of leaves, twigs and branches had 
fallen down. He said: “enough! enough! What havoc you have 
created! Get aside.. We don’t want to have mangoes this way.”

It is common knowledge how Bhagavan was keen that 
everyone was served alike whether it was a costly item or 
of the quality of routine like the buttermilk or the quantity. 
Anything not shared by all was like poison to him. Once when 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   560 06-05-2011   10:54:04



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 561

somebody served him more of a rare item, he looked up and 
said “Do I eat with only one mouth?”

It was a rule with Sri Maharshi not to take any costly food 
at all and if a rich dish was brought to him, it was invariably 
distributed equally among all the diners.

Even when his health was deteriorating  fast he refused 
to have fruit juice and nourishing food saying he would not 
have it unless it was distributed to all. “How can we afford to 
have such a luxurious diet? For us there can only be the poor 
man’s ration.” (Surpassing Love and Grace, page 85).

Someone sitting in the hall had a very painful headache. 
Holding his head with his hands, he mentally prayed to 
Bhagavan for relief. The next moment he got relief and opened 
his eyes only to see Bhagavan holding his head with his hands.

Instances such as these are legion indeed and fortunate are the 
devotees to have had Brahman embodied moving in their midst.

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 563

Paraphrase: 
Those who always worship Me (the Ātman) 

meditating on Me alone with Ātmabhāva to the exclusion 
of even an iota of anyother thought and are ever united 
with Me (the Ātman), to them I vouchsafe to bear on my 
head their yoga (attainment of what they have not)  and 
kshema (security in what they have).
Commentary: 

Ātma yoga is nothing but the union of para and jīva and 
not the jīva remaining as the worshipping one and Ātman the 
other, worshipped. This is ananya bhakti. Bhagavan explains 
this “I approach Iswara and pray to be absorbed in Him. I then 
surrender myself in faith and by concentration. What remains 
afterwards? In place of the original ‘I’ perfect Self surrender 
leaves a residue of God in which the ‘I’ is lost. This is the 
highest form of devotion (Parabhakti) Prapatti, Surrender 
or the height of vairagya’... The I and mine are given up in a 
stroke.” (Talks no. 26).

“Those persons who have no object of vision and who 
thinking of the inmost Self as non-separate see ‘Me’ (Self) 
everywhere and to them I arrange for the acquisition of what 
they lack (yoga) and the preservation of what is attained 
(Kshema). I carry gain and security” is the import of this verse.

This is a highly celebrated and key verse in the form of 
a promise of the Almighty to all true devotees. If yoga and 
kshema are to be understood in their esoteric content, it should 
be taken to mean making the yogī attain the union of jīva and 
para which hitherto had not been attained and guarding him 
from slipping from that state.

A true bhakta or a yogī surrenders ‘I’ and ‘mine’ to the 
Lord Himself. Ennaiye Unni means thinking of Me (that 
inmost Self) harbouring no desire except that of the Lord 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   563 06-05-2011   10:54:04



564 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

(Self). Ennile ondrum – those who see Me as their own 
Self and abide in it. Taking care of them and guarding them 
becomes His bounden duty and responsibility. He ever remains 
as their saviour providing the needed things just at the time 
needed.

For those who are established in non-dual vision and are 
absolutely desireless making no effort of their own, how can 
there be acquisition of what they lack and protection of what 
they have? Hence He arranges for them on His own even 
though they do not hanker after it.

Although the Lord arranges for the yoga and kshema 
of everyone without exception, still in the case of others he 
arranges for it through Self-effort. He arouses in them a desire 
for these but in the case of jñānis who cherish no desire for 
life or death the Lord Himself secures to them gain and safety.

The original Sanskrit verse runs as follows:

Chadwick’s translation initially had ‘I bring the power’,

Bhagavan has very significantly introduced two new

taliyāl (on my head) I bear. This reemphasis of this assurance 
emanating as it does from Bhagavan, inspires and emboldens 
the resolve of devotees to stay anchored in him.

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 565

A legend that has traditionally been told, reveals the 
aptness of the use of the word ‘On My head’ by Bhagavan. 
There was a great scholar devotee of Lord Krishna who eked 
out his living by delivering discourses of scriptures like Śrīmad 
Bhāgavatam and Gītā. Though the income was meagre to 
support his large family, he lead a happy and contented life 
with his sole faith and love centred on the Lord. He was writing 
a commentary on the Gītā and when he came to this verse was 
puzzled as to how the Lord could bear (vahamyaham) for his 
devotee everything he needed, he concluded that it must have 
been an interpolation. He scratched out the word vahamyaham 
(I bear) and substituted it by dadamyaham (I supply). Once 
his work took him to villages on the other bank of the river by 
the side of which he was living. That day after he finished his 
discourse, he found to his dismay that the river had become 
swollen with flash flood and was not fordable anymore. He had 
to remain there for a few days perforce but he was distraught 
with worry about the fate of his wife and children; who he 
thought would be starving with nothing to eat and none to 
provide for them while he was stranded on the other side. 
However, during his absence, a young boy drove a cart laden 
with necessary provisions and fruits and handed them over to 
the lady of the house saying “your husband will not return till 
tomorrow. So he has sent me with this”. The lady on noticing 
some red scratches on his forehead, lovingly enquired the 
boy about them with concern. The boy replied “your husband 
scratched my forehead before he sent me”. So saying he went 
away. The devotee-scholar on his return was relieved to see 
his family safe and came to know what had transpired in his 
absence. The wife admonished him on his cruel behaviour 
towards the boy saying there were traces of blood. The devotee 
was struck dumb with the revelation that the Lord Himself 
had carried to them what they needed. Needless to say he 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   565 06-05-2011   10:54:04



566 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

immediately restored the word vahamyaham (bear the yoga 
and kshema) and repeated it thrice.

But Bhagavan goes further and assures that the Lord 
bears the burden of providing both on His head. Bhagavan 
once remarked “there is no need to remind God about His 
business which is to keep an eye always on our welfare.” 
(Unforgettable years, page 122).

The stories of nāyanmārs are replete with instances when 
Lord Siva Himself brings food and sustains the lives of Appar, 
Sundarar and Sambandhar and on one occasion he brings 
food obtained by begging Himself. Saints Thayumanavar and 
Kumara deva at Vriddachalam and Guhai Namasivaya were 
all fed by Devi Herself.

The Lord of Pandarpur served not for a day or two but 
continuously for 12 long years as a domestic servant to sage-
devotee Ekanath . Lord Panduranga relieved Sakku Bai form 
her home prison and enabled her to visit Pandarpur. While 
referring to this Bhagavan “recollected the appearance of a 
mysterious Moulvi on his way from Madura to Tiruvannamalai 
in 1896, how he appeared, spoke and disappeared suddenly.” 
(Talks no. 83). But the direct proof of this truth amply borne 
out can be seen in the life of Bhagavan right from the days 
he stepped into Arunachala as a lad of sixteen with total 
renunciation and Arunachala as his sole refuge. The perfect 
nature of surrender that elicits the Lord’s bearing the burden 
of yoga and kshema of the surrendered is best revealed in his 
life. Bhagavan did nothing to satisfy the needs of the body. 
Everything happened by divine chance. His thoughts were 
on the Father and His Kingdom, the Self. His throwing away 
of all his belongings in the land was symbolic of his total 
surrender and jettisoning of all the non-Self. He never again 
touched money. Discarding the sacred thread signified his 
transcending varṇa and ashrama while casting off the cloth, 
the vow of holy poverty. Henceforth with earth as bed, arms as 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   566 06-05-2011   10:54:05



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 567

cover, palm as plate he lived in the ‘many mansions’ (caves) 
of His Father’s House (The Hill) and the one who feeds the 
toads in stones fed and clothed him. He lived the Truth that 
he experienced: “The son was contained within the father.”  

A long line of people chosen and appointed by the 
Lord took care of his food: Ratnammal, Mounaswamy, 
Uddandi Nayanar, the temple priest, Annamalai Tambiran, 
Palaniswamy, Keeraipatty, Mudaliar Patty and Echchammal. 
Then the ashram grew up. About one and half years after his 
first visit to Tiruvannamalai he was given a second bath at 
Gurumoortham by a granny. Bhagavan reminisced “There was 
no question of a bath; who was to make me bathe; who was the 
one to bathe?” (Letters). Minakshi brought all necessary things 
for a bath, heated the water and said “Swami, please come, get 
up.”. Bhagavan did not move. She pulled him by the arm and 
he had no choice. (“I would just be a trifle for a single hand 
of hers”) ......tamil text......... The hair looking like a basket 
or a birds nest, having collected stones and dirt had become 
a clotted mass. After the bath it became clean and spread out 
like the mane of a lion. He would never ask for anything but 
everything came unasked. Whether it was the desire of the 
mother for ladles, or urgent need for myrobalams to control 
cough or raisins or oranges, somehow they all came. Later 
when the Ashram was in straits and though Bhagavan showed 
no concern, some unknown benefactors would supply them 
or known devotees would arrive with just the things needed. 
Perfect submission and delight were his and Arunachala 
became his loving benefactor. Muruganar hails that Bhagavan, 
verily the Brahman, bears 

“On his dedicated head carries 
As if were his own, all burdens 
His devotees should bear.” 
                                  (Ramana Sannidhi Murai, Verse 937)

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 569

Commentary: 
Four types of virtuous men worship the Lord as stated 

by Lord Krishna in the verse just earlier to this. The man in 
distress who worships for relief and protection called ārthie, 
the one who worships seeking knowledge called jignyasu, the 
seeker of enjoyment and material wealth called arthārti and 
the man of knowledge called jñāni, who perceives all that is 
perceived as the very form of Self, are those four categories 
of devotees. Amongst these four classes of righteous men who 
worship the Lord, the jñāni ranks first and foremost, excelling 
them all; hence called periyan superior to all. He is endowed 
with constant steadfastness and one-pointed devotion and he 
is endrum vida yogī never away from but ever absorbed in 
the Self, the Lord, who is the indwelling spirit.

A jñāni is all these four types of bhaktas rolled into one. 
He is one who does not view the Lord as the other from him 
and has no other object of attachment and therefore he is an 
ananya bhakta. Ever integrated with the Ātman, he is a yogī too. 
A greater wealth than jñāna, there is none. There is no wealth he 
needs to ask for. A jñāni himself is the repository of all wealth. 
Most of all, that which is most dear to the jñāni, is his own Self. 
He is exclusively devoted to the Self. What Nammalwar, the 
famous vaishnava saint sings explains the state of a jñāni. “I 
kept Thou in me and kept me in Thee – where the drop becomes 
the ocean and the ocean becomes the drop.” “Whatever path one 
may choose, the ‘I’ is inescapable, the ‘I’ that does the nishkāma 
karma, the ‘I’ that pines for joining the Lord from whom it feels 
separated, the ‘I’ that feels it has slipped from its real nature 
and so on. The source of this ‘I’ must be found. Whereas all 
the paths are approved in the Bhagavad Gītā, it says, the jñāni 
is the best karma yogī, the best devotee or bhakta, the highest 
yogī and so on.” (Day by Day, 22.3.46). “Yoga is only a sādhanā 
and jñāna is the siddhi.” (Talks  no. 580).

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   569 06-05-2011   10:54:05



570 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Hence the Lord declares that He, the Supreme Self-non-
different from the indwelling Self – is exceedingly dear to 
him – dear as an object of unqualified love – and the jñāni, 
who ever remains as the Self, is superabundantly dear to him. 
This is borne out by the declaration of the Veda also, namely 
“The Self is exceedingly dear to all”. Lord Krishna declares in 
Bhāgavatam: “Neither Brahma My offspring, nor Sankara My 
own emanation, nor Balarama My brother, nor Sri, My consort 
nor even My own Self is so dear to Me as you (devotee) are. 
I always follow the footsteps of a sage who desires nothing, 
who is always tranquil and who has enmity to none, in order 
that all the worlds within Me may get purified by the dust of 
his feet. None else – including aspirants for moksha – can 
experience that state of desireless Bliss attainable by those 
devotees who have no wealth except Myself, who have deep 
attachment for Me; who have universal love for all beings and 
whose minds are free from the stain of lust.” (11-14-14 to 16).

For a knowing one, there is no other love for him than 
the Lord (Self). Those who are endowed with knowledge and 
experience attain to His Transcendent State. “The knowing one 
is therefore the most beloved of Me, for through knowledge he 
bears Me ever in himself.” (Ibid, 11-19-4). Bhagavan, while 
explaining this śloka said, “of them the best is the man of 
wisdom for extremely dear am I to the Wise man (who knows 
Me in reality) and he is extremely dear to Me. You see what 
the jñāni likes most is the ‘I’. He worships only the I. He is 
dear to Me and I am dear to him. It means the Ātman which 
always says ‘I’ ‘I’ is dear. In the same manner wherever in the 
Gītā it is said “Serve Me, Surrender to Me. I am everything” 
it relates to the Ātmaswarūpa and not to the form wearing 
Shanka, Chakra, Gada and four arms. The references made 
by all mahātmās to ‘I’ are to that Ātmaswarūpa and not to 
the body. To them, nothing other than the Self is evident.” 
(Letters, page 689).

‘And ever’ is the only insertion by Bhagavan for

Once there was a pious couple living in a village and 

they had no issue. The woman was declared barren. A little 
away from the village was a great devotee who, it was said, 
talked to God everyday. She visited him regularly and one 
day explained her pitiable plight and requested him to find 
out from God whether she was destined to have a child at all 
in this life. The devotee, promising her to do that, put that 
question to God that night when he appeared as usual. He very 
clearly declared that she had no chance of getting even a single 
child in this birth. That woman, highly dejected on knowing 
this, was on the verge of committing suicide by entering into 
a river when she heard a sweet voice calling her name. She 
turned back and saw a sadhu, with body covered with dust, his 
dishevelled hair almost covering his face. His voice, despite 
his frightful physical appearance, was sweet and he questioned 
the reason for her extreme step. On being told the reason the 
sadhu with a calm and serene face, said in a soothing, but stern 
voice: “Mother, who told you that you are a barren woman? 
You’ll have not one, but three children. I speak the truth. Go 
home and be happy.“ These words were like nectar to her and 
she went home. True to his words three children were born to

Paraphrase: 
Having worshipped the Lord in various ways in 

successive and countless births, one becomes a jñāni in 
his last birth. That jñāni always meditating on Me in his 
heart knowing that Vasudeva, the Supreme, is all that is, 
reaches Me. Among men of repute he indeed is great and 
rare to find. A mahātmā he is.
Commentary: 

The realization of the Truth that there is naught that is 
not He, is accomplished over ages and at the end of countless 
lives. The spiritual evolution and transformation of a man into 
God is indeed a long but most rewarding journey.

Jñāna is unattainable except through merits accumulated 
over innumerable births. Performance of daily karmas 
enjoined by the scriptures, observance of meritorious acts 
like fasts, vows, yajñas, charity, tapas and worship over a 
number of births decimate the latencies. These latencies or 
anātma vāsanās are difficult to overcome because of their 
strength acquired in a number of previous lives. They can be 
liquidated only by the persistent and continuous culture of 
ātmavāsanā, like nithya anithya vastu vivekam (the distinction 
between Sat and asat) and or the Sarira mimamsa and the 
practice of Inquiry into the Ātman. Vāsanākshaya or extinction 
of vāsanās occurs then and the grace of God descends upon 
and assuming the form of guru instructs one verily is the Self 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   573 06-05-2011   10:54:05

that dwells within. Many births are necessary for the anātma 
vāsanās to wear away.

Such a one constantly contemplating on the Ātman in his 
heart and by the strength of the dhyāna directly experiences 
the Ātman, his own Self and realizes that all that is perceived 
is Vasudeva and that there is naught else that is not He. To him 
“everything and I are Vasudeva” – the object of unqualified 
love, the object of all love. Such a jñāni is called a mahātmā 
(manma) – a high souled – to whom there is neither an equal 
nor a superior one and therefore such a one is very rare indeed.

Vasudeva who is the Self is attained by the Self – 
Vasudeva.

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 575

In the place of ‘worship’, this translation had ‘Cometh 
unto me’ and ‘And says Vasudeva is all’ has yielded to place 
to the phrase ‘thinking the while’ – significant in content.

Once when someone while cutting vegetables in the 
wee hours of the morning in the kitchen asked what sādhanā 
Bhagavan performed while at Madurai, he remarked “What 
sādhanā did I do?  I ate three times a day and fetched water 
in big vessels” at which remark everybody laughed. “Though 
this was in a lighter vein”, he explained it later. 

Mr.D.S.Sarma asked Bhagavan what sādhanā did Bhagavan 
perform. Bhagavan stated “I have never done any sādhanā. I 
did not even know what sādhanā was. Only long afterwards I 
came to know what sādhanā was and how many different kinds 
of it there were”.... “The Self is not attained by doing anything 
but remaining still and being as we are”. (Day by Day, 4.10.46). 
When someone wondered how Bhagavan attained realization 
without any sādhanā, Bhagavan immediately replied “I must 
have left at this stage in the earlier birth.”

If great personages have become jīvanmuktas in their 
present lives, it only means that during their past lives up to 
the present, their vāsanās have been gradually diminishing 
to the extent of complete extinction. Saint Vamdeva gained 
knowledge even while in the womb of his mother. He died in 
his previous birth with a thin layer of ignorance left behind. 
But he remembered whatever he has been practicing and 
released himself from the last vestige of ignorance even while 
in the womb through the dint of the knowledge of the Supreme, 
like a hawk kept forcefully in a net, tears it and flies high up in 
the sky. The story of Jadabharatha is another apt illustration of 
this truth. It is relevant to recall that to a question whether there 
had been ativarnashramis like Bhagavan earlier. Bhagavan 
readily recalled, that they there were three namely Vamadeva, 
Jada Bharata and Sri. Suka.

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 577

Until the desires from the heart are completely wiped out, 
one’s own real form will not be seen. ‘Just as thread split in the 
end cannot enter the eye of a needle’, even if the last vestige 
of a desire lingers one cannot realise the Ātman. Unless one’s 
true form is perceived, happiness or contentment in oneself 
will not arise. The Bliss of the Self is the only permanent 
happiness. Desires delude the mind and distort the reality. 
Desires can be renounced for they are not properties of the 
Self but of the mind.

When the bliss of Ātman shines without any let or 
hindrance in a heart rendered pure by the renunciation of 
desires, the yogī abides and revels in It. One, who desiring 
nothing else and is content in the bliss of the Self within, is a 
jñāni who has known the Self.

tannil tannal uttran: In the self by the Self without 
desiring any acquisition extenal to himself.

uhappu tanil uttran: fully contented in the Self which is 
identical with Supreme bliss.

He is a man of steady wisdom who has abandoned 
all desires concerning progeny, wealth and the worlds and 
renounced all activity and delights in the Self and sports in 
the Self. He is fully contented in the Self which reveals itself 
as Self-effulgent consciousness, and the contentment he 
experiences is identical with Supreme Bliss.

An echo of this verse can be found in Śrīmad Bhāgavatam 
as well where Krishna says as follows: “Oh Uddhava! In the 
case of one who is free from all worldly desires and who 
has offered himself heart and soul to Me (Self) I shine in his 
heart as his very Self. The joy arising from this experience is 
something that a sense-bound creature can never realise. All 
the world is full of joy for one who is without any attachments, 
controlled in mind and senses equipoised and even-sighted 
and finding complete satisfaction in the Self.” (11.14.12).

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 579

Paraphrase: 
When one abandoning all desires, is freed of every 

attachment, longing for the unattained, and is bereft of 
the feelings of ‘I’ and ‘mine’ – then that man of glory, 
the best among men, achieves everlasting Peace. Be sure.
Commentary: 

Having renounced objects of desire in their totality, a 
jīvanmukta moves about, his efforts having been reduced to 
securing just what sustains bare life. But seeking nothing, he 
would be indifferent even in the upkeep of his body. He has 
no sense of ‘mine’ even in regard to those few things needed 
to maintain the body and has forsaken desires even for the 
essentials like shelter and clothing. Nor does he entertain a 
thought of them much less yearn for them. 

Icchai ellam – (all the desires) stand for all enjoyable 
things – of three kinds; external (house, wife and son) 
and internal in the form of day dreams or mere hankering 
Ihandavanai – he is one who rejects or is indifferent to even 
when they present themselves. Even in what comes his way 
without his volition by way of food and clothing that are 
indispensable for day to day living, he has no sense of ‘mine’. 
Neither has he ‘egoism’ being free from all feelings of Self-
esteem based on anything like knowledge. Such a sage of 
stable wisdom having attained to a pure state free of desire, 
attachment, ego-sense and the sense of mine is the best among 
men and Supreme peace will be his. With the cessation of all 
forms of transmigratory sufferings, he becomes assimilated 
in Brahman and this is nirvāna.

When the longing for the unattained desires is given up, 
contentment in what one has attained will rise on its own. But 
human nature is such that neither contentment in what one 
has nor the relinquishing of the hold on unattained is possible. 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   579 06-05-2011   10:54:05



580 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

But desires, properties of the mind, can surely be removed by 
renouncing the mind. The egoless one makes no effort for the 
‘I’ in him does not arise asserting itself. When the ego sense 
has died there can be no room for ‘mine’. The idea of egoism 
in the form of “this is mine” with regard to even a loin cloth 
or a covering for the body is not in him.

“When all desires clinging to the mind or heart fall off, then 
a mortal becomes immortal, attains Brahman even here.” declares 
Kathopanishad (6-14) and it further says “He himself is Brahman.”

The outstanding example in ancient spiritual lore of such 
a one is King Janaka of Mithila who is said to have exclaimed, 
“If Mithila burns, nothing belonging to me is burnt.”, when 
his teacher caused an illusory fire to impress Janaka’s fellow 
students who were anxious about their petty belongings, the 
superiority of Janaka over them.

“‘No want’ is the greatest bliss. It can be realised only by 
experience. Even an emperor is no match for a man with no 
wants. The emperor has got vassals under him. But the other 
man is not aware of anyone beside the Self. Which is better?” 
asks Bhagavan. (Talks no. 648).

In recent times Bhagavan shone as the example par 
excellence of a mukta purusha, totally devoid of ‘I’ and ‘mine’ 
and as the stita prajñā.

The tribute in verse, Municharya Panchakam that 
Narayana Guru composed on Bhagavan and sent provides the 
best description of Bhagavan: consuming for the maintenance 
of the body the food, unsought couch unsolicited and given 
by divine design, sanctifying the ground beneath with every 
fall of feet, sleeping with arm as pillow, floor as couch, with 
no worry, though in a body conditioned by time, ever abiding 
as unconditioned Knowledge Supreme, transcending all 
enjoyments, enjoying the realisation of ‘That Thou Art’ is this 
sage. He is often described as a beggar who never begged. 		

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   580 06-05-2011   10:54:05



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 581

      Once in Skandasramam when there was not even salt and 
somebody suggested procuring it from the town, he forbade 
it saying the gratification of the palate will lead from one to 
the other. Yet, Kunjuswamy records, with all that “Those 
were the happiest days.” Suri Nagamma records an incident 
narrated by Bhagavan himself. “My koupinam (piece of cloth 
usually a small strip worn over the privities) got torn. I do not 
usually ask anyone anything. Bodily privacy has however to 
be maintained. Where could I get a needle and thread available 
to mend the koupinam? At last, I got hold of a thorn, made a 
hole in it, took out a thread from the koupinam itself, put it 
into the hole and thus mended the cloth and so as to hide the 
place where it was mended, I used to fold it suitably before 
putting it on. Time passed like that. What do we need?” 
(Letters, 5-12-1947); and again quoting a verse which sang 
“Oh! Lord Thou hast given me a hand to use as pillow under 
my head, a cloth to cover the loins, handswherewith to eat 
food. What more do I want? This is my great good fortune!...... 
Is it really possible to say how great a good fortune that is. 
Even the greatest of kings wish for such happiness. There is 
nothing to equal it... These beds, sofa, articles around me... all 
this is bondage.” Once the towel he used for wiping and other 
purposes became so tattered as to be a rag of a towel and lest 
some devotee should notice it and bring a new one he hid it 
in a hollow of a tree. He had two pens (one red and one blue) 
and would not accept another till the two, though broken, 
worked. Similarly somebody would present him with a deer 
skin and another who wanted it for himself would approach 
him when nobody was around, ask for it and take it away. 
Nothing, totally nothing, did he regard as his. Later when the 
Ashram grew up around him, even if he wanted something 
to be done for someone, it would only be a mild suggestion. 
He would never ask anybody to do anything.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   581 06-05-2011   10:54:05



582 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

As Narayana Guru describes in his Nivritti Panchakam:  He 
enjoys the inner felicity of the One Self of all, who asks none to 
come, go, not to go or where one is going; who refrains from 
enquiries about the name, native land, caste or clan, who has no 
differentiation as I, you, he, that, within, without and who remains 
the same with known and unknown and free from distinctions as 
oneself and others and the assertion of non-difference.

He obeyed the rules of the administration more than any. 
When during his last illness characterised by the excruciating 
pain which revealed no sign of suffering on his face with his 
heavenly spirituality unaffected, he was requested to resolve 
to heal himself he simply answered “There is no mind. So the 
question of resolve does not arise.” 

Yoga Vasishtam describes such a sage thus: “He does not 
fasten (his mind) on anything. He has a satisfied form and an 
unattached mind. The person liberated while living, with his 
attachment gone lives as if he has the nature of paramount 
sovereign. The wise one does not fear, nor does he assume 
helplessness or dejection. He stands like a mountain, even, 
silent and with a mind at ease (Self-abiding)”, Verses 2310 
and 2313.  “The jñāni is the finality because he has become 
the Self and there is nothing more to do. He is also perfect 
and so fearless – dwitiyāt vai bhayam bhavati – the existence 
of a second gives rise to fear. This is mukti. It is also bhakti.” 
(Talks no. 650).

Paraphrase: 
He from whom this world is not perturbed out of 

fear in the least and who is not afraid of and perturbed 
by the world and who is free from joy and sorrow (likes 
and dislikes) fear and anxiety – he indeed is very dear to 
Me. Be certain of this Truth.
Commentary: 

This verse also describes the nature of a muktapurusha. 
Generally people, afraid to approach or be friendly with 
people possessed of desire and hatred shrink, shun and shy 
away from them.

But a jñāni often called Priya darsana is one who gives 
ananda by a mere darsana  to all. People throng the presence 
of jñānis and filled with joy and peace that they exude, await 
eagerly a look of grace or a word of blessing from them. He is 
one from whom the world is not afraid (evan pal ulaku bhayam 
edum urado). No one, and not even an animal, is disturbed or 
afraid in his presence, owing to his having realised non-duality 
and his being apt to forgive by virtue of his being supremely 
compassionate in nature.

Just as the world is not afraid of him, he is not afraid or 
harassed by the world. He is not disturbed out of fear by any 
mischievous person whose sole vow is to cause distress to 
innocent people.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   584 06-05-2011   10:54:05



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 585

This is the meaning of the phrase (even ulahukku 
anjano – who is not afraid of the world). Fear arises out of 
the existence of a second entity. It is out of factors regarded 
as external like wild animals, thieves, enemies and loss of 
property and internal factors like thoughts of forbidden 
deeds, fear of death, etc. The agitation consequent of fear 
is the state of an antagonised mind But the jñāni who is 
the Self, who remains as all, has nothing other than him to 
cause fear in him. The remover of all fear is the non-dual 
knowledge where nothing exists apart from the Self. He is 
not a source of fear or grief to any nor can any make him 
afraid or aggrieved.

Joy, anger, fear and anxiety have left him by themselves 
as a result of his having realized the oneness of being.

That, tranquillity and peace that prevailed in the 
presence of Bhagavan surpassed all understanding has been 
uniformly felt and reported by all the devotees who visited 
him. Bhagavan was ever brimming with the milk of divine 
kindness and even members of the sub human species had 
their share of the unbounded love of the master. The monkeys 
walked with great liberty up to him to claim their share of 
eats. In turn they shared their joys and sorrows with him and 
on occasions of quarrels among rival groups, had him as their 
mediator to restore amity and peace. Squirrels scrambled up 
fearlessly to his couch. So did the peacock and the cow. He 
was the universal father to human beings and beasts alike. 
Tigers, dogs and cobras listened to him. A hound of the then 
Collector preferred Bhagavan’s company to his own master. 
When the Collector returned after visiting Bhagavan in the hill 
he found one of his hounds missing. In the evening Bhagavan 
himself leading the dog on a string brought it back to him. 
(Prof. K.Swaminathan, Ramana, the Self Supreme). Children 
loved to be in his presence.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   585 06-05-2011   10:54:06



586 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

What was there for him, the non-dual Self, to be afraid of? 
He was totally unconcerned, whether it were the thieves who 
broke into the ashram and frustrated at not finding anything 
worthwhile beat them all up not sparing even Bhagavan or the 
likely summons to court in a frivolous law suit that agitated 
everybody. A similar attitude was discernible when the whole 
ashram was agog with excitement at the anticipated arrival 
of dignitaries like heads of religious mutts, maharajas of 
fame, literary luminaries or respected leaders of the freedom 
struggle. Osborne records, “He called nothing as his. He 
refused to have any special consideration shown to him. He 
refused to have an electric table fan because the devotees 
would not benefit equally. He never asked anyone to come or 
to go. He never pressed any to stay yet he watched over each 
one with loving solicitude of a mother for her only child.”

Excepting when he was served more than the others he 
was never known to be angry. Grant Duff records, “Bhagavan 
is gentle to a degree that surpasses gentleness.” His presence 
also elicited what was best in one. In short he lived the content 
of Gītā and was proof in flesh and blood of Gītā’s inner 
meaning. Yoga Vasishtam describes such a sage: “He has a 
mind which is quite full (or satisfied). He is silent, highly 
honoured and immovable (or undisturbed) among enemies. 
Though living among riches, terrific dangers, pastimes and 
festive occasions, he is not having excitement, nor does he 
attain joy. He lives as if he is a doer of actions, having a 
liberated mind within, always.”, (Verses 2311 and 2312).

miperiyan- (very dear to Me) while the original says “he 
is dear to me” in Bhagavan‘s translation such a one is extolled 
as being ‘very dear’ to the Lord.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   587 06-05-2011   10:54:06



588 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Paraphrase: 
He who is equal in honour and dishonour that he may 

face, the same to foes who oppose and friends who love 
him as their dear life and who, on his own has moved 
away from all initiative of endeavours that never leave 
one but hold on fast due to strength of vāsanās, know 
him to be one who has gone beyond or transcended all 
the gunas (qualities).
Commentary: 

This is yet another verse that dwells on the nature of Stita 
Prajña whose nature remains unchanged in all states and in 
all situations.

Praised or insulted, the jñāni feels neither joy nor misery. 
A knowing one will view the body and the world connected 
with it as one woken up a man views the dream body and the 
dream experience. Though he is in the body he is not of it 
and the world is not the other of him. Calumny and praise are 
merely the form of words. Honour or dishonour are particular 
forms of actions of body and mind without words. A jñāni 
is one, in whose perception there is neither the body nor the 
world as ‘other’ than the Self. Therefore none of these so 
much as touches him.

He is one whose kartrutva bhāva and bhoktrutva bhāva 
(sense of doership and enjoyership) have been burnt along 
with the ego. Enmity and friendship do not affect him. When 
the doer is dead, along with, karmas and the initiative to 
endeavour are lost. Hence he is called akarta or mahakarta.

A sage will not lavish praise on persons who favours him 
by word or deed; nor will he be offended with others who 
do the contrary. A liberated sage is one who does not view 
his experiences as favourable or unfavourable to himself but 
remains even-sighted always, same in honour and disgrace, 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   588 06-05-2011   10:54:06



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 589

the same to friend and foe, relinquishing all undertakings.
He has transcended all the three gunas, the manifestation 

of prakriti. Bhagavan referring to this śloka says that it speaks 
of  “gunatita (one who has transcended the gunas). That is 
the final stage. The earlier stages are asuddha satva (impure 
being), misra satva (mixed being) and suddha satva (pure 
being). Of these, the impure being is when overpowered 
by rajas and tamas; the mixed being is that state in which 
the being -satva- asserts spasmodically the suddha satva 
overpowers rajas and tamas. After these successive stages 
there comes the state transcending gunas.” (Talks no. 73).

He has transcended the gunas – the manifestation of 
Prakriti. The qualities diligently developed before the dawn 
of enlightenment by one eligible for knowledge and practised 
as spiritual disciplines remain as effortless characteristics 
of a jñāni. As the avadhuta in Bhāgavatam says, “These 
two alone are free from worries and immersed in joy. The 
child, thoughtless and without purposive effort and the 
sage who has gone beyond the three gunas of Prakriti.” 
(Bhāgavatam, 11.9.4).

All the traits that this verse mentions were present in 
Bhagavan from the time he came to Tiruvannamalai whether 
it were the hostile children who plagued him with their 
mischievous pranks or the band of robbers who came to loot 
the tamarind fruits attempting to pour the milk of euphoria 
trucalli into his eyes, or the sadhus who tried to hurt and harm 
him, or the band of robbers who dealt blows on everyone 
including Bhagavan. But he was unmoved and showed no 
concern to what might happen to his body.

Perumal Swamy, one of the earliest to attend on Sri 
Bhagavan rendered yeomen service in the initial days on the 
hill. Later on due to some reason he turned hostile and painted 
the whole town red with abuses on Bhagavan denigrating him 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   589 06-05-2011   10:54:06



590 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

vehemently. When devotees reported this to Bhagavan, he only 
recalled his earlier services. Later when better sense prevailed 
over him, he regretted his earlier obnoxious behaviour, came 
to Bhagavan and confessed that he would only rot in hell for 
all his unpardonable sins. Bhagavan assured him that he would 
come there too.

On another occasion a letter was received wherein 
several things were alleged against Bhagavan decrying him. 
When everybody came in Bhagavan wanted Venkataratnam 
to fetch it so that it could be read out and heard by all. 
When Venkataratnam  demurred saying it was not necessary 
Bhagavan said “look how he behaves. When anyone writes 
saying Bhagavan is great he has it read out. But he does 
not want this letter to be read out. Why?”. Suri Nagamma 
records that this reminded the devotees how Bhagavan in 
earlier days faced with equanimity the attempts to decry him 
by Mallaswamy and Jadaswamy. Everyone was reminded of 
this verse of Gītā then.” (Letters, 14.4.49).

More than anything else the way Bhagavan described 
himself before the Commission that had come to enquire on the 
basis of a law suit filed by an erstwhile disciple claiming that 
he was the legitimate sarvadhikari, reveals how Bhagavan, 
the stita prajñā of Gītā in flesh and blood was a yuga purusha 
(the only one who appears in every yuga) comparable only to 
Vamadeva, Jada Bharatha and Sukha. Some of the answers 
like:

“the property is thrust on me. I neither love nor hate it”, 	
       “But this body is considered swamy in the world. The 
body is this. It reduces itself to myself.”, 

“I do not call myself a disciple or Guru” 
(about not signing his name): “By what name am I to be 

known? I myself do not know”, prove the transcendental level 
that Bhagavan was anchored in.

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 591

The following question and answers throw more light 
on “that state”.

Q: Why do you not touch money? 
A: I cannot eat money. What shall I do with it?”,
Q: Can atiashram own property? 
A: There is no restriction on them. They may do what 

they please.”,
“Their conduct is not regulated according to any rules 

or codes.”
Finally when it was all over a devotee asked whether it 

caused strain, Bhagavan replied: “I did not use my mind and 
so there was no strain”.

Such is the spontaneity and grandeur of a jīvanmukta. 
(Talks - ‘Sparks from the anvil’ – 15-11-1936).

When some disciples asked why the robbers should 
molest the sadhus and why the sadhus would not protect 
themselves and their dependants from them, Bhagavan’s 
reply marks him out as a jīvanmukta. “There were rishis like 
Visvamitra who could duplicate the universe if they wished. 
They lived during the life time of Ravana who caused agony 
even to Sita and Rama among others. Could not Visvamitra 
have destroyed Ravana by occult powers? Though capable 
he kept still. Why? The occurrences are known to the sages, 
but pass away without leaving an impression on their minds. 
Even a deluge will appear a trifle to them; they do not care 
for anything.” (Talks no. 421). So many pictures pass over the 
cinema screen; fire burns away everything; water drenches 
all; but the screen remains unaffected. The scenes are only 
phenomena which pass away leaving the screen as it was. 
Similarly the world phenomena simply pass on before the 
jñāni, leaving him unaffected.

Though the jñāni abandons all endeavours his non-action 
is unceasing activity. Once when a saying of Laotze was 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   591 06-05-2011   10:54:06



592 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

read out in the hall “By his non-action the Sage governs all”, 
Bhagavan explained: “The Sage is characterised by eternal 
and intense activity. His stillness is like the apparent stillness 
of a fast rotating top (gyroscope). It appears to be still because 
it cannot be followed by the eye. So is the apparent inaction 
of a sage. This must be explained because people generally 
mistake stillness to be inertness. It is not so.” (Talks  no. 599).

The Sage feels that there is none other than the Self. 
He sees Brahman everywhere. The sage, whether pushed or 
disregarded, slighted, beaten, hindered or having urine and 
faeces thrown upon him by vicious persons is not perturbed 
and thinks well of them.

Paraphrase: 
For him who is never away from the Ātman and revels 

and rejoices in the Self alone, who is content with the 
Self and delights with joy in the Self alone, there indeed 
exists nothing that needs be done at any time.
Commentary: 

The one who renounces the evanescent comforts and 
pleasures of this ephemeral world as trivial and revels instead 
in the Self alone is called Ātma rati (one who revels in the 
Self). For a liberated man an object of pleasure does not 
produce delight and trouble does not cause grief. While others 
derive delight and contentment from the possession of external 
objects, one who, dissatisfied with the enjoyment of objects 
of pleasure like delicious food and exotic elixirs or creature 
comforts is satisfied instead in the Self alone is called Ātma 
trupta (one who is satisfied in the Self). He does not fasten 
his mind on anything for he perceives no duality anywhere. 
How does one become released from desires? (nishkāma:). 
Only by fulfilment of desires (apta kāma:) But how does he 
become one with desire fulfilled? It is by desiring the Ātman 
alone (Ātmakāma:). Ātman without an inside and outside 
remains as all, as the form of awareness. If one is anchored in 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   593 06-05-2011   10:54:06



594 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

it, nothing whatsoever remains to be gained. Therefore there 
is no more karma for him. As there is no more karma he has 
no transmigration anymore. He may perform action but it will 
not bind him. Though he appears to be with a body, the body 
itself is like a shadow to him. His nature in life and death 
remains the same. He ever remains as Brahman.

“Such a one lives as if he has the nature of Paramount 
Sovereign. He who has gone beyond everything is free from 
seekings and is satisfied only in the Self, neither acts nor 
desires.” Yoga Vasishtam, (Verses 2310 and 2314).

One who is not happy with fame, renown and wealth and 
instead is happy in the Self is called Ātma Sāntushta – ever 
happy in the Self. “For one who is satisfied by the nectar of 
jñāna and remains a krita kretya (who has done all that needs 
be done) there is not even a little that needs be done. If there 
is, he is not a jñāni”, declares Uttara Gītā. One who is ever 
happy in the Self will desire no other joy. He is one who is 
desirous of nothing other than the Self and is called a stita 
prajñā. Mundaka Upanishad also (3.1.4) echoes the same: “He 
sports in the Self , delights in the Self and is engrossed in the 
Self. This one is chief among knowers of Brahman.” He has 
no duty whatsoever whether Vedic or secular for the ground of 
eligibility is lost. He is declared tranquil within to whom there 
is no taste anywhere in any object, though having to perform 
worldly affairs. There is nothing he needs to perform himself 
or get performed by others; nor is he under any compulsion 
to do anything. 

One living on the banks of the Ganges will not search for 
a well to drink water. Nor is a lamp required when the Sun has 
risen. Where is the need for a hand fan when the salubrious 
southern breeze blows? A Sage after the bondage with the 
body is relinquished will not again identify himself with the 
body and perform actions.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   594 06-05-2011   10:54:06



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 595

Such a one is released from the bonds of karma and is 
called Sarva karma parithyagi (one who has renounced all 
karmas).

“When a thing distinct from the Self is obtained desire 
arises there. Where nothing whatever exists distinct from 
one’s Self what possibly can the Self run to or reach desiring 
what and remembering what?” (Yoga Vasishtam, Verse 2359).

Yet he is one whose deeds are desired by everyone but he 
desires nothing. He is one possessed of joy which gladdens 
everyone but he does not rejoice in anything except the Self. 
“Happiness is born of peace. Peace can reign only when there 
is no disturbance. Disturbance is due to thoughts which arise in 
the mind. When the mind itself is absent, there will be perfect 
peace. Unless a person had annihilated the mind he cannot 
gain peace and be happy, unless he himself is happy he cannot 
bestow happiness on others.” (Talks no. 597).

Paraphrase: 
A jñāni has nothing to gain by performing actions 

in the world. He has nothing to lose nor does he incur a 
sin by abstaining from actions. Indeed no object worthy 
of attainment through dependence on any created being 
remains for him anywhere or in any way.
Commentary: 

The reason why a jñāni, who is a stita prajñā, does not 
engage himself actively in endeavour of any sort is explained 
in this verse. All the virtues or auspicious enterprises that are 
undertaken in this world have just one goal, that of attainment 
of the Ātman. As there is nothing higher than the summum 
bonum of this spiritual experience all efforts are fruitless after 
attaining it. For a man of knowledge no purpose is served 
either by renunciation of actions or by having recourse to 
them. The sense of doership having been lost neither gain by 
non-performance of actions nor loss nor sin nor degradation 
of the Self by non-performance of actions accrues to him.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   596 06-05-2011   10:54:06



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 597

Besides there is naught else to be gained by a man of 
knowledge through dependence on any, right from Brahma 
down to a worm. Dependence is the seeking of patronage by 
means of activity for securing or furthering a desired aim. 
There is no object to be gained by depending on any being 
for which he needs to engage himself in activity.

Liberation is not a product of action and therefore does 
not come from action.

The non-achievement of ever achieved liberation which 
is the nature of the Self consists in mere ignorance of it. And 
that is removable by knowledge alone. For knowers of reality 
no need whatsoever remains to be fulfilled either by action 
or Knowledge.

Apart from the Self which he is, and which alone is, 
nothing else exists and therefore the question of attaining 
anything does not arise. “The jñāni is fully aware that the 
true state of Being remains fixed and stationary and that all 
actions go on around him. His nature does not change and 
his state achieved is not affected in the least. He looks on 
everything with unconcern and remains ever blissful himself”. 
(Talks no. 607). The form of Chit that is ever present shines as 
He. Since that alone, the One shines as all – filling everywhere 
without a second – and remains within him as the Self, there 
is nothing else either to be gained or lost. This is the hallmark 
of a jñāni who has gained his natural and real state of being 
the Self. Such persons knowing the nearer and further banks 
of the ocean of Existence neither give up nor desire the affairs 
relating to the world. 

They always follow action which has sprung up by chance 
like the fall of a palmyra fruit when a crow alights on it. They 
do not do anything truly since there is no grasping or purpose 
for them anywhere. “Persons whose ego is destroyed are so 
detached that even if they appear to see they do not see..... 
and whatever they do is not really doing” (Letters, 3.12.1947). 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   597 06-05-2011   10:54:06



598 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

The jñāni goes through all the activities without the notion 
that he is the doer of them. Though it is hard to understand 
how this is possible, the illustration normally given is that of 
a child roused from sleep to eat; eats but does not remember 
next morning that it ate. But these explanations are not for the 
jñāni but for the onlookers.

Bhagavan explains this, “A jīvanmukta always revels 
in the Self alone... His silence is the highest expression of 
the realized non-duality which is after all the true content of 
the Vedas. ... Although he may appear grief-stricken like any 
other man in bereavement yet he evinces just the right love of 
and pity for the senses which he earlier controlled before he 
realized that they were mere instruments and manifestations 
of the Supreme Being. When he seems keenly interested in 
the wonders of the world he is only ridiculing the ignorance 
born of superimposition.... All his actions should be taken 
to be only divine manifestations on the plane of humanity.... 
He lives only for the good of the world.” (Talks no. 449). 
Sometimes he gave the example of the actor on stage playing 
a certain part as the author has scripted it although knowing 
that he is not really that person; sometimes of a bank cashier 
who pays out thousands coolly and efficiently knowing that 
it is not his money that he is paying.

Bhagavan also warned devotees against the mistake of 
disparaging a jñāni for his apparent conduct and to prove it 
cited the example of the story of Parikshit, a still born child 
due to the effect of the missile of Aswattama (apāndava astra). 
Krishna said then that if the child be touched by one eternally 
celibate, the child would revive. None around including many 
rishis and sage Suka dared. Finding none Krishna went to 
the child saying “If I am eternally celibate, may the child 
be brought back to life” and the child revived. Bhagavan 
remarks, “just consider how Krishna surrounded by 16,000 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   598 06-05-2011   10:54:06



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 599

queens is a brahmachari! Such is the mystery of jīvanmukti. 
A jīvanmukta is one who does not see anything separate from 
the Self.” (Talks no. 449).

Brihadaranyaka Upanishad declares “Things done or not 
done do not trouble him” (1.4.10) and “Even the Gods cannot 
prevail against him for he becomes their own Self.” A jñāni 
has no action other than that of revelling in the Self. Even if 
he appears to engage himself in worldly activities he is one 
who never trespasses the boundary of nivritti mārga.  A jñāni’s 
actions are Gods and therefore always right.

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 601

Commentary: 
A jīvanmukta is freed from all actions. Not seeking objects 

of enjoyment that have not come his way and enjoyment of 
those that have come naturally, is the characteristic of a man 
of knowledge. “He is one with the marks of the mud of desire 
washed out and the bonds of his own delusion broken. He is 
liberated from the evil of duality. He is one who has crossed 
the ocean of worldly existence.” (Yoga Vasishtam, Verse 2344). 

uttradam peru means what comes unsought or by chance. 
He is one who has the feeling of satiety in what comes to him 
unsolicited, without hankering for more and without the effort 
in the form of entreaty or premeditation. Scriptures declare 
that such a one will never be desirous of laying by or storing 
even alms by forecasts of calamities. (Chaitanya Mahaprabhu 
sent away a disciple who stored a myrobalan for the morrow). 
Since nothing can be gained without one’s self-effort how can 
he live when afflicted with cold and heat? He is one who has 
transcended the dualities or rather they have left him, for his 
mind is untroubled though assailed by dualities, for the mind 
along with the dualities that afflict it, has been sublated into 
the Self – that is non-dual, non-doer, non-enjoyer and Supreme 
Bliss. The wise man though assumes or engages himself in 
mental effort, or sees names and forms, in reality does nothing 
whatsoever. He sets himself against none. Excellence in 
scholarship, renown in wealth, austerities and fame in others 
do not incite his jealousy. He is rid of the competitive spirit 
and therefore intolerance of excellence in others or desire for 
one’s own excellence is non-extinct. As there is none other 
than the Self which he is, with whom will he compete?

Once Bhagavan clarified to Yogi Ramiah the following 
point about endeavour or effort. Purusha or Swarūpa cannot 
make any prayatna (effort). Jīva is the one who makes it. 
“So long as egoity lasts, Prayatna is necessary. When egoity 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   601 06-05-2011   10:54:06



602 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

ceases to be, actions become spontaneous. The ego acts in the 
presence of the self. He cannot exist without the Self. The Self 
makes the universe what it is; yet He does not Himself act.”

He who has renounced all attachments is happy, 
equipoised and possesses the sameness of mind whether 
chance brings or fails to bring food essential for the upkeep 
of the body and in success and failure, devoid of elation and 
depression. Whether his basic needs are satisfied or not, he is 
not defiled within by notions of exultation, jealousy, fear, anger 
or wretchedness. He is a sarva sanga parithyagi – renouncer 
of all and even if he apparently engages himself in action, he 
is not bound, for the sense of doership has been annihilated 
along with the ego. He is a non-doer though he may seem to 
engage himself in action and he is bound by nothing; for he 
has risen above sankalpas (willing and wishing) and vikalpas 
(doubting).

“Distinctions such as ‘this is desired’ and ‘this is not 
desired’, do not touch or influence the Self. Therefore in the 
state without desire the Self does not do anything on account 
of the oneness of the doer, the instruments and action; nor is 
inactivity of the desireless Self admitted, on account of the 
absence of a second idea.” (Yoga Vasishtam, Verse 2360).

Though engaging himself in actions by virtue of the 
regular course of place, time and activity, he is not seized even 
a little by the pleasure and pain arising from such actions. 
A jīvanmukta acts with his excitement or anxiety extinct, 
is possessed of silence free from egotism, is stainless and 
exceedingly tranquil and even within, though in the midst of 
weal, woe, pleasure and pain, love and hate. Non-doership of 
the mind is the highest samadhi. That is the state of ‘aloneness’. 
He is verily a non-agent by his own experience but to whom 
agency is ascribed by others. Karma and its cause, the root 
of bondage, have been consumed by the fire of knowledge.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   602 06-05-2011   10:54:06



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 603

One is invariably reminded of Bhagavan while going 
through the content of this verse. Nothing ever perturbed him 
right from the time he reported his arrival to Arunachala to 
the end. A life of solitude in the rugged hills, hostile weather, 
impish children indulging in acts of mischief, scarcity of food, 
assault by robbers or the arrival of men of eminence from all 
corners of the world, thronging of the devout, excruciatingly 
painful trauma of the sarcoma did not bother him in the least. 
Whether heat of the midday sun or the pouring rain, his slow 
pace never changed. 

Bhagavan never thought of his next meal. If at all he 
begged he was immensely happy with a handful. “You 
cannot conceive of the majesty and dignity I felt while so 
begging”, he reminisced later. Sometimes receiving stale 
gruel without salt or any flavouring, “Taking it in the open 
street before great pandits who used to come and prostrate 
themselves before me at the asramam, then wiped my hands 
on my head and passed on supremely happy and in a state of 
mind in which even emperors were mere straw in my sight. 
It is because there is such a path that we find tales in history 
of Kings giving up their thrones and taking to this path.” 
(Day by Day, 30.5.46). Similarly whether it was sitting on a 
floor infested by ants constantly crawling over him or sitting 
on a sofa with the fragrance of incense around, it mattered 
least to him. Recitation of devotional songs in a monotone by 
devotees with no great pretension to a good voice which was 
far from pleasant – nay even and grating and harsh – was the 
same as the excellent rendition of music. He was one ever 
established in the Self.

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 605

Commentary: 
Even as the operator of a merry-go-round mounts children 

on the figurines of various sizes and shapes and revolves 
them or one who revolves the totally non-independent 
marionettes or wooden frames tied to strings, so the Lord by 
His bewitching power of māyā – delusion – mounts the jīvas 
on the wheel of saṁsāra and whirls them round.

The Lord who rules the Cosmos is also seated in the heart 
of every being and though He reposes in Stillness, will not let 
the jīva rest. Just like the marionettes mounted on a machine 
are moved about, the jīvas are animated and moved about in the 
performance of karmas by the lord. The power that determines 
events is his māyāsakti which, in the presence of Paramātman, 
assumes the power of action and moves the jīvas to act like the 
figurines tethered to a revolving wheel are moved about. Then 
the question arises whether the jīva has freedom in performing 
karmas. As long as the three gunas are not transcended the 
jīva is whirled round by prakriti or māyā. The Lord is simply 
‘Sarva Sākshi’ the Witness of all. The only freedom that the 
jīva has is not to identify himself with the body.

The Supreme is the inmost of the jīva’s existence. All 
the powers and acts of jīva are derived from Him but in all 
ignorance he imagines himself the Self-initiated worker 
and forgets this truth, thereby making his entanglement in 
māyā deeper. Realising this truth, one, rather than claiming 
independent agency, should submit to be a willing vehicle.

The body is often compared to a cooking pot and the 
mind, intellect and sense organs are compared to the water, 
rice and vegetables held inside the pot. When the pot is put 
on fire, the contents of the pot become heated, yet the heat is 
not of the pot, nor the contents of the pot. Likewise the power 
in man is not his but that of the Lord who dwells within. That 
is why Ramakrishna Paramahamsa often said

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   605 06-05-2011   10:54:07



606 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

ami yantram (I am a machine)
tumi yantri (Thou, the Operator)
“Because people think that they are jīvas, Sri Krishna 

has said that God resides in the Heart as the operator of the 
jīvas. In fact there are no jīvas and no operator. The Self 
comprises all. It is the screen, the pictures, the seer, the actor, 
the operator, the light and all else. Your confounding it with 
the body and imagining yourself as the actor amounts to the 
seer being represented as an actor in a cinema picture. Imagine 
the actor in the picture asking if he could enact a scene without 
the screen. Such is the case of a man who thinks of his acting 
apart from the Self.” (Talks no. 313).

Bhagavan would narrate a story to emphasise the need 
to get over the sense of doership. There was a powerful king, 
proud of his might. Suddenly one day he handed over his 
kingdom to the neighbouring king and went to the forest to lead 
an ascetic life. After some years the king came to his capital 
for begging alms and went away content with it. As he was 
thus trying to erase his ego, the king of one of the kingdoms 
where he went died without heirs and the royal elephant threw 
the garland round the neck of this King-turned-beggar. He had 
to accept the kingship of that kingdom. Meanwhile, the king 
to whom he had entrusted his own kingdom also died without 
heirs and pleaded by his former subjects he consented to 
become their king too. But there was a world of difference in 
his mental attitude. Earlier he prided himself on his greatness, 
his good reign and renown. Now he was conscious that the 
strength was the Lord’s and not his and that he was merely and 
instrument of the divine”.  (Unforgettable years,  page 47).

Sri Krishna says whether Arjuna liked it or not he would 
be forced to fight. “When there is work to be done by you, you 
cannot keep away; nor can you continue to do a thing when 
you are not required to do it, that is to say, when the work

and you must take your share in it – the share that is allotted 
to you – like an actor playing his part in a drama – free from 
love and hatred.” (Talks no. 653).

Surrender to the Lord who is the friend of all as the sole

alone makes possible the attainment of Supreme Peace and

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   608 06-05-2011   10:54:07



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 609

well. Lord Krishna also teaches this grand principle to Arjuna. 
Further perception of Unity in diversity is yoga or equanimity. 
“The seer is only one. Nothing appears without the seer. There 
is no change in the seer however much the seen may change.

	 Yogh karmasu kausalam = Skill in work is yoga,
	 Samatvam yoga uchyate = Equanimity is yoga,
	 Mamekam Sharanam Vraja – Only surrender to Me,
	 Ekamevadwiteeyam – Only one without a second.

representing Karma, Yoga, Bhakti and Jñāna convey the 
same meaning. They are only the single Truth presented in 
different aspects.” (Talks no. 319). Bhagavan further clarifies 
it. “And this is the same as enquiry. Those that take refuge 
in ‘Me’ means those that engage themselves in an enquiry of 
the Self and take refuge in that ‘I’ can cross over the māyā.” 
(Letters, page 689).

A vaishnava devotee once very reverentially approached 
Bhagavan’s couch and asked: “Bhagavan, why have you not 
chosen the verse sarva dharman parithyajya (abandoning all 
righteous deeds seek Me, as thy sole refuge; I will liberate 
thee from all sins; do thou not grieve (Verse 66, Chapter 18), 
which has been cited by great sages as the most important 
śloka of Śrī Bhagavad Gītā and which is the charama śloka 
(the last word) of vaishnavites?” Bhagavan replied “you will 
see that I have chosen instead an earlier verse of the same 
chapter. (Verse 62, Chap 18).

Sri Balarama Reddiyar has clarified this cryptic 
statement as follows. In verse 66 a negative aspect 
“abandoning all righteous deeds, seek Me as the sole refuge” 
is stressed but in verse 62. “Unto him alone surrender O 
Bharata with all thy being”, the positive method is given! 
(Moments remembered,  page 6). Further, as both the verses 
emphasize surrender and Grace there exists only distinction 
without difference. Bhagavan himself clarifies it: “Grace is 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   609 06-05-2011   10:54:07



610 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

both the beginning and the end. Introversion is due to Grace; 
Perseverance is due to grace; and Realization is Grace. That 
is the reason for the statement: ‘Mamekam charanam vraja’ 
(only surrender to Me). If one has entirely surrendered oneself, 
is there any part left to ask for Grace? He is swallowed up by 
Grace.“ (Talks no. 319). Hence Liberation is effected by grace 
and sarva karmam all karma drop off automatically.

“What does the Gītā say? Arjuna refused to fight and 
as long as he refused he had the sense of doership. “You are 
being manipulated by a Higher Power. You are admitting it 
by your own refusal to submit to it. Instead recognise the 
power and submit as a tool.... Rather be fixed in the Self and 
act according to nature without the thought of doership. Then 
the results of action will not affect you. That is manliness and 
heroism.” (Talks no. 58). Thus, ‘inherence in the Self’ is the 
sum and substance of Gītā teaching.”
