614 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Śrī Dakshināmūrthy Stōtram

Avathārikai: (Genesis)
Sanaka, Sanandana, Sanatsujata and Sanatkumara, the 

four sons born of the thought power of Brahma – the Lord 
of creation – came to know from their father that furtherance 
of world creation was the mission for which they had been 
brought forth. Highly dispassionate by nature and averse 
to their mission, these renunciates, seeking the Supreme 
Quietude, were in search of one who would enlighten them. 
The Lord of Supreme Compassion – Parameswara – appeared 
for the sake of these exceedingly earnest and ripe seekers in the 
form of Lord Dakshinamurthy seated under a banyan tree in 
perfect repose of the Self displaying the Chin mudrā. Instantly 
attracted to him as iron filings to a magnet, they also sat near 
Him and like Him abided in the natural state. Āchārya Sankara 
reveals through this hymn the Sarvātma Tattva that everything 
is the form of the Self including the power that evolves and 
devolves as the world, perceiver and the perceiving light – the 
main obstacle to ripe sādhaks lacking the intuitive awareness 
of realizing the perfect silence as the truth of one’s Existence 
– is not other than the Self.

– Bhagavan
Later when Suri Nagamma showed Bhagavan the Telugu 

translation of this avathārikai (origin) Bhagavan said with 
a smile: “Look! I mentioned briefly in the preface only that 
part of the story related to the hymn. The real story is very 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   614 06-05-2011   10:54:07



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 615

interesting. When the mind-born sons of Brahma, highly 
dispassionate by nature and therefore reluctant to engage 
themselves in acts of creation and desirous of gaining 
upadēsa to attain jñāna were wondering who would impart 
jñāna to them, Narada just then appeared and divining their 
thoughts said, “Who can impart Brahma jñāna other than 
Brahma himself? Come, we shall go to Him.” They all went 
to Satyaloka, the abode of Brahma and found Saraswathy 
singing and playing on the veena. Brahma was found to be 
enjoying and appreciating the music, keeping time with beats.

On beholding this scene, they wondered how such a one 
could instruct them on Ātmajñāna and lost all hopes. Instantly 
Narada said, “Let us go to Vaikunta, the abode of Vishnu” 
and thither they all went. The Lord was in the inner chamber. 
Narada, the triloka sanchari, who can move at will in all the 
three worlds with ease and liberty, asking the four to wait 
outside, went in.

Within minutes he was back and told them “There Brahma 
was seated a little away from Saāāraswathy who was singing 
and playing on the veena. Here Goddess Lakshmi, seated on 
the very same couch is massaging the Lord’s feet. This is 
even worse. How can this saṃsārin (householder) render us 
any help in our undertaking? Behold! This is what the glory 
of Vaikunta is all about! Enough! Enough!”

Then Narada suggested “Let us seek the help of Lord 
Siva”, and to Kailasa they repaired with great expectation and 
desire rekindled. In Kailasa, Lord Sankara, in the midst of a 
vast gathering as Ardhanāri (with Uma as the left of his body) 
was performing Tandava, the cosmic dance of Bliss. Vishnu 
was playing on the percussion and Brahma was keeping time 
with cymbals.

The seekers in search of spiritual guidance became 
speechless. They exclaimed “Alas! Even Siva is enamoured 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   615 06-05-2011   10:54:07



616 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

of a woman. Brahma had Saraswathy only by his side. Vishnu 
was in physical contact with Lakshmi; while Siva has enfolded 
Uma within His very body.” They, saying “enough of all this,” 
departed in despair.

The Lord, realizing this, felt sorry for them who dismissed 
the three Gods as dispossessed of jñāna, out of mere 
association with women. “What delusion on their part!... Who 
else can impart Ātmajñāna to these ripe and serious seekers?” 
(Letters, 7th Sep. 1987). Bhagavan stated then, “Guidance 
should be only from the best of Masters. Who could it be but 
Siva – the yogīraja.” He, the embodiment of compassion, 
seated Himself under a banyan tree on the northern side of 
lake Manasarovar as Lord Dakshinamurthy with Chin mudrā 
on their path of return.

“Being yogīrājā should He practice yoga? He went 
into samādhi as He sat; He was in perfect repose. Silence 
prevailed. They saw Him. The effect was immediate. They 
fell into samādhi. Their doubts were at an end. “Silence is 
the perfect upadēsa and it is suited for the most advanced 
seeker.” (Talks no.569)

Bhagavan concluded the story saying “This is how the 
avatar of Dakshinamurthy took place mainly to claim the four 
ripe souls by preaching them through silence.”

Āchārya Sankara, being an avatar of Siva was full of 
Compassion for fallen beings. He wanted all of them to realize 
the blissful Self. He could not reach them all with His Silence. 
So he composed Dakshināmūrthy Stotra, in the form of a 
hymn, so that people can read, chant and understand the Truth.

Dakshinamurthy is one aspect of Siva. He is usually 
pictured as sitting under a banyan tree, facing south in virasana 
posture, with right leg on the left thigh, exhibiting Chin mudrā. 
Mudrā is a mystic pose and Chin mudrā is formed when the 
tips of the index finger and thumb are joined together to make 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   616 06-05-2011   10:54:07



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 617

a circle. Chin mudrā, the most auspicious, is variously called 
as jñāna mudrā, badhra, and vyakkyana mudrā (mudrā of 
exposition). Many are the interpretations given to explain 
this mudrā of jñāna .

The union of index and thumb indicates the identity of 
para and jīva and the three fingers spread stand for the negation 
of the triputi – jīva, jagat and Iswara, (the individual soul, the 
world and god) – signifying they have no existence apart from 
the Self. The leg that is let down is pictured as stamping on 
a demon called Muyalakan – the embodiment of nescience.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   617 06-05-2011   10:54:07

Paraphrase: 
That Sankara – who out of Compassion for the four 

best of rishis with intense yearning for liberation, fortified 
with unflagging dispassion and in search of the quietude 
of the Self – as Lord Dakshinamurthy, seated in the shade 
of a banyan tree, and facing South granted them perfect 
repose and perpetual abidance in It by revealing to them 
clearly His true state of Absolute Silence and stated the 
Sarvātma tattva (that everything is the form of the Self) 
– that Sankara abides in me.
Commentary: 

That Āchārya (Guru) Ramana is but an avatar of the 
aspect of Lord Dakshinamurthy can be proved by recalling 
many incidents from his life. Most of the time he would be 
found seated in the hall facing south. He always (excepting 
when questioned by devotees) abided in the natural state of 
absolute silence. His upadēsa was mainly through silence.

The traditional invocatory couplet to this hymn in Sanskrit 
runs thus: “It is wonderful that under the yonder banyan tree, 
a youthful teacher (is sitting surrounded by) disciples who are 
aged. The Guru’s exposition is in silence. Yet the disciples 
have their doubt dispelled.”

Chitram Vataratrár mule vriddhÅ sishyÅ gurár yuvÅ
Gurástu mounam vyakkyÅnam sishyÅstu chinna 

samsayah
The beatific spectacle of Bhagavan at the age of sixteen 

as the king of youths and in silence settling on the slopes of 
Arunachala is but a proof of the term Gurōryuva (a young 
teacher). That, many were the disciples venerable in age like 
B.V. Narasimhaswamy, Sivaprakasam Pillai and Gambhiram 
Seshayya, who by merely remaining in the powerful presence 
of this King of yogīs, gained sublime experiences is a fact 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   619 06-05-2011   10:54:07



620 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

widely known and recorded bearing testimony to the term 
Vriddha Sishya (disciples, advanced in years)

What Lord Sri Dakshinamurthy seated under a banyan 
tree (a symbol of eternity), imparted through silence to the 
four in the hoary past was revealed and imparted by Bhagavan 
seated on the sofa in the old Hall to ripe souls coming from 
the four corners of the wide world.

To him Silence was the most powerful expression 
of ‘Being’ and his method of instruction was through the 
unspoken word. This penetrating silence, the most powerful 
transmitter of knowledge and experience, became the hallmark 
of this young sage.

The silent teaching of Lord Dakshinamurthy dispelled the 
doubts of the four disciples. “Their doubts dispelled means 
they lost their individual entities.” (Talks - no. 398). Nothing 
can be more true of Bhagavan. Legion is the number of 
devotees who have gone on record reaffirming repeatedly how 
the mere stillness of Awareness that Bhagavan was steeped 
in, dispelled all their doubts and transmitted the spiritual 
experience of Swanubhava. But the manner and the mode in 
which it operated defies human comprehension. Paul Brunton 
and others had their unasked questions answered in Silence; 
at other times Bhagavan would himself preempt the unasked 
questions harboured by some, directing a genial look at them 
or someone else would voice the very same questions that 
others had in mind and after replying to them, Bhagavan’s 
eyes, full of light, accompanied by a meaningful smile would 
be directed at them.

The most classic example is that of the Kashmiri 
attendant, who had accompanied his master from Kashmir. He, 
who knew no other language than his native Kashmiri, came 
to Bhagavan one night, and spoke rapidly in his language. 
Bhagavan, bestowing his look of grace on him, was silent. 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   620 06-05-2011   10:54:07



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 621

After a while he saluted and left the hall. The next morning 
his master came to Bhagavan and complained of Bhagavan’s 
unfairness in not letting him know that he could speak 
Kashmiri so well and explained how his assistant had all his 
questions posed to Bhagavan answered in his language.

(Source: A Sadhu’s Reminiscences, Chadwick)
Many devotees have vouchsafed the fact of Bhagavan 

being none other than Dakshinamurthy, based on their 
experiences in his potent presence and powerful silence. 
Bhagavan himself confirms this view. Just as plantain tree 
produces shoots and these shoots when transplanted do the 
same again, “So also the original primeval Master of antiquity 
who cleared the doubts of his rishi-disciples in silence has left 
shoots which are ever multiplying. The Guru is a shoot of that 
Dakshinamurthy.” (Talks no. 17)

The dhyana sloka that Ganapathy Muni wrote and was 
approved by Bhagavan runs as follows:

“In showering grace he is like the Moon, the friend of 
the white water lily

In the same way in lustre he is like the Sun, the kinsman 
of Lotus

In his Brahmic state he reminds us of his father abiding 
under the banyan tree

Him, the moveless one, we lovingly remember” 
(Ramana Gītā, Chap. 18, Verse 13)

Let us pay our obeisance to Bhagavan along with Swamy 
Desikananda:

How gracious art Thou Lord Dakshinamurthy,
To have blessed mankind by Thy ministration
To Bhagavan who is but the form of Satyam Sivam and 

Sundaram.
Do I offer my Salutations again and again.

(Surpassing Love and Grace, page 68)

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   622 06-05-2011   10:54:07



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 623

Paraphrase: 
Let us hail and hymn the Supreme Father, the Lord 

of all, who as Lord Dakshinamurthy, the Parabrahman, 
the child forever, the most exalted guru, of a joyous 
countenance, with ananda as the very form, revelling 
in the inherent bliss within and with the Chin mudrā 
of the hand and surrounded by most eminent disciples 
ever established in Sivahood graciously indicates ‘That’ 
through the greatest exposition of Silence.
Commentary: 

‘Sri’ ‘Dakshina’ and ‘amurthy’ together form the word Sri 
Dakshinamurthy. While Sri stands for māyā sakthi, Dakshina 
means “Competent” and “in the heart on the right side of 
the body and amurthy means “formless form”. Therefore 
Dakshinamurthy means “that Supreme Content, the form of 
Chit, though adept at creating sustaining and destroying by 
that indescribable power of māyā, is the formless Brahman.” 
In fact “A lot of Commentary on this is possible. Isn’t it?” 
says Bhagavan (Letters, 7th Feb. 1947)

One meaning refers to the incarnation of Siva in which 
He represents a guru teaching the summum bonum of spiritual 
wisdom to his disciples. The second reference is to the 
unconditioned formless Divine Being.

Dakshinamurthy is also the perceivable Brahman and 
easy of being worshipped as Brahman alone shines as 
Dakshinamurthy – the form of Guru both as instructor on 
and as Brahman.

It is pointed out here that the hidden import of the divine 
wisdom of the Vedas namely, the Absolute Content, can be 
indicated only by Silence.

The exposition to reveal the ‘Content Beyond’ is couched 
in the language of Silence. Chin mudrā is the indication that 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   623 06-05-2011   10:54:07



624 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

announces it. The teacher is a child, the very form of Brahman. 
The face radiates the joy of Awareness and the bliss of Being 
as a result of constant revelling within. The disciples who 
surround him are the ideal ones and the best of all such who 
are firmly poised in the Ātman. The divine resplendent teacher 
who exhibits all these is called formless’ or unembodied 
though with form.

This south-facing Lord is hailed by Bhagavan as Appan 
(Father). He is the Father of all embodied forms.

While the Sanskrit invocatory verse describes 
Dakshinamurthy as a youth Bhagavan uses the word valan – 
child. During the course of conversation, G.V. Subbaramiah 
remarked about a child creating the “home” atmosphere. 
Bhagavan responded as follows. “Yes. Children are always in 
the ‘home’. We too are there but are dreaming and imagining 
that we are outside the ‘home’. I have rendered the word yuva 
(youth) in Dakshinamurthy Stotra by the word valan (child). 
This seems more appropriate . To be reborn is to become 
children over again. One must be reborn before gaining jñāna 
, that is, recovering natural state” (Talks no. 414)

It will be interesting to note here that the then Pontiff 
of Sringeri Mutt, Sri Narasimha Bharati, who himself was 
a jñāni of great renown, used to direct his disciples to have 
a darshan of Bhagavan whom he always referred to as “the 
Bala Swamy” (Child Swamy).

In sacred literatures, utterances like “said without saying” 
and “showed, remaining still as ever” will occur only too often. 
The ‘unspoken word’ referred to here is “Silence “. A realized 
sage uses the best of language, namely Silence. T.K.Sundaresa 
Iyer records how on a Sivaratri night a sadhu requested 
Bhagavan to explain the Dakshinamurthy Stotra. Bhagavan 
asking him to sit down sat in his usual poise. There were no 
words, no movement and all was stillness. Hours ticked away 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   624 06-05-2011   10:54:07



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 625

but all sat motionless not conscious of the body, space or time. 
“Thus eight hours were passed in Peace, in Silence in Being 
as It is. Thus was the Divine Reality taught through the speech 
of Silence by Bhagavan Sri Ramana Dakshinamurthy.” (At the 
feet of Bhagavan, page 32)

Bhagavan once told Muruganar the following story. The 
four venerable munis, sensing the greatness of Siva sat at 
his feet and plied him with shrewd and pertinent questions 
about the nature of Reality and the means of attaining it. 
Overjoyed to see their earnestness, wisdom and maturity, Siva 
full of Compassion and fatherly love gave apt replies. As he 
answered, further doubts arose and this question – answer 
session went on for a whole year. Finally the Lord sensing that 
there would be no end to their questions and ajñāna, merged 
into Supreme Silence and after Him the disciples too merged 
into the true state of the Self – the Supreme Silence.

On hearing the story Muruganar remarked, that no book 
has ever mentioned about the Lord speaking thus, Bhagavan 
(adu appadittan oi)shot back firmly, “But that is how it 
happened”. From this authoritative way and tone Muruganar 
realized that Sri Ramana was none other than Dakshinamurthy 
himself. (The Silent Power, pages 48-49)

“What one fails to know by conversation extending to 
several years can be known in a trice in Silence or in front of 
Silence – eg. Dakshinamurthy and his four disciples.” (Talks 
no. 246)

It is worth recalling here that Bhagavan seated in silence 
was also surrounded by eminent disciples, scholars, poets, 
mahātmas, tapaswins, ripe souls and earnest seekers.

When Bhagavan’s uncle, Nelliappa Iyer came to 
Tiruvannamalai, after knowing his whereabouts and visited 
him, on his way back, a learned man discoursing to a small 
audience, by way of an answer to Nelliappa Iyer’s question 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   625 06-05-2011   10:54:08



626 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

about Bhagavan informed him that “he was an ignorant boy 
who knew nothing, sitting there without any education and 
with a crude philosophy. But during a later visit of his uncle, 
Bhagvan was explaining Dakshinamurthy Stotra. His uncle 
came in, listened and was convinced that (in the words of 
Bhagavan recorded by Suri Nagamma) “his nephew was not 
an ordinary person, that he knew the subject very well. He 
went away fully satisfied.” (Letters, 4.11.1948)

Paraphrase: 

May our obeisance be to that Primal guru Sri 
Dakshinamurthy, who, at the time of spiritual awakening, 
experiences directly (without the aid of any medium) 
his true form as one without a second even as a dreamer 
on waking up sees only himself but who, hitherto out 
of ignorance, perceived the world existing within (the 
mind) as if manifested without (or outside of him) like 
the reflected image of a city seen to exist within a mirror.
Commentary: 

This entire hymn can be classified into three parts, namely, 
the world, the perceiver of the world and the light that reveals 
it – the triad or triputi of jīva, jagat and Iswara. “The first four 
stanzas deal with the world. It is shown to be the same as the 
master whose Self is that of the seeker also, or the Master to 
whom the seeker surrenders himself. The second four stanzas 
deal with the individual whose Self is shown to be the Self of 
the Master. The ninth stanza deals with Iswara and the tenth 
with the Siddhi or Realisation. Such is the scheme of the 
stotra.” (Talks no. 569)

The example of sleep is provided to clarify how what is 
within appears to exist without. What is not within the Self 
in truth appears to be within the Self and is depicted through 
the example of the reflected image of the city in the mirror 
which appears to be within the mirror when it is really not so.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   627 06-05-2011   10:54:08



628 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

All the Universe that is within appears to exist outside of 
one by the strength of the power of māyā, like the reflected 
image that appears to be within a mirror. “Which is the 
darpana (mirror) here? A mirror we know is an insentient 
object which reflects light. What corresponds to a mirror in 
an individual? The light of the Self-luminous Self is reflected 
on the Mahattattwa. The reflected light is the mind-ether or 
pure mind. This illumines the vāsanās of the individual and 
hence the sense of ‘I’ and ‘this’ arises.” (Talks no. 569). Further 
“The mirror reflects objects; yet they are not real because they 
cannot remain apart from the mirror. Similarly, the world is 
said to be a reflection in the mind as it does not remain in 
the absence of mind. The question arises: If the universe is 
a reflection, there must be a real object known as Universe 
in order that it might be reflected in the mind. This amounts 
to an admission of the existence of an objective Universe. 
Truly speaking, it is not so.” (Talks no. 442). Therefore the 
illustration of the dream is set forth.

The dream-ego that perceives the objects and experiences 
the dream-world is not aware of its true identity as the real 
ego. The objects seen in dream do not have an existence, (for 
there is no activity of instruments of action or perception) 
independent of one’s own existence. In dream the objects 
are illumined by the light of the mind which in turn is 
illumined by the light of the Self. On waking up from sleep 
one perceives that he alone exists and none whatever of 
the dream-stuff. As in dream, in jagrat (waking-state) he 
imagines a world and as in dream where the experiences 
appear to be interminable, he imagines he will live for ever 
in jagrat. Jagrat is akin to the dream state. Thus the jīva 
thinking that the world that appears within by the play of 
māyā like the reflected image of a city in a mirror, is without 
and thus deludes himself.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   628 06-05-2011   10:54:08



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 629

On waking up to reality from the slumber of delusion 
he realizes that the ephemeral and insubstantial nature of the 
phenomenal world is just like the transient nature of the dream 
world. All things perceived externally exist within. Within 
one is the whole universe. The mighty power of māyā makes 
it appear without.

In the oft-used example of snake and rope, the truth of 
the snake is the truth of the rope. Even as the appearance of 
the snake is rejected by the reality, namely, it is the existence 
of rope, the fleeting dream state is rejected by the reality of 
the waking state. And the reality of the less-fleeting jagrat is 
rejected by the reality of the Truth-the Ātman. Just as a dreamer 
will no longer see the dream world on waking up one waking 
up to reality will realize the advaitic truth of ‘Infinite I’ that 
is worldless.

While the dream-world is projected by the ego out of 
the impressions gained in jagrat, the phenomenal world is 
the outcome of one’s vāsanās or proclivities. But in both the 
worlds everything seen derives its astitwa (existence) and 
light only from the light of the Ātman. Then the question 
arises: how did these vāsanās originate to start with? There 
must have been a world sometime. Bhagavan answers, “the 
straight way to find an answer will be to see if the world is 
there. Admitting the existence of the world, I must admit a 
seer who is no other than myself. Let me find myself so that I 
may know the relation between the world and the seer. When 
I seek the Self and abide as the Self there is no world to be 
seen. What is the Reality then? The seer only and certainly 
not the world.” (Talks no. 442)

Just as, though the food before partaking of it, was thought 
of as separate from oneself and after consuming it, the ‘I’ 
or Aham includes the food consumed, an Ātmajñāni’s Self 
that is Infinite and One, encompasses everything including 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   629 06-05-2011   10:54:08



630 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

the world, he has swallowed. All that appeared alien to the 
Self are reduced to only forms ensouled by the Self in whose 
being they exist. Bhagavan explains the one real thing which 
exists, “The one only is the Sat, the existence that appears as 
the world, the things that we see and we ourselves.” (Talks 
no.186.) Ātman is the screen on which the pictures – worlds 
– dream, wakeful – appear. It is like the newspaper on which 
various items of news appear. We see the pictures and read 
all the articles therein but do not care to know anything about 
the screen or paper. “We take the chaff but not the substance. 
The substratum on which all this is printed is the paper and 
if we know the substratum all else will be known (like wall 
and paintings)” Ibid.

 But for the grace of the realized guru whose guidance 
comes from his experience, attainment of jñāna is well-nigh 
impossible. Upanishads proclaim “One who is blessed by a 
spiritual preceptor knows the Truth” (Chandogya Upanishad, 
6.14.2). When guru’s grace and upadēsa cause the spiritual 
awakening one realizes oneself to be the Infinite Self – that has 
swallowed up the individual self and the world – his natural 
state of bliss and light of awareness as ‘I am’. He realizes 
the advaitic truth of the Self that is sleepless, dreamless and 
unborn.

 Talaiyuru Guru or ādi guru (the first and foremost 
guru) – Dakshinamurthy that God, is the primary guru, who 
transmits spiritual truth, that paratattva, through a succession 
of human gurus.

Reality is one. Ātman by the power of māyā appears as guru 
and disciple. The jīva, by the upadēsa of a jñāna guru and rid 
of nescience, realises he is the form of Awareness. “Obeisance 
to that Dakshinamurthy, the weilder of omniscience, who is 
of both the forms of jīva who knows thus and the Guru who 
so instructed” is the content. Hence the refrain Pottri. When 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   630 06-05-2011   10:54:08



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 631

the sleep of nescience is ended the truth that the jīva, the guru 
who woke him up to reality and the ‘indweller’ who shines 
within both are all one is clearly realized. In the ultimate sense 
there is neither guru nor disciple. This is expressed in the line 
jñāna nilaiyuru neran tannai oruvana evaner kanban (at the 
time of enlightenment who sees him as a single Self).

“Obeisance to Sri Dakshinamurthy who is the form of 

God, Guru and Ātman, who is all-pervading like the sky” is 
the content of this sloka.

But there is a note of warning provided by Bhagavan. 
“A superficial reading of the slokas makes one believe that 
the bondage and liberation, etc. are all related to the Master 
namely Dakshinamurthy. It is absurd. ‘Surrender to Him’ is 
meant” (Talks no. 569)

Dr. Sayeed once asked Bhagavan “Why did the Self 
manifest as this miserable world?” Bhagavan stated, “in order 
that you might seek it. Your eyes cannot see themselves. Place 
a mirror before them and they see themselves. Similarly with 
creation. ‘See yourself first and then see the whole world as 
the Self’”. (Talks no. 272)

Paraphrase: 
May our obeisance be to Sri Dakshinamurthy, who, 

by the sheer power of His will, like a siddha or a magician,

Commentary: 

The world perceived by us is a phenomenon of māyā. 
Prior to creation it was in an unmanifest condition like the 
sprout in a seed by the power of māyā of God. Even as the 
mighty tree with its roots, trunk, branches, leaves, and fruits 
and flowers exist in a seed in an undifferentiated form, so 
does the world with its panoramic names and forms remains 
unmanifest. Time and place are projected by the powers of 
māyā and due to their association and karma countless forms 
come into existence and are known as the ‘world’. Therefore

Jīva, world and god, the three 
Prime principles are pieces for māyā

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   632 06-05-2011   10:54:08



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 633

The Great Awareness which is Being,
In her eternal game of chess
Played on the board which also is
The Self – same still and blissful Being”.

(Guru Vāchaka Kovai, Verse 1215) 
The classic example of a magical feat is the contrived 

illusion by a conjuror who throws a rope into the air where 
it appears to remain vertical without support. Not merely 
that, a boy very soon climbs the rope and on reaching the top 
vanishes into thin air. Muruganar in a verse compares the Self 
to the conjuror, which, itself remaining unchanged, creates 
the illusion of the world, by throwing into the mind’s sky, the 
strong rope of three states, mounted on which the jīva plays 
his tricks, sustained by what he knows not. 

A mahayogī, by his yogic powers, creates wonders. Sage 
Viswamitra, by sheer sankalpa, without resorting to any 
external aid, created by his yogic power a heaven in mid – 
air out of nothing. Likewise, God, who is the repository of 
all powers, by his power of will, rolls out this world like the 
unfolding of a mat.

Many scriptural references are given as proof of this. “In 
the beginning Sat alone existed” (Chandoghya Upanishad, 
6.2). “Let me become many” and “That from which all these 
things are being born.” (Taittiriya Upanishad 3.1)

This verse represents the vedantic view of creation. 
What exists alone can get ‘created’. Nothing can come out of 
nothing. The sprout by virtue of its existence comes out. The 
effect preexists in the cause in a subtle form.

Here it is worthwhile to note how the sage, Rishi Uddalaka, 
instructed his son Svetakethu on the Self by using the example 
of a seed. Asking him to break a seed of the nyagrodha tree 
(Indian fig tree) he asks his son to take out the smallest seed 
within that seed and break it to see what is inside. When the 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   633 06-05-2011   10:54:08



634 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

boy replies ‘nothing’ the sage says “the subtle essence you do 
not see; and in that is the whole of this tree; that which is the 
subtle essence – in that have all things their existence. That is 
the Truth. That is the Self. And That, Svetakethu, Art Thou”. 
Likewise the world remains unmanifest in its causal form is 
the view of the Vedantins.

The world is an illusory appearance. One who made it 
appear is a great magician (mayikan) and the magical power he 
wields is called variously as māyā, prakriti, pradhana, avidya, 
nescience, avyakta (unmanifest), avyākrta (undifferentiated). 
The power of māyā operates with time, place, karma and name 
and form as its chief aspects.

When words like “prior”, and “later” indicating time and 
creation are used instantly curiosity is incited and a volley of 
questions like when, where, what, why and from what springs 
forth. 

Kabir once witnessed how people were astounded by the 
feat of a street magician, who keeping one end of a thread in 
hand, threw a ball of thread into thin air which stood vertical 
and a boy walked on it. He at once said he could also do the 
same (by his yogic power) and did the same but in addition, 
he threw the other end of the thread in hand also into thin air 
but still it stood vertically. This is but an instance to show that 
the illusion created by a magician can as well be accomplished 
by the sheer sankalpa of yogic power.

Creation does not happen without differentiation resulting 
in particularities based on name, form, time and place and 
karma. These, the sine-qua-non for the projection of creation, 
have no permanent form or existence of their own. They 
follow the mind which is their support. That the manifold 
world of plurality of names and forms should spring forth 
from existenceless and impermanent factors bespeaks of the 
wondrous power of māyā. The power of māyā belongs to the 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   634 06-05-2011   10:54:08



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 635

Lord. The Lord is the Self of all. Apart from Him, the Ātman, 
realised as the Self, there is no other support for multiplicity; 
yet He remains unchanged. The apparent doership of the 
Lord in creating this world is also mayikam (illusion). May 
the Lord Dakshinamurthy who makes the world appear thus 
by His will be praised.

Many theories of creation have been postulated by various 
schools of thought. They are Vivarta, Drishti-Srishti vada, 
Srishit-Drishti vada and ajata doctrine. 

Vivarta Siddhanta is the doctrine of illusory appearances 
according to which the illusory world appearance is an unreal 
projection of the perceiver.

Dhrishti-Srishti vada is known as yugapath srishti or 
simultaneous creation wherein with dream experience as 
example, one is told “All that you see depends on the seer. 
Apart from the seer there is nothing seen.” This argues that 
one first creates out of his mind and then sees what the mind 
itself has created. “To those who argue the dream experience 
is so short while the world always exists; the dream experience 
was limited to me. But the world is seen and felt by so many 
and we cannot call such a world non-existent” the argument 
called Srishti-Drishti vada is addressed and they are told ‘God 
created such and such a thing out of such and such an element 
and so forth..’. That alone will satisfy this class. Otherwise they 
ask themselves “How can all geography, all maps, all sciences, 
all stars, planets and the rules governing or relating to them 
and all knowledge be totally untrue?” To such it is best to say 
“Yes – God created all this and so you see it”. (Day by Day, 
15.3.46). This vada is also called krama or gradual creation 
and includes all other theories of creation either as explained 
in scriptures or by natural processes as explained by scientists.

Ajata vada states there never was any creation (ajata 
means non-creation). The rope, they say, never became a 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   635 06-05-2011   10:54:08



636 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

snake. To say that the Self has fashioned itself as the world is 
to say the rope has fashioned itself into a snake. The snake, it 
is found, does not exist at all.

Muruganar, in Guru Vāchaka Kovai, says that though 
Bhagavan did expound various doctrines “we have heard him 
say that his true teaching, firmly based on his own experience 
is Ajata”. “Only if there is creation, we have to explain how it 
came about. All that we may not know. But that we exist now 
is certain. Why not know the ‘I’ and the present and then see 
if there is creation.” (Day by Day, 17-2-46)

Bhagavan often used to quote the 32nd Verse from 
chapter II of Mandukya Upanishad Karika: “There is neither 
dissolution, nor birth, neither anyone in bondage nor any 
aspirant for wisdom; neither can there be anyone who hankers 
after wisdom nor any liberated as such. This alone is the 
Supreme Truth.”

This verse was translated into a couplet in Tamil by 
Bhagavan

(Ådalazi vÅrppavizha vÅsaimuyal vÅrndhÅril ≠du 
paramarttamendru en). Interestingly the last two words 
meaning ‘Supreme Truth’ were used to name Guru Vāchaka 
Kovai as Paramartha Deepam (The lamp of Supreme Light) 
by Muruganar.

Bhagavan also used to say this pre-eminent truth was taught 
to Arjuna by Krishna in the Gītā. “For the very first sloka of 
Sri Krishna’s upadēsa starts ‘No birth and no death, no change 
etc.’... but Arjuna did not understand it.” (Talks no. 611).

Bhagavan used this illusory appearance to explain world 
creation for not everyone can grasp the truth of this doctrine. 
But out of infinite Compassion, he condescended to come 
down to the levels of various seekers who approached him 
and answered them from that level in order not to unsettle 
them in their faiths.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   636 06-05-2011   10:54:08



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 637

The intention of the scriptures in describing creation is 
also to promote enquiry into the one Truth. One need not 
doubt as to how a formless form of Sat can be the cause of 
the manifested universe. Cause and effect, part and whole, 
substance and attributes, action and agency and others like 
these are imaginary forms of the one Light and viewed from 
which absolute level discussions of creation and destruction 
are also mere illusory excercises. Bondage of the jīva, its 
release and instructions are all mere māyā–vilasam, the spread 
of māyā.

This sloka emphatically affirms the truth that this 
panaromic world is in the Self. Due to māyā it appears as if it 
is without. When Ātman is realized as the unsublatable Truth, 
the beginningless māyā, though not apart from Brahman, 
vanishes in the Supreme effulgence of jñāna, when, becoming 
one with the Self-revealing effulgence as its form, it becomes 
existenceless, true to its name.

May our obeisance be to Guru Dakshinamurthy 
whose inherent and revealing effulgence (of the nature

Commentary:

aspect of the Ātman that indwells or interpenetrates everything. 
The objects do not announce themselves on their own. The

which functions in the reflected light of the Ātman. ‘Being’ 
or existence (astitva) and light (awareness) are not inherent 
in the objects but they are the attributes of the perceiver, their 
source and support. The snake in the rope is non-existent; yet 
the snake appears partaking the existence of rope. The light 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   638 06-05-2011   10:54:08



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 639

that reveals both is the light of the perceiver. If the rope is 
turned, serpent is gone, yet the snake is not Sat or real but it 
appears real and causes fear. The Sat of the substratum is the 
Sat of the superimposed. The “light and being” that appear in 
the phenomenal objects which remain neither as Sat or asat, 
and indescribable by words, is the light and being of the Ātman.

The existence and light in all objects that are momentary 
and almost non-existent proceed from the eternal Brahman 
and become mingled with them. Having their being in the 
being of Ātman and shining by the light of Ātman, they have 
no existence of their own.

Just like the sun being the common matrix of both the eye 
and the form it perceives, Ātman, the one Reality, is the cause 
of origin and knowledge of all asat or anātman - existenceless 
things, like deha (body) and the ulahu (world).

The sphurana of the Universe is the sphurana of Ātman. 
Knowledge of various kinds and objects are strung together 
on ‘I’ or aham – the Self. If Reality is but one, why is it not 
perceived? Even as a mirror covered with dust cannot reflect 
clearly, Ātman, veiled by the cover of ajñāna (in the form of 
upādhis or adjuncts) envelop the glory of Ātman leading to 
the non-perception and the misperception of the one Reality 
and permanence in the unreal and ephemeral world. This 
leads to lives of strife and suffering which, when they become 
insufferable, drive the jīvas to seek refuge at the feet of the 
realized Guru to find a way out of this mire of existence.

Such a guru, the embodiment of compassion and jñāna 
instructs those who have taken refuge in him, in the content of 
mahavakya and makes them experience it as the most intimate 
and non-mediated experience by his grace and protects them 
from the repeated fall into the ocean of saṃsāra. No words 
can describe adequately the greatness of the guru in saving 
mankind. Spiritual enlightenment blossoms solely due to the 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   639 06-05-2011   10:54:08



640 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

grace of the guru so much so the scriptures proclaim that only 
one who is blessed with and by a teacher, can know the Truth.

	T he mahavakyas are four in number.
	 1. Prajñānam Brahma – Consciousness is Brahman. 

Aithreya Upanishad 3.3 Rig Veda
	 2. Aham Brahmasmi – I am Brahman. Brahadaranyaka 

Upanishad 1-4-10 Yajur Veda
	 3. Tat Tvam Asi – That Thou Art. Chandoghya 

Upanishad 6.8.7 Sama Veda.
	 4. Ayam Ātma Brahma – This Ātman is Brahman. 

Mandukya Upanishad – 2 Atharva Veda.
The mahavakya ‘Tat Tvam Asi’ is repeated nearly nine 

times in the Upanishad. Here it should be remembered that this 
is not instructed for contemplation of it but to remain abiding 
as that condensed form of Pure Consciousness (as jnapti alone) 
by isolating one’s awareness and freeing it from all upādhis.

The perception of snake in a rope, a mistake, none the less 
creates panic and perturbation. When the snake is realized in 
light to be nothing other than a rope it ceases to cause concern 
and fear.

Once the true nature of this misery-ridden world is 
realized in the light of Awareness, the bewilderment born 
of the confusion of mistaking the ephemeral for the eternal 
does not recur again. Nevertheless, the world will continue to 
appear but it will not inspire a sense of reality in it even as the 
appearance of a mirage will not delude one who knows it for 
what it is into thinking that it will serve to quench one’s thirst.

The billows and bubbles in water shine along with 
water but not in the form of water though they are of water. 
Though the universe stands shining to all, it has no other light 
or existence (reality) than that of the light of the Sat - the 
substratum – the Self.

Paraphrase: 
May our obeisance be to that ‘moveless’ guru 

Dakshinamurthy whose luminous awareness like the

and following whom, the Self-certifying effulgence, the

Commentary: 

The resplendent lamp of the Ātman appears to be caged 
inside the pot-like body. The beams of light of a lamp within 
a many-holed pot, stream out through the holes of the pot, 
take the forms of the objects outside and remove the darkness 
surrounding them. Likewise the effulgence of Ātman, the 
form of jñāna , the indweller of the body, floods out through 
the holes of the pot-like body, namely, the antaḥkaraṇa or 
the organs of cognition like the eyes, assumes the forms of 
those objects and removes the ignorance of the knowledge 
of those objects. That light of Awareness that illumines the 
objects perceived, causes the awareness of the knowledge of 
them as “I know them”.

If, in the objective consciousness “I know it”, the one 
who, feels so were not manifest as ‘I’, to whom will anything 
shine? Or what is there to shine? Then, like a lamp, lit but kept 
buried in a deep cavern or in an opaque rock, no object will be 
seen by any as in the state of sushupti (sleep) where nothing 
is seen. The Universe, therefore, depends for its manifestation 
upon a light beyond itself. Likewise that it depends on another 
for its existence as well, was explained in the earlier verse.

The knowledge of the objects is grasped by the 
antaḥkaraṇa (the inner organs like intellect) along with other 
organs of perception. This inner organ, being the most subtle of 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   642 06-05-2011   10:54:08



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 643

all upādhis, is where the light of Ātman is reflected the most. 
This light of awareness of the Ātman flows out through the 
senses and illumines the objects and the knowledge of them 
is gained by the same light of awareness.

The effulgence of the Ātman is reflected in the objects 
that are revealed. But for the luminosity of the Ātman, they 
cannot shine on their own, for they are not endowed with 
Self-revealing light.

Ātman shines by Its own Self-certifying effulgence and by 
its resplendence lights up everything else. Hence the scriptures 
proclaim “There the sun does not shine, nor the moon nor the 
stars. Neither do these lightnings shine; what to speak of fire, 
then? All shine following Him who is resplendent. All this 
shines by His light.” (Mundaka Upanishad, 2.2.10)

If objects could shine by themselves, independent of 
another light, then all objects would appear and shine to all 
individuals and at all times. But never do objects announce their 
existence by themselves. It is the perceiver who establishes 
them and says “there they are”. In short the ‘I Consciousness’ 
is responsible for the awareness of ‘this’ or ‘that’.

The knowledge of the snake wrongly inferred on its 
substratum rope was not there before and after the dispelling 
of the delusion. Likewise the external objects having no 
independent ‘being’ or Sat either before they appear to come 
into being or after they appear to go out of their ‘being’, have 
no real ‘being’ even when they are seen. True being belongs 
to the Ātman that has neither the state before nor after and the 
‘being’ of all things depends on the ‘being’ of Ātman.

A lamp reveals itself without the aid of another lamp. 
Ātman reveals Itself. 

May our obeisance be to Dakshinamurthy, the form of 
Ātman.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   644 06-05-2011   10:54:09



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 645

Commentary: 
Numerous are the adamantine adherents of various 

religions who, besides deluding themselves with the foolish 
ideas of body, breath, sense, intellect or the void as the Ātman 
– the object for the experience of ‘I am’ – delude others as 
well by their vehement advocacy of the same. 

The reference here is to the votaries of various schools of 
thought that asserted the various kosas as the Ātman. These 
foolish and misguided contenders, devoid of real knowledge 
subject themselves to mighty delusion. Ignorance of the real 
content of ‘I’ that ever remains as the uninvolved witness, 
Awareness and the imagining of illusions contradictory to each 
other is but the brilliant play of the power of māyā.

Charvakas are the epicureans or ultra materialists. 
According to them pratyaksha or direct perception being 
proof or authority of knowledge, objects pertaining to realms 
beyond perception could not be proved. Ātman is not perceived 
and therefore is not accepted. Changes like birth and growth 
pertain to the body and varnashramas are body-based. Carnal 
pleasures and wealth conducive to the fulfilment of pleasures 
are ends in themselves. Heaven and other worlds are not seen 
either. There is none who creates and hence these exists no 
Ātman apart from the body.

Some postulate and conclude that pranan or the vital 
breath is the Ātman. Living, hunger and thirst are functions 
of the vital breath. With the exit of pranan, the body though 
it looks of the same nature, is not self-conscious nor does it 
perform the functions of vital air. Therefore pranan is Ātman 
whose presence makes the body alive and whose exit makes 
it a corpse.

In sleep and swoon, though body and breath are there no 
action is performed. The worldly transactions take place only 
when the sense organs function. Therefore this sect argues that 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   645 06-05-2011   10:54:09



646 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

as self-consciousness arises only with the activity of the senses 
on the basis of experiences like ‘I hear’, ‘I see’, ‘I smell’, they 
conclude that the indriyas – the sense organs – are the Ātman.

Everything shines and the past is remembered due to the 
intellect. Activities go on due to the presence of the intellect. 
Hence intellect or knowledge is Ātman, is the contention of 
yet another school.

In sushupti, there is absence of any kind of knowledge 
or śūnya prevails. Intellect rising from śūnya abides in śūnya. 
Therefore Buddhists declare śūnya as Ātman.

All that is perceived is anātman. The body, perceptible, is 
insentient and depends on something else for manifestation; 
is made up of five elements. It has no sphurana of ‘I am’. The 
content of ‘I’ is different from the human body for even men 
devoid of discretion consider the body as apart from them and 
say ‘this is my body’ as if it is like an ornament that belongs 
to them.

If pranan is Ātman, in swoon and sushupti when it is 
active, the awareness of ‘I’ must be there. Pranan is also not 
the Lord of sense organs for if it be the Lord when it is active 
in sushupti, its subordinates cannot remain inactive.

The sense organs are insentient and not known as ‘I’. 
One sense organ cannot do the job of another. If indriyas are 
the Ātman, there must be more than one Ātman as there are 
many sense-organs. Further people devoid of sense organs like 
the deaf and dumb must be ‘Selfless’ and therefore insentient 
anātman, which is absurd.

Intellect is a momentary phenomenon that comes 
and goes. Further it is not Self-revealing but is illumined 
by Ātman’s reflection in it. Intellect is born in Ātman and 
dissolves in Ātman. Also the origin and end of a thing cannot 
be perceived by the thing itself.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   646 06-05-2011   10:54:09



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 647

Ātman, the form of Chit, the ruler of intellect and other 
sense organs, is distinct from pranan. These cannot be facts 
of experience unless perceived by some conscious entity – a 
revealing light – that simply remains as uninvolved witness.

Śūnya cannot be the Ātman for there is a conscious entity 
who perceives it and knows it as Śūnya. Ātman manifests 
Himself by His all-pervasive nature in different kinds of 
bodies.

All these arguments are due to delusion. All the dissenting 
disputes that the scriptural scholars – deluded and impelled 
by māyā – engage themselves in, disappear if sadasiva, Lord 
Dakshinamurthy is seen. Discrimination must originate in the 
perception that from the body to the intellect is distinct from 
Ātman, the content of ‘I’. The Lord, free of delusion alone can 
destroy the mighty power of delusion of māyā.

Those who contend various things as Ātman are deluded 
indeed. As true knowledge is eclipsed by delusion in them, 
they not only assert what they think as right but even 
proceed to establish it by indulgence in specious arguments 
as well. Such delusion is hence called “mighty delusion – 
mamayakkam. When the delusion of an ordinary jīva itself is 
hard to overcome, who else other than Lord Dakshinamurthy, 
free of delusion, can remove the mighty delusion of such 
learned dissenters? 

Our obeisance to him who has neither body nor sense 
organs nor vital air, whose nature is inaccessible to all organs 
of perception, who is Consciousness and bliss in essence.

Jñānat tadaiaru guravam can also be interpreted as 
follows: “Obeisance to Sri Dakshinamurthy, the one who 
removes the delusion born of the expansive display of māyā 
caused by the ignorance of one’s real form and the obstacles 
encountered while pursuing the path of jñāna.

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 649

Commentary: 
The five instruments of perception and mind subside 

in their cause while the jīva sleeps. Then the jīva, with all 
instruments and organs stilled from activity, subsides in his 
source, becomes moveless and quiescent as the Ātman. When 
the mind becomes outward bent, impelled by the vagaries of 
vāsanās, on waking up, he becomes aware that he slept well 
before waking up. The one, who remaining awake while the 
jīva sleeps, causes him to wake up and makes him aware that 
he slept till then, is the eternally existent vastu – the Ātman.

The state of jagrat is when the mind functions in 
association with the indriyas. The dream state is when the 
mind alone – and not in association with indriyas – functions. 
When the mind also is at rest, that state is called sushupti.

The nature of indriyas is to rush towards their respective 
objects, their action controlled by the intellect. Perception, 
non-perception or misperception of sense objects through 
sense organs depends on the state of antaḥkaraṇa – the 
intellect – functioning through the reflected light of the Ātman. 
When the sense organs are withdrawn in dream, the jīva is 
conscious of the mental images generated by impressions of 
jagrat. The withdrawal of even the mind is called sushupti 
when he subsides into the causal state – nescience. The 
sushupti is the state of deep sleep in which the jīva is in the 
prajñā (awareness) aspect. “Just as a hen after roaming about 
in the day calls the chicks to her, enfolds them under her wings 
and goes to rest for the night, so also the subtle individual 
being, after finishing the experiences of jagrat and swapna 
for the time being enters with the impressions gathered during 
those states into the causal body made up of nescience.” (Talks 
no. 617). “At sunrise the rays emerge forth and are collected 
again at sunset. Similarly when the ego displays itself, it 
does so with all its paraphernalia. When it sinks everything 
disappears with it.” (Talks no. 286)

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   649 06-05-2011   10:54:09



650 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Deep sleep is nothing but the experience of pure being. 
Every person, after waking up, is known to say “I slept 
soundly and happily; I was not aware of anything”. Two 
facts emerge from the statement, unawareness of anything 
and the happiness of sound sleep. During sleep there are no 
other external source – or instruments or even sādhanas that 
can give ananda (happiness). It is the true form of Bliss of 
Ātman that was experienced in sleep and recognised after 
waking up from sleep. Bhagavan explains this state: “Unless 
these (the unawareness of anything and the joy) existed and 
were experienced in sleep they could not find expression by 
the same person in the waking state. Just as the eye sees the 
darkness which remains enveloping all objects, so also the 
Self sees the darkness of nescience which remained covering 
the phenomenal world. This darkness was experienced when 
it (the Self) emerged in dots of Supreme Bliss, shone a trice 
and fleeted away in such fine subtlety as the rays of moon 
which peer through the waving foliage.” (Talks no. 617). 
The experience was however not through any media (such as 
senses and mind) but bears out the fact that Consciousness 
does exist in deep sleep. The unawareness is owing to the 
absence of relative knowledge, and the happiness to the 
absence of seething thoughts. The recollection of the feeling 
of awareness and bliss of sleep is a remembrance of what 
has been experienced. The one who says he was not aware 
of anything is very much present. The experience of bliss of 
Brahman in deep sleep is transitory. Thus, inspite of varying 
states of being, Ātman – sat-chit-ananda – is revealed. “The 
Self is the basis of all experiences. It remains as the witness 
and support of them all. The Reality is thus different from 
the three states, the waking, the dream and the deep sleep”. 
(Talks no. 617)

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   650 06-05-2011   10:54:09



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 651

The remembrance or recollection of the non-awareness of 
anything and the bliss is called prathyabhijna. “Pratyabhijna 
= Prati + abhijna.

abhijna is direct perception; prati is to be reminded of 
what was already known.

“This is an elephant” direct perception
“This is that elephant” is pratyabhijna
In technical works, pratyabhijna is used for realising the 

ever-present Reality and recognising it.” (Talks no.333)
The light of the sun and moon during the period of eclipses 

is not like their light before and after; yet one cannot say there 
is no light during eclipses. Like the sun and moon that do not 
shine in full effulgence during eclipses, during sushupti there 
is no qualified or special knowledge as indriyas and mind 
have been withdrawn.

What was before and after should also have been in 
between is the inference. The jagrat states before and after 
sushupti denote a continuous and unified awareness of one’s 
being, enabling one to recall the joy and unawareness of 
anything else. The one before and the one after sleep is one – 
He I am – is pratyabhijna. Pratyabijna is the Consciousness 
that refers to the continuous existence of one and the same 
thing. In sushupti the jīva is shining as mere form of ‘being’ 
(Sat alone) and not in full effulgence for he is enshrouded 
by māyā or nescience just as the sun and moon do not shine 
fully during eclipses as at other times; yet still shine as the 
form of being.

The contention of the Buddhists that Ātman is Śūnya and 
that in sushupti there is no Ātma prakāśa (light of Ātman) is 
answered here. Is not the one who says he knew nothing in 
sleep an existent one? He is the Ātman. Therefore the Ātman, 
through seemingly non-luminous in sushupti due to the absence 
of special forms of cognition, as indriyas have subsided, yet 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   651 06-05-2011   10:54:09



652 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

shines as the Self-luminous witness and Awareness. What is 
experienced in sushupti must be consciously experienced in 
jagrat and all sādhanas are aimed to achieve that. This verse 
provides a practical tip to sādhana. 

 “This ‘I’ is the one who experiences the waking, dream 
and sleep states. The three states are changes which do not 
affect the individual. The three states alternate with one 
another leaving the Self unaffected. The waking and dream 
states are creations of the mind. So the Self covers all. To 
know that the Self remains happy in its perfection is Self-
Realisation. It’s use lies in the realisation of perfection and 
thus of Happiness.” (Talks no. 486). In this context Bhagavan’s 
definitions of Sravana, Manana and Nidhidhyasana have great 
relevance. “Listening to one’s own Heart declaring itself as 
the root of the I-thought, different from the body (and mind) 
– this is Sravana in reality. Manana, in reality, is enquiry 
into Being (The Self). Firm abidance in Being is termed 
Nidhidhyasana.”      (Ramana Gītā, Chap. 15). Bhagavan calls 
this as antara Sravana.

 The shadow not connected with the effulgent form of 
Sun hides the Sun. Then the sun is not seen as it is. Likewise, 
the Ātman that is totally unattached and unrelated to any 
shines in Self-luminous effulgence. Like the sun coming out 
of the eclipse shines in all its effulgence, with the dawn of 
wisdom, the veil of māyā removed, the Ātman shines in all 
its luminosity. Māyā eclipses or conceals Ātman and vidya or 
Knowledge unveils It. 

That Ātman who, when enshrouded by māyā, remaining as 
the aspect of existence alone (Sat aspect) with all the indriyas 
merged, remained as one who slept well and who on waking 
is recollected as the one who slept and by whom one’s being 
is known, to that guru of sentient and insentient Universe, 
may our obeisance be.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   653 06-05-2011   10:54:09



654 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

the handpose of Chin mudrā reveals graciously to those

Commentary: 

That Ātman is of eternal or continual and persistent 
nature was confirmed in the earlier verse on the strength of 
recollection of the Self-identity. At any one time, there is but 
one avastha and not another. Just like the states of dream and 
waking, pain and pleasure, experienced in the states of infancy 
and childhood, the various changes caused by the dharma 
or nature of body, and in all matters of the empirical world, 
we ever remain constant simply as witness – Awareness, as 
the true content of the I-st person I, having no connection 
whatsoever with any of them is explained in this verse. 

Though this luminosity of Ātman permeates and appears 
from body to mind and is not distinct as Itself, and as It always 
pulsates as the sphurana of ‘I’, we are devoid of the various 
changes of states and that we, as That which lights up these 
states forever, remain the same changeless Self.

Infancy, youth and old age relating to the gross body and 
dream, waking and sleep, relating to the mental world are 
common to the entire humanity. The one who remains through 
all these states that follow one another in quick succession 
remains without undergoing any change, thus proving that He 
is not subject to those varying avastas or states.

For example a youth may delightfully recount the innocent 
pranks he indulged in as a child; yet the state of childhood 
he speaks of is not present now but having become bygone 
lies buried in the past. If he had been identical with the state 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   654 06-05-2011   10:54:09



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 655

of childhood he would not now be able to recall and speak of 
them. Along with that state his thoughts of them also would 
have disappeared once and for all. But not having been so, 
that he is able to recollect and recount proves that the one who 
experienced childhood state then is one who experiences now 
his youth and he is different from these two states. Thus the 
states are many but the one who experiences them all is just 
one otherwise there would have been a childhood Ātma, an 
youth Ātma and so on.

Likewise the one who dreamt on waking up says “I had a 
dream” which clearly reveals that the one who dreamt is the same 
one who woke up. Whatever be the states that one is revolved 
in continuously, one after the other, the ‘I’, unchanged, pulsates 
persistently in us throughout the various states continuously and 
without change. This ‘I’ is the sphurana of Ātman.

The object of former experience or even the experience 
itself might have disappeared but its memory abides as 
samskara (vāsanās) and the Ātman, never vanishing, in 
association with antaḥkaraṇas, recollects the object that has 
been dissolved in him as latent impressions.

The Ātman continues as the same through the various 
bodies necessitated by karma – not born when bodies are born, 
and not dying when the bodies die. Hence Ātman exists the 
same even in different bodies. The presence of the persistent 
Ātman alone provides the reason for the instinctive recollection 
of former experiences. This is explained with an example in 
Vivekachūḍāmaṇi. One small built Devadatta of Kasi is seen 
in Chidambaram after ten years, in a hefty frame. His identity 
is established by obvious similarities as the Devadatta of Kasi 
as the one seen in Chidambaram, though the time, place and 
even physical frames have changed. If attributes such as spear 
for a soldier and a badge of ownership for a slave are removed 
both alike belong to the genus, man, in the same way though 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   655 06-05-2011   10:54:09



656 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

the attributes of Devadatta and factors like time and place 
have changed, yet the content of ‘I’ in him, which others refer 
to as ‘He’ has not. The body, time and place are not part of 
his svarūpa and are not permanently abiding objects. Though 
they have changed they are rejected as not part of him and 
the form permeating and appearing as Devadatta is the same. 
Thus bodies and states may come and go but ‘I’ the sphurana 
of ‘I am’ goes on forever.

Incidentally it is worth knowing what Sadhu Natanananda 
records as Bhagavan’s teaching: “As the jīva himself is 
the substratum for the rise and subsidence of the mind, 
unceasing practice of the witness state will lead to a gradual 
reduction of the rising of the mind. When practice matures, 
the mind will totally cease to exist.” (Sadhu Natanananda, 
Ramana Darsanam, page 80) and it is aptly described by 
Thayumanavar as follows:

“It is there that the mind is born; it is there that the mind 
died and became clear. All the states are there. It is also there 
that I remained as One without a second. It is fit to meditate 
on the witness, the clever one who, while creating, preserving 
and destroying, remains absolutely untainted by all these acts.”

Obeisance to that form of Guru Sri Dakshinamurthy, who 
reveals the sphurana of Ātman, as ‘I’ ‘I’, to those who have 
surrendered to him through Chin mudrā.*

In this verse, Bhagavan, by the introduction of two 
significant words “kazhal vizhuvorkku” (to those who 
take refuge at His Feet), which are not in the original, has 
emphasized the importance of surrender, the only alternative 
to Self-enquiry.

* Chin mudrā is a gesture or physical pose that reflects the inner 
(mystic) state. It is called a blessed symbol (badra) or symbol 
of consciousness, and also a symbol of vyakyana (exposition), a 
symbol of tarka (investigation) and a symbol of jñāna (wisdom).

May our obeisance be to that Teacher of the world, 
Sri Dakshinamurthy, the Purusha – the Self, who, deluded 
by māyā perceives in manifoldness the Universe in the 
nature of Cause and effect, as master and servant (with a 
sense of possession), as disciple and teacher (with a sense

and with various perceptions in jagrat and sushupti.
Commentary: 

That form of Parabrahman during waking and sleep, 
dwelling unceasingly within, assuming the form of jīva by its 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   657 06-05-2011   10:54:09



658 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

power of māyā and getting deluded by its own māyā (which 
is but ignorance of the Self), perceives the world as the form 
of cause and effect and with manifold distinctions as sire and 
servant with a sense of possession, with a sense of connection 
as guru and sishya or with a sense of ‘mine’ as father and 
son, – that form of Ātman, Sri Dakshinamurthy, is hailed and 
prayed to here.

That which is perceived as the world is the unreal and 
imagined projection of māyā, that indescribable power which 
is not apart from Brahman. All imaginations – in their entirety 
– are but the expansive display of māyā. This power of māyā 
is totally subservient to the Self. That is why vedānta śāstras 
explain the phenomenon of world as that created by the Lord 
himself, entering into māyā and assuming the form of jīva. 
Bhagavan calls māyā as “only Isvara-Sakti or the activity of 
Reality” (Talks, no. 399). This verse also explains this view. 
Upanishads also speak of how Brahman by māyā became two 
birds ever together. (Mundaka Upanishad, -3-1)

Two birds of golden plumage, inseparable and of equal 
stature, live in the same tree. While one eats the fruits, tasty 
and sour, the other witnesses without eating any. Though 
living in the same tree one bird (jīva), deluded, losing its 
nature, reaches states lowly and grieves. Whenever it looks 
up the other, perched high, alone and Lordly bird, perceiving 
that greatness to be its own, it gives up grief. Whoever is 
capable of perceiving, perceives the Brahman, Lord (shining 
with golden effulgence) of creation and his Source, then that 
mighty soul shakes off all sins, becomes taintless and attains 
oneness with that purusha”.

The verse from Upadēsa Undiyar also is worth recalling 
here. “By their existing nature, God and soul, are only 
one substance. Their adjunct (upādhi), knowledge, alone 
is different. Knowing oneself, having given up adjuncts 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   658 06-05-2011   10:54:09



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 659

(upādhis), is itself knowing God because He shines as One’s 
Self.”

Though the world perceptible to the eyes, instead of 
remaining as one and Eternal Existence, appears with varied 
distinctions, it does not exist as apart from that one Self-
Luminous Existence. The Universe has, for its basis and 
support, the Existence of the One Truth.

If nothing exists apart from Ātman, the One Light, how 
do all the experiences happen? One a Guru, another a disciple, 
bondage to the disciple, initiation from a guru to be relieved 
of misery and bondage, all can happen only if there are many. 
The answer to this question is also provided by this verse.

To imagine in the one Self, the non-dual Existence, 
‘notions of many and otherness’ like cause and effect and 
other mental projections is like imagining the head of Rahu 
(for all that Rahu has, is only head and no trunk – when one 
speaks of Rahu none can presume that the head exists distinct 
or apart from Rahu) or empty space in Ākāśa or to say “my 
Ātman” (I and myself are one) .

When the Lord is spoken of as the cause of the Universe, 
it should not be understood that the universe exists distinct 
from the Ātman. Likewise all distinctions based on varied 
relationships relate to the One vastu only. The Lord assumes 
Himself, of His own accord, these forms of worshipper, 
worshipped, master, servant, etc. This is called Leela 
Kaivalyam (the divine play of the Absolute).

If they are not illusions, a father must always remain 
a father. But he who is a son with reference to his father, 
becomes a father to his son. One vastu is imagined in various 
distinctive forms by mere twist of terms. On enquiry into 
the Supreme Truth, the Light of Awareness alone exists. All 
notions of difference or distinctions in the One Ātman are 
mitya which stand negated with the dawn of Knowledge. 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   659 06-05-2011   10:54:09



660 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Then distinctions like master and disciple, the one instructing 
the other, disappear like dream objects becoming untrue on 
waking up.

All mundane experiences are due to the play of māyā 
which stands nullified on waking up to reality.

Then the question arises, if with the dawn of knowledge; 
everything, including the Universe, stands proven unreal, 
then, Brahman taught by vedānta is also unreal. The figure 
of a tiger drawn on a wall is not real but the fear induced by 
the lifelike picture is real. Likewise Vedānta, though it pales 
into the realm of unreal with spiritual enlightenment, teaches 
the Sat or ‘Brahman’.

Mind, the product of māyā, constantly alternates among 
the three states which cause the delusion of difference and 
distinctions. Karmas which cannot be done without the notion 
of distinctions entangle one in saṃsāra. This mind is illumined 
by the witness, Ātman, like the Sun who is not affected by the 
activities on earth by various beings, though he illumines them 
all. The uninvolved witness, Brahman, will not be bound by 
any activity; the one witnessing a duel between two acquires 
no bandha by way of grief or punishment, both of which 
belong to those who fought. The mind alone is the cause of 
bondage or mukti. In the ultimate sense “To know that there 
never was ignorance is the goal of all the spiritual teachings. 
Ignorance must be of one who is aware. Awareness is jñāna. 
Jñāna is eternal and natural. Ajñāna is unnatural and unreal.” 
(Talks no. 289). And finally “All explanations are merely 
mental and intellectual and nothing more. Still all of them 
are true according to the standpoint of the individual. There 
is no creation in the state of realisation. When one sees the 
world, one does not see the one Self. When one sees the Self 
the world is not seen. See the Self and realise there has been 
no creation”. (Talks no. 455). 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   660 06-05-2011   10:54:09



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 661

Like the fire, though covered by smoke, is bright and 
aflame within, Ātman, though covered by the effect of māyā 
– the world of names and forms – is resplendent as the light of 
jñāna, within. To that form of jñāna that shines within – Lord 
Dakshinamurthy – may our obeisance be.

Paraphrase: 
The one whose eight-fold form shines as all this 

moving and unmoving universe, earth, water, fire, air, 
ether, moon and sun, the one who remains the Content 
Beyond pervading everything and apart from whom 
there exists naught else – to that form of compassion and 
infinite peace, Sri Dakshinamurthy, may our obeisance be.
Commentary: 

This verse suggests the way to overcome māyā. If non-
mediated experience of Aham Brahmasmi is the way, how 
to gain it? Though the Universal Self is present everywhere, 
permeating everything, it is immediately perceived in eight 
forms that the world is classified into namely earth, water, 
fire, air, sky, moon, sun and jīva. The one who enquires into 
the truth behind the principle of these eight forms will realize 
that they are but forms of the Lord.

Worship of the Lord in these eight forms and realizing 
Him is called Akanda upasana. The worship of this is an 
excellent guide to realize that everything that is perceived 
is the form of the Absolute Itself. This very same Truth, the 
Lord proclaims in the Gītā: “He whose Self is harmonized 
by yoga, seeth the Self abiding in all beings and all beings in 
the Self; everywhere he sees the same.” And “He who sees 
Me everywhere and sees all in Me; I am not lost to him nor 
he lost to Me.” (Chapter VI, Verses 29 and 30). Worship of 
the eightfold form in mind will elevate a yogī to the mind-
free state. One who so worships cannot perceive or think of 
anything as other than the Content beyond. Hence it is said, “to 
those who perceive He is the One who is all.” As everything 
is perceived as nothing but ‘He’, it is said there is nothing 
aught apart from ‘He’ – Viswam Vishnuhu (Universe is Vishnu) 
which is the worship of all-embracing unfragmented Brahman.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   662 06-05-2011   10:54:10



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 663

Upasana is nothing but viewing a small object as a great 
one worthy of reverence and obeisance. Worshipping a small 
idol viewing it as Devi or Lord Murugan is upasana. Of the 
various forms of worship prescribed for realization of the Self, 
worship of eight forms is spoken of here.

This type of upasana removes the impurities of ‘I’ and 
‘mine’ and induces one to engage oneself in the enquiry of 
the Self. Such a one, by the grace of Guru’s instructions 
,realizes that the jīva has no existence apart from Him, and 
that other than ‘He’, the jīva has no distinctive existence and 
gets released from the bondage of saṃsāra.

Of the various principles which are the bodies of 
Parameshwara, the immediately perceivable are these eight 
forms. As the mind cannot easily ascend high to grasp 
incomprehensible matters, the guru teaches contemplation of 
the Universal Self, the Sarvātman in these eight forms.

Then by the grace of the Supreme, the non-mediated 
experience of the effulgent Self results.

The entire Universe is made up of the aggregate of eight 
forms. The aggregate of 36 basic principles (five elements, 
five pranas, fourteen indriyas, mahat, time, pradhanam, māyā, 
avidya, Purusha and Bindu) constitute the microcosm and the 
macrocosm, everything at cosmic and individual level. The 
devotee should contemplate that the soul indwelling both is 
the same. 

Obeisance to that Guru Dakshinamurthy of the eight-fold 
form on whom everything is imagined and apart from whom 
there is naught and none other.

Paraphrase: 
When the content of this verse which reveals lucidly 

the Sarvātmatva (the Universality of Ātman) – the Self 
remaining as everything – is listened to with faith from 
a guru, the content thus heard is reflected upon well and 
enquired into and contemplated upon or sung sweetly, 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   664 06-05-2011   10:54:10



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 665

the exalted wealth of the divine state of Iswaratva 
(Lordliness) – remaining the Self of all – will accrue to 
one along with the eternal wealth of the eight-fold siddhis 
like anima which reach one on their own.
Commentary: 

This verse is in the nature of phalasruthi, a conventional 
conclusion wherein the benefits that will accrue to one who 
recites the hymn are enumerated. Constant reflections on 
the contents of this hymn, after listening to it with faith and 
sincerity, will endow upon one the incomparable wealth of the 
grandeur of being the Self of all, by being one’s Svarūpa or 
Self, otherwise called Sarvātmatva. This power rests with Lord 
Parameshwara. He remains the indweller, the Self or Ātman 
of all and when He is the Self of everything He becomes the 
‘Self’ of us too. As such He is our real ‘I’ and we are not other 
than Him. Therefore Sarvātmatva is within us.

The one Universal ‘I’ becomes many and detached 
only by restricting it to the body and thus the Content of ‘I’ 
becomes limited. When this narrow outlook and restrictive 
attitude is overcome the content of ‘I’ expands to Infinitude 
to include everything. When the truth of the dictum Sarvam hi 
etat brahma, ayam ātma brahma – all this is verily Brahman 
and ‘This Ātman’ is Brahman – is experienced by one as 
the most intimate experience, everything is experienced as 
consciousness in both the immanent and transcendental aspects. 
Each and every atom of this infinite creation is perceived as 
the immanent aspect of that very same consciousness and no 
difference whatsoever is perceived between the unmanifested 
infinite consciousness and the manifested universe, both being 
simply Pure Consciousness alone. In the words of Bhagavan, 
“The Transcendental state of identity with Brahman places the 
man in harmony with everything and there is nothing apart 
from the Self.” (Talks no. 2)

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   665 06-05-2011   10:54:10



666 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

The way or sādhana for the union of jīva and para – the 
attainment of mukti - has been very lucidly explained in this 
verse. One who hears it from a competent teacher, meditates 
and reflects on its import and knowing it with clarity, and hails 
and sings it will attain the greatest of all siddhis, namely the 
experience of Aham Brahmam.

Siddhis like anima, mahima and others, held high by 
jñānis, also seek and reach him on their own though he 
seeks them not like the one who carries a flower enjoys its 
fragrance wily nily. He remains the master of siddhis, they 
being subservient to him. There is nothing that is not attained 
by one in whom the truth of being the Self of all holds an 
unceasing sway.

Vibhuti is a manifestation of the glory or wealth of God. 
The worldlings regard one who owns some possessions as 
one with wealth. With the dawn of spiritual enlightenment, 
“I am the Self of everything”, all the objects of the universe 
– in their entirety – become one’s own. There cannot be a 
greater vibhuti than this. This summum bonum of spiritual 
experience is indeed the summum bonum of all wealth. This 
is the Brahmi stiti – namely, the state ‘I am Brahman’. “One 
who has the highest love for God and for Guru as for God, to 
that Mahātman, the truths taught here shine in full” declares 
the Sruti. He who is Primal Guru to all worlds, the repository 
of all Ātma vidhya, the quintessence of all vidhyas, the form of 
pure jñāna, the physician curing the disease of transmigration, 
He who by His power of Light affords light to all lights, who 
lights the whole universe, to that Guru, Sri Dakshinamurthy 
may our obeisance be.

in all the verses from two to ten as “tasmai Sri Gurumūrthayē 
nama Utham Sri. Dakshinamūrthayē” (to that form of Guru,
