668 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Sri Ānma Bōdham

Origin
A Muslim scholar, Mr. Minna Nuruddin, a Law officer 

with some knowledge of Sanskrit had translated and published 
this highly venerated work of Sri Sankara, Ātma Bodham in 
Tamil. That the Muslim gentleman himself had sent by post 
to the Ashram two printed copies of the book which along 
with the daily letters, found their way to Bhagavan’s hands is 
one version. The other version has it that the author himself 
had come to see Bhagavan with Professor K. Swaminathan, 
who introduced him to Bhagavan when he handed over two 
copies to Bhagavan personally.

On receiving the book, Bhagavan was found leafing 
through the book frequently. His repeated act of closing the 
book only to take it back to read it again, puzzled many and 
an inner urge was apparent on his face.

Bhagavan was very fond of this masterpiece from his 
Virupaksha days. Perusing through this prolix paraphrase in 
Tamil (this rendition was in verses of eight line stanzas) he 
felt an urge to pack the content of each verse in a composition 
of terser, more faithful and compacted translation and chose 
the veṇbā  metre to accomplish it. Asking Venkataratnam to 
bring the original Ātma Bodham by Sankara in Devanagari 
script from the library, Bhagavan perused it and forthwith 
started and completed the translation of two verses in the 
Tamil veṇbā  metre.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   668 06-05-2011   10:54:10



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 669

An intrigued Gurram Subbharamaiah, who was observing 
all these wondered what that book was. Then Bhagavan 
showed him the two translated verses. Echoing at once the 
desire of all the devotees present he remarked: “Wouldn’t it 
be good if Bhagavan translated the rest of the verses in the 
Text?” Though Bhagavan declined saying “Why all that to 
us?”, something from within must have been prompting him 
to do precisely that.

Within the next two days he translated two more saying 
“Even if I remain quiet, it looks as if it will not leave me 
alone; verse after verse appears before me.” Asking for a 
freshly stitched note book, be completed the work within days. 
T.P. Ramachandra Iyer records, “Bhagavan completed the work 
sitting the whole night with candle light by his side, straining 
his already weak eyes and when the new printed booklets were 
ready, he had one sent to the Muslim Professor and another to 
Professor Swaminathan.” (Moments Remembered, page 43)

Bhagavan then remarked, “This text finds a place in that 
small note-book with Malayalam verses – the first possession 
we acquired nearly forty years before.” Someone remarked 
that for every occurrence, there is an appropriate time to 
happen. “Yes! After I complete one another appears suo motto. 
I also feel like having read it before. I hope nobody has written 
it already”, responded Bhagavan with a smile.

Muruganar, who was opposite to Bhagavan, assured 
saying, “none has written in veṇbā  metre.” Further Muruganar 
continued, “Can there be any wonder or surprise in their 
appearing before Bhagavan one by one? Even history of 
Epics bears testimony to the fact that in the beginning of 
every kalpa (aeon), Vedas appear before Brahma. Is not this 
exactly similar?”

Bhagavan wondered further with a chuckle and a smile 
whether as in the case of Saint Jayadeva, “will someone appear 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   669 06-05-2011   10:54:10



670 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

claiming authorship to this text and accuse me of plagiarism?” 
Some devotees wanted to hear the story of this saint-scholar, 
devotee of Lord Krishna, from Bhagavan.

The story of Jayadeva is found in Bhaktavijayam which 
text was read aloud by Bhagavan on many occasions. Jayadeva 
wrote Bhāgavatam in Sanskrit. His fame had spread through 
the length and breadth of the country through his earlier 
composition Gīta Govindam. The king  of Orissa (Krauncha in 
olden days) who was himself an ardent devotee of the Lord and 
an admirer of Jayadeva requested him to read his Bhagavatam 
in his royal court. Lord Jagannath of Puri in the guise of a 
Brahmin Pandit came to the Durbar Hall and after blessing the 
king introduced himself as a Pandit well-versed in śāstras and 
residing in Gokula Brindavan and that he had been searching 
all over for his equal in śāstraic knowledge and was itching 
for discussion with such a one, and knowing that Jayadeva 
was with the king, thither he had come. When Jayadeva was 
introduced to him, he said: “Oh! You are Jayadeva! Let us 
discuss any one of the śāstras you have studied.” Looking at 
Jayadeva steadily, he said, “What is that in your hand?” and 
without waiting for a reply snatched the book from his hands 
and said, “Oho! This is Bhāgavatam. So you are a pauranika 
(one who gives discourses on the Epics).”

Jayadeva said  with all humility and devotion, “Sir, I am 
not a Pandit to hold discussions with you. I seek the blessings 
of elders like you. Though I do not have the courage to say I 
wrote this book as it is not a fault to utter the Truth, I admit 
I am its author.”

That Brahmin pretended surprise and said, “What! If it 
is you who wrote it, tell me, how could I have learnt all its 
contents by heart?” So saying without opening the book, he 
repeated the contents, chapter by chapter. While the king 
and audience were amazed, Jayadeva realised that the Lord 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   670 06-05-2011   10:54:10



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 671

Himself had come in that guise to shower His grace on him 
and hailed him with hymns full of devotion. The Lord, pleased, 
blessed him and disappeared.

Bhagavan concluded “in the same way someone may 
quarrel with me saying that he had written Ātma Bodha.”

Only here, the roles of Lord Jagannath and Jayadeva seem 
to have been interchanged.

Ānma Bodham took shape in Tamil in the light of this 
interesting backdrop. There lies an interesting background 
to every work composed by Bhagavan since what Bhagavan 
wrote on his own were few and far between. As none has left 
a record of these incidents, only a few are available to us now.

Initially these verses were written in veṇbā metre, but in 
Sep. 1948 Bhagavan changed them from veṇbā  to kaliveṇbā 
metre to facilitate easy parayana. This text is the final 
composition of Bhagavan.

That, one, not a practicing Hindu, was prompted to 
attempt a translation of Ātma Bodham, a purely Advaitic Text 
in Tamil is strange enough and stranger still is that it should 
prompt Bhagavan (the all-knowing Pure Awareness that he 
is) to bring forth a fresh translation saying: “I feel like having 
read it before.”

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   671 06-05-2011   10:54:10

Paraphrase: 
Can Āchārya Sankara, the enlightener of the Self 

through his treatise Ātma bōdham be, ‘other’ than the

(What else is there other than the Ātman?)

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   672 06-05-2011   10:54:10



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 673

Commentary: 
Ānma Bōdham* is one of the most quoted and highly 

extolled of the numerous Vedantic texts composed by Sri 
Sankara Bhagavadpada. This text, concerns itself with 
Brahman, the delineations of its characteristics, the emphatic 
pronouncement that Brahma jñāna, Knowledge of the Self, is 
the only way – the royal way – to mukti and the nature of mukti 
explained and illustrated with ample examples. This is written 
exclusively for the sake of mumukshus, intensely desirous of 
mukti.

What Āchārya Sankara, the Teacher of all, abiding 
himself as the Self, penned in Sanskrit in days of yore, is now 
reiterated in these dulcet verses of veṇbā  metre in Tamil by 
Guru Ramana, the same Self.

Bhagavan concludes this verse with the question, “Who 
else, other than Sankara, speaketh that Knowledge of Ātman 
now in Tamil?” The same non-dual Eternal Ātman sports 
as these two forms of Guru, namely, Sankara of yore and 
Bhagavan of now. Bhagavan emphatically affirms that 
Sankara, abiding as the innermost Self in him, bespeaks it now 
in Tamil. Conversely it can also be said that Sri Ramana, who 
utters the Tamil verse now, spoke in Sanskrit then as Sankara. 
Both the gurus are but forms of the non-dual Brahman, bearing 
testimony to he truth of the ancient declaration.

	 Iswaror Guru Ātmeti
	 Murti bheda vibhaginē
	 Vyomavat vyapta dehaya
	 Sri Dakshinamurthaye namaha.
Iswara, Guru and Ātman are the one Essence differentiated 

by mere forms. Our prostrations to Sri Dakshinamurthy, with 
the frame spread like the vast sky.

When Bhagavan had completed translating Ātma Bodha 
into Tamil verses, a scholar-devotee pleaded with him that he 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   673 06-05-2011   10:54:10



674 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

should also bestow a mangala-sloka (an invocatory verse) for 
it. Bhagavan, as usual, complied with the request and this is 
that verse.

It is worthwhile recollecting that all the invocatory verses 
of Bhagavan for all his translated works, centre around the 
Self, that Bhagavan is. Even the invocatory verse  for the 
translation in prose form of the Vivekachūḍāmaṇi has the same 
as content and runs as follows: “May the heart ever rejoice at 
the Feet of Ātma Deva, the Lord, the Self, shining forever as 
‘I, I’, unaware of day and night and putting the ego, the root 
of nescience, to flight.”

Paraphrase: 
This treatise Ānma Bōdham teaching Ātma Jñāna 

(Knowledge of the Self) fit to be gained by mumukshus 
is the right refuge for seekers of liberation from the 
bondage of transmigration who having expiated their

Commentary: 

A mumukshu is one who desires emancipation from all 
sense of bondage, intensely. All beings desire unalloyed bliss, 
bliss unmixed with misery. The bliss of liberation ranks the 
highest of all happiness. As every one, in essence, is verily 
the form of bliss, desire for the bliss of release is inherent in 
one and all, and it is indeed, one’s birthright.

Serene peace and tranquillity is what the merit earned 
from the observance of prolonged austerities culminates 
in. Tapas (austerities) has to rigorous for the anātmavāsanā 
and impurities deeply embedded in the mind, acquired over 
countless previous lives, call for equally strong and sustained 
tapas and discipline to be liquidated.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   675 06-05-2011   10:54:10



676 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Sinful words, thoughts and actions make the mind 
impure and the code of expiatory conduct prescribed involves 
austerities of the body, namely, vows, like krichchara* and 
chandrayana**, celibacy, nonviolence, devotional practices, 
religious observances, codes of cleanliness, austerities of 
speech, like utterance of truth and use of inoffensive, pleasant 
and beneficial words and austerities of mind, like practise 
of dhyana, control of the senses, of mind, discrimination 
and dispassion. Dhyana promotes concentration and single 
pointedness.

Just as the body, starved of food and sleep, shrinks and 
weakens, austerities may shrink the sins but cannot extinguish 
them, nor eradicate their vāsanās completely. It is only the 
fire of jñāna that burns up the mala (impurities) of the mind 
and scorches the bonds of desires and attachments.

Unless the buffeting thought waves (induced by the 
anātmavāsanās, perception of Reality in non-real things) that 
a mind is subject to, cease altogether, shanti is not gained. The 
agitations of the mind are caused by the perishable pluralities 
of the world into which the jīvas have projected themselves 
with the strong assumption that they could derive eternal 
and unbroken happiness from them which, in turn leads to 
attachments and desires. As Bhagavan rightly points out, “The 
vision of Reality is only for those in whom the experience of 

* Krichchara refers to physical mortification by way of penance or 
expiatory act.	
** Chandrayana is a religious observance or expiatory penance 
regulated by the period of waxing and waning moon. In this 
observance, the daily quantity of food, which consists of fifteen 
mouthfuls, on the day of the full moon is diminished by one 
mouthful everyday during the dark fortnight till it is reduced to 
zero at the new moon and is increased in like manner during the 
bright fortnight.	

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   676 06-05-2011   10:54:10



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 677

sense pleasures – consisting of the same experiences again and 
again – has become bitter and who can therefore give them 
up.” (Pādamālai, Verse 38)

The desire for Release arises only to a man of discrimination 
and detachment and who has effectively controlled, subjugated 
and sublimated his mind and senses. This intense desire for 
liberation paves the way for jñāna. 

This verse is verily like a preamble to the text for it list in 
seriatim the various requisites that are demanded of a serious 
seeker of release and only he who satisfies these conditions 
is  competent enough to read this text, reflect on its contents, 
meditate and finally gain the Knowledge of the Self. Sravana, 
manana and nidhidhyasana of this text form the several rungs 
in the ladder of mukti.

Ātman is an ever-attained Reality and no penance need be 
performed to attain what is attained already. All endeavours 
are only to remove the obstacle (namely, the cogitations of 
the  mind) that stands in and bars the way of realizing the 
ever present Truth. “It being of us and in us, any amount of 
discrimination (vivechana) can lead us only one step forward, 
by making us renouncers, by goading us to discard the seeming 
(abhasa) as transitory and to hold fast to the eternal truth and 
presence alone.” (Talks no. 29)

Hence abidance in the Self alone releases one from all 
bonds. “The fragrance of Paramātman is hidden by the dust 
of vāsanās, productive of evil. When it is purified by being 
rubbed against prajñā it is clearly perceived like the smell 
of sandalwood”, proclaims Sankara in Vivekachūḍāmaṇi 
(Verse 275)

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   677 06-05-2011   10:54:10



678 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Commentary: 

Traditionally various paths like karma, bhakti and yoga 
are advocated for the attainment of liberation but Release is 
not obtained in the absence of the Knowledge of the Self. This 
is explained by an analogy. One may have all the necessary 
items ready for cooking like rice, stove, water, utensils, fuel 
and spices but cooking cannot be done in the absence of fire. 
These are all contributory factors but by themselves cannot 
constitute food. Fire alone is the direct cause of cooking. In 
the same way mukti can only  be a fond hope in the absence 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   678 06-05-2011   10:54:10



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 679

of the fire of knowledge. “By knowledge alone is liberation 
gained” is the vedantic truth.

“Let one read śāstras, do sacrifice to the Gods, perform 
karmas and meditate on the divinities; liberation will not 
arise even after hundreds of Brahmakalpas without the 
knowledge of the unity of Ātman”, emphasizes Sankara in 
Vivekachūḍāmaṇi (Verse 6).

The various other forms of discipline are factors helpful 
in fostering and furthering the spiritual growth by creating a 
conductive mental climate to pursue enquiry which heralds 
the dawn of jñāna sooner or later. All the other paths are aids, 
or external auxiliaries, that cannot by themselves lead directly 
to liberation by providing the direct experience of the Self, 
the non-dual brahman.

Without direct knowledge or abidance in the Self, the 
inward journey cannot culminate in release from the ocean of 
saṃsāra. What the other paths bestow at best is an intellectual 
grasp of jñāna or paroksha jñāna but cannot take one beyond 
that to a direct experience or aparoksha jñāna.

Just as by proper reasoning followed by conviction born 
of personal experience, the reality of the rope is gained and 
the illusion of snake no more causes fear, with dawn of direct 
knowledge, the grief of saṃsāra is destroyed. Other paths are 
mere aids.
Svetasvatara Upanishad points out the impossibility of 
attaining Him except through Knowledge which dawns from 
meditation. “Only when men could roll up the sky like a piece 
of leather, there will be the end of misery fro them without 
realising Him. It is impossible to free oneself from the miseries 
of the world without realising the Supreme Being as one’s 
own Self, the Self of all.”

Possession of knowledge will renders other aids redundant 
for knowledge by itself destroys ego and delivers one from 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   679 06-05-2011   10:54:10



680 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

ajñāni. Abidance in the Self is rigorous penance, excellent 
charity, one’s own dharma, duty and bhakti too.

Bhagavan once used an incident to explain the content 
of this verse. While Bhagavan was in Virupaksha Cave, the 
devotees with Bhagavan started to reach  the summit of the 
Arunachala Hill, with all the necessary things for cooking and 
eating on the way. It was a hot day and on reaching the seven 
springs they bathed and got ready to cook. They found, to their 
dismay, that though they had brought everything necessary, 
they had not taken the most important item, namely, the match 
box. The cave was too far away to go and fetch a match box 
from, and it was hot and everyone was hungry. They tried 
several ways of making a fire by striking flint stones against 
one another, rubbing one piece of wood against another as 
they do in yagnas to light the sacrificial fire. But none was 
successful. Then Bhagavan, who was reminded of this sloka, 
explained the meaning and kept them all in good humour , till 
a match box was procured from Virupaksha Cave. Bhagavan 
continued to explain to them during the walk to the summit 
also. “For preparing food we had no fire, so nothing could 
be done. Similarly you may have everything for teaching 
and learning but without understanding there cannot be full 
ripening of wisdom. With that fire of jñāna all worldly things 
must be mixed up and swallowed to attain the highest state.” 
(Letters, 30-09-1948)

Action or performance of karmas with a view to

Commentary: 

Śāstras speak of manifold karmas and that the fruits 
obtainable by their performance are also diverse. Wonderful 
indeed is the power of karma. Karmayogīs, who, with a view 
to attain the desired ends, performed karmopasana (worship 
through karma) and obtained fulfilment of specific desires, 
are indeed many. Cannot mukti be gained by karma alone 
possessed of such potency? Where then is the need for the 
knowledge of the Self? The reason why śāstras have not 
declared so is explained with an illustration in this verse.

Any object can be destroyed only by another that 
is conflicting with or opposed to its nature. Fire can be 
extinguished only by water and not by any fuel or inflammable 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   681 06-05-2011   10:54:11



682 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

substance like petrol. Fuel and petrol have great affinity to 
fire, being friends of fire. Instead of dousing they will kindle 
the fire more.

Karma and ajñāna are not conflicting in nature, but 
promote each other. The ego, endeavouring to perform karma, 
indulges in it with a strong sense of ‘doership’ and enjoys its 
fruits, thereby fattening itself and the one who was sought to 
be eliminated grows strong and invincible.

The ultimate Reality is non-dual Ātman; whereas 
multiplicity and duality (in the sense of doer, performance and 
the objects of attainment) belong to the realm of ignorance, 
for the destruction of which karma is undertaken. In fact the 
very basis of existence of karma rests on ignorance. Therefore 
karma cannot remove ajñāna or nescience.

Secondly, Knowledge of Ātman is not produced by 
karma for Knowledge of the Self is an ever present Reality. 
Knowledge only reveals the Self that has never been 
nonexistent. Therefore, It need not be striven for and obtained 
anew for It is already within us. Therefore karma of any 
kind, divine or mundane, cannot be the cause of the dawn of 
enlightenment. Karma is only to remove the obstacles that 
stand in the way of knowing the ever existent Truth of the Self.

Light and darkness are opposites of each other. Likewise 
jñāna, knowledge and ajñāna (ignorance), being the opposite 
of the other, cannot remain together. The ignorance that 
conjures up the relative world of  multiplicity will disappear 
when the one worldless jñāna dawns. Sankara affirms this in 
Vivekachūḍāmaṇi: “the fire of knowledge of the Oneness of 
Brahman and the jīva totally destroys the forest of avidya. To 
one who has attained the sense of this oneness, what will be 
there of the seed of saṃsāra?” (Verse 347).

Just as a small light drives away the darkness of years in 
a room, however dense it may be, the light of chit, shining 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   682 06-05-2011   10:54:11



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 683

in its effulgence, removes the ignorance that was all along 
veiling the Ātman. Performance of karma is like sweeping 
a room plunged in darkness to illumine it. Sage Vasishta 
proffers the same exhortation to Lord Rama, “Rama! Men 
of great intellect have crossed over the ocean of worldly 
existence which is very difficult to be crossed, in a moment, 
merely by the raft that is the expedient of knowledge”, and 
“There is no means other than knowledge for the mind 
with bondage like fetters in crossing over the saṃsāra.” 
(Yoga Vasishtam, Verses 1652 and 1653).

Commentary: 
The all-pervading omnipresent Ātman seems to have 

been concealed due to ignorance. When this delusion of 
nescience is dispelled by the practice of sravana, manana and 
nidhidhyasana, the Ātman shines in Its own natural effulgence 
and resplendent glory even as the sun shines brilliantly when 
the clouds hiding its view move away.

ekamatāi niraivāi tanāi ilahume: “The Ātman, as the 
One, Whole and Full, shines by Itself” – meaning It, being 
Self-luminous, shines as Pure Awareness by Itself without the 
need for any medium or any other instrument or factor such as 
rituals, study of religious literature or prayer seeking favours.

Just as the Sun lies hidden behind clouds, the Self remains 
concealed behind the layers of non-self, (like the various 
sheaths) projected out of ignorance and does not shine clearly 
due to the sheaths, which have arisen out of It’s own power 
– Māyā – even as the clouds have arisen by the power of the 
Sun itself.
Therefore all sādhanas are to remove the concealment caused 
by ignorance and to rediscover the ever present Content and 
not to attain It anew. Verse 44 of this text also speaks of the 
‘ever attained’ nature of the Ātman and Bhagavan instructs 
in Spiritual Instructions that there is no time when the Ātman 
does not shine.
	 A lamp is required only to see objects in darkness and 
a second lamp is not required to see another lamp. With 
nescience dispelled, Ātman shines in Its own effulgence.

The long and repeated practice of pure knowledge 

(enquiry based on discrimination, sravana, manana, 
etc.), totally destroying the impurities of desires and

and disconcerted due to the beginningless nescience – 
itself disappears just as the powder of the cleansing nut 
(kataka) after removing the impurities in water, itself

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   685 06-05-2011   10:54:11



686 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Commentary: 
The jīva, deluded by the illusion of nescience, while 

referring to himself as ‘I’, means both his body together with the 
Supremely Immaculate Ātman. Thus he, and by superimposing 
the dharma of the body, its nature and characteristics onto 
the Ātman, becomes perplexed and bewildered. In reality 
the Ātman is neither the ‘doer’ nor the ‘enjoyer’; yet the jīva 
interweaving the body and Ātman inseparably misconstrues 
the Ātman as the ‘doer’ and the ‘enjoyer’. The Absolute has 
become the relative and the one has become the many. The 
Self stands polluted by this nescience.

If this insurmountable delusion is to be overcome, 
sravana, manana and nidhidhyasana will have to be practiced 
for a good length of time which, in turn, leads to Self-enquiry 
with the aid of which the distinction between the body and 
the ‘dweller’ in the body, namely, kshetra and kshetrajna, 
must be known. And by rejecting all the non-self one must 
become aware of one‘s real form as that of ‘Pure Awareness’ 
and abidance in this Awareness removes the delusion of 
the jīva and he becomes undefiled by being stamped in his 
divine nature. The knowledge that helps to end the delusion 
also disappears  along with delusion. What remains left is 
the Ātman alone. The knowledge which is the instrument 
disappears into Knowledge, the goal – the Self.

The powder of the nut (kataka) used as a cleaning agent, 
being denser, settles down at the bottom, carrying along with 
it the minute particles of dust and dirt, that the water had 
become contaminated with earlier. “When the five sheaths are 
set aside, this Ātman that is pure, blissful indwelling, Supreme 
and self-effulgent, appears clear, untouched by anātman.” 
(Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, Verse 153)

Here the jñāna, that is used to remove the ajñāna, refers 
to vritti jñāna, whereas Ātmajñāna is called Svarūpa Jñāna, 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   686 06-05-2011   10:54:11



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 687

Knowledge of the Self. Vritti jñāna refers to the movements 
of the mind and though it is not jñāna in the real sense of the 
term, it is euphemistically called so.

The prolonged practice of Enquiry (the Vrittijñāna) that 
helped in the attainment of jñāna also disappears, for there is 
no longer an entity. The impurities of water are not natural, 
but alien to it. In the same way, all ideas of non-self, the 
‘impurities’, are eliminated along with the agent itself, and 
the mind, through which it was adopted. When a mind, which 
is but the thought-flow, becomes void of vritti, it becomes 
pure and clean and rebounds, back to its original nature, the 
Self. Just as by washing a lump of earth sticking to the hand 
by another lump of earth, in water, great purity of hand is 
acquired, by the destruction of the two lumps of earth, on the 
mind destroying itself, Ātman alone remains.

“The thought ‘Who am I?’ will destroy all other thoughts 
and, like the stick used for stirring the burning pyre, it will 
itself, in the end, get destroyed. Then there will arise Self-
Realization.” (Who am I?, question no. 10)

as long as it continues, seems real, the worldly saṃsāra

Commentary: 

Saṃsāra is the Universe or the relative world. The 
question how can the world, that is directly perceived, be 
said to be non-existent, is answered with an illustration in 
this verse.

The objects of the world (which also include persons 
and thoughts on them) do not harm us as long as no personal 
contact is established with them. Once we associate ourselves 
(senses and mind) with them, attachments for the loved ones 
and aversions for those disliked, develop, bringing in their 
wake sorrow, pleasure and pain. What is required to steer 
clear of these evils is not the destruction of the world, which 
is impossible, but to keep away from these dwandwas or dyads 
that are the support of the relative world. As Bhagavan rightly 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   688 06-05-2011   10:54:11



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 689

remarks, if walking on bare earth causes pain one can not 
cover the entire earth with leather but one can protect one’s 
feet with leather.

Attachments and aversions will not develop, if, by 
enquiry, the world is known to be a mere illusion. As long 
as one dreams, the dream objects and the dream experiences 
appear real to the dream-ego. But on waking up, the dream 
objects and experiences become unreal and the dream-ego 
has no reality as well. The objects, experiences of the world, 
in jagrat have only as much substantiality as the dream stuff 
and that they are as transient and ephemeral as those of the 
dream world is experienced on the dawn of jñāna.

Sleep is the basis for dream. The sleep of ajñāna is the 
basis of for this dream-like life. The end of sleep causes the 
dream to disappear and on waking up to jñāna, the dream 
of the world, saṃsāra, disappears, too. “Waking is long 
and a dream short; other than this there is no difference.” 
(Who am I?, Question no. 22). With the dissolution of the 
ego on the dawn of jñāna, the grief of saṃsāra becomes as 
non-existent as the cry of a severed tongue to announce that 
is has been sundered.

Commentary: 

While the earlier verse dwelt on the illustration of the 
dream state to prove the unreality of the life in jagrat, another 
analogy – that of the appearance of silver in an oyster shell – is 
used here to stress the same truth.

Viewed in sunlight and from afar, the mother of pearl 
keeps shining with a silvery gleam till a closer scrutiny 
disproves the presence of silver. As long as the substratum of 
everything that appears, namely, the imperishable Brahman, 
is not known through enquiry, so long will the unreal world 
continue to ‘shine’ with seeming reality.

The Sanskrit word adhishtana means the substratum 
which, by itself remaining unperceived and changeless, 
lends an air of reality to an illusion based upon it. Brahman 
is the adhishtana of all that is manifest and the illusory world 
that appears on it is called ārōpitham or a superimposition. 
Adhishtana also means that presence through the real 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   690 06-05-2011   10:54:11



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 691

knowledge of which, the unreality of what is superimposed 
on it becomes known. In the celebrated example of a rope 
and snake, the rope, unseen, but the basis for appearance of a 
snake, is the adhishtana. The illusory appearance of a snake, 
which appears real as long as the rope is not perceived, is 
the superimposition or ārōpitham. The ‘mother of pearl’ is 
the substratum for the illusory appearance of the silver on it. 
Brahman, though unperceived, lends an appearance of reality 
to all that have names and forms. When jñāna dawns by the 
grace of a satguru aided by the śāstraic and scriptural proofs, 
the illusion of names and forms perishes and Brahman alone 
remains as All. Mere knowledge of śāstras cannot remove 
ajñāna. Aparoksha jñāna or direct experience of the Reality 
alone can destroy nescience, paving the way for the Self to 
shine in all Its glory and effulgence. “This indeed is the Truth 
and accept it whole heartedly”, says the Teacher.

ulahaÙ-ga¿ ellÅm all the perceived worlds

Paraphrase: 
Know that all the perceived worlds, like bubbles that 

appear on water, rise and appear, stay and dissolve in that 
Supreme Self, the whole, prime and the material cause 
–  and support – of everything in the universe.
Commentary: 

By an extension of the same logic offered in the previous 
verse, namely, that the adhishtana or substratum alone is real 
while the ‘superimposition’ (ārōpitham) is unreal, it is proved 
that Brahman, the Self-created or unborn substratum, alone is 
real and all that is seen is unreal.

Bubbles arise from water, remain in water but are not 
independent of it and finally dissolve in water. Water alone is 
the basis and substratum for the origin, stay and dissolution 
of the bubbles.

Similarly, all the worlds, with the manifold distinctions, 
appear, remain and dissolve in Brahman. Names and forms 
are simply a play upon the Infinite Consciousness.

The bubble, born of water, cannot be separated as water 
and the form, bubble. Bubbles in water are but water. Water 
becomes water. In all the changes water alone is the Truth. The 
appearance and the existence of the bubbles are mere illusions. 
The Teacher instructs that the Supreme Brahman undergoes 
no change and as such the manifestation, stay and absorption, 
of worlds of multiplicity are merely illusions. Brahman alone 
is the material cause of the Universe.

In any creation three types of causes come into play, the 
Material, the Efficient and the Instrumental. In the example

694 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Paraphrase: 
Just like the ornaments of various names and forms 

like bangles and bracelets that are wrought in pure 
gold, all the manifested world with its manifold names 
and forms, projected by imagination are not other than 
or different from the eternally existent primeval, all-
pervading, unmanifest Brahman, of the very nature of 
Sat-Chit-Ananda (Being-Awareness-Bliss).
Commentary: 

This verse speaks of the Svarūpa Lakshana of Brahman 
(the characteristic of Brahman as “It is”, the unconditioned 
Brahman), while the earlier verses spoke of the Tatastha 
Lakshana (indicative characteristics of Brahman). That which 
is, remains as Sat, Chit and Ananda, infilling everything, 
eternally present and not appearing at one time and disappearing 
at another, Itself formless, though appearing with a diversity 
of names and forms, and shines in Its own effulgence. Here 
the word ‘Vishnu’ meaning ‘All-pervading’, denotes Brahman.

In this One, non-dual, all-pervading Brahman, the 
phenomenal world, with multitudes of distinctions of names 
and forms appear. Yet the world is not apart from Brahman. 
The names and forms associated with objects and subject 
to constant changes, appear to distinguish and distance 
themselves from Brahman and seem to be real, partaking the 
reality of their substratum, Brahman. When the names and 
forms undergo changes, Brahman Itself remains changeless 
as It is. This is illustrated with an example. The various 
ornaments made of gold, though manifest distinctions in 
names and forms – thereby seemingly distinguishing them 
from the original gold – are not other than gold. In the same 
way, the world of diverse distinctions of names and forms is 
not other than Brahman.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   694 06-05-2011   10:54:11



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 695

Names and forms of ornaments are changeable, therefore, 
unreal, while gold, ever existing as gold, is real. Likewise 
Brahman, the substratum alone is real though couched in 
diverse names and forms that are subject to constant change.  A 
comparison of what Chandhogya Upanishad declares is worth 
noting: “And as, my dear, by knowing one nugget of gold, 
all that is made of gold is known, the difference being only 
in a name, arising from speech but the truth being that all is 
gold...” (6-1-5). What differentiates the gold from a bangle is a 
name, a mere convention of speech. Apart from this, there is no 
intrinsic difference between gold and bangle. In the same way 
there is no essential difference between Brahman, the cause, 
and the phenomenal world, It’s effect. Names and forms that 
create the distinctions exist only in one’s mind. ‘That’ alone 
shines when stripped of names and forms. The traditional 
story that is often quoted to prove this point is that of the 
householder – turned monk. He could not realize Brahman 
because of the sole impediment of the form of she-buffalo he 
loved dearly as his very life, that kept appearing in his mind 
during his meditation on Brahman. The guru, then instructed 
him to continue to see that but  stripping of the forms of both 
the buffalo and himself. Ultimately he reached the goal. Hence 
Vedānta declares, “All this is verily Brahman.”

Just as gold is the cause and ornament is the effect,  an 
oyster shell the cause and Sat-Chit-Ananda Brahman is the 
cause and the world, an illusory appearance on it. This is called 
vivartha siddhanta wherein, the effect cannot be described as 
the same as cause and nothing beyond can be said. Vivartha 
refers to the quality of a vastu that, without giving up its real 
form, manifests as another seemingly silver effect – real. In short 
vivartha is the doctrine of illusory appearance which states that 
the world appearance is an illusory one and that it comes into 
existence as the unreal projection of one who sees it.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   695 06-05-2011   10:54:11

Paraphrase: 

Just as the sole, vast expanse of pure ether appears 
to be diverse (fragmented by clouds or disintegrated 
into pot-space or room-space), the All-pervading 
Supreme, shining as the One, taking up the countless 
bodies (upādhis) appearing in Him appears diverse and

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   696 06-05-2011   10:54:11



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 697

distinctions of names and forms. When the differing 
upādhis fall off, He shines as the One and Whole.
Commentary: 

The Undifferentiated, Impartite (Indivisible) nature of 
the One Truth is explained here with the illustration of ether.

Though the space that pervades everywhere is one and 
indivisible, yet, when in association with pots (ghata) and 
room (mata) it appears to be of diverse forms like pot-space 
and room-space. Ghata and mata are called upādhis - a 
terminology in Vedānta – meaning the conditioning or limiting 
adjuncts. The one space or ether, due to the limiting adjuncts, 
comes to be cognized as many and multiple. When the pot is 
broken or walls of the room are pulled apart, the distinctions 
caused by the upādhis too disappear; yet the nature of space 
remains unchanged during all the three times, namely before 
the pot and walls appeared, when they existed and when they 
were broken down. The infinite ether appears to be finitised 
by upādhis. 

The all-pervading (Vibhu) Brahman, that shines infilling 
everything, is One and Indivisible – incapable of being parted 
by any – and remains without distinctions. The all-pervasive 
nature is such that there are no gaps or interspace in between 
and therefore nothing can impart It in anyway.

The countless upādhis of bodies appearing distinct from 
each other in the phenomenal world makes the all-pervading 
form of Brahman appears to be fragmented into distinct 
entities of names and forms. Sankara reiterates this truth in 
Vivekachūḍāmaṇi also as follows: Freed from the thousands 
of upādhis of a pot, a pitcher, a granary, a needle, etc. the 
space is only one and not diverse. So too, is the paramātman 
one only when divested of the upādhis like ahamkara. One 
should look at the Ātman as full and of unlimited nature like 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   697 06-05-2011   10:54:11



698 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

the sky, freed from all the upādhis, namely, body, the sense 
organs, the mind and the ahamkara imagined on account of 
ajñāna.” (Verses 386 and 385)

The association between Ātman and the upādhis is not a 
real one but illusory. There can never be any contact between 
the two, totally contradictory in nature, like light and darkness; 
hence this association does not affect the nature of Brahman.

The distinction between Brahman and living beings and 
between the diverse living beings is illusory, superimposed 
out of ignorance. When these upādhis are destroyed by 
the dawn of enlightenment, the aparoksha jñāna, Ātman 
shines in all its effulgence as the One and Impartite. All the 
Upanishads declare this Truth in various ways: “The one Lord 
is concealed in all beings”*, “It is indivisible, and yet It is, as 
it were divided among beings”**, and “In Brahman there is no 
diversity whatsoever”.***

Therefore “all upādhis from Brahma to the minutest worm 
are unreal. One should realize one’s nature, which is infinite, 
as the eternal one and single.” (Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, Verse 387).

Paraphrase: 
All distinctions spoken of as name, caste and ashrama 

(station of life) refer to the various upādhis of diverse 
bodies that are imagined illusory appearances on the 
Ātman (the distinctions are to the upādhis -bodies – and 
not to the Ātman).  As the tastes like salinity, sweetness 
and insipidity and colours like red, yellow, etc. appear 
in water, distinctions of names and forms are imagined

Commentary: 

The distinctions of characteristics, communities, names, 
varnas and ashramas originate from the body and the sarīra 
dharma, the nature of each body, exhibits distinctions 
according to its actions in previous lives. Species like man, 
cow, bird, varnas like Brahmana, Kshatriya, Vysya and others 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   699 06-05-2011   10:54:12



700 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

and ashramas like Brahmachari, Grihastha, Sannyāsin, etc. 
are all body-based and do not at all pertain to the Ātman. 
Whatever be the physical name and form, Ātman is One, 
the same everywhere and in all beings. The all-pervading 
consciousness is simply consciousness and pure and pristine, 
and there are no distinctions in it as ‘dog consciousness’, 
‘human consciousness’, etc. nor as ‘rich-Ātman’, Hindu-
Ātman or old-Ātman. It always remains unaffected by and 
unattached to all outward marks. The effulgence of Ātman 
has no difference whatsoever.

As Bhagavan rightly points out, if these distinctions 
were real, one should be aware of them in deep sleep too, 
when one is closest to one’s native purity. Again, if they were 
real, realized sages would be conscious of them in their most 
sublime spiritual experience, when they remain as their real 
Form, but it is not so.

Yet due to our inability to separate the superimposition 
from the substratum, the body from the Ātman, or the non-Self 
from the Self, due to nescience, we attribute the characteristics 
of the body to the Ātman and thus delude ourselves. Water, by 
itself, is colourless, though a given sample of it may be red, 
white, yellow. Though devoid of smell and taste, sometimes it 
is sweet or saline and carries even a distinct smell. Those who 
know the truth are aware that none of these properties belongs 
to water but the changes are acquired through association with 
or admixtures of, extraneous objects with distinct qualities. 
Similarly fragrance carried by wind and water is often 
mistaken to emanate from air or water. Earth alone, of all the 
five elements has odour as its intrinsic property. Water and 
air, due to their association with earth, seem to possess odour.

Therefore the distinctions of body, varna, causes, effects, 
qualities are all mind-produced and they do not exist in the 
absence of the mind and are superimposed on the Ātman. 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   700 06-05-2011   10:54:12

clan, name and station in life which are associated with your 
living body (which is really a corpse through which blood is 
coursing).” (Verse 298).

This panchīkaraṇam happens both at the cosmic and 
individual levels. By Panchikarana process, the five gross 
elements ether, air, fire, water and earth are solidified and get 
their clear forms. One, two, three, four and five qualities are 
seen to exist in ether, air, fire, water and earth respectively.

has two, sound and touch, fire three, sound, touch and form

five gross element the Cosmos is created.

inspired his fellow student to do so too. One of the boys asked 
him what would they do if they were to be deported by his 
father? He being the son of a king would sure be taken care 
of but they, the children of his father’s subordinated, would 
suffer without food and shelter. Prahlada laughed. When 
Bhagavan came to this stage he laughed as Prahlada did. The 
atmosphere was surcharged with spirituality and indescribable 
thrill coursed up the spine of everyone present. Bhagavan 
continued. Prahlada assured, “Don’t you know that all you 
have eat (experience) has already arrived and awaits you.”

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 707

As explained in the earlier verse, the five elements that 
make up all creation, were in the beginning in their subtle form. 
They become grossified after mixing with the other elements.

While the gross body of the jīva is made up of the five 
elements after (panchīkaraṇam) admixing with each other the 
subtle body of the jīva consists of the five pranas, namely, 
prana, apāna, vyana, udhana and samana, five organs of 
perception called jnanēndriyas (eye, ear, nose, tongue and 
skin), the five organs of action, called karmēndriyas (the hands, 
the feet, the organs of speech, evacuation and generation) and 
mind and intellect (the antaḥkaraṇa), totalling seventeen in 
number. Prana, though one, is divided into five, according 
to the five functions it performs. Prana is a life force, whose 
presence is felt as breath. Apāna  moves downward to expel 
unassimilated food and drink. Vyana moves in all directions 
pervading the entire body. Udhana is the ascending life force, 
that helps the soul to pass out of the body and also causing 
vomiting. Samana helps in the digestion of food and drink 
and in the conversion of them into various materials of the 
body. While ‘mind’ is the wishing and willing part of the 
antaḥkaraṇa,  intellect is the determinative faculty.

All these seventeen instruments are formed of the five 
subtle elements before they mix with others by the process 
of panchīkaraṇam. Hence it is called kalavāda nuṇbhūtā 
kāriyamām - the effect of five elements unmixed. These are 
called pancha tanmatras (hundred percent in their subtle 
specific nature) or apānchikritkam – subtle elements (elements 
without the admixture of other elements).

The five subtle elements are the basis for the creation of 
the subtle body – the instrument to experience the unending 
rounds of pleasures and sorrows.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   707 06-05-2011   10:54:12

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 709

The Ātman, is the other of these in the sense It is the witness 
of the three bodies and is never to be identified with these.

All the three upādhis (three bodies) are the veil (āvarana) 
that conceal the Ātman. Therefore the Truth or Reality is veiled 
and not known. This is non-perception or avidya). Hence the 
Reality is misinterpreted through imaginations of the mind 
(misconception - vikshepa) and mere illusions are projected 
(āropa or superimposition). None can say when this avidya or 
causal body came into existence. The beginning of avidya cannot 
be known by mind for the mind which creates the concepts of 
time, space and causality, is itself a product of avidya. Though 
called beginningless, jñāna – true knowledge, puts an end  to 
it; hence it may be beginningless but can be ended.

This avidya which makes the One, non-dual Brahman 
appear as manifold, the Absolute as relative, is indescribable. 
A thing which exists can be brought under the realms of 
expressions and explanations. But avidya is the cause for the 
instruments of perception and, therefore, falls beyond the 
ambit of speech. It is not non-existent, it being the cause of 
this vast creation. Further as it perishes with jñāna, it cannot 
be said to ‘exist’ forever. Avidya can neither be said as existent 
nor as non-existent (or both) and therefore inexplicable.

Like fire and heat, māyā resides in Ātman and is 
inseparable from It; nor can it be said to be with Ātman, the 
Self-effulgent. Nothing definite can be said about it. Hence it 
was spoken of ‘indescribable’.

All the glorifying epithets attributed to Ātman, the form 
of Vidya (like beginningless, indescribable, beyond speech 
and mind) are all bestowed on māyā or Avidya as well. The 
difference in their names hangs on just a single letter, ‘a’. All 
the Avidya, creations of māyā, take place in the darkness of 
nescience; but vidya, encompassing the creations of māyā 
within, shines by Itself illumining everything.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   709 06-05-2011   10:54:12



710 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Finally Vidya is the goal and not Avidya. Being light, the 
Self within (covered by the bushel of this body) seeking to know 
māyā is like going with a lamp to locate darkness. If we jettison 
the upādhis of the three bodies, the Ātman shines as ever.

That the Ātman is other than the three bodies is explained 
in Panchadasi by Swamy Vidyaranya with an illustration. The 
gross physical body is compared to a royal court and the jīva, 
a reflection of the Ātman, the king, mind the prime-minister, 
the five pranas, ten senses and five objects of senses to various 
officers, courtiers, entertainers and servants. The Ātman, the 
Self-luminous Consciousness, is the grand chandelier. Ātman 
illumines all the activities of the gross and subtle body during 
waking and dream states like the chandelier illumining all 
the activities of the court. When everybody retires, the light 
continues to shine, illumining the absence of all activities. 
Likewise in deep sleep, Ātman alone shines revealing Its own 
immutable reality and the absence of activities of the body and 
mind. Ātman is the uninvolved witness of the experiences of all 
the three states. It is Itself detached from all the three bodies.

Paraphrase: 

The colourless crystal, due to contact with blue or 
red cloth placed in front, appears to be endowed with 
that colour. Likewise the Immaculate Ātman, though the 
taintless purity that cannot be touched or impacted by any, 
due to proximity to the upādhis of five sheaths like food, 
prana, etc. appears to be the form of those very sheaths.
Commentary: 

In this verse how the three bodies as the five sheaths 
(kosas) conceal the Ātman which is ‘other than’ the five 
sheaths, is explained.

The five kosas (sheaths), namely, the food sheath 
(annamaya kosa), the vital air sheath (pranamaya kosa), 
the mental sheath (manōmaya kosa), the intellectual sheath 
(vijñānamaya kosa) and the bliss sheath (anandamaya kosa) 
comprise the three – gross, subtle and causal – bodies.

The gross body is called the food sheath which is born 
of food, lives by food and dies without it. It does not deserve 
to be the Ātman, for it does nor exist before its origination 
and destruction, undergoes changes, is not of the same nature, 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   711 06-05-2011   10:54:12



712 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

material and visible like a water pot. It cannot be the Ātman 
which knows the changes of existence.

The vital air sheath is composed of five organs of action. 
Mind together with the five organs of perception forms the 
mental sheath. Vijñānamaya kosa houses the intellect. These 
three sheaths together form the subtle body which therefore is 
compressed by seventeen entities. It also connects the causal 
body with the gross body.

The causal body the fifth Bliss sheath is, of the form of 
nescience – the jīva, the enjoyer. The Immaculate Ātman, due 
to association with these five kosas, appears to be the very 
form of each kosa. Besides veiling the Ātman, each sheath 
poses as the Ātman itself. The vital air sheath, the effect of 
wind, like wind, goes in and comes out, is unaware of good 
or evil anywhere or anytime, either of itself or of others and 
is dependent on others as well. Hence it cannot be the Ātman.

The manōmaya kosa is the cause of ‘I’ and ‘mine’. Mind 
itself is avidya, the creator of bondage and itself disappears in 
deep sleep. It’s rise and disappearance are known, it is subject 
to modifications and it is itself an object. Therefore it cannot 
be the Ātman. Chit is reflected in vijñānamaya kosa, by virtue 
of which it has the power of illumination. (The reflection of 
a luminous body is also luminous). Jīvahood originates here. 
This itself is nescience. The vijñānamaya kosa cannot be the 
Ātman for it is insentient, subject to change, limited, an object 
of perception and not present constantly. Therefore it cannot 
be Ātman.

The anandamaya kosa is a modification of avidya, having 
for its attribute pleasure on obtaining a desired object. This 
also cannot be the Ātman because it is connected with upādhis.

Therefore, though of the same form, and without any 
change, by virtue of association with upādhis (kosas), the real 
Ātman too, as if of the nature of upādhis, acquires its qualities 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   712 06-05-2011   10:54:12



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 713

even as colourless crystal takes on the colour of the object 
it comes into contact with, like a blue cloth or a blue flower.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   713 06-05-2011   10:54:12



714 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Upanishads and enquiries into śāstras. (The grain of the

Commentary: 

When one refers to oneself in the empirical world, 
invariably one includes the five kosas and the Self too. This 
is the outcome of superimposition – a habit that has come 
through countless births. Just as paddy, after being pounded 
well with pestle and mortar, dehusked and the rice grain is 
obtained, one, instructed by a Satguru and duly undergoing 
the stages of sravana and manana, must enquire well, fortified 
with strong discrimination and stern dispassion, armed with 
the conviction born of scriptural statements, logical inference 
and should separate the matter envelopments, namely, the 
kosas, and realise the ever present Ātman within.

But unconsciously, even in the absence of conscious 
enquiry and consequent separation of the Ātman from the 
anātman, one saying involuntarily ‘my body, my mind and 
my intellect’ separates himself from the anātman. But through 
enquiry as to who is the person who says so, kosas must be 
set aside as chaff from the corn and the truth, must be known 
and experienced.

As one does not identify oneself with the shadow of one's 
body or with the reflected image of the body in a reflecting 
medium or with the dream-body, so also, the Ātman should 
not be identified with any of the three bodies or the five kosas. 
Even as the tender core of the īsika is carefully separated from 
its coverings in the munja-grass, the kosas must be discarded 
and the Ātman  must be known.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   715 06-05-2011   10:54:13



716 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Commentary: 
That though all the five kosas appear as the Ātman, they 

are not the Ātman, and Ātman is the ‘other’ of them and the 
three bodies, was declared in the earlier verse. Where then is 
the Self which is apart from the five kosas and three bodies and 
how to find it are the questions that are answered in this verse.

Ātman, being Infinite by It’s very nature, is all-pervading 
and present everywhere, It does not shine in everything. Just as 
reflection is clear only in a stainless, clear, polished medium, 
held steady Ātman is manifest only in the serene quietude of 
a settled, sharp, pure and subtle intellect.

As It is all-pervading one need not go anywhere searching 
for It. Even if so sought It will not be attained for the object 
sought shines in the very intellect of the seeker. When all the 
outward-turned senses are controlled and the mentations of 
the mind are stilled, the intellect, shorn of impurities, cleansed 
and rendered, sharp, subtle and clear glows. The intellect, by 
virtue of its closest proximity to the Ātman, is the best aid to 
attain the reflection of the Ātman. Intellect is pellucid by nature 
and has a preponderance of sattva. If the intellect is tainted by 
blemishes like attachments, aversions, the reflection of Ātman 
will not shine clearly or at all.

Commentary: 

Though the Ātman dwells in the body, interpenetrating

association of assorted vastus like instruments, pranan, mind, 
intellect and the ego sense. Ātman resides in this coalition of 
sorts. Despite the seeming association, without being impacted 
by the nature and dharma of them, It shines all by Itself. It is 
the Supreme Illuminator who illumines the subtle workings 
of the intellect, grosser thoughts of the mind and still grosser 
movements of the body. As the illuminator is different from the 
objects illumined, He is always a Witness, never a participant. 
He illumines knowledge and even the absence of it. He is 
called the ‘Universal Witness’.

The King sits ensconced on the throne as the observer of 
the activities of the ministers, counsellors and others and is 
perceived to be different from all by his lordly majesty. The 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   717 06-05-2011   10:54:13



718 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

King, without engaging himself in any work himself, gets 
everything done by his mere presence. Likewise, the Ātman 
simply dwells in the body as a mere witness of the functions 
of the body, mind,  senses, intellect and the ego. But no action 
can escape from this witness. “Without action a non-agent 
and one without a second, ‘I’, the Universal Self, makes the 
world go round like a King who is only a witness or like the 
loadstone which moves iron by its sheer proximity” (Upadēsa 
Sāhasri, Chap. 17, Verse 80).

 When the body, mind and organs undergo/changes 
through various phases in life like childhood, youth, old age 
and several avasthas or states,  undergo changes, yet He who 
calls the body ‘his’ from then to now, remains the same without 
undergoing  any change. When ‘Who He is’ is enquired into, 
it will be realized that He is the Universal Witness, the Ātman.

Just as one does not have the sense of ‘I’ in any limb of 
the body, the sense of ‘I’ in the body (all the five kosas) must 
be given up.

“This Ātman which is Self-effulgent, distinct from the five 
kosas, the Witness of the three states, without change, untainted, 
which is always of the nature of Ananda, that is to be known by 
the wise as one's true Ātman.” (Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, Verse 213).

Except during hours of sleep, the mind and other 
instruments continuously engage themselves in actions in their 
respective fields. While senses rush out towards sense-objects, 
mind, externalised, moves outward through the senses and 
engages itself in various activities of the empirical world. In 
case of the non-availability of opportunities to be exteriorised, 
it rules over an empire of its own, an imaginary one, indulging 
in daydreams or lapsing into reveries.

The actions are of the indriyas and mind, and not of the 
Self, which endows the organs, with their capacity to manifest 
activity, by It's mere presence. Such actions are recognised

and experienced in the light of the Self. The qualities of the

lamp that illumines them. Ātman is a non-doer. The aviveki, 
one who lacks in powers of discrimination, unable to separate 
and know the nature of Ātman and that of the body, considers 
the actions of the body as those of the Self.

The fast movement of clouds on a moon-lit night creates 
the illusion, that the moon is moving and the children believe 
that, it is playing hide and seek. To one seated  in a fast -moving 
train, the trees, the countryside plains and hillocks appear to 
move fast though it is the train that moves. Those who are well 
aware of the nature and characteristics of Ātman and Anātman 
will not be deluded so. That  the 'moveless' Ātman appears 
to engage Itself in activity is due to the delusion of the mind. 
Ātman is often called the Kutasta for It stands forever like an 
‘anvil’ with no movement.

That which is superimposed by those subject to delusion 
of the mind cannot affect the substratum.

Commentary: 

People, ignorant of the nature of the Self, superimpose 
on the Self the dharma of the body, mind and intellect with 
all their limitations, namely, the attributes of the physical 
body like birth, growth, old age and death, its functions like 
locomotion, speaking, seeing, etc., the attributes of the senses 
like sharpness or dullness of vision, deafness, etc. and the 
functions of senses like hearing, touching, etc. But the Self is 
Pure, free of all stains like Māyā and its effects like ignorance 
and the notions of doership and enjoyership.

Space, one of the five elements, is devoid of any colour or 
attribute. The property of colour belongs to fire, another of the 
five elements. The infinite space of the summer-sky appears 
blue. One devoid of discrimination attributes the quality of 
blueness to the colourless vast space. One well-informed about 
the attributes of the five elements is well aware that the sky is 
colourless and that the infinite sky so endless vast and as to 
elude physical perception makes it appear blue. 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   723 06-05-2011   10:54:13



724 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Ātman, ever remains as Sat, Chit and Ananda. Out of the 
delusion of ignorance, the nature and functions of the body 
and the notions are superimposed on the Ātman. Therefore 
discretion  lies in separating and knowing the Self and Its 
nature (Svarūpa) as distinct from the non-self as the body 
and senses.

This superimposition does not affect the Ātman in anyway 
as the traits of one object (blueness) on another (sky) does not 
affect the substratum (sky). The Ātman, like the sky, is beyond 
all the imagined divisions. Like the sun, It is different from 
the illumined. Like the immovable mountain It is permanent 
and unmoving. Like the ocean, It is without a shore. “If 
heat and cold, good or evil touches the shadow of a man, it 
does not affect the man who is different from the shadow.” 
(Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, Verse 505).

Paraphrase: 
The movements of the water in which the moon 

is reflected are imagined, out of ignorance, to be the 
movements of the moon that stands still in the sky. 
Likewise the agency of action and enjoyment (sense

Commentary: 

Everybody is known to say “I did this” and therefore “I 
experienced this effect of that act”, thinking wrongly that the 
‘I’ sense and the notions of agency and enjoyership are not of 
the body but of the Ātman.

That Ātman, in reality, is devoid of the ‘I’ consciousness 
(the sense of ego) and consequently free of the notions of 
doership and enjoyership and that they are experienced 
only by the jīva, the apparent soul, is explained with an apt 
illustration here. 

When the reflection of the moon is perceived in the 
undulating surface of water, small children think that it is the 
moon that dances and enjoy the spectacle. If the truth of the 
matter is to be impressed on them, their perception will have 
to be directed towards the still moon in the sky when it will 
be realised that is the water that moves and not the Moon.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   725 06-05-2011   10:54:13



726 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Upādhi is a limiting adjunct or a conditioning medium. 
Water here is an upādhi for the still moon. In the absence of 
water , there can be no reflection. The intellect where the light 
of Awareness of the Ātman is reflected, becomes an upādhi of 
the Ātman. This Bhagavan refers to as “manamām upādhi” – 
the upādhi that the mind is. 

The nature and qualities of water, the upādhi of the moon, 
have no connection whatsoever with the moon in the sky 
and cannot affect it in any way. In the same way the sense of 
doership and enjoyership, actions or their fruits, all belong to 
the mind, an upādhi of the Ātman.

If the surface of the water is not disturbed, it calms down 
and becomes steady and the reflection of the moon dances no 
more, but appears as one, whole and intact. Likewise if the 
upādhi of mind is purified, emptied of thoughts and stilled, 
the reflection of the Awareness is clear and total. That these 
senses of doership and enjoyership are to the mind alone and 
not to the Ātman can also be proved from dream and sleep 
experiences. In dream, when the mind alone functions, one 
perceives the ego with its various characteristics such as 
happiness and unhappiness, all of which disappear in deep 
sleep, when the mind remains actionless.

To those who cannot separate one from the other and 
know them as such, out of delusion, Ātman appears as the 
jīva and the jīva as the Ātman and the actions of jīva are 
erroneously  perceived to bind the Ātman.

The Ātman is pure Awareness, unattached to anything. 
The jīva without realising that he, in essence, is this pure 
Awareness, and also mistaking himself to be the body, binds 
himself by the cord of the body, sense organs and mind, draws 
himself up and down with a sense of agency and enjoyment, 
among objects produced by his actions.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   727 06-05-2011   10:54:13



728 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Commentary: 
Here comes the answer to the Tarkikas (logicians) who 

argue that Ātman is an active participant in actions and the 
actions of pranan,  and the experience of pleasure and pain 
are but proofs of the existence of the Ātman.

Love towards children, the desire for wealth, feelings of 
bliss and happiness on the fulfilment of heart's desire, misery, 
aversion and hatred when they are not attained are all natural 
to one. The logicians argue that they belong to the Ātman.

If that be the case, they must occur for ever, as the Ātman 
is 'ever present'. Manifesting in wakeful and dream states they 
are absent in deep sleep state, thereby proving that they are 
not the eternally present Ātman. In the absence of external 
objects in the dream, the mind by itself creates everything, 
namely the dream enjoyer, the dream objects etc. by its own 
power. So too the waking state is not different from but 
identical to the dream state. These are but the ramifications 
of just the thought waves of the mind. “It is well known that 
there is nothing in dreamless sleep when the mind is stilled. 
Hence the saṃsāra is a creation of the mind. It does not exist 
in reality.”(Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, Verse 173). As they are stilled 
along with the stilled mind in deep sleep, Bhagavan remarks, 
“sondamavai pundikkē” – these belong to the buddhi, intellect, 
alone. 

Producing attachment to objects like body, etc. the mind 
tethers a man with a rope as if he were an animal. Later, the 
same mind creates an aversion for them and liberates him 
from that self-fashioned fetters.

This being the truth, how can these (the non-existent 
things) be ascribed to the Ātman, the Only vastu that exists? 
Therefore Bhagavan queries wonder  with the single word 
“Atmāvirkāmō?” – can it be to the Ātman?

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   728 06-05-2011   10:54:13



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 729

Sankara voices the same truth in Vivekachūḍāmaṇi when 
he says: “How can there be talk of difference in the Supreme 
Reality which is unitary? Who had experienced difference 
in the state of dreamless sleep characterised by pure bliss?” 
(Verse 404).

Commentary: 

The nature of Ātman is explained in this verse with

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   729 06-05-2011   10:54:13



730 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Sat (Existence), Chit (Awareness) and Ananda (Bliss). In 
addition, It is Eternal, unlike other objects that exist at one 
time and go out of existence at another, and immaculately 
Pure, without the taint of the admixture of an other. All these 
are intrinsic to the Ātman. It must ne noted that Eternity 
and Purity  are not qualities of Ātman, but Its very innate or 
essential nature. They are always present in Ātman though 
obscured by Māyā.

Just as the effulgence of light cannot be separated from 
the Sun, coolness from water and heat from fire – they being 
their intrinsic nature or dharma – so also, Sat, Chit, Ananda, 
Eternity and Purity, cannot be separated from the Ātman. 
Nothing can run away from its very essential nature. There 
has never been – nor ever will  be – a ‘dark’ Sun or ‘cool’ 
fire. Ātman is the very form of Sat, Chit, Ananda, Purity and 
Eternity.

Verse 17 of Yoga Karzattri of Orzhivil Odukkam speaks 
of this: “Who taught water its cooling nature, fire its burning 
property, the wind its mobility? As they are their inborn nature, 
the clinging on to an object is the very nature of the mind; 
ascertaining the object held is the nature of intellect; desiring 
the object so ascertained is the nature of chitta (memory). 
None can keep these – mind and the antaḥkaraṇas, away.”

If, desiring  to remove them, they are controlled more and 
more, they will keep bouncing back, even as the shadow buried 
under sand pops up again and again. Yet, without allowing to 
be impacted by any, if one remains perceiving, like the vast 
space, they are rent asunder.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   731 06-05-2011   10:54:13



732 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

sense of ‘I know’. This sense of ‘I’ is called the jīva. Since he 
emerges out of the combination of chit and jada, Spirit and 
matter, he is called chitjada granti (the knot between chit and 
jada) by the Vedānta śāstras. Ātman neither perceives nor is 
perceived.

The chit of the Ātman is reflected in the intellect. The 
reflected chaitanya (sat and chit aspects of the Ātman) acquires 
a sameness with the intellect. Hence it is that the chaitanya is 
spoken of as non-distinct from jīva, which considers itself as 
‘I’. As the reflection of a luminous body is also luminous as 
in the case of a reflection of sun in a mirror which illumines 
dark places where the sun's rays cannot penetrate, the intellect 
acquires the power which is of the nature of illumination. As 
the ‘I’ sense emerges here, the duality of the perceiver ‘I’ and 
the perceived world appears along with notions such as ‘I see’, 
‘I know’ (also rise forth). This is the interesting story of the 
birth of jīva. The origin of both, the world and the one who 
says “I know the world”, though baseless, is wonderful indeed!

This union of Ātman and intellect is the result of 
ignorance, cannot be real, for no real union is possible 
between two mutually conflicting things such as spirit and 
matter or light and darkness. It is an illusory superimposition 
and Ātman remains ever, unattached to māyā. Sankara in 
Vivekachūḍāmaṇi says, “This association of one’s Ātman 
with the intellect  is preceded by incorrect knowledge. It's 
disappearance will arise by correct knowledge and not 
otherwise.” and “the jīva bhava’s satta (existential character) 
persists so long as there is delusion as it is born of  mithyājñāna 
(false knowledge). The serpent in rope endures only during 
the pendency of the delusion.” (Verses 2030 and 199). The 
perceived wold appears when Ātman, identifying Itself with 
intellect, becomes the jīva. The jīva, when through enquiry, 
gets released from his ajñāna, the jīvabhava gets annihilated 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   732 06-05-2011   10:54:13



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 733

and Ātman in full splendour shines forth where he realises 
that universe and the perceiver both are illusory appearances 
originating in Himself.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   733 06-05-2011   10:54:14



734 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Commentary: 
Ātman is ever changeless. Changes due to space, time, 

and causality occur only in material objects. Ātman is all 
spirit. Further devoid of the sense of doership, activity and 
attributes, It neither perceives nor performs nor knows and 
therefore  never undergoes change.

The intellect is inert and insentient and cannot know 
anything. The jīva, superimposing knowledge, the aspect of 
Ātman, which is Knowledge itself, on the insentient intellect, 
deludes himself into thinking that he knows everything and 
falls into a deeper delusion.

“Jīvahood which is imagined in the Ātman due 
to association with upādhis  is  not  real;  for the 
Ātman is really different from it in essential nature.” 
(Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, Verse 202)

When we say, “I know this”; “I know that”, the chit aspect 
of the Ātman and the jada aspect of the jīva come together 
mixed with each other. In “I know”, ‘know’ is the aspect of 
the awareness (chit) and ‘I’ is the aspect of being (sat). ‘This’ 
and ‘that’ are aspects of jada or insentiency. When Ātman is 
finitised to the measure of the body It becomes a jīva; in other 
words Ātman in a body is jīva.

The ‘awareness’ aspect of Ātman, Knowledge itself, 
shrinks into the limited knowledge when spoken of as “I 
saw this, that”. A jada always remains a jada and though the 
knowledge of the Self be eternal, with the new emergence 
of the thought-waves of the antaḥkaraṇa, namely, intellect, 
he thinks “I know”. “Pure ether cannot take reflections; only 
the ether of water can do so... Similarly pure knowledge does 
not contain objects in it nor reflects objects. Only with the 
limiting adjunct the mind, it reflects the world... Mind is a 
mixture of chit (intellect) and sankalpas (thought) reflections... 
Chidākāśa (chit-ether) is pure knowledge only. It is the source 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   734 06-05-2011   10:54:14



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 735

of mind. Just at the moment of rising up, the mind is this ‘I’ 
thought forms the jīva and the world.
	 The first light is pure mind,... its modes manifest as objects. 
Knowledge does not consist in knowing objects; this is relative 
knowledge. But knowledge in its purity remains all alone. One 
unique, transcendent Light.” (Talks, no. 589).

The jīva who unifies the sat and chit aspects with 
the thought-wave of intellect assumes the bhava “I know 
everything” and gets deluded. This superimposition of 
qualities of one on the other leads to the wrong sense of 
identity between the bearers of these respective qualities 
which makes the delusion deeper. Such identification is the 
result of ignorance. Bhagavan was vividly explained it and 
with an illustration too. Pointing to his towel he said, “We 
call this a white cloth, but the cloth and its whiteness cannot 
be separated; and it is the same with the illumination and the 
mind that unite to form the ego. The following illustration is 
given in the books: The lamp in the theatre is Para Brahman 
or illumination. It illuminates itself, the stage and the actors. 
We see the stage and the actors by its light, but the light still 
continues when there is no more play. Another illustration is 
an iron rod that is compared to the mind. Fire joins it and it 
becomes red hot. It glows and can burn things like fire, but 
still it has a definite shape unlike fire. If we hammer it, it is the 
rod that receives the blow, not the fire. The rod is the jīvātman, 
the fire the Self or Paramātman. The mind can do nothing by 
itself. It emerges only with the illumination and can do no 
action good or bad, except with the illumination. But while 
the illumination is always there, enabling the mind to act well 
or ill, the pleasure or pain resulting from such action is not 
felt by the illumination, just as when you hammer a red hot 
iron it is not the fire but the iron that gets the hammering.” 
(Gems from Bhagavan, Devaraja Mudaliar, page 12).

Commentary: 

This bondage of saṃsāra has its origin in delusion. A 
way out of this delusion – and therefore from saṃsāra – is 
spelt  out in this verse.

When darkness is about to envelop during twilight, a 
wayfarer happens to see a rope moved by wind on his way. 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   736 06-05-2011   10:54:14



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 737

Mistaking it for a snake and overwhelmed with fear, he runs 
shouting for help. A friendly soul on hearing the shouts arrives 
with a lamp, and with the help of the light proves it to be 
only a rope and not a snake. On knowing the truth, the fear 
is overcome.

By the defect of abhyasa (superimposition) of the 
mithyaātman (the false Ātman like the intellect, etc.), the 
Ātman, which is all, attains limitation and looks upon itself 
as different like pots from the clay.

Fear is out of the existence of a second. Even a slightest 
difference between two perceived beings will lead to the fear. 
The perceived plurality, the world, is the cause of saṃsāra. 
The jīva or the individual living being, thinks he is limited by 
space, time and is subject to birth and death. In reality, Ātman 
never becomes a jīva; hence the fear is groundless.

When one's true Form is not known, this non-perception 
of reality leads to the misperception of reality, of looking 
upon the aggregate of body, senses, mind and intellect as ‘I’. 
With this the jīva performs actions in the empirical world. 
The world of plurality and duality appears bringing in its 
wake all the attendant sufferings. Abiding satisfaction from 
the fulfilment of desires can never be possible in a world that 
teems with dyads.

Through the upadēsa of a Satguru, aided by discrimination 
and enquiry of the Self, the jīva knows himself to be not the 
jīva but the very form of Paramātman, Sat-Chit-Ananda and 
dispelling the delusion born of nescience and the fear, he 
becomes a fearless hero. 

“Bondage and liberation are imaginations due to māyā, 
they do not pertain to the Ātman. It is like the appearance 
and disappearance of the serpent in the inactive rope.” and 
“a wise man, free from grief, compacted of bliss, is not 
himself afraid of anything from anywhere. To the seeker 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   737 06-05-2011   10:54:14



738 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

of liberation there is no path for freedom from bondage of 
saṃsāra other than the realization of one's true nature.” 
(Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, Verses 570 and 224).

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   738 06-05-2011   10:54:14



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 739

Commentary: 
This verse answers the question that while the instruments, 

antaḥkaraṇas (inner organs), mind and intellect are capable 
of analysing and evaluating very minutely all the objects 
outside of them, including the most subtle and secret mysteries 
of atoms, why can't they know the Ātman that is at closest 
proximity to them?

The light of a single lamp illumines all the objects like pot, 
jar and reveals them to us. But objects like pot and jar cannot 
illumine the lamp for they are insentient and having no light 
of their own, they themselves require another to reveal their 
existence. How then can they reveal others, especially a lamp? 

The lamp, the Ātman, with Its self-revealing light, 
illumines intellect, mind and sense organs, etc. The intellect, 
with the help of the light of Awareness that the Ātman beams 
out and by that light, illumines everything and knows them. 
The eyes perceive forms, ears hear sounds and other sense 
organs grasp and absorb their respective objects, only by 
the light of awareness of the Ātman for all of them are non-
luminous  by nature. These can never illumine the Ātman for 
they themselves shine in the effulgence of the Ātman. “That 
which cannot be seen by the eyes but by which the eyes see 
other objects – that alone is Brahman.” (Kenopanishad). If 
indriyas, that illumine objects of the world, can be compared 
to lamps -which cannot illumine the Sun – the awareness of 
intellect cannot illumine the Ātman, the Sun of Knowledge. 
Ātman in the entire creation is the only vastu with the 
effulgence of the Light of Awareness and all the rest are 
insentient and non-luminous.

“What can be there to manifest that by whose lustre, as 
of the Sun, shines all that is the anātman, asat (unreal) and 
insignificant?” (Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, Verse 28).

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   739 06-05-2011   10:54:14
