Just as to reveal the form of a lighted lamp burning 

bright with light, the light of another lamp is needless, so 
also, the Ātman, ever-shining as the form of knowledge, 
to know itself requires no other knowledge, Ātman being 
effulgent with Self-revealing light.
Commentary: 

It was said that Ātman cannot be known by intellect or 
mind or sense organs. This verse explains how then ‘That’ 
can be known.

The existence of objects in the world is cognized by the 
light of either sun, moon, stars or lamps. If the question, in the 
same way, what is the light that reveals the Ātman were to be 
posed, the answer is: no other light is necessary to announce 
Its existence. If so, can Ātman be never known? Ātman is 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   740 06-05-2011   10:54:14



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 741

Self-effulgent and It shines in It’s own Self-revealing light, 
requiring nothing else to illumine and reveal It. 

Just as the sun illumining all the objects in the world 
by its light, illumines himself by his own light, the Ātman, 
illuming everything else, shines in Its own light. There is no 
other effulgence that can illumine it. It is Self-effulgent and 
shines in Its own Self-revealing light.

In order to cognize a lighted lamp, we need no other lamp 
but to turn our eyes towards the lamp. To know the Ātman, the 
very form of Consciousness, no other awareness is required. 
All that we need to do is to turn inward and proceed towards 
the Heart. It, besides announcing Itself, will make us also of 
Its Form. “To see the world or external objects, the mind and 
the reflected light (or chidabhasa) which always arises with 
it are necessary. To see the Self, the mind has simply to be 
turned inside and there is no need of the reflected light.” (Day 
by Day, 21-11-1945).

None can deny or doubt the existence of one’s own Self. 
Ātman is the Self of even the one who denies or doubts Its 
existence. No thinking is possible without the Consciousness ‘I 
am’. The real ‘I’ behind ‘I am’ is Ātman. Watching the source 
where from ‘I’ rises will lead us to the Ātman.

“To realize that you yourself are the Self, why do you 
require any light other than being Consciousness, the light of 
the Self.” (Pādamālai, Verse 33).

“When a person wants to see if there is an article in a dark 
room, he takes a lamp to look for it. The light is useful for 
detecting the presence and absence of a thing. Consciousness 
is necessary for discovering if a thing is conscious or not. If 
a man remains in a dark room, one need not take a lamp to 
find him. If called, he answers. He does not require a lamp to 
announce his presence. Consciousness is thus Self-shining.” 
(Talks, no. 591).

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   742 06-05-2011   10:54:14



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 743

of the mahavakyas that speak of the non-difference or 
identity of the upādhiless jīvātmā left after negating 
all upādhis and the unsublatable Primal Content, the 
Supreme Self, and be realized.
Commentary: 

Though Ātman is Self-luminous, It is not perceived for 
the three bodies conceal It; just as the Sun though the very 
form of effulgence is not perceived when hidden by clouds.

Not withstanding this, the body, etc. which, conceals the 
Ātman, but shines in the light of the Ātman is regarded as 
Ātman out of delusion.

If such non-perception and misperception of the Ātman 
is to be overcome, all the veiling factors must be removed. 
Jettisoning of all the upādhis through vichara requires a sharp 
intellect which is acquired by engaging oneself in the study 
of Vedantic texts and the practice of sravana, manana and 
nidhidhyasana after being instructed by a Satguru.

The distinction between the seer and the seen is done by 
a mind, by separating the Ātman from the anātman even as 
the mythical hamsa  (swan) separates the milk from the water 
in the mixture of the two.

The import of the four Vedantic aphorisms that declare 
the total identity of the Supreme, devoid of upādhis and jīva, 
who is divested of all his upādhis, must be deeply enquired 
into, and clearly known: One with the awareness of upādhi 
is called the jīva and one devoid of upādhis is called para.

The Upanishads advocate the process of ‘neti-neti’ (not 
this – not this) to discard all the upādhis. This way all upādhis 
that are extraneous to the Ātman, belonging to the realm of 
ignorance, namely, the causal, subtle and gross bodies, all the 
objects of the outside world that form the vishaya or content 
of all the instruments and organs of action, time, space and 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   743 06-05-2011   10:54:14



744 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

causality are all negated. The Upanishads teach that finally, 
when THAT, which, negated of all upādhis as “not this-not 
this”, which can neither be rejected nor accepted, is Brahman.

All our endeavours are only to remove the veiling and 
not to illumine the Ātman. Ātman can never be made known 
as ‘this’ by affirmation. 

“Without the total removal of the concealing power, it 
is difficult to get over the projecting power. That concealing 
power will get destroyed naturally only if the seer and the seen 
are distinguished clearly like milk and water. This conquest 
over the projecting power will be surely effected without any 
obstacle if there is no resting (of the mind) in the false things 
of the world.” (Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, Verse 345)

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 745

Paraphrase: 
The whole world of objects perceived like deha 

(body) et al, born of nescience, the effect of māyā, are 
evanescent and perishable like bubbles on water. The Self 
is not these. That taintless immaculate Brahman distinct 
from all these “I am”, thus, through ceaseless enquiry 
without becoming weary, know forever and be.
Commentary: 

The body, senses, mind-stuff, intellect and the ego 
are creations of avidya or māyā. But māyā is non-existent, 
therefore, the effects of māyā, all these creations, are also 
mithya, non-existent. They are as mysterious and false(non-
existent) but  they do everything like their parent, māyā. The 
snake in the rope, did not exist in the first place; hence the 
effects of this illusion namely fear and attempts to drive it 
away, also need not exist. Māyā has the quality of making the 
unreal appear real. But Ātman shines transcending māyā and 
unknowable through māyā; nevertheless it is eternally existent, 
imperishable vastu that is uncontaminated  by māyā and its 
effects. The imperishable Ātman cannot be known through 
perishable objects like the bodies.

The Self, in its identifications with the gross, subtle and 
causal bodies, becomes the waker, dreamer and the one who 
sleeps deeply. Therefore the Self, in Itself, must be something 
other than Its manifestations in these three states. The body 
is but an object, the seen and the Self is the Eternal Subject, 
the Seer. Things illumined are always different from the 
illuminator.

Therefore armed with the strength of conviction of the 
Truth proclaimed by the Vedas, fortified with the power of 
discriminating objects of impermanence from permanence, 
one should realise one's real nature.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   745 06-05-2011   10:54:14



746 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

“The nature and characteristics of the possessor of the 
body (sariri) are different from the nature of the possession, 
body; hence none of these body or its components am I. 
While they are perishable, like the bubble, I am Imperishable 
and Eternal.” “That taintless Parabrahman, am I, thus 
untiringly reflect and know”, is the upadēsa, the content of the 
mahavakya, provided in this verse. In this context Bhagavan’s 
advice to Miss Merston: “All things are like bubbles on water. 
You are the water and the objects are the bubbles. They cannot 
exist apart from the water, but they are not quite the same 
as the water.... Be the water and not the froth. This is done 
by diving in..... But even without diving in, you are That.” 
(Talks, no. 625).

In order that the delusion of māyā should not hold and 
grip the seeker even in the slightest manner, a seeker is 
instructed on the impermanence and the illusory nature of 
the phenomenal world with its plurality, the effect of māyā. 
That the delusion given up, does not stage a ‘come-back’, 
the seeker is asked to resort to the nidhidhyasana (reflection) 
ceaselessly. “That Brahman I am”......

There can be no better aid to effect the annihilation 
of mind than this upadēsa is the highest teaching on the 
knowledge of the non-dual Brahman.

“For, the fire of the knowledge of the oneness of Brahman 
and the jīva totally destroys the forest of avidya. To him who 
has attained the sense of this oneness, what will be there of 
the seed of saṃsāra?” (Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, Verse 347).

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 749

Commentary: 
This verse, like the earlier one, negates the other 

constituents of the subtle body like vital breath and mind and 
their functions as: “The Self, this is not”, and confirms the 
real nature of the Self. The earlier verse negated senses and 
instruments of perception, here the powers that activate them 
are negated. Mind is characterised by an unending flow of 
thoughts that keep changing for ever. Thoughts spring from 
desire which gives rise to the attendant and opposite thoughts.

Since I am not the mind I am not attached to attachment 
and aversion, desire, fear, pleasure and pain, all of which 
are experienced by the mind. Nor am I the vital breath that 
belongs to the same group. None of these kinds belong to me 
noe do I belong to any of this kind. Sri Sankara says, “do not 
the Vedas declare so?”

“Desire, deliberation, doubt, faith, want of faith, patience, 
impatience, shame, intelligence and fear – all these are but 
of the mind and not the Self.” (Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, 
1-5-3)

“Since He is birthless, therefore He is without vital force 
and without mind; He is pure” (Mundaka Upanishad, 2-1-2).

“From It are born breath, mind and all organs of sense, 
ether, air, light, water and earth which is the support of all.” 
(Mundaka Upanishad, 2-1-3)

Sankara says as the Vedas proclaim this truth to the beat 
of drums, know that and be clear in the mind.
With certainty born of the conviction of the truth of the Vedic 
declaration about the real form of the Self which is beyond 
the ken of human mind, a seeker must proceed on the path 
of enquiry according to Vedic instructions, must absorb and 
assimilate the Truth.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   750 06-05-2011   10:54:14



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 751

Transcending all principles that are subject to change but the 
substratum of all these principles, the one form of Awareness 
without a second am I. I am, like the Sun in whose presence 
unbaked  pots undergo changes but myself remains without 
change, changeless though associated with bodies and 
indriyas. Therefore I am Nirvikaran (changeless), I am without 
a body.  The four Vedas proclaim the Ātman as the formless 
Form of Awareness, like the sky and nameless. Having no 
limbs and form, I cannot be cut or burnt and I, illumining 
the other organs and organs of perception cannot become an 
object of them Therefore I am Nirakaran.  Hence none of 
the impurities of the physical body can touch Me. Qualities 
of māyā like satwa, rajas, tamas and their manifestations 
like bravery, fearlessness, miserliness and munificence 
belong to the mind. I, transcending all the creations of māyā 
like God, jīva, and	 the world and creation, sustenance and 
dissolution, yet remaining as the cause of it all, am boundless 
as the form of bliss everywhere. Therefore I am Nirgunan.

Desire and hatred, outcome of vāsanās of actions are the 
taints of the mind. As I am not the mind, I am free of taints 
of all kinds. Remaining as ‘other than’ the reprehensible 
bodies and their impurities, the elements and their impurities 
and the greatest impurity of being caught up in the grievous 
cycle of repeated embodiments due to endless karma and the 
experiencing their fruits, I am Niranjanan.

Time is an effect of māyā on Eternity. I am beyond time. I 
am eternally existent, pre-existent to time, by whatever length 
of time it is lengthened.

Impurities are of three kinds; those of the gross body being 
sweat and other wastes and of the subtle body, desire, hatred, 
attachments, etc. and of the causal, the nescience. Since I am 
none of the three bodies, none of these impurities can taint 
me. Hence I am immaculate - suddhan.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   751 06-05-2011   10:54:15



752 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

All actions are of the body, mind and senses. I am not 
any of these, therefore, I am actionless – nishkriya, sankalpa 
and vikalpa (wishing and willing, doubting and distorting) are 
of the mind. I am devoid of these therefore I am nirvikalpa. 
Devoid of the ajñāna of nescience I have no bondage and in 
the absence of bondage, mukti is also not for Me. I am eternally 
liberated without bandha and moksha.

Thus when all these have been negated what remains 
is asmi – ‘I am’, the One Awareness of Being on which 
substratum hangs all this wold of matter, anātman, the 
product of māyā. That ‘I am’ illumining all thoughts stands 
all by Itself in ‘Immaculate aloofness’. That ‘I am’ spoken 
of variously here, know that I am. “For me, ever of the same 
form and without parts, there is no activity nor withdrawal. 
How will anything act which is ever identical, compact and 
undifferentiated?” (Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, Verse 504).

[How will That, which is without limbs or parts and 
therefore change, and which is one through and through, 
closely compacted and without intervening space like the 
sky ever act?]

Paraphrase: 
He, who like the immaculate sky, pervades filling 

everything within and without, is deathless and eternal, 
homogeneously the same in all, eternally – realized,

Commentary: 

The nature of Ātman, It’s real form is described further 
here, comparing It to ether. Ether, on account of its subtlety, 
permeates all things in and out. Space, though it provides 
existence and accommodation to other things, is not 
contaminated by any of them contained by it. None of the 
properties of objects that appears on it, like lightning, thunder, 
hues, or content of the clouds can ever contaminate the space.

Ātman, the subtlest of all, is present in everything as 
Existence, Luminosity and Bliss. What is born only, is subject 
to death. I who am never born will never die and therefore, 
eternal. Being birthless It is eternal and deathless. Like the 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   753 06-05-2011   10:54:15



754 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

ether that homogeneously pervades everywhere, resides 
everywhere without exception and preference; hence He is 
called Sarva Saman (always and everywhere, the same).

All the objects of enjoyment of the phenomenal world, 
are created and made ready with the help of other things. The 
attainment of objects not possessed but desired and therefore 
obtained as the fruit of endeavours put forth is called aprapta 
praptavyam (attainment of what is not possessed). But the 
Ātman is in the seeker, nay, he himself is the Ātman. It is 
already attained called prapta praptavyam (attainment of that 
which already remains attained).  Ātman is eternally present 
and ready to be realised. He is a siddhan – ever attained 
Reality.

“I am that Brahman itself which is without a second, 
which is like the sky, subtle, without beginning or end, in 
which the whole universe, from the unmanifested to the gross 
appears as a projection. Let there be changes in Prakriti in tens, 
hundreds and thousands. What is my connection with them? 
I am unconnected chit. For, the thunder of the cloud does not 
affect the sky.” (Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, Verse 513 and 512).

Paraphrase: 
Know that, that Content which is eternal, ever pure, 

ever unbound and free, All-alone, of the form of ceaseless 
and unbroken (indivisible) bliss, non-dual without a

Commentary: 

The nature of our own Self is reiterated further so that 
constant awareness of this becomes the jñāna abhyāsa – 
practice of Knowledge.

The Ātman is Eternal, present at all times. Nothing other 
than Ātman is eternal, therefore the only Eternal among all 
the impermanent ones. It is unattached to and unimpacted by 
any; hence undefiled by contamination of any sort. It is free 
without any bondage – bondage from relativity – marked by 
birth, death and other changes.

It is One or ēka with Its existence unlimited by any other 
entity. The words Akanda inbu can be taken together to mean 
ceaseless and unbroken Bliss or separately to mean Indivisible 
and compacted Bliss. Ātman is Indivisible for none of the 
kinds of distinctions made in material objects is possible in 
Ātman for It is one without a second, partless, homogeneous, 
Awareness.

“That which shines as Truth, Awareness, Eternal and 
Supreme, that Brahman – I am. Know this well.”

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   755 06-05-2011   10:54:15

A few verses of Vivekachūḍāmaṇi also affirm and reaffirm

which constitute the manana of Ātman landing one smoothly 
into the next and important stage of nidhidhyasana.

“Of the nature of existence and chit, whole and entire, 
permanent, compacted of bliss, inactive Brahman is one only, 
not dual, Internal (to all), homogeneous, full, endless, facing 
everywhere, Brahman is one only, not-dual, not one to be 
discarded or accepted; not one resting on another, nor having 
any support or base. Dualityless without parts, subtle, without 
change, without blemish, Brahman is one only, not dual, there 
is no manifold here. Of indemonstrable nature, beyond mind 
and speech, Brahman is only one, not dual, there is no manifold 
here.” (Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, Verses 465 and 471)

Commentary: 

This verse speaks of nidhidhyasana or reflection. 
Engaging a mind freed of its restlessness in intense reflection 
is nidhidhyasana.

What was listened to (sravana) is contemplated (manana) 
upon, with the help of scriptural proofs, upadēsa of the guru 
and logical reasoning and when the mind is made to inhere 
single-pointedly in that truth so ascertained by contemplation, 
namely  the bhavana that “That Brahman I am”, it is called 
dhyana. Scriptures say manana (thinking) is hundred times 
better than hearing; a lakh of times better than thinking is 
reflection (nidhidhyasana).

Constant practice, intense contemplation and single-
pointedness that admits no other thought, are emphasized, 
for the vāsanās acquired over countless births demand such 
practices for their total elimination and only by the fruit of such 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   757 06-05-2011   10:54:15



758 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

intense dhyana, the thought waves of the mind that veil and 
conceal the Ātman (āvaraṇā – non-perception of the Reality) 
and project the illusion as real (vikshepa – misperception of 
Reality) are destroyed. This contemplation of ‘I am Brahman’, 
bhavana, is like the rasayana (a class of Indian medicine, 
made of chemicals reputed to contain the secret of rejuvenation 
and longevity). It is odourless, sweet to taste, destroys the 
malady, promotes health and provokes no adverse reaction 
or side effects, and is cool and soft on the system.		
Likewise, the rasayana of Brahman bhavana, “I am Brahman” 
is the ideal medicine for the disease that has been harassing 
the jīva from time without beginning, namely, the diseases of 
āvarana and vikshepa. The disease of ‘I am the body sense’, 
is the most irremediable of all disease.

If a sādhak, in place of ‘I am the body’ idea maintains 
the constant remembrance that ‘I am Brahman’ it will create 
a new set of ‘Divine vāsanās’ which will act as an antidote to 
the earlier body-based vāsanās. While the jīvabhava – sense 
of ‘I’ of the jīva – brings about more and more agitations, 
Brahmavāsanās quieten the thought flow. This process will 
continue until the last of the thoughts ends in the supreme 
silence of the mind, and Brahmavāsanā also ends, like 
the kataka nut mentioned in verse 5, leaving the seeker to 
experience the Self.

While āvarana prevents our knowing our true form 
vikshepa, dislodging us from our Svarūpa, throws us into 
body-mind complex making it appear as if it is our Svarūpa.

Bhavana here is not at the simply level of the intellect. It 
has to be a mixture of thought and feeling and both must be 
woven harmoniously together.

Commentary: 

The disciplines that have to be observed by the sādhaks 
to strengthen  the Brahma bhavana, are detailed here.

A traditional adage says, “One alone for tapas; two for 
learning; and three for travel”. There is no one great who has 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   759 06-05-2011   10:54:15



760 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

not extolled the sweetness of solitude. Solitude is ideal and 
most congenial for the furtherance of tapas. Śāstras ordain 
that a seeker intensely serious in knowing his Svarūpa (real 
form) must keep himself away from the crowd of society and 
remain in solitude. Gītā declares: “Let the yogī try constantly 
to concentrate his mind on the Supreme Self, remaining in 
solitude and alone, self-controlled, free from desires and 
(longing for) possessions.” (Chap. VI, Verse 10)

Living in the midst of society compels one to reorient 
oneself towards that from which one has moved away. In 
short it exteriorises one while solitude helps one to go inward 
further and helps one to know one's real form.
Despite remaining in solitude if one yields to desires and 
attachments that besmirch the mind, allows a free rein to the 
unbridled senses ruminates over the past and dreams of the 
future forgetting dhyana with Brahma bhavana, solitude can 
help in no way.

“Living alone is the means of dama, the cessation of 
sense-organ activity. The dama is the means to sama, the 
control of the mind. By such sama, the tendency of the ego-
sense is attenuated. By it accrues to the yogin, the unceasing 
blissful experience of the Brahman. Therefore one given 
to meditation should always control the mind with effort.” 
(Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, Verse 369).

Here the instruction given is that Brahman, the One 
eternal Ātman, must be contemplated on by the mind without 
entertaining any other thought, but single-pointedly fixed on it. 
The ‘One’ refers to the Lord and essence of all that exists is the 
same as Self, the witness of the three states and stages of life.
	 The speech in mind must be restrained. The mind must 
be restrained in the intellect and the intellect must be merged 
in the infinite Pūrnātman and thereby one can attain Supreme 
Peace.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   761 06-05-2011   10:54:15



762 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Commentary: 
Buddhiman or man of wisdom, is one, who by the diligent 

practice of sravana, etc. has attained purity and clarity of mind. 
He is of the firm conviction that all the perceived objects are 
not other than Brahman. When all that is perceived is unified in 
the perceiver, the True eye, the Self, shines as the Eye without 
perception, as the mere witness.

The phenomenal world is a mere superimposition on the 
Ātman; it is one with the substratum. In the illusion of the snake 
in a rope, it is the rope alone that exists. The snake is one with 
the rope. The substratum alone is real and the superimpositions 
are seen on account of the association of a name and form. 
But they are in essence the substratum. The name and form of 
the snake is superimposed on the rope, which is the essence 
of existence for both the rope and the snake. Through such 
reasoning a discriminating sādhak should realise the non-
existence of the world apart from Brahman and merge the 
universe in Brahman. This is the content of the word onḍṛal 
purivittē – merging it in the Ātman that shines like suddhamām 
viṇ - the pure taintless sky – clear cloudless sky.

All that is perceived must be merged in that Supreme 
Space of Awareness, is the meaning.

“Whatever is made of clay like the pot, etc. is all, through 
and through, clay only always. Similarly all that is the effect 
of Sat (Brahman) is of the nature of Sat and is entirely Sat 
only.” (Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, Verse 253)

Srimad Bhagavatham gives the same message: “See the 
Self in yourself like the pure ether in all beings in and out. 
Unashamed, fall prostrate before even an outcaste, a cow or 
an ass. So long as ‘I’ am not perceived in all, worship all with 
body and mind with right knowledge, see all as Brahman. 
This once clear, all doubts are at an end and you will remain 
withdrawn in the Self.”  To view all that is perceived as not 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   762 06-05-2011   10:54:15



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 763

other than the Self is Ātma bhavana which leading the mind 
inward, inheres it in the Ātman.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   763 06-05-2011   10:54:15



764 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Commentary: 
Ātman will not be realised  so long as the truth of the 

Supreme Content is not known. So long as the nature of 
Ātman is not realised, the objects of the perceived world 
cannot be divested of seeming differences of their names, 
forms, virtues, faults and distinctions of castes, etc. For 
these to be discarded the name and the form of the perceiver 
of the distinctions of names and forms must be jettisoned. 
The best way to transcend one's own name and form is to 
practise the Ātmabhavana – that all that is perceived is but 
the form of Ātman.

Whoever incessantly practises and knows 'that which 
is', the Ātman, he overcomes once for all the delusion of the 
illusory  multiplicities that the world is teeming with. His 
perception having become one of jñāna, the names and forms 
of all the perceived objects disappear and the essence alone, 
that shines in all, as the very form of joy of awareness, remains 
resplendent in all its Fullness, including his own form.

As long as one conceives of oneself with forms, so long do 
name, family and caste persist. If he realises that he is without 
a form, then the world also has no form. Such a one shines as 
the very embodiment of Sat, Chit and Ananda.

“As a lamp in a windless place flickers not, to such is 
likened the yogī of subdued thought who practises union with 
the Self.” (Gītā, Chap. VI, Verse 19) and Vivekachūḍāmaṇi 
echoes this: “If the mental functions are established in the 
true, unchanging, higher Self, Brahman, this awareness of the 
phenomenal world is not experienced. What remains thereafter 
is merely a matter of meaningless word.” (Verse 399).

One day, while going  round the Hill, a devotee saw an 
apparition. On returning back, he asked Bhagavan, “Do ghosts 
have form?” Bhagavan was greatly amused. He replied, “If 
you can have a form, why not the ghosts?”

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   764 06-05-2011   10:54:15



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 765

The same was emphasized by Bhagavan by way of an 
answer to another devotee who felt that perceiving everything 
as Vasudeva is easier than knowing the Self. “But you cannot 
escape the Self. You want to see God in all, but not in yourself. 
If all are God, are you not included in that ‘all’? Yourself being 
God, is it a wonder that all are God? There must be a seer and 
thinker for even the practice. Who is he?” (Talks no. 254). The 
practice with the attitude of everything is Brahman makes the 
mind exteriorised. But attempts to know the Self, the Ātman 
makes the mind interiorised.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   765 06-05-2011   10:54:15



766 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Paraphrase: 
The distinctions of triputis (triad) like the knower 

(who knows objects other than himself), knowledge, and 
the object of knowledge, cannot occur in the Supreme 
Ātman, the Being. Since that Content, the very form 
of joy and awareness abides nondually as One (Being, 
Awareness and Bliss, all these three as one), without 
requiring anything else It alone shines as Sat and  also 
by the light of It's own awareness.
Commentary: 

The question “Will the triputi of knower, known and 
knowledge persist for an ātmajñāni, who realises the Ātman 
that is worldless?” is answered here.

To perceive and know the objects, other than oneself, 
in the world, a perceiving consciousness is necessary. The 
objects of the world being insentient cannot reveal or announce 
themselves. Only the one with consciousness can become 
aware of their existence, through his own awareness. Yet to 
know oneself, one does not resort to another ‘awareness’. He is 
the very form of consciousness, and he is aware of himself. For 
Rama to know that he is Rama, he does not require a Krishna to 
come and make him know that he is Rama. He knows himself 
to be so beyond doubt and if even others were to contradict, 
it he would simply and silently turn a deaf ear to it.

In the Ātman, the form of Pure Knowledge, the triputi, 
knower, known and knowledge is not present. If it persists, it 
is not the natural state. Ātman, the Sat (Existence) also shines 
as the Chit (Awareness) and Ananda (Bliss) and one without a 
second shines in Its own light, without the aid of another light.

In the continuous practice of “I am Brahman”, when the 
vāsanās are completely eliminated, the mind is brought to a 
grinding halt. Just as when a cloth is burnt every warp and 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   766 06-05-2011   10:54:15



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 767

woof of the cloth gets burnt, with the ending of mind, all 
the modifications of the mind, including “I am Brahman”, 
are destroyed. There then remains only the reflected 
consciousness which, unable to illumine the Supreme and 
the Self-effulgent Brahman, becomes overpowered by it. 
Further on the destruction of the mind, the reflection reverts 
back to the Supreme Brahman just as the image of a face in a 
mirror reverts back to the face when the mirror is broken or 
removed. Then the subject and object, Pure Consciousness 
and the perceiving consciousness become one. There remains 
only the Supreme Brahman without a second. “As light and 
illumination are identical, so also are the knower, known 
and knowledge. Self-Knowledge has three aspects, the 
knower; an acme of purity; known – the enveloping space, 
and knowledge – the divine light.”(Uma Sahasram, Chap. 
37, Verses 3 and 11). 

This experience, utterly indescribable in words, is known 
only to him who has attained it and thus is borne out by what 
Bhagavan says in Ramana Gītā, “The difference between the 
seer and seen is only in mind. For those, abiding in the Heart, 
the perception is unitary, one.” (Chapter V, Verse 19).

Sankara also affirms, “How can there be difference in 
the unitary Reality which is devoid of the distinctions of 
Seer, seeing and seen, which is unchanging, unembodied and 
qualityless?” (Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, Verse 401).

Paraphrase: 

When in the Arani of jīvātmā the  (lower) arani of 
antaḥkaraṇa (mind) with the inward meditation of ‘I am 
Brahman’ (as the upper arani) is ceaselessly churned with

Commentary: 

The fruit of contemplation of the Self devoid of triputi 
is dwelt in here.

The fire that is used for ritualistic purposes was prepared 
in ancient days in a special way as the fire used for purposes of 
cooking was not considered good or fit enough. Arani refers 
to one of the two pieces of wood used  for the sacred fire 
created by friction caused by the churning one wood into the 
hollowed – out socket of the other. This is called ‘churning 
of the arani’.

This analogy is used for the ‘churning of the knowledge’. 
By constant inward churning by the upper arani of the 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   768 06-05-2011   10:54:15



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 769

meditation on the Self (I am Brahman), on the lower arani of 
the mind, the fire of knowledge is generated and with persistent 
perseverance rises to a mighty conflagration that burns up the 
fuel of ajñāna (two fold, non-perception and misperception) .

In Arunachala Ashtakam Bhagavan uses the same simile 
wherein he says, “When the impure mind is churned by the 
whet stone of the enquiring mind it shines with the light of 
Thy grace by shedding its vāsanās.”

The ‘fire of Knowledge’ that is enkindled by this inward 
churning is also called Ātmakāra Vritti  – thought mode of 
the nature of Ātman. This knowledge burns up ajñāna with 
its root and itself getting destroyed finally attains peace and 
quietude. What remains is simply the Ātman in all its glory.

Ordinary thought-modes are called vritti. This manovritti 
by the strength of contemplation of ‘I am Brahman’ becomes 
Ātmakāra Vritti which annihilate all vāsanās and finally 
destroys itself,  just as the remedial medicine taken after curing 
the disease itself disappears along with the disease.

Kaivalyopanishad also speaks of this inward churning: 
“Making the Ātman the (lower) Arani and OM the upper Arani, 
by the repeated friction of knowledge a wise man burns up 
the bond.” (Verse 11).

Gītā speaks of jñānagni, ‘the fire of knowledge’. 
“He whose karmas are burned up by the fire of jñāna” 
(Chap. IV, Verse 19).

It is interesting to note that while the original has 
dhyanamatanē (with meditation as the churning) Bhagavan 
has introduced a very significant word dhyana ahamatanam, 
adding aham considerable emphasis to the inward churning.

Vivekachūḍāmaṇi also echoes it: “By attaining to a state 
of yogāruda by firm knowledge of Brahman, let one raise 
one’s impure mind steeped in the ocean of saṃsāra by one’s 
pure mind.” (Verse 9), and, when burnt as everything turns 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   769 06-05-2011   10:54:15



770 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

into dust “all that is the object of sense-perception like the 
body, the organs, the breath, the mind, etc. burnt by the fire of 
jñāna becomes the Paramātman (attains Paramātmanhood).” 
(Verse 564)

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 771

Commentary: 
The knowledge that dawns by the constant and diligent 

practice of the spiritual discipline that destroys ajñāna and the 
experience of the Self that springs forth following is described.

Even as the dawn appears heralding the sun in the 
east before the sunrise, darkness is driven away. [In Hindu 
mythology the dawn is personified as Aruna (meaning 
crimson), the charioteer of the Sun God]. In its wake the 
sun emerges shining in all its radiance. In the same way the 
dawn of knowledge that destroys ignorance is followed by the 
revelation of Ātman, the Self that shines in its own splendour. 
All sādhana is to destroy the nescience which, veiling the 
Ātman, broadcasts its might.

Ātman is eternally present and ever realized. It need 
not be created anew. The best spiritual discipline to destroy 
nescience is the ātmakara vritti. Ātmakara vritti is the pure 
intellect with the reflected image of the Ātman. Like fire 
attracting the swarms of moths into the fire in which fall and 
perish, all mentations and vāsanās with their seeds, attracted 
by the flame of ātmakara vritti fall into it and are burnt up.

A parallel to this is found in Bhagavad Gītā: “But for 
those in whom this ignorance is destroyed by the knowledge 
of the Self, that knowledge, like the sun, reveals the Supreme.” 
(Chap. V, Verse 16)

This ātmakara vritti arises, as was mentioned in the 
earlier verse, by churning the ego of the lower arani and the 
higher Self with the mahamantra of “I am Brahman”. In the 
conflagration of this fire all thought forms and vāsanās with 
their seeds fall into it, as oblations. Just as fire in yagnas 
burns up all the libations offered into it and then eases itself 
into quiescence this vritti jñāna, burns up all mental modes 
and finally abides as silence. With the darkness of nescience 
dispelled, Ātman shines in full glory. This churning is often 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   771 06-05-2011   10:54:16



772 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

compared to the burning of camphor which burns itself 
completely, leaving no residue whatsoever. Such a mahātma, 
with actions and vāsanās burnt away like a fried seed never 
more falls into the transmigratory cycle.

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 773

Paraphrase: 
At all times the Ātman is an attained reality. Owing 

to ignorance It appears as if it is yet to be attained. On the 
destruction of ignorance the Ātman shines as if attained 
anew. This is just like one who, forgetting the ornament 
around one's neck, mistaking it to be lost, searching high 
and low and ultimately after the ornament being pointed 
by a friend who knew the cause of search,  realizes that 
the ornament is around one's own neck as ever yet feels 
as if it has been regained.
Commentary: 

That Ātman is ever present and eternally realised is a 
Vedic verity. ‘Why does It appear then, as if attained anew?’ 
is countered in this verse.

Ātman is perceived at all times by a knower of Brahman. 
He knows it, as Being, Awareness and Bliss, to be the basis 
of all perceptions. Even in the case of an ignorant person, the 
Ātman is the basis of all awareness, though it is not realised so 
by him. “We imagine that we would realize that Self sometime, 
whereas we are never anything but the Self.” (Talks, no. 609).

A new worldly object that one does not possess, and to 
has attained  after hard toil and fervent endeavour, is found 
to one's dismay that it does not abide permanently with one. 
Attainment of Ātman is unlike this. It is absurd to say that we, 
ever the form of Ātman, attain the Ātman. Thought in Reality 
we remain as the Self, mistaking the body and other things 
as the ‘Self’ out of ignorance, we get perplexed. Ajñānanēna 
āvrutam  - concealment is due to ignorance.

“Consciousness is the Self of which everyone is aware. 
No one is away from the Self. So each one is Self-realized. 
Yet what a mystery that no one knows this fundamental 
fact and desires to realise the Self? This ignorance is due to 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   773 06-05-2011   10:54:16



774 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

mistaking the body for the Self.... The truth is Realization 
is eternal and already there, here and now. Realization 
amounts to elimination of ignorance and nothing more or 
less.” (Talks no. 482). Further if it were nor present here 
and now, “How can It, newly got, be of any use? What is 
permanent must be eternally present, can it be newly got and 
be permanent also? ...Once veiled by ignorance and later 
revealed, Reality looks as if newly realised. But it is not new.” 
 (Talks no. 439)

When the ornament around the neck was thought to be 
lost, when searched for and when discovered to be around 
the neck itself, it was, during all the three phases of times, 
around the neck. The lament over what was not lost and the 
joy over what was apparently gained, both are delusions born 
of nescience.

Even while one is deluded into thinking that Ātman is 
not known, one remains as the Ātman. Remaining as the very 
Ātman, he pursues the enquiry of the Ātman. Remaining as the 
Ātman he enjoys thinking he has attained the Ātman. “The Self 
is always realised. The Realization is now obscured. When 
the veil is removed, the person feels happy at rediscovering 
the ever realised Self.” (Talks no. 490).

Paraphrase: 

Just as the stump or a post appears in darkness to 
be a thief, the Pure (indivisible) Brahman, owing to the 
delusion born of nescience, appears to be a jīva, a mere 
illusion. When the true nature of this imagined form

Commentary: 

So long as the two conscious entities, the jīva and the 
Lord, remain, even if the unreal world is not cognized, how 
can the Advaitic truth that ‘what is’ is one, be reconciled, is 
dealt with here.

Though just an imagination is responsible for the 
apprehension of a thief in the post, the real cause of delusion 
is darkness. Clarity of vision being obstructed by darkness 
(non-perception) one is mistaken for another (mis-perception) 
and the mistaken identity leads to confusion and fear.

When viewed in the light of a lamp, the truth of the post is 
known and the imagined delusion of the thief stands exposed 
and no more will one be assailed by the fear of a thief.

Never did a thief come and go but the delusion did.
In the same way, due to the delusion born of māyā, 

Brahman conjoined with the limiting adjuncts, the effects of 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   775 06-05-2011   10:54:16



776 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

māyā, appears as jīva. The jīva, having no existence of his own, 
cannot be away or apart from Brahman. Out of Brahman the 
jīva appears as an illusion, allows his own illusory appearance 
to conceal his real identity and considers himself as Brahman 
and suffers.

If the upādhis, the creations of māyā with which the jīva 
identifies himself with and deludes, are jettisoned there is no 
individual jīva and ‘what is’ is Brahman alone. The notion 
of individuality disappears and in its place the universal 
consciousness, Brahman alone, One without a second, shines.

A lamp was required for the post to be known as a post 
and not a thief. In the same way if the upādhis are subject to 
close scrutiny in the light of pure intellect, duly instructed by a 
satguru, they become meaningless and unsubstantial. Then with 
the illusory appearance of the jīva dissolving, the experience 
of ‘I am Brahman’ dawns. If jīva and para were two different 
vastus never can they mingle nor can there be an experience of 
unity. The non-difference between the two becomes a matter of 
experience only when the upādhis are shed.

Commentary: 

While the sense of ‘I’ in the body and the sense of 
possession of 'mine' related the body, are deep-rooted in the

Until ignorance of one’s real form persists, the sense 
of ‘I’ in the body and of ‘mine’ will prevail, accompanied 
consequently by the notion of the ‘otherness’ of Brahman 
as apart from oneself. When these upādhis that seemingly 
differentiate the jīva and the para, the individual and the 
Absolute, are removed, the oneness of the Truth behind both 
stands realized. This experience of the Self as one universal 
Reality ever the same, instantaneously destroys the nescience.

After knowing oneself as Brahman through experience, 
the sense of ‘I’ in the body and ‘mine’ in things related to it 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   777 06-05-2011   10:54:16



778 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

will not appear. Then no thought will surface, as the mind that 
thinks, has itself gone out of existence. The unreal upādhi, 
existenceless, disappears when the vastu tattva  – the nature 
of Reality – is known. The Truth – that which is – shines 
without concealment. In Tattva here Tat means That and tva 
means Thou. The annihilation of ‘I’ and ‘mine’ is the direct 
fruit of Brahma Vidya. The sense of ‘I’ is cancelled in the 
cognition of ‘I am Brahman’ like the idea of thief is cancelled 
and Brahman remains like the pillar. With the annihilation of 
‘I’, ‘mine’ cannot remain. Therefore a realized one is death 
to sense objects.

“When the sun has arisen, darkness and its baneful 
consequences are not seen. So too, when the nectar of non-
dual bliss is enjoyed, there is no bondage, nor even a trace of 
misery.” (Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, Verse 320)

dīk - bhramai – stands for confusion of directions. After 
dawn, the darkness of the night, and all the host of evils 
attending it like affliction of eye-sight, the danger from thieves 
and the straying away from proper road, are not experienced, 
so too, when the nectar of non-dual Brahman is experienced 
as the result of the inner realization of Brahman, there will be 
no identification of Ātman with anātman or bondage or even 
a trace of grief.

It is worthwhile noting here that while the original 
Sanskrit verse contains just the word jñānam, Bhagavan uses 
an epithet uttama, meaning exalted and thus glorifies such 
jñāna.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   779 06-05-2011   10:54:16



780 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

The usage of ‘I am the All’ spoken of as the perception 
gained from the direct realization of the Self is only by way 
of conventional usage. As 'what is' is but one, to speak of ‘all’ 
in aparoksha anubhuti is but a contradiction in terms. Yet it 
is accepted as a decorative usage.

The ‘Eye of jñāna’ or the ‘perception of jñāna’ means the 
‘Infinite Eye’ that remains as Eye with nothing to perceive as 
other than Itself and perceives only Itself. This is the Ātman 
which is both the perceiver and the perceived. An old saying 
of a siddhar proves this:

	 The Self is the Eye
	 The Self is the Seen
	 The Self is the dharma observed
	 The Self is the speechless Silence
	 The Self is the All
	 The Self is without All
The Infinite Eye is the gnoetic Eye or the Eye of jñāna.
As all the perceived objects are but the perceiver, the  Self, 

Ātman, is the One Infinite Eye. This perceptionless, Eye of 
wisdom, is the most sublime of all. The one possessed of this 
eye of wisdom will shine with the distinctionless perception 
of the entire world as the Self and he, the One Self, remains as 
the all. This alone is jñāna dhrishti (perception of jñāna) and 
not knowing what others think, clairaudience, clairvoyance, 
and knowing the past and future, says Bhagavan.

A verse from Ribhu Gītā emphasizes this: 
“The world and beings and others seen in Consciousness
Are not apart from Brahman, which is of the nature of 

Consciousness
I am not apart from that Brahman
Likewise Brahman is not apart from me.
By realizing the undivided, non-dual Supreme Knowledge
That all kinds of appearances are Brahman

Paraphrase:

whole and Full Content, the Ātman. Nothing, not even a

perceives the whole moving and unmoving cosmos as 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   781 06-05-2011   10:54:16



782 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

the Self. Are pots and jars, though of different names and 
shapes seen, other than the basic clay that they are made

Commentary: 

This verse explains how the world of multiplicity with the 
multifarious distinctions of names and forms can be perceived 
as the Ātman, the One.

Out of the mud are fashioned various kinds of pots and 
pans by the potter. They came out of mud, exist as mud and 
go back to the mud. The mud cannot be separated from the 
names and forms of pots. “It is not possible for anyone to show 
the form of pot apart from the clay. Hence the pot is imagined 
due to delusion. Clay alone is the abiding reality of the pot.” 
(Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, Verse 231)

Without mud all these different shapes and forms could 
not have come about. The mud has become the pots. There 
is no change in the fact that at all three times, before their 
creation, after their creation, and after they are broken, they 
have been the form of mud. Names and forms, given by the 
potter, are unreal; mud alone is real.

Likewise, the ever existent Ātman, unchanging and the 
same ever, is the only Reality. The world of names and forms 
that appears in it, is unreal and are mere forms of imagination. 
The  multiplicity is a projection upon one Eternal Infinite. If 
the forms of these appearances were real, it will be impossible 
to see them as the same One Ātman. But in the experience of 
Sages who have realized the Self, the unreal world disappears 
and the all-pervading ever-existent Ātman alone is cognized.

As there is not an atom apart from the Ātman, the 
Indivisible Ātman alone abides with nothing ‘other’. Like the 
wave seen in water is the same water from beginning to end, 
the world, the jīvas and all that is seen in creation are all but 
Ātman, the Consciousness. Therefore in the words of Sankara:

pure existence; there is nothing apart from It. If one says there

sleep.” (Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, Verse 232).

784 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Paraphrase: 
A jīvanmukta, a sage called a vidwan (a knower), 

who has well realized the Brahman, relinquishing all 
his previous upādhis of body, mind and intellect and 
the qualities like satva etc. that he had acquired through 
his earlier vāsanās (from previous lives) instantly gains 
his real nature, the form of Sat-Chit-Ananda even as 
the worm constantly stung by the wasp and thinking 
ceaselessly of the wasp attains the very form of wasp. 
Likewise you abide firmly as the Ātman.
Commentary: 

Verses from 49 to 52 describe the characteristics of a 
jīvanmukta.

“He is said to be a jīvanmukta whose prajñā is firmly 
established, whose bliss is continuous and to whom the world 
is a thing forgotten.” (Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, Verse 429). Śāstras 
say that as such a one abides as Brahman always – there does 
not arise the sense of ‘I’ in the body and its organs and the 
sense of ‘this’ in other things, both of which are traced to pūrva 
vāsanās (previous predilections) and even if traits of previous 
upādhis were to appear, they are merged in Brahman.

Yad bhāvam tad bhavati – as one thinks so one becomes. 
The prārabdha (of pain and pleasure) of every jīva does not 
come of its own accord but is purely what the jīva intensely 
thought of and sought for in previous births.

Jīva, in essential nature, is the very form of Sat and Chit. 
Enveloped by the might of the three gunas, the handwork of 
māyā, he regards himself as an ajñāni or an ignorant one. He 
becomes a saṃsārin, caught up in an inescapable bondage, 
when this thought, strengthened by memories of countless 
births, becomes difficult to be dislodged. The bhava “I am 
Brahman” has to be equally strong – and even more – to 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   784 06-05-2011   10:54:16



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 785

overcome and displace the “I am the body” sense successfully 
and herein lies the importance of the intensity of ceaseless 
sādhana. The jīvabhava gets destroyed by the sheer strength 
of the Brahmabhavana and one attains the form of Sat-Chit-
Ananda.

The wasp builds a mud nest with just a small hole as its 
outlet, and places a worm in it. Now and then stinging the 
worm, the wasp sits at the door constantly. The helpless worm, 
weary with fear and pain, constantly thinking of the wasp 
single-pointedly grows itself wings and totally metamorphoses 
into a wasp itself. Bhagavan has described this in detail 
from his personal observation. This analogy the importance 
underscores of sustained and intense nidhidhyasana with the 
stance of “I am Brahman” so as to displace the upādhi assumed 
and developed over countless number of births.

In this verse, a jīvanmukta is called a vidwan – one who 
knows, even though in common parlance, the word vidwan 
stands for a scholar in any discipline. But ‘knowledge’ in the 
real sense of the term, is only the Knowledge of the Self and 
only a jñāni can aptly be called a vidwan or scholar.

him up in the prison of the dehātma bhava and the ocean of 
māyā appears shoreless even as the shore of an ordinary ocean 
is beyond human perception.

At this stage his release from imprisonment is effected 
by the upadēsa and grace of the Satguru earned by virtue of 
the merit acquired over many births.

He, then releasing himself from the delusion of māyā 
by the strength of Ātma Vidya fortified with the practices of 
sravana, manana and nidhidhyasana, and with a mind clear 
and pellucid vanquishes the armies of the demons – passion 
and avarice –  that arise from within with formidable force. He 
rediscovers and regains shanti imprisoned so long and shines 
forever revelling in the bliss of Ātman – his essential nature.

Scholars are of the opinion that Sankara has fashioned 
this verse on Adyātma RamÅyaṇa – an allegorical version of 
RamÅyaṇa teaching the Ātma Vidya through symbolising the 
various characters of RamÅyaṇa. The yogī spoken of here 
Ātmaraman (in Sanskrit) -Yogī Anmāvil inbattil amaindoḷirvan 
(in Tamil), scholars say, refers to Rama.

The very word RamÅ means the one who revels in all 
bosoms. The Self (the jīva) Rama, wedded to Sita, to his own 
nature of peace – lives unperturbed with equanimity both in the 
Kingdom of Ayodhya and in forests of exile. Rama’s sorrows 
begin when Sita is abducted by the demons of moha. (Ravana 
is a ten headed demon, the ten heads represent the ten organs 
of action and perception). Just as Rama wallows in despair 
and the jīva (the Self that has become the jīva) suffers with 
shanti (peace) lost. Just like Hanuman, who finds the place of 
imprisonment of Sita, by his prowess, announces it to Rama, 
the Satguru, by his upadēsa reveals the place where Shanti 
resides hidden.

Thus Rama, the jīva fortified builds the bridge of sravana, 
manana and nidhidhyasana across the ocean of delusion and 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   787 06-05-2011   10:54:16



788 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

crossing over the nescience routs out the demoniacal armis 
of kama, kroda, etc, redeems Sita (Shanti) unites with her, 
reaches his real Home, Ayodhya (the Self) and revelling in 
the bliss of that Kingdom shines forever.

Once a devotee begged Bhagavan for the bestowal of 
peace of mind. Bhagavan, with a smile, replied, “Oho! Is that 
so? First find out what is meant by the mind. If you enquire 
thus, the mind will disappear. What is left is peace itself. Even 
the Vedas begin with Shanti (peace)...whenever the Vedas 
are recited, the words Shanti, Shanti, Sahnti will be repeated. 
But no one bothers to find out the meaning of those words. If 
they understand they would realise that what is begun with 
Shanti and what is concluded with Shanti must have Shanti 
in between also. The whole thing will be full of Shanti.” 
Whereupon when Venkataratnam mentioned that Sankara has 
said the same thing in Ātma Bhoda, where he has described 
jñāni as Ātmarama and Shanti as Sita, Bhagavan quoting this 
sloka said, “Yes, it is this sloka.”

Paraphrase: 
A jñāni devoid of desire for transient and ephemeral 

pleasures of sense objects ever satisfied with the bliss 
of the Ātman, shines within as his own Self by his own 
effulgence like a lamp in a bushel.
Commentary: 

A jīvanmukta has totally detached himself from all 
attachments, external and internal – his consciousness having 
been entirely withdrawn from the sense-objects, outside and 
from the identification with the body, mind and intellect.

The state of the joy of jñāna or the pure consciousness 
and the bliss of Pure Being, that a jñāni ever abides and revels 
in the state where there is nothing but the Self to illumine the 
Self, in the Self, is explained by a delightful analogy.	

When a lighted lamp rests on a surface, its glowing 
illumination illumines the various objects in the room. If it is 
placed in a pot, it can illumine only the inner space of the pot 
and will not be seen outside. Similarly when the consciousness 
is withdrawn from the upādhis and made to inhere in the Self, 
it illumines the Self within. He shines within the Self, as the 
Self and forever revels in that bliss of Awareness and the 
bliss is known only to himself. “This yati who enjoys bliss 
forever with his mind resting in Brahman only, unchanging 
and inactive is a stitaprajñā ( a man of steady wisdom) whose 
mind is firmly anchored in Brahman.” (Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, 
Verse 427).

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   789 06-05-2011   10:54:17



790 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

What Lord Krishna says can be compared with this. “O 
Partha, when a man completely casts off the desires of the 
mind, his Self, finding satisfaction in Itself, then he is called 
a man of steady wisdom.” (Gītā, Chap. II, Verse 55)

One ignorant of the bliss of Ātman searches for happiness 
from sense-objects, and finds the pleasures gained besides 
being meagre, is transient as well. Sense-pleasures, far from 
yielding the desired satisfaction create more craving like 
kindling the fire with ghee. In these there is neither satisfaction 
nor annulment of grief.

Of all the happiness that we think as happiness, derived 
from sense-objects, the highest is that of an emperor. This 
is the human happiness. Higher than this is that enjoyed by 
ghandarvas. Higher still, is that of the devas. Like this various 
increasing levels and grades of happiness are mentioned in 
scriptures end in the ananda of Brahma (the creator), but even 
that (the creator) equals just a drop in the ocean of the Bliss 
enjoyed by an ātmajñāni.

A jñāni who enjoys the bliss of the Ātman, in all the 
majesty of an ocean that is waveless, shines in his own light 
like a lamp on a windless place.

“To one who has known (realised) his Ātman and 
drinks the nectar of the bliss of Ātman, there is no other 
higher source of joy than silence, free from every desire.” 
(Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, Verse 528)

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   791 06-05-2011   10:54:17



792 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Though he continues to remain in the body, associated 
with the upādhis, like mind and sense-organs, he is merely 
a witness to their activities. He abides constantly in the 
Knowledge and its illumination and as such, the limitations 
or upādhis do their activities and do not touch him.

The sky, by nature of its all-pervasiveness and subtlety, 
though appears blue or grey due to the dust in the air, itself 
is not defiled by it. In the same way, a jīvanmukta may seem 
to be associated with upādhis and may seem to wander about 
as an ordinary man, he gets into that role and comes out of it 
unattached, like a lotus leaf in water.

“Although a jīvanmukta is associated with a body...he is 
only pure, like the ether which is always itself clear whether 
covered by dense clouds or cleared of clouds by currents of 
air. He always revels in the Self alone.” ... “All his actions 
should be taken to be only divine manifestation on the plane 
of humanity.” (Talks no. 449)

“The jñāni’s mind is like this moon (looking like a speck 
of cloud) before sunlight. It is there but not shining of itself.” 
“The moon shines by the reflected light of the Sun. When the 
sun has set, the moon is useful in revealing objects. When the 
sun has risen, no one needs the moon, although the pale disc 
is visible in the sky.” (Talks no. 460 and 98)

Unlike the ordinary ignorant men of the world, he does 
not identify himself with mind and other upādhis.

The fire of jñāna has burnt up his karma entirely and he 
dwells in the body that moves about as long as the momentum 
of prārabdha remains. It is a singular blessing and fortune 
that such a jñāni's contemporaries derive by virtue of their 
accumulated merits, earned in the past to have such a one in 
their midst.

That jñāni, moves about in the world in the body, is only 
from the perception of the onlookers. Just as the wind remains 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   792 06-05-2011   10:54:17



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 793

unaffected by the good or bad odours it carries, the jñāni is 
unaffected by the dharma of the upādhis. “As the all-pervading 
ether is not tainted by reason of its subtlety, even so the Self 
that is present in everybody does not suffer any taint.” (Gītā, 
Chap. XIII, Verse 32)

Neither the changes of the physical body, nor the pleasures 
and pains of the mind affect him. Praise or slander leaves him 
unaffected, like the sky that remains the same whether the 
sun rises or a vast collection of clouds appears. Though he is 
omniscient, he will appear like an ignorant fool.

“The wise man always enjoying bliss goes sometimes 
like a fool, sometimes as one learned, sometimes with royal 
magnificence, sometimes as mad, sometimes auspicious, 
sometimes unmoving like a python, sometimes evoking 
respect, sometimes derided and sometimes unknown to 
anybody.” (Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, Verse 543).

794 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

upÅdi-yil vi„hœu vinu¿¿É in the upādhiless ‘Vishnu’ 
(the all-pervading Brahman)

abÉdamÉ uŸuvÅn tÉr vÅi nondually, and without a

this.

Paraphrase: 
Know that a jñāni, on the destruction of upādhis – 

gross and subtle – (which appear to belong to him during 
his lifetime in the perception of others), acquired through 
prārabdha, merges non-dually and without a difference 
in the upādhiless all-pervading Brahman, like water in 
water, ether in the immaculate ether, and fire in fire.
Commentary: 

The state of a jīvanmukta on disembodiment is spoken 
of here. With the realization of the Self, the causal body 
(nescience) perishes. Gross and subtle bodies remain till 
prārabdha lasts after the expiry of which, they also fall off. 
Scriptures say that the appearance of a jñāni, who appeared to 
remain with these two bodies, while embodied also disappears 
and he becomes a videhamukta (a mukta unembodied).

When the momentum of prārabdha is exhausted, gross 
and subtle bodies merge with their cause, namely, the five 
great elements. When the upādhis, that separated the jīva 
from the Self and revealed the jīva and para as two distinct 
entities get dissolved, that jñāni merges without distinction in 
the upādhiless Brahman, for what appeared as jīva and para 
are but the one form of Consciousness.

‘Vishnu’ mentioned in the verse refers to the form of space 
that is all-pervading. 

When the pure water taken from Holy Ganges is poured 
back into Ganges, both mingle as one without any distinction 
or when a pot submerged in water is broken, the water inside 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   794 06-05-2011   10:54:17



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 795

the pot becomes one with the water outside. When an empty 
pot is broken, the space inside the pot merges in the all-
pervading space. When fire is merged with fire, both become 
one. (Another explanation is sometimes offered: when a light 
is extinguished, the flame merges in the great fire which is one 
of the five great elements of the material universe; or when a 
lamp is extinguished in the daytime, the light merges in the 
all-pervading light of the sun).

In all these three illustrations, each mingles with that of 
its own commingle with each other. Otherwise, if they are not 
of the same kind, they cannot be merged. The Consciousness 
of the jīva and para is the same. The upādhis that are not of 
their kind, move away.

There are two Vedantic schools of thought. While one 
accepts liberation in embodiment is supreme and a mukta, 
though in a body, is unaffected by the actions of the upādhis, 
the other school believes the jīvanmukta retains a trace of 
ignorance due to association with the body and that complete 
absorption in Brahman occurs only when he becomes free 
from the body.

“Mukti is synonymous with the Self. Jīvanmukti and 
videhamukti are all for the ignorant. The jñāni is not conscious 
of mukti or bandha...There is only mukti and nothing else.” 
(Talks no. 266) and again “Jīvanmukti and videhamukti are 
differently described by different authorities; videhamukti is 
sometimes said to occur even when the man is seen with the 
body. The fact is that mukti is another name for Aham (‘I’)” 
(Talks no. 256)

Therefore, truly speaking to say that the Self once 
separated as jīva now merged as one, cannot carry much 
conviction for never were they separated. Appearing to have 
separated is a mere illusion. When that delusion is destroyed, 
it appears as if merging anew.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   795 06-05-2011   10:54:17



796 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Distinctionless union with Ātman alone is mukti and the 
three illustrations are used in this verse only, prove that living 
near Siva or Vishnu in Kailasa or Vaikunta is not mukti.

A comparison of this verse with the following verse from 
Vivekachūḍāmaṇi will be fruitful.  

“The muni who is a knower of Brahman attains oneness 
with Ātman, as milk poured into milk, oil into oil and water 
into water becomes identical with milk, oil, and water, 
respectively.” (Verse 567)

“As when the pot is broken, the space in it becomes one 
with the outerspace, so too, the Brahmavit becomes Brahman 
when the upādhi vanishes.” (Verse 566).

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 797

Paraphrase: 
That pure Vastu, the attainment of which leaves 

nothing more to be attained, beyond the blessed bliss 
of which there is no bliss aught else, and beyond the 
knowledge of which there is naught else higher, know 
that to be Brahman and realize it.
Commentary: 

The following three verses extoll the glory of Brahman, 
explain its nature or Svarūpa and the bliss of Svarūpa. 
Here Brahman is described not by affirmation, as It defies 
description but by a process of negation such as ‘That’ other 
than which nothing greater or higher exists.

We ourselves being the very form of bliss in essence – the 
Ātman – whatever be the nature of pleasures enjoyed, whatever 
be the amount of pleasures experienced, we suffer from a sense 
of incompleteness in us until we attain our real form.

In spite of possession of endless variety of objects of 
pleasures and comfort, there still remains an infinite range of 
articles to be attained and enjoyed. Satisfaction ever eludes and 
whether he be the sole emperor, or a rich millionaire being no 
exception to this and this is mainly due to the imperfection and 
inadequacy in the pleasures gained. The imperfection belongs 
to the individuality. For a jñāni, who has attained the bliss of 
Ātman, there is nothing more to be gained, for Ātman is the 
farthest boundary of all  the glorious and the sublime that are 
attainable. Having enjoyed the Bliss of the Self, none will 
strive for a greater bliss. The knowledge of the Self is greatest 
gain for It is the Supreme purifier and the greatest secret of 
all the Vedas and Gods.

A jñāni need not go in search of sukha or pleasure. Ātman 
is the very form of joy and comfort, being higher than all the 
celestial and worldly happiness.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   797 06-05-2011   10:54:17



798 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

A jñāni with the knowledge of the Self, will have no more 
thirst to know anything more.

Despite the rapid advances made in the field of scientific 
research, there is still so much to be known and there is no 
end to research in this field. But a jñāni who has experienced 
the true knowledge stands and shines majestically at the very 
frontiers of all knowledge to be known.
	 Brahman is that beyond which there can be no greater 
gain. 
	 Brahman is that, beyond the sukha of which there be no 
greater pleasure.
	 Brahman is that beyond the Knowledge of there can be no 
higher knowledge and all the three rolled into one is Brahman.

“This is his highest goal, this is his highest success, this 
is the highest bliss. Altogether world creatures live on a small 
fraction of that bliss.” (Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, 4-3-32)

Lord Krishna speaks of such a jñāni as one who, 
“on gaining That thinks there is no greater gain beyond.” 
(Chap. VI, Verse 22)

Commentary: 

This verse dwells on the truth, that for a knower of

The jñāni who has known his real form and has become 
the Eternal Being, the Subject, there is no longer any other 
object than It for Itself to illumine. His mind, intellect and 
all indriyas have become the very form of Brahman. Other 
than the Subject there is nothing else. The world that is the 
effect has become the cause Brahman and he himself remains 
Brahman. As such there is nothing whatsoever for him to look 
at with wonder, either to hear, or to think likewise.

The various celestial and heavenly worlds obtainable as 
a result of merits earned, are all as transitory as the world of 
human beings. After the exhaustion of merit, a return to this 
world is inevitable.

800 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

But a knower of Brahman becomes Brahman and having 
rent asunder the bondage of continuous births, becomes 
immortal and shines eternally.

Knowledge to be gleaned from books, practices to be 
observed or enquires to be engaged in, all become meaningless 
for a jñāni who has known the Self. However great knowledge 
or scholarship may be, before Ātmajñāna it pales into 
insignificance, like the moon seen during daylight.

Where one sees none other hears none other, knows none 
other, attaining which state one does not come back to earth, 
that form of Awareness is Brahman. The Lord affirms, “It 
is My Supreme Abode and they who reach it never return.” 
(Gītā, Chap. XV, Verse 6)

“His body, constituted  of avidya, having been burnt  by 
the realization of the ever existing sole, Ātman, he becomes 
Brahman here and now. Whence will there be birth for him 
again?” (Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, Verse 569)

Sage Uddhalaka questions his son Svetakethu: “Have 
you ever asked for that instruction by which we hear what is 
unheard, by which we perceive what is not perceived, by which 
we know what is unknown?” (Chandogya Upanishad, 6-1-3)

Paraphrase:

Commentary: 

There is no expression or indicator available so that

inferred as the basis of this perceptible world.

This phenomenal world is characterised by five main 
aspects, namely, Sat, Chit, Ananda, name and form. If the 
source which the world sprang from, is sustained in, and 
finally resolves into, is enquired and known the substratum, 
Brahman will be known.

Bhrigu was instructed by his father Varuna on Brahm,an at 
his request: “That  from which all these beings are born, That 
by which they subsist after birth, That to which they proceed 
and into which they merge – crave to know That well. That 
is Brahman.” (Taittiriya Upanishad, 3-1 to 6)

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   801 06-05-2011   10:54:17



802 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

When the real Form of Brahman is known, it will be 
realised that Sat, Chit and Ananda is its characteristic trait.

Names and forms are the exclusive characteristics of the 
constantly changing world and its activities. In the absence 
of names and forms there can be no activities. Whenever 
something is enquired into, if the name and form of what 
is enquired into is unknown, the enquiry becomes fruitless. 
The world is but a synonym for names and forms. Even 
though these names and forms keep continually changing, the 
world forever in some form continues to appear and provide 
happiness.

The appearance, the joy and the ‘being’ of perception, 
continue to exist in every perception of ours though names 
and forms change. These three bear no relation to the names 
and forms but are related to the light that is the basis for the 
perception by which alone they are seen.

When these three are seen as the world, It appears as 
the ‘being’, appearance and the joy of perception. When the 
world’s appearance disappears in the experience of the Self, 
jñāna, they are realised as the characteristic of Brahman.

All sense-happiness is this bliss in different garbs veiled 
by names and forms. The essence of everything, that by which 
the whole universe is constituted, is this Bliss. These names 
and forms, subject to change, cannot cover the Infinite; but 
the names and forms exist because of ‘That’.

That which pervades and fills all the divisions that the 
dimensions of the whole world may be segmented into as 
top, down, above, below and cross as Sat, Chit, Ananda 
imperishable, the Eternal, Endless and shines in its own 
effulgence, is Brahman. When there is nothing other than 
this One homogeneous mass of Consciousness who can say 
up or down, etc. Mundaka Upanishad says the very same 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   802 06-05-2011   10:54:17



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 803

thing, “The Immortal Brahman is before, that Brahman is 
behind, that Brahman is to the right and left, It has gone forth 
below and above. Brahman alone is all this. It is Supreme.” 
(2-2-11).  Sankara packs the content of this verse into a verse in 
a celebrated hymn called Dasa sloki. “ I am neither above nor 
below, neither inside nor outside, neither middle nor across, 
neither the east nor the west; for I am indivisible and one by 
nature and all-pervading like space. Therefore I am that One, 
Pure and Auspicious, that alone remains.” (Sivah Kēvaloham).

The infinite nature of Brahman is made clear: “That 
(invisible Brahman) is full, this (visible Brahman) is full. 
This full (visible Brahman) proceeds from that full (invisible 
Brahman). On grasping the fullness of this full (visible 
Brahman) there is left that full (invisible Brahman).” 
(Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, V-1-1).

Paraphrase: 
Realize with a clear intellect that Content to be 

Brahman which remains as One, forever Indestructible, 
unbroken Bliss and which the Vedānta, namely, the 
Upanishads, indicate and explain as ‘not this – not this’ 
by a process of elimination thus negating the world of 
names and forms, the body and the senses, etc.
Commentary: 

Brahman, being beyond the reach of speech and mind, 
cannot be explained by any trait or characteristics but can 
be known only through direct experience. That is why even 
Vedas, that are divine revelations and not of human origin, 
resort to the process of negating the perceived world to explain 
It in a subtle and indirect way, that is, by way of ‘neti-neti’ 
(not this-not this).

None of the bodies, gross, subtle and causal, is that 
Content. Neither the jīva, who fondly considers the body as 
‘I’ nor the world of plurality and its objects which he claims 
as his is that Content. That which remains as the irreducible 
substratum of everything after the negation of all tangible 
objects which is Eternal, Imperishable and the Spring of 
unbroken Bliss,  is to be known as Brahman, with the help of 
a sharp intellect.

The considered verdict of the Vedas is that Brahman is 
not knowable through mind or indriyas. 

The content of certain words in normal usage is commonly 
known to all.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   804 06-05-2011   10:54:17



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 805

Everyone knows that honey, sugar and jaggery are 
sweet in nature and does not require a special explanation. 
Yet the flavour of sweetness in one is different from that in 
the other. If we were to describe it in words nothing beyond 
their tasting sweet can be said by way of further description. 
The experience of tasting it alone can reveal the difference 
among them. What is explained through words is literal 
meaning (vachyārittam) and the intended meaning is called 
lakshyarttam. The intended meaning can be comprehended 
only by experience. Intellectual comprehension of Brahman 
as Sat-Chit-Ananda through the upanishadic teaching is the 
former while knowing it as such through direct non-mediated 
experience is the latter.

Thus the Upanishads which negated all perceptible 
objects as not Brahman, attempt to explain that which is 
beyond the ken of mind and speech by its real characteristics.

Brahman, ever without change, is not the changeful world. 
In the words yādondru – lends itself to be interpreted in two 
ways, ‘That which’ or that which is ‘One’.

The One Brahman is not the manifold world. Brahman, 
the very form of unbroken Bliss, is not the worldly happiness. 
After negating all that is perceived and thought of, that 
unsublatable Content which remains as the One without a 
second, form of unbroken Bliss, should be known as Brahman.

The process of ‘neti-neti’ is explained by saint Vidyaranya 
in Panchdasi as follows. “An object which the senses can 
perceive, can be said to be ‘like this’; an object which is 
beyond the range of sense perception is said to be ‘like that’. 
That which is the subject cannot be an object of the senses. 
But as it is the very Self of everyone, it cannot be said to 
be beyond the ken of perception. In every perception Its 
presence is felt; centred in it, but without it being made an 
object, all perceptions take place. As It is felt directly, It must 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   805 06-05-2011   10:54:17



806 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

be Self-revealing. So It is not void. This Existence cannot be 
negated for if It perishes who will be the witness to the act 
of perishing? When all perishable things are destroyed what 
remains is the Self.

The Consciousness which witnesses the absence of names 
and forms still remains and that is Brahman.

In ‘neti-neti’, the first neti negates māyā, the second all 
its effects, the gross and subtle creation including time, space. 
When the entire world referred to as “ ‘this’ can be negated, 
the thing which is not ‘this’ can never be negated and this 
indestructible witness is the Self. Thus Sruti or Veda negates 
all objects (Having names and forms) but keeps the ‘that’ (i.e. 
Ātman) intact.” (Panchadasi, Chap. III, Verse 31-34).

Paraphrase: 
All the Gods like Brahma, Indra and the devas, 

attaining an infinitesimal part of the unbroken Bliss 
of Ātman according to their level and standing, obtain

Commentary: 

The Supreme glory and magnificence of Brahman, filled 
with torrents of the immortal nectar, which cannot be described 
in words, nor even thought of by mind, is hailed and extolled 
in all grandeur here. The sense of happiness obtained on the 
attainment of a desired object varies in grade and quality.

Ananda Valli of Taitiriya Upanishad gives a calculus of 
joy starting from human joy and ending in the joy of Brahma 
(the Creator). The happiness of an emperor ruling over the 
entire earth, in the prime of his youth, possessed of the might 
of mind, and the prowess of physique is taken as the basic, unit 
of human happiness. The happiness of others of the world is 
not taken into account at all it being infinitesimal. Based on this 
unit, the happiness enjoyed by the denizens of higher worlds 
(higher levels of consciousness) is measured. The Upanishad 
mentions ten higher levels consciousness: ghandarvas, 
celestials, pitris and so on ending in Brahma (the Creator) 
and says that in each succeeding level of consciousness, the 
joy is hundred times that of the preceding one. Thus the joy 
of Brahma is the human joy of the world emperor multiplied 
by the number one followed by 20 zeros, which is difficult to 
grasp by the mind.

If the human joy of one unit enjoyed by the world emperor 
is not possible to be experienced by any human being, who 
can speak of Brahma’s joy? And this joy of Brahma is stated 
to be an infinitesimal fraction of the Bliss that is Brahman. 
To compare Brahma’s happiness to a spray and the Bliss of 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   807 06-05-2011   10:54:18



808 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Brahman to all the oceans of the world put together may not 
reveal the Truth even partially.

The most exalted positions considered worthy of 
attainment are those of Indra and Brahma, and are attained by 
performing the severest of all penances; yet the joy of such 
attainments is but a spray from the ocean of Brahmananda. 
Thus a relative picture is drawn here to give us an idea of the 
vast magnitude of the infinitude, in terms of a finite yard-
stick as the quantum of happiness, in terms of the quality of 
subtlety, the Bliss of Brahman – being subtler than subtlety 
– falls beyond the scope of mental gauge.

Sankara has beautifully described this transcendental 
experience of Brahmananda thus: Having realised the oneness 
of Brahman and Ātman “the modifications of the intellect have 
completely ceased and their interaction with the objects has 
melted away. I neither know ‘this’ nor the ‘not this’. What 
is Bliss par excellence? Where is the limit of this Supreme 
Bliss? I do not know.” (Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, Verse 482) and 
in the next few verses “Like the hailstone dropping into the 
ocean disappears into it mind merged in a minute fraction 
of that ocean,....where has the universe gone?....I do not 
see anything here; I hear nothing; I do not know anything.” 
(Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, Verses 482 to 484)

If even the ananda of Brahma is a mere trifling, how can 
a seeker evince pleasure in the joys of the transient world?

Awareness, Ananda) gets reflected in the form of happiness 
we derive, when we come into contact with objects. We come 
to know by enquiry and realise that objects are not the origin 
of happiness but the pervasiveness of Brahman in them is the

As He is the illuminator of all actions and thoughts, 
whether within or without, all actions have, as their basis, 
the Ananda of the spirit of Consciousness – Brahman. The 
happiness that people derive in the world is because of the
