Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   809 06-05-2011   10:54:18



810 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

That is why It (Self) becomes dear to everybody. The love of 
the Self manifests Itself as love for near and dear ones.

Brihadaranyaka Upanishad states that “the Ātman in 
oneself is the dearest among all lovable objects and it is for 
this sake of Ātman that everything else is loved.” (1-4-8). All 
objects of love such as wife for her husband, son for the mother 
and father, wealth, animals, other persons, this world as well 
as the heavenly worlds, gods, scriptures, in short all objects 
and beings are dear to one, not for the sake of the object or 
beings but for the sake of one’s own Self only.

In the perceived world Ātman alone is the Awareness; all 
the rest are mere jada (insentient). Bliss or happiness is the 
form of Ātman. Ātman and Bliss are not two but just one. There 
is no inherent happiness in the objects of the world. The jīva, 
out of ignorance, assumes that it comes from the objects. The 
musk deer carries the fragrant musk within itself. Unaware 
of this and assuming that it emanates from a source outside 
itself, it wanders all over searching for it. Until the jīva knows 
that his own essential nature is matchless bliss he will, like 
the musk deer, be confused and misled.

“Happiness is the very nature of the Self; happiness and 
the Self are not different. We imagine through our ignorance 
that we derive happiness from objects... In fact when desires 
are fulfilled, it returns to its own place and enjoys the happiness 
that is the Self.” One walking in hot sun feels cool in the 
shade. “A wise man stays permanently in the shade. The 
mind of one who knows the truth does not leave Brahman.” 
(Who am I?, question no. 24).
	 Swami Vidyaranya explains how the Consciousness, the 
Self of the very nature of Supreme Bliss goes unfelt in the 
empirical world. The Self is the object of greatest love and 
love for the Self is seen in every man who wishes, “May I 
never cease to be; May I exist forever.” If the Supreme bliss 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   810 06-05-2011   10:54:18



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 811

of the Self is not known, there cannot be the highest love for 
it. (But it is there). If it is known, there cannot be attraction 
for worldly objects (That too is there). So we say this blissful 
nature of the Self thought revealed, is not strictly revealed. So 
love of both the Self and the objects is found. A father may 
distinguish the voice of his son chanting (the Vedas) in chorus 
with a number of pupils but may fail to note his peculiarities 
due  to an obstruction of his voice having been mingled 
with other voices. Similar is the case with Bliss. Because of 
obstruction, it is known but unknown. The obstruction here 
is due to other loves rooted ignorance – the one cause of all 
contradictory experiences, namely, Avidya.

The reason for the love  of the anātman, the body, is its 
association with Ātman which is its Essence and the pervader.

Though butter permeates milk through and through, 
it cannot be seen directly as such in the milk. As butter is 
extracted from the milk by churning, so Brahman can be 
separated from the world of names and forms through the 
churning of intense meditation. And when Brahman is thus 
obtained, the world of plurality is no more perceived as no 
more milk is left in the butter.

Paraphrase: 
Observe keenly and realize That to be Brahman 

which is without birth, destruction, form, attribute, caste, 
name and which is neither gross nor subtle; nor long nor 
short.
Commentary: 

The all-pervasive nature of Brahman, spoken of in the 
earlier verse, is further elaborated here. All the finite objects 
conditioned by factors of time and space are either gross or 
subtle. All the gross objects of the perceptible world, when 
viewed by the physical eye, appear long or short; or flat or 
circular and in diverse other shapes. Senses cognise subtle 
qualities that are imperceptible to eyes, like taste, sound and 
smell. Thoughts, even more subtle in nature and ungraspable 
by senses,  are all known by the mind. Thus the power of 
awareness decides the grade of subtlety.

None of these perceivable gross objects, nor the subtle 
objects known by senses, nor the subtler thoughts known 
by the mind, nor objects measurable with name, attributes, 
colours and birth and death is the Ātman. That which is 
devoid of all these, that which remains as only 'Being' is 
the Ātman. Sage Yagnavalkya instructs Gargi: “O Gargi, 
the knowers of Brahman say this Immutable Brahman is 
That. It is neither gross, nor minute neither short nor long, 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   812 06-05-2011   10:54:18



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 813

neither red nor moist, neither shadow nor darkness, neither 
air not ether, neither savour nor odour; unattached without 
eyes or ears, without the vocal organ or the mind, without 
vital force or mouth, without measure, without exterior or 
interior. It does not eat anything nor is It eaten by anything.” 
(Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, 3-8-8)

Ātman is the timeless Eternity and the spaceless Infinity 
and hence cannot be confined to space-time causation but 
can only be defined in negative terms  such as ‘neither gross’ 
‘nor subtle’. 

That which is irreducible  after all the aforesaid qualities 
have been negated by the process of ‘neti-neti’ is Brahman. 
The process of negation provides many pointers, though not 
positive, indicating the Truth. The one who negates is the 
Self, the Master.

Paraphrase: 
That Content by the ‘light of being’ of which fire and

Commentary: 

The Svarūpa or nature of Brahman is further explained 
here. 

The cognition of any object in the phenomenal world is 
accomplished by organs of perception. Physical perception 
of objects needs, besides the eye, the organ of perception, a 
light to illumine the objects to be perceived, for the eye by 
itself can perceive nothing in darkness. The sources of light 
are either the sun or the moon or a lamp.

Sun, Moon and other illuminators are not  self-luminous 
and therefore cannot reveal even themselves. The same light 
of awareness that illumines the organs of perception in us 
illumines them as well. Hence the verse says, “by which light 
the Sun and others shine?”

While they themselves require the light of the Self to 
illumine them how can they illumine the Ātman, the Provider 
of light to them?

All lights, including the greatest and most powerful light, 
the sun, shine because they are illumined by this Light of all 
lights which is Pure Consciousness, the Supreme Brahman. 
Kathopanishad says, “There, the Sun does not shine, neither 
the moon, nor the stars, nor do the flashes of lightning. How 
can this fire shine there? He shining, all these lights shine 
and through His lustre which is Consciousness, all these are 
variously illumined.” (11-2-15)

Without the light of Ātman which alone illumines the 
world and the objects, neither the world nor the objects will 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   814 06-05-2011   10:54:18



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 815

appear. None can cognise an unillumined world. Ātman alone, 
pervades the whole world and by Its power of māyā appears 
as the world of plurality with diverse names and forms.

There is no world apart from the body. There is no body 
apart from the mind. Mind is not apart from the Chit, the 
form of awareness. Chit is not apart from Sat, ‘that which 
is’. “That by which the whole world shines, know that to be 
Brahman” is the instruction here. That which illumines and 
makes everything known is Itself not known by anything that 
is illumined by It, is Brahman.

While physical lights such as sun have rising and setting, 
the Light of all lights shines eternally.

The ordinary light cannot illumine darkness for darkness 
vanishes with the flooding of light. But this Light of all lights, 
illumines in addition to light, darkness as well. Though 
knowledge is said to destroy ignorance, Consciousness 
illumines both ‘knowledge’ and ‘ignorance’; yet remains 
unchanged as it is the Knowledge of knowledge and ignorance. 
It is the knowledge which makes it possible for one to say 
‘I know’ and it is ignorance which makes one to say ‘I do 
not know’. In both statements ‘I’ know that ‘I know’ and ‘I 
know that’ ‘I do not know’, the ‘I’ illumines the functions 
of the intellect, in the form of knowing and not knowing 
i.e. knowledge and ignorance. This ‘I’ is the pure light of 
awareness, the Light of all lights, the Self in us, that also lights 
up the Sun, moon, etc. It is worth recalling the 7th verse of 
Supplementary Verses to Ulladu Narpadu:

Paraphrase: 

Know that the Supreme Content, Brahman, permeating 
in, out and through the whole world, illumines all that 
is in the world and glows by Itself even as the fire in a 
ball of iron well heated in the fire with rising tongues of 
flames glows by itself like that very fire.
Commentary: 

That which is beyond expression and comprehension – the 
Svarūpa of Brahman – is variously explained from verses 54 
to this one. The all pervasive nature of Brahman, permeating 
through and through in and out of the world, is explained with 
an illustration that is easily comprehensible to all.

The sun and moon, illumine only those that come in direct 
contact with their luminous rays of light. In the same way 
will not Brahman also illumine only those associated with it? 
How can It illumine everything? This verse clears that doubt.

An iron-ball, in contact with fire long enough to become 
red-hot, glows red like the fire itself. Yet, the heat and glow 
are not the properties of the iron. They are the properties of 
fire, but imbibed by the iron ball due to long association with 
fire. Further, though fire appears in the form of a round ball, 
what appears so, is not the form of fire but that of the ball. Due 
to the association of fire with the iron ball, the fire appears to 
posses that form.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   817 06-05-2011   10:54:18



818 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Similarly the characteristics like the ‘Being’, ‘Awareness’ 
and Ananda that the world appears with, are not of the world 
but of the Ātman that shines pervading in and out of the world. 
The names and forms, likewise, are the essential nature of the 
world and not of Ātman.

Burning is the intrinsic property of and natural to fire and not 
of iron. Yet when contact with a red hot iron happens, we say “this 
iron has burnt my hand”. Thus, the heat of fire is superimposed on 
the iron. So also, the light of the Self, that illumines everything, 
is superimposed on the sun and moon, which are spoken of as 
‘shining’. The light of the sun and moon is but the light of the 
Self, the Light of all lights. Thus Brahman is proved.

“As the sun is a mere witness of an action, as the fire 
makes for the burning quality of iron, as the rope is associated 
with the object (snake), superimposed on it, so too is what 
pertains to me who am the Chitātman in my inmost being.” 
(Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, Verse 507).

Paraphrase: 

Brahman is distinct from or other than the Universe. 
Nothing, not even an atom, exists that is not Brahman. 
(The Universe has no existence except that of Brahman). 
Should anything other than Brahman appear to exist 
and shine, know that to be an illusion like the water in

Commentary: 

This verse summaries the conclusion of Advaitic Vedānta.
If Brahman remains always, everywhere and as all, the 

question: why should knowing It involve so much pains 
and trouble? Why then Brahman, then should not be known 
through the objects of the world, is reconciled here.

In the example provided in the previous verse it was stated 
that the iron ball is other than fire. Is then the Brahman other 
than the Universe which has an empirical existence?

Though the perceptible universe appears as other than that 
Brahman in reality it is not other than Brahman. If it appears 
so, it is an unreal appearance like a mirage in a desert.

It is true that Brahman pervades everywhere. Yet the world 
itself as such, is not Brahman. Pervading in and out of the 
world, remaining as the ‘other of it’ is the nature of Brahman. 
While the world is impermanent, and is subject to change, 
Brahman is eternal and changeless. The world is insentient 
matter; Brahman is the form of awareness. The world is the 
form of misery; Brahman indeed is the form of Ananda.

Therefore the world is not Brahman and by knowing the 
world Brahman cannot be known. When the world is said 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   819 06-05-2011   10:54:18



820 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

to be not other than Brahman what is meant is that there is 
nothing that is the ‘other’ of Brahman. The pure Awareness 
on which the world is said to be a superimposition is not 
available to our cognition as the world is. But space which 
is everywhere cannot be seen or touched. If one loses one's 
grossness and becomes subtle like ether one may touch it and 
even become part of it. So long as one lives in identification 
with the matter envelopments, Brahman which permeates 
and pervades everything in the world cannot be known. This 
identification, however faint, creates a  mountainous block 
of a mind, riddled with its unavoidable sense of ego which 
conceals the Ātman. 

In fact each fact of experience implies a double 
consciousness, namely, the real and the unreal. Real 
consciousness is that one which is never absent. Unreal 
consciousness is that of which the awareness is impermanent. 
The consciousness of existence is real, while the consciousness 
of names and forms is unreal; in other words, the awareness 
of ‘I am’, is the substratum and the real awareness.

What appears as the manifold universe to the ignorant, 
is realised by the illumined to be the indivisible and non-dual 
Brahman. It is ignorance that sees multiplicity in place of 
Brahman. But this superimposition of multiplicity does not 
defile Brahman.

The common question while Brahman is not seen 
the world is seen is explained with the illustration of the 
appearance of mirage in a desert. In the case of the mirage 
and desert, the desert alone exists and without the desert, 
the appearance of mirage cannot exist. Therefore the unreal 
appearance of mirage, as if real, corresponds to the unreal 
world appearing real. Just as the water of mirage cannot wet 
even a grain of desert sand, the world of plurality is not real 
and Brahman is undefiled by its appearance.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   820 06-05-2011   10:54:18

But then the ignorance, through which Brahman appears

Ignorance,which is ultimately destroyed by knowledge, has 
no absolute existence.

The reality of the universe is not negated because the 
universe as Brahman cannot be negated. What is aimed at 
is the destruction of illusion which projects the universe of 
names and forms and makes it appear as other than Brahman.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   823 06-05-2011   10:54:18



824 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

as the resplendent sun that illumines all perception is not

Commentary: 

Why Brahman, instead of appearing as Sat – Chit – 
Ananda, appears as the world and why not all can know 
Brahman that shines pervading everywhere as the very form 
of effulgence, are answered here.

The truth is that the Supreme Content is everywhere, 
always and as all, and as nearer than the nearest and yet 
not everyone perceives It. The truth gleaned is that just the 
proximity to anything will not suffice to acquire a knowledge 
of it but the faculty of perception must be sharp and subtle 
enough to grasp the Truth.

“He is apprehended neither by the eye nor by speech nor 
by the other senses, neither through penance nor through good 
works. When a man's nature has become purified by the serene 
light of knowledge, then he sees Him meditating on Him as 
without parts.” (Mundaka Upanishad, 3-1-8)

Even as a blind man cannot perceive even the object 
nearest to him, we immersed in the darkness of nescience, are 
not able to perceive Brahman that shines as ‘the resplendent 
sun of jñāna’. The sun shines ever bright and brilliant. It is 
blindness of the person that makes the sun dark to him. Ātman 
is the ever present and ever attained Reality; but the limiting 
factors in the seekers of Truth veil and distort the effulgence 
of the Ātman, Brahman is not perceived by an ajñāni. “There 
is no time when the Lord remains unknown. If the light of 
the sun is invisible to the owl it is only the fault of that bird 
and not of the sun. Similarly can the unawareness by ignorant 
persons of the Self.” (Spiritual Instructions, Chap. II, Q. 7). 
“In the sunshine cotton does not burn; but if the cotton be 
placed under a lens it catches fire and is consumed by the 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   824 06-05-2011   10:54:18



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 825

rays of the Sun passing through the lens. So too, though the 
awareness of the Self is present at all times, it is not inimical 
to ignorance. If by meditation the subtle state of thought (the 
mind of sushupti must be brought on in jagrat) is won, then 
ignorance is destroyed. And Vivekachūḍāmaṇi also says the 
exceedingly subtle Supreme Self cannot be seen by the gross 
eye.” (Talks no. 624).

“Knowledge is enveloped by ignorance, thereby creatures 
are bewildered” (ajnanenÅ vrtam jnanam, tena muhyanti 
jantavah – Gītā, Chap. V, Verse 15).

As was pointed out earlier, the eyes in the absence of light 
that illumines, can see nothing. The eye, or the perception, 
now the form of ajñāna, can only perceive objects of the 
world and not the true Content, Brahman. In the same way a 
light is required to illumine the perception, the light of jñāna 
is indispensable to know Brahman. With this as the eye, the 
gnoetic eye only, can Brahman be known.

In Arunachala Ashtakam (verse 4) Bhagavan voices the 
same idea: “Those who look for Thee, who art Being and 
Consciousness, elsewhere and do not know Thee, they are 
indeed the blind who do not know the Sun.” The Ātman is 
the true Eye. That is the Eye of jñāna, for that is the perceiver 
and It itself is the perceived. One who knows not the Ātman, 
is one without the eye of True Perception. 	

The Eye of wisdom can be developed gradually by 
enquiring into the Self with the mind made pure by the 
observance of austerities, armed with sufficient discriminative 
power to reject the unreal from the real, and with the resultant 
light of knowledge, and with a single pointed devotion. Then 
the mere perception changes into a perception of jñāna and 
everything is seen as Brahman, Being and Consciousness.

Commentary: 

The gold mined, full of impurities,  is heated and smelted 
in fire and the molten gold, freed of dross shines in its innate 
purity and brilliance. In the same way the jīva when heated 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   826 06-05-2011   10:54:18



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 827

well in/subject to the fire of jñāna, kindled and set ablaze by 
the incessant practice of jñāna, consisting of sravana, manana 
and nidhidhyasana, becomes taintless with all the impurities 
of vāsanās, attachment, aversion, anger, etc. burnt away and 
shines as the Self in all resplendence. 

The process of smelting the gold is not to brighten it 
– for brilliance is its very nature – but only to remove the 
impurities that have settled on it. The impurities admixed 
with gold eclipse its natural brightness and, when removed 
allow the gold to shine in its natural glow. It is not a quality 
attained anew.

Likewise the impurities, the jīva is covered with, in the 
form of avarana (concealment) and vikshepa (distortion) 
and the consequent blemishes like vāsanās, attachments, etc. 
acquired from beginninless time, have veiled the Ātman, the 
form of Bliss, and have disguised It as the jīva.

In order to know the truth of his real nature, when the jīva, 
approaching a Satguru, carefully listens to the Upanishadic 
truths taught by him, meditates on their  meaning and practises 
nidhidhyasana, the jñāna within brightens and in that fire of 
jñāna all the impurities, are burnt away.

“The fire of the Knowledge of the oneness of Brahman 
and the jīva totally destroys the forest of avidya. To him who 
has attained the sense of this oneness what will be there of the 
seed of saṃsāra?” (Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, Verse 347)

This practice of sravana, etc. is called brahmābhyasa 
or atmābhyasa which is accompanied by sarva sankalpa 
sannyāsa, which is the giving up of all stimuli to every 
kind of action. Bhagavan once explained not only are there 
outward sravana, manana, etc there also inward sravana, 
manana, etc. “Antara sravana means the knowledge of that 
Ātman which is in the cave of the Heart always illuminated 
with the feeling ‘Aham-Aham’ (‘I’-‘I’) and to get that feeling 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   827 06-05-2011   10:54:19



828 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

to be in one's heart is manana and to remain in one's Self is 
nidhidhyasana.”

Then the jīva, like the burnished gold, with his impurities 
turned to aches, shines as the Self.

All sādhanas are only to remove blemishes of avarana 
and vikshepa, and other impurities acquired due to the above 
reasons and not to make the Ātman shine. The destruction of 
the impurities by these spiritual disciplines results instantly 
in by the spontaneous revelation of Ātman. “The fragrance 
of Agaru which has got hidden by long contact with water 
appears well only when that external odour is removed by 
rubbing.” (Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, Verse 274).

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 831

Commentary: 
This verse, the concluding one, encapsulates in a nutshell 

the essence of this text.
The Ātman, transcending space, time, constantly 

without duality, all-pervading, shines as the Self. It does 
not need a place or a time or purity. “The mahātman whose 
mental modifications have been rendered ineffective, 
does not depend on place, time, posture, direction, mental 
disciplines and objects of meditation. To that mahātman, 
what regulations can there be in the knowledge of himself?” 
(Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, Verse 530)

Many wonder whither the state of being the Self is 
possible at all in view of the insurmountable obstacle of 
demerits accumulated over many births. This verse addresses 
itself to this and answers this in full.

Scriptures prescribe pilgrimage to holy places and dips 
in holy waters to expiate the sins and earn merits and also 
mention the auspicious times for them, like the day or night 
of the occurrences of the eclipses, etc.

The places where the holy rivers turn back towards their 
sources (uttara vāhini) are extolled further. Holy Ganges, 
though worshipped throughout its course is held most 
auspicious at Prayag, spots where rivers turn northwards, 
towards their source, are considered holy.

Such change of course and flowing back towards their 
source, probably is a reminder to the jīvas to plunge inwards 
seeking the source. This at once recalls an incident wherein 
a youth from Andhra wanted to know the way to moksha, 
when Bhagavan with a smile stated: “Go the way you 
came.” The crestfallen young man, confused at this cryptic 
remark, was later comforted by devotees by explaining that 
he was privileged to get the upadēsa direct and that it meant 
to reach the source by the method of enquiry ‘Who am I?’ 
(Letters, 2nd Dec. 1945)

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   831 06-05-2011   10:54:19



832 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

All these holy rivers will not come to the place we reside; 
only we have to go seeking them. But there is one river most 
holy, readily available where we are without involving the 
difficulty of seeking the holy time, holy river, holy place or 
direction. It is the most holy Ātma tirtha, remaining in the 
very place where we are, within us, as the Self.

Further by the merits earned by bathing at such places 
one may go to heavenly spheres. But as the Lord points out 
in Gītā: “Having enjoyed the spacious world of heaven, they 
return to the world of mortals, when their merit is exhausted; 
thus they obtain the changeable (what is subject to birth and 
death).” (Chap. IX, Verse 21)

Yet one, who, immersed in the Self, drinks the elixir of 
the bliss of Ātman, gains the state of Brahmahood and never 
again ever goes through birth and death gaining immortality.

Holy waters situated in Himalayas are either very cold or 
the hotsprings  there too hot. But this tirtha of Ātman, is most 
soothing and induces one to get immersed in it.

The Mahābhārata describes Ātman as the real sacred river 
bathing in which the soul becomes free of impurities. “The 
river of Ātman is filled with the water of self-control; truth 
is its current, righteous conduct its banks and compassion its 
waves. O son of Pandu! Bathe in its sacred water; ordinary 
water does not purify the inmost soul.”

Unlike some holy rivers which having become impure, 
makes one hesitate to have a dip, Ātma tirtha cannot be tainted 
by any. Śāstraic injunctions lay down that holy dips should 
be accompanied by dana, observance of charity. But one who 
is immersed in Ātma tirtha has neither the Vedic duties like 
yagas or yagnas nor the empirical ones like pilgrimage to 
holy places. Such a one “inactive though acting; experiencing 
fruits of actions but not enjoying them; though embodied yet 
not afflicted by the body, he is everywhere, though localised.” 
(Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, Verse 545)

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   832 06-05-2011   10:54:19

Śrī Guru Stuti

Avathārikai: Origin
(Bestowed by Śrī Bhagavan)

Śrī Sankara, the world Teacher, travelling through 
the length and breadth of India triumphed in debates over 
leading exponents of alien schools of thought and came to 
the town of Mahishmathy in the North, where, on conquering 
an inhabitant of that town, Mandanamishra, the foremost 
advocate of karmakanda (Vedic ritualism) in debate, his wife 
challenged him that unless she be vanquished too, his victory 
would not be complete, engaged herself in debate with him 
only to be vanquished after which, she argued in kÅmaśÅstra 
(the śÅstra relating to conjugal intimacy). Sankara pleading 
for the permission of a month’s time, leaving his body to the 
care of his disciples in a cavern in a mountain and entering 
into the body of king Amaruka, who had departed just then 
was sporting and enjoying with the hundred queens of the late 
king when, anxious at the expiry of the period specified by the 
guru, some of his disciples donning the robes of wandering 
minstrels hailed him in his presence in the court, through this 
hymn.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   835 06-05-2011   10:54:19



836 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Paraphrase: 
That Form which, after all the gross forms and subtle 

bhavanas that are not the form of Ātman, are rejected as 
‘neti – neti’ (the Self, not this; not this) as per the Vedic 
injunction remains as that which can neither be rejected 
nor be accepted and which jñānis of indescribable glory, 
well learned and with erudition, realize in their hearts 
as their Self (Ātman) – that primeval cause, the blissful 
form of Awareness – that Sat-Chit-Ananda Brahman – 
art not thou That? (Thou Art That). (The Content of the 
mahavakya, Tat Tvam Asi is the refrain at the end of each 
verse in this hymn).
Commentary: 

When an enquiry as to ‘What exactly is the Ātman?’ is 
made within, objects of gross form and subtle bhavanas of 
thought appear. Ātman, being beyond speech and thought 
forms all these must be rejected as “this is not Ātman”. In so 
far as even the external objects are cognised only by the mind, 
they are also in truth internal or mental concepts. The aim of 
all paths of meditations, carried on through and by the mind 
is to transcend the mind. Bhagavan expalins this ‘neti – neti’ 
process. “There is now wrong identification of the Self with 
the body, senses, etc. You proceed to discard these, and this is 
neti. This can be done only by holding to the one which cannot 
be discarded. This is iti alone.” (Talks no. 366)

Consciousness is the illuminator of the mind and 
consciousness alone expresses itself as subject and object. 
When all the anātma vastu, asat, or transient and impermanent 
objects are discarded, the subject alone exists without an 
object. Finally the one who thinks “I am the one who reflects 
all these things” alone is left. This 'I', the real subject, Self as 
pure Awareness, can never become non-existent for who then 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   836 06-05-2011   10:54:19



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 837

will cognise the non-existence? He remains as witness and was 
viewing it all. He cannot be rejected or accepted. This Content 
of ‘I’ is the eternally present Ātman. Every object, gross or 
subtle – a mental concept – is a limitation superimposed on 
Pure Awareness. The process of ‘neti – neti’ eliminates all 
limitations. In ‘not this’, ‘this’ signifies everything that is 
comprehensible by the mind.

When a devotee asked how is the Self to be found by 
‘neti – neti’, Bhagavan explained “The Self is said to be 
the hearer, thinker, knower, etc. But that is not all; It is also 
described as the ear of the ear, mind of the mind, etc.; and by 
what means to know the knower?”.... “Not this – not this”. 
Yet the devotee complained that the Self is not pointed out. 
Bhagavan explained, “A man wants to know what he is. He 
sees animals and objects around him. He is told, ‘you are not 
a cow, not a horse, not a tree, not this, not that and so on’. If 
again the man asks saying ‘you have not said what I am’ the 
answer will be ‘It is not said you are not a man’, He  must 
find out for himself that he is a man. So you must find out for 
yourself what you are.” (Talks no. 620)

The Vedas are eloquent in neti – neti and then remain 
silent. Their silence is the real State. Silence denotes that the 
questioner is himself the Self to be found. In Svayamvara the 
maiden goes on saying ‘no’ to each one until she faces her 
choice and then she looks downwards and remains silent. “This 
is the meaning of the exposition of Silence. When the source 
of ‘I’ thought is reached, it vanishes and what remains over 
is the Self.” (Talks no. 130). In other words the false ‘I’ will 
disappear and the real ‘I’ will be realized. The former cannot 
exist apart from the other. He who has negated everything 
including his body and mind remains. ‘This’ (that remains) 
is not the intellect or mind or the ego. The result of this ‘neti 
– neti’ process of meditation is the attainment of being one's 
real form which is liberation.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   837 06-05-2011   10:54:19



838 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Jñānis of great glory who have seen the shore of the 
ocean of knowledge revel in the bliss of the Ātman, having 
realized It as their ‘Being’. The refrain each verse has at its 
end, namely, “You are that form of Ātman” is emphasized as 
if to wake up one to Reality from the slumber of nescience.

Paraphrase: 
That Form, that imperishable, eternally realized,

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   838 06-05-2011   10:54:19



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 839

realize in the hearts as the Self and revel in, by pounding 
well within with the pestle of reasoning spoken of in the 
scriptures and rejecting the husks of the five sheaths like 
the food sheath by investigating and enquiring with a 
sharp intellect even as the rice grain is obtained threshed 
dehusked and winnowed from the paddy – art not thou 
that Content?
Commentary: 

The Self that has created the body and the world by the 
mixing up of the five elements shines – residing in and out 
of the creation – pervading everywhere. Just as the rice grain 
is covered by the husk this Self is covered by the five kosas 
namely five sheaths of food, vital air, mind, vijñāna and 
ananda one after the other. Just as bangles, ear-rings, house, 
etc. known as ‘mine’ are all other than the knower, so too, 
the five sheaths etc. are known by the Self as my body, my 
pranan, my mind, my intellect and my knowledge and are not, 
therefore, the Self. Transcendence of the five kosas, the sheaths 
which cover the Ātman, is still another form of ‘neti – neti’ 
through which the whole world – including one’s own body, 
the subtle senses, the mind, the intellect and the ego, which 
are mistaken for the Self – is eliminated as not the real ‘I’.

Kosas are mere appearances and there is no reality in 
them. “They are sheaths and not the core which is interior to 
all these. That is Reality and consists in true ananda.” (Talks 
no. 619) If we look on the Self as the ego, we become the ego. 
If we look on the Self as the mind, we become the mind, and 
if as the body, we become the body. “It is the thought which 
builds up sheaths in so many ways. The shadow in water 
is found to be shaking. Can anyone stop the shaking of the 
shadow? If it should cease to shake, you would not notice the 
water, but only the light. Similarly take no notice of the ego 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   839 06-05-2011   10:54:19



840 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

and its activities but see only the light behind. The ego is the 
‘I’ thought. The true ‘I’ is the Self.” (Talks no. 146)

Therefore even as the grain is separated from the husk, 
using the strategies of logical reasoning with a sharp intellect 
guided by the spiritual wisdom contained in srutis (Vedas) 
and scriptures, each kosa must be separated and the Self that 
is ‘other’ than each of these kosas after rejecting all of them 
must be known. 

Experts in tattva jñāna, namely jñānis, seers or sadhus, 
perceive and realize the ever realized Ātman in their hearts 
and ceaselessly enjoy unchanging Bliss. This verse instructs 
‘thou art that’ which the Sats perceive in their hearts as the 
Content Beyond.

Paraphrase: 
That to which, the wise who are well versed in firm 

Knowledge stable and tether the wild horses of the unruly 
senses that gallop towards sense objects by whipping 
them with the scourge of discrimination, making them 
realize the defects in the experiences of sense objects 
and pull them inward with the rope of discrimination 
and enquiry – that Content Beyond which transcends all 
knowable objects – that Ātman, indeed, art thou, not?
Commentary: 

All forms perceived, all the sweet sounds heard, afford 
unbounded happiness at times and at others  plunge one to the 
depths of despair. The senses that identify themselves with 
these are comparable to horses that gallop on rugged paths.

Whipping the senses by the intellect is to repeatedly 
make them aware of the inherent defects of the objects of the 
phenomenal world.

While the wind runs faster than the horse, the restless 
mind led by the senses flies faster than wind thereby shaming 
it. The jñānis thwart and control the senses that gallop swift 
and fast towards sense objects, turn them inward and tether 
them firmly to the Self.

The universe appears to be split into a diversity of objects 
by names and forms. When these names and forms are whisked 
away, Brahman, Pure Being, alone abides.

Paraphrase: 
Thou art indeed that Ātman, that is subject to neither 

creation nor destruction, in which sages, the true knowers, 
get immersed in their hearts and which remains the 
support of the various revolving states of being like 
wakefulness, dream and sleep and the gross, subtle and 
causal bodies, but which abides as ‘other’ than all these, 
perceiving them all as the uninvolved witness like the 
thread that runs through the flowers in a garland is apart 
from them, despite being their support.
Commentary: 

That all-pervading Content Beyond appears finitized 
when limited by a measure and that measure is called an 
upādhi of the Ātman. Just as infinite space when constrained 
in a room or pot becomes room-space or pot-space, the True 
Content, which is all pervading, can be known clearly in 
gross, subtle and causal bodies. These three bodies become 
the upādhis of the Ātman. Though the nature or dharma of 
these upādhis keeps perpetually changing that which ever 
remains the same and unchanged as mere witness of all those 
upādhis and their changes is that Supreme Content – Ātman. 
One (the Self) is resting in the body and is different from the 
body – gross, subtle and causal.

In deep sleep, the intellect disappears completely and 
there is neither knowing nor not knowing of objects. It 
illumines the presence or absence of knowledge in waking 
and dream states and the absence of both in the deep sleep 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   843 06-05-2011   10:54:19



844 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

state. It always shines and there is no rising or setting for this 
Consciousness which is without an object. It is by virtue of 
remaining the witness of the three states and aware of the 
nature or dharma of the three bodies that, a change from one 
state to another is accompanied by the remembrance of the 
previous states; otherwise, the end of an avasta or state would 
mean end of the remembrance of that state and one cannot 
recall and speak of the experiences of the previous states. But 
it is common knowledge that everyone recalls one’s memories 
of childhood and the nature of the body and experiences – 
pleasure or pain – while speaking of them. Hence the Ātman 
is called the “Universal witness”.

The eternal consciousness can be compared to the 
white screen in the film show behind the moving shadows. 
When the show stops the shadows cease to exist but the 
screen still remains unchanged. When the knower, known 
and knowing have coalesced into one, what remains is the 
Self – the Witness.

“Talking of the witness should not lead to the idea that 
there is a witness and something else apart from him that he is 
witnessing. The ‘witness’ really means the light that illumines 
the seer, the seen and the process of seeing. Before, during 
and after the triads of seer, seen and seeing, the illumination 
exists. It alone exists always.” (Day by Day, 18-7-1946)

When the bubbles, foam and waves of this apparent 
external world of duality subside in the ocean of Consciousness, 
there remains nothing other to Consciousness and one is That.

Sages perceiving this Ātman in their hearts become 
merged with it non-dually. It is without an origin and an end. 
None can create or destroy it. “That Content art thou”, so does 
the verse remind us.

Bhagavan explains the same Content with a different 
simile in Ashtakam (Verse 5) wherein he says “Like the string

in a necklet of gems it is Thou in Thy unity who penetrates 
all the diversity of beings and religions.”

universe is in truth but the form of Chit (Awareness). That

Commentary: 

The ornaments of gold that shine sharing its glitter may be 
many and even varying in their size, form, weight, names and 
forms; but in truth they are all gold in essence. “Gold is not 
an ornament but the ornament is nothing but gold. Whatever 
shape the ornament may assume and however different the 
ornaments look, there is only one reality namely gold. So also 
with the bodies and the Self. The single reality is the Self.” 
(Talks no. 396)

When the Supreme Content that pervades everything 
and infills everything appears as the world and the 
jīvas, the forms may exhibit a variety of distinctions 
but the indweller in all of them is but one that is non-
differentiated. All Vedas proclaim this Sarvātmatva. 
Purusha Sooktam says: “Purusham eva idagum Sarvam”, 
Purusha is all this.

“yah sarvāni bhūtani antaro em adyesha ta ātma antaryam 
yamritha” (Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, 3.7.15). “Who resides 
in every being and by whom the beings become eternal.”

“Gods, human beings, animals, birds, trees, rivers, 
etc. These countless forms without distinction are the form 
of Vishnu. Knowing this, perceiving the entire universe 
as Vishnu – the very Self – is cosmic vision.” (Vishnu 
Puranam)

The insentient world has no ‘being’ apart from chit. 
The world that rises in the Self shines as such. As nothing

The all-pervading Brahman that shines in the sun also

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   849 06-05-2011   10:54:20



850 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

rare and exalted Vedas and which Content, the pure and 
meritorious Vedic scholars who have attained to greatness 
by performance of good dharmic (virtuous) acts, like 
religious gifts, exalted yagas, reciting (and making others 
recite) the rare Vedas and by worshipping (their Content) 
with great śraddhā in their hearts are greatly desirous of 
knowing.
Commentary: 

Śraddhā is the essential life force of sādhana. Only the 
one who has inordinate faith in the vedic verities and in the 
teachings of the guru can register spiritual progress. Bhagavan 
emphasizes the importance of śraddhā as follows: “With 
shraddha, the Self will become manifest. Śraddhā, Grace, 
Light, Spirit are all synonymous with the Self.” (Talks no. 381)

Bhagavan used to narrate a story to prove this as reported 
by Suri Nagamma in Letters (in Tamil dated 27-7-48) While 
a sparrow was flying over an ocean holding its egg in its beak 
the egg slipped from the beak and fell into the ocean. In order 
to retrieve the egg, the bird repeatedly dipped itself in the 
ocean, sucked water in its beak, came to the shore, released the 
water and fanned its wings in an attempt to empty the ocean. 
Narada, the celebrated celestial sage, saw this act of the little 
bird enquired and came to know the reason for. When the sage 
wondered at the impossibility of the accomplishment of the 
aim, the bird replied that whether possible or not, it would 
continue to persevere in its endeavour and that beyond a point 
it was in God's hands. Sage Narada struck with and pleased 
with the śraddhā of the bird went to Garuda (the mount of Lord 
Vishnu) and pleaded for help from him to one of its own tribe. 
Garuda then flew to the spot and flapped his wings and the 
waters of the ocean separated exposing the egg of the sparrow. 
Immediately the bird picked it up in its beak and flew away.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   850 06-05-2011   10:54:20



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 851

In the same way, if spiritual aspirants who follow the 
canons of conduct for sādhaks persevere in their noble 
endeavour undaunted by the uphill task, divine succour comes 
automatically.

The Vedic pandits who worship with great śraddhā in 
their hearts  the knowledge gained through the vidya of the 
Vedas (by reciting the Vedas, performing great and rare yagas, 
and practising charity and austerity and having gained thereby 
purity and renown), evince the keenest desire in knowing that 
principle that remains the whole prime and concealed Content 
of the Vedas. 'That' which the Vedic scholars are so desirous 
of realizing “art indeed thou” – thus is the guru (in King’s 
body) reminded.

Mind attains purity by the observance of swadharma or 
the duties enjoined by scriptures on people of various varnas 
and ashramas. A serene mind bereft of any turbidity engenders 
an intense desire to know the Truth. When observance of 
swadharma (the dharma enjoined on one) is coupled with 
upasana or worship, strength and power capable of erasing 
the taints and flaws of the mind are generated. One possessed 
of such a blemishless mind will harbour a desire for nothing 
except to know and be the Self – the True Content. That 
Content, in the attainment of which men of immaculate heart 
are desirous of – indeed art thou – is the instruction.

The state of abidance as svarūpa, which is true 
consciousness, vast and pure, is an obligation that should be 
firmly observed by all the beings in the world.

“Swadharma is abidance in the pure Self only. All other 
perceived duties are worthless.” (Pādamālai, page 299)

Commentary: 

Dama is destroying the exteriorised nature of the senses

Śrī Hasthāmalakam

Avathārikai:  Origin
(Bestowed by Śrī Bhagavan)

While Sri Sankara, the jagatguru (the Teacher of the 
world) was on his triumphant peregrination in the region of 
the west coast of India, Prabhakara, a brahmin of the village 
Srivali, on coming to know of the visit of the Āchārya, took 
his thirteen year old son to him and making his son prostrate 
before the august presence of the guru, he also prostrated and 
narrated the history of the boy and how right from childhood 
he had been behaving like a dumb boy, disinclined totally to 
any activity, without likes or dislikes and regardless of insult 
and praise.* The teacher, on hearing this, touched and lifted 
the boy lying prostrate with his own hands and looking at him 
with great delight, questioned him thus: 

*Note: This is but an echo of the pen-picture of a jñāni that Sri Sankara provides in 
Vivekachūḍāmaṇi: “A jīvanmukta lives dumb like a witness and unmoving like the nave 
of a wheel. His mind, full of the ecstasy of drinking the elixir of Bliss, he does not direct 
his organs towards sense-objects nor does he use them (for anything else) he being an 
unconcerned spectator and he does not care even in the least for the fruits of actions.” 
(Verses 552 and 553)

What is your name? Whence have you come hither?

Commentary: 

The moment Sri Sankara’s eyes alighted on the boy, he 
immediately gauged the exalted spiritual stature of the boy. 
A mere glance sufficied to reveal that he was anchored in the 
Self. Hence the array of questions he shoots at him are all 
about the inner pervader of All – the Ātman. That the world 
may know that he is simply not a dull-witted, supine boy but 
is the very embodiment of the fullness of Awareness and to 
proclaim that too in his own words that he fires these rapid 
questions in quick succession at him and elicits the answers 
that prove his real nature.

Scriptures proclaim that a jīvanmukta remaining in the 
plane of chit may appear to be like a mad man, like a child or 
a ghoul and ignorant people of the world cannot know their 
true worth.*

If all questions posed by Sankara were of the nature 
of those addressed to one with the idea of self in the body 
(dehātma bhava) neither the comprehension of them nor 
replying them suitably will entail any difficulty for everyone 
knows the mundane answers to those common place questions. 
The boy who had remained silent like one dumb all along, 
now opened his mouth only to bespeak the glory of the eternal 
Truth he was steeped in. 

 His song springing from the Silence of the Absolute 
is the most lucid expression of his experience of the Self as 

* Note: “Having attained the non-dual, one should behave in the 
world as though one were dull-witted.” (Mandukya Karika, 2.36)	

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   857 06-05-2011   10:54:20



858 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Self. “Though he remains silent like one devoid of learning 
yet his supineness is due to the implicit duality of the vaikhari 
vak (spoken words) of the Vedas; his silence is the highest 
expression of the realized non-duality, which is after all the 
true Content of the Vedas.” (Talks no. 449)

The import of the very first question inguru nī yār pillāi? 
(Child, who are you who have come here?) is: who are you 
tenanting this body as ‘I’ and sojourning in it? [Incidentally the 
original Sanskrit version has kasthavam Siso? simply “Who 
are you, child?” The addition of a simple word ingu  (here) 
in Tamil by Bhagavan at once stresses the nature and tone of 
the transcendental level from which the questions are asked.]

The next question “Whose son are you?” implies “What 
is the cause or source of your appearance here?”  The next 
“Whither are you bound?” means “Which is the place of your 
abidance?” 

The poser “What is your name?” has for its content, 
“What is the name of your real form?”, “Whence have you 
come here?” connotes “From which Original Content have 
you come to dwell in this body?” 

All the enquiries, though seem to refer to the body, are 
esoteric in nature referring to the inner pervader, the true 
Content within and elicit answers in eleven dulcet verses of 
a song of ecstasy – all wonderful and lucid expressions of the 
experience of the Self, ever anchored in – from a child who 
appeared dumb and dull-witted.

Sri Sankara’s request to the boy to gladden his heart by 
answering his questions (ennuḷḷam inbuṛa isaippāi) struck the 
spring of the Eternal Truth in his heart and strands of divine 
music of nectarine wisdom gush forth from the bliss of Being 
and the joy of jñāna, that he revels in always. 

Sri Sankara, the jñāni that he was, was quick to recognize 
the jñāni who tenanted the physical frame of the boy. Only 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   858 06-05-2011   10:54:20



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 859

a sage can know another sage for they are the birds of the 
same feather.

Bhagavan once narrated a story from Prabhulinga Leelai 
to prove this. “Once Marula Sankara was living like a madman 
near the place where leaf-plates after eating were thrown away 
in front of a mutt. Neither the head of the mutt nor the disciples 
knew anything about this man. But when Allama Prabhu went 
that way, Marula got up and prostrated himself at his feet 
and Allama Prabhu in turn took him up and embraced him. 
For, each knew the other’s worth. Only a jñāni can recognize 
a jñāni. One who indulges in kriya, charya or yoga can be 
recognized by these activities which he goes through. But in 
the case of a jñāni there is no such external thing by which we 
can recognize him.”  (Day by Day with Bhagavan, 6-10-1945). 
Devaraja Mudaliar further goes on to say that he recorded this 
incident because someone who came to the ashram used to 
feel and say that what is there about Bhagavan to say that he 
is realized for he eats, sleeps and does everything like others. 

Does not Sankara say “Without any marked features or 
any external attachment, the knower of Brahman experiences 
all sense-objects through this body like a child, as they come 
to him by the wish of others but without identification with 
them.”  (Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, Verse 540).

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   860 06-05-2011   10:54:20



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 861

varnas of Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vysya and Sudra. Neither 
am I a noble and disciplined brahmachari learning 
the vidya of the Vedas. Nor am I a householder who 
provides help and succour to many; nor a vanaprastha, 
who, renouncing the enjoyments of the world takes to a 
life in forest, nor a taintless sannyāsi (monk) worthy of 
veneration. I am none of those belonging to the aforesaid 
categories of people. I am of the form of true knowledge

Commentary: 

Though this boy by birth belongs to the human race and 
bears the body of a Brahmin, he has transcended both race 
and caste. He has fully realized that neither the nature of the 
human race nor those traits of Brahminism are his real form 
and therefore declares that he is neither a man nor a Brahmin. 
Likewise in his many previous births he might have been 
embodied as a deva or a yaksha or on earth either as a warrior 
or a merchant or a worker. That none of these embodiments 
is his real form is the clear and emphatic implication of the 
answer of this child-sage. Embodiments may have been many 
but what remains left behind after all of them have gone is 
my real form. Bodies may come and go but ‘I’ go on forever.

“I am the body” is the quintessence of nescience or 
ignorance of one’s svarūpa or real nature. The sense of 
distinctions based on this primal erroneous perception of ‘body 
as I’  such as varnas and ashramas, the offshoots of the basic 
ignorance, is equally erroneous and cannot be the real form 
of one. The experience of the awareness of the Content of “I 
am” alone is one’s real form.

Ashramas pertaining to human beings are four in number. 
Brahmacharya is for learning and reciting the Vedas. By 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   861 06-05-2011   10:54:20



862 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

saying “Alan nal Brahmachāri”  (I am not a celibate) the boy 
clearly implies that “I, who am ever the form of Brahman, 
need no brahmacharya ashrama, to learn and recite the Vedas, 
the whole and ultimate Content of which is Brahman alone.” 

The dharma of the grihastha, a householder, is to provide 
succour and help to brahmachārins and sannyāsins and 
discharge the obligations to forefathers by due observance 
of rituals. The boy while saying alan grahi (I am not a 
householder) implies “I am That which the householders aim 
to achieve by the proper observance of their dharma; hence I 
am beyond the grihasthashrama.” 

The purpose of adorning ochre robes and observing 
the dharma of sannyāsa is to know Brahman. “I am not the 
taintless holy monk”  (kedahal sannyāsi) means “as I am verily 
of the form of Brahman I am not a sannyāsi aspiring to know 
and become Brahman.” A vanaprastha is one, who divesting 
himself of all worldly responsibilities and renouncing all 
mundane enjoyments, takes to a life in the forest with the 
sole aim of attaining Brahman. The boy denies his being a 
vanaprastha for he is “Brahman – that Being that knows no 
distinctions.” Further the boy denies emphatically his being 
one of the crowd divided into the four varnas and ashramas.

Body is nothing but matter, but the mutual superimposition 
of matter on spirit and spirit on matter leads to regard the Self 
as the body and the body-based distinctions like varnas and 
ashramas as belonging to the Self. With the dawn of nija 
bodha, true knowledge of the Self, the Self is realized to 
transcend all limiting factors like body, name, form, space 
and time. Though all objects, including the body, (which is 
but an object) are varied and constantly change, the Self as 
the “awareness of I am”, is the same and changeless in all. 
Birth, death and changes apply to the body, the adjunct of the 
Ātman in embodiment; Ātman, on the other hand, is the Self-

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   862 06-05-2011   10:54:20



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 863

Conscious witness beyond all that is gross or subtle and is the 
like ākāśa (ether) that is changeless and endless.

The boy declares, loud and clear, that none of those is his 
real form and the eternal and Pure Awareness, the Self, alone is 
his true form. This reply also contains the answer to Sankara’s 
question “Whither are you bound?”. “I am not a benumbed 
fool. The whole insentient Universe moves before me. Hunger 
and thirst, old age or disease are to the body and not to me. I 
am ‘That’ alone that is bereft of birth, stay, appearance, growth, 
change, decay and death.”  Even as a snake, after moulting 
its skin does not reenter into the moulted skin and cares not 
even to look at it, a jñāni who has jettisoned the upādhi of the 
three bodies will no longer be associated with either the body 
or the body-based distinctions.

Thus the siddha-boy spake the highest and eternal Truth 
in clear terms and delighted Sri Sankara.

This hymn is but an echo of what issued forth from the 
bosom of Sankara himself in reply to his own guru who asked 
him the same question, “Who are you?” when he met him for 
the first time on the banks of the Narmada river. “None of the 
elements or their aggregate am I. I am neither castes nor the 
rules of castes, society and custom; for all this illusion of 'I’ 
and ‘mine’ are rooted in the non-Self... Therefore I am That 
one, Auspicious and Pure, that alone remains.” 

When Lord Vishnu, taking the form of a hamsa (swan), 
appeared before sages like Sanaka and others to explain the 
ultimate Truth to them, they, in all reverence, asked him “Who 
are you?” The Lord’s answer couches the same truth: “O! 
Holy men how is this question ‘Who am I?’ relevant when 
the Ātman, in reality, is not so many? (For only when there 
are many Ātmans can I distinguish Myself and say who I am). 
On what basis, therefore, can I answer your question?.... All 
the entities, other than the Ātman, are false. The body and the 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   863 06-05-2011   10:54:20



864 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

body-based institutions... are equally false like the objects seen 
by a dreamer.” (Bhagavatham, 11-13-22 and 31)

The hymn containing the reply of Lord Siva appearing in 
the form of a chandala (untouchable) to Sankara when Sankara 
on his way back from a bath in Ganges ordered him to move 
away out of his path lest he be polluted by his proximity (he 
being a chandala) is reminiscent of this perennial Truth. “Do 
you ask matter to move away from matter or you mean to 
separate spirit from spirit by saying ‘move away’? Is there any 
difference in the space as such, be it in a golden pot or in a mud 
pot? In the ocean of Consciousness without a thought ripple, 
how can there be this delusory distinction ‘this is Brahmin, this 
is a dog-eater’?” Sankara prostrated to Him and exclaimed: 
“He alone is my guru, be he a dog-eater or a Brahmin, who 
has realized that he is the one Consciousness that is the sole 
witness of the entire play of the universe.”

Commentary: 

The denizens of the earth engage themselves in their

an instrumental cause. “Without desire, resolve or effort, 
the sun rises; and in its mere presence, the sunstone emits 
fire, the lotus blooms, water evaporates, people perform 
their various functions and then rest. Just as in the presence 
of the magnet, the needle moves, it is by virtue of the mere 
presence of God that souls governed perform their actions.”

the Ātman in the body, the eye perceives, the ear hears, mind 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   865 06-05-2011   10:54:20



866 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

thinks and intellect determines. Ātman, like the sun, is simply 
an instrumental cause for all these functions.

The only one who remains pure, like the sky, 
uncircumscribed and unaffected by the body, though clothed 
in the three bodies – the gross, subtle and causal – is a jñāni. 
The reason for the appearance of the reflected image of the 
sun in water is due to water, an upādhi. If water, the reflecting 
medium, is removed, no reflection appears. When water, the 
upādhi of the sun, is removed, the image of the sun in the sky 
continues to shine as ever, all by itself.

In the same way though the Ātman shines reflected in the 
minds of all individuals, yet dissociated with the upādhis and 
their dharmas, like the minds and bodies of the jīvas, It shines 
like the pure sky changeless and the same forerver.

“God (Ātman) has no resolve; no karma attaches 
itself to Him. That is like the wordly actions not affecting 
the sun, or like the merits or demerits of the other four 
elements not affecting the all pervading space.”  (Who am 
I?, question 17)

The sun’s reflection may fall in the water of the Ganges 
or in a ditch water but that does not affect the sun. A man’s 
shadow may fall on the waters of holy river or on filth; yet 
the man himself is unaffected by it.  Similarly  one may read 
Bhagavatham while another may forge a signature under the 
same light but the light itself burns unaffected by either. In 
the same way the body and mind may engage themselves in 
actions virtuous, or vile, but the Self does not become holy 
or foul on account of that.

Even so, the Ātman, devoid of the limiting adjuncts ever 
abides in His natural state in It’s unchanging nature filling 
everywhere.

The child-sage declares with heroism born of firm 
knowledge that “That Ātman of the changeless nature that 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   866 06-05-2011   10:54:21



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 867

ever reveals Its presence incessantly as the experience of the 
awareness of the feeling of ‘I am’ – am I.” 

While the Sanskrit verse simply reads Pravritti (activities) 
of mind and senses, Bhagavan has used attam (dance) of mind 
and senses in common Tamil parlance means ‘indisciplined 
mind’.

868 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Paraphrase: 
Like fire and its heat that abides in fire, the One who 

shines as the One without a second, ‘moveless’ without 
the least vibration and depending on whose power, the 
inner instruments like the inert mind, intellect and senses 
like eyes, ears, etc. pursue action in their respective fields 
and who is eternally existent and constantly experienced 
as the form of Awareness (the Content of ‘I’) – that Ātman 
am I.
Commentary: 

The effulgence of Ātman is ever inseparable from Ātman 
like the heat, ever dependent on fire is never away from it. 
All the insentient inner organs and instruments of perception 
function in their respective fields of action depending on the 
ever present form of Awareness, the Ātman, but for which 
they  cannot function on their own. Just as an iron ball heated 
in fire looks exactly like fire, so too mind and senses appear 
to be sentient in the presence of Awareness.  Just as fire with 
its lighting and burning property is different from the fuel it 
burns, so is the Ātman, the Self-luminous Seer, is different 
from all objects seen including the gross and subtle bodies 
forming Its instruments of perception.

That which all the inert things depend on is the One 
without a second and though making the insentient organs 
and instruments engage in their respective fields of action, 
is Itself moveless without the least vibration and shines in 
its own nature of Awareness that is moveless and effulgent. 
Everything shines partaking the Light of Ātman. Hence 
Upanishads declare that everything including the sun, moon, 
stars and fire shine following the Light of Ātman.

“He shining, all these (the sun, moon, stars and fire) 
shine; through his lustre all these are variously illumined.” 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   868 06-05-2011   10:54:21



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 869

(Kathopanishad,  II-11-15) and “Kindled by which light, 
the sun shines” (Taittriya Upanishad ) “That splendour of 
the sun that illumines this whole world, that which is in the 
moon, that which is in  the fire, that splendour, know as mine.” 
(Gītā, Chap. XV, Verse 12), and “He that is in the sun is in the 
right eye.” (Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, 5-5-2).

Even inert and insentient objects, partaking the light of 
the Ātman function as sentient beings. Creating the world with 
manifold distinctions and with multifarious forms, the Ātman 
shines as the One non-dual indweller through all of them like 
the thread in the necklet of gems.

“That form of non-dual Awareness – moveless and the 
eternally cognised presence as the experience of the awareness 
of the Content of ‘I’ – I am”, so declares the boy-sage from 
the farthest frontiers of knowledge, having drunk deep the 
nectarine bliss of the Self.

Paraphrase: 
The image of the face reflected in the mirror is not an

jīvas, the reflections of chit in the intellect are but the forms of 
chit, the Ātman and have no reality of their own. That Ātman

Commentary: 
The reflected image of the face produced by a mirror, has 

no separate existence from the real face, and is not an object 
different from or other than the face which is responsible for 
causing the appearance of the reflection.

The reflection of face in the mirror is a mere appearance 
and the parts of the reflected face can neither be touched nor 
felt. Only the mirror can be touched and felt. The face is the 
only image and cause of the reflected image which has no 
reality to it.

In the same way, the chit or Awareness of the Ātman 
gets reflected in the intellects and the reflections are called 
chidabhasa jīvas or embodied souls. These chidabhasa jīvas 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   870 06-05-2011   10:54:21



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 871

not being other than the chit and being merely reflections of 
chit produced by numerous buddhis (intellects) are not other 
than the chit, even as the face reflected in the mirror enjoys 
no separate existence other than that of the face.

The empirical world, an unreal appearance, projected and 
witnessed by the chidabhasa jīva, with all its activities, beguiles 
and deludes the jīva appearing to be real in the chidabhasa, the 
reflected consciousness namely the mind. But its appearance 
and movement are nothing but illusions in the bright light of 
Pure Awareness. Just as the yellow colour fades and disappears 
in sunlight, the world projected by  mind disappears in the 
Light of Knowledge or Awareness. The world-picture, though 
many coloured, is but a reflection seen in the darkened mirror 
of the impure mind. The dirt and stain that the mirror may be 
covered with should not be misconstrued to belong to the face. 
If the upādhi or the reflecting medium is pure and clear, the 
reflected image is equally pure. But the chidabhasa jīva, who 
identifies himself with the upādhi, the reflecting medium of 
the intellect, imagines himself to be impure, while in reality 
he is ever pure.

“The world is seen with the mind, that is by the reflected 
light of the Self. It is perceived with the aid of the mind. When 
the mind is illumined, it is aware of the world. When it is not 
itself so illumined it is not aware of the world. If the mind is 
turned in, towards the source of light, objective knowledge 
ceases and ... the source of illumination shines forth by itself.” 
(Talks no. 98)

“That unfragmented, non-dual sole whole without an 
another source from which all these reflections emanate, 
the support of jīva, the constantly realized presence as the 
experience of the awareness of the Content of ‘I’ – am I.” – 
thus does the boy-sage declare.

ANUVADA NUN MALAI 873

Commentary: 
In the absence of the mirror, the reflector, there will be 

no reflected image. But in the absence of the reflected image, 
the real face itself does not disappear but continues to exist as 
the sole object without the other, namely, the reflected image 
of the face.

The intellect, the reflecting medium, is the upādhi of the 
Ātman (like the mirror). If this intellect perishes (the reflector 
becoming extinct) the reflected image of the chidabhasa jīva 
will also disappear. Then activities like reflection, reflecting 
and causing to reflect will no longer be there. 

Then Ātman, sole and whole, shines radiantly in all its 
effulgence. “That Ātman which shines as the experience of 
the awareness of the Content of ‘I’ – am I – announces the 
sage – a mere lad – with supreme delight.

Sri Bhagavan offers a valuable tip for the seekers to remain 
as the chit minus the abhasa of the jīva or the individuality. 
“Only the Supreme Self which is ever shining in your Heart 
as the reality is the Sadguru. The pure awareness, which is 
shining as the inward illumination ‘I’, is his gracious feet. 
The contact with these (inner holy feet) alone can give you 
true redemption. Joining the eye of reflected consciousness 
(chidabhasa) which is your sense of individuality (jīva bodha) 
to those holy feet which are the real consciousness is the union 
of the feet and the head that is the real significance of the word 
asi. As these inner feet can be held naturally and unceasingly 
hereafter, with an inward mind, cling to that inner awareness 
that is your own real nature.” (Sri Ramana Darsanam, page 35)

Bhagavan expresses the same in verse 15 of Upadēsa 
Undiyar as: 

	 “Mind extinct
	   The mighty seer returns to his own natural being
	   And has no action to perform.”

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   874 06-05-2011   10:54:21



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 875

instruments like eyes and He who cannot be mingled with 
by the mind, intellect and eye, He, the imperishable and 
eternal Ātman, constantly and directly experienced as the 
awareness of the Content of ‘I’ – I am.
Commentary: 

Mind, intellect, eyes and such organs and instruments 
of perception do not have innate sentience but deriving their 
sentience from the Ātman, function by the power of Its’s 
Presence. None of them can be what it is, in the absence of that 
power. Hence the Ātman is spoken of as the Eye of the eye, 
Ear of the ear and Mind of the mind, Speech of the speech, 
the Life of life. Therefore He is the Seer and the instruments 
and mind are all reflecting media, gross and less gross. The 
Upanishads, hence, proclaim “Give up Self-identification with 
these and renouncing the world (as real), become immortal.” 

Ātman Itself is without inner organs like the mind or the 
instruments of perception like eyes. Yet remaining as the Eye 
of the eyes, It endows the eyes with the capacity to perceive 
and remaining as the Mind of the mind bestows on it the 
capacity to wish and will, doubt and decide, think thoughts 
that ramify into waves of ideas and attitudes.

As It remains ‘apart’ from and dissociated from the 
mind and eye, It cannot associate or unite and become one 
with them. Yet in the absence of this chit or the sentience 
of Ātman, not one of them, devoid of any power of its own, 
can function. “He is the unseen Seer; unheard Hearer, who 
thinks but cannot be thought; who knows but cannot be 
known. There is none other than Him who sees; there is 
none other than Him who hears; none other than Him who 
thinks; none other than Him who knows; He is the Ātman, 
the indweller and the imperishable.”  (Brihadaranyaka 
Upanishad, 3.7.23)

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   875 06-05-2011   10:54:21



876 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Bhagavan in Akshara ManaMalai in an ecstatic outpour 
hails Him thus:

“Who can ever find Thee? The Eye of the eye art Thou, 
and without eyes Thou seest, O, Arunachala!” (Verse 15)

The real ‘eye’ is the Self; as He is formless, being pure and 
infinite Consciousness, He does not see forms. This ‘I’, the pure 
awareness, as it arises does not announce itself as an object in 
front, and hence incomprehensible to the mind and senses. He 
remains inaccessible to these and can neither be approached nor 
penetrated by them. Hence the Upanishads proclaim: “Failing 
to reach, words along with the mind, turn back.”  

When the roar of the mind with the clatter of the senses 
subsides, hushed into the silence of the natural state, that which 
shines without the aid of any of these inner organs and senses is the 
Ātman – the bliss of simple Being and the joy of pure Awareness.

The instruction that Bhagavan imparted to Humphreys is 
based on training attention on the Seer, or the Eye of the eye. 
“We do not realize that It is the One and only one, illimitable 
force responsible for:

a. all the phenomena we see, and
b. the act of our seeing them.
Do not fix your attention on all these changing things of 

life, death and phenomena. Do not think of even the actual 
act of seeing them or perceiving them, but only of that which 
sees all these things – THAT WHICH IS RESPONSIBLE for 
it all. This will seem nearly impossible at first, but by degrees 
the result will be felt. It takes years of steady, daily practice 
but that is how a Master is made.” (Self-Realization, page 112)

Such a Master, Hasthāmalaka proclaims: “The one 
who remains unmixed with mind and senses, He who remains 
the Eye of the eye and Mind of the mind and who cannot be 
commingled with by them, He – the imperishable and ever 
realized experience of the awareness of Content of ‘I’ – I am.”

Paraphrase: 
Just like the sun being just one, though seen severally 

as the images reflected in the waters of numerous 
pots (that Ātman) though shining in every heart of the 
multitude of the embodied jīvas as diverse and varied, 
He, who as the very form of Awareness, shines all by 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   877 06-05-2011   10:54:21



878 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Himself in His own resplendent light without resorting 
to any other source, He – who is never gained anew but 
ever abides as the continually and directly experienced 
awareness of the Content of ‘I’ – that Ātman I am.
Commentary: 

The Sun, though one, when reflected in many pots of 
water appears as many, one in every pot. Though Ātman 
shines resplendently as the One form of Pure Awareness, yet 
reflecting through the buddhis or intellects of many beings, 
appears severally as so many jīvas, with various distinctions 
characterised by the virtues, blemishes and peculiarities of 
those jīvas. But Ātman shines eternally as the One without 
a second with absolutely no change or appearance in it 
whatsoever. Whether reflections appear or do not appear, 
Ātman shines eternally as the ever realized Content.

In the same way the pot becomes an upādhi or a limiting 
adjunct for the image of the sun, the mind becomes an upādhi 
for the Ātman. The various distinctions and their merits and 
demerits caused by the manifold forms of these upādhis will 
not touch the Ātman, the form of pure Awareness for there is 
no manifoldness in the Supreme Truth. The manifoldness is 
in the adjuncts in which the Reality is apprehended as of the 
various pots in which the sun is reflected.

Further, the Ātman, besides being of one form, is never 
attained anew. He is the truth of the experience of the 
awareness of the Content of ‘I’ that exists ever cognised. Just as 
the sun when he rises only removes the obstacle to vision from 
the eye, namely darkness, but does not create anything new 
to be seen, so jñāna removes the ignorance when the Ātman 
shines as it has always been shining. Nothing new comes into 
being. He is Self – luminous Consciousness, unoriginated and 
unfathomable.

Paraphrase: 
Even as the  Sun, the form of light, illumines 

simultaneously the eyes of all, the world and the objects

Commentary: 

The sun that illumines simultaneously the eyes of so 
many enabling them to see the world is but one. Likewise 
Ātman, the very form of awareness, illumines at once the 
minds of all with the light of awareness. Though the buddhis 
or intellects so lit up may vary in many aspects like those of 
devas, demons, humans and gandharvas, there is no distinction 
in the effulgence of the light of Ātman which is the very form 
of non-dual Awareness.

The white radiance of the sun passing through many 
coloured glasses is reflected diversely. So also the radiance of 
Brahman may be reflected in the minds of diverse dispositions 
and may appear several and varied.

The intellects are many and different for they function 
according to their predispositions and qualities. But the 
awareness of the Self that lights up all minds shines uniformly 
without a distinction as is proved by the feeling of ‘I’ in all.

That which abides unconditioned by time and place in 
the heart of everyone ceaselessly as the experience of the 
awareness of the Content of ‘I’ is the form of Ātman. That 
which abides as the simple awareness (of being) as “I am”  is 
the form of unbounded Bliss. “That Ātman – I am”,  says the 
child-sage condensing his experience of Truth in words as an 
answer to Sankara’s query.

882 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

Commentary: 
The earlier verse stated that the sun illumining the eyes 

of all enables them to perceive the world of objects. The eyes 
illumined by the sun alone can receive and absorb that light 
and the others, not so illumined, cannot perceive the forms 
in front.

The effulgence of the sun that illumines everything is 
not his own either. The effulgence of the Ātman illumines 
the sun who in turn lights up the world and the eyes. Ātman, 
shining inmost in the beings, reveals Itself from moment to 
moment and by virtue of its natural illumination, enables our 
eyes and indriyas to function as does the sun enable the eyes 
to cognize the world of objects. But nothing can illumine the 
Ātman – the ultimate illuminator of all and the form of all 
effulgence.

Bhagavan describes Ātman as “The Infinite Eye” 
(anthmilāk kaṇ) in verse 4 of Uḷḷadu Nārpadu and also how 
It abides as the “Eye of all”  in Ātmavidya Keerthanam, verse 
5. “You see the world with the small light called mind. You 
find it full of different colours. But if you see it with the big 
light known as Self-Realization (Ātma jñāna) you will find 
that it is one continuous Universal light and nothing else.” 
(Letters, 25-9-1947).

When the mind is illumined, it is aware of the world and it 
is not itself so illumined it is not aware of the world. Bhagavan 
often used the example of moon and the absence of it on the 
new moon day to explain the function of the mind. It shines 
by the reflected light of the Sun (the Self) but has no light of 
its own. And the new moon day is compared to the state of no 
mind. “To see the world or external objects, the mind and the 
reflected light (chidabhasa) which always arises with it are 
necessary. To see the Self, the mind has simply to be turned 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   882 06-05-2011   10:54:21



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 883

inside and there is no need of the reflected light.”  (Day by 
Day, 21-11-1945)

	 “When I say ‘I see the world’
	   What do I really mean?

	   Both appear within Me, the pure I
	   Whose being is space of
	   True Awareness, flawless light.” 
			         (Guru Vāchaka Kovai, Verse 870)
Hence Bhagavan questions “to realize that you yourself 

are the Self, why do you require any light other than being – 
Consciousness, the light of the Self.” (Pādamālai, Verse 33)

“That Ātman, the ultimate illuminator illumining 
everything abiding as the formless and ever realized as the 
directly experienced entity as the awareness of the Content 
of ‘I’ – am I” – thus spells out the boy-sage the Truth with 
clarity born of direct experience.

Paraphrase: 
The sun, though one, appears as many in undulating 

and wavy surfaces of water. The same sun appears as the 
only one in still and steady surfaces of water. Likewise 
He who, though when reflected in varied and ever active 
intellects appears to be many and changing, yet abides

constantly experienced as the awareness of the Content 
of ‘I’ – that Ātman I am.
Commentary: 

When the sun is reflected in the undulating waves set in 
motion on the surface of the waters of huge reservoirs, the 
reflected image of the sun will appear as a separate sun in every 
wave giving the appearance of the existence of numerous suns. 
The same sun when reflected in the still waters appears solitary. 
Neither the movements of water nor the distinctions of many 
forms have any bearing on the lone sun in the sky. The wave-
tossed movement of the water is the cause for the appearance 
of many a sun. In the manifold minds with the innate nature 
of perpetual movement, the reflected Ātman may appear as 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   884 06-05-2011   10:54:21



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 885

many even as the sun in agitated waters seems to break up into 
many. But when the buffeting thought waves are stilled into 
quietude, the Ātman, as the sole sun in the sky, will shine as 
the Lordly One, the cause for the Ātman appearing as many 
being the mind ever restless and never constant. Ātman, just 
One, ever abides as the waveless ocean.

The fickle mind, by superimposing its own movement 
on to the moveless one, deludes itself and is stupefied. The 
removal or extinction of the mind’s oscillation becomes the 
mighty treasure of inestimable value; for as the old adage goes 
“he who slayeth the mind is redeemed from treachery”. When 
the  mind stops being restless and becomes quiescent, vāsanās 
become extinct and one gets established in mona – the farthest 
frontier of jñāna – and whatever seen becomes Brahman.

“That which appears as many in an oscillating mind and 
abides as one when the mind is stilled and hushed into quietude 
and who is ever cognized as the experience of the awareness 
of the Content of ‘I’ – that Ātman am I”  – so does the boy-
sage explain with lucidity.

Commentary: 

When the perception of the sun becomes veiled due to
