ignorant fool, not realizing that his perception is veiled by 
the clouds, thinks instead, that the clouds encircling and 
enveloping the sun have caused the sun to lose all its power 
of natural brilliance. This is the conviction of a deluded mind 
devoid of investigation.

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   886 06-05-2011   10:54:22



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 887

In the same way, in the perception of an ignorant fool, 
drowned in the darkness of nescience, having forfeited 
knowledge, the Ātman appears as the jīva constricted by the 
bondage of saṃsāra and entrapped in the whirlpool of desire 
and attachment.

Ātman appears as the bound jīva, to an ajñāni, just as the 
sun seems to be lost to a fool. The cataract of nescience blinds 
us to our real Svarūpa – the ever effulgent Self. “What appears 
in ignorance as Truth does not remain so after discrimination; 
but it becomes one with the Reality – not separate from it.” 
(Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, 387) and again “Bondage and liberation 
are both false. Fools imagine the qualities of buddhi on the 
Ātman as covering of the sight caused by the cloud is attributed 
to the sun (saying the sun is covered by cloud). But the chit is 
non-dual unattached intelligence, one only and indestructible.” 
(Vivekachūḍāmaṇi, 572)

The clouds which are produced from the sun and are 
lighted by the sun can obstruct sight, which is a power derived 
from the sun. This is how one effect  of the substance can be 
affected by another effect of the same substance. Just so, the 
light of the Self makes one say “I am ignorant.”  – while ‘I’ 
remains constant to both knowledge and ignorance. The I sense 
which is derived from Brahman and which is also revealed 
by Brahman can itself be an obstruction for the jīva which is 
itself Brahman experiencing his own nature of being Brahman. 
“Wherever particular objects are known it is the Self which has 
known itself in the form of those objects. For what is known 
as knowledge or awareness is only the potency of the Self.” 
(Upadēsa Manjari, chap. II, quest. 6)

But one anchored in true knowledge – a  mukta – perceives 
the perishable and impermanent world and beings as the 
form of Self. The perception of many is the bondage. To him, 
the mukta, the eye of ignorance has been totally blinded by 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   887 06-05-2011   10:54:22



888 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

the dazzling light of true knowledge and that gnoetic Eye, 
becoming the All, filling everywhere, perceives everything 
as Itself – the whole Content, the ever – directly experienced 
entity as the sphurana of the awareness of ‘I’. “Aham sphurana 
(the light of ‘I-I’) is unbroken, continuous. After the (clouds 
of) thoughts subside, the light shines forth.” (Talks no. 307)

“That moveless form of awareness – the entity ever 
experienced directly as the awareness of the Content of ‘I’ – 
that Ātman I am”,  declares the child-sage and establishes the 
state that is Knowledge of knowledge.

“The sage who has realized the Svarūpa direct, immediate 
as the light of Being, the formless light revealing every form, 
is the King who rules the space of awareness.”  (Guru Vāchaka 
Kovai, Verse 1153).

Paraphrase: 
Though fully and continually pervading and

Commentary: 

Though pervading homogeneously as the One, as the 
Ātman transcends everything and is uninvolved with the 
senses It is inaccessible and no object can either associate 
with or touch It. Yet remaining as the All, It supports and bears 
everything pervading through all, simply as the awareness of 
Being.

The direct proof of the all-pervasive nature of Ātman 
known to everyone is the awareness of being as “I am”  in 
the hearts of all. In all the objects of the world known through 
the five senses Ātman remains as the true Content. When the 
mind, speech and body remain still, what shines within as 
the ‘sphurana of I’ – a dance of stillness in the heart – is the 
Ātman. As Bhagavan states:

	 “By virtue of this nature you are the Supreme Being
	   The perpetually radiating sun of the Self
	   Which is the true reality,
	   Impossible to reject or deny

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   889 06-05-2011   10:54:22



890 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

	   Shining out in the darkness (of ignorance)
	   As the light (of jñāna)
	   The “I am”  of even he
	   Who denies your existence.” 

(Ramana Puranam, lines 461-462)
Bhagavan clarifies amply what and how this sphurana 

is like. Making the body corpse-like when one remains not 
even uttering the word I “there would shine in the Heart, a 
kind of wordless illumination of the form I-I. That is, there 
would shine pure Consciousness which is unlimited and one, 
the limited and many thoughts having disappeared. If one 
remains quiescent without abandoning that (experience), the 
egoity, the individual sense of the form ‘I am the body’, will 
be totally destroyed and at the end, the final thought viz. the 
I-form, also will be quenched like the fire that burns camphor 
(without leaving any residue).” (Self-Enquiry, page 6)

The great sages and scriptures declare that this alone is 
Release. When Devaraja Mudaliar was reading this passage, 
wondering what sphurana means, he asked Bhagavan about 
it. Bhagavan replied “It means which shines or illuminates” , 
and when asked whether it is a sound Bhagavan replied “We 
may say it is a sound we feel or become aware of.”  “The word 
means throbbing, springing on the memory... Thus both sound 
and light may be implied in the word. Everything has come 
from sound and light.”  and finally “the Self is without even 
this sphurana.” (Day by Day, 24-3-45)

Remaining as the natural awareness of “I am”  is the form 
of our Self. The admixture of the world and jīva in it manifests 
in the form of I am ‘this’ or I am ‘that’. Yet within the world 
and jīvas Ātman alone abides continuously without a gap as 
the feeling of the awareness of being, like the thread on which 
different gems are strung.

“The Content which interpenetrates everything, bearing 
all, yet abiding apart from and unmixed by anything – 
the Ātman – this I am”, declares the child-sage with firm 
conviction born of experience.

Paraphrase: 
The colourless and pure crystal takes on the various 

hues of the objects in front and appears coloured. Likewise, 
even you of true perception, bereft of distinctions exhibit 
the fragmented perception of distinctions such as ‘you’, 
‘me’ and ‘he’ due to association with the upādhi of 
the intellect. Even you, the totally distinctionless all-
pervading Fullness that you are, superimpose the nature 
of movement and perception of distinctions of the mind 
on you, just as the movements of the reflected moon in 
water are mistaken to be the dance of the moon shining 
still in the sky.
Commentary: 

While the first verse contains the various questions posed 
by Sankara to the boy, the second verse consists of tabling 
of various kinds of beings and an emphatic denial of his 
belonging to any kind of these beings.

The verses from three to fourteen are a lucid exposition 
on pure jñāna or knowledge by a mere boy seated on the 
throne of the pinnacle of knowledge. A lad of just thirteen 
years appearing to the world to be an inert idiot describes 
the characteristics of Svarūpa, the Ātman, with great majesty 
and skilled mastery and proves it with illustrations, not from 
śāstraic testimony, but from those born of his direct experience 
of the Self.

Śāstras are traditional wisdom experienced and 
transmitted by sages and seers – a body of compilations 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   892 06-05-2011   10:54:22



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 893

or a compendium of experiences of far-sighted sages. The 
expressions of their experiences take the form of śāstras which 
alone serve as the guiding light for the world of mumukshus 
to come. Their utterances are verily upanishadic mantras.

The fourteenth verse, though seemingly an answer is a 
question to Sankara himself, who queried him “Who are you” 
and “Why are you behaving like a benumbed one?” 

The colourless crystal, taking on the colour of objects in 
contact with, spoils its own colourless clarity. Likewise chit, 
the form of which one is, becomes chittam (mind) – acquiring 
tam which represents the defilement by sense objects that is 
māyā. As Muruganar says:

	 “Even as a piece of glass acquires
	  Redness from the red flower near it
	  Chit, awareness pure, becomes
	  Chitta, the mind, by imposition
	  Of sense-impressions. remove this ta
	   And chitta becomes chit again,
	   Awareness pure. This ta then stands
	   For Māyā, mere illusion.” 

(Guru Vāchaka Kovai, Verse 244)
 Bhagavan explains further thus: “The ego is simply 

wrong identity of the Self with the non-Self, as in the case of 
a colourless crystal and its coloured background. The crystal 
though colourless, appears red because of its background. If 
the background is removed, the crystal shines in its original 
purity. So it is with the Self and the antaḥkaraṇas (the 
mental faculties)”.  But Bhagavan issues an apt warning for 
the illustration cannot be stretched far: “For the ego has its 
source from the Self and is not separate like the background 
from the crystal. Having its source from the Self, the ego must 
only be retraced in order that it might merge in its source.” 
(Talks no. 398)

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   893 06-05-2011   10:54:22



894 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

The boy addresses Sankara with the following reply: 
“Indeed even to you, the all-pervading distinctionless Fulness 
that you are, due to association with the fickle mind, restless and 
ever-moving, distinctions like ‘you’, ‘I’, ‘he’, ‘fool’, ‘inert’, and 
‘scholar’ appear in ‘Me’. There is absolutely no distinction in the 
Ātman that dwells and shines in the hearts of both of us. Even 
the Ātman appears to possess various upādhis and distinctions 
due to the movement of the mind.”  (Due to the limiting adjuncts 
like the limited intellects, differences are felt).

This verily recalls to our mind the questions shot at 
Sankara, the world Teacher, by the Lord, in the guise of a 
chandala (a social outcaste) as mentioned earlier.

Concluding verse by Bhagavan

Paraphrase: 
As the stuti reveals the Ātman as clearly as the 

amalaka fruit held on the palm of one’s hand, gaining 
a celebrated status, it received the name Hasthāmalaka 
Stotram. Moreover that boy, ripe and proficient in the

Commentary: 

This verse, not part of the original, is a composition by 
Bhagavan.

That which is clear and easy to perceive is compared, 
in normal parlance, to a fruit of gooseberry (amalaka) on 
the palm (hastha) of one’s hand. The principle of Ātman 
is explained with so much ease and clarity that the hymn 
itself came to be called “Hasthāmalaka”  and as the boy-
sage expounded the principle of the Self through this 
hymn with such lucidity he himself came to be called 
“Hasthāmalaka” .

He was admired with awe and wonder held high in esteem 
and was praised by men of the world saying, “He looks a mere 
boy but in experience of the Self he is ripe and old.”  Right 
from birth up to the age of thirteen without engaging himself 
in any activity the boy remained like an idiot and the very first 
instance he spoke was only to reveal the Truth of the Supreme 
Content with such felicity and all admired saying “Amma! 
(Oh! Dear!) What a wonder!”  

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   895 06-05-2011   10:54:22



896 ANUVADA NUN MALAI

None is struck with wonder when a tapasvin attains jñāna 
after an austere life of an anchorite with due observance of 
rigorous penance forbearing great obstacles and difficulties 
with fortitude.

But when a mere boy remaining all along like a benumbed 
fool and without any activity suddenly rains in the Truths 
of Ātman, the world struck with wonder at this awesome 
phenomenon, hails and praises the boy. When questioned by 
the jagatguru (the Teacher of the world) as to “Who are you?” 
and “Whence are you?”, floods of nectarine bliss contained 
and revelled at in the Heart rush out through the flood-gates 
of speech like unstopped floods, drenching those around and 
sweeping all off their feet in astonishment and wonder. If 
this is not a wonder, then what else is? So much so, the great 
Āchārya himself felt it meet to write a detailed commentary 
on this outpour of the ecstasy of Brahman from a mere boy, 
that contains the quintessence of all the wisdom of the world.

Sri Bhagavan:
Sankara, addressing the father, who was then beside 

himself with wonder on hearing these words said “It is your 
good fortune to have begotten this boy born out of austerities 
left to be completed. He will not be of any use to you in this 
world. Let him be with us.”  So saying, after bidding the father 
go, he took the boy with him. 

On being questioned by the disciples as to how this boy 
has attained abidance in Brahman without observance of 
traditional sadhans like sravana, etc. the guru replied, “When 
his mother leaving her two year old child under the care of a 
siddha yogī – a sadhu with the accomplishment of the entire 
wealth of austerities practising tapas on the banks of the 
Yamuna, and had gone to the river with other ladies for a bath, 
the toddler slowly walked towards the river, fell in and was 
drowned and out of compassion for the disconsolate mother, 

Anuvada Noonmalai_Combined.indd   896 06-05-2011   10:54:22



ANUVADA NUN MALAI 897

the sadhu relinquishing his body, himself entered into that of 
the child and therefore the boy has attained this exalted state.”

SRI RAMAṆĀRPAṆAMASTHU
